Normally I wouldn't recommend something like this because of the bad writing but I think the concept is important and it was successful despite its other flaws. This is a game that says more about the player than the subject matter.
The main concept of the game is that you can't force people to do what you want. Since we're talking about reproduction the  reviews of this game are very emotionally charged and more eye opening than the game itself. I read a lot of them and watched people on both sides of the issue express their impetuous anger at the main character for not doing what they think is best. It's an interesting concept but, sadly, the game has some serious problems.
The style of the graphics is simplistic. It uses a few different pictures or colorful backgrounds for the text which tells the story.  I have no complaints about the style but I think it would benefit from more variety.
The biggest problem with the game is the poor writing. The game is dealing with a very serious topic: the assault and subsequent pregnancy of a teenage girl. It doesn't seem like the writer(s) were ready to handle something so complex. The subject matter is talked about in a very simplistic way. It seems like the topics either weren't well researched or were just poorly expressed. It doesn't seem like the main character has been through a trauma at all. Despite a pretty graphic flashback, the assault itself seems very remote.
The main focus of the game is on the character's pregnancy but when a pregnancy results from an assault things just aren't that simple. The character goes through a very generic story of unexpected pregnancy. She could be 40 years old or 14. She could have gotten pregnant from a hot night with her boyfriend or an assault by a stranger. None of the specifics of the story are really a factor. It's not this girl, this situation, this pregnancy, it's any pregnancy. The characters, like-wise, seem very generic and have little personality. The game didn't do its subject matter justice and that's unfortunate.
The thing that makes the game stand out is the main concept and the reactions people have to it. My perspective on the events of the game is somewhat different from most people's. Throughout the game the player makes dialogue choices which influence the main character's final decision. My goal was to be supportive and not judgmental. I picked dialogue options that seemed kind, cautious, or as hands-off the situation as I could. In the end she decided she wanted to be a mother and I was happy with that because it was what she wanted.
To me that said making her feel ashamed of her pregnancy and her struggle with it was the wrong thing to do. Being supportive of people in these situations makes it easier for those who do want to continue their pregnancies to do so. Pushing your opinions on people and going into things with an outcome in mind isn't a good practice when it comes to reproductive issues. The game made me think and I like that.

I have to admit that I have not gotten around to try the actual adventure part of the game too much, I've been mostly running my own "gladiator ludus" in the arena mode, so this review is mostly based on that. This game keeps pulling me back "for just a few fights" every now and then, and the arena is perfect for that.
I think the 1-on-1  fighting mechanics are simply excellent. Initially they might feel a bit clunky, but after you get the hang of them, they are quite realistic and deceivingly simple. Mastering it takes a lot of practice and you still get your complacent behind handed to you every now and then. In the end it all comes down to mastering two things, range and timing, and when you succeed  winning the opponent quickly without sustaining any damage, you really feel like a master swordsman.
I love the fact that there is always danger of (perma)death related to combat, all you need is couple of small mistakes leading to catching that cleaver with your head and it's all over. When you get better armor, the danger of death is realistically reduced but not entirely removed.  I also like the way that the armor is layered and the way the damage works, once again the most realistic thing I've seen in games.
Things I like:
-The arena mode
-Different combat styles needed with different weapon setups and opponents
-No special moves or power attacks.
-Combat, balancing between attack and defence and utilizing your weapon setup strengths pays off
-Physics are great and realistic looking.
-Fights are varied, some last 5 seconds, some 5 minutes.
-Fights are realistic, if you are facing 2 enemies, you will probably lose. If you are facing 3 enemies, you will surely lose.
-Sounds are outstanding. The sound that your weapons make when you hit your opponent will tell wheter hit was blocked, connected with effective/ineffective part of your weapon and what kind of armor was hit. Opponent grunt tells how much it hurt. And that squishy sound of hitting opponents unarmored head with a bill is so satisfying...
Things I hope to see improved
-Inventory management is messy, especially for armor
-A lot of user feedback is still missing.
-There are some arena fights with very low light. Sure, sometimes you might have to fight in the dark but I don't like it

Most people who give negative reviews on this game seem as if they just didn't spend the time to get the know the mechanics of the game well enough. It's not trying to be very realistic, as many people seem to think, it's just supposed to be an interesting (and I think very fun) take on how medieval combat is done. It is quite hard to learn at first, but the combat system is very deep and, once you get the hang of it, very rewarding. Every blow really seems to have weight and power because all animation, movement, and damage calculation is physics-based. This makes for some incredibly satisfying and difficult fights. The story mode is ok, but the best part is really the arena mode. Being able to craft your fighters from the beginning with specific skillsets and watch as they improve to become the ultimate gladiators works really well. I would say that the one downside, though, is the lack of updates recently. It used be updated quite frequently, but as of right now, there hasn't been an update since February, which is rather frustrating for an early access game especially. Overall, though, I would definitely recommend this game for anyone looking for a rich and rewarding combat system that they are willing to get to know.

Nice puzzle game with only a couple of rules to learn, but can create extremely complicate to resolve puzzles - you have to fill in the entire grid from a given start point (later puzzles can have multiple start points to work with) by choosing any of the three hexes ahead of each branch of the path you are creating, if you go straight ahead then only that hex is filled, if you turn left or right it will fill in both, if they are not blocked.
This means you can rapidly start creating a branching path, and you need to decide which branch to expand first, and in which direction to go to avoid cutting off areas from being filled in.
While nothing gets added to this apart from some later puzzles having multiple starting parts to consider/use to your advantage as needed, the concept is strong enough to create enough interesting and different puzzles to last a while (depending on how quickly you get your head around the way you need to attack each level).
So overall a fairly nice puzzle game that will keep you thinking for a while, probably not a huge amount of replayability though.

After putting in a good 80 hours into the original Deus Ex, Revision is a pretty welcome change. The gist is that the mod adds a few new handy gameplay mechanics and some nice features. For example, if you've invested in the Power Recirculator augmentation and you activate another aug with high energy consumption, the Recirculator will activate automatically. Little handy additions like that.
If you wanna play Deus Ex for the first time but think the original is too outdated, then you should probably skip this because MILD SPOILERS
Graphically, the mod was a hell of a lot better than the original, but that's to be expected. One thing that particularly annoyed me was that a lot of important characters weren't given HD models, which means that you can have a particularly sleek-looking J.C. talking to a mass of polygons with eyes. Characters like Manderly, Tong and Everett seemingly got the boot, while characters like Nicolette are given HD textures. Just seemed inconsistent, basically.
Level design-wise, the mod really overhauls it. It fixes a lot of sections where level design was pretty lacking, while still remaining true to the original Deus Ex. The lighting is also a hell of a lot better, so certain areas will look much better than before, like Hong Kong's market. Also, certain sections of Vandenberg were completely revamped.
Other than that, it's still pretty much the same Deus Ex, story preserved. The soundtrack was done-up, too. Turned out pretty nicely, although you can still disable it from the options menu if you need to. And this mod also fixes up the technical problems with the game a lil bit. I didn't even need to run through any fixes to play the game at 1920x1080 and in fullscreen on Windows 10. For a game released in 2000, that's pretty impressive.
Altogether, good♥♥♥♥♥♥ Great for pretty much anyone with an interest in Desu Ex.
EDIT: Forgot to add the game kinda runs like♥♥♥♥♥♥in certain sections. I managed to drop my frames down to 30 at times, depending on where I was standing and what I was looking at. A GTX 970 should be more than able to handle a mod of a game from 2000.

For the past year or so, over a couple of steam accounts, I've been accumulating little & cheap indie games that have caught my eye from the Steam store. This was on sale for around 50 cents when I bought it, so I figured I'd give it a spin.
The Big Picture:
You are a group of survivors in a Zombie Apocalypse looking to strive in the harsh conditions. You need to manage your food, ammunition, and scrap (I'll get to this later), and your shelter.
Mechanics:
Crafting - Very simple but gets the job done. Scrap is the main building supply, but in order to build things you also need "hammer points" (for lack of a better phrase), which I assume comes from each turn you've been through.
Scouting - Have you ever played Bethesda's Fallout Shelter? Well, the scouting is basically the scavenging in that game sped up to around 3-4 seconds. You pick a character to scout (scavenge) and equip the desired weapons and equipment, then send them off to the wastes. They come back in a few seconds with some supplies and maybe some currency. Overall a good system.
Leveling/Skill Trees - This game's leveling is so very simple yet perfect for the purpose of a lightweight mechanic. You have a variety of available skills you can choose upon leveling up (in which your character glows yellow until you pick skills), and have four max at any given time. Some of these skills are class beneficial, where others are more universal. It adds the aspect of the importance of management, because you have to spend your points wisely.
Traveling/Moving Settlement - Very simple. Ties into scouting in which new locations are found, and then are available to inhabit. Not sure of the importance of certain settlements, but this review will be updated eventually*.
All other Mechanics - I haven't made it very far, but all of the mechanics that I've seen and messed with seem to work quite well.
Pros and Cons:
Pros:
-Cheap & Goes on sale often
-Good Developers & Updated often
-Decent Graphics
-Fun & Casual (Not much effort is needed in Normal mode(Not sure if that is supposed to be, but whatever,))
-Overall Good Game so far
Cons:
-Bit confusing (Maybe update Tutorial???)
-Menu Text sometimes goes over borders
-Resolution is default set to 4k (Maybe just me)
-Options are limited
-Characters are sometimes cutoff by screen
-Crafting menu isn't compatible with scroll wheel
-+ A lot more simple and not that bad things that don't really need to be mentioned.
Summary:
If you have some leftover money in your Steam wallet then this game is quite the deal, for .99USD full price and common sales, it's a downright bargain. It is a very good and from what I know an original idea, with no major bugs that make the game unplayable. The bugs that do occur often only effect the asthetics and resolution rather then any gameplay mechanics. It's an overall good game, and even though it might have some bugs here and there, and maybe some confusing bits to it, it really has room for improvement.
+rep for not copy-pasting more Unity assets onto Steam.
P.S. Please feel free to comment any revisions for this review if you feel they are needed.
*I'm quite a lazy person so don't expect anything too soon if something does change.

I have not enjoyed a new baseball game as much as this one in the past ten years, probably since MLB Power Pros.  If you want a super simulation baseball game, this is not for you.  I find those types extremely boring, especially when they try to be so realistic that it takes two hours just to play one game.  If you like your baseball games to be more arcade style, you will probably like this.  I was excited to play RBI Baseball '15 when it came out and find it pretty fun, but Super Mega Baseball is much more fun.
The good:  The art style for all the players is very cartoonish, but done well.  The game is fast paced, and you can get through an entire game in 30 minutes or less.  There is decent replayability in seasons as your team levels up and you can hire staff to make your team better, then play the next season at a higher difficulty for better rewards.  The game is satisfying to play, and the various players have lots of character.  Difficulty can be adjusted across a very wide range from extremely easy to very hard.
The bad:  There are no real baseball players or teams in the game.  This is no problem to me, but I know it will be for some people.  An issue I thought was going to be a major negative when I started playing is the automatic fielding your players do for you.  It looked like you could basically just let your team play defense for you, which would be bad.  However, if you let your fielders track the ball themselves, they will not move very quickly, so you will give up far more hits and runs than if you do most of the fielding yourself.  In the end I see it as a slight negative, but not enough to detract from my enjoyment of the game.  Finally, I have occasionally had an issue with the game crashing in the middle of playing (has happened in maybe 2% of my season games), which unfortunately results in a 1-0 loss for you and counts no stats from the game, even if you were winning 40-0 in the bottom of the ninth.  It happens rarely enough that I have not been overly frustrated from it.

A cool and impressive remake to the classic point-and-click adventure game, Leisure Suit Larry. This game is a lot of fun, especially thanks to the great work done and time spent on this quality remake.
The only drawback, in my opinion, is the exagerated use of the narrator in the game. Wherever you go, whatever you do, everytime you click the left button of the mouse, you get a long and well-acted presentation from the narrator. Why is this bad, you ask? All in all, despite the tedious narrator, I had fun. Definitely worth buying if you like point-and-click adventures, and especially if you've played one of the previous versions (the original from the late 80s, I think, and the point-and-click remake from the early 90s).

So. SickBrick. Got it in a bundle a while ago and finally felt like giving the game a whirl. Here's my entire opinion on it:
SickBrick has you waking up (I assume) in a city, but scattered all around are messages saying that you're in a game. Alright, cool--you're self-aware, let's see where you take this. Then you wind up in a strange testing facility guided by  a robotic voice, and that's when I started getting worried, thinking to myself, "Okay, now you're aping Portal.. well, I'll give you the benefit of the doubt." About ten minutes later I was blasting geometrically-shaped robots with a shotgun, and I finally quit. The gunplay is passable but needs refinement, the visuals are in the same boat as the gunplay, and there's some kind of mouse-smoothing on in this game that drove me mad.
However, those aren't the reason I quit playing and immediately uninstalled it. No, the reason for that was simple: the game was trying to be funny, but it wasn't funny. Say what you will, but almost anyone who has played Portal can remember several lines by GLaDOS that made them snicker. Maybe it gets funny later, but trying to listen to what sounds like a person with a robotic-voice doing amateur night while trying their hardest to impersonate someone else isn't my idea of fun. Sorry guys, I don't hate your game, but your 'comedy' killed anything enjoyable about it for me.

I suppose this is potentially intentional and realistic, but I've tried pretty much everything and can't seem to solve it.
Anyway, the game no longer suffers from nearly as many translation issues, the highly confusing GUI that it once had, and especially the lack of information. There's a lot of depth here; global diplomatic relations, scientific research trees, the ability to set specific policies in each area.  I'm pretty sure I've only scratched the surface in terms of what the game has to offer.
Also, the soundtrack is amazing.
Finally, the developers are highly active and seem dedicated to updating the game.  We've had two patches in the past week and some free DLC coming.  So the game is only likely to get even better over time.
If you are willing to get past the initial roughness, Crisis in the Kremlin is well worth your attention.

This game expands and improves the old game with the same title and, incidentally, is one of the really pure political games that exist. One of its strong point is that it doesn't try to be generic (à la Democracy), but it is tied to a very specific situation (URSS/Russia, and specifically its crisis) which makes it a richer experience.
The frustrating part is that the game could be improved significantly with few easy and very evident stepsand these steps haven't been done up to now. I hope the creators will consider the following (even more than the promising expansions of the game).
- the consequences of the various buttons are not immediately evident, so in many occasions it feels like going in total darkness. Some description could be welcome. Even few words can be enough. Every button should have a description in three parts. First, a short summary of the meaning (especially as several things are very Russian-specific and not well known to the Western audience!). Second, the requirements. Third, the possible consequences. In this moment only the requirements exist, which is a pity.
Even if not all events or options can have automatic consequences, at least some qualitative indications could be welcome.
- the options that are not available because the requirements are not fulfilled should be greyed out (this is especially annoying in the world map, where there are many countries which are empty or with options that cannot be clicked at a certain moment, but this is not clear and one has to click all the time to the various nations to check).
- it shouldn't be too difficult to ask someone to clean the English up, because sometimes it's really difficult to understand the meaning!

Great RTS game with TD elements.
I expected usual Tower Defense game when I was buying this game, but I got a kinda innovative game with a lot of cool features. Creeper World is a game where you build towers to defense yourself in the early game and then you build towers to offense the enemy :D
Every game starts with placing Command Center. It produces few energy. Then you need to "conquer" as much as possible neutral territory with Collector building to increase production of energy. While you are doing this the blue thing called Creeper is constantly conquering other territories. Then it tries to conquer you. You start building towers. It costs energy. Towers are shooting, CC sends extra ammo. It costs energy too.
So, there comes the first great feature of the game, Creeper World is a strategy game where you need to find the perfect balance between production and consumption of energy. It is easy to conquer territory in the beginning, but it is much harder to defend it, because each tower consumes a lot of energy. The larger territory produces more energy but requires more towers. If you are greedy you will lose. In this game you need to think strategically. Find the safest place, make defense, be sure that it is unbreakable. Then start your offense.
So as I said at first this game is a survival city management. Pretty cool!
Usually you need to kill all Creeper hosts to complete a level. So there starts the second part of the game, Offense. When you have unbreakable defense you need to produce enough towers, prepare enough energy for ammo and find the place where you will attack. In the first missions of campaign you just take enemy territory by small steps. In the later stages it doesn't work. You need to find the weakest spot of enemy, make artillery preparation, when send air fleet and then comes with ~15 pulse cannons. After that you will have 10 seconds to clean a small piece of territory from the creeper and build a Relay for recaharge ammo of your towers. It is really easy to lose, but you will feel incredible feelings when your the small assault succeed and you will have an small blockpost in the heart of enemy territory.
Actually, it's the hardest part of each mission,  make an succeed assault. You are like commander Eisenhower which controls Operation Overlord. Awesome experience.
There is also a good story line with a kinda interesting plot. Game designers made great jobs, each new story missions offer you new buildings/enemies/game features. So it engages you until all campaign is finished. I passed it in less than 12 hours for 2 days. It was a game with really fresh gameplay mechanics for me. I was surprised
Pros
- Fresh gameplay idea. It's really cool
- Well done campaign with good story and interesting variation between missions.
- A lot of stuff after completing the campaign: custom missions, daily missions, missions made by community.
- A lot of ways to complete any mission.
Cons
- Sometimes confusing controls. You can't deselect unit with right button. You must click Cancel button.
- No difficulty settings. I suppose it could be really hard for casual players.
A great strategy game with fresh mechanics. Someone could find the graphics outdated, but you will forget about it after 30 minutes of gameplay. I recommend this game for both strategy and TD fans.

DX:R attempts to enlarge upon the world of Deus Ex with new expanded settings, some new weapons and various other tweaks. On top of that, they’ve also bundled in some graphics mods, like New Vision, that enhance the original’s look and feel.
While there are some things to like about DX:R, for the most part it fails to improve upon the vanilla experience. I think the main issue comes down to adding world complexity without adding any new things for the player to do.
Here’s an example. You’re in the expanded Hell’s Kitchen and there’s a locked house. You pick the door, explore a couple of new rooms, perhaps read some flavour text, and pick up some ammo. Unfortunately, Deus Ex already had plenty of this type of thing; it didn’t need more. What you won’t find are new conversations, new story additions, new characters or new conflicts to resolve (such as the fight between Sandra Renton and her pimp). It’s pretty much just pick that lock and we’ll give you a multitool, or multitool that keypad and we’ll give you a lockpick. That’s not what made Deus Ex great!
Frustratingly, there are a couple of places where the devs did add a new NPC and some new voiceover work (although recorded at low quality) so it seems this wasn’t an impossible challenge.
Worse, in many cases, the mod doesn’t add new ways to reach a goal; it actually eliminates some of the options in the original while artificially pumping up the difficultly with more enemies, tweaked AI and more powerful weapons.
As things stand, DX:R simply dilutes the original – making it a more tedious and more ‘run-and-gun’ FPS experience on the whole. That said, a couple of the areas that Ion Storm didn’t perhaps spend enough time on have been improved by the modders (notably Paris, a hub area that is considerably better and now 'feels' French and very distinct from NYC and HK).
I would actually like to see a stage two of DX:R – adding fresh characters, events, conversations and stories to the new areas already in place. Of course, that will demand writing and acting talent, not just Unreal engine skills. Frankly, a team of good actors could re-voice the entire game and improve it; the original acting was terribad! So yes - think story, characters, writing and this mod could be made genuinely great. Of course, matching the quality of the original game is a tough challenge; but what do you expect if you want to try modding the ‘greats’?
Worth playing? Sure, if you’re an old hand at DX. If you’re a new player, just grab New Vision and perhaps HDTP. Then I'd highly recommend trying GMDX. If you hit a tenth playthrough it might be time to try DX:R.
TLDR: Revision is an interesting diversion for those who have finished the vanilla game multiple times and have tried other, better mods like GMDX. It’s certainly not a new ‘definitive’ version (it actually detracts from the original in many ways) so don’t use this for a first playthrough.

It's a nice little puzzle game. It can be quite tricky in places to work out which way to go but that is part of the attraction. It's simple but addictive and the developer seems very willing to take on suggestions. He added trading cards and achievements really quickly after I asked which is very rare.
You basically have to fill in every hexagon by creating chains or snakes around the board. The trick is finding the right path. Some chains will break into two so you can start a new chain. You will get it wrong a lot. There is a handy rewind button for this though. There are also bonuses which can help you if you are stuck. There are no tutorials for these bonuses. A stone will fill in any missed hexagons and an energy cell will start a new chain from anyhere on the board. You can also show the solution if you are really stuck.
The music is great and the puzzles are challenging.
I would highly recommend this for puzzle game lovers and at this price it is a bargain.

I can't see whether this moniker has already been assigned, but a more appropriate title might be Lifeless Design; or Mediocre Planet. Now that opening sentence may seem a tad savage, but hopefully upon further inspection of the review - or your own explicit experience of the game - you may go so far as to agree to such a damning critique.
I will preface the remainder of the review with the following statement; I only played an hour of the game and the method with which I played was via Keyboard and Mouse.
TL;DR the game is mediocre in almost every aspect - except the audio design department - which is the only reason for the game's just below average final score.
I have conducted surface level research as to the development of Lifeless Planet, to which I discovered the game is a "solo" effort by the indie developer David Board. While it remains impressive that it was developed by a one-man band, it doesn't excuse the rather ham-fisted mediocre design throughout the experience. There is a severe lack of material variety in the game. Establishing a wider variety of materials - such as more varieties of metal, varieties of wear and tear or different rocks - would've gone a long, long way in breaking up the slow pacing of the game. Additionally, this may have lead to more exploration of the environment, which would have further emphasised the feeling of isolation and miniscule scale in this desolate landscape.
While the sole addition of a wider of variety of textures would have greatly boosted the game's visual design, it wouldn't have been a one-size fits all solution. The game needed much more variety in it's 3D model geometry. Examples include the lifts you use at approximately 45 minutes into the game, or the various pieces of concrete which are very clearly repetitively tiled, and finally the lack of moderation of the application of rust textures (also over tiled and over used).
A final comment relates to the lack of imagination to the game's platforming elements - which as far as I'm concerned - is the primary mechanic. The above walking simulator is hilarious, but fails to capture the mediocrity of said platforming gameplay. In my experience (again, 69 minutes total) there was no hazard other than gravity. To have gone so long without any sign of hazards such as unstable ground (there was one falling boulders hazard), or timed platforming sections is a major crime against platformers in my opinion. The mechanic of platforming is about traversing an environment - regardless of it being devoid of life - or spatial navigation. Both of these core values are ignored thus making the primary mechanics very, very disatisfying.
Unforunate the experience panned out this way, but none the less I do not recommend this game.

I read other's people reviews, and I'm still wondering if they played the same game that I did.
I start the game, and the first thing I notice is the standard-Unity graphics configuration panel where you can pick your graphics details from "fastest" to "fantastic". Ominous, but to be fair there are nice Unity games out there.
After going for "fantastic", strong in my hardware configuration, the second thing I notice is that the graphic is *not* fantastic. And oh! The game *lags and stutters* on the very first level.
Don't get me wrong: I don't have a Steam-VR ready machine or anything, but I just finished Batman Arkham City, and *that* game (which indeed looked fantastic) ran at full detail in full-HD on my hardware, so the that the barren and (quite bad looking...) planet surface is proving too much for it, is just preposterous (even by Unity standards).
The game is basically a platform: go through a level of obstacles (very plain and boring ones, with occasional annoying spikes in difficulty), with the aid of a broken jet-pack that gives only small boosts (which look like small farts ¡­), reach a building, get a clue. Rinse and repeat.
Everything else in the game is heavily and (sloppily) scripted.
Your character can have a very limited interaction with the world around him, and even that feels horribly clunky: you can push things, but the effect is all but satisfying and all you can do is give small pushes to objects (barrels, rocks, etc), not shove them around continuously. [REDACTED].
Around the planet you'll find a number of Soviet recordings: you have an automatic translator, so your PDA will be brought up and you'll be able to read the content. Pity that the voice-over in russian is absolutely distracting, so you have to patiently wait for blabbering to stop, to be able to actually read (and in case it's not clear, I'm not having a go at Russian, as a language, but on the opportunity of having people talk while you try to read…)
Occasionally you need to push a button.
When you do, it's connected to a moving platform. Wait (for what will seem) an eternity for a it to arrive. Walk on it. Press another button (isn't that fun?!). Travel (painfully slowly) on the platform through a chasm, step down, and it's Farting Mario Bros all over again…
Some other time you get some dynamite that you can use to destroy an obstacle. You pick it up, place it near the offending rock and go hide. 3.2.1. ­ Boom! You're dead. Why? Because the game does a rather basic check on the explosion (no ray-casting: maybe just a distance check?) and you where not in the right place, or at the right distance.
But tt doesn't matter anyway: you'll just re-spawn nearby: the obstacle is removed and you get to even keep the dynamite that should have supposedly exploded, so you have you cake and you can eat it too!  Isn't that great? :D
Water is your own kryptonite: you are walking in a pressurized suit (so you are basically a walking inflatable puppet), still you sink like a rock. [EDIT: as someone in the comments has correctly  pointed out, space suits *do* sink, so this one is on me. Not that it changes the overall judgment much...]
The graphic is plain and unassuming, when it's not just bad. The only two NPC in the game, your wife and another woman, are a thing of nightmare.
To give an example of how bad the graphic can just be, early in the game, there is a huge vent with a rotating fan. Put some sort of hard garbage while it's spinning and get through it: classic. The vent is just plain horrible to look at, the aforementioned physics is embarrassing and, in the end, even the vent's explosion seem to be ripped directly from a Half Life 1 era game.
There are a lot of interesting settings on the planet: a small village, a long big hulking building near a chasm, etc, but you can't actually visit them: you can just look at them, pick some hint that might be laying around, and that's it. Farewell.
I dutifully jumped and farted my way through the game, but the mechanics where atrocious, dull and repetitive, the graphics plain, the story not so good that you might feel hard pressed to move on, and the final attempts at introspection and at pulling som "2001 Space Odissey" s..t, laughable.
I just wanted the game to finish and get over with it, but it kept shoveling at me the same repetitive stuff over, and over. I don't know if I hated more this game for the boring chore it is, or for the wasted potential, of what it could have been.
The sound compartment is adequate, though still on the boring side. At some point during one of the lava background noise samples, I heard someone coughing. I don't know if on purpose.
This is a horrible game, probably the worst game I played in more than a decade, and I regret every minute I spent on it so don't make the same mistake that I did, and stay clear from it: it's not worth it, even if you get it for free.
The promotional text says: "Equipped with a limited-use jet-pack and a mobile robotic arm, the player must use wits and skill to solve puzzles, unravel the mystery, and survive the Lifeless Planet!". Please…
AWFUL.AWFUL.AWFUL.

Well, at this point I've played barely over an hour of this game, so maybe it's too soon for me to say, but I strongly disliked it. Lifeless Planet is simply not worth any more of my time.
The graphics were quite poor, as was the control scheme (the character turns on a dime, and whenever you need a flashlight this becomes dizzying). Jumping can be a bit obnoxious and hard to gauge, and the textures look pretty abysmal. This is all, in my opinion, entirely forgivable, if the story is fantastic. Which, unfortunately, it was not.
Although I can't imagine anything more intriguing than discovering a cold war village on a deserted planet, it's existence is quickly explained away in perhaps the most unexciting way possible, turning it from a fascinating mystery story to a boring run of the mill sci-fi game plot. The hints at zombies (talk about a mysterious illness, phrases like "they're coming, I'm the last one left") whether misread by me or not, also added to the feeling of retread ground. Additionally, I was shocked early in the game to find no agknowledgement of liquid water or the living creatures one encounters on what is supposedly a "lifeless planet". Considering one of the main mysteries is "why is this planet barren of life", you'd think discovering the alien life on the planet would register at least a few words from the main character. Nope. You pass by a few green squid-things in a pool without so much as a reference to them later. The player character has just commented: "I don't understand why there are absolutely no traces of life" when he sees a rocky outcropping, but apparently finding that life is too unimportant to mention. I was puzzled and frustrated and spent a while trying to find the action that would make them relevant to me. it's one thing to add a few fish to a pool in a game, another to do so when the game's setting is a desolate lifeless alien planet.
I finally stopped playing because I made a puzzle much harder than it was supposed to be (I missed a pretty obvious button that would have made life much easier) and on restarting the game I found myself at a checkpoint that was a few too many obnoxious jumping puzzles away from being worth doing them again.
So take this with a grain of salt, because the game could turn around just after the hour mark (although the other reviews don't suggest so) but I'd strongly suggest some other, more well crafted, space exploration game. I just couldn't find it in me to keep playing it.
TL;DR At least for the first hour, the controls, graphics, puzzles, and story are all bad. The concept is cool.

TL:DR;
This game is not what it appears to be on a first glance. I cannot recommend it without few conditions and without explaining what it really is - read on!
Review:
Envy the Dead might appear at first glance as tactical combat mixed with survival in post-apocalyptic world.
In reality this is more of a board game, where you move your pawns around and make decisions every day.
Combat sucks. Random events are usually combat related, so they suck a bit as well.
Graphics as on screenshots is somewhat of a lie - it's not bad, but not really that great either.
There is virtually no tutorial in the game, except of few explanation screens.
If you are into post-apocalyptic zombie survival board games, this might be it for you.
There are however few things about the rules that you need to know to play it succesfully.
Rules:
- scouting ends the day. Set your toons to training/scavenging before scouting.
- you can only train skills when you use them or if character has proper equipment. If you toon carries rifle, he will not train melee fighting.
- in stage 3 you will not be able to recruit anyone. make sure full party makes it to level 3 or you will suffer
- melee weapons become useless very fast, but ammo is very limited. avoid fights whenever you can
- barricades and traps won't work against non-zombie oponnents or bosses. use flammable oil barrels instead.
- skills are being unlocked during a playthrough and this is global. your first playthrough will only let you unlock skills it's the second where it starts getting serious.
If you are in that type of the games or a great fan of a genre, go ahead and grab it - you will enjoy it for a dozen or so hours, but just don't expect too much.

A click-for-click re-re-retelling of Larry Laffer's first outing!
Sounds outstanding on the surface, but once you're inside, the inherent flaws in the outdated and clunky control system become glaringly obvious within the first 5 minutes of play.
Gaming has come a long way from Sierra's halcyon days in terms of control aesthetics, simplicity, and approachability -- all of which is ignored by this game's creators. Granted, the interface is supposed to work over all platforms including touchpads and tablets, but that's still no excuse to ignore about 25 years of advancements in intuitive gameplay design. There's no sense of nostalgia here, just overly-complex tasking and needlessly wasted time fumbling with an inaccurate radial menu, hard cycling through an incomplete series of options, or dragging the mouse to the top of the screen to temporarily pause the game as you decide what to do.
The new jokes are raunchier, but also were not written by Al Lowe at all -- those duties instead passed on to this Josh Mandel guy, who might have voiced a good King's Quest king, but lacks any real talent for writing witty dialogues. This is probably the most disappointing thing about LSLR, since Al was the guy who made me laugh for a decade, and the man who I believed when he said HE was bringing back Larry.
The new artwork and areas are pretty, but very, very generic and don't really capture a sense of 'Leisure Suit Larry', so much as 'colorful-but-bland and self-serving set pieces'.
Larry retains the voice of Jan Rabson, as we've come to know and love it from the LSL6 talkie onward, but they apparently couldn't get the talent of Neil Ross, the original narrator -- who's pretty prolific in his body of work and couldn't be THAT expensive...
...What, with havin pulled in nearly three-quarters of a million dollars through Kickstarter supporters like myself...That is an awful lot of money...I'm sure it put enough in the budget for "Series Staple Voice Actors"... Damn, this sure doesn't feel like a million dollar title...
Perhaps there were contractual agreements from previous studios or some other, more nefarious reasons for changing this beloved presenter of shenanigans; however, their replacement (some guy named Brad Venable?) leaves much to be desired. His voice isn't smooth, or appealing, and even his insults fall flat and oftimes ruin a joke for lack of comedic timing and odd choices of inflection.
If this is how they plan to continue and retell the series, it could be the death nell for our loveable loser... WHY HAVE YOU FORSAKEN US, AL LOWE?!?
GET BACK TO THAT WRITING DESK!!

The Seven Years War (1756-1763) was a crucial historical event involving all of northern Europe, great parts of North America and India. Its conclusion set the stage for both the American and French revolutions, the second British Empire and securing Prussia’s role as a major player in European politics. Oddly, no strategy game has taken an in-depth look at this conflict. Paradox’s Europa Universalis IV and Sega’s Empire: Total War take almost abstract approaches to this war while AGEOD’s Rise of Prussia only deals with individual campaigns.
The subject deserves more detailed analysis. Fortunately, one man, Oliver Keppelmüller, spent years making an extremely detailed RTS game of the war.
The campaign mode allows play as Britain, Austria, France, Prussia and Sweden. Each has a campaign starting in 1750 and going through 1763 and a campaign beginning in 1756 and finishing the war. On top of this are country-specific shorter scenarios, e.g. Britain’s crisis in North America. The goals for all of these are unique to the country. Hence, Britain need only run the French out of North America while Prussia must fight hard to survive. The tools of play reside in several levels of panels. For instance, opening the financial panel reveals further panels of action. Handling these levels becomes second nature after some hours of play.
The key to successful campaigning is not moving troops around but finance. Under-supplied and unpaid soldiers and sailors don’t fight well and tend to desert. The Seven Years War handles money through a very detailed supply and demand system.
The production chain resembles that of Civilization III: resources are exploited by building mines, farms and so forth but these facilities need resources themselves. Products are brought to cities and trading outposts by traders and merchant ships. These traders and ships move automatically around the map looking for the best deals. Although their profits go directly to the player, traders may ignore the country’s own products if they are overpriced, making production irrelevant. Adjusting prices and demand priorities in cities influence traders indirectly and aid cities.
Cities are also crucial to population morale. Factors like religion, health and level of corruption contribute to happiness. Players can influence these factors by building “Feel Good” facilities such as schools, doctors’ offices and forts. A high level of happiness allows for tax increases. Cities are also where soldiers are recruited and ships for the fleets are built.
The general status of a nation can be enhanced via research and government policy. New technology can yield better production and new weapons. Policies can decrease corruption and initiate popular reforms. If all of the above seems a bit much for a wargamer, never fear. The military focus option turns all of the civilian functions over to the AI, leaving players to concentrate on why they bought the game – imposing their will on the world.
All in all a beautiful and deep wargame covering an important historical period often forgotten.

I am a long time enthusiast for the history of the 7YW and have toured most of the major battlefields in Germany, Czech Republic and Poland and a long time wargamer. While not an A title game, this is a well executed indie game that is really well executed. Overall, I'd recommend the game but don't expect a seamless experience.
First the bad:
* There were immediate bugs encountered. Everything from running the game under Windows 10 to game crashes to mangled troops. That said, I wrote the developer and he *immediately* either gave me a workaround or actually fixed these bugs. I've never seen support like this before and this alone makes me recommend this game.
* The play balance is still a bit off. Certain commodities like cotton are only found in the colonies, so only England and France have access to them. If the AI is running these countries and doesn't develop them, everyone ends up short. There are plenty of similar examples.
* The AI is really bad. Even with the agressive option set it can't really offer much of a threat. That said, it's still fun to stomp on. But the objectives you need to win are trivial to accomplish.
* There are various UI annoyances, from poorly designed interfaces to stuff like trouble dragging troops around (half the time they snap back and you've got to do it again).
Second the good:
* Really detailed economic model. You not only can develop resources and build production buildings, but you can trade with foreign powers. Most of the trade is automated and made simple, despite there being ~20 resource types. You can also dominate a given commodity and force the price up, making a ton of money. Playing the economic game was as satisfying as the military.
* Very cool system of troop recuitment and organization. Both troops and officers are recruited separately, with officers limiting the number of battalions your army can have while troops fill in the bulk. Reorganizing armies is easy and makes a huge difference in the tactical battles.
* Good quality graphics for an indie game.
* Excellent developer support (bug fixes in days!)
* Active improvements. I expect once the bugs and balance issues get worked out this will be an excellent game.
Overall I'm giving this a positive review despite the negatives, mostly because I believe it will work those out soon and be a truely good game.

The Seven Years War is a gem, but make no mistake: this is a game meant for enthusiasts. The economic system is dense and takes several hours of getting used to, even after reading the 60 page manual and playing through the tutorial. If you're looking for a game that you dive right into and will hold your hand, this isn't it. However, if you're either an avid wargamer or fan of the period (or both!) and don't mind graphics from circa 2002 and a spotty UI, than I can't recommend strongly enough that you buy the entire bundle. There's simply no other game on the market that covers the dometic, political, and military (both strategic and tactical) aspects of the Seven Years War as well as this game. The attention to detail is truly impressive and it really shows that this is a labour of love. Yes, there are still some warts, but the developer is actively engaged in this product and puts out regular updates. If anything, the game's faults only highlight the fact that is isn't yet another homogenized, big studio release using a paint-by-numbers approach to grand strategy. Watching a Highlander regiment emerge from an autumn forest and charge across the field into enemy fire while striking up "Scotland the Brave" on the bagpipes evokes a kind of gaming joy that few modern titles can match.

Where to start....
Well I am not one to bash on games. I feel most games have at least one good thing going for them. This game has a few things, but the few "good" things about this game... are nothing that should keep you playing.
I bought this game as part of the bulletproof bundle on bundlestars. So that made the game worth it. As a rule of thumb, I like every dollar I spend on a game to transfer to 1 hour of game time (at least). Steam says I put 2 hours on the game, but I feel the game time I spent is closer to 1.5 hours. That would not make it worth the $9.99 price tag. That leads into the replayability. Is this some great game that you can replay over and over and pick up something every time? Nope, not at all. I feel that I could not spend another second on this game again and be happy.
Ok after that little bashing lets talk about some good stuff. The gun models are pretty good, each one is different but same enough that they fit in the world of the game. The textures of this game will be talked about in a few moments, but the textures of the guns, are not half bad. The level design pretty straight forward, albeit basic and somewhat boring, and so I never really got lost or had a question of where I was suppose to go.
Ok... here comes the not so great parts of this game, for the sake of brevity I will only touch on a few points. First is the story (SPOILERS START HERE). This is pretty much a Portal wannabe. The whole test subject and evil robot overlord theme going. I feel like this story could have done some pretty cool things. Maybe having the main character question his humanity and what it means to be a human. Have him fight the urge to just follow the orders, but no, we got a flat character who was of course a robot! The plot was so flat and simple and didn't go anywhere. Unlike portal, there were times where we would go from room to room without any real story or narrative driving us forward.  So the story falls flat, go play portal instead if you want a good laugh and a deeper story. (SPOILERS END).
Load times are not to bad, but longer then I would have expected. I am confused though about some of the "level" changes. There are few "outside" parts where you are driving a tank (oh my for the reticle having a seizure when you are driving) and you have to get out of the tank to pass though a pointless door so that the game can load a new level. Then once the level is loaded, you get right back into a tank.
Last thing (that I will at least talk about), is the difficulty of the game. I died a few times (which I will give it credit that the autosave and checkpoints seem to be forgiving [the two that I used]). All but one time were just to environmental obstacles, and not enemies killing me. The game was way too easy. I dipped below half health... once... during the final battle, that is all!
The graphics... oh boy. They are another thing that is flat. They are boring and not noteworthy at all. The physics are super strange, and dead bots have body parts that sometimes float in the air. All the controls feel so floaty (not in a good way).
Ok, enough beating up on the game. Would I say buy this game? No, there are plenty of other shooters that do what this does but much better. Want an interesting story about an evil robot overlord, play portal.
TL;DR - Don't buy

I love shoot 'em ups, but I will be the first to admit I am not very good at them.   One of the great things about this game is that it is very approachable for all skill levels.  In fact, I actually cleared this game (there are no continues, so every clear is a 1cc), which is a first for me as I have never cleared a shmup without using a continue (terrible thing to have to admit, I know).  It only took a few practice runs of the 2nd and 3rd stages, and a couple replays that I watched from the leaderboards to achieve this too.  However, there is alot more difficulty and depth in the scoring, plus numerous challenges to satisfy you after you have gotten that first clear.  In addition, each stage has multiple routes, some of which require conditions to unlock, so the stages have alot of replayability.  My favorite way to play this game is just practice one stage, experimenting with different routes and rotating in different areas to shift bullets for better scoring, or to find more items or destructible objects.
From the video and screenshots you can see that the graphics are very unique and original, and quite good too.  The first time you play this game, make sure you try the challenges first.  The beginning ones are what actually teach you to play the game.
The rotating mechanic is also very original.  It feels like you are actually changing the shape and pattern of the enemy bullets and I think this game is worth playing just for experiencing this neat new system alone.

The only complaint I have about this game is that sometimes it is a bit difficult on the eyes for me-- but that's just me. You might have a different experience dependent on your color contrast and ideal monitor setup.
That said.
I am by no means an expert, professional shmup player. I love them, I have a passion for them, but I'm not spectacular at them. This game makes me feel like I'm a professional anyway. You will slowly learn the game as you continue practicing it, figuring out ways to make seemingly impossible attacks become trivial. You will watch yourself destroy massive hulking behemoths of nightmarish blue metal and you will feel invincible.
I often watch replays of top players just to watch the backgrounds, just to see the details in the landscapes that I'm otherwise not paying attention to. The optimization is top-notch, and I'll be shocked if the game runs at anything shy of 60FPS the entire time.
This game is absolutely worth full purchase value.

This is a strategy game where you focus on base-building, slowly expanding your territory to push back against a spreading ooze. It's great if you are more into the building and defense side of strategy games than the attacking or offense.
There are a variety of units you can employ to take different approaches to each mission—some directly push back the ooze while some are more defensive. The campaign does a great job of changing up the missions so you have to try different strategies and use all the different units.
There is a campaign, hundreds of standalone maps (including challenge ones), and a map editor. It's a great game to play in short bursts (smaller maps take around 15-20 minutes to complete), but you can certainly spend a lot of hours on the game, if you'd like.

Creeper World 3 isn't for everyone, but offers galaxies worth of "tower defense"-like content. Constantly pushing against your semi-mobile turret defenses is the grey goo cousin named Creeper. The objective is to hold ground against the Creeper until you can slowly push back and envelop the Creeper itself, destroying its spawning locations. It's a tug-of-war for your survival. Along the way or during the start you will be deciding which resource nodes to prioritize or upgrades to get. Most missions should be approached like puzzles, and pausing to plan or place buildings is a must for quicker times, but it can otherwise be played like an RTS.
The campaign provides tutorials and unlocks for the various defenses available, although the details of the story are forgettable. One common issue is that the difficulty spikes at a later mission. The soundtrack is some good, dramatic strategy music, but only lasts so long before getting repetitive.
The extras like the map editor, alpha sector (mini-games/rule changes), and scripting ('playing' as Creeper!?) are all much-appreciated icing on the cake if you enjoy the main portion.
Who ever has a few hundred hours to spare and has no idea what to do with them; just sink 'em in this game.

With a few simple turrets you must hold back the oncoming tide long enough to build up your forces and push back.
The story mode was fun and there are a ridiculous number of extra maps to play.  If you enjoy it and fancy something similar, I also enjoyed Creeper World 2 which takes the basic idea and changes the axis so you are fighting up, or down, or even both instead.

This is one of thoes games, that I will return to, every few months, and play for a few days straight. It's har to put in a category, because it is really kind of its own. Put I guess, some sort of advanced tower defence, is the best description, it's great for just spacing out an entire weekend, trying to crack the harder levels.

Deus Ex: Revision isn't a bad mod, all things considered. I feel like I should get that out of the way first. The problem with it is that it doesn't do anything that really makes it worth the 5 GB extra download.
Revision tries to combine most of the well-known mods like the HD texture pack, Shifter, and Biomod, along with some new additions, but the package feels poorly put together. The new soundtrack is okay, but it's never good enough that I thought it was noticeably better than the original iconic music, and the only times I really noticed it were when I didn't like it as much. It includes various HD graphics mods, but they all fall into the same problem that every Deus Ex HD mod falls into. They slap fancy high-res textures all over the maps, but only occasionally change the extremely flat, blocky environments of the original game, leaving it with a "Minecraft HD Texture Pack" feel that just looks worse than the original textures in the end. The HD characters are a whole other story, ranging from bug-eyed UNATCO soldiers who look like their respirators give them a constant supply of crack cocaine and JC looking like a 40 year old cosplayer who's past his prime, and I can't imagine anyone actually playing the game without disabling them within 20 minutes. Walton Simons doesn't even seem to have an HD model, even though he's one of the only two important things in the opening cutscene.
The Revision part of the mod does make some noteworthy changes though, aside from just removing "Deus Ex" from the title in every possible place that it can as if they think their mod is so substantial that it justifies being its own creation. Various levels have small additions to the level design, adding new structures or rooms that in general are pretty well-made. If you could just use those changes as a solitary mod, it would be nice. Unfortunately, Revision also does plenty of things that annoyed me. The major issue is that they altered the difficulty settings to make them impact more things, like what items appear in what difficulties, and those minor changes pretty severely alter Realistic. I always considered Realistic the go-to difficulty for Deus Ex because of the way it provides enough challenge to encourage you to make the most of your augmentations and the environment without putting you on an unfair playing field, but Revision's Realistic does things like removing a significant amount of augmentation upgrade cannisters from the game and other various things that turn it into more of a masochistic Very Hard mode. They also add a lot of guards that are just annoying, like a seated guard right at the start of Liberty Island that essentially forces you to abuse the AI in order to get the baton at the start. Gunther's cell also now has two seated guards facing each other, making the room effectively impossible to stealth. I'm really not sure what their reasoning for doing those things are.
I really just don't really see any benefit to playing Revision over the base game, or even the base game with other mods. The mod includes Shifter and Biomod and lets you choose one of them at the start if you want, but it doesn't explain anything at all about what either of them do, so you're still much better off just reading about them and downloading them seperately. I don't think anything else in this mod is substantial enough to be worth being a download 5 times the size of the base game, and the basic Revision changes come with too much dead weight to be worth it. It isn't necessarily a terrible mod, but I wouldn't prefer replaying it over replaying vanilla Deus Ex. Really, I didn't even prefer playing it once over replaying the original, even though I've played the original game several times by now.

Deus Ex: Revision is an incredibly fun mod which refreshes the original game.
Instead of being a total conversion like the well-beloved "The Nameless Mod", Revision reworks major elements of the original game while retaining it's storyline.
Many (if not all areas) have been redesigned and expanded upon, these expanded areas feature many secrets and new events, and of course i need to mention that the mapping is very well done, bringing the best out of the Unreal engine.
More so, new weapon models reflect the mods used on them - meaning that for example a pistol with scope and laser will actually look the part.
The mod features an optional exclusive soundtrack, giving the player a choice between original music or the revision tracks.
Overall i highly recommend this mod both to people who (like myself) replay the first Deus often and wouldn't mind experiencing new things in their beloved game, and to stubborn people who always wanted to play Deus but couldn't get past the game's "age".
To me the first Deus Ex will always be a perfect and beautiful game, no matter how much time passes.
As for this mod, it only makes these feelings burn even stronger.
To finish off i would like to compliment the developers on the tech support which assisted me in solving a technical issue i had.

Lifeless Planet surprised me.
Actually, the moment the game started and I looked around at the desolation and then took my first steps into the unknown, I knew I was going to love this game.  It just had that kind of promise to it.  And I'm glad to say that playing it was totally worth it.
The game starts out innocently enough - an astronaut stranded on an alien planet, looking for the rest of his crew, hoping to survive it all.  But then our hero stumbles into a deserted town and it looks all too familiar, exactly like a scene from Earth: even a Russian flag flies in the alien wind.  Strange indeed, but it's just the beginning of more strange and weird but spectacular things to come on a very personal journey about surviving loss.
You can't help but wonder what lies behind the next dune, the next giant doorway, the next turn in the path and where it is all going to lead to.
You get to explore the seemingly lifeless planet, learn about what has happened there, using your jetpack in the lowish gravity to get to otherwise unreachable places and solving puzzles by interacting with the environment.  The controls are uncomplicated and the scenery is stunning.
Lifeless Planet gets my vote and I'm definitely going back to experience it again.

The more I played this game, the more I came to love it. I initially went in without reference to the manual, and eschewed the tutorial scenario, so my learning curve was longer than you`ll likely experience. That being said, there`s still enough to keep track of to keep you occupied. The limited resources you begin with in the full campaign makes for a slow start while you prioritize things, but once your economy is up and running (i.e. you`re not losing money hand over fist) there`s lots to do. Make no mistake though; you`ll never be able to satisfy all you wants.
Battles are fun, although I harbour the suspicion that cavalry by this time was a little less reckless than the AI allows. I do enjoy the restraints put on the player by the command and control features, which puts a premium on fighting your brigades as brigades, which gives things a more realistic feel. It`s also nice to see a game that doesn`t ignore the supply issues that dogged every single army (and navy) of the period.
The only thing I would like to see going forward is some form of player-controlled naval combat, but this shouldn`t dissuade anyone from purchasing an otherwise excellent product.

Feel compelled to write a positive review after seeing the 'mixed' rating this game gets.  There's no justice.
This is the kind of game I've been wanting to play for years...a historical strategy game with an excellent campaign system that beats anything I've played by the big developers.
As a total package, that melds all of it's disparate elements together in an engaging and innovative way, it can't be beaten.  No tedious single sprite fights, numbers, stats and sound FX to represent battles (Paradox and Ageod), no Benny Hill arcade battles and uninspiring strategic layer (Total War), no strung together bunches of battles with some occasional core units promoted masquerading as a campaign (Panzer Corps and 100s of others). Pike & Shot (and Sengoku Jidai) impressed me with great battles but the campaigns were bare bones.
This game nails what a historical campaign should be, perfectly.  A fascinating strategic layer that creates a meaningful context for the realistically paced battles.
The game is not perfect, the graphics are dated but functional, the learning curve is steep (especially for the economic simulation) and the English localisation has quite a few errors, but the developer of this game has shown some real ambition and talent to put this together.

If you are a Total War Empire or Napoleon fan, this is definitely worth experiencing, although leave any preconceptions and expectations at the interface.
With highly detailed economic infrastructure, trade and diplomacy, there is an awful lot of shaping that has to take place before you even bring your military force to bear. This is ideal for those who play a historical campaign and have deep knowledge of the era and resultant hostilities. The AI is sufficiently aggressive to take you by surprise, whilst comprehensive strategies require co-ordination not present in Total War games where you can basically fund your entire campaign through conquest; here you have to develop your civil infrastructure.

Ignore reviews whining about the combat system being too hard. People shouldn't give bad reviews just because they couldn't manage to figure out how to play the game. I couldn't kill a single enemy the first couple of hours I played, but I practiced instead of going on steam after 30 minutes of playing and writing a bad review.
There comes a point where you simply "get it" and start destroying enemies and ranking up in the arena. There is no other game like this in existence. It's absolutely skill based. A peasant in rags with a blunt weapon can knock out a fully armoured, skilled up knight. There are no walls that keep you from progressing in the game like in other RPGs, where you need to be a certain level, learn a certain skill or have a certain piece of gear to proceed. You could go from start to finish without ever putting on any gear (although it would be hard).
The combat system is what actually makes this game. There is no game that gives the same satisfaction in defeating an enemy. Once you figure out how your weapon of choice acts, you will be addicted to smacking opponents in the face. Once you switch to a different weapon, the learning begins all over again, as all weapons act differently and are reacted to differently by the AI. The AI in this game is decent, as well. The only thing I can predict about the AI is that it will attack me if I step back and wait too long.
The one thing that is actually negative about this game: Some scenes are too dark and you can't see anything, so you absolutely need to use your torch. One thing that actually annoys me is having to switch between the torch and your weapon in the story mode if you're using a 2 handed weapon, or having to drop the torch on the ground so you can actually see while trying to defend yourself.

The concept is sound: fully physics-based combat model where you have to be very careful of position and momentum, among many other variables. Unfortunately, the control setup falls flat by trying to do too much with too little. There are no visual aids or mouse cues to tell you what your character is actually doing; instead, you have to struggle your way through the system until you eventually manage to get a feel for the rudimentary basics of the movement and combat system, part of which requires you to either manually move the camera or hold down a button to re-orient the camera behind your character. Why do you have to do this? Well, you don't strictly have to, but movement direction is relative to the character, not the screen, which is fun in zero-drag space games, but not so much in a down-to-earth sword-slinger.
Your weapon is controlled entirely by your mouse; hold down your mouse button, move the mouse, and the weapon follows the same general direction. Unfortunately, the game treats everything as a ragdoll; stumble on a chair and you fall into a sprawled heap, as opposed to natural human reflexes kicking in and helping you catch yourself, or at least turn a fall into something a little more controlled. Running away from a fight you can't win? Great! Just make sure your aim is good, because turning is clunky and you'll probably run into a wall at some point, since your character is a ragdoll with no reflexes, and after hitting the wall and falling over, your pursuer with catch up to you and bash your brains in while you try to stand.
Now, if you hold ALT and move forward before holding down the mouse, your char will attempt to perform the worst thrust in the history of thrusts. Aside from that, there are no buttons to switch your stance or your grip, and levelling your character to higher skill tiers does not make them less clumsy: they will still swing a sword like a rank novice no matter how skilled they supposedly are, and no amount of player skill will make them move like a fighter instead of a ragdoll with rudimentary movement skills. Everything else is mouse hold, mouse move. Now, if this were a simple hack'n slash, that would be fine, but it isn't; it's a physics-based medieval combat sim and it needs more buttons.
TL;DR:
Exanima is a game which tries to do too much with too little even though it doesn't need to limit itself in that way. The movement system is completely unintuitive, the camera has no follow control beyond a manual (and generally mandatory) button press, and the combat needs to utilize more buttons to perform all of the functions which it tries (and usually fails) to do. THere is so much potential here, but until these issues are fixed--whether it's with alternate control scheme options or complete control system overhaul--this game remains, for all intents and purposes, unplayable.
If you are in for fighting and roguelike games - this will give you lots of fun.

This is among my favorite games, and certainly tops most of the games I've played as far as innovation goes.
Piercing damage doesn't magically kill wearers of heavy armor. A heroic man at arms wearing leather armor, armed with a short sword, won't kill somebody wearing full plate armor, wielding a halberd. On the other hand, blunt damage, in high quantities, will easily trump heavy armor, and another person wearing full plate armor, wielding a halberd will kill the same. This game takes realism to an impressive level, while still keeping the gameplay fun and somewhat simple. Don't believe the reviews claiming that this game has a "poor contol scheme" or is "too challenging" to those two complaints, I say: git gud. Just actually give this game a chance for what it is. Know what you're getting into, as this game certainly isn't for everyone. But that goes for just about every game in the Steam Store. Also, please keep in mind that this game is a Tech Demo sideproject of the developers, so you shouldn't expect regular updates or a finished game at any point. However, if you're like me, and well-simulated scenarios give you a boner, you should definitely give this game a try, even if you refund it after half an hour of gameplay. And even if you're not like me, just ♥♥♥♥ing try this game, I mean seriously, where else can unarmed builds be actually viable in serious gameplay?

Revolver 360 is an STG (or "Shmup") that is innovative in its mechanics whilst remaining respectful to the classics and fundamentals of the genre. To summarise, Revolver 360 is a 2.5D STG taking place in 4 stages, with branching paths and bosses at the end of each level. The player shoots enemies and objects coming from all directions in a 3D plane whilst moving within a rotatable cylindrical playing field. Bullets can be rotated-around and cancelled through abilities which use up constantly-recharging resources. The scoring system is based around cancelling bullets and enemy chaining (although the chaining is not nearly as strict as games like Dodonpachi, which is notorious for its perfection-demanding enemy chaining). There are also 50 short challenge levels which test the player's knowledge of the different game mechanics, as well as their memorisation.
As someone who usually plays STGs for survival and tends not to care about getting high scores, the scoring system in Revolver 360 is so addictive that it has gotten me hooked and trying to improve my scores regularly in spite of my preferences for survival play.
The scoring system is based around two multipliers: a first multiplier which is based on chaining enemy destruction, it is capped at X16, although this limit can temporarily be broken through using overdrive mode; the second multiplier is a count of how many bullets you have cancelled. Bullets are cancelled through destroying enemies as they are firing lasers, using your ship's own lasers, or using the emp shot (a powerful charge shot which breaks through blue beams which lasers cannot cancel) and overdrive, which cancels all bullets on screen once activated. Larger enemies fire more bullets at lower health, so the player has to be careful to leave them on as little health as possible to cancel as many bullets as possible. The effect this has on the gameplay is that it encourages players to be constantly taking risks, as it requires them to rotate clouds of bullets directly towards them to cancel them out with a well-timed/positioned laser cancel. The nature of the first multiplier encourages players to mix up their main shot (which works as you would expect from a basic STG shot type) and their laser for the most optimal chaining. This combined with the fact that there are many routes to take throughout the meticulously-crafted and gorgeous levels (there are even secret routes!) means that there is a ton of player freedom and replay value.

From time to time, I like to wind down from games leaning heavy on the action side and simply play something that involves no violence or quick reflexes. A story which could be enjoyed and finished in a short amount of time. Visual novels nail that definition and the one I’m reviewing today is a bit of a novelty in regards to its many counterparts on Steam. Developed by a dev team which had previously launched a conventional 2D visual novel in 2014, Winter Novel features an art style composed entirely out of ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) symbols.
If something can be drawn or pieced together, you can bet some human tried to make art with it. And rightfully so, ASCII art occupies a well deserved niche of its own along with a decently sized fanbase. Never attempting it myself, I did enjoy glancing over the works of some truly talented individuals and what they can do with this character encoding standard, should they have sufficient patience and predisposition towards any of this. I strongly recommend you watch a special version found online of 1999’s The Matrix movie in all its green ASCII glory!
Onto the actual game now. Since it’s rather brief, clocking at less than an hour if you’re reading at a normal pace, I shall focus on Winter Novel in general terms. As with most visual novels, at its center lies a complicated love story (when was true love ever an easy thing to achieve?). You could breeze through the game by spamming the Enter button, but you know better than to do that, right? Read carefully and ponder upon what the dev team has layed before your eyes. It’s a decent story too, as far as I’m concerned. I did wish it had some form of voice acting, but I’m aware that would have driven the price tag up by quite a lot. What you see is what you get and it’s ultimately up to you to decide if the ASCII visual style is easy on your eyes or not. Bear in mind that only a handful of Steam games use it so far and I had no qualms about it but it is an acquired taste, I guess.
Against all odds, I’ve decided to recommend this game simply for the way it looks and the Steam auxiliaries which shall please most collectors of games, Cards or Achievements. You either hate Winter Novel the moment you see it, or you accept its relatively nice and creative visual representation, quite rarely exhibited in Steam video games. You can’t deny it has its own distinct charm, setting it apart from similarly priced visual novels but if you’re still not convinced, wait for a Steam Sale or bundle containing it.
