I'll start by saying though I'm enjoying Disposable Heroes very much I have to admit it does have it's problems, but I still find the game playable and keep finding myself playing 'just one more run'.
The gameplay itself is very simple, room by room you must destroy the enemies you're faced with using random weapons, potions and your own wiley movement skills!
You start by picking one of two characters (with two unlockable later) and then are popped right into the game. The levels start without telling you much but the game is pretty easy to work out. Defeat the enemies and advance  picking up items and weapons as you go along.
The game has an abundance of weapons, items and enemies to keep you busy and though the levels are predetermined there are minor RNG elements so there is re-playability. The balance is slightly off on some of the weapons so some are pretty useless imo and some are super overpowered but this is the case with pretty much every rogue-lite out there.
You collect gold throughout the levels and gold carries over after dying and can be spent at the market for various upgrades to make your gameplay a little easier so it's not the same grind over and over with nothing to show for it.
Though lacking it story (and I mean completely lacking) the gameplay makes up for that as it doesn't pretend it's deep or well written it just does what it says on the front of the tin. It also has some fun achievements to get so achievement hunters should be pleased!
Disposable Heroes has co-op as well as single player mode so you can play with another person locally which is appreciated because as I've said before local co-op is often overlooked these days in favour of online multiplayer which can die out very quickly.
The graphics are really simple and nothing to call home about but they work in a weirdly charming way. I also enjoyed the voice acting at the start even if it there was only a little of it, it definitely made me smile.
Now onto the problems I've found. I have no idea if it's just me but I cannot cancel the intro EVERY time I start up the game.  Considering my sessions are around 10 minutes, having to watch a two minute intro every time gets annoying. Secondly is the instadeath that happens randomly without any warning. Some levels are designed very poorly and can result in your dying in under 5 seconds which can be hell if you're doing really really well or have weapons and items you like. And my final issue is the fact that once you clear a room it throws you right into the next room without allowing you to pick up any of the gold, chests or items that may have dropped. That is my biggest issue with the game as certain weapons are better than others and they spawn randomly so if a weapon spawns and your complete the level without grabbing it, it's gone and you're screwed.
All these issues can be fixed fairly easily though and I hope the developer takes note because it would make the game ten times as fun.

Disposable Heroes is a difficult rogue-like game. It seems to feature some RNG elements into the mix of the game, but doesn't really go all out on it very much. Fighting enemies that are in rooms, and just trying to get to your objective will become a real challenge with the random weapons you will find that may (or may not) help you along the way.
Disposable Heroes is a fun local co-op game that has a few issues here and there with some balancing issues with the enemies and the way that you get hit which I will explain later. Although the graphics aren't all to be looked up upon, don't underestimate what the game really is. It's a very content-rich sort of game that doesn't focus much, if at all, on story but more of the gameplay itself. There is a nice variety of levels, weapons, special powers and such that you can find throughout the entire game. This does mean that you might be constantly switcing weapons and having to adjust to how the new weapon works in the next couple of seconds of obtaining it. Obvioulsy some weapons are better than other, and some of them are just damn OP, but we as gamers like OP stuff. The way that you will play through the game is rather simple. Your objective is to clear out each room in order to progress to the next one. You will continue to do this, with some RNG deciding what rooms you will encounter, until you get to the end of the area. You will face countless amounts of different types of enemies along the way, some of them throwing swords at you while others are just walk to you. This does however take me to a few of the issues that I had wit the game, and what it set up to be in my opinion to what it really is. When I first started playing Disposable Heroes I assumed that the game would run along the lines of a Dungeon Crawler. However, the game itself doesn't do that unfortunatly. You only have to kill the enemies in the room and then you get teleported to the next room. I found this a little odd, as there are sometimes 2 doors that will open after you have killed the enemies in that room. I also found out that you can't actually grab the dropped loot once you have killed all the enemies in the room because you get instantly teleported to the next level. Nothing too major, but the next point is one of the things I really don't like about this game. Once you get hit I would expect to get a small amount of invinsibility to get out of whatevers attacking me. You don't get that here, which leads to a lot of cheap deaths as your stuck in a corner and get continously hit by enemies.
+ A nice co-op game

+ Trading cards & Achievements

- Get teleported to the next room automatically, meaning you can't grab any gold or weapons once you have killed all the enemies

"Kim is a top-down perspective open world RPG set in Rudyard Kipling’s colonial India. A peculiar choice of setting to be sure and if that name seems kinda familiar, Kipling is the guy who wrote The Jungle Book. The actual Book-book, not the Disney stuff.
The game is inspired by the eponymous Nobel-award winning novel, which tells the story of a street urchin named Kimball whose dusty and worn shoes you’ll be walking in during game-time. The game also isn’t some sort of linear adaptation or interactive graphic novelization either, it basically takes the setting, characters and events and allows you to play throughout as you see fit."

Normally I don't do reviews on the games I play, but when it comes to Kim I really felt that I should do one because of two things.
1) First is obviosuly the merit to the game itself. It is really enjoyable, unique and probably one of the best indie games i have come across. Once you start a playthrough, you just immerse yourself in the character, the beautiful settings and the writing it offers. The music is lovely, so the deluxe edition is reccommended.
Gameplay wise, having to weigh in the pros and cons of actions as well as taking into account of the limited time and resources available to the character in the playthrough is the strongest element of the game. Basically, you have to make smart choices to score high but at the same time you also get to choose the high road or the low road in making decisions and that will put your own morality to the test, which I really like to see in all kinds of games.
I did 3 playthroughs so far, and the 3 playthroughs were completely different to each other even though the main quest line does not change. This is because you practically can't do all, which again makes you choose smart and makes the game replayable which is I believe is value for money.
2) The developers are really responsive to community feedback and constantly with all ears on how to improve the game by taking into account of our experiences.
Best example is, when I encountered that reading books (character can buy books) in the game does not have excerpts from the actual book itself, I pointed that out as a weakness to the devs. They responded immediatly and said that they will add this feature to the next update in May, and i'm really ecstatic about it.
Then I as well as a lot of people playing the game has complained about the shortness of the playthrough, and they addressed that also. So, it's really good to see the devs listening to us, the community.
So yes, I reccommend this game with full thumbs up!

I'm really enjoying Kim! I like the feeling of geniune consequences, I'm learning from my own mistakes constantly. Admittedly I probably shouldn't have gone near that tiger. You live and learn. Sometimes with tigers you just learn actually. The living part is optional.
The writing is a little difficult at times, but that's because it's super faithful to the source material. Once you get used to it it's real beautiful.
The art is pretty as all heck. There's a real feeling of texture and life in everything. There's a lot of character in the faces of the people you meet, but also in each of the towns I've been to.
The other thing that's nice is I feel like I'm getting a window in to this interesting, contentious period of history that I don't know that much about. I'm learning about all these factions and groups as I go, and how they feel about each other. I've only played for an hour and already I've learned a little about the various different religions vying for prominence in colonial India. I've also learned that tigers are really dangerous, but I think I mentioned that already.

Kim is a special little game - at first glance it seems like a linear story driven game, but after the tutorials ends the game really opens up and you can practically go everywhere, live to story of Kim as you please. Along with the amazing audio and cute hand-drawn art I found Kim to be a lovely experience

On the good side: trying to play with timing and variations, one can beat some levels waaaay below the "par".

Interesting game with a lot of potential. Still can't recommend at this point:
While physics based combat sounds nice on paper, it is implemented in a very unresponsive and complicated way. As a result, fights are random and can (will) be lost just because controls got in the way.
Even the slightest hint of criticism gets shut down immediately. Community managers and a band of fanatic "fans" yell down any attempt of openly discussing the game or providing feedback with "GID GUDDER! This game is hard on purpose! LEARN TO PLAY!!". Games being hard and unforgiving is OK. Using the intended difficulty as an excuse for sloppy implementation of fundamental game features (i.e. physics based combat) is NOT OK.
The vague combat controls lead to a lot of "at game" frustration to a point where most (non-masochistic or elitist) players just give up. Which is a shame.
Given the way the developers handle any feedback in that direction, I do not see this issue ever being adressed. And therefore, no recommendation.
TL;DR: General athmosphere is great, the layering (and visual style) of armor is awesome. However, the core mechanic of physics based combat is lacking and ruins an otherwise great game.
EDIT: My playtime displayed is incorrect. Since I wrote a save game manager which started the game directly (before I noticed and fixed it), my actual playtime is about 80 hours more than displayed by steam.
When I posted a github link to the source code of my (harmless and helpful) tool, it was immediately flagged as hacking and the post removed for violating the terms.
The way the developers / community managers sabotage any notion of modding or community support - even calling well meaning fans cheaters and hackers - is another reason to avoid this game.

The kind of game you play when you want to relax during a hot summer day, with the fan humming besides you and the cicadas singing outside. Or maybe during a cold evening, after a hard day at work and before going to bed.
Anyway, this game is not about action, challenge or solving head-scratching puzzles. It's not even exploration per se. It's all about the atmosphere. You just wander on a mysterious planet (not as lifeless as it seems), admiring the landscapes and unravelling the story of the earthlings who lived here. This is not an open world, the puzzles are easy to solve and the platform sequences won't give you a hard time. It still feels rewarding as you're constantly progressing through the game and discovering new environments.
However, the game is long enough to keep you entertained for several hours.
The various environments are coherent and fascinating, even if the graphics are simplistic.
The music is nice but could have played a greater role.
The gameplay is simple and the character reacts smoothly.
The background story is just oppressive enough to make you beg for more.
A few bugs -like falling through the floor- but nothing serious.
Loved it.

It should be noted that having knowledge on the history of the USSR is extremely helpful for the game (it can sometimes even help you make decisions), not having any prior knowledge will cause you to get lost due to not knowing what an event is about or what the consequences are.
For a summary of the game: you basically play as a Soviet historical entity, replay the Fall of the Soviet Union and see if you can turn it around. You can choose several different approaches to the matter, reform the Soviet Union, go on a hardline path or go full on liberal. You can decide how to approach historical events (occured before the game's timeframe but can still use it to influence your stats) and current events (the events basically advance time a month at a time). The timeframe goes from as early as 1985 to as late as 1996, a total of 132 turns excluding historical events (where a victory scene will show telling you how you did). There are several numbers you need to keep track of: budget, science points, political power points, and loyalties. Budget is used to allocate around and make things run, science points can be used to unlock tech and ultimately win the space race, political power points can be used to export revolutions or enact reformation and loyalty ensures you stay in power (don't mess with the KGB or the military, those are quick ways to lose the game).
All in all, fairly interesting, nice replayability especially if you want to try out different idealogies.
很有意思的一款游戏，很便宜，但是物有所值。基本上的意思就是你被钦点“中央都决定啦，你来当(苏共)总书记。”，于是乎你来建设苏联特色
社会主义（你也可以选择走民主路线或者是共产主义路线）。
游戏是按回合进行的，每年12回合，一回合一个月，从最早的1985到1996年游戏结束（可以继续，但是1996年会给你评分）。游戏开局的时候可以选择玩历史事件（基本上就是选择有几个事件来决定你的初始数据）。游戏最关键的几个数据，钱，政治点数，科技点数，忠诚指数，自由指数，中美关系。钱是用来让鬼推磨的。政治点数可以用来实施政治改革以及影响他国。科技点数可以用来加科技，特别是对于喜欢科技取胜的（里面如果不废除和平号空间站的话，可以进行火星登陆）。忠诚指数包括克格勃，将领，知识分子和左翼右翼等等，时常注意好克格勃和将领的忠诚指数，这两个比较要命，太低的话容易被推翻。值得一提的是克格勃，克格勃很多时候都可以用来轻松帮你解决问题，但是比较耗经费，如果不给经费的话需要他们的时候他们就不会出动。自由指数可以用来让你决定往后的政治走向。至于中美关系，美国关系初期比较重要，不过玩的时候可以把美国政府推翻，一旦推翻美国政府，立刻会解锁大量的外交选项，比如统一两岸建立台湾特别行政区，让日本割让北方四岛以及让西欧诸国退出北约等等；中国关系不是很重要，但是到后期会有一些事件可以选择把海参崴还给中国等等等等，中国最大的好处就是有一个大大的市场，一旦开放就是可以拿来赚钱的，如果选择向中国开放市场，可以解决一定程度上的的轻工业不足（后面还可以向天朝出口军火）。游戏里面还需要注意其他苏联加盟国的忠诚指数（太低的话他们会分裂出去）还有极个别的有苏联驻军的国家（亚非拉同胞们）。如果一定想出口革命的话也可以，但是比较困难，比较耗金钱和政治点数，建议先照顾好东欧再说。
不过这个游戏翻译比较粗糙，不会讲俄语的可能会比较吃亏，游戏的英语翻译也是比较毛糙。玩这个游戏最好有一些历史常识，稍微了解一些东欧剧变的历史对游戏里面各种事件都会有所帮助。

This seems like a cool concept for a game. In fact, it seems like that this might be an interesting game based on how many different factors and mechanics there appear to be. Unfortunately, the tutorial for this game is a mess and it detracts from the game itself.
For instance, in the tutorial the buttons to advance to the next page vary between the top left, bottom right, and bottom left corners. There really isn't any good reason for this and (because of other arrows that appear on the screen) it makes advancing to the next page unnecessarily confusing.
Another issue I have with the tutorial though is that (despite it telling you to "explore the cabinet") it doesn't actually let you do anything with any of the things that you use in the game. If you click on the globe or the map for instance you can't actually get an idea yourself of how things work. Instead you get fed a bunch of information in a way where you aren't in the position to use the screens for yourself.
Its not even like these pages are conveyed in a way that are easy to read either. In the tutorial there are probably 6-7 pages that look like this.
Why is this text center-aligned instead of left-aligned? Why aren’t the different factors split up by paragraph? Why are you using letters (a, b, c, etc) to divide them?
(also in this case you used “d)” twice)
Basically, instead of just getting an info dump I think the game would be better served with a clearer, more interactive tutorial.
Also, the game suffers from cases where words get jumbled together incorrectly. Take the screenshot below.
I wish I could say this was the only case where I saw this in the 20 minutes I've played. Unfortunately, its surprisingly frequent. There are also other basic proofreading issues as well (like incorrect capitalizations, spaces missing between words and commas, etc). In a larger game this wouldn't be as much of an issue, but in this case issues like these stick out.
TLDR: There might be a good game here. But the developer needs to take some time to seriously proofread the text in this game.

I have mixed emotions about this game. I will recommend it,because if you love baseball,its a great game.
In itself it is an awesome baseball game. The physics off the bat and in the field of play are great. You can see the ball change directions on the lip of the grass or deflecting off the mound. The ball also plays very well off the fences.
I do wish it was a little deeper. A 10 season Franchise mode with star points of course,more teams/divisions,aging players, pick offs,pitcher warm ups,deeper rosters,track errors, because they are a problem. I would also like to see it keep your W/L records for different egos, and be able to save multiple seasons.It could also use a stadium for each team(or at least for each team in a division) and the ability to pick your home stadium. I would be willing to pay for these additions. They would make a very good game better.
It does have problems in my opinion....
I start at a certain ego to start the season (65),every time I win I add 2 ego,and everytime I lose I subtract 2 ego. I hold steady from 67 to 73 ego. I have never won a game at 73. I believe the game has issues at higher egos. At 73 ego I can generally predict how a game is going to go. I will score a few runs(2-4) early. I will hold them for till 7th or later. Then the AI will start hitting the ball in nearly perfect areas on the infield, where you have to dive,but wont catch it and the throw will not be in time, or my team will commit 2 to 3 errors in the inning. I wont have an error all game till the late inning with a lead. If I'm losing, errors are not an issue.Player errors grossly outweigh the AI errors. Also there are issues with fielder control. I was trying to field a ball with a left fielder ,charging the ball and suddenly I switch to the SS. The ball drops in front of the LF and the tying run scored. This is because its perfectly placed between the LF,3B and SS, and I have learned it is usually better to use the OF.
These issues are very frustrating. There is also times at high egos that if you throw a strike it gets hit hard. You can not throw a ball by the AI. This seems to be in big games vs. Division leader or a team ahead of you in the standings. Its generall early in the game...and doesnt last after a good lead.
Why you ask do I still recommend this game? Because even with these issues...this is a great game. The physics ( which are a big thing for me in a baseball game) are excellent. Its fun and challenging. If you enjoy a good baseball game its right here. Play/load times are fast. It could be a little deeper ,but its a good game.
Also I think the fooled/anticipated idea needs to go. Why would a guy anticipate a pitch out of the strike zone and swing at it. On the other hand a batter who is fooled will smack it to the fence.

Revision looks better then stock Deus Ex, but it's unfortunately not
much better. The unreal engine is unfortunately not really capable of much better then what you get in the stock game. However, Revision's changes to the hub worlds are pretty nice. New York and Hong Kong are now both much larger, though Hong Kong now has a loading screen in the middle of it, which is a bit of a shame. Additionally, these changed level designs means the game refers to locations that have changed, for instance Smuggler, who used to be near the entrance to the subways, is now hidden in the basement of a building.
The music of Revision is the other major change. Objectively, the music is nice. Subjectively, I don't love it as much as the original's game. The new OST is a combination of covers of the original (which do sound nice and fit the game), and more cinematic orchestral music (which, while nice sounding don't fit the original).
The only other thing worth a mention that's specific to Revision is that the game world (but not UI) will disappear, until you switch resolution or change out of Fullscreen mode.
Revision isn't a bad mod, but it's also not a substantial improvement over the original game. If it's your first play through, or you just want an excuse to play through the game again, it's pretty good, but for most other people it's probably not worth it.

I got the chance to play this game early, and I must say, I was really impressed with it overall!
The game has an interesting art style, that might fool you into thinking this game isn't too hard, but you'd be surprised at how quickly this game just picks up in difficulty! The game obviously has a few minor issues, since it's still in early access, but they were very minor, and did not detract from the game substantially.
Here's a video of me playing the game, and giving my first impressions, should it interest you!

While the art looks like it was done in MS Paint, it does grow on you after a while. From the charming little rodents and bandits to the nearly inescapable death traps, this game is truly a trip. It's like the Dark Souls of dungeon crawling. It is hard. It is unforgiving. And yet, it's also addicting and encourages you to play more. The weapon choices are even endearing, from your starting weapon of a wooden spoon, to the futuristic lazor gun.
That being said, there are some improvements I would like to see. For one, it would be nice to have online or LAN multiplayer. This game was definitely made to be played with another person, and I feel as though it's restricted by only having "couch" co-op. It would also be nice to see difficulty settings, especially if a person feels like going it solo.

It's a game about a man who drank too much, ran away from responsibility by going to work forever and left his family. Now after his wife is dead he suddenly gets a chance to make up with his daughter and gets a happy ending. Poor daughter. Poor wife. I just found him to be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who left his family and who was forgiven for doing nothing. One could argue that the journey itself would be the trial/trail he must cross to come to terms with his past.
Okay, then, as beautiful as the journey is, it doesnt amount to much narrative-wise. He walks, sits, remember. Maybe the gameplay is supposed to implicitly suggest that we are in a way "making things right" by huh, altering the scenery around him, I guess? Notice that we are the ones doing this. He just walks.
He doesn't, at the very least, say "im sorry" at the end. Maybe for a wordless game, this would be an interesting twist at the end.
Forgive me, the art is so pretty, but there is something inherently mean spirited about this naive story where bad decisions are romanticized ("I am a man of the sea, I like yatchs so bye forever") and forgiveness seems to mean so little ("okay mom is dying I forgive you, you really liked boats, right? lets go sail on one").
If this emotional journey was anything but the point of the whole damn game, maybe it would be palatable. But it's not.

Kim is a top down adventure game where you play as the boy Kim. Kim was orphaned at a young age and lives the life of a vagabond doing tasks for money. In this game, the player travels around 1800s india during the "Great game". You have to manage your money, happiness and health (Including sickness and hunger). The player has the choice to work for the money (at the cost of time) or steal (at the cost of merit). When Kim turns 18 years of age the game ends and the score is tallyed based on your actions. The game loosely follows the story of the original book by Rudyard Kipling but gives the player the freedom to explore and discover the secrets of 1800s india. With detailed dialogues, descriptions and a very pretty, drawn graphic style, KIM is a very enjoyable game based on exploration. It challenges the player with little money and little food to survive on as a vegabond boy. Although it can feel like the game is rushing you at times, it has plenty of replay value with random seeds for the game world and the oppertunity to make different choices or discover something that you never expected to...

Would the helpful math underlying this game be group theory? Graph theory?
Whatever it is, KNIGHTS is a rare type of puzzle game: it doesn't involve any numbers (unlike in the Hexcells, SquareCells, and CrossCells, and Cross Set games), and each puzzle doesn't involve discrete solvable subparts and doesn't really introduce any new gameplay mechanics as you progress (unlike in say, Hook, Zenge, PUSH, and klocki).
Rather, you play by moving around the finite permutations of a set of chess knights on a small playing board to achieve a desired configuration; the mechanics are simple enough to grasp with a glance. This ends up making the game more difficult in a way, especially by the later levels, but it's a pure, fair, and classic sort of difficulty.
The general aesthetic, which includes graphic+UI design and music, is as pleasant and relaxing as any other minimalist puzzle game. The puzzles are short and sweet enough to play in a few convenient minutes of your time, and there is enough pure difficulty from the way the game is designed so as to never really be reduced into a few algorithmic strategies.
You can also unlock a rather difficult Daily Levels pack after you finish the game too, so the game does have its replay value.
All in all, a solid puzzle game. Would definitely recommend.

Despite its flaws, Crisis in the Kremlin is a major improvement on the 1991 version of the game.
The first major improvement is that your regime doesn't intend on committing suicide like it does in the 1991 version (unless you're playing on hard.) You run the USSR in an oddly very democratic way, a way that challenges you to think and rewards you as such. You have to remember to be careful with your ambitions, which DO have realistic concequences for things like overspending. It's ironic, because in Democracy 3, a so-called Democracy simulator does a horrible job of presenting to us. Secondly, like all games, it's confusing at first - but very easy to learn for a geopolitics game of this depth. Your country will effectively collapse if you overspend and make risky foreign investments, but it will boom if you manage to spend enough on both supplying your people with what they need, making enough profit for economic growth, while remaining economically independent enough.
P.S.: There's a weird bug where you start off even on Utopia difficulty you start off with nothing in your economy. I'm sure as of now that this is just a bug, and not a major aspect of gameplay.
Foreign policy (note that this is heavily impacted by pregame events that you can either skip over and go the historical route or change by not skipping over) nonetheless needs some improvement. On anything above normal, if you don't funnel what's left of your budget into fueling loyal regimes, they grow tired of you, break away from you, and then suddenly collapse. On Normal, however, the game does a good job of presenting foreign relations effectively. Romania is lead by an oddly authoritarian maverick regime - as in real life under Ceaușescu - Bulgaria has tendancies to sway toward Yugoslavia, but are nonetheless loyal, as with real life - Czechoslovakia is keen on reform, but can be kept in place, as with real life - Poland is loyal, but occasionally requires support or intervention to be kept loyal, as with real life, East Germany is a firm ally, as with real life, and China has mixed feelings on you, as with real life. It could use a bit of brushing up, though; although it's benefitial to start and win an immediate civil war in South Africa by backing labor unions, it ignores both pre-war elections and the possibility of having an interesting diplomatic scenario revolving around the civil war in South Africa. Communist sympathy and the extent of reform also needs some patching up, as well as 'supporting revolutions.'
The individual decisions you can make and party management are what make the game challenging. There's a lot of variety in what can happen and the AI isn't always predictable, plus, your actions have such a grand impact on the overall game that it requires you to read over things when they appear, and to put thought into your choices. And that is exactly what makes the game fun. The music also greatly improves the experience. I personally enjoy Soviet political music and military marches, but that definately needs to be expanded on, as well as most of the music. I suggest
as an addition to Soviet political music.

The adventure / story mode also never appealed too much to me. I find it too hard to be honest, too punishing, too slow if you're trying to find good gear. And I kept getting lost on the map!
I find that the arena mode that was added later is the strongest point of this game. You have a sense of progress, it's not that easy to lose all of it and it's cool to rank your characters up and gradually equip them with better armor and armaments until you own an awesome Knight's armor with e.g. a halberd or polehammer to hurl at your opponent. And the innovative and unique way of fighting in this game makes it all more interesting.
Character customisation is formidable but I'd like it more if you could change your character's face. However the game is of course still being developed.
To me it's not a game I can put hundreds of hours in, the gameplay doesn't give enough variety for that, but I still confidently recommend it for its price. and the boobs on the female characters look great btw.

What an amazing game! This is a mix of real-time strategy, tower defense and liquid physics. It is an excellent example how you don't need lifelike 3D graphics, a great story or a bombastic sountrack - as long as the gameplay is rock solid like here. After 200+ hours not a single negative quality comes to my mind. It's still as much fun as when I started and I still find myself challenged by some maps.
The amount of content is truly mind-boggling. I've honestly just scratched the surface. There are thousands of pre-made maps and an infinite amount of randomly generated and community-made maps. There's everything from easy 5min runs you can sleep-walk through to 5-hour-long battles where you always find yourself on the brink of extinction and claw for inches against overwhelming amounts of creeper. If you ever tire of the gameplay - there's dozens of achievements to chase and some really clever community maps to play, that take advantage of the scripting capability. And every single map has an online leader-board if you are looking for competition.
I've never encountered a bug or technical problem. All the settings, from hotkeys to color schemes are customizable. The game loads and runs extremely fast, even on my rather anemic computer. You can play everything at your pace, since you can pause or save/quit at any moment, so even multi-front battles are quite doable. The base mechanics are simple, there's about two dozen buildings at most, but there's still a lot of different play-styles and unit preferences, which are all pretty viable.
If you are at all interested in strategy or tower defense this is a must-buy! But if you are still hesitant - check out the demo from the developer's website or play the old Creeper World flash game.

Overall I enjoyed this game greatly, although there are some caveats.  Although Lifeless Planet is referred to as a "walking simulator" it doesn't neatly fit into that category, insofar as there is a LOT of platformer action throughout.
The Good:
The story is what is at the core of this game, however and it is pretty awesome.  The way it is slowly told throughout the game keeps your interest up.  The visuals also match the narrative very well--they help set the mood and whomever designed them did an outstanding job.  The game's length is also great...not short by any means, but not so long that things get drawn out needlessly.  I enjoyed the fact that despite the vastness of the world, the correct path is fairly evident (in most cases).  Also, the storytelling elements (notebooks, recordings, etc.) are not hidden--i.e. you do not have to scour every corner of the map (which can be vast in some areas) just to look for "clues" or narrative elements.
The Bad:
The platformer sections, however, are very hit or miss.  I appreciated this element of the game, but the experience was undermined in places by the game's most obvious flaw--the controls.  I played Lifeless Planet both with Keyboard/mouse as well as the Steam Controller.  Control of your character could be very sloppy in places, making certain timed jumps extremely difficult to execute.  On one section, I literally had to try to execute 6 consecutive jumps well over 50 times.  This particularly section was poorly designed and the fact that your avatar "drifts" was borderline unfair and marred the experience.  Although not consistently a problem, when your avatar is in a tight environment, the camera perspective is every bit as poor as the original Alone in the Dark from the early 90s.  Finally--and this is sort of inexcusable--there are a number of areas on maps where you can "get stuck."  If you happen to jump in some areas (e.g. between rocks or next to a structure) you can be stuck there and have to re-load from the last checkpoint.  I have no idea why some of these negative elements were not patched, but expect to encounter them and be annoyed.
Verdict:
I really liked the game and would highly recommend it to folks who enjoy slow, story-rich "walking sims."  The story, not the platformer elements, are what makes the game so watch the trailer and if you feel drawn in by the narrative, you'll probably really like Lifeless Planet.

Alright, I really enjoyed this game.  A lot.  It's everything I would want in an indie sci-fi.
The positives are that it really genuinely feels like an alien planet and the atmosphere is really good.  The music really worked well for me.  I enjoyed the story.
Now, if you're expecting this to be a AAA game with Crysis level graphics you may be disappointed.  But from what I understand this was a kickstarter game and mostly developed by one person over the course of a few years.  So keep that in mind before reading too much into some of the less positive reviews.
This is more of a platforming game than a walking simulator.  The puzzles are pretty straightforward and easy.  If you get stuck it usually just requires a bit of backtracking or paying closer attention to stuff.  I didn't have too much trouble with it.
People say the game is short, but it felt reasonably long to me.  Dunno if it has a lot of replay value.
Minor nitpick is that the transitions between levels are not at all seamless, you end one level it like hard cuts to a different area where it doesn't seem like it's all that connected to the previous level.  It may be daytime in one level, then when the next level starts it's suddenly nighttime.
The textures are a bit low resolution and sometimes feel a bit dated.  It may not satisfy you if you expect photorealism.  It feels like it might be a bit older of a game at times because of this.  It's fine for an indie game.
Overall I just had a lot of fun and I can recommend this to sci-fi fans, especially if it's on sale.  Although it does have some tense moments, it isn't that fast-paced for the most part, definitely more exploratory.  So it may not appeal to you if you enjoy twitchy games where timing matters a lot.

Its a lot of fun when not being unfair, the story is actually quite interesting it feels like something from an old classic Disney movie with an extra comedy touch, the design is simple and the music is outstanding with a medieval theme.
To those coming here hoping for an experience similar to binding of Isaac PLEASE note that this is NOTHING like it if anything its quite similar to castle crashers in game style except for the perspective of-course.
- You'd be impressed by the amount of levels this game has so far, unlike the game might suggests, this is not really a randomly generated dungeon type, it has a set of levels you need to progress through to reach the next stage, the map is very similar to castle crashers looking like this
so levels are pre-made however, some levels have a random chance of appearing in your current play through or not.
- Simple battle system, Up down left right for movement and 1 button to attack and one to cast the spell in hand alongside with buttons from 1 to 5 to use inventory slots "Potions".
- A lot of enemies, boss fights, cut-scenes, weapons, items and a market level "think of it like the blacksmith level of castle crashers"
- A talented female narrator, that narrates the story and whenever you pickup an item and do basic commands like that.
- Special levels like the one in the 6th screenshot in this store page and more similar stuff, great music, funny animations, hard to acquire achievements and trading cards.
+ The game play is fun , controls are simple, its fun enough to play alone and more than that to play with a coop buddy "local only"
+ Great music, hilarious artwork, nice animations, a plus for the narrator and her beautiful voice.
+ Fun levels, good content so far, check points after finishing each stage "they consist of several levels each"
+ Its really fun to play alone and 10 times more fun to play with a local coop bud.
+ Dev looked active in forum and reacting with community thats always a huge plus. "as far as I know the game has only one developer for it and someone else for the music "
- The game gets too difficult and unfair if you got close enough to a monster, because their attacks resets when they hit you, so if you're close enough they can land 14 hits in 1 second and you die instantly considering your character has no fade-time after taking a hit, same thing for any spike obstacle or trap.
- At later levels the control scheme suddenly changed for me from arrows to wasd, I died without moving because I had no idea they'd change suddenly so this is a bug "on level 3 the cave"
- The controls feels clunky with character movement, its not that easy to attack enemies though you'd get used to it but its still not as satisfying as you'd hope it to be.
- I love the narrator's performance, but she doesn't really have to say everything you do it gets annoying, like when scrolling the main menu "1 player, 2 players, options " yeah those ... either reduce it or give an option to do so.
- In certain levels that has traps throwing daggers or shooting lasers, considering that the character's movements are not as smooth as you'd hope it to be, it gets really tough to dodge them.
- Due to the fact that enemy attacks has no cooldown and your character has no fade-effect when hit, you can die INSANELY fast if got too close to an enemy so you'll die a lot and feel frustrated from this unfair difficulty.
- Having the controls on keyboard to use inventory potions set from 1 to 5 is not a good idea, I really died so many times without using them because the buttons are too far : |
- Sometimes after picking up a potion or weapon then you try to walk over another one to pick it up, it don't work so you'd have to walk away and walk over it again.
- Level transition is annoying to say the least, I mean the idea of moving to the next level automatically after killing the enemies is dumb, so much loot gets lost, however some levels requires you to reach the end to pass it.
- I don't believe there is a button to get back to main menu, pressing esc only freeze's the game and the narrator says "take a break", screen stays the same just frozen, pressing F2 restarts the game, pressing - or + reduces window size, those are all weird but whatever.
I know I mentioned a lot of things the game needs work on, try to remember this is an early access game and a new one nevertheless, so I am still expecting more updates and I know that most of those issues I talked about are simple to fix, so please don't let what I said shy you away from getting the game, it is really a lot of fun to play with a friend if you can ignore the unfair difficulty hoping it gets fixed soon.

Old Man's Journey has a fairly interesting game mechanic at its core (aligning different levels so that the old man may reach different parts of the map), but this game truly shines when it comes to its poignant message and imagery. It probably takes some maturity and life experience to be able to fully appreciate its story, since it deals with making choices between the people and things we love, and often having to abandom some of them in order to pursue our other dreams. I have been there, and sometimes I'm not sure walking away was the right choice. This game has made me question some of my previous decisions. It has also forced me to confront the prospect of aging alone, since freedom and happiness are often antithetical and mutually exclusive. Poignant and brilliant gaming experience, even if a bit short.
As a side note, the game is themed with Mediterranean / southern European imagery and is stunningly beautiful.

Absolutely exquisite game. It is rare to find a game that is more like an artistic masterpiece, but this is one of them.  The music helps immerse you in the touching plot and light pastel colors are combined beautifully to create the levels where the environment itself is the puzzle. It's so refreshing to see a point-and-click game that doesn't make you collect items, so in that way it's quite reminiscent of Samorost 3, another great game. There's no dialog, but thanks to the game's simple mechanics, it's not too difficult to figure out what to do to progress. The game may be short, but the story is well expressed in a coherent way that makes it feel like it didn't need to be longer. This game is an OK game. Nothing crazy good, nor insanely bad. I enjoyed playing it, with gunplay reminiscent of a combination of Counter Strike and Call of Duty. However, there are a few things that need to be fixed for this game to get better.
Its looks...alright? Nothing particularly amazing. Better than CS:CZ, but less that CS:S. Straight out of 2009-looking thing. Maybe that'll make more sense.
HUD/UI is simplistic yet clean, and sound design was surprisingly good. Footsteps, weapons (shooting and reloading) and other actions sounded good. Though the voice acting sounds kinda cheesy.
Like most MMOFPS games, BlackShot has an EXP, Shop, and Inventory system. You earn in-game BP, spend it on weapons, items, etc. Nothing particularly new. However, it does have a character select system, where you choose a character of either gender favoring speed or health, as well as effecting starting weapons (although an extensive starter pack was obtained upon character creation). You can also apply different buffs that increase health, movement speed, etc. to varying degrees.
The gunplay is actually quite fun: fast-paced, and weapon recoil is actually pretty consistent, meaning you won't have to compensate much for it like in other CS-clones. And, finally, I've seem to have found a much more fair use of timed-weaponry in this game when compared to other similar ones. Essentially, most weapons you buy with in-game currency (not sure about Premium weapons/items) have a time limit: 3 hours, 1 day, etc. These times onnly drain for as long as you actually use it, not just how long they've been on your account. This is GREAT. No longer are you pressured to use the weapons immediately. Until you activate them, you can keep them in your inventory as long as you want. The Shop itself is pretty fair too, as earning BP through gameplay and achievements honestly didn't feel like a terrible grind, though don't expect anything to come easily.
The NA servers are practically always barren, meaning you'll have to play in the "World" server. This wouldn't be a problem if latency wasn't so bipolar all the time. In addition, I've run into 2 hackers in the small amount of time I've played. Thankfully, the majority of the community is nice and kicks the suckers out, but if you're stuck in a small server, it'd be better to leave.
Plus, this game is sorta-pay-to-win. What I mean is that the Premium weapons are still difficult to master, but do offer stats that are straight up better than most of the other weapons. Mastering these weapons makes you a GOD in TDM and S&D. Spawn-camping has also been an issue, but most gamemodes won't have this problem.
I'd give BlackShot a 7/10. It's fine, better than other CS-clones and MMOFPS games. It has a few additions that keep its painfully overdone formula fresh, and its gameplay was fun and reletively fair. However, the issue that do plague this game are too severe for me to grant it a higher score. It's average, and you know what? It's free. I gave it a try, so why don't you?

Fun little physics puzzle game. Your goal is to get a blue square or circle to a blue area to complete each puzzle. Items start stationary but when you click on them gravity is activated and the blocks will move accordingly.

Using these tools, you'll make catapaults, swings and other interesting tools to help you throw blocks around in ways that would give Newton a boner.
The graphics are pretty minimalistic, it's all done on graph paper and with pencil, so it's still aesthetically pleasing.
The music I really enjoyed, just simple playful little tunes that will have you unashamedly bobbing while you sling blocks around.
The overall theme of the game is simplicity hiding some pretty complex features.
It will only take a few hours to complete. The game isn't super challenging, but it will make you think a bit. Definitely worth a playthrough

ExGen=Exanima/Sui Generis
NPC=Non-Player Character
PC=Player Character
BM=Bare Mettle
MS=Motion Synthesis
The future of gaming has never been more exciting to me! In Exanima, you are witness to the footnote of possibly the finest sandbox fantasy RPG of all time, Sui Generis. Already, there are supreme demonstrations of innovative melee combat that not a single other game can match. They can't possibly because ExGen's physics integrations are one of a kind and ingenious, and that's only one facet in which ExGen will slap an ungloved gauntlet across the face of the mediocrity that is AAA.
Such classic, cheesy proverbs are imbedded in BM's philosophy with games, and the inherently awkward controls solidify the meaning. ExGen wants you to take it seriously. As an initiate, you must feel your way to get your bearings. Punishment is swift and consistent for those who attack the game with common mindsets. This is because no respect is given, but must be earned at every turn. Not that ExGen is immensely challenging. In fact, most of the challenge offered is merely a consequence of the control and realism BM aimed for.
The violence is lethal and brutal. Mishaps can lead to decisive or fatal outcomes. What you do, intentional or incidental, is from your creative input, and the input is refreshingly open ended. While offense currently consists of only four attacks, MS—the replication of genuine, anatomical movement and balance through a simulation of body tissues—allows for unprecedented dynamics and fluidity in the control of avatars. You aim attacks and decide their path via cursor which controls the torso and arms. Due to MS, control is not 1:1, and that's where it gets interesting.
Footwork is a major aspect of combat, and it can affect melee control as much as the cursor. In combat mode, persons broaden their form and take quick, stiff steps to retain balance at all times. Due to orientation's exclusive control by cursor, and the camera being static, step movement is directed within a full 360°. For defense, persons automatically try to intercept trajectories of opposing strikes in the most efficient way possible, and they can even pan out from or neutralize an attack's trajectory. These defensive measures are reliable, but the player does need to orient the cursor and their avatar to a logical position to guarantee success.
Exanima's controls and MS are typically why newbies quickly give up, become frustrated and/or confused (and go on to give a pathetic/mindless/knee-jerk negative review). Also, the camera—especially in relation to the controls—is unusual. Constraints on player input are fairly cryptic, and again, mainstream mindsets may lead to oversimplification or underestimation. The other side of the coin sees players flailing about, rather than making deliberate, precise movements. The finalization of MS and especially any planned elaborations for combat are a long way off, but it's always up to the player to achieve practicality and finesse in their avatar's form.
The differences in gameplay of practiced and experienced veterans, versus greenhorns, or even moderately seasoned players, is staggering, and refining one's form and the art of slaughter becomes a game in and of itself! The most exciting part, to me, is how complex techniques, strategies, and ideas IRL can be applied to the combat! Another exciting benefit of MS is the differences in style that players can develop, and the significant role that preferred equipment plays in applying a style. There's only a glimpse of what is to come in these regards because systems, such as procedural weapon assembly, have so much to offer.
The final aspect of combat is stamina and encumbrance. Stamina currently has no aesthetic or definitive effect, other than incapacitation once it is depleted by non-lethal damage, or death once it is depleted by lethal damage. Stamina recovers from non-lethal damage while out of combat, but lethal damage may only be recovered through healing effects. Encumbrance effects mobility and freedom of movement. High encumbrance will significantly slow all actions, while armor can impede flexiblity and make movements stiffer.
Dark, forgotten dungeon full of unknowable danger, scum, and villainy. Check! Numerous paths, halls, and mazes to explore and get lost in. Check! Chests, armories, workshops, hidden items, and treasures to plunder. Check!
The Underworld is about survival and discovery. As the Unknown, you start bare and with relatively poor combat prowess. Remember, ExGen wants you to take the world seriously! It's important stay vigilant and open to the possibilities. NPCs and the environment itself are not simply fabricated elements for our enjoyment. They have motivations separate from the player, while the environment is arranged to be as sensible and immersive as possible. The level design lives up to what BM is trying to accomplish, but NPCs still have long-due updates to fill out their identities and make interaction more consequential. Still, if you pause to observe NPCs, you'll find they do have unique and genuine behaviors.
When it comes to exploration, there is much ground to cover and a plethora of nooks and crannies to inquisite. On that point, Exanima currently represents a small fraction of final content. That includes the combat, which will be expanded with ranged weaponry, more melee actions, and the mystical powers of Thaumaturgy. While no one knows exactly what to expect, those who've explored every nook and cranny and uncovered every plot understand how much there is to look forward to!
Persons are governed by an immersive advancement system. Experience is gained through actions and experimentation, great and minor. Presently, experience's only use is to train, but it will have various dynamic effects in the future.
Arena is a work in progress, but if you're an action junky, you delight in crushing your enemies, and you want to experience ExGen's legendary melee combat, I highly recommend it to get your fix!
Arena is basically a gladiatory sim. To start, you create a manager. Currently, the manager is of little consequence, asides that if they die, they drag associated save data to the grave. "Recruit" starts additional inept PCs, while "Hire" allows purchase of hirelings to bid into matches and/or pair with as allies. There's also merchant hirelings that ease obtainment of items.
Equippables are purchased from the shopkeep or merchant with match prizes. Purchased items are transferred to the arena stash, but PCs/NPCs have a personal inventory and stash. On equipment: clothing and armor come in many grades and colors. There's so many combinations, you can't hope to stash all without accruing attrocious load times. Still, if you're going to gather an absurdly large reserve of equipment, I suggest you spread it between your roster.
Match types are plentiful, but Arena isn't very immersive yet. Although players can forfeit, winning demands the death or KO of all opponents. Elimination is the most offending because opponents always start maxed out, though you may have taken damage previously. Arena lacks personality too. There's no taunting or weapon flourishing. No victory celebration. No blaring, memorable fanfares. No guards. No master of ceremonies. Most importantly, there's no audience!
Exanima is as elegant as it is rough around the edges, and despite its youth and lite content, what it currently offers is nothing short of phenominal! Arena and brutal combat gives Exanima a hardcore edge, however, it ultimately leans more towards adventure, immersion, and roleplay. Still, early play means an early grasp on the massively complex combat, but there's no guarantee that you will master it without steadfast dedication!

I'm sure some people won't have a problem with it, but for me the game just feels terrible.
The biggest issue is the movement. Firstly, movement is relative to the character. i.e., if the character is facing to the left and you hit 'w', the character steps forward, to your left. In combat mode, you can only step in cardinal directions, and only in lunging steps. You can take smaller lunging steps, but there's always a significant delay before you can step again. This makes for very restricted-feeling combat. And not in combat mode, there's tank controls; 'a' and 'd' turn your character left and right. Why? It just makes moving around that much more difficult. I was suprised when the 'main' game felt significantly worse than arena practice mode. Honestly if the game had twin-stick style controls I'd probably be recommending it instead.
Two other (not so) minor issues: the weapons feel wrong and the characters don't know how to use them.
To my understanding, the weapons are supposed to feel heavy. But heavier weapons aren't just slower on the wind up, they're slower throughout the swing, which doesn't really make sense unless air resistance is slowing them down. Hence, they feel like they're made of foam.
And the swinging, it's all done from the shoulder. Generally to get power into a swing you use your hips, putting your whole body into the movement. But the characters don't, so if you don't throw your character into a blow, it just doesn't hit very hard. For me, this feels bad because I feel like my skill in the game is being limited by my character's lack of skill. But also it feels like to fight I have to make the characters wobble around like they're made of jello.
Since these are a result of design choices by the developers, I don't see this ever getting better (for my tastes). I don't recommend it.

basically they let you change bullets into points and increase your multiplier so you can have like billions of points OH BOY
The rotation mechanism is very interesting. What you see on your screen is not always the whole picture. There's enemies in the background, as well as ZOMG HUGE ASTEROIDS AND SPACE JUNK (and other crates that can help your ship but those aren't too frequent). So, how do you destroy these things if you can't see them at present? You rotate thorugh your 360 degree field of view, of course! That way, even though you're looking at your ship and the approaching enemies from the side, you can also blast background objects and enemies away, whether they're above or below you! It's a fascinating concept that really sets this game apart and makes it that much more enjoyable.
You really should get this game if you enjoy a challenge. It is a challenge, honestly. Not that you'll die all the time, of course. But y'know, you could just have rotated through the 3D space to avoid that humongous helicopter's laser.
Okay, whatever, just get the game already, it's breathtaking! No joke!

I don't often write reviews, but for this game I thought I'd make an exception.  I happened to see it on the store front and checked out the video - at that point I knew the game was for me!

I wouldn't describe the game as bullet hell, but more like a Cave shooter; there are plenty of bullets for sure, but every single one of them is there to be used to increase your multiplier.  Although you only get a single life, the game isn't so punishingly hard that you can't progress a few levels with some practice, but like any good shooter you can choose the risky play styles which could net you much more points at the expense of progress.
Graphically the game has a unique look to it, very reminiscent of the demoscene product "cdak" by Quite and Orange.  On level three things get shaken up a bit which is welcomed at that point.  Musically this game is incredible, covering a wide range of styles but remaining high quality throughout, and the soundtrack is right there in the game folder.
A fantastic game then and one that I'm sure I'll keep replaying not just for the score but for the sheer enjoyment of it.

Creeper World used to be an old favorite of mine, back when it was a small flash game on Kongregate or some other gaming website. Imagine my surprise when I saw it on steam....and a third edition, no less! Needless to say, the game has come very far since its flash days. I think it may even still be a flash game. Regardless, this version has so much content to offer, it is ridiculous. You start the story with a few towers and have to fight the Creeper, which is basically a fluid that flows down different terrain levels. You can collect energy in the early levels, which lets your command node send out packets of ammo and construction to build things or destroy Creeper. Later, you unlock Anticreeper which uses the same mechanics as Creeper, but it helps you out instead! Each level unlocks more towers and more areas of the game, such as the super-hard Alpha Sector and player-made maps on the DMD(Dial Map Device). Play any number of thousands of missions provided for you after you beat the story (not the best, admittedly, but for this type of game, great). Get bored of that? Make your own maps to grind achievements on or challenge what you thought was possible! Hate the colour purple or light blue? Change the colours of both Anticreeper and Creeper to suit your eyes. Simply a unique game that will provide hours of enjoyment for tower defense fans.
If I only had one complaint, it would be that after you initially hold off the Creeper and get yourself set up collecting energy, you can always win and steamroll over the Creeper. It has no AI so there is nothing that will surprise you after you beat the storymode. That being said, the amount of different towers and ways to win each level are great to provide some variety instead of simply using a blaster and mortar each time.

Having got excited by the prospect of this game when Kotaku listed it as one of its most anticipated adventure games of 2016 and then doubly so when it got the approval of Indie Game Mag, I took the plunge and backed its Kickstarter campaign.  I'm happy to say that it was money well spent, as this game is a little beauty...although "little" is a bit misleading as there's loads to explore and do in the atmospheric world of Kipling's most impish creation.
Colonial India, with all its charm and craziness, is wonderfully brought to life by the hand-painted illustrations, the awesome soundtrack, and the use of Kipling's original text.  The gameplay is solid, with the choices you make having a constant effect on Kim's character, both in terms of his happiness and his skillset.  I seem to find myself in moral quandaries way too often, but maybe that's me!
Have only had a couple of sessions so far, but am looking forward to many more. Would definitely recommend to anyone, particularly if, like me, you're a fan of the original book.

If you have any interest in Kim, Kipling or colonial India, or if you just want to be immersed in a fascinating and colourful world, definitely check it out!

I recommend you take a look at ‘Kim’ but if you are interested in the era or the source material it’s an essential buy.

Kim is a beautifully crafted little indie game based on the book Kim by Rudyard Kipling. The music combined with the illustrative hand-painted art style are a killer combo and whisk you away to a period of time and place that I have never experienced in a game before.
I'll write a more in-depth review once I've delved deeper into the gameplay systems but loving it so far!

Just finished the first of many imminent sessions playing this charming new indie game. Hadn't read Kim in years and was pleasantly surprised by how quickly the book came back to me and how faithful this new medium is to the original, with great graphics and an interface that really gives you a feel for the period.
Keeping both the tone and character of the book could have been heavy handed or confusing but delightfully neither is the case and this game of exploration, spiritual questing and intrigue recreates Kipling's story in an accurate, fun and accessible format.
You gain both information and respect as you encounter more characters throughout your journey, and there are plenty of different ways to increase your skillset and ease your exploring - though theft has thus far been my favourite shortcut to success.
Looking forward to seeing how Kim progresses, both as a character in my charge and as an engaging new game in my arsenal.

I'm really enjoying this game so far. Wonderful atmosphere - the soundtrack and art style really give the feeling of India at the end of the Raj. Kim is a favourite book of mine so it's amazing to see it brought to life in this way.
There seems to be a huge amount to explore -- I managed to get the train to Umballa to carry out the secret mission of the stallion's pedigree, but you can travel in many different ways and many different directions from each of the top down map areas. I chatted to a Sikh policeman and met a regiment of Irishmen, and can't wait to see what new adventures this world may have to offer, and what strategies will open up for surviving Kimball o'Hara's quest for enlightenment.
Anyway, for anyone with an interest in books, india or beautifully produced games, I think Kim is very much worth playing.

I really want to give this game a good review.  I did enjoy certain puzzles where there was a rube goldberg type of chaining going on, but unfortunately the negatives outweigh the positives for me.  That said, I'm really rather neutral on the game but wanted to put this as a negative review so that people know that there are serious flaws and it's not simply a "Brilliant physics puzzler" as the top review currently states.
Pros:
+ fun art style and music
+ when it works it works well and can be quite satisfying.  there were a couple puzzles which just came together beautifully and I even replayed those levels to see it again.
Cons:
- Outcomes are nondeterministic: If you do the same exact thing twice, you WILL get different results.  Often those results are the difference between a solution working and not working.  In a physics puzzler, this is an absolutely HUGE deal.  Likewise, the Undo doesn't completely revert to the previous state and will often leave you in a slightly in-between-moves state.  This means a lot of redoing to get something that works which makes it feel like you're cheesing your solution.  You can also exploit the broken Undo to get a solution that would otherwise not be possible.
- The physics are based on actual physics, so there's gravity and momentum, but there are noticeable gaps where things don't behave according to how you'd expect.  The most jarring for me was a solution that required you to exploit the wonky physics to make one rectangular block turn while another square block flips to stay on top of the rectangular turning block.  That was the only time I used a hint in the game and it left quite a bitter taste.  Outside of that one puzzle, it's more quibbles than actual annoyances.
- The menu system is absolutely terrible: there's about ten different tabs for different puzzles but you have to navigate between them in really odd non-intuitive ways and can't access a single list.  it tries to be nonlinear and give the player options, but really is just confusing.  You can't just select 'next puzzle' from the main menu and it doesn't remember what you were working on last so you have to find it in the maze of options.
Neutral:
* Very short: about two hours total with the newly released Master II puzzles.  But it's cheap, so I won't fault it for this.
* The vast majority of the puzzles are trivial tutorial-esque puzzles that hand-hold you though the solution.  Only a few will require more than a couple minutes to work through.  Of the puzzles that are nontrivial, about half of them require guessing or trial-and-error to find what esoteric solution the designer thought would be really difficult to figure out (it is and it's not fun).  The other half are the good ones where you can concoct a plan, have that plan mostly work or mostly fail, tweak things, and finally achieve your goal.  It winds up feeling more like "what did the developer expect me to do?" than "what can I figure out that will work?".
Overall, I'd say it's a solid 5/10.  If it was deterministic, I'd give it a 7/10.  A bit more of the fun puzzles would be an easy 9.

This tool turned out to be surprisingly useful to me. Some games have problems running at fullscreen (at least for me), but lack borderless window mode (Dark Souls 3 and Resident Evil 7 to name a couple), making this (or any other) external solution a must to play comfortably. It's a really simple program with no extra features at all, and that's exactly what I love about it - simple and easy to use, it just gets the job done. As automated as it gets - you add the certain app to the list and it runs fullscreen borderless (as long as this tool is running in the background).
One very useful trick not everyone knows about: V-sync is not needed if the game is in windowed mode. Let's take Batman Arkham Knight for example. It runs on stable 60 FPS on my hardware, but cuts to 30 FPS should you enable the V-sync. Without the image is heavily torn every few frames so that it's untolerable. Disabling the game and running it in windowed mode solved it 100%, running smoohly at 60 FPS. And that's where this little tool shines: it lets you run windowed games fullscreen with no drawbacks, literally eliminating the need for V-sync and thus saving a lot on performance.
It surprises me, just how much difference such simple app can make. Definitely a must-have for me for a while now.

At the time of writing this review I only have 2.5 hours on record. AND, I don't normally write reviews. However, I was so impressed with Exanima that I felt compelled to write something.
Wow. This is the most fascinating dungeon crawler I've ever encountered. And how they dev'd the physics such that processing isn't so completely overwhelmed is impressive. You can even drop a torch between the legs of a chair and watch is stand up!
The combat makes you think on your feet, instead of mashing buttons. You think through every interaction and actually grow a personal bond, if you will, with, not only your own character, but others you encounter. Tip #1: Don't attack everyone you see! NPCs remember your mercy later and leave you alone. I'm still early in the game so I'm looking forward to other benefits of leaving them alone.
Tip #2: Read the manual! Press the esc key, and read the friggin manual! You'll thank me later!
This is NOT your typical hack and slash crawler. This is physics extraordinare, combat physics like nothing you've ever thought of, and, while it takes a bit of practice to get it down, it's so satisfying when you win your first fight you'll fight the urge to jump out of your seat and cheer like a girl! And while on that note, you'll lose your fights, you'll lose many fights! The key is, don't fight! if you can avoid it.
I bought this as early access as I like the larger project they're working on. There's a go fund me for the larger "Sui Generis" that looks absolutely fantastic. And if this crawler is just a taste of what they're working on, I can't imagine it with a story line and mission and.. and...
Ten thumbs up, and counting!

Fast, blue, stylish and clean. Ikaruga's wilder, more futuristic cousin I think. That's a good place to start when discussing RE:ACTOR. From Cross Eaglet, this bullet hell shmup takes a simple premise and adds a unique mechanic, instead of polarity, you're dealing with rotation. The field of play can be rotated along a 360 degree axis around your ship. In effect, you're flying through a "cylinder" as opposed to a flat playfield as is often the case, with enemies swirling all around you, and the landscape forming a three dimensional tube that often branches and splits, with numerous junctions appearing that will allow you to choose your route (this offers -immense- replayability as you high score hunt or figure out new routes through various stages).
As you rotate the field of view, the bullets also rotate, so a near impossible field to navigate suddenly becomes a flat line that's easy to dodge, and all of a sudden the game forces you to think in three dimensions, with objects often coming at you from "depth" as well as from the top, sides, front and back. It would be a bit easy to lose track were it not for the utterly gorgeous aesthetic which keeps things simple and easy to keep track of. Everything is presented in a washed out, futuristic neon blue, clean lines and clear presentation keep the game running at a flawless 60fps no matter what you're doing, with everything maxed out on my rig the game looks nothing short of artistic (Oh god please let there be an occulus rift option down the line).
As is the norm for such japanese bullet hell games, the music is energetic, electronic and upbeat, it maintains a strong pace and a good sense of place, but isn't exactly going to reach the heady heights that Ikaruga managed (but then nothing is ever going to manage the soundscape of Ikaruga, let's be fair). It's good enough though, as is the sound effects, which do the job with satisfying explosions and gun noises, everything sounds correct, which is really all that needs to be said. You don't buy these games for the sound, but it's good to see that Cross Eaglet got everything lined up and the sound presentation is clearly up to spec.
What makes this game stand out is the rotational mechanic, which is nothing short of inspired, it imposes a learning curve, and with an Xbox or PS pad, you'll be wise to map it to the shoulder buttons, but after half an hour of getting used to it, you'll be swooping back and forth like a pro, and the game opens up, once you make it past the opening stage, you'll then find junctions everywhere, and you'll be able to navigate through a gorgeous cityscape.
It's hard, as any good bullet hell should be, but it's worth every second of your attention, offering visual and gameplay delights as you duck and weave your way through a constant barrage of firepower. Each boss makes full use of the rotation mechanic too, forcing you to quickly improvise and adjust to the constant incoming flak that they toss your way, and within a few goes, rotating will be second nature, you may even look at other bullet hells and feel a little... lacking... when you try to change perspective and find you can't.
At this price, it's an absolute steal as well, for what you are paying for, you're getting one of the best experiences since Ikaruga, if you're a fan of the shmup genre, this is an easy sell, if you're new to the genre, getting this and Ikaruga should be high on your priority list. Both of these games are well worth your attention.

Greetings as always!  So, I have a guilty pleasure and that is these ‘creeper’ games and today I’m reviewing Creeper World 3:  Arc Eternal.  If any of you have been following my reviews you may find this odd as it is an older game from my first experience of this series:  Particle Fleet (made by the same developer) but the honest reason is I didn’t know this game type even existed until Particle Fleet and I still wasn’t sold that this wasn’t a one hit wonder so I cautiously bought the game you see now.
I’m doing what:  This game is an odd mesh of genre’s:  Part tower defense, part base builder but all real time strategy when it comes down to it.  However, you aren’t going to see many controllable units (aside from fighters / bombers) and even those you really aren’t micro-managing as they are told to strike an area and generally left alone (nothing in the game can actually damage them).  Your first encounter with this may leave you with a “That’s it?” kind of thought but as you keep playing you will find the complexity comes from the buildings themselves and not the core game (as all great strategy games have).
Loud Noises:   Like the later game of the genre (the above Particle Fleet) the music is very good, though I do tend to turn it off after several hours of playing it.  My friends have an overwhelming annoyance with the cannon sounds…not sure why.  To be fair, the gun sounds can be obnoxious from an onlooker’s perspective.  I just don’t mind all that much as I’m usually listening to something else.  In addition the graphics are very simple; but I’m glad they are as the game is about the gameplay not the graphics or particle effects or really even the sounds (though, again, the music is really good).
Multitasking:  One of the amazing things about this game is the ‘casual’ nature of the gameplay itself with the possibility of improvement to a competitive level.  That sounded a bit word-salad but what I mean is the game isn’t really ‘hard’ but more of a challenge that can be relaxing like a brain teaser and I found myself using this game as a wind down at the end of a night or after work along with watching a movie or podcast; nothing too intense.  Now, if you are trying for the leader boards then get ready to white knuckle because there is some serious optimization to be had.  In the end, however, I am happy with my slow paced game for the purpose I’ve set for it.
Overall, I make no qualms in that this game is a guilty pleasure of mine.  This game is not for everyone; it can be a bit slow paced (or fast depending on you).  I’d earnestly recommend that everyone gives this a try, especially if you are a management, strategy or puzzle fan.  I also have to mention that there appears to be a near endless amount of content.  I actually forced myself to uninstall this game as I was playing it instead of moving on to other games in my library.  At worse, wait for a sale as the game does get pretty cheap during those.  As always, regardless of your decision I hope you enjoy your gaming!
