Old Man’s Journey feels like a kids book that was made for adults.
Before we start I just want to get this off my chest.
Alluring, appealing, charming, cute, dazzling, delicate, delightful, elegant, exquisite, fascinating, fine, good-looking, gorgeous, graceful, grand, handsome, lovely, magnificent, marvelous, pleasing, pretty, splendid, stunning, superb, wonderful, admirable, angelic, beauteous, bewitching, classy, comely, divine, enticing, excellent, fair, foxy, ideal, nice, pulchritudinous, radiant, ravishing, refined, resplendent, shapely, sightly, statuesque, sublime, symmetrical, taking. — There that’s every synonym for beautiful and how I feel about Old Man’s Journey’s art. Yes, I even learned a new word pulchritudinous; go google that one.
Why go to all that trouble in listing those words? Well, Old’s Man Journey is definitely a game that falls into the category of gamer art. This is a short bite-sized sweet experience that you will enjoy wrapped up in your blankets while sipping hot chocolate.  This isn’t as robust as other ‘GameArt’ titles such as “Everything” or deeply engrossing like “Journey”. Old Man’s Journey is pleasant, simply put. It does exactly what it needs to, in the correct amount, and never hits a snag. This game is made extremely well and I can’t recommend this game enough.
I have seen a recent surge in these types of games and I hope it continues and flourishes. If you enjoyed Burly Men at Sea, then this is right up your alley. Old Man’s Journey is a storybook that you get to play with, gasp at its superb art and probably cry a little. One thing of note though is that while the games tone is delightful, it may raise some trigger flags for younger kids. Especially those without fathers, so take that as you will.
At its core Old Man’s Journey is a story but it also has to be a game too right?
Just like everything else about this title, the game mechanics are short and sweet. You play the old man on his journey. Duh. While on his journey though, you will help him along as he traverses terrain. Formerly a Navy man, he picks up his stick and bag and starts hot footing it across hills, cities, plains, you name it.
Where you as the player come in is adjusting how the terrain is laid out, literally. You can pull and push hills, roads, and tracks around so that they line up. This is purely done with your mouse as there is no controller support. Then the old man just simply hops to the next layer to get where he needs to go. At first it feels a little odd watching the old man sink farther into the background or move closer but you eventually get a zen going and you hardly notice. The puzzle aspect is simple but the developer adds a little more complexity as you go. Hills become two sided, old stone walls begin to block your path and waterfalls must be managed.
Rest assured though nothing is really that hard. It’s more of relaxing experience then any kind of a puzzle game. You are going to make progress no matter what usually and there is no game over. Now this is the only ‘game’ aspect to Old Man’s Journey and I am completely okay with this. The rest of the game more then makes up for it with its (looks at list) DAZZLING art and soundtrack. There are moments when the game mechanics shine and make me smile. When you board a train and have to quickly begin lining up the tracks ahead was fun and challenging to keep up with.
As you complete sections of the game you are rewarded with a memory and this is where the art kicks into breathtaking detail and the story unfolds.
Did I mention the art was (looks at list) angelic?
While I am sure you are growing tired of me mentioning the art, the details, the use of color in playful ways never ceased to amaze me. The art itself does tell its own story on top of the actual story. There was an anime that I watched long time ago called Robot Carnival. The anime displayed a broad range of stories, art styles and themes. Old Man’s Journey captured for me those same feelings. At the start you feel wondrous and adventurous, then there are times you will feel sad and lonely. This never stops you from admiring the storm and scenery even in the bleakest of moments. That speaks to how well controlled the tone is in Old Man’s Journey.
Then Old Man’s Journey will shift its tone and the storm clears and you are seeing a whale jump out of the water. These moments, while small, have a huge impact. They did for me anyway.
Usually now is when I would start talking about story. I am not going to do that. This is a title that is best enjoyed on your own. What I will say is, Old Man’s Journey does deal with some rather serious topics. Even if it approaches those in a family friendly and delightful way. There are times this feels odd. The entire aesthetic feels very warm and friendly but there are times where as they say, “s**t gets real.”
To balance, control, and support that tone we have the music and everything else.
The soundtrack for Old Man’s Journey is as playful as its art style. There are many styles of music that were incorporated into the game. While it is all instrumental, that doesn’t stop the game from exploring music as much as you are exploring the world in your journey. Visiting an exotic village location usually has some really fun beats to match. There is as much attention paid to the music as the rest of the game.
The sound effects are expertly crafted to coordinate with the games sound effects. I could listen to the sea crashing against the cliffs for hours. Thunderstorms feel even more powerful with the soundtrack coming behind it. It’s something you will hardly notice but that’s because the developer weaved it together so well.
You can currently purchase the soundtrack on Steam and if you enjoy instrumental music, you won’t be disappointed.
There are very few issues I could find with Old Man’s Journey.
The game does what exactly what it set out to do. That said, there are areas that the game will come up short because of what it is. For one, the game does have a heavy App like feeling. You can tell that this game is on multiple mobile devices. This is abundantly obvious from the menus and how you navigate the game. While this didn’t particularly bother me, it might be irksome to others.
Old Man’s Journey is a short adventure, topping out for me at a total of two hours game time. You could stretch that in either direction but its not going to stray too far. Like I said earlier, it’s a short but sweet game. Replay value is also going to be questionable at best. You may enjoy playing this title over and over again for its relaxing nature, but just keep in mind what it is. A lovely little story.
Currently there are Steam cards but no achievements and I don’t really expect there to be any. It just doesn’t seem like it would fit for this type of game. That can change of course.
We have come to the end of our own journey.
I had an amazing time with Old Man’s Journey. It was fun, unique, sad, and wonderful all at the same time. For that alone it deserves your attention, as its hard to capture all that in one experience. It may not be reinventing the wheel as far as the game industry goes, but its perfect for what it is. I personally want more titles like Old Man’s Journey. These experiences are akin to books, in that they let you escape the ordinary world, giving you access to explore art, music, and emotions. If that isn’t what gaming is all about, then I don’t know what is. The cherry on top is that you can get Old Man’s Journey for relatively low price.
If you are looking for something that you can relax, enjoy, and surrender to on a emotional and visual level, then look no further than Old Man’s Journey.

Picked up this game tonight on sale for just under $7. I played for 5 hours and completed it. I couldn't put it down! There were 2 maybe 3 areas where I wasn't sure where to go and it took me a bit of running around to figure it out. (hint: In the volcanic area, look in every direction and make sure you've gone down every path... you'll get out eventually).
All in all, this game was well worth the sale price I paid (probably not so much the regular price due to only being 5 hours (for me anyway) to complete. But definitely glad I bought it. Replay value is probably nil since once you've completed it and know the story, it won't interest you to go through it again - not immediately anyway.
I'd give this 4 out of 5 stars. Grab it now if it's still on sale. It's worth the few bucks to kill 5 hours. :)

I'm not going to question why you're looking at reviews for a 0.99 game. But this should be one of the last ones you read. After this paragraph or so of text, you're going to scroll upwards, buy this game, and enjoy your life.
Just do it.
KNIGHTS is a game about, you guessed it, moving knight pieces on little checkered puzzle boards. Do you need to know jack about chess? Not really, but it helps if you've played a few casual games, just so you're familiar with a Knight's moves, since it's definitely the least intuitive of the pieces. But, even if you've never played a game of chess in your life, this game indicates quite clearly which spaces you can and can't move to.
KNIGHTS takes the mechanics of moving a knight chess piece, and builds a fantastic little puzzler around it. Your task is to move knights to certain preallocated positions, which gradually becomes more and more complex as your chessboard shrinks, and the number of pieces increases. You can do this by just brute-force clicking at everything you can until it works, which is only viable for the earlier puzzles, or carefully try to map out how you want things to look like X moves from now, and work backwards. At the point I'm at, about 2 hours in, I'd go crazy if I even attempted to brute-force these monsters...
The game also apparently has dailies, which I haven't looked at too much so far. These might have varying difficulties day to day (the was Duet does it), or  just a set difficulty. I'll update this review on my thoughts on dailies once I give them a look. At a glance, though, just that should be enough to add a good number of hours to your time with this game.
Really, it's just a fun and cue little puzzle game for a dollar. Literally a buck.  Just skip on your next coffee flavor/espresso-shot, and you'll be good to go.

Knights is a simple relaxing puzzler based on the classic movement of the Knight chess piece. Designated pieces must be moved about the board methodically to their matching colored spaces. There are several puzzle packs which ramp up in size and difficulty, as well as the ability to unlock daily procedurally generated levels as you progress through the game. The puzzles are all logically solvable, and in the King pack in particular, random movements to attempt a solve will generally not yield the desired fruit. As the game is based upon a single concept I found it easier to play in short bursts, rather than try to solve 100+ similar puzzles one after another. My only complaint is that of a sore neck as I found myself inadvertantly angling my head 45 degrees to give a more traditional perspective of the puzzle board.
It's cheap. It's fun. The end.

As the name suggests, this is a classic "moving pieces" puzzle game. The base mechanic is incredibly simple and easy to pick up. But make no mistake - this is not a casual puzzle game where you can mindlessly brute-force yourself to victory - the chess-style movement means you can easily find yourself trapped in a loop. Once you've gotten over the initial confusion, patterns start to emerge. With a little planning, careful thought and clever management of your empty spaces you'll still find success rather easily.
The 82 pre-made levels are pretty much an optimal length. They provide a nice progression and never really feel boring. The game also features an endless mode in the form of randomly generated daily levels (75 of them each day), although I wasn't blown away by them. Even though they variy widly in difficulty, they feel very samey and tiresome as they are always on 5x5 grids and have 2 or 3 spaces empty. I would have liked customisation for difficulty, grid size and difficulty (empty tiles). But this is a very minor gripe as the price-tag leaves nothing to be desired. You get a
of bang for your buck, even at full retail price. My playtime of 7-8 hours includes beating the game, around 30 daily levels and getting all the achievements.
The game is technically solid. It has a pleasant and consistent style in terms of visuals and sound, sometimes even a little too much style. The initial load time feels long and the fade-out upon closing the game is pretty annoying. I would have also liked to see a separate volume control for sound effects and music and at least "Escape" bound as a keyboard shortcut (there are none).
I like puzzle games and Steam has been recommending this to me for a while. I'm not much of a chess player so I never really put a lot of thought into it. Even though it is somewhat of a one-trick pony, I was very pleasantly surprised and can wholeheartedly recommend this game, even at full price!

One of the greatest arcade baseball games I've played. It's like Backyard Baseball but much more difficult and in depth, and it has a ton of replayability due to its varying skill levels and high skill ceiling in general. Best Baseball game ever!
This game presents the mechanics,strategies, details, stats, and game play experience of Real Baseball, but in a graphic style that is cartoonish in the best ways - big heads, huge jaws, overdone gestures, great fan animations - and fast, deep, and fun to play. Almost all aspects of the game are presented here in delightfully entertaining details, from a pitcher throwing so hard, he closes his eyes on release, to a glove-pump before throwing the batter out at first.
You have two modes, exhibition and season, each customizable; there are three season lengths, a dozen teams to choose from, and a fully remappable selection of detailed controls; yet, you can play the entire game with just the mouse.
The gameplay is smooth, the animations are believable and reflect excellent baseball motions and actions.
The pitches are easily selected either with middle mouse button or from a clickable grid, or keyboard. Batting is as simple as a click at the precise moment, or take a chance on a power swing, which has a limited-time hold-down effect to improve power, but you better make good contact!
You have a full pitching rotation. You have a bench of subs, and every player is rated in two positions.
Once you select your team, you can customize them in incredible detail, change the uniforms, but the most impressive addition is the staff; you can hire coaches, trainers, gear-suppliers, etc. Each one has multiple factors to consider, each is different, and all add skills to specific players, up to three per staff member. It will make all the difference in a penant run - you must use the staff to your best advantage.
Personally I made a bad choice when I installed, adjusting the base-selection sensitivity (set too low) and I couldn't throw properly from the field; even with this handicap, by batting the way real teams do - forcing the pitcher to throw strikes, going to the full count, etc., and by pitching with both variety of type and position, I was able to win championships. Then, thanks to the great tech support, a correction to my settings brought the full game back into my reach, and allowed me to increase a fully adjustable difficulty level (change it at any time) of my own liking.
Double plays, triple plays, throwing out steals, leaping catches, and diving saves are all part of a fantastic in-game experience.
Hands down, the BEST SPORTS GAME I HAVE EVER PLAYED.    THIS IS A MUST-HAVE!
Addendum:
This game is really much, much deeper than a simple arcade sports game; I missed that aspect the first times around. The STAFF function turns this game into a deep, strategic, and flexible baseball management experience. Without going into details, there's a lot of fun to had and results to be enjoyed from carefully and lovingly assigning the right staff to the right players, and the displays make it easy. When you have great players sitting on the bench, and you start rotating and developing your players, it is more fun than ever.
Finally, you can modify default teams into more interesting and different looking and differently named teams that you have personalized; then setting up a season, you can toggle on the newly modified team in place of its default. Very cool.
This game continues to impress!

There's a good mix of good and bad elements in this management simulator, and it can be entertaining.  There are some specific programming choices that just ruin the simulation for me which is primarily the routines/math used to determine mission success or failure. For example, if you have a mission package researched to 95% and save that mission before a launch which then fails, then no matter how many times you reload (even several turns back) and redo the mission, it will always fail.  So in my experience random factor is basically zero, you're just clicking buttons in a pre-determined outcome that changes with each new simulation.  It's for this one reason I find myself giving this a thumb's down, otherwise I've enjoyed the mechanics and strategies involved with this management sim.

At a $30 price tag I cant recommend this game.
TLDR: The game is short (5 hours for me) , the puzzles are very boring (Most can be solved by simple first order thinking, and there are no failure states if you get a puzzle wrong), and only real saving grace is that it looks and sounds nice,
Ill start with the good things that i did like,
Firstly, the game is very very pretty, the colour palate is varied and vibrant, the characters are 3d moddeled and look well designed onto what seem to be a mix of 2D and 3D enviroments, the music fits and sounds amazing, even if some of the tracks are just the theme from the Whispered World, and the voice actors performances were good, although get somewhat grating after a while as they dont like shifting off of one or two emotions through the whole game, especially with Renie and Noah, who have the most lines in the game.
And for the things I didnt like.
Without looking up a guide, I beat the game in 5 hours. Most of that time was spent waiting for animations to play out instead of thinking about the game. Most puzzles will require you to use Item A, on item A. There is no inventory system and items will be used regardless of whether or not you know you should use them there. Occasionally there will be a slightly harder puzzle such as listening to a short riddle, and turning symbols to match the riddle, or tuning instuments, but those are still brutally simple. Comparitivly, in the whispered world, which ill admit i havent completed there are a few great puzzles, such as "To get item required, close the door after walking in to reveal it" or "Change the time on the clock to match a thing you had on a list since the beginning of the game, after realising that the riddle meant a certain item on that list". There are 2 bad puzzles in PnC games which are A. Diversions that dont require much on the player or B. Guide dangit puzzles which are ones that are rooted in moon logic and cant really figure out. This game has plenty of A.
Secondly, the story and writing seem to fall flat. The best example of this is the ending. Otherwise this seems to be filled with some lines that feel just, off for some of the characters to do. There is swearing from some of these people, which have been living in a magical fairy land all their lives.
MAJOR SPOILER, if it wasnt obvious.
The ending of the game, is that it was all a dream.
Thats right.
You are given the choice to continue the dream, or to wake up.
This cliche is by far one of the worst ways to end a story. And it is somewhat justified in the story but its still, as a friend of mine said after I told him this "A giant middle finger to you for playing the game" because, everything that you have done to that point was ultimatly POINTLESS. Only one character really grows over time, being Noah, who changes from someone who wants to be a hero, to an absolutely selfish jackass because he's a sad clown now, and you are going to like it, and finally a somewhat redeemable jackass.
I could handwave all of this as a "Its meant for kids" and it would be a great game for kids, but the writing tells me its not necessarilly for them, as the forementioned swearing and the game features strong themes such as rebellion, war, death, loss, not necessarilly meant for them. I very much doubt a child young enough to have the puzzles as easy as they were, would understand and grasp the concept of air raids.
Again, at its price point, for a 5 hour adventure I cant really recommend it.
I would say your money is better spent picking up its prequel, the Whispered World, which it itself has some probelms, but it is a much much better adventure game than this, and fills the craving for a fantasy adventure game very well.

Wow! What a fantastic game! I absolutely loved this game for the idea of the game and how well it was executed. I've got a lot more to say about it, but I'll run through a list of the pros and cons of the game first.
Pros:
- Low Price
For only 1 dollar off sale and even less when it’s on sale, this game is quite worth it! Imo it could be a little bit more on the shop and I still would have bought it!
- Fantastic Idea
I've loved the puzzles that deal with the knight piece from Chess for the longest time, but the idea of putting a bunch of them on a chessboard and then working puzzles around them was also awesome. It was especially rewarding that one of the achievements led to you thinking a little bit outside the box on a certain level as well.
- Infinite replaying
Even though I'm not really sure how it works, it seems that there are 75 new puzzles generated for the game for each different day! I didn't play through a whole bunch of them but I did notice the changes between the different days, and (bonus!) the puzzles are still quite challenging.
- Colorblind mode
I feel that a lot of games of this type don't give too much thought to the colorblind players of the game, but I really enjoy that this dev took the time to make a separate colour palette so that everyone could enjoy the game.
Cons:
- Lack of "saving"
The only real problem that I had with this game is that there wasn't any way to save the progress that you made with a given level. It was a little bit annoying knowing that if you started a level you were stuck there and had to finish it up before you could step away again (otherwise you'd lose all progress).
Overall, I'd say the execution, idea, and time that were put into making this game make it a fantastic buy and the low price makes it that much better in the end. If you can get it on sale, that's cool but it's worth it even if it isn't! Overall, a solid 9.5/10 and like I said if there was "save mechanic" this game would have gotten a 10/10 from me!

This Review has to deal with two seperate questions. First: Is Deus Ex a good game? And second: Is Revision a good mod?
Question No. 1 is easily answered. Yes, Deus Ex was and still is the best game of all times. Even more than 15 years after release it provides a much more sophisticated gaming experience than it's sequels or the majority of action games - let alone shooters - around. The amazing level design invites and rewards exploration. The game is hard to learn but incredibly fun to master. The setting, characters and story are fascinating and extremly well told. And, first of all, the degree of freedom the player has in it is absolutely unmatched. Yes I'm a fan, but for good reason.
The second question is more difficult to answer. All in all, Revision is well done. Graphics are tuned up. The Levels have been overhauled and a few nice details added. But this is simply not enough to merit a recommendation because I expected much more. Most of the game is still the same and in some respects like music or atmosphere Revision even takes some steps back. I have a feeling that the modders were not really sure what they were doing and just couldn't live up to the task of remaking such a classic. It is one thing to put in a few new models and textures - and this is fine. But expanding and improving Ion Storm's work is a task, which exceeded the skills of the team. If you look at outstanding mods like Black Mesa, you can see how a classic from 10+ years ago can be successfully hoisted into the present. But this takes a lot of aptitude and time. Maybe remaking Deus Ex is just too much a venture for a non-commercial title.
So, if you want to play DX again or, for some inexplicable reason, haven't done so yet. Get the original.

Deus Ex Revision is a quite impressive, albeit not perfect, mod that is worth your time. Okay, so literally just finished playing through the game an hour ago. I’ve played the original around 4 times before and playing it through Revision will be my 5th. It offers a new and fresh experience for veterans of the game to enjoy while updating its game to be more accessible to first time players. Let me break it down using their own description. Single-player only.
-New environments-
A lot has been reworked and crafted to make old environments seems foreign. New York gets a face lift to appear more modern, Paris feels like you’re exploring a city rather than some alleys, Unatco headquarters feels like an actual headquarters with every agent having their own office instead of Gunther getting some corner of a hall like in the original. Most major areas are heavily revamped and ignite my sense of exploration again. I found myself looking around every corner, exploring every room, and being surprised to find come handy loot. But while great, this modernization creates its own issues. For one, now that New York and Paris feel more up to date, both in architecture and size, they end up feeling a bit barren. The levels were smaller before and when you expand them out, or at least give the feeling that they are expanded out, you have more to fill with the same content. They try to mitigate this, at least in my experience, with NPC's that just stand there with no dialogue to offer (or they should be talking but glitches) and computer terminal in added rooms that have nothing on them. Another issue is the expanded locked houses and buildings that end up having nothing interesting to find, expect for a plethora of candy bars and soda. Countless times through the game did I come across an inaccessible door I broke into only to find it not worth the two lock picks I wasted to get in there. More often than not, the new buildings added to bring the architecture of the level up-to-date can be ignored. Having sad that, Paris subway now feels like a subway, Hong Kong and Paris clubs don’t look like crap anymore. Most of the smaller areas look so much better. There are definitely issues you'll identify while playing the game but the fact that I can enter a level and not be sure which way to go; giving me a chance to explore this game as I did the first time I played it more than makes up for it.
-New music-
The new music is hit-and-miss. They changed pretty much every song you encounter in every level; from the calm explorative moments, to the action queued moments. Some are pretty good that I prefer it to the original, others are not as good. Thankfully they have an option to revert to the original soundtrack. I found myself switching back and forth to see which I liked better. I did run into one music glitch when entering the Lucky Money in Hong Kong; the music just didn’t play, yet the original club music would. Still, it’s a great effort to put it in and it does for the most part blend well with the style of its original. A for effort, A+ for giving us the option to switch back.
-New world-building detail-
This gets all the praise I can offer. Building signs are clear, the colors are new and interesting. Computer terminals are great, even with the copy and flipped, over-sized keyboard. New areas are decorated to make sense. Unatco has a more appealing color scheme, the design of certain doors makes more sense. They have story-driven changes, such as a certain character's office being cleared out when they are no longer part of Unatco and gameplay-driven changes such as lock/unlocked/powered on changes with lights and text that let you know that whatever you just did or went through did something right here. Random computer screens, both large and small, are amazing. Most notably, the ocean labs. Holy crap did the Ocean labs look amazing. Darker, more interesting lighting, floating e-mail screens, alert screens you can read that help bring out the atmosphere of this dead laboratory. Dynamic changes with broken down doors, added effects, even a voice that repeats a system warning through a part of the level bring this once dull area to life! They even had buttons and switches on certain newly created screens which surprised me. I really wish they did that throughout the entire game, but I only found it here. They gave the overall game a lot of love, but they gave the Ocean Labs A LOT of love. I found Area 51 just as pleasing to the eye as well. It felt like a mission was just here. One complaint I’ve heard was how much darker this game is to the original. While I did find myself using my flashlight more often, it felt appropriately used, like it should have been this dark in this certain area in the original. The signs, the advertisement in cities, citiy lights, new decorations, clearly readable text, I love it all.
-Bundling of the best modifications that the fan base has made over the years, including Direct3D 9 rendering, high-resolution textures, high-detail 3D-
They use a HD version of a lot of textures here. That game looks much better that it did in its heyday, but the weapons and items don’t look too different. The stealth pistol doesn’t reload correctly in the characters hand (You can’t see the clip exit the gun) and the stun prod isn’t as cool as the original. The items and weapons are good, but I feel like I’ve seen better mods that do them better. Luckily though, they didn’t go with that retextured version of JC. I always hated that one. But I do love those shiny floors!
When it’s said and done, this mod gives players something new to enjoy. It breathes new life into a game I love and it is immediately clear the team that created the mod loves it too. I searched rooms as if for the first time. I've explored areas I’ve never seen before or looked completely foreign to me. I’ve read screens that weren’t originally there that gave me information I never knew I wanted to know. It gave me something I never thought I would ever get in Deus ex again; another chance to play it for the first time. Download it. Enjoy it. Love it. It isn’t perfect. It does have issues. But this is the absolute best we could ever hope to get from a source that wasn’t the original publisher.

An unfortunate case of a game's quality not living up to its potential. The potential I see for a game like this lies in its story and atmosphere, but neither manage to impress all that much.
The story is minimal, or at least stretched thin enough to seem minimal, and has the foundation of something compelling. Unfortunately, most attempts to heighten the plot's mystique fall flat in the earlier sections of the game. Really only during the last quarter or so do things become intersting, but by that stage I'd already lowered my expectations for overall narrative quality.
Secondly, and arguably more importantly, everything about the game screams that it is an absorbing atmospheric experience. The title itself is a statement of setting, game environments are left wide and sweepingly open, and the camera typically soars right over the player to focus on the vistas surrounding them. The problem is that these environments and vistas really aren't visually impressive. From the barren, stretched textures of the distant hills to the matte, ill-defined features of human characters, the graphical fidelity here is on par with something out of the PS2 era. I was honestly a little shocked to learn this was a 2014 release after being so thoroughly underwhelmed by the visuals.
Despite these gripes, it's not like the game is aggressively bad. There are good moments of contemplative silence and solitude, and many of the puzzles and progression bits are logically well thought-out.  In this way, I think this game feels more like a proof of concept in the state it's currently in. It feels half finished; technically functional but not polished at all. I can't recommend it for the $20 price tag, but it is at least worth playing through once if you can grab it on sale.

and it's ispiration,
. The mods are really both the same, however Biomod focuses on fixing and improving the broken/stupid parts of Shifter. You can choose between either, or none of them at all. I'm writing a negative review not because I didn't enjoy the game, I really did, but I want to highlight my criticisms and feel this is the best way to go about it.
Cons:
-The enemy is non-reactive, having no ai of its own.
Now, this IS NOT a bad thing, but it creates problems when coupled with other design decisions.
-Every level, is winable. This means that, once you know what's going on, if you can build a stable base in the beginning, you have already won the map. Victory is inevitable so long as you dont over-extend yourself. This KILLS any real thought of strategy once new elements stop being introduced or combined in new ways.
-The real question is how QUICKLY you can win, which means the only true challenge you'll face is when a level has a time limit of some kind or has a component within it that requires fast progression.
This ALSO isn't necessarily a bad thing. There's a sort of catharsis to this game's war of attrition, even if the deck is decidedly stacked in your favor
-The game DOES have scripted sequences where unexpected changes occur, changing the map and, likely, ruining your immediate plans and requiring a new strategy. But they arent used to their fullest potential and rarely occur if at all.
What I was looking for:
This game is very good for what it is. (it is the THIRD game in a series of similar games after all. Lots of refining has happened). That said, once its novelty passed for me, I just couldnt stay interested, even WITH user generated contet.
-Once I realized that victory is basically inevitable in ANY situation without a timer and learned how to deal with any situation a map could throw at me, I lost interest.
-What I REALLY want from this game, that it CANNOT deliver on due to its own systems and design, is a war of attrition decidedly in the enemy's favor. Where DEFEAT is inevitable, but preventable and the only question is how long you can survive.
-The strategies you have at your disposal are not varied enough to make this kind of play truly interesting. The game is set up so that, outside of timing and basic idea, you are constantly just improving on your initial strategy adding more and more units as you build your base.
--Initial decisions have virtually NO bearing on later strategies. Outside of success or failure, the strategy you start with has no bearing on whether you'll be successful in later parts of the level. I would have LOVED a "path less traveled" sort of design where one decision means you CAN'T have somthing else down the road.
So ya, it's a good game, worth the buy, but it didn't really scratch the particular itch I had.

This is a fun and charming game about the race into space.  The equipment is all historical, and the race between the US and USSR is compelling, on both sides.  Replayability comes from having completely different hardware between the two nations, plus multiple pathways forward as you plan your missions and milestones on the road to prestige (and funding!)  Even the low-budget graphics match the style of the day, which I found nostalgic.  There are a couple of detailed guides on steam for when you are ready to kick up the difficulty and maximize your efficiency on the path to the moon.
I think it is great for kids, with two qualifications.  The first is that astronauts will die: the RNG is merciless.  This will not be fun.  So start out on the normal difficulty, and take yout time building up equipment reliability, rather than racing the clock the first time out.  Secondly, there is a strong spreadsheet element to the game: each mission has percentage chances of success based on equipment and skills that are also rated by percentage.  This is a little bare, since each turn boils down to a handful of numbers.  Not bad, just not terribly engaging.
I would honestly like to see the game extended to programs past the 70s; the fundamental structure would still work.  And the game engine isn't demanding, so I could see this as an indy-level goal.
Good luck!

Choppa is an amusing little helicopter rescue game that plays a bit like Choplifter, but with bigger explosions and psychotic seagulls.

You start of with the basic choppa. Playing the game rewards you with coins that you can use to upgrade your "bird" with better tougher chassis, more powerful engine, and taller ladder.
Level 1 starts and the handling is like 'mmeh, could be better' as the choppa responds to keyboard controls a bit slowly. The first couple of levels are just a piece of cake but then it gets a bit trickier. The rescuee may be standing in between to vertical cones and the ladder on your choppa is too short, and that darn seagull is on to get you. As it leaps onto the blades your dear choppa is going down in one black piece of charcoal! And you had just figured out how to swing the short ladder to the person!
Fortunately you can use your hard earned coins to opt in a replay of the level where the turmoil that darn bird caused is still visible. This is an interesting game mechanic as the levels are randomly generated but if you waste your choppa to clear out an easier fly patch that is blocked by, say, explosive barrels, you may replay the level and get more easy access to the rescuee.
And once you've earled enough coins and you always seem to crash land at level 5, then that is the time when you remember the upgrades. The coins you earn and collect from rescues and and random coin boxes are good for an extension for the ladder. And maybe you also want to spend some on that engine, too, and some shields so you can fend off those haunting seagulls. Off you go! Oh, how smooth the ride is now! You may want to update that feeling of 'mmeh' to 'oh, cool!' at least once you reach max engine level 'cos that is when the game really begins to feel fun! It shouldn't take more than 30-45 minutes to reach that level so no heavy griding required.
The more you play, the more fun it gets. It is interesting to notice that at level 15 you will need to rescue two people on opposite sides of the map and the reward for the rescue of each is equalent to the amount of coins replay costs so you may want to make sure you get at least either one of them rescued before you end up sleeping with the fishes. That way should you crash and burn, the (replay) fun never ends! =P

I like it. It has a nice lonely, tense atmosphere that can catch you off guard and spook you when a person comes out from the dark a golem wakes up and cheses you, or when you open a door and someone comes out swinging. There's not much of an actual tutorial, which is mostly fine since you get the hang of the motions, but it would be better if it told you some things (I still don't know if I parry automatically or not or see any difference with that skill.)
The main drawback of the game is that it is so slow and tedious that if the combat and/or atmosphere don't do it for you, you'll be bored mindless. There's hints of lore, but not enough to understand what happened. The story is like if you took out all the dialogue and cutscenes out of a dark souls game: "you're a little sh*t nobody; git gud and go." There's no map, which means unless you have a good mental one or some paper and a pencil, you'll get lost. The graphics aren't bad, but the areas are so samey and bland looking. Don't expect much more than dark, cobblestone hallways in its current state.
Arena has some more unique areas, but that mode has problems too. It takes forever to win enough matches to get enough money to get better armor and weapons, and even if your character gets max level and great gear, you'll not want to use them since if they die, you lose all progress. Plus, you won't be able to partake in some matches since you'll need ally fighters. You'll have to hire fighters for a pretty penny and level them up over time hoping they don't die. I don't mind it too much since it adds to the realism for me, but it can be pretty tedious since the matches pay so little compared to what gear costs. I have yet to be in a Beast match because everyone dies before they git gud enough to help me. It's also tedious how you have to manage gear for every single level for you and your team. There should be an "apply to all applicable" button or something.
The combat is good, but has a few issues. Blocking is weird since you can do it with any weapon with roughly the same effectiveness. As long as you hit their weapon before hitting them, they won't get hurt. Your attacks lose all momentum on contact with their weapon or shield. Enemies probably shouldn't be able to so easily block all incoming damage from your warhammer swing with their rusty little cleaver. Often enough, the littlest swishes and pokes seem to do more damage than they ought to, and the heaviest swings and stabs that would kill an average person don't seem to do enough (more so the former than the latter.)
Even with those problems, I had fun with the game. A good fight can feel very satisfying and look pretty cool too if nothing dumb happens. Getting a clean blow that knocks down enemies never gets old. Exploring and making progress can be pretty satisfying, especially when you manage to find sweet loot. The physics can be fun to mess with like putting buckets on your and npcs heads, or running into a chair trying to trip, or accidentally tripping over a body while backing away from an angry man wielding a prosthetic leg.
If that sounds fun, you'll probably have a good time. But for others, you may want to be cautious because of how dull it can all get what with the samey areas, lack of enemy variety, lack of much music (which does well for the atmosphere), and the nuances of arena mode.
The game's still being worked on, so this stuff is subject to change to a degree, but this is what I think of it as it is now.

There isn't much to be said about this game that hasn't been said before. Many of the reviews here sum up the experience whilst playing Onikira. However, I do differ in opinion compared to some.
Firstly, I find the graphics dull and bland. There are a total of 3-4 enemy types in the first 3 levels (that's all I bothered playing), and the differences between the protagonist and the antagonists are minor colour wise. So, if you're coloured blind, then you're going to wonder where your character went to on the screen.
As for game play, you can get away with spamming the jump (A button) and slam (Y button) and beat most enemies that way. The levels are highly linear and employ a standard 80's game technique that should have been abandoned long ago. Every few seconds, as you run along, the game forces a pause by putting up two impenetrable barriers either side of you and drops enemies into the play field. You need to kill these before the barriers will disappear allowing you to progress for another few seconds.  As mentioned, this was routinely done in the 80's, mostly because earlier computers just weren't as powerful as they are today, so need an artificial way to stop the players progress, to limit the amount of things happening at once on the screen.  This is lazy gaming making nowadays and should be avoided.
Adding to that, the game is repetitive. You run, get stopped by these barriers, hack a bunch of enemies to dust, rinse and repeat over and over and over again.  There's the occasional  'run from the burning stuff' sequence, but these have all been done before, and usually done better.
Unlike a lot of people, I did not experience any crashes or lost game saves, however, I only played the game through one session and am highly unlikely to ever go back to it. The game just isn't enjoyable enough.
In the end, save your money or go buy something else. Unless you enjoy playing repetitive, graphically dull, linear hack and slash games with contrived and cliched stories.

I wish I could’ve played more of Onikira, but the game kept crashing on the first level when continuing my game. Looking at the forums, it’s a common thing with no fix in sight. What I did experience with the little time I had seemed promising, with one inexcusable fault.
Checkpoints don’t save your progress in the level! It saves your progress for the current level you’re on, so if you die, you go back to that checkpoint. However,
Why would you design something like this for game that was published in 2015? Even worse, is that there is no confirmation “y/n” for going back to the Main Menu. If you accidentally click it, boom…start the level over. There’s no warning message either about having to start the level over.
On the plus side, the combat seemed decent with room to grow as you’ll obtain a few more weapons and can buy additional moves with the in-game currency. It’s mostly a button masher but integrates combo moves as well. I wouldn’t say it’s very responsive like the store page states, however.
Graphics didn’t seem too sharp at 1440p, but were vibrant and colorful. No issues with the sound/music during my time playing but there are no voice-overs and I think it would have benefitted to have some type of speaking dialog in the game.
I noticed some of the menu options (like Fullscreen and VSYNC) wouldn’t activate with my 360 controller and I needed to click on them with the mouse.
+60fps
+Good visuals (although not sharp)
+Expandable combat system with combos
+Good tutorial in first level
+Game crashed when continuing on the first level. I can’t play it anymore
+Checkpoint system doesn’t save overall progress (see rant above)
+No voice-overs
+Load screen lags
While it has some promising attributes, steer clear of this game as it’s unstable. My final score reflects that.

TransPlan is a puzzle-simulator game with a fun 'doodle' appearance.
The game uses basic physics of gravity and collisions, and you are tasked with getting the blue item to the end position. While not particularly difficult, it does provide challenges by tasking you to complete levels 'under par'. This coupled with 'pins' lets you find very unique solutions to each puzzle. It's particularly rewarding when you manage to get the game to produce a result in a very small number of moves.
The music and appearance match the difficulty, being very light-hearted, and if you ever get stuck you can use 'hints' to show you where to get started on a level. I do feel as if the game provides a bit too much help though, as if you keep asking for more hints it will essentially solve the level for you.
Not particularly difficult, but fun nonetheless.

It's a fun mechanic, and sometimes a fun game, but there are things I really don't like about it. It feels too much like an amateurly produced indie game, even though really the game is solidly designed. Challenge has little to do with survival -- it's more like, if you screw up, you're going to spend another half an hour building something that actually works. And the mechanics of unlocked tech are often poorly explained, leading to exactly the kind of confusion that causes you to screw up. Since tech is unlocked in almost every mission, as far as I've played, the result is a somewhat frustrating experience. To be clear, I don't think this is the developer's fault -- the game is solidly put together, it's just that its mechanic tends to overwhelm and destroy when you make a mistake. I'd recommend it if you're looking for inspiration in your own game design projects -- but not so much if you just feel like playing it.

I bought this game knowing that it probably wouldn't be the most polished or sensical thing I had ever played, and I can enjoy simplistic, "clearly showing their budget" games, but even with those somewhat lowered expectations I have still come away thinking this is a poorly made mess. This game seems very imaginative and cool conceptually (a pirate, dreams, etc..) but its execution and implementation is horrible.
The best thing this game has going for it is its unique setting of creepy goblins versus a pirate dude in somewhat "dreamy" locales. Unfortunately, playing the game is a complete mess, with very little feedback or explanation to any of the combat or actions you take. Instead, you're just thrown into the opening levels with a ton of goblins swarming you, who constantly jump and flail around wildly swinging their clumsy attacks as you do the same, flailing your sword and just assuming that you're hitting them, aside from an obnoxious "bell-like" sound that triggers every now and again I suppose indicating that you're hitting them. There is a UI / comic-book looking "ARGH" that pops up over and over from you and the enemies, meant to indicate damage being done (I guess?) but it all just feels very sloppy, like most of the game.
There is very little structure to anything you're doing, and not in an abstract, charming, minimalistic way present in other games but instead it comes off shoddy and poorly put together. You aren't even told what to do beyond there being an Exit cave in one of the rooms of the level you need to eventually reach. For example, during one level with about 15 of the same generic looking goblins running around aimlessly, apparently I needed to defeat all of them in order for the Exit tunnel to be activated (despite it being visible) So I had to spend a few minutes swinging at and hoping to hit this higher health, different colored (but same model) goblin, flailing my attack against him until he eventually just disappeared, then I could go through the exit. The next level consisted of a very simplistic platforming area, but the character's jumping and landing handles so horribly it's like trying to navigate an icy surface everywhere, with your character landing and then drifting an extra 2 or 3 feet to fall off the ledge and force you to restart the sequence. The level after this involved a very basic looking sphere meant to be a boulder rolling back and forth down a tunnel which you would have to evade by hiding in a few alcoves, then reach the exit (EXCITINNNNNG) After this level it was another level strewn with goblins and some bland-looking 'traps' and my character became lodged in an overhanging log after jumping into it and couldnt get out, forcing me to quit, so I logged out of the game and am now writing this review.
There are signs scattered around the level that say things like "Secret Passage (Under Construction)" which is then just a boulder wall that clumsily retracts as you approach it. While I think this is a tongue-in-cheek acknowledgment from the creator(s) that it doesn't look great, at the same time it pisses me off to see this kind of blatant "HAHA our game kinda sucks, right???" self-awareness after you've spent your money to experience the title.
This game might open up a little if you get past these horrible opening levels but I don't feel like bothering to sift through garbage just to ~maybe~ get a morsel of enjoyment from some of the later settings.

This game puts you into a NASA program manager role -- this is less about running missions yourself but rather about making the hard decisions on how to accomplish the goal of landing on the moon.  Starting in 1955, you build your facilities and undergo the research to work your way up to greater and greater accomplishments.  It actually features a lot of the real decisions that had to be made back in those days at NASA -- there were different approaches to getting to the moon (direct ascent or lunar orbit rendezvous) and they all have trade-offs.  One recurring theme here is how willing you are to make risky decisions.  You can research your technology until its reliability is high enough but risk losing to the other side or you can gamble on it with the potential loss of money, prestige, and even the lives of experienced astronauts.
It is a fun game for some types and you will learn a decent amount of history behind the space race if you take a few moments to look at it and think.  That said, there are some downsides to this game.  After you have landed on the moon, there is really not a lot to do other than a few interplanetary probes.  These probes can take a long time to get there, which is entirely accurate but you may wind up just blowing through your turns if you are a completionist.  The probes are also a serious distraction if you are racing to the moon like the game wants you to.  It is a shame that the game doesn't engage in some additional missions after that -- for example, the last lunar landing had the announcement of the space shuttle, so why not add that?  Or perhaps, like in real life, add Skylab (which was the direct result of leftover Saturn-V rockets) or Mir and then the international space station.  The game hints at permanent moon bases but they are absent.  Perhaps even planning a Mars landing would be in the realm of possibility.  If they had added support for modding, that would have been awesome so we could have done these ourselves.
Ultimately, a fun space-themed game, but it is tough to get more than twenty or thirty hours out of it.

Whoa. It was my 9th time, when I finished the game. I loved (and still love) original game so much, that I was quite hyped about this mod. For the first time I had enough motivation (thanks, achievments section!) to finish without killing anyone ("animals" doesn't count, so... :D ). I don't fully understand people, who dislike it, but I'll try to explain it.
Pros:
-Graphic. OMG, it is so, so, so nice now, that's sometimes hard to express it. Shame that they didn't finish with all models, but new Walton Simons, Anna, Nicolette - looks just fantastic. Of course, they aren't shaped so well as bright new models, but hey, this engine is mature now.
-Improved AI - I've made over 400 saves during my playthrough. Never should have done that so often, but AI force me to do so. They finally SEE, when we are close, they FOV doesn't end 3 meters in front of them. Also - they've got MUCH BETTER aim. Of course, it equals harder game, but far from Omega MOD (skill farm), but also equals more fun. Even at the end, with full bioupragrades, skills etc, you could still be easily killed by Commanos or MiB.
-Few nice changes into locations - that's two-handed sword. Some people dislike it, I do like. It's not much, rather few extras during whole game, but Paris finally looks like Paris (much wider), as well as MJ12 Prison (it's not so easy to escape now). Few extra implementations have been made, as well as few extra areas, passages and keys (around 15 new nanos could be founded). It's always good to find some new place, even in old and well-known game.
Getting skill points from takedowns/kills is also two-way. I'm not gonna say anything wrong about it, but it does make your life easier. Shame, that non-lethal way is sometimes less valuable than killing (vide, for example bustin' heads). Also, about busting heads - it is much harder to do it now - rats should die instead of moving around our feet. But, that's not a big deal.
Minuses:
-Music. Don't get me wrong - it was so, so strong task to make a new music to old and well known classic. In some areas music is much less irritating, few places work better now (catacombs, Sector 4), few other - worse (MJ12, NYC, Paris catedral). It would be great if option to choose prefered soundtrack will be avaliable from main menu.
-Few, incompatible moments. I'm not gonna cry, because there's no Illuminati's hand in intro, but that's a shame. Few other symbols were also kinda crushed and removed. Hoping, that it will come back in one of further (if they will ever come) patches.
Overall - I've spend superb time. New look of the areas gave much fun, in my opinion all of them were made to fit current place in map. Nice try with music, but there should be an option (maybe it is somewhere?) to bring original, timeless UMX back to place. It's good to finally see some action there - that game is just amazing itself. And, if You bored, there are The Nameless Mod, Revision, ZODIAC, HD models and few other things that will make game playable and visually good, after all this years. Thats proving loud and clear, that the game is just amazing. Thank you for all good memories, that came back to me.

This is a really fun baseball game, something that the PC has been sorely lacking. Don't let the cartoony characters throw you off. There is a lot of depth and challenge here. I especially appreciate that the difficulty sliders, or "ego" settings, can be varied in four categories; batting, pitching, fielding, and baserunning.I've always enjoyed the batting and pitching part of PC baseball, and less so the fielding, so I let the AI handle more fielding than the others.
Hitting has a very solid feel to it. When you jack one out of the park, you really do feel a sense of getting all of it. Solid base hits and extra base hits feel equally rewarding.
The "mojo" facor and emotional reactions are a brilliant touch. Watching the pitcher and batter literally sweat it out in a duel at the plate in late innings in a close game really brings the game alive.
There also seems to be a very nice balance in letting the AI batters swing at pitches off the plate rather than having a perfect eye like so many other baseball games have had. Even the umpires seem to have some leeway in their strike zone.
Congrats to the developers. They were also very responsive to an issue I had posted in the dicussions page, which did indeed turn out to be a problem with my controller.

If you're looking for a game that is an accurate recreation of the actual game of baseball, this is not for you. Awful AI, wonky, cartoonish mechanics, and bugs galore. It would be a good cell phone game to kill time, but as a stand-alone PC game, it needs a lot of work.
This game would be a must own if it had online Multiplayer. If you have friends, use them for this.

There need to be more sports games like Super Mega Baseball. Metalhead Studios understands that this is what a baseball game is at its core, and in polishing it, they’ve made their game very compelling. Most baseball games feature realistic pitchers with 3-5 reliable pitches, just like in real life. Those games can be great, but adding more pitches and having them break like crazy really amps up the fun, even though it is unrealistic. But again, Super Mega Baseball throws caution to the wind when it comes to realism, all in pursuit of a fun game.
The pitching in the game is perhaps one of the best, if not the best, pitching system in any baseball game I’ve played. For one thing, each pitcher has an eight pitch arsenal, with breaking balls that curve so much they seem more suited to a game of wiffle ball. Each pitch can be thrown two ways - normal or power - which changes the dynamics of each pitch, causing some to break more, and others to increase velocity. This adds an incredible layer of depth to the pitcher/batter interactions. Those interactions - between the batter and pitcher - are the smallest constituents of ‘game’ that exist in a baseball game, and they really polished it to a mirror shine. They understand that this is what a baseball game is at its core, and in polishing it, they’ve made their game very compelling. Most baseball games feature realistic pitchers with 3-5 reliable pitches, just like in real life. Those games can be great, but adding more pitches and having them break like crazy really amps up the fun, even though it is unrealistic. But again, Super Mega Baseball throws caution to the wind when it comes to realism, all in pursuit of a fun game.
Batting is a joy as well. The success of the batter depends on a few things - where the cursor is placed within the strike zone, their contact stat, and their power stat. For my first 150 hours or so, I relied on getting lucky with pitch location to hit home runs. I would place the cursor where I anticipated the pitch, and hoped it would appear there. As I reached EGO levels of 80+, I realized this was no longer going to cut it. I started a new technique - shifting the cursor in the zone towards where the pitch may land as it's flying through the air. This requires quick, snap-like movements with the analog stick, and so far I have been wildly successful. Most recently, I eclipsed the 90 EGO threshold season that I was having trouble with for awhile, and won the championship at that. Though it is somewhat derivative of ‘zone’ hitting from prior MLB licensed games, I haven’t really seen a batting system reach these levels of skill depth.
All this being said, there are some things I would like to see added in Super Mega Baseball 2, slotted for release in Spring 2018. Firstly, some added depth in the gameplay. They already announced that defensive shifts would be added to the game. Pickoff attempts to curb base stealers would also be a great inclusion. But season mode needs the most work, I think. Selectively adding some tried and true features from other baseball games into SMB’s season mode could be fantastic. The game begs for a seamless ‘dynasty’ style mode, for example. Negotiating with other managers about trading players could also add a great level of depth. Each season would naturally create its own storylines with players being traded and the league generally taking on a mind of its own. The league would be shaped differently each season.
Also, a fantasy draft mode would be absolutely incredible. Having a fantasy draft creates an entire league of new teams every time. That would be very compelling. Due to the fact that each team has a specialty (power, pitching, speed, etc.) they tend to feel a little too one-dimensional. Adding some power hitters to the Crocodons, for instance, would really balance out the roster. Of course, some would argue that each team having a specialty creates a kind of game balance in itself - each team has their own emergent style of game and strategy to uphold. The Overdogs won’t be hitting lots of home runs, but they’ll be stretching a lot of singles into doubles and doubles into triples, for instance, and so that ‘small ball’ style of play is their specialty, and this is all part of the strategy of choosing the Overdogs. Shaking up the players on the teams would make most of the teams in themselves balanced, but perhaps would take away from the balance of the ‘league as a whole’ as the teams become more homogeneous.

This is a pretty adorable little kingdom simulator that has more depth than you might think, given the straightforward premise and the low-poly graphics. It follows the basic pattern: you can place building blueprints and set your villagers a small variety of tasks and just watch them try to do your bidding, keep them alive, and if you keep them happy and make room for them, more villagers show up.
You're primarily pursuing three resources to survive and expand: wood, stone, and food. Wood can either be auto-harvested (and renewed) through placing a forester building or you can direct specific plots of trees to be chopped. Stone must be quarried from a grey stone tile and occupies a fair number (at first) of your population to do so. Food has to be grown from either farms or orchards AND stored in food buildings (or it spoils), and if you don't pay attention to the seasons, you can easily end up starving your population with no way to counter it until new food is grown.
Later you're also going after gold (through taxes) and ore (which allows you to build a military and also clear unharvestable stone).
Expanding is a lot of fun, because space is at a premium, so there's a lot of consideration to go into how you slot your buildings around your roads for maximum travel efficiencies and, of course, your own aesthetics. Kind of reminds me of the classic "Cathedral" boardgame
Dragons and vikings and then eventually ogres show up to wreak all sorts of havok on your poor town/village/city and you start worrying about archery towers and strong walls. Fire occasionally break out and require fast action by your villagers.
The game doesn't do much outside of that - I'd have loved to see a quest system and maybe a wider variety of threats, but for what this game does - boy does it do it RIGHT and I can easily lose an afternoon or an evening to it, and end up quite proud of your little medieval population.

TransPlan is a very enjoyable puzzle/physics game at a very enjoyable price. If you have a penchant for this sort of game, this is definately one NOT to be missed.
The goal is to cause one geometric shape to be delivered to the same spot as another shape, locked in place (so far at least.) This is done by a combination of manipulating the moving shape, as well as other shapes, using the force of gravity. Shapes are manipulated by using pins, much in the manner of Crayon Physics Deluxe, or by erasing. Perhaps other means further on, and some of the shapes fall into sometimes partially controllable PILES of shapes. It can be somewhat complex, and so far the number of suggested necessary movements has gone as high as eight. The "reset" and "undo" buttons will be well used, and should be, without shame. I've had fun failing deliberately, just to watch gravity at work. (If you have a touch screen this game is a little piece of heaven! VERY well thought out.)
So far I've just passed the 40 puzzle mark, apparently of 70. Nothing is crazy-frustrating, and in fact can be fairly easily accomplished, though without the feeling of being a gift. (I've returned to a few, rather than become frustrated.) There is thought required for success, and since many can be solved below "par" (basically under "budget", or in less than the suggested number of movements) there is an additional challenge that can be quite a bit more interesting, even after initial completion. (I've come in as much as 5 below, on a 7-movement puzzle, and there are two achievements to recognize that very thing.) The map is well conceived, as is the process of becoming eligible to access certain puzzles and groups of puzzles. At any time there may be numerous puzzles available for consideration, grouped into categories such as "catapult" and "sling" (my personal favorite!)
Don't expect this to be Crayon Physics Deluxe, and at this wonderful price and degree of accessibility, it shouldn't be. Every puzzle solved has given me a nice feeling of accomplishment, without the frustration so often a game-ending part of the journey. Since I am in no way an engineer, I am grateful for this really fun, well designed game with a very well conceived learning curve. And the DEVs will respond quickly, sometimes within minutes. For me, that can be the BEST feature in a game.

The game generally looks as if someone drew it at school, it also has pins and rubbers that you can use to progress to the next level as those will be needed. It seems as if they designed this to be for kids, but that is my opinion only.

Deus Ex was an amazing experience where you truly had options on how to achive your mission objectives.
In the past, FPS's were all about run-and-gun. While this was always an option in Deus Ex, often, the enemies were too numerous to overcome with bullets alone. This game gave you an option of choice. You need to get into an enemy base to get a hostage? You can gun your way through, you could hack into the security to open the doors, you can find a contact to get you in, or you can sneak in through the vents. Options are what this game was all about.
However, this game has not aged well. While this was one of my all-time most memorable games, today it is a rough ride to get through it. The interface and navigating through it can be rough, a lack of auto-save or checkpoints can erase a lot of progress if you make a mistake, and the character progression doesn't have all the bells and whistles of today's games. REVISION enchances some of the features of this game, but it is still a journey that may not be worth your time.

I made sure to play through it first and then comment on it, even though half way through I realized they botched a huge section of it, perhaps inadvertently.
Understanding the fact that Caustic Creative does not have the ability to create new gameplay content (i.e new maps/map changes supported by new assets, voice-overs, features, etc. that expand the game in a meaningful way), the question you should be asking is what does Revision really add to DX, and whether these additions really +add to the classic experience as opposed to -detract from it.
Here's what Revision adds:
-Map changes
-Difficulty hike
-Remix of the Deus Ex OST
I'll start with the easiest one - soundtrack remix.  As a big fan of the original, I found the remix to be... acceptable.  The subtleties are not lost on me, make no mistake it is different, and in some cases the remix tracks completely change the underlying tone of key locations.  A more diehard fan would probably rebuke the remix for the reason stated, but I'd let that one be.  it is a fan's interpretation, and whether you agree with it or not, ultimately it's not the biggest deal when playing.
...which brings me to gameplay.  I played on realistic difficulty from start to finish, and I equate Revision's hike of the difficulty to what a few other mods have done - by simply ramping up a few parameters.  A.I. is hyper reactive to player action, and accuracy is needle-thread as if every fresh-faced NSF is a famed western outlaw.  Running past a doorway at an extreme angle so as to be exposed only for a split second?  Yup, get shot in the head.  The result feels mechanical, artificial.  You will get raytraced if you play realistic.
Finally, the map changes.  During early game, map changes consist of additions to the classic DX maps.  More trash on the ground, a new garage with a hence; at times they are furnished with a bit of pickup.  Later on, map changes are quite extensive - Hell's Kitchen, Hong Kong, Paris, etc., always with existing DX content intact, but the key locations and their NPCs are reshuffled.  Essentially they play the role of interior design - in other words, purely aesthetic.  I remember this one time I was wowed quite literally, though not by any fresh gameplay so much as the rearrangement of existing DX assets to create a natural setting.
When combined, the experience is inconistent.  You will find changes that you don't agree with, you will find additions of certain readables to be subpar, trite, even stereotyped (an invasion of 2015 internet into the world of Deus Ex circa 2052...).  Without a doubt, a lot of effort was put into the Paris maps.  The underground terminal with the three MJ12 troopers, security bot, and the lone "shopkeeper" who asks you to take care of them - my favorate location by far.  Elsewhere though, the effort is canceled out by a monumental lack of due diligence.  Hong Kong, equally as extensive in its modification as Paris, is severely marred by the horrendous gibberish that pass for "signs" everywhere.  All the new neon advertising that I can see are spouting complete and meaningless nonsense.  I feel 110% justified in wanting to say: "get some help with that for ♥♥♥♥ sake."  It makes Caustic Creative looks like a bunch of morons.  If I had filled this review with only gibberish, then I deserve to be called nothing less.
In the end, Revision works in a few ingame instances.  But others have done Deus Ex real justice in the area of its individual parts.   For true original content, there is Deus Ex: Nihilum, Nameless Mod, Redsun 2020, etc.  For gameplay tweaks, there's Shifter, BioMod.  For an experience overhaul, there is the newly released GMDX v8.0 which I'm currently playing and is vastly superior - simply because it doesn't subtract from the original, only enhances.
I enjoyed Revision's fine display of prop arrangements, but that's not why I play Deus Ex.

So this is the developer Stanislaw Truchowski's second game, his first one being a free game from 2016 known as Mind's Eye. To be honest, I really did not like Mind's Eye that much, I thought every sequence in that game had a flaw and it took so many missteps that it just wasn't enjoyable. Mind's Eye had so many problems with it that I could sit down writing an essay on it, but there was a few kind of interesting things tucked away in it especially for the guy's first game though. So when I started up his second game release and first commercial one, A Girls Fabric Face, I didn't have my hopes up that high.
However, to my surprise this game was a real little gem, a HUGE improvement over Mind's Eye, and more so A Girls Fabric Face did some interesting things I haven't seen very often in the horror scene.
It's kind of a paranormal investigation horror game, you play as a girl coming to a worn-down house, you carry a camera with you as you go and set-up a few other cameras and a place to rest as well. Your goal is to find paranormal happenings and capture it, though your camera has a charge of how much it can record at once and you have a battery life on the camera, but a mechanic I actually ended up liking while I hate this sort of thing in most horror games as the environments are small enough and there's several 'charge stations' you set-up around the place which has unlimited charges to get you back to 100% battery life rather than finding finite batteries. Due to their stationary nature, this mechanic mostly lead to you going to certain parts of the house more often (which as the house wasn't that big, wasn't really tedious and m ore created opportunities for things to happen on your small trek to it than a hassle), which ended up being an okay addition rather than an annoyance.
The game's biggest strength comes through its subtlety, keeping a few interesting mechanics balanced, and some atmospheric imagery and exploration. It has some surprisingly well done subtle scares, there are a few minor jump scares but they happen to be the good kind I feel with some good build-up or having an affect on the world rather than being hollow or empty, plus with the paranormal recording function of the game adds a little meat to them sort of like the 'passerby ghost' scenes in Fatal Frame you can capture. You might notice in the screenshots I used above that there's a "Paranormal Findings" percentage, there's more than 100% to capture as I found but basically getting your percentage up unlocks certain drawers and cabinets in the house with some additional stuff to uncover. Kind of a neat way to handle it, and it leads to not punishing the player for being bad at capturing stuff but giving some extra incentive to do so to unlock some small things.
Most of the game you're in full control and explore as some increasingly surreal and unusual things begin to happen and solving some light puzzles, but once you've done your objectives you can go rest, and when you rest you control the green stationary nightlight cameras you set up, and switch between them looking for paranormal happenings and clues to what to do or what's changed overnight. It allows some good chances to get more paranormal happenings and leads to some intuitive hinting systems. I don't want to spoil too much, but this game does work due to some well-executed scenes and the house itself being interesting to explore. The game also has four different endings to obtain based on some things you can do in game, so that's neat.
I did have a few quibbles with it. So the game isn't that long, but it actually does not have a save system, so you have to play it in one go. This isn't too much of a problem as it should only take an hour or two to get through the game your first time, but I did run into one bug where I got stuck by my character accidentally standing up in a crawl space and getting stuck in the ceiling leading me to starting all over, but in the end knowing what to do it didn't take too long to get caught up to where I was and I found some interesting differences between runs by restarting it then. My only other kind of complaint is while the story isn't all that bad, I feel some elements of it aren't implemented well, and I feel like the very end of the game isn't as interesting as the rest of it, but it's brief so whatever.
I do think this sort of set-up could be very interesting in a more open-ended format. In the end despite some slight differences you can do and the game not being a linear path, what you need to do to progress is rather linear, and though I enjoyed the game I feel it could've been better suited for some open exploration and allowing the player to do several different things at their own pace like a few moments in the game rather than most of it being in the end a rather linear affair.
Still, I was pleasantly surprised by the title and some parts of it have stuck with me a few days later, and I'm not interested to see what this developer does in the future, so consider me a fan of this one. It's definitely worth a try if you like some atmospheric paranormal investigation stuff.

It mostly succeeds in building a half decent atmosphere, and is paced fairly well. It has a few jump scare attempts but is not over the top and the puzzles are pretty light. The game also has multiple endings. However in all honesty I only played through to one ending. Decent as the game is, I did not feel invested enough to play through to see the others.
Biggest gripes are the finnikey hot boxes for interacting with items and doors, which could do with being more generous as you need to be very precise. Also the torch, when your battery is low you need to charge it up from a charging station. Whilst it is better than the usual battery hunting simulator, it adds nothing to the game except padding.
Also be warned there is no saves, you have to play through in one sitting. However the game can be played through in about 45 mins.
So all in all not a bad game for the money, but not a great game because of the length.

Great indie horror game!
First, my bias: the majority of indie horror games I play are off of
, so I have a really low bar.
Story: It actually has one! I won't give any spoilers, but it wasn't exactly groundbreaking, but more than enough to keep me interested to see it to the end as well as to justify the well made creepy house.
Atmosphere: Looks nice! Full of spooky sounds (I didn't even run into any cheap jumpscares. Some exist, but I didn't think they were cheap). It's not the best looking graphically, but I'm not one to be caught up on that sort of thing.
Gameplay: Mostly fetch quests, but an interesting camera mechanic and variety of tasks to accomplish keeps things feeling fresh.
Replayability: Decent replayability! A second time through you'll be able to unlock more achievements just from knowing when things will happen, and there's 3 different endings to get which all do their own little thing to add to the lore.
Conclusion: It's cheap. Get it if you're into indie horror games and have a good 45 minutes to kill!
