First off I would like to say the thumbs up is very much conditional upon the asking price. The appropriate price needs to be in the five to six dollar range, and this is very much a run and done affair. There is not much in the way of replay on offer in this particular title. You will probably finish it in four to five hours, and after that you will probably never touch the title ever again. Those four or five hours however are pretty decent gaming hours.
The developer has gone to some lengths to keep the experience fresh throughout, and while the game is not gorgeous by any stetch of the imagination. It certainly has its moments. The same holds true of the sountrack and sound effects. The controls are somewhat floaty, but I am sure that is by design, and the interface is actually pretty bad, but like I said this is a four to five hour long game. So compound that with no inventory management, and what you get is something you cannot possibly get frustrated with. The game is over before you even get a chance to get frustrated.
That said this game falls terribly short in one respect. The story is just good enough to get you intrigued, but after just a couple hours of playing. You will see the intrigue has degenerated into pure drivel. No character development, almost no plot to speak of, and the storytelling itself is atrocious. Everything is disjointed from beginning to end. Which can be an asset at the beginning of a story, but becomes a serious liability if it is allowed to persist. The games story will leave you feeling ambivalent or terribly unsatisfied.
This is merely a good enough game. It is more good then bad. Its greatest asset is its novelty. Its greatest liability is that it is underdone. It will however hold together for the four to five hours you will play. That said it could have been so much more. There is the seed of a great game here. Had the developer been given the resources and the time. This could have been a great game rather then an okay game.
Buy it as an okay game at the right price, and you will most likely not be disappointed.

This could be a really great game.But there are some things that often make it frustrating. It's not the challenge that's at fault. It's because someone decided to include a penalty in some of the launch scnarios. If you have a problem durning launch the game extorts a huge amount of money from you to "fix" the problems. These charges sometimes amount to many times the cost of the launch and can quickly drain your reserves. The developers could have inserted the variable in some other way but choose not to. This one flaw diminishes the enjoyment of playing by almost half. Save before every launch and be prepared to go back and cancel. These charges can happen many times in one launch (I've had it happen five times in one launch). If you save and use the option to skip to the conclusion you increase your chance of success. If you cannot get a successful launch, scrub and try again a quarter later. Research your components to 90%. Look at the history of the programs and skip missions when you can to get to the moon landing by 4/1969. I thought years ago someone should make a game on this subject in almost the same way this one was made. But it needs to go on into the future with a shuttle, space station and mars colony. Then beyond that to true interstellar program.  All this having been said, the game does have it's good points. If you can tolerate the down side. Need to have more than just a thumbs up/thumbs down rating because this is right in the middle. If they would just fix the "Tiger Teams" flaw, and make it less expensive to use.

= Please note that this review was originally meant as a reaction to AshenRowan's review =
= We seem to find the same pro's/con's, but in a minorly different measure of importance =
= Leading to a different recommendation total =
Review:
After having finished the game, i agree with most of what AshenRowan said.
- The music/ambient sounds were wonderful. They acted out the exact role they're supposed to; drawing the player further into the game, rather than just being distracting random music. While never truly noticing any sounds/music, i always felt it there. As strange as this may sound. Think of it as air: you know it's important, you know you're always inhaling it, but you never really realize or appreciate it as such.
- The scenery, especially in cinematics, were beautiful. I have to say, however, that i don't completely agree with the comment on the graphics quality being a lot worse at times. I noticed (pretty late) that the image quality seems to be directly linked to the center of the screen. Looking directly at parts of the scenery seem to brighten, sharpen ánd enhance the overall quality of that specific part of the scenery. The point that's actually sharp is pretty small though. (Please note that i have my graphics set to "fastest", as i'm working on a laptop that doesn't fully accept its own graphics card)
- The enemies are absolutely awesome! The design is wonderful, and they're placed at good locations in the game. I find some points about the enemies quite confusing though. Some seem to be programmed to follow a specific path, while others seem to act either at random, or to your movements. Don't get me wrong, i wouldn't consider this a Con, it's just... if you don't know, it can be a bit confusing, i guess.
- I didn't really mind the "Put the rock in the whole" thingy, to be honest. However, this could've been made a bit easier, or at the very least, they could've taken out the cinematic leading up to the necessary equipment.
- AshenRowan seems to have encountered more environment issues than i have. I agree that some parts of the environment doesn't work well with the intensity/air-movement of the jetpack, but that's a matter of feeling it a few times, and it'll be fine until the next time you need to slightly alter your technique. Only once have i encountered a seemingly solid piece of environment to be completely intangible. However, again, after knowing that, i managed to jump that gap with the second try.
- There's one thing AshenRowan didn't say in his review, that seems pretty important to me: the end. It doesn't seem finished at all. There were so many things i still had to do to feel like i had completed the storyline, but it seems that only one part of the storyline is officially considered the storyline? and that one honestly only seemed minorly important, considering how the storyline developed throughout the game.
| In conclusion, i also agree with AshenRowan: I'm not necessarily satisfied (especially due to that last bit), but it's a very enjoyable game. And if you don't feel like playing for a while, and you're in a fully safe spot, just leave the game open and enjoy the ambient sounds and the music while you're busy doing other stuff.

Greeting Everyone!  Today I will be reviewing a little game called Kingdoms and Castles.  To be honest I had to double check the name because it is not exactly memorable.  The game is unfortunately in the same vein, but is it worth a purchase?  Let’s find out.
Job’s Done:  At the core this game is more of a building simulator than anything else.  In classic city builder style you build a keep, some house and farms moving slowly towards more advanced resources with the obvious goal of getting more residents and keeping them happy.  One of the differences of this game (aside from graphics) is that you will occasionally get attacked almost in an RTS style.  The attacks the come really don’t cause too much so I unfortunately can’t really consider this a revolutionary design choice and some games have already done this as well.  The game really doesn’t have a tutorial but if you’ve played any city builder this shouldn’t be an issue for you.
Serenity or Boredom:  The graphics hearken back to the ‘bit-genre’ of games; which does seem to be a common trend in games today.  The graphics are easy to follow and the game does a good job at representing items.  The audio is more or less the same, some calming music with basic sound effects for events or actions.  Nothing really to write home here, which is sad as you will notice this is kind of the theme of this review…It’s okay, but you’ve seen it before.
Fast-Forwarding:  So, bugs?  None really.  So, great game?  Hold your mining there…The game is just a bit boring for anyone who’s had a deep dive into city-building games and provides nothing new to the genre apart from a new aesthetic of the ‘bit-genre’ style.  Yes there are attacks, but they are mostly harmless and there really isn’t much to do other than expand.  If you are a hardcore city builder you may appreciate this game or you may be equally bored.
Unfortunately, this game is not a hidden gem but neither is it a piece of coal.  It is ultimately a solid city-builder with an interesting graphics style.  I do wish it had a bit more substance but for $9.99 you really can’t expect that much.  Do I recommend it?  For the city building veteran, no not really; there just isn’t enough here to keep you occupied, especially in the world of vastly more expansive games.  If you are new to city building or as a gift for someone who doesn’t normally play these types of games?  Sure.  I could definitely see someone on a budget or new to the genre loving this game.  Myself, I must unfortunately pass.  Enjoy!

I don't know where to start. Massive Chalice is probably one of the best games I've ever played.
It's so amazing how much story you can get on just a simple premise. The story ends up being as procedurally generated as all the other elements of the game. If you play in a way to just let things happen, then you end up with an amazing and unique story that spans multiple generations of multiple family lines combating a common enemy. Things don't go to plan sometimes and that just adds to the beauty of it.
You planned for someone in your party to marry another? Well he dies when another party member accidentally throws a bomb on him. Then you have to find another suitor. But then they still end up with an amazing family line.
That war veteran who battled the Cadence whom retired and had children? Well, the cadence attacks their castle in their old age! But wait! Due to their experience in battle, they fight honorably against overwhelming odds!
Brother can fight alongside brother. Mother can fight alongside daughter. Even grandpa can get into the fray!
The randomized traits and personalities also add spice to the mix. This family line produces offspring that are each strong as an ox? Well, they might all be prone to depression.
That wise old master you have teaching all your young heroes? Well he might be an alcoholic and you created a whole generation of drunkards.
And don't get me started on the philosophy. You effectively play as a god for a span of 300 years. You care about these people and you see them be born, fight, and eventually mourn their passing, but their legacy lives on! Whether you believe in a god or not, it certainly makes you think about what it's like to be one, the effects of decisions, cause and effect, control, how much omnipotence does a god actually have when you factor in free will and randomness? Does a god actually care? Are some people more favoured over others?
This game also gives you a big picture look at life. It changed my perspectives and pre-conceived notions. Aren't we all expected to grow up, contribute to society, get married, and have children? But the reality is that not everyone will live that life, whether by circumstances or by choice. But whether or not you end up living that life, you can still contribute greatly to society. Some of my greatest heroes in this game never had children. Some go on to mentor others, and in a sense carry on their legacy that way. You don't have to get married and have children to be great or to have epic stories told about you or continue your legacy.
Some will die too young, some will live long lives. Some will have boring lives, some will have amazing lives. Even if you lived a boring life, did it still have meaning? Imagine being chosen for something, in this case being able to fight the Cadence. You are able to do this thing that not many are able to do. You have trained to do this thing. It is your speciality. Yet, the when the opportunity comes to show what you're made of, you were never chosen. You never got to do anything. This was the fate of some of the characters. They never got the chance to fight. They never got the chance to have a family. They never got the chance to teach others. How many people in the world today live this kind of life? Did it still have meaning? It's quite sobering to think of this.
The narrations by the Chalice's two personalities were entertaining throughout the epic saga. The random small story popups were sometimes hilarious and refreshing. As the game progresses, the stakes keep getting higher, and culminate in a final thrilling battle, and the revelation at the end was just spinechilling.
Although the graphics weren't that great, it had a certain charm. The music was amazing. The gameplay was exhilarating and fun.
I only wished that I could have recorded it all so that I can revisit the stories and my decisions anytime in the future. As of now, they are fated to disappear with time.

Massive Chalice is one of my favorite strategy/roguelike games, mechanically up there with the XCOMs, Darkest Dungeon, and the like. It's hard. Really hard. It's generational kingdom management fantasy XCOM that takes place over 300 years. But you skip through most of it.
Stylistically, it's Double Fine through and through (think Brutal Legend, Psychonauts, etc.) although in world lore and setting only since aside from the narrators and yourself, there are no other set characters - but MAN does it work.
The music and art is gorgeous. The narrators are comical, light-hearted, and whimsical, but it only adds to the feel. This *is* Double Fine we're talking about.
It's main feature is a lineage system allowing you to pass on the genetic, personality, and statistical traits of your retinue of randomly heroes, by retiring heroes as rulers or mentors from combat. These aren't always good stats and traits though - which can be frustrating, but honestly just adds to the fun for me.
There's a research system a la XCOM for items, equipment, and passive bonuses that *also* includes kingdom construction as well as research. Time is your most precocious resource, and there are options to speed up research, by retiring otherwise useless heroes as Sagewrights.
The lineage system is mechanically made more robust by the fact that the different pairings of the three base classes with a talent system (Alchemist - throws bombs, Hunter - sneaky ranged, and Caberjack - beats/stuns things with logs and endures pummeling) result in a number of additional hybrid classes, combining the base classes in different ways (each one has different quirks off of its "base"). The pairings are based on the primary and secondary ruler - which can be frustrating but is actually loads of fun once you get into it.
Finally, the last facet of the lineage system is that if a character becomes experienced enough and gets a "handle" from killing a ton of the enemies (or you get lucky through one of the randomly generated options), they have a chance of leaving a Relic behind for a chosen Family member, which is a super upgraded artifact weapon that gets stronger as its user gets EXP. This is honestly one of the most awesome facets of Massive Chalice on top of the others, in that the artifact weapons all have a visually distinctive look and name.
If you like hardcore strategy games like XCOM, or are interested in the lineage system, check it out. Or if you just like Double Fine games, of course! If you can't handle loss, then I still recommend it - save state scum if you have to. Just don't play on iron.

is a simple, yet addictive puzzle game with exciting game modes and lots of hours of gameplay.
Check out this review and many others on Save or Quit:
The concept of the game is simple. In each level, you are assigned a color and once the colors start spreading from their "spawn points", your color has to spread across more lines than other colors. Since you never start in a winning position, you are given different options to improve it, depending on what mode you're playing.
The main mode just gives you a few spawn points to place across the blank lines, then you also have the eraser mode (erase one of the other colors),  knife mode (cut one of the blank lines), and others. Each mode contains fifty levels and you can only unlock the next mode by finishing at least ten levels of the previous mode. Not all levels in a single mode are unlocked automatically, though - to unlock all fifty of them, you have to beat one level with a gold trophy (win the level ten times in a row), to give you the short version.
The rules of the game are really easy to understand, although you probably understood nothing from my description above. The tutorial takes ten seconds and it shows you everything you need to know about the game to be able to successfully complete all levels. The puzzles are rarely very easy though, to complete most of them in the first try you need to think a lot about how to use your tool. Some of the levels are really really hard, though, so you might even need to try ten times before you manage to beat it.
The spawn point placement is random on every level, which has an obvious effect on the difficulty of the level. Sometimes, you manage to complete a very difficult level just because the RNG gods really weren't in favor of the other colors and you're more or less just given the victory.
A lot of attention is given to beating the same level multiple times in a row. As I indicated below, you need to beat one level with a bronze trophy (3 times in a row) to unlock levels from 35 to 40, a silver trophy for levels 41 to 45 and a gold trophy for the rest of the levels. I think this is a good enough motivation to make people try replaying the same level over and over, something which I would otherwise never do for sure. To really show you how much the developer actually emphasize winning streaks, just take a look at the achievements list for this game: you can get one for winning the same level 100 times in a row.
Daily challenges are also a thing in this game, which is certainly a good option for players who have beaten all other levels already. Every day, you have to beat one level from around 2-5 times, depending on the level. The daily challenges don't appear to be too difficult, at least not from what I've experienced.
If you happen to be a Twitch streamer, Lines also supports a so-called Twitch mode, which lets you play the game with your viewers. The grid divides the screen into sections with different names, which can be chosen by your viewers to either help you out or play against you. How cool is that?
For all of you who play puzzle games late into the night (like me), you can turn on the night mode, which does what you expect it to do - changes the white background into black, ensuring your eyes can stay pain-free for longer periods of time. And it looks really rad if you ask me, so I just keep it on all the time. Plus, you get an achievement when you finish one level in night mode.
There is no music in this game, everything you hear is sound effects, played when lines collide or when the level is finished. It's nothing special, really, but it fills your ears with some pleasant piano sounds.
I know that people like to be creative, which is why the Workshop support might be of interest to them. A built-in level editor lets you create your own level, share it with the community and play it instantly. The Workshop button in the Play menu lets you choose among all community-made levels you're subscribed to and the game keeps the winning streaks just like it does for ordinary levels.
After briefly looking at the paragraphs above, you may notice that I haven't mentioned any bad things yet. Well, there aren't many. The first thing that bothers me is that the lines move a bit too slow. Now, this is not even a problem if you're not repeating the levels, but once you try to get the 100-in-a-row achievement, waiting for the lines to finish their journey is not always a pleasant experience. I wish there was a way to speed things up a bit. The only other complaint I have is the lack of Linux and MacOS support. I do use Windows at the moment, but I know plenty of casual gamers who use Linux and this game would be perfect for them.
For $5, this game offers plenty of fun. I needed about 4 hours to beat every level and I will definitely keep playing the game to try to get the rest of the achievements. If you're a fan of games like Mini Metro or other puzzle games, you will surely have a good time playing Lines, too.
With love,
BirdCute

From what I've seen, the later games in the series can be a bunch of fun, but this first game strikes me as completely pointless. It is too easy, looks hideous, and the physics have not aged well at all. Even with patches downloaded to enable resolutions which have become standard in the decade since this game came out, it still has to be run windowed on an ultrawide monitor.
I managed to play around 50 minutes before I was so bored I had to give up. I didn't manage to die once, despite rushing headlong into every conflict, and the story was already getting on my nerves. (Is it just me, or did they pitch-shift down the voice of the guy who gives you your missions? Was he not "tough enough"?) Beyond the story and gameplay not aging well, the basic control scheme is also really rough. Mouse-look feels like a complete after-thought, and every vehicle's tires feel like they're made of butter. Also, if the opening turret sequence is any indication, the auto-aim function reduces some of the interaction to "Hold down Mouse 1; repeat."
The core thing this game has done for me is really hammer in the fact that if you buy something as a lark because it's on sale it's worthwhile to fire up right away so you're not well outside the refund window when you realize what a waste of money and time something is. Even though it was just a dollar, I wish I had that dollar back.
If getting the better later games ends up being cheaper in a package that includes this game (so when it costs negative money, that is), then go for it. But - even if you have some nostalgia for this game - I can't recommend this in any other instance.

Editing this review to be a little more constructive.  Suffice to say, this game made me grumpy.  TLDR: this is a beautiful game with terrible writing.
First, my play time is a bit of a lie because I had to pause and run away at one point.  I actually played only about an hour.
In the first five minutes there were a few emotional non-sequitors which had me wondering what I was in for, and I was leery because the writing for Deponia was the worst thing I've ever experienced in a video game.  But I liked the setup and the characters, and the art in Silence is truly wonderful, so I decided to try to ride out the intro.  However, once the game actually gets started, the characters start making incoherent dialog references like, "Oh, there's that train I rode through the sky."  What??  Did I miss a cutscene or something?  And then a major character is introduced as my good old buddy, and of course I already know this character so there's no reason to explain them to me, the player.  If this game is a sequel, and if you need to play the prequel to understand this world, then this should be clearly called out somewhere, and ideally this should just be "part 2 of something else" instead of its own title.  I'm assuming that that is the explanation, because otherwise I have no idea what the writers were thinking.  Whatever the reason, I felt a bit conned because it's either bad writing in the game or bad advertising in the Steam store.
I kept playing because I was hoping to get through whatever backstory references they forgot to explain, and just get into this world.  For a bit I almost succeeded, despite some bugs in the dialog timing where characters would start speaking too soon or over each other and completely break the immersion.  I actually like most of the character personalities - none of them go terribly overboard in any annoyingly stereotypical fashion, and they interact in some fun ways.  But due to the timing and backstory issues, I also never really connected with any of them in a way that made me care whether or not they made it through this unexplained world.
The puzzles were simple yet fun to play through, and I liked how the story was interwoven pretty well with the puzzle sections.  However, after breezing through the first several scenes, I got to one that seemed to stump me.  I noticed that some of the objects in this area were extremely difficult to get the game to highlight, even when I knew that they were there, so maybe I simply never found the object needed to solve the puzzle.  Either that, or the difficulty went from like 2 to 10 instantly.  But after several minutes of trying to figure out why objects weren't highlighting and whether I was missing something or just dealing with bugs, I realized, I don't care at all about this story or these characters, and the puzzle system isn't interesting enough to engage me. Silence is a sequel to the first Daedalic's international success - The Whispered World. Which I've played twice and don't like all that much, by the way. And it hits all the points every Daedalic's title hits - it has amazing visual style, except now it's 3D+2D, it has really nice soundtrack, it has fantastic ideas for the story, and then it falls apart at everything else. The studio did make a few point and click adventure games that worked (more or less) fine throughout the entirety of the playthrough, with solid gameplay ideas and actually good story execution, but Silence is not one of them. In fact, I'd say Silence is one of their worst attempts.
Be it the first foray into the world of 3D adventuring or some other reason, but Silence feels like a quarter-baked idea released as is. It has the story arc fit for a full feature, story for about 20 minutes and then a bunch of "adventure game" gameplay in between. Which isn't actually adventure gameplay, but more of a "guess where you have to click next to trigger the next thing to go to another place to trigger another thing to trigger the story", in the worst possible way. It's like watching a movie, only for it to pause and present you with a bunch of boring busywork so it unpauses and continues, with busywork having next to nothing to do with the story. Which, by the way, is a boring and non-impactful rephrasing of the same story as in The Whispered World, but with forgettable disposable secondary characters, pointless "character arcs" (oh no, I so care about this character I'm seeing for the third time and know nothing about who might die now!) and nothing of its own. I hope Daedalic manages to make a good game with this visual style. But Silence is not it.

Forewarning: This is less a review and more a rant about certain aspects of this game that I either hate, enjoy, or otherwise feel neutral about.
This is, without a doubt, my favorite game I've found in what must be the last three or four
. Definitely what I put up in top five catagory. It is not without it's flaws, however. And it definitely isn't for everyone. But I do recommened that you at least put forth a good effort to enjoy what Bare Mettle has to offer in Exanima.
First and foremost, all the talk about difficulty is codswallop. The initial hump of getting over movement and combat is negligible at best and frankly overblown. I myself is included in exaggerating this task and I imlpore everyone to disregard what people say about it. That is not to say that you are not in for an easy ride. The term "easy to learn, hard to master" is in full affect here. I find myself getting my rear handed to me on a silver platter on occasion at totally my fault, I'll admit. The most difficult fights you find will be from special enemies that I won't mention.
Exanima is currently in development by a very, very small team of developers (read as "three devs, one composer, one artist, and one guy who acts as IT AND legal"). Many of you have already correctly guessed that updates, while meaningful, come less than often. It is what it is, but from the quality of improvements that range from overhauling the terrain system to making movement more fluid - a necessary evil. I would most certainly say that being this early in development is what holds Exanima back the hardest and what will probably hold most from buying it. Exanima, after all, is a prelude to Bare Mettle's actual love child Sui Generis. A game I will most probably buy if Exanima continues development in this way.
This game absolutely reaks of being a work of passion. Everything to the art style, to the music, to writing, and lore is drenched in the sense that the devs want to bring it life. For the most part, I think they've succeeded. The notes, books, and writings you find are dropped in the perfect places to find them without feeling like you're actually looking for them. It feels natural, and I can't wait to keep learning about the world and what's inside of it. The music is great as well, but a little limited. A current seventy-odd minutes I believe is there. Some of it can only be found in the Arena mode, and others in various sections. The Underworld themes are beatifully haunting, and genuinely leave me uneasy whenever I hear them crop up. I need a buyable soundtrack to keep hearing them, please Madoc, I beg of you.
The biggest problem I have with the game is its pacing concerning items. There are a planned 15 levels to Exanima, but by the time you get to level 4-5/6, you will have a set of superior full plate armor. Do you see what I mean?
Enemy variety is also fairly stagnant. If you count the skeletons on floor four as the same on floor three, as you should, there are a whopping five enemy types in the campaign. Seven if you count arena humans and the monster types. I would love to see some new things to kill added. Even if it is just bandits that fight like a drunk child as I did when I first started playing.
As of right now, the last update was about three months ago, but Madoc has said that the next update is coming pretty soon and with a lot of significant content. I cannot wait until the next few levels release so I can create another poor sod to condemn to the horrible depths.

This is one of those games where I wish there was a 'Maybe' button for do you recommend.  I'd have to err on the side of 'no' on this one, though.
The premise is cool and the story is interesting, which are pretty key points in a game like this.  However, to make a game interesting, it has to be more tha a series of bright spots on the screen that you walk to in order to advance the story.  That's where things start to fall down.
I'm the kind of guy, that presented with an open environment, will try to seek out the nooks and crannies.  I quickly found that with this game, there was no real reward for doing so ... Exploring just seemed really unsatisfying and it turned into me marching from journal entry to journal entry, largely ignoring everyhing else.  There's a lot of big, open expanses of nothing.
The structures (houses, buildings, etc.) are weird lifeless props.  I would have liked to have gotten to see a little bit more, gotten a feel of an abandoned place.  Instead, it felt like a low budget movie set.  The main character's early reaction that this is all fake rings way more true than anything else.
Some people say this game is beautiful, some say its beautiful in places and ugly in others.  I'd say its pretty bland all the way through.  The color palette changes, that's about it.
I will say I actually liked that the puzzles were relatively simple ... I didn't really get stuck on anything, which I liked.  What I didn't like is the jumping mechanic.  There's one part in particular where I failed so many times I was starting to question if it was the right path ... it was the right path, just a pain in the butt jump.
Despite all this, I plan on finishing the game.  I think I'm near the end as it is ... interesting story, and I want to see how it ends.  And that's worth a lot.  So, consider that when you're considering the game ... want a neat sci fi story?  Well, maybe it's worth giving this one a try.

I love this game. At first when i saw it i was tempted but the negative reviews put me off, but after watching my friend play and getting it myself i am not certain what the negative reviews problems are.
Firstly the games style is simple but delightful. I love the art style. I think if it was hyper realistic or anything like that it would feel too much like banished. The simply art style is very clear and gives it a cheerful colourful atmosphere. Lets be fair..if a triple AAA place got this it would be really dismal and grey.
Secondly the game play is simple too. Buildings do not require too many resources which means its quick to get going and gameplay naturally escalates at a normal pace. I have never felt that the game was 'cheating' against me like i have on some games.
Thirdly; the game has a reasonable amount of longevity for me. If you just want to build your ultimate fortress then play the non-combat mode. Its also good to practise and learn the games mechanics. The easy mode, where you first encounter raids and dragons, is not OTT and so it gives you time to respond and react. I have not yet tried the hard mode, however 13 hours in i am not bored of the game.
More content is also coming which i look forward to seeing.
If i had any criticisms at all, its that there needs to be a more obvious alert when theres new messages from your castles 3 advisors...but thats a small gripe.

Game is fun and has alot of potential but the developer needs to update it a little. mainly fix combat&balance issues.
DIFFICULTY ISSUES (game is way too easy):
- needs to be much harder to maintain a food surplus
- its too easy when 20-30 of workers auto-immigrate each year. cut spontaneous immigration to once every few years and add reproduction/aging. this would add an extra incentive to build medical structures and make a more life-like community.
- need more causes of citizen death (for example, make it so people can freeze to death if they don't have coal or shelter).
- libraries are wayyyyyy too good (especially relative to churches)
- defense is only an early-game concern.
- i've never had my citizens riot even when they were angry for years.
COMBAT ISSUES:
- towers are too powerful relative to troops. no real reason to raise troops.
- troops models are bugged and their graphics jitter if they are standing still.
- vikings don't scale into late game. IMO they need a 3rd unit type to help them with late game sieges.
NITPICKINGS (minor stuff):
- max map size is too small
- happiness system is too polar. more things should affect happiness, but no one thing should affect it entirely.
- irrigation system potential distance from freshwater source needs to be increase by 2x.
- freshwater needs to be more common.
- can't choose color of castletops (i don't know why, but weirdly important).
- no alternative models for homes/churches/etc.
- no way to select a group of trees for cutting.
- only 2 sources of food.
- not enough structures.
potentials:
>smaller medical building
>school (higher worker productivity if they attended a school)
>tailor (clothes decrease chance of workers freezing to death & increase worker happiness)
>fishery (or other alternative food-sourcing structure)
>bigger coal structure (or alternative to coal)
>amphitheatre (source of plays. luxury structure. matches style of castle. increase local city happiness)

Oh. My. God.   I just finished Knights, and my brain hurts. It really does.   I don't get much time to play games, so I have to cram everything at the weekend.   Thinking in "L" shaped patterns, and working out chains of moves is NOT my forte!  Let's just get it out there: I suck at chess.  I really do.  I once put a chess computer on "zero ply" (which is AI-speak for 'don't be clever, just move random pieces to places they can go), and I still didn't manage to win.
So, a game which is all about trying to put pieces in a specific location is supremely brain-busting for me.    Nevertheless, I persevered through, and managed to finish the main game.
The game is split into five 'levels', and each level has between 9 and 30 'boards'.. Each board is set up so that you have to move knight chess pieces around in order to put the red or blue knights back onto their red or blue squares.   Sounds easy?  Well, to begin with,  it is :)
Pretty soon, bit of the board become un-usable, and then there are yellow knights whose sole purpose is to get in the way.   Once the little yellow b*****ds turn up, the game starts to turn into a really brain-bending challenge, because you often have to move a bunch of yellows out of the way, in a specific chain in order to get your coloured knight into the right spot.
As the game continues, you start to 'see' patterns.  There are ways to get your knight from one spot to another spot at a relative position away.  There are some hard moves (moving immediately next door) and easy ones (moving two squares away, or to your diagonal neighbour )..   Once you start to see the patterns, the game starts to flow a little better, and all of a sudden you begin to 'see' the chains of moves you need to make, and before long you're planning ahead to get the knight where you want it to be.   I guess it's sort of like a kingergarten level sense of 'ply' that real chess players have when they can scan the board, and plot a number of moves in advance.
However, chess masters can simulate the moves in their heads, which normos like me can't so the game really helps by allowing you to 'see' the valid target jumps for a knight by clicking on it, and doing chains is easy because you can just keep clicking the place you want to move it to.  moving back and forth incurs no penalties, so you can move things about all over the place.    One of the most frustrating things is that the boards can be set up so that specific knights have to be in place before you tackle others.  It's vitally important in the later levels that you nail those first, or you're just going to spin for ages, moving one piece all over the shop.
I'd say my experience to begin with was very impressed by the way you could 'milk' a game out of one chess piece.  This turned into being impressed by the way the board managed to be set up in increasing ways.  This turned into being impressed by how the boards are set up beautifully, but are, indeed, solvable, when they REALLY shouldn't be.   This then turned into dogged determinism to get the darned game finished.   Yes, I have to admit, midway through the 'queen' level, I started to really struggle.  I'd say the estimated time to complete a board started out at about 10 seconds, and midway through 'queen' ended up being a solid 10 to 15 minutes.   Strangely,  by the end of queen, I'd really started to get back into whatever flow you need, and the king level was relatively easy compared to queen.
Once you get to (say) Queen level, you are well-enough armed to tackle the Daily puzzles.  Like Lyne, Race the sun,  and a few other indie puzzlers, the daily puzzles are all procedurally generated.  The first one I tried was solved in two clicks.  The next one had be beat.  The difficulty level is all over the place, because the computer doesn't know what makes a level hard for a human.  What's really impressive is that the designers have figured out how to make boards procedurally generate that are still solvable!
I really enjoyed this game, and despite my frustration in 'queen', I think it's well worth a play if you like logic and puzzle problems:  Especially if you like chess, or just like indie puzzlers like Lyne.

Also, there is no "do this in the minimum number of moves or it does not really 'count' as a win" type mechanic. There is no counter. This gives it the feel of a physical puzzle that you can feel free to fiddle with until you get it. You do not get stuck after almost getting it and have to start over. For me, this makes it perfect -- fun, not work.
If you like puzzle games at all, this is one you really should get.

Although steep in price, I'm sure sports fans from all ages will enjoy this one. I got it on sale and do not regret my purchase one bit. Yes, it's Baseball (my least favorite sport) represented in the form of a cartoon but it's game play does not lack whatsoever.
First off, the game is local co-op. I just wanted to make sure everyone knows this because this is an awesome thing on steam. Second, the game play is also varied in it's works. At first, all the batting styles and pitching styles may seem relatively the same. Upon reading the instructions (as I usually do after an hour into the game) you can definitely mix up your style in order to meet the demands of the play. The batter can swing using "A" in which is a straight through swing. "B" will let you bunt while holding "X" will let you decide how much power to put into your swing. Alternatively, using the right thumb stick will let you sort of have a say in where the ball goes. This selection also uses a power setting in which starts at 0 and goes all the way up to 99 then back to 0. Timing is important in the game and plays a role from batting to pitching.
When pitching (playing solo), the player will have to line up his pitch into a small box that is displayed. The game is even nice enough to show you where the ball is planning to go. These arrows may point in a different direction depending on what type of pitch you choose. I believe there are 8 different pitches to choose from including fast balls and forkballs. Playing local co-op though, there are no boxes displayed as to where you should line your shot up. This doesn't take away from the game as you can still get some fancy throws off.
Playing out field is relatively simple and you'll feel almost in complete control of your players. "LB" tells all players to run around the bases while "RB" tells everyone to run back to the previous. You can tell individual players to run to certain bases and even play some tricks running back and fourth. Pressing "RB" while playing outfield will make your player jump while pressing "RT" will make them dive. These are fantastic features but can sometimes be slightly misleading. Spacing sometimes plays an issue as I'm unsure whether to press one of those buttons or not in fear of completely missing the ball. You, as the player have to give some time to the actual players to pick up the ball. The ball is throwing accordingly to the button layout (Y - 2nd base, X - third base, A - home and B - 1st base) and holding down the throw button brings up a power meter of how hard to throw the ball. Releasing at the right time will give you desired power. The controls overall are pretty on point and you'll be blaming yourself more than it for mess-ups. Level of difficulty can be adjusted but be aware, anything over 20 is pretty tough (and 20 is medium)! The teams also have different characteristic settings as some are better at bat than pitching. All teams have ridiculously funny names.
The graphics are very enjoyable and the character designs are fantastic. Everything seems like it was taking slightly over the top but it's absolutely suiting. I wish they would add maybe one or two more arenas to play in. The ones that are given are none the less pretty.The local co-op scheme is absolutely phenomenal and well organized. Don't know whose pitching? Don't know whose batting? Don't know whose playing outfield? Don't know whose controlling what? Take a quick glance before the pitch is thrown and you'll see which player is assigned which task. Sounds are funny as the umpire will have you laughing when he sends you off the field (YOOOOOUUUURRRR OUTTAAAHEEERREEE isn't the start of it...  a deep low voice will be saying some random stuff that you'll have to listen to carefully to make out what the guys yelling in a mumbling fashion). From the bat making contact with the ball to the throws themselves, everything seems on point.
Overall, a really fun baseball game that closely mimics a real one. Don't let the cartoon graphics fool you, this game will challenge you. Just wish there was
.

Here are some quick pros/cons:
PROS:
- Excellent/fun gameplay, smooth animation.
- 6 beautiful baseball stadiums with their own configurations and characteristics.
- Simple and intuitive hitting and pitching interface.
- No bugs that I have noticed yet.
- Attention to detail in the stadiums and player animations (some funny player reactions).
- CPU teams seem to make the right plays in the right situations.
- "Ego" adjustment so you can play at varying levels of difficulty.
CONS (but not really... I mean, for this price these aren't that bad):
- Not very deep stats, just the basics. In season modes, you can look at the stats for your own team or the top-10 league leaders in the basic categories. Unfortunately, you can't compare total team stats with other teams. Errors are not counted. So all runs are earned, no matter if runs score because of dropped balls.
- No Home Run Derby! This is too bad, because it's really fun to hit homers in these stadiums. There are all kinds of features over the fence for the ball to hit and bounce around a bit. It just doesn't "disappear" into thin air like some games. Please add a HR Derby mode!
- All pitchers can throw the same pitches, although with various degrees of velocity and movement.
- Not really a CON because this is probably just me... Baserunning with keyboard/mouse setup is quite tough to get used to. I understand how it works now, but I still screw it up. I've lost count of how many times I've run myself out of an inning because I have runners going in all kinds of ridiculous directions. But I did figure out that yelling and screaming at the monitor does NOT help.
That's all I have for the moment. Hope this helps!

Here's a small selection of my review of Lines from my YouTube series, The Show. You can find the full review in the youTube video below.
Self described as a zen puzzle experience, Lines is a beautiful mixture of abstract minimalism and spatial logic, where your ability to map out cause and effect in a 2D plane is tested by a flood of colour. Each level you’re presented with features a predefined shape, made up of a series of interconnected lines, and some coloured dots. After placing or removing additional dots - or performing some other actions depending on the game mode - the dots burst to life, pouring their colour at a fixed pace through the lines, until the whole shape is flooded. Your goal is to ensure that the colour you represent occupies the majority of the available space.
What I love about this is that it’s incredibly easy to pick up, and even though every scenario that you’re presented with is winnable, it’s not always immediately obvious exactly which choices will lead to your victory - you really have to think about what the distances between dots and junctions, and how the different colours on the playing field are going to interact. Add to this a vibrant colour palette, creative level designs, and an almost improv-like piano soundtrack that seems to be generated by way the colours fill the shape, and you’ve got instant puzzle appeal.

I just refrained from getting a refund on this, hoping that it will become both a crazy hard game and an enjoyable one. I'm really not sure about that last part though.
While the originality and uncomprimising nature of combat in this is really appealing, it's just too clunky to feel rewarding. Controls completely changing in and out of combat (a rage-inducing mechanic that I thought had died with the AC franchise), unprecise hitboxes (drive a pike through some dude's head? Too bad, the game decided your trajectory was off even though you did put it all in his forehead, and ignores your attack so that you can get instantly countered!), and a camera that remains miles away from the action: everything that should help you ease into the whole "think of it as a real brawl" thing actively prevents you from learning, because most of the time you can't even tell wth happened.
Now everything else seemed as good as promised before ragequitting ensued: minding your distance from your opponent, following his movements to block or dodge, carefully looking around in the middle of combat so that you don't back up into a pile of junk that will make your trip at the worst possible time, all of this felt like it could actually become a very fluid and fair experience, the game just doesn't have the interface to support these features.
I hope we can get more options in the future, be able to choose when and how the controls change, decide which actions we want to work with the keyboard or the mouse, and most of all: get some goddamn alternate cameras. The exact same concept with the ability to switch to a simple overhead 3rd person, Dark Souls style camera would change everything in how the player is introduced to the game, and let one learn a lot more quickly from one's mistakes. Well it would also require ceilings to be added, but I think that'd be a small price to pay to make it playable.

I don’t often rite reviews but I can see how this game could get undeservingly down voted into oblivion. Look the game is hard, not like Dark Souls hard like something "new" hard. This game is unlike anything you have probably played and it is unapologetic about it. Exanima is a physics driven game, it's like learning to ride a bike with a mouse and key board. Saying this game has a learning curve is a gross understatement. This game has a learning mountain surrounded by a learning wall complete with a learning moat. Things that have never posed a challenge in any other game will challenge you "Walking". I downloaded it yesterday and put in 8.5hrs in the first night and I’m still♥♥♥♥♥♥ but not frustrated. I can see improvement. I have completed practice mode with the long sword but not on expert, and I’m finally making progress in the arena. I am only just now beginning to be ready to try my hand at the dungeon crawl.
If you want a game that is based solely on skill I cannot recommend it more. The depth is incredible as someone who has takin fencing and been a part of HEMA (Historical European Martial Arts… Like fencing with long swords.), this game is as close to a real sword fight as a game can get. If you are someone who doesn’t like change or gets butt hurt when something is hard or actually punishes you for being bad "DONT BUY THE GAME". You will trip and be tripped, you will die and lose everything, it will be hard, but it’s that difficulty that make the games so rewarding. When you block the blow that would have killed you and repost to land the finale strike, it is a rush. Exanima is not for everyone I suggest doing some research, but I for one love this game.
TL;DR
Game hard don’t buy if bad.

This is a nice little tactical game, but let me tell you, If you are expecting something as good as XCOM you will have a bad time.
I had a GREAT time during the first few hours of this game, sadly the longer you play the more troubles that start crawling in, enemy variety (like 7 at most), Class Balance (I dont want to say wich is wich, but 1 class is overpowered as hell, another one is perfectly designed BUT all the enemies can counter it in some way or another and the last one is simply horrible in late game and barely useful before that), Lack of gameplay depth and tactical options (No cover system, very few usable skills per class, only 3 real classes even if you can get some minor variations if you breed "hybrid" versions of them, et.) , and so on.
So... why do I still recommend it? Well... it still trows you one or two new things once in a while to keep you hooked (random events, some new  mechanics and technology that you can research, etc.) at least until the end of the campaign and I actually had a pretty nice time with the game, making your empire grow and prosper while breeding heroes that defend its borders is actually quite fun, but as I said, I expected something much worse so your mileage may vary.

If only the game got more development to expand the tactical options and make some of the strategic choices more interesting the game would be amazing, as is you'll get bored as soon as the novelty begins to wear off.

This game is the unofficial successor to Buzz Aldrin's Race to the Moon for MS-DOS which I loved to play because as a space-enthusiast there weren't enough games about the race to the moon on the market. So I like to compare today's gameplay with the prior game. Generally does it look better, but it's sometimes unorganized.
The space center is a bit chaotic and buildings like the headquarter, VEB, SET, mission control and co. are less visible on a first look than earlier. The game reduces the locations for the bunch of data. You simply have a lot of menus hidden in the buildings and sometimes it takes too much time to go from A to C and back. This is the victim of a tablet-strategy I think.
But the old game on DOS had a better atmosphere. Although the videos were ugliers in earlier times, these old media from NASA and Soviet archives transferred the feeling of being the director of a space agency during cold war. Sure, the drawings are fine (although I can't skip as I did with a click in Race to the Moon), but it's fine. More disgusting are the names and photographs of astronauts, engineers and controllers. Names are too mixed, photos too new. Honestly, in the 60s it is really unlikely to have an Afro-American astronaut in space (unfortunately).
Sometimes missions are less dependant on the reliability than expected. I could play the same mission x-times and still loose despite of a reliability of 90%. This is a huge disadvantage. And I'd like to do more after landing on the moon. This game isn't Race to the Moon, but Space Program Manager and so I want to do more, maybe rebuild Skylab or its Soviet counterpart.
However, I'd recommend it because the challenge with the AI is great and the background, the race between the USA and the USSR is still fantastic and dramatic.

I avoided that mistake this time and the gameplay changed because of it.  Deus Ex is about choices and I can see where one could play this game 3, 4 or more times and have a different experience each time.  The Deus Ex world is also incredibly immersive.  The developers created a world with an atmosphere of foreboding that few others are able to achieve.  It has been named the best PC game of all time by several major publications and I can see why.  If you haven't played this game, put it to the top of your list. You won't regret it.

Now this is a game I really enjoyed, I haven't played it in a while, but I'm writing a review for the Black Friday event.
A cool end of the world calamity event that constantly having you constantly debate the best choice to make. Choose some families to fight to the ends of the earth... literally. Wed, have kids, and force them to do the same... for generations. They use turn based combat which I'm always a fan of, however the % hit chances could cause you to pull your hair out, and if your an alchemist... may actually burn the hair off your allies. Decide the path to take on random quests, find weapons that turn into family heirlooms to pass onto the next generation, develop your technology trees, and choose what buildings to construct on which territories.
I only wish there were more classes than the 3 standard. You do have the option to mix classes together as you wed families, but 4 or 5 different models would have been really neat. A playthru could last you 20 minutes to several days depending on your difficulty and unfortunate luck.
I was glad I picked this game up, and if it's on sale I'd recommend it even more.

A turn based strategy game along the lines of X-Com, only fantasy based and the graphics are a bit cartoonish. With that being said, the 'world view' requires you to breed heroes together to create the next generation of (hopefully) better heroes to continue the fight against the 'evil' Cadence. The overall war lasts 300 years so each generation might see only a handful of fights before dying of old age (if they don't die in battle). I like the aspect of choosing breeders in the royal houses based on their traits and personalities, always striving to maximize the offspring for the coming strife when they come of age. The undesirables are ignored or cannon fodder...
The battles themselves are turn based, with 3 main character classes each with 2 sub-classes, each class with specific abilities. The vanguard is up to 5 of your heroes on your roster, and if some of them die, you should hopefully have more for the next fight, but they're probably "second-string" heroes, so be careful. There's no "cover" like in X-Com, but you can use the terrain to your advantage with knockbacks and stuns or some terrain fauna that will explode when touched. Mostly just flank and overpower, but the AI is fairly good.
The real challenge comes on Brutal mode, which, along with the RNG, becomes a formiddable challenge, as the Cadence become stronger as the years progress, just like your heroes should. Each Cadence has a special abiity that can be a real problem if you don't have the right hero abilities to counter them.
Overall I enjoyed this game very much, almost as much as X-Com. For an indie game, it's worth looking at.

Can't estimate this game well having months of life behind spent on original Buzz Aldrin's Race Into Space. It could be my subjective niggle but it just does not feel right and here is my remarks why.
Most of the time you just get *Catastrophic failure*, *Crew perished* with no explanation whatsoever. Violent explosion? Did escape system fire or something got wrong after separation from the faulty rocket? You are left confused with no food for thought.
There are a new game mechanincs with affection to mission reliability from flight control crew skill levels and it should be part of interesting complicated gameplay. But when your crew *perishes* on lunar insertion burn, you just need to know if it was an explosion onboard, or those dumn f*cks on Earth failed plotting course and smashed your crew into the Moon. Because in the event of ignition failure ship is still on the free return trajectory to home, so you are forced to suspect game in cheating and developers in laziness on every corner.
Even though game guides you to learn history, you are forced in the bad way to repeat existed schemes. I felt myself constrained with 7K-L1 orbiting only with single launch having no opportunity for EOR/LOR joint launch. Instead we now have tons of rockets in historical configurations which have human-rated restrictions. Engineers are requiered to learn separate skill to develop piloted rockets *sick* !Your escape system is still not working, just give me launch whatever I want already!
Another word to probe programs. For example, game offers you to develop historically existed programs in NOT historically chronological order. It's obvious flyby is simplier than orbiting or landing, and it's okay that game mechanics expects you to do each step before more complex task. But launching Venera-15 orbiter before Venera-7 lander and Venera-10 after Venera-11 later is a mess. Just give player to develop his own sequentially numbered probe missions as in the original game instead of confusing him with educational bias.
Wandering in gorge of menus while trying to manage programs doesn't help either. You are not allowed to freely plot a combined task for flight, instead you are expected to choose from limited existing flight configurations. For example convenient filter from the original game allowed to launch joint docking+duration+spacewalk+whateveryouwant configuration back in '92.

I can understand that burden of the copyright doesn't allow to put real names or photos of envolved people in personell info, but why do I need to know that Alexsandr Popov is black random guy anyway? 95% of faces presented in game is nothing you expect to see as an employee of NASA or especially soviet space program back in the sixties. I don't feel heat of the space race staring in those faces, I see imprint of nowaday multiculturalism misconceptions and it totally ruines zeitgeist.
Artworks for game are done in really great details, but you don't expect to find game full of poorly animated slideshows in product for such cost. Graphics is no matter for the gameplay anyway, but inability to squander of flat and monotone sketches through the mission makes you sad in memories of good-old-fashioned poorly digitized chronicle videos you believed in BARIS.
Also confused with tiger teams mechanics. What are they? When something goes wrong you have an option to gather help team for some ridiculous ammount of budget compared to whole launch itself.
I understand how it works in the real life with brainstorming onboard issues while inflight, but it just looks out of place. Success of flight is greatly depends on MCC, but money can't buy you a life of the man left in space.
Again, all those thingies in the game like a solar system and other confusing menus looks nice, but have nothing to do with comfortable gameplay even compare to imperfect old original game.
No mention of the dead multiplayer.
I can't find things BASPM done right compare to BARIS except for Ivan Ivanovich. And it's unlikely anything changes in the near future.
Better go play oldie hotseat with your friends.

This was met with some strong negativity when it came out, due to the mod having several flaws that become apparent right from the first level. However, after playing through the game I would say that the mod's improvements outweigh its downsides, but it's not the ultimate version of Deus Ex that the description makes it sound like.
The changes in level design are quite subtle in the first levels, but become more apparent in the later levels like Paris or the underwater lab, which are much more impressive to look at than the rather dull and gray originals. That is the most notable feature of this mod, as all other improvements are taken from other mods like New Vision.
So, overall this could be a really great and convenient bundle, but there are some aspects that hold it back.
First of all, it's only on Steam. Obviously I don't have a problem with that, but it nevertheless was a really unnecessary move by the developers in my opinion that earned them a lot of negativity towards their mod.
The new soundtrack is also quite pointless, however good it may be, but I don't think anyone would prefer it over the fantastic original soundtrack.
Furthermore, the mod manages to create performance problems in a 15 year old game, which is quite an achievement in itself. In some areas the framerate drops noticeably and there occasionally are weird mouse lag issues.
Also, there are some minor mistakes, like giant bushes that enemies can see through, and plastering some walls in Hong Kong full of Japanese letters.
In the end, I would recommend this mod if you're looking for a reason to play Deus Ex again (not that you'd need one), if you're playing for the first time play with something less involved like New Vision first.

Although I did like some of the improvements, sometimes I do feel the original game had more capability to create atmosphere.
The original is more rough around the edges, sure... though this MOD - although great new level design was made for some specific locations like Paris - did feel a bit 'empty' at times as well.
Overall recommended for a good revisit to this great game.

This game is for you if you enjoy at least one of the following:

The most interesting part of this game just so happens to be the biggest let down of this game. To say the controls are clunky and the animations are bland, is an understatement. This game sells its self on 'physic's based combat', but in reality it's more or less wildy moving your mouse left/right/forward to sling whatever weapon like a ragdoll, juiced to the gills on novocaine at an equally awkward ragdoll doing the same. After you get a feel for the game, you learn that your character inherently blocks incoming attacks, as long as your cursor is positioned so that your toon faces the another character. You also learn that every match is basically the same, as you will wait for an attack and counter. I often found myself strafing to the left and stepping forward after dodging an attack, and plunging my mouse to the left to swing my weapon and often it being blocked or catching a knee. It's comical stepping into an enemy as they swing. You'll watch your $14.99 toon tangle up with your enemy as each flail their limbs in every direction as if this were a "I can't dance simulator" before eventually separating. As if this wasn't complicated enough, the camera angle is awful. This honestly killed the game for me. As you move around, you'll be forced to spam the space bar to keep the camera angle on your side. Because if you don't, as you move around the map, left will become right, right will become left, etc. It makes the game nearly impossible to play without the space key function. So as you're preparing to flail your mouse in an awkward motion, you'll also have to make sure your camera angle is correct or you just might swing in the wrong direction. AWSD just doesn't feel good in this game. Now before the reddit nerds come and say 'I need to learn the game mechanics' or 'that I'm just bad, and that's why I don't like it' or 'if you don't like this game you obviously don't know how to play it' - you're wrong. I gave this game a fair chance and I geniuenly wanted to like this game. Lol i think one of the top comments for this game starts out with "skill based combat", which, has me rolling in my chair. There's no skill in this game, outside of wait to counter. This game is hard for literally no reason other than; just becasue. Its not Dark Souls hard, where your enemies are super difficult, but hard in the sense that the game mechanics are fighting you and winning. With better a fixed/locked camera setting and some polish on the controls, this game could be cool. This also feels like a game that could be fun multiplayer game. But so far, all the game really offers is a difficult transition from modern gaming to Windows 98 WASD running game.

1)  It actually feels like a revolution. The liberation missions are so much more chaotic, friendly and enemy soldiers are plentiful and people die left and right as bullets fly and cars explode, rebels patrol in convoys and in helecopters in their territory, and many times, especially on popular roads, gunfights are everywhere with factions getting some backup more offten than not. Whereas in jc2 it merely feels like you are a lone lunatic who occasionally helps out streetgang esque idiots that sometimes patrol around and immediately die as soon as they run into military because they are all there is. While a blackmarket mod does allow you to spawn a friendly soldier that's immortal and that follows you, it doesn't solve this problem however. Maybe if said mod allowed you to spawn 30x normal friendly troops like it does with 30x enemy troops, you could have more fun, but as it stands factions feel better in jc1 though some faction mods in jc2 claim to remedy this, but i cant say for sure since i haven't tried them yet. Even if they do, base attacks in jc2 would still be crap. Picture a small handful of idiots with guns, following you into a mostly deserted military base, and there you have jc2's base liberation missions. And afterwards the only indication that your friends now own the base are a few faction cars outside the front gate, the rest of the base remains deserted. As ive stated above, definitely not the case with jc1.
2) In jc1 you can run towards gunfights and expect them to not be over in 2 seconds because the factions spawn pretty frequently often join in existing firefights, and because of how frequent the skirmeshes are, and how restless civilians are, it makes you feel like a small part of something bigger as opposed to being the bigger part of something smaller like in jc2.
3) In jc1 you get full support from your allies, meaning safehouses from the factions prestocked with vehicles and weapons and access to better vehicles and weapons as you rank up, agency safehouses which offer better vehicles for the most part, and free vehicle drops. In jc2 you have to pay for it, listen to sheldon's dumb a$$, and do so multiple times if you want to stock up on weapons/ammo. I know, there's mods that disable it and allow you to spawn many things, and using those makes jc2 much better, but it's still an annoyance to individually drop all your equipment. jc1 did it right in that you get weapons, and full ammo all at once at safehouses, and you get them for free but lose them on death
4) Speaking of weapons, in jc1 weapon variety is commendable, with different weapons of the same class that all have different stats and performance. The weapons in jc2 were lackluster in my opinion, and very dry, not to mention the stupid upgrade feature which somehow allows you to cram about 10 super shells into a sawnoff shotgun. I never like to upgrade my weapons past certain points in jc2 because i feel it makes things too easy when only 7 bullets from your AR can blow up a military jeep or helecopter. In jc1 the weapons handle better, and feel less crazy. I like the thought of upgrading my weaponry, but it could have been done, much better with more weapon variety.
1) For one, the graphics in jc1 are not that hot, and jc2 takes the cake in that department, which is a given since jc1 is a lot older. If graphics is a big thing for you, this may matter.
2) The play area of jc1 is only slightly smaller than panau but it feels bigger to me. Still in terms of play area and places to go, i think they are equal, or as equal as you can get when comparing an old and somewhat newish game.
3) Vehicles in jc1 are pretty cool, but in jc2 vehicular combat is a little bit more fun, then again my childhood memory recalls glorious times driving around and blowing $hit up in many fun vehicles in jc1 so im sort of in the middle on this. However, speaking of vehicular combat, if you count pc auto-aim i'd lean toward jc2 heavily in this regard. But minus auto aim, jc1 wins hands down.
4) 5) Moddability is obviously much more superior in jc2 than jc1, but even though jc2 takes the cake in this regard it doesn't mean many of the mods are actually good. Overpowered weapons, flying mods, mods that give god mode, invincible vehicles with super weapons, and player skins/visual ambient changes make up most mod choices. Mods that actually add fun things without making you godlike are rare, and serious enviromnet changes (like sky and moon) are also rare, joke mods making up the majority of visual mods. So while jc2's handful of good mods beats jc1's 0 mods, it's still not good enough to be considered a pro either in my book.
5) Story wise they're both similarly cheesy, the actual narrative is meh for both games, and while jc1's more immersive feeling revolution remedies this somewhat, it's still meh. I never did play these games for the story, i always played for the fun chaos and open world warzone settings, a setting which i am very fond of, and a setting that sadly feels watered down in jc2, never the less causing chaos is fun in both games, and i screw around more often than actually playing the stories. In jc1 id usually only play the agency missions when i want to unlock more fun stuff to play with honestly.
1) World feels overall more alive, roads are overall more populated when driving around in jc2, visible spawns are less frequent as well. Jc1 feels dead sometimes, and offten durring pursuits cars will spawn literally right infront of you and cause you to crash. The npc spawning is much less subtle, and sometimes detrimental when traveling at high speeds. Even on console i remeber this problem, that always pi$$ed me off a little.
2) Gunplay is actually much better in jc2, despite the guns themselves being crap, shooting them feels good. You can also dive, grapple, crouch, shoot from stunt position, and gunfights always feel overall better in jc2 over jc1, even though jc1 has pretty fun gunplay too, but you are limited in what you can do, and also limited in mobility.
3) Better driving and stunt mechanics, much better. I haven't driven much in jc1 on pc, but from the times i have driven, it's much more dificult than i remember. Crashing also doesn't much feel like crashing in jc1, vehicles seem to lack impact, in jc2 your vehicle gets visibly heavy damage from impacts, and peices fly off your car as you death tumble through the air, overall i love driving, jumping, and crashing injc2 much more than jc1. Using a keyboard also doesn't help much, but a controller wouldn't fix bad mechanics for jc1. Driving can still be fun, but it's just more fun in jc2.
4) Vehicle upgrades work well despite using the same system as weapon upgrades, and as you upgrade vehicles you get more armor, speed, handling, and im like 90% sure higher damage weapons, with many unarmed vehicles adding weapons at full upgrade level, and this is a good plus since vehicle combat in jc2 is more fun.
Overall, i think jc1 is more enjoyable, but it has some serious problems, especially with the dumb auto aim crap that's forced on you for some reason. But if you can get over those problems, then this game could be very great.

I wanted to get into the Just Cause series, so I've started with this game. After beating it, I'm here to tell you to SAVE YOUR MONEY. This game is AWFUL!!! Where do I start?
Story:
You're Rico Rodriguez, you work for the "Agency," and you're called to a fictional island by your superior to overthrow a dictator who possesses weapons of mass destruction. That's all you need to know, and it's probably all you'll remember. Cutscenes and short and feel rushed, and each one boils down to Rico receiving similar orders while often being patronized. Mission types are: fetch quests, eliminations, and base destructions/takeovers. Main and side missions are very dull and repetitive, and the game plays out so slowly that you may just forget what you're doing in any given mission as you succumb to the boredom.
Gameplay:
Driving- Some of the worst mechanics you'll find. Steering is extremely frustrating. The slightest turn sends Rico into a 360 spin and triggers a slo-mo camera effect. Nearly all the vehicles look and feel the same, save for specialized vehicles. They really differ in speed, and the slower ones are a NIGHTMARE to drive. Slower vehicles like trucks will stop in the middle of the road on uphill drives, which makes pursuits 1,000,000x worse. If you happen to veer off road and are about to slide off the face of a mountain, you can't drive back up. Despite your best efforts you'll only fall and trigger another annoying slo-mo sequence on the way down. When you hit the ground, your car will ricochet and bounce around like a Fisher Price toy. It's both annoying and funny and I hate myself for laughing when it happens.
Pursuits also make fetch quests or missions where you need your vehicle intact absolute nightmares. Enemies respawn infinitely in this game, and the game LOVES to drop enemies RIGHT IN YOUR FACE. You'll constantly find yourself in situations where maybe you're low on health or your vehicle is almost destroyed, and from nowhere comes 3 vehicles with NPCs on the mounted guns to put you out of your misery, or two choppers to fire missiles at you with surgical precision. Vehicles in general don't feel very fast, but let an NPC get behind the wheel and suddenly gain godlike speed and handling. In several pursuits, enemies have gotten into cars and within 0.73 seconds have rammed and boxed me in. What's more is that there is no drive by shooting... for you. Enemies can do it, but you can't, so have fun with that!
Some vehicles are bugged. On several occasions I've gotten into a vehicle that won't even move. Once, I even hopped into an APC tank just to get launched and start flying across the map. I couldn't make this up if I tried!
Combat- EXTREMELY dull. Every pistol and rifle feel the same. The game promises better weapons as you progress, but don't hold your breath. You'll spot the cookie cutter thing going on with each gun.
Rico is extremely squishy and takes very little effort to kill. This will be the MAIN SOURCE OF FRUSTRATION for you throughout the game. From the jump, enemies eat headshots for breakfast, and must be engaged at mid-range whether you're using a pistol or rifle. They become more and more bullet spongey throughout the game, while you become squishier.
Anything you drive will be shot down within seconds during pursuits, and you can take damage while driving. When your car turns pitch black and it's time to bail, you'll be surrounding by one of the never-ending spawns of enemies and finished off. This will happen to you AGAIN and AGAIN and AGAIN, and you'll rip out your hair or some other appendage before you break your monitor and beat your pc to death with a sledgehammer.
Grappling hook- It was obvious that this was supposed to be the game's one quirk, something to set itself apart from the competition, and boy does it SUCK! It's not a separate action and has to be selected from your weapons cycle. It's only meant to latch onto vehicles, which it does %40 of the time. You can reel into or push yourself away from attached vehicles, but often the hook disengages before you can do anything, making it a very unreliable tool. If you do reel in close enough, you can hop onto the attached vehicle and hijack it. Often when I got the prompt to jump onto the attached vehicle, Rico would perform a Hulk-style leap across the map to jump on a totally different vehicle and take me further from my destination. Good luck trying to hitch onto aircraft for a ride too. The game has a feature that allows you to call in Agency vehicles to your location, and once it arrives you can hook onto it and catch a ride, but this is only good if you're lucky enough to have the chopper depart toward your destination. You can try hitching onto enemies’ choppers too, but when you do, they just shake the line. If you're lucky enough to reach the cabin, Rico will commit suicide by flinging himself into the blades. The hook is a complete and utter failure, driving mechanics are god awful, and Rico's run is little more than a glorified snail's pace. Traversing this world in any method is a complete pain.
Overall:
I can honestly say I've never played a game where every single thing you do is a complete chore. From movement to combat to story missions, every aspect of this game is either dull or broken. AVOID THIS GAME AT ALL COSTS. Take your $7 and get yourself some lunch instead. The game could go on sale and still be overpriced. This game could be free and still be overpriced. The devs should be PAYING YOU to play this garbage, and even then, you'd still lose because that's time that you could spend playing games that are better than a solid -1/10.
