This game is great. Basically, it's an XCOM style strategy game in which you have to control a group of heroes of varying classes from 5 or 6 bloodlines in order to fight the Cadence, the monsters infecting and conquering your lands. The main mechanic of the game, outside of the implied gameplay, is that of the player character being the Immortal Ruler, having been formed by the titular Chalice and rooted to it, controls the heroes and their many decendants, as well as how they come to be, over the course of 300 years. During this time, your heroes will age, get married (to whom-ever you choose), and reproduce before eventually kicking the bucket.
Each stage of life, as well as their inherited and aquired traits, determine their specific attributes and how well they'll perfom in the field and home base. (This could range from their old age and natural intellect making them the perfect researcher or their great sight and youthful agility making them a great soldier.) Alongside this, you can research stuff, make weapons/gear, and expand your facilities much like XCOM. In this same vain, the passage of time and the Chalice itself are very pivotal points of the narrative as well as the gameplay itself. They are most used as a sort of buffer for your heroes by naturally aging them until eventual death, ensuring your need to continuously switch off to the next generation after another and strategically marry off certain heroes to breed effective heroes of stronger classes and ability for future battles down the line.
One of my personal favorite mechanics are the special items you can make with the corpses of certain Cadence spawn, after approriate research, in which you can use a weapon to literally punch your enemies into next week. Another is the "Bloodline Relics" that are made from a particularly successful hero killing enough Cadence to earn a title and a new weapon, the latter being passed down after their death to their remaining heirs and, with any luck, fulfilling their full potential after being used to kill enough Cadence, which is pretty cool.
Lastly, there is the time between the battles where you take a decade-long nap between upgrading and micro-managing your base, which can be interrupted with little events related to your heroes. These can often improve a hero, bring in more, involve the departure (sometimes permanant) of one or more that could be called away for years at a time to help a civilian, serve a prison sentence, go on a long spirit-quest, and even be sent forward through time an indeterminate number of years.
Overall, I liked it. I beat it in just under 24 hours on my first run, on normal, with many achievemnets gotten. It was fun, had many interesting mechanics, and had very balanced gameplay. I actually beat the campaign without restoring an old save (save-scumming) despite not being on the "Iron Mode" that allows for only one save for the whole game, so that every move you make is irreversible. I say the game is balanced because I have not had a drop of the luck since that which brought me through my first game because I have tried three times after with each ending in failure soon after the first level. That's still not including the Brutal difficulty, for those RTS masters.
I would expect nothing less from Double Fine.

I really enjoyed playing Massive Chalice.  It's an X-Com style game with buildings, research, ever increasing difficult enemies etc.  What is completely unique is that your heroes don't last really long.  You begin with a group of level one newbies, full of negative traits and personalities.  But you establish bloodlines and need to breed characters in arranged marriages to develop a strong bloodline.  You also will eventually get relics, which are super weapons that level up through the generations.  Overall I found the mechanics fascinating and unique.  It also had that, just keep playing for one more combat addictive-ness.
The final battle occurs after 300 years (if you survive), with battles every 8-10 years or so.  So, there is a balancing act of who to fight with, who to breed with, who trains and who researches.  There is also an extensive research tree and you won't have time to research everything, so choose wisely.
There are 3 main classes (fighter, archer, mage) with 6 different hybrid subtypes for the skill trees.
The game also has the ironman mode, which I'm playing through now on hard as my second playthrough, which will likely only take 10-12 hours as I now know what is happening.
Massive Chalice received some negative views form sickly starting heroes and not enough variety in the fights.  But the types of enemies have some really cool twists and I thought offered a lot of strategic thought when fighting.  I think most of the negative views don't hold much weight and I see them more as "features" than imbalances.  I loved every minute playing this through. 9/10 for a very unique TBS game.

Combat is overly simplified and lacks pretty much everything that would make it interesting in the long run, like a rudimentary cover system for instance. AI doesnt perform as well as one would like and is far to predictable to be enjoyable in the long run.
All in all massive chalice had the potential to become an interesting addition to the turn based tactics genre, if only the developers hadnt rounded so many corners.

+ Really good pace. Judging by the trailer and artwork, I thought the game was going to be an slow artsy feast, but that is not the case. That melancholy tone doesn't mean the game is a snooze fest at all

Overall, Lifeless Planet is an excellent atmospheric and captivating Sci-Fi  indie title that I would recommend to  every story lover.

You spend most of your time exploring the world, occasionally jumping across gaps or pushing rocks but mostly just walking around. The few puzzles really aren't anything extraordinary and the solutions to all of them are immediately obvious. The real enjoyment comes from exploring the vast and impressive environments and finding clues about what happened to this world and the Russians who first settled it. The story is definitely intriguing and kept me entertained the entire way through the game, which is good, because the exploration part unfortunately becomes quite boring by the end of the game.  The first two hours are fantastic!  The last two to three hours, are mediocre and bland.
Early on there are rock specimens, scientist logs, and intractable locations all over the place, but by the end of the game, there's pretty much nothing hidden for you to find. I feel the designer, by placing these items throughout the early levels, deliberately designed the game to make you waste time looking for something when there is nothing to be found. Either that or he just ran out of ideas for the second half of the game. I stopped bothering to explore about 75% of the way through the game and instead just kept to the obviously marked path since there was apparently nothing else to find or see in the giant open areas.
There are a few areas where the game gets in the way of the immersion. These are only minor at first, but they quickly become more prominent in the late game. Two minor aspects break the game's own rules: oxygen that you only need sometimes and jet fuel that is infinite until you move into the next area. The major problems I constantly experienced were:
- the astronaut sometimes hits an invisible wall that prevents you from progressing down an otherwise obvious path
- a rock will look like something you can stand on but the game doesn't let you
- the astronaut suddenly dies mid-jump because you jumped toward an area you are not supposed to be able to reach
- when walking forward up a steep incline, if you jump you lose all forward motion and actually go backwards (this one is a huge annoyance considering how often you have to jump uphill)
More commentary on that last major flaw... This game is a platforming game, and the fact that the platforming is broken is a huge dissapointment.  I was honestly getting angry at the game with how difficult the jump mechanics make it to follow an obvious path through the world.
The story and environments start really strong, but they significantly decrease at the end of the game. If you want to experience a good story and uncover an interesting history of a fictional distant planet, then certainly give this a shot. If you want a good game, you are probably best off looking somewhere else.

I know this company doesn't exactly have a great reputation as far as standing behind their games and I've been pretty disappointed a couple of times myself. But in all fairness, I've played this game a short bit and it was at least "OK". It ain't exactly epic and there are things I would add to it, but I did find it entertaining so far and intend to go back and play it some more. Considering Steam's new refund policy, if you think you might like it, it might be worth a try because you can always get your money back. A lot depends on what you think you expect the game to be... It's pretty basic and uncomplicated. At least I haven't found any glaring bugs or anything like that yet.
I'd describe the game as a basic simulation in which you start off with a horse (with single log trailer) and a chainsaw. It seems like you can pretty much fall any tree in sight of the town you start in, saw it into 4 sections, then haul each section (one-by-one) back to the lumber mill for money. There's a light RPG element as you gain experience/level for selling logs, for which you get a point to allocate toward a skill (higher selling prices for logs, cheaper equipment prices, etc.).
I've only gotten so far in the game as of this review, but after level 3, you can buy a garage (which opens up the ability to buy tractors and other logging equipment... Couldn't afford them yet myself). A level 6 you can buy an office to accept contracts and so on. In higher levels, it appears (I haven't got that far yet) that you can hire employees, possibly buy the lumber mill, make stuff to sell there, etc.
Anyway, I think this game may suit some, but not others. For me, I give it a tentative thumbs up, subject to change. I know buying again from this company is scary, I almost didn't do it either. But so far, even though there's things I think they could/should add, I do like it better than anything else I've bought from them. And I haven't seen much about the game itself except people angry at the company for past burns (rightfully so). So, I thought I'd try to post something informative to help those on the fence. Good luck with your choice.

For 51 cents (on sale) you get an everlasting puzzle game.  Usually with cheap puzzle games they are short and once you finish them there is no replayablity factor.  Here, with the addition of daily puzzles - 3  new sets of 25 boards/levels every day, it's unending and you certainly get your money's worth out of it.  In main game, there are 5 sets of puzzles, each set of varying amount - 82 boards in total.  The first 3 sets are very easy.
If you don't random click your way through the easy beginning sets but make sure you work it out, then it will greatly help you with the King and daily levels and get you used to patterns.  This puzzle game has nothing to do with chess (apart from how the knight moves) but I would say you do have to be able to think ahead at least 2-3 moves - actually backward from the solution.
It's a pick it up just do one board type game which is great but I wish you could save mid way through a board.  I did find most dailies to be a bit harder than the King pack.  For achievement hunters, wanting the quickest/easiest route - some daily level tips -
- Don't even try and do a daily pack, know you are going to play this over a few days.
- Some days just seem quite a bit easier than others.
- On each day in each of 3 pack I found 3-5 boards that were about King level.
- Sometimes A1 etc boards are the easiest but not always.
- Only play boards that have 3 spare spaces in them - ignore the two space ones, I found having  space to move around easier.
If you love work it out puzzles, no timer just point n click then I do recommend this really fun game.  I loved it.

The game Knights is a very relaxing, but a game that needs focus. The game is very good for its style and its puzzles. The game also has a lot of replay value.
Knights is in a chess style, with the only pieces being knights that you move, this style is accompanied by a chessboard that the pieces lay on. The knights thus move in the same way they do in chess, this is a very good game mechanic, as it gives you something you are familier with, such as a chess knight, and making you use it differently, as in these puzzles. This use of only the knight is interesting, as it is the only piece in chess that can jump over blocked pieces, as it moves the strangest out of all the pieces, thus giving it a special interest.
The puzzles in Knights are very fun, and challenging, you have to move the red knights into the red spaces, and the blue knights into the blue spaces, which is easy at first, but it ends up getting challenging quickley (as this is a bloody video game!), and you need to find new ways to move pieces around to achieve the end goal. Eventually more obstcles are introduced, such as blocked spaces, and outcast knights (with no space to go, so they end up getting in the way).
Knights has a system that is not unlike Lyne's, where you unlock daily puzzles. These daily puzzles help to provide much more replay value. If you finish the main puzzles, you can just play the daily puzzles. The only problem I have encountered with the daily puzzles thus far is that, because they are randomly generated, they will sometimes be generated solved. I am unaware if I have come across an impossible puzzle, as it's hard to tell if my failure is from a lack of skill or the lack of solvability. A massive pro to having daily puzzles is if a puzzle is too hard, you can always wait till tomorrow to get a puzzle matching your skill level, and you are not unable to progress.
Overall Knights is a very well made game, if you enjoy puzzle games like Lyne, Knights is a great choice, or even if you love a game of chess, Knights will be a familier friend. The puzzles are quite addictive, once you get the hang of it, and the daily puzzles give you a reason to not uninstall it after completing.

A very familiar game to any returning chess players. The game delves into numerous possibilities of positioning your piece and making "the right move", as highlighted by where you should put the coloured Knight in its corresponding tile. The only one chess piece featured, The Knight, quite obviously, is secretly a brilliant concept to improve one's ability to perform in an average game of chess.
The game specializes in providing the perspective of the game limited to only the Knight, meaning you are able to narrow down your opportunities in taking out another player's piece by considering the move limitations and potential of your Knights you are playing.
Moreover, I would like to commend the creative input they put in the interface. Using not only simple buttons to navigate a player but also provide content that is straight to the point and adds to an overall polished product.
Other than that, there's nothing much to say about it anyway. I find the game engaging and would definitely try to get all the achievements up , post-review.

You know when you play something too much, to a point you dream in it's mechanics, with it's UI (I know some of you know what I'm talking about).
Well this is the first time those dreams have ever reinforced tactics that are relevant to real combat/combat sports.
Circle away from the power (weapon) hand, be all the way in or all the way out.
These are principles I was taught when I trained and are tactics that also work well in Exanima.
I have never tried fencing, but someone who has said they had used fencing techniques to win fights in game.  Which makes sense, as when combining the all the way in/out technique with thrusting you get a very convincing fencing simulator.
But even beyond that, because of the way an arm falls or the way one weapon parries another, it' possible to continue an attack after a parry and with good aim still reach your mark, which makes for some very fencing like action.
When you are playing well and against the more advanced AI, fights can look just as beautiful and or sloppy as any real brawl, and you can really see where the devs are going with this.
At the beginning though, when you are flailing around like a marionette piloted by a drunk puppet master, it is far less fight sim, and far more Thunderbirds on ice.
(*The game looks crap when you are crap at it.)
This learning curve is nearly motion sickness inducing, but it is a curve and not a cliff like say, dwarf fortress. It's intuitive and once you get it, it sticks.
I had never heard of the open world RPG this serves as a form of prequel for, but having read up on the project, I'm intrigued. While I will say it sounds grand and ambitious, it's certainly doable to some degree and the devs have shown good knowledge and expertise in the field.
There are currently 5 levels to explore in story mode, with many lore filled books to discover.
This is a work in progress, and while I thought the combat was a grand undertaking, it sounds as though the devs have even more ambitious plans when it comes to their A.I. system. Having yet to be implemented, I'm very intrigued to see where that goes.
What has been implimented is very cool, as not all npc's are hostile which can make for some tense stand offs.
There are some nice puzzles, and as a testiment to this game I was actually intrigued enough to spend my time working them out and earning that feeling of satisfaction through completion. (I hardly ever do that, and often grab a walk through so as to get back to combat etc.)
The only issue with some of these puzzles is how frustrating it can be to orientate objects exactly right in order hold up or down a lever etc.
Arena acts as a form of campaign, all on it's own. Where you can be a "Shadows and dust" style manager of Gladiators, equiping your warriors and sending them to either die or return victorious.
There is also a system for hiring A.I. controlled warriors who fight for or with you, though I have found these guys to be dead weight so far.
(*Correction. Having learned to better equip/train and select which bouts to send my hirelings into, they have proven a quite valuable and fun filled edition to Arena.)

Wow, where to start, I'm not usually a fan of dungeon crawlers or games that are somewhat limited yet this game somehow has me addicted and it's definitely down to the combat and physics system.
There are so many ways this game could have gone wrong and there are some ways that it did (or has currently) gone wrong yet the pro's outweigh the cons by a mile. The game's physics work well and make the game so much more interesting, the Arena mode is very entertaining and thrilling, the main mode is good for what it is and even though I haven't got very far in it currently I can see myself completing it. However one thing I would like to suggest is a random dungeon mode if possible, even if it was just a bunch of pre-built ones for different levels of the dungeon it would make it a whole lot more interesting and fun.
So the main juice of the gameplay is the physics and it does it almost perfectly, there are some minor things that could be tweaked and changed or added but currently I have no major or really minor issues with it personally. You have to play the game tactically if you are going to win, you can't just charge at someone and expect to win because you won't although charging someone isn't nessesarily bad as that can be used to your own advantage if you know what you're doing, an example of this would be stopping them from attacking because they won't be able to swing at you very easily.
Each way of fighting is unique and requires altering your strategy. Got a long♥♥♥♥♥pipe? Get some distance and fight from afar. Got a small cleaver? Get up close, dodge and counter. The enemy got a long♥♥♥♥♥pipe? Don't try dodging left and right because you will get most likely get hit.
Blocking is done automatically (From my knowledge I haven't actually used the manual really as I prefer figuring it out on my own) and works quite well and depending on your characters skills that will alter how well they do at it. Enemies also block your attacks quite well so be careful.
Final note, dodging someone and then smashing them in the back of the head with a steel pipe is extremely satisfying.
Final Final Note, so is slitting someone's throat with a knife.
Arena - Recurit characters to fight for you and Hire characters to fight with you as you run a gladiator school (I guess that's what it's called). Fight small to begin with but make your way up the ladder getting better equipment to fight the harder people. Very fun and very satisfying.
Campaign/Story/Main - Wake up in a dungeon with a torch and try to survive inside the cave trying to find better weapons and armour.
Not needed and won't effect the review but will definitely make the game better.
Random Generation - Survive as many floors of dungeons as possible as it gets progressively harder.
Random Variants - Same as above but just pre-built dungeons, maybe not infinite but with a boss at the end.
Exanima is an amazing game and is something I cannot wait to see progress, I believe there is another game that will be coming after this based with the same gameplay so I cannot wait to see that and will definitely be purchasing that aswell.

The original Deus Ex is a classic game. It was from an era where it was normal for games to have demos. The demo of the original Deus Ex is something that people played repeatedly back in the day in an attempt to see and do everything that they could in the demo. It felt like there was so much to do and see that you'd always find something new if you played through again.
That many of the locations were real world locations was also something that was neat back in the day. Okay, it's still cool today. Back then however, it was special. It was interesting to see real world pictures of Liberty Island along side the locations in the game to see how close they came to recreating it.
The full game was full off all sorts of neat and fun things you could see and experience, especially if you took the time to explore the levels. It's not uncommon to hear tales of people discovering something new even after playing through the same countless times.
It was from a time when (unless I'm remember wrong) playing at 1024x768 (if even that) was about the best most could expect.
After years of development, we now have Deus Ex: Revision.
So, does Revision make for am improved version of Deus Ex that will make it the game we wish it could have been back in the day?  Or, is it an unwanted, unneeded renovation that ruins a classic game that was perhaps best left alone?
In a way, it's both. I think your opinion of it will depend on what you're looking for.
If you're looking for Deus Ex with updated technical aspects (i.e., textures, works better with high resolution that wasn't available or practical back in 2000 etc.) but want the maps to remain the same with perhaps a fresh coat of paint, you might be disappointed.
If you want a more renovated Deus Ex with in some cases, expanded, more complicated maps in some places and a more up to date look in others that can (at times) allow you to re-experience Deus Ex from a somewhat fresh perspective then this mod might be for you.
Deus Ex: The Revision is an ambitious mod. This isn't just Deus Ex with improved textures and higher resolution.
As the name suggests, this is also a revision. Renovation could also apply when it comes to the maps.
In some maps, the basic layout is the same with some changes and/or additions. There are some that are more or less the same just with updated textures.
In other cases, the maps are a lot different with only some familiar elements remaining.  It's almost like an alternate universe version of the places we know. Being in a place that is and yet isn't what you remember might be disconcerting depending on what you're after in the game.
If you don't mind change and perhaps even needed some change to give yourself a reason to play Deus Ex again (i.e., perhaps feeling that as good as it is, it's become too repetitive) you might be in luck.
If however, you just want to play through it again as part of an (as an example) annual play through then the changes might leave you feeling lost with a feeling that this isn't your Deus Ex.
The changes do go beyond the maps and textures.
Some of the augmentations are also not as effective. As well, JC's weapons skills seems less effective until upgraded to in some cases, advanced. There are also more enemies in some locations and the locations of some others have changed. As well, from what I've seen, you do take more damage and the enemies can take more damage compared to playing on the same difficulty level on the original Deus Ex, but this might be my imagination. Whether or not these are good things is a matter of opinion. Some will like it, others will not.
There is a new soundtrack. I personally found it to be hit or miss. I generally prefered the original tracks but this is a matter of opinion. There is thankfully an option to switch back and forth.
There is also one nice fix from the original. There is one character that you can save early on in the game. In the original, he wouldn't make another appearance. There were conversations for him in the files however. In the revision, he will be at the location of the character who sends you on the mission to save the character at the two other times you can visit said character. I know that probably sounds too generic but I don't want to spoil anything for those who haven't played the original.
Another neat change is that some of the newspapers now have at least some legible text that matches the story you can read if you click on them. I believe the same also applies to some of the books, but may be mistaken. Yes, it's a minor thing, but I think it's an example of something that did enhance the experience. I'm sure this is something that also required a lot of work. Kudos to the team for taking the effort and time to do this.
Speaking of time and effort, I think it's important to recognize the work and time that went into this mod, especially given that it's free (although it does require the Steam version of Deus Ex to be installed). Even if one doesn't like or agree with the changes, I think we still need to remember how much time and effort the team has put into this.
If you're looking for your next (annual or however often you play through the game) play through but want the Deus Ex you know and are fine with it, it might be better to stick with the original. However, given that this mod is free, it still might be worth a try if you're willing to take the risk that you won't like it.
If you haven't played Deux Ex in a while and need an excuse to play again and/or just want a new challenge and can accept the changes then this might be worth at least a play through.
I've you never played Deus Ex (or at least never played from start to finish), I honestly think it might be better to play the original at least once before giving this a try.

Let's be clear here: I didn't dislike this game, but I wouldn't really recommend it to anyone, either. The love and care of a single man is shown in beautiful atmospheric music and, occasionally, the environments. However, this isn't enough to carry the whole game.
PROS:
- As I mentioned, GREAT music and occasionally magnificent environments
- Draws you in
- Interesting story
- Enemies are awesome
CONS:
- The jump and the fact that the game is built around it
- Put the rock in the hole puzzles
- Very noticeable changes in quality
- Poor pacing
Lifeless Planet's first hour drew me in; I wanted to find out more about the mystery. I was genuinely curious. But as the game continued, bits of story were more and more sparse and rapidly decreasing in cohesiveness. By the end, I found the story component of the game intriguing but not quite satisfying.
My first impression of the graphics were that they were pretty mediocre; in fact, I even thought the game looked pretty ugly in one of the first few environments, approximately an hour in. Then, suddenly, the next level was gorgeous, colour-rich, and stunning to look at. Unfortunately, the game kept going back and forth between beautiful and meh scenery. While the music really helped me enjoy the game, the change in quality sometimes broke the immersion.
But man, were the enemies cool. I loved them. I won't give anything away, but if you're into interesting enemy design, you'd probably like this game.
My least favourite part of this game was the jump (as well as the mechanical arm, but that part felt rushed and rather dumb). The jump was SO annoying that I became increasingly frustated with the mechanics of crossing a simple path. Some environments paired with the jump simply did not work, and it was infuriating just how simple the platforming I was screwing up was.
Even the extended jet-pack time mechanic, by far the most fun thing in the game, kept being taken away at convenient times after I'd stopped needing it; same with the threat of running out of air. It doesn't seem real, but like it's an in-game scenario. The puzzles were occasionally interesting, but were basically never challenging, which saddened me. Some moments in this game were really cool, but it feels like a mixed bag.
In the end, I liked this game somewhat. The story definitely had some interesting parts, and I was invested enough to want to battle the jump out to the end. I'm not completely satisfied, but I am hopeful for what the creator could make with more money and resources.

You spend the entire game as a little astronaut man running around this planet with seam-heavy level transitions and a very linear path (not straight but definitely always on a rail). Given the type of gameplay, the linearity is definitely appropriate, it's just that it's a big, dull planet with some pretty ridiculous obviously computer heightmap generated canyons and crevices that steal away any suspension of disbilief.
But it does make for some interesting sci-fi. The concept is interesting. It's kind of a movie type of plot where all you do is sit back and learn, slowly, what it is you're looking at. The gameplay is extremely dull, however, because the only challenges, with the exceptional of three or four mini-puzzles, are "don't jump too far" and "*splat!* no not that ledge, the other one". You have no weapon and there are only about three types of things you can push or carry. That's it, the rest of the time you're running. Run! Run, Forrest, run!
With simplistic graphics and limited gameplay, I still recommend the game, but I rate it a 3.3/5.

I don't review many games, although there are several that I really do enjoy playing.  This Buzz Aldrin Space Program Manager (BASPM for future reference in this post) is a very addicting game to play.
BASPM is not anywhere near as interactive as Kerbal Space Program, so keep that in mind; and the grapics are 2D images of 3D renderings without animation (Just X,Y translation through the frame), however it is an extremely good and rewarding strategy/management game to play.
BASPM combines a sandbox in one aspect with the cold war space race (you may pick the CCCP or the USA) and rewrite history.  Also, with the GSA side, it allows for future ideas and designs so as it isn't limited to just the cold war.
Although I haven't tried the multiplayer, it seems that BASPM could be as interesting as a 4K strategy game with a strong focus on managing finances, people, each program in general, as well as extras such as EVA and docking (and things of that nature that generally don't appear on the flight plan that I have found).
All in all, BASPM is a very enjoyable game especailly if you're a fan of the space program.  If you're a space history buff, I can't recommend this game enough.

This is in fact a VERY interesting game. Not only for those who like management of a corporation which has to deal with timeplanning, staff improvement, money and pioneer work but for all who like space and science and history too.
It brings you near the development of spacetravel since the 1950's, with conquest and failure, and it tells you the story about the journey to the moon, with prooven background from no less an astronaut than Dr. Edwin Buzz Aldrin - yes, the one who was with his colleagues Neil Armstrong and Michael Collins on the mission that first landed a manned craft on the moon.
I mean, folks, the man who helped develop this management simulation was actually on the moon! And he was not just there, but on the first ever mission that landed on it!!
In my opinion this alone is reason enough to buy this game.
But anyway: it is not just a game, this is history made into a game with lots of fun, a pioneer simulation management with first hand perspective - where you can take this "first hand perspective" literally, indeed!
If you are a space and history enthusiast this is a "must buy".

The game is really cheap and the puzzles, while falling a bit on the "just try and it will eventually get solved"  problem are still interesting enough.
But this game made a mistake, a big mistake. The layout of the background together with the transitions from a menu to another (or level to level) is super awkward for the eye and creates a really unpleasent effect. As dumb as it sounds, you are constantly changing levels in the game and so it becomes tiresome and hardly bearable really fast, because of this, I cannot recommend it.

Not a bad time sink for a little bit, but the later levels really become tight and oppressive. There later levels feel less like a chess puzzle and more like a one-by-one slide puzzle, which drains you fast. I'd recommend Lyne over this game, if you had the option. But, if this is on sale and you're looking to kill an hour or two, it's hard to argue with the price, just don't expect an enjoyable late game.

Gameplay:
How to play the game:
Very simple, anyone who's ever liked playing chess will definitely learn how this game is played instantly. The game is about moving red and blue knights over boards of chess to red/blue highlighted tiles, as in a game of chess, knights can only move in L-shaped direction (2 tiles straight and then 1 tile to side), the knights can jump over whatever it's standing in their way, as long as the tile they're meant to go to is empty. To clear a level, every red knight has to stand in a red tile, as well as every blue knight in blue tile (the easiest  levels only contain knights of 1 color).
What to expect of the base game (level packs and levels):
There are 82 levels in the base part of the game total divided into 5 level packs - the pawn pack, the rook pack, the bishop pack, the queen pack and the king pack. With pawn being easiest to king being hardest, resembling to value of the chess figures (rook is easier than bishop). Why exactly 82 levels? It's rather simple, allow me to explain: Pawn pack is the easiest, the board sizes in pawn pack are 3x3 tiles, so 9 tiles total, there are 9 levels in the pawn pack. Rook is on 4x3 tile sized boards, meaning there are 12 tiles and levels. Bishop is 4x4 (16 levels), queen is 5x4 (20 levels) and king is 5x5 (25 levels).
If you struggle with one specific level, you can always skip it and return to it later or not return to it at all, as unlocking new pack doesn't require you to complete all levels in the pack you are in, only most of the levels in a pack have to be completed in order to unlock a next one.
Additional information about the levels:
But of course, to make every one of the levels unique and more and more challenging as the game gets harder, most of the levels have some tiles on the board blocked, meaning no knight figure can access them. Even later in the game (starting from queen pack), there will also be yellow knights. It doesn't matter where yellow knights stand at all. They are there just to make the game harder for you by blocking the red and blue knights resulting in more trouble of getting them to the highlighted tiles. Of course you can move the yellow knights, but also only in the L-shaped ways. You can reset and exit any level at any time, everything auto-saves.
Daily levels:
The game has also a feature that automatically generates completely random 75 levels you can play everyday, divided into 3 25-level packs. Pack A, B and C. Those packs reset daily and have no influence on the main packs that are the same forever.
Motivational words:
Upon pausing the game or finishing any of the main packs, you are given motivational texts, being reminded how capable you are, really nice little addition to the game.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Game's design:
Before launching the game, you'll see a small options window allowing you to set the graphic settings, the resolution of the game, and whether you want the game to be windowed or not. Even on the highest graphic settings and resolution, the game design is still so simple that every computer/laptop without exception could run it.
The music was great to the theme of the game. Simple and calming.
Overall the way the game looks is just the way a puzzle game like KNIGHTS should look like in my opinion.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary of pros & cons:
Pros:
-Great and challenging puzzles, over 3 hours of fun in levels of various difficulties
-Easy to run on any PC
-Nice base price of 0.99€, discounted to 0.49€ during sales
-Very easy to understand
-Ideal for people of all ages, from children to elders
-Great atmosphere of the game, relaxing music and fitting graphics
-Almost endless, considering there are 75 new levels automatically generated every day
-Great motivational texts
Cons:
-Being a simple puzzle game could also make the game repetitive and boring for some people
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Final words:
I did not know what to expect of the game when I've been buying it for the discounted price of 0.49€, but after starting it, I could almost instantly tell the game is great. I got more addicted to it than I would expect and even though I'm generally not a big fan of puzzle games, I really couldn't help myself but to leave this one a positive review. Definitely worth buying even its full price, though waiting for a 50% discount can always work too. Since the game also drops trading cards, big % of the game's price will still return to you through selling the trading cards, even though the game itself is already pretty cheap. If you are a big fan of puzzle games, I'd suggest to give KNIGHTS a shot as soon as you're able to, I am pretty sure you won't regret it.

Onikira looks like an awesome game by the video and pictures on the Steam Sales Page... However, for a game just out of Early Access it has a few too many basic day one glitches that should have been sorted out in general tests before even considering leaving EA. Also in its current state, it’s worse than what it was in Greenlight.
Firstly, I haven't finished the Campaign as I played 1hour, quit and came back only to find out I had to start the level again as checkpoints don't save and there is no save game. Along with no save-game I can’t even continue a level due to Crashes and Re-Validating Steam Files deleting my Save File for this game. With that said I can’t recommend you buy this and here is why in my Pro’s and Con’s so far.
Pros:
♦ Decent Storyline so far (I can't comment fully as I haven't finished the game fully as of release due to crashes and Save File Deletions)
♦ Good Soundtrack
♦ Awesome tooltips for some of the controls (I say some as some are still fully not explained and are in Controller talk all the way through the game even if you are using a keyboard. Also, I'm not sure if these tooltips would change from Keyboard to Controller if I had a controller plugged in, but they worked for Keyboard)
♦ Perfect Controller/Keyboard Support (I say this in terms of working, figuring out what buttons do what may be a different story)
♦ Awesome Artwork
♦ Stunning Graphics
♦ Cool hidden level features such as the Photo frame Switch lock idea (Keeps the game interesting and unique)
♦ Awesome Re-mappable Controls for Keyboard
♦ Steam Trading Cards
♦ Awesome number of Achievements
♦ Nice variety of weapons, attacks and enemies (See cons Relating to Weapons)
♦ Great variety of scenery, obstacles and such between fights sort of adding a nice platformer aspect to the game
♦ Awesome Devs who seem to try to listen to feedback as best as possible (I’ve talked to multiple Devs before but it looks like they have let this die… I’ve just posted in the Discussion part of the game and will wait to hear from them)
♦ Eargasmic Sound effects (For when there isn't a really loud highpitched crackling sound)
Cons:
♦ Porting to Fuse when the Game has never worked properly on Steam (Someone asked where the Devs had been and they responded “Busy Porting to Fuse”. I find this weird as there are many bug/glitch reports and crash reports for the Steam Version that haven’t been fixed. Plus Onikira, has never worked more than 50% in Greenlight and out of Greenlight for it to warrant being ported to another platform.
♦ No Difficulty Settings (This is annoying as there is no incentive to play the game over on a harder difficulty or for bragging rights etc)
♦ Checkpoints aren't actually Checkpoints (I say this in the sense that I played for a long time and got past the first boss and went to main menu and had to start the whole level again, not from checkpoint)
♦ No save points (This is really bad as you have to play a whole level before you can leave and come back and from the looks of the first level the levels are really long)
♦ 50% of the time the controls are in controller language and 50% in keyboard (This is bad as it confuses both markets and doesn't satisfy one. There should be a way to select your method of input which converts the whole game into the method of input chosen)
♦ Can only scroll backwards through Highscores until Light On Your Feet (This is annoying as you should be able to loop through the categories and not hit what I call is a "Brick Wall". Also if you try to scroll backwards past Light on your Feet and then Scroll Forward through the categories again, you have to keep clicking forward until it changes category depending how many times you clicked to try and go backwards past Light on your Feet)
♦ Continue isn't a Continue (It's more a Level Select as you aren't continuing off where you left but infact the start of the Level you have selected to continue you from. In my understanding continue would be to continue where you left off)
♦ Can pay $20 to get an extra copy of the Game but the game doesn’t have multiplayer (Why would I want an extra Game? I’d rather ingame content)
♦ No advanced graphics options
♦ No multiplayer whatsoever, not even co-op or verse mode
♦ You can pause on the Combat Arena Main Menu and still choose game modes whilst the Pause Menu is Open (This is bad as each Menu overlays each other and you can click on both menus at once)
♦  You can pause over the top of Tooltips and Dialogue in game (This  shouldn’t be able to happen until the tooltip or dialogue box has gone)
♦ No voice over (Not needed but would really enhance the game)
♦ Inconsistency between game names On the Main Menu it's called Combat Arena... however it's called Challenge Arena when you enter it (This is an inconsistency that shouldn’t ever exist)
♦ No way to tell what keyboard control lines up to what xbox control (For example on an Xbox Controller it says "A" is "Jump" on an Keyboard it says "Jump" is "SpaceBar" but "SpaceBar" is not "A")
♦ Can buy Upgrades from the Soul Shop for Blades I don't seem to have yet (This is weird, as I shouldn't be able to purchase an upgrade to a blade if I don't actually own it)
♦ Beat the First Level and didn’t unlock a new Weapon (This I found weird as mentioned above I can buy upgrades for multiple Weapons when I don’t own them)
♦ Default controls for PC have conflicts (This is because "W" is set as up and "W" is set as special. Both these have default Alt buttons but this shouldn't be the case)
♦ Souls stack on death (You can get a checkpoint near a bunch of vases, enemies or whatever containing soul points for the soul shop, collect the souls and just keep dying and repeating to collect an unlimited amount)
♦ Leaderboards are broken (Blank names, scores and positions until you highlight over them to make them appear. Some people’s names are just ????. Also, no way to easily locate your Steam Friends or your own score)
♦ Have to press the "Main Menu" button twice to get to the Main Menu from within game
♦ Level Select is broken (I Started a new game, beat The Breach and says I got a different score and rank to what I got. Also says I have beaten Daimyo's End as it has a score and rank when I haven't played it in this playthrough yet. All other levels are still locked)
♦ When continuing levels they randomly Crash (I've witnessed crashes on the first two levels, as I can't progress any further due to the crashes, after the level loads and during fights.
♦ Re-Validating Files Deleted my Save-File (I re-validated to try and fix the crash problem and lost my current save which should never happen unless stated in an update as nothing should have been broken)
♦ Random Crashes when on menus (I went to select a level and got a random crash even before I got to the loading screen)
♦Load Screen animation is laggy and slow (This just makes the game look poor even before you have got into the game, which is bad in any case).
♦Combat Arena 100% Broken & Never Worked (Major Game Modes shouldn’t be broken)

Oh man, I'm 7 hrs in and let me tell you this game is hard, the combat is hard. I've only spent about an hour dungeon crawling. After getting beaten to a pulp in the main game a few times I decided to spend most of my time in the arena and practice modes. The learning curve is steep on this one. At first the combat feels very clunky and frustrating, however this makes it great. The first time I sidestepped an opponents attack, only to dash forward and thrust my sword into his gut was soooo satisfying. Or to step forward into your opponents two handed hammer and stop their swing short, then step back and take a wide swing right at their head... that solid connect feels so good! Eventually all of your bumbling around becomes gracefull once you start to feel out the nuance of combat. Dashing forward to lock weapons with your enemy, then dashing to the side with a quick turn and nailing them in their exposed back side! The difficulty of the combat really rewards skilled/patient gameplay and leads to a lot of satisfying moments.
But like I said, I am 7 hours in, and I still feel like I"m getting the hang of it! I feel like I could sink in another 7 and still not have it completely down. As I said above, I have spent most of my time thus far in arena mode, just grinding through matches. The main game seems very difficult, wandering through a dungeon with permadeath hanging over your head and not a healing potion in sight. I look forward to playing through it once I have mastered the combat a little better.
I recommend this game, I would've been happy to spend the 15$ just for arena mode and the chance to play around with this really neat combat system. I would also recommend though that you don't just throw your money at this game without doing a little research, as it is not for everyone. It is definately not a pick up and play sort of game, you will NEED to practice. So go watch a few youtube reviews, I've also seen a few instructional videos that help explain how the combat works.

Before I bought this game, I watched some gameplay of it on YouTube. I thought "Hey that doesn't look so hard"
Oh how wrong I was.
This game is hard. Very hard. Harder than Dark Souls. Damage is based on speed and location, as well as resistances. Combat is at first wobbly, and just moving is wack as all hell (movement is my number one problem with this game. The movement controls on keyboard are wonky and rediculous. This may ruin the game for some, but personally I find the rest of the gameplay to more than make up for it) Aside from moving, this game is very enjoyable. Combat is instense, and hits are meaty. Kills look and sound brutal, and the health system is great. Not sure what the blue bar is for yet, though it's likely it will be used for magic abilities like it is in Sui Generis (another game the devs are working on. Built on the same engine as Exanima). I also feel to make up for the movement and hard to adjust to controls, the devs had damage deal in favour of the player. While you can still be one or two hit killed, this happens rarely and only to enemies which can understandably do that. Your lesser enemies will hardly do this. I was however able to kill an enemy in two swift strikes, which also made me fell (excuse my French) ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic.
Overall, a very hard and satisftying game. Perhaps in the current state not worth the $20 I payed (god damned conversion rates), but I'm confident the devs will update the game further, and warrant that price.

-when you have to blow up a ship there are two extra reinforced doors.

Revision clearly pushes the limits of what the original game's engine is capable of, and with the addition of the high-res textures it looks great for what it is. The expanded locations also give more of a sense that there is a world outside of your immediate surroundings, especially in Paris and Hong Kong. The soundtrack is also excellent; like everything else it's instantly recognizable as Deus Ex, but adds additional atmosphere and depth that just wasn't possible when the game was released more than a decade ago. It's a world so familiar, yet different enough to be new again.
One thing to note - the game is harder than the original, at least on realistic difficulty. There are also a few things that are harder to find, such as Smuggler's hideout on New York.
I'm also experiencing a bug which causes the assault rifle to be unable to use the 20mm HE ammo - every time I try to switch ammo types to use the HE it switches immediately back to bullets. None of the other weapons with multiple ammo types do this. Maybe I'm doing something wrong?

Firstly, some context: way, way back in the year 2000, my dad brought home the latest monthly instalment of PC Powerplay magazine (I forget the month, my memory's not *that* good). Much like any other month, there was a disk on the front, containing a bunch of demos for all the hot new games which were due to be released in the next couple of months. Out of all the demos I played and subsequently forgot about, one in particular caught my attention, one for a game called Deus Ex.
The gameplay was fun, the level design was brilliantly unconventional, but the thing that really drew me in while I was exploring Liberty Island was Deus Ex's unparalleled freedom of choice. I ended up playing that demo over and over again until I'd found all possible routes for assaulting/sneaking into the Statue, saved my pocket money for the full thing and have done a full playthrough of it at least once a year ever since. I love it inside-out back-to-front upside-down, it is still the closest thing to a perfect game that I have ever played.
So, as a huge Deus Ex fan since day one, how do I feel about Revision? How does one improve upon perfection? Revision aims to do this by taking the game's existing levels and fleshing them out for a more satisfying experience. Some updates are minor to the point of being simple touch ups (Liberty Island, Battery Park), some make the originals completely unrecognisable (most Paris levels, Area 51), but all have a distinct flavour and, relatively speaking, feel less like video game levels and more like real locations.
The only two levels which I feel could do with a bit more work are the Hell's Kitchen hub (confusing layout) and the Paris Catacombs (I ended up running around in circles for nearly 30 mins before finding the exit), but these are relatively minor gripes when taking into accout how good the mod is overall.
And then there's the little details. New Vision and HDTP come with Revision by default, as do Biomod and Shifter, meaning that Revision is all you'll need to install for a fully updated Deus Ex experience. It's unfortunate that the GMDX mod wasn't included aswell, fingers crossed for a future update.
It's worth mentioning that the new soundtrack is really well done, too. While the originals do provide a nice hit of nostglia, objectively speaking the ugly midi samples of the original have not aged well at all. The new soundtrack maintains the same feel of the originals while showing some tasteful restraint, walking a fine line which should please newcomers and purists alike.
Overall, this mod is a must for anyone who's played the original Deus Ex to death and wants something new to explore or anyone who's had Deus Ex recommended to them but can't get into the vanilla game. And hey, if you're skeptical it's totally free, so it's not like it'll cost you anything anyway.

This is a one of its kind gem of SIM/Management genre.  The game play is exactly as described in the title - Space Program Management.  You do not fly any space craft manually, nor do you get your hands on any parts to assemble one.  What you do is management - draw the roadmap of space race for your country (US/USSR), recruit the most talented people of the era, set up goals and projects and beat your opponent to moon.
My favorite part of the game is how it successfully captures the tension you would feel in that position.  Each turn (season) you will get reports on the missions (read: progress) your oppenent carried out in alerting red background.  Those reports sometimes really make me nervous as beating opponent to certain key milestones can be crucial to my roadmap and the success of the whole program.  Another good part is the uncertainty of space missions.  However well you prepared, your mission could still blow up right in your face in the very beginning of launching stage.  Not to mention you can't afford to get nearly well prepared in the tension of the race a lot of the times.
9.5/10  would be 10/10 once those tiny little things got polished.

Massive Chalice is an overall great game, but not without its flaws. For starters, because The Cadence attacks semi-randomly, you may only get one or two battles out of a given team of heroes before their children take over for them, with the heroes being on the far side of decrepitude before their first deployment. On the other hand, you may get the experience of entering battle with a team of fresh young heirs to their respective houses, who then battle again and again, well into their winter years, as they come out of retirement for one last defense of the kingdom. Naturally, this latter case always feels pretty awesome. That said, individual members of a house can end up feeling indistinct if they don't see enough action during their lifetimes, and that you can have six different houses but only five deployed heroes can result in one house being completely forgotten unless you find some other way for them to contribute (such as staffing various kingdom facilities). This trend can be mitigated through the system by which the weapon used by a truly legendary member of a house can be passed down through the bloodline and level up independently of the heroes wielding it.
All in all, if you like tactical games like X-COM, Massive Chalice is absolutely worth a look. The tactical gameplay is solid, the ability to hybridize classes through breeding is interesting, and the random event system keeps things interesting between battles. It's not a must-play, but if you're into the genre, this is one of the best examples of it in recent years.

Before I got this game I was really turned off by some of the reviews and never felt comfortable purchasing it at it's full price. A huge sale made me gamble on it and I have to say knowing the game experience I would have been fine with this game at full price. This is a satisfying game with some great ideas, not all of which are necessarily followed through to conclusion but which make for a fun game regardless. Once you get used to navigating marriages based on traits and your desired classes you are free to devote much of your actual thinking into the combat, which is good but is probably a few steps from great. I would have liked to seen a little more complexity in this area. Some real terrain advantages/disadvantages like height or hazards (there are a few hazards/interactables but, again, it is just not followed through with all the way) and more variations between classes could help make combat more exciting.
The core of Massive Chalice is a realm management system which (Sages/Keeps/Crucibles) allows for some depth and until you really grasp the flow of the game they can be challenging, but once your kingdom is up and running you can manage these systems rather easily and I think a lack of complexity in the Realm Management is the game's major downfall. I feel like there are a lot of events with random and occasionally extremely harsh outcomes that were thrown into this game as a way to make up for the fact that the realm management is rather shallow. I chose to build a particular kind of building (from an event list) and was punished by having one of my territories destroyed, which didn't feel like a deserved loss. With a few more options at research and a few more challenges from the enemy I don't think you would need these random terrible consequences. A more complete realm management system, events system, and maybe ways to upgrade/specialize the 3 main types of building would really help to complement the lineage system. As it is the bulk of the game just revolves around managing the trainees of your keeps.
Still, the game is fun. It has a lot of heart and clearly a lot of effort was put into it. It has great ideas, they are just incomplete. I think this is just as much game as they could afford to make. For it's price it is quite worth it.

Old Man’s Journey is played entirely with your mouse. For the majority of the journey, you’ll be rearranging roads and hills and even train tracks to ensure that the Old Man gets to where he needs to go, pausing occasionally to click on or hover over people and creatures that will react to you interference.
Because it is such a story heavy game, it’s difficult to discuss it without spoiling anything, so I’ll simply say that it follows the memories of a lonely old man.
Puzzles consist of moving and aligning surfaces so that the Old Man can make his way across the scene. Clicking reveals a series of line segments, which indicate the path he can take. Some surfaces can be moved and others cannot, and once two surfaces are aligned, a dot appears to mark the intersection. You can instruct the Old Man to move by clicking, but he will refuse to move, a question mark above his head, if the path is not clear.
You are required to move in one direction, rearranging surfaces so that you can make your way across the scene until you find a resting place where the Old Man will put down his pack and reminisce--after which you have to click on an object in the scene that will trigger a memory. These memories tell the story of his past and they are absolutely gorgeous snapshots of a moment in time.
The atmosphere is where the game shines. Not only is the art nice to look at, the small details like swaying leaves, critters and people that go about their lives and passing vehicles breathe life into every scene, making the world a living, breathing—not to mention realistic—one. Ambient sounds like the trickle of water or even something as small as shuffling cards can be heard over the background music, which changes with each scene change.
There’s just something incredibly charming about the layers of detail and I found myself stopping on more than one occasion to see what I could click on and how it would respond. Your cursor can part or block the flow of water, startle birds shift power lines, and prompt creatures and people to move and change positions. Some objects prompt the Old Man to resume his journey, while others just provide a lovely little distraction.
And that sense of wonder will linger even after you’ve complete your playthrough, which will take you anywhere from 1 to 2 hours depending on how leisurely your journey is. I didn't find any bugs during my time spent in game and performance was good. No, there are no sound sliders, which is not unheard of in games that are released on mobile devices as well as Steam, or an exit button, but that is in no way game breaking. I'm a grown up, I can use windows or alt+tab and close out my games--no big deal.
The game is linear, moving along after you go from point A to point B. The latter half of the game adds on some interesting mechanics to the standard land mass shift, but I didn’t find any of the puzzles to be too difficult. Most can be solved after pausing to think, but the main focus of the game is the story.
.Pros.
.Cons.
.Bottom Line.
The Old Man’s Journey is a fantastic, albeit short experience. It’s one of those games that you just have to play to understand its charm and if you’re a fan of poignant stories or atmospheric games, then you're in for a treat. I enjoyed every moment of this game and there were moments where I just had to smile because there was a clever puzzle or a triumphant moment after solving a puzzle.

My first impression of this game was: hack-n-slash, artistic.  This is exactly what it is.
So why don't I recommend it?  Well, I first bought the game a while back while it was in early access.  Some issue that I was never able to determine prevented the game from opening.  Steam would show that I was running it, but it wouldn't start.  A minute or so later, Steam would say I was no loger playing it.  After trying multiple things, I gave up.  Recently I got a new computer and thought I'd give it another shot.  It worked!  I understand that it is very challenging for a developer, especially a small team, to get a program to work for every possible set-up.  But!.. with my new set-up, I have still had the game crash on me three times in 1 1/2 hours of play.
Now for the actual game features:
Graphics: In all fairness, the game looks really nice!  Although I have not completed the game, the areas, animations and characters look excellent.
Sound: Very bland.  The music repetitive and does not stand out to me while playing the game whatsoever.  I stopped playing the game about five minutes ago and already cannot remember any music or sound besides the *shing* of the slashing blade.
Gameplay:  It is a hack-n-slash, but a fairly dull one.  I enjoyed it for the first 10 minutes or so.  It didn't take long to realize that every fight was the same bag guys on a flat platform.  And by the same guys, I mean the same three: basic slasher baddie that prett much waits for you to kill him, shield baddie that forces you to start your combo with a certain move then  slash him until he dies, and the flying head that shoots.  After a while I ran into two more guys: the baddie that shoots a gun occasionally but mostly just waits for you to kill him, and the big guy that you slash endlessly until you see the attack queue frame so you can dodge, then continue.  I thought it got dull very quickly.
Killing bad guys gives you points to upgrade.  Never a bad addition, but I do have problems with it.  The store lets you buy moves you can't even use until you find a weapon at some point later in the game.  I was getting bored of fighting, so I bought some moves that looked like they would require specific timing to use, hoping this would make it more interesting.  I figured since it let me buy them I could use them.   Nope...  I'm still stuck with 3 basic combos and a knock-into-the-air/smash to the ground attack.
As I mentioned before, I had bought this during early access.  Up to this point, I was thinking, "Well, they aren't done with the game yet, they'll probably fix a lot of this".  I then decided to see at what rate the developers were progressing.  I was suprised to discover that the game was "finished" in September...
A few other concerns I ran into:  hit an enemies bomb to know it back, but instead it stops in mid-air and floats there eternally.
On several occasions I dodged past an attack only to find that I still took damage, even though my guy made no sound or indicated in any other way that I had been hit.
In one very few fight areas that aren't just a flat, the floor started to drop out from under me.  Unfortunately, I was standing in the wrong spot and fell to my doom without any warning or any chance to move.
Overall, the gameplay feel very unpolished and lacking.  As a long-standing fan of side-scrolling action games, this falls very low on my list.  In my opinion, Steam has many other, better options (Rainblood Chronicles, Super Panda Adventures, Bleed, Castle in the Darkness, etc.)

Highly recommend this game for those looking for a fairly difficult perma-death dungeon crawler (with great visuals and attention to detail) with a fantasticly unique physics based movement and combat system. Although the physics based movement and combat is very different and may throw some people off due to its learning curve.
The games visuals are fantastic, with a very dark (pitch black in some areas), mysterious setting and beautifully done dynamic lighting and shadows. You are forced to take the game slowly if you wish to find every advantage you can to survive the dungeon. Most of what you see is interactable, within reason. Lost your weapon? Have an approaching monster down the corridor? Go ahead and pick up that candle holder on the floor and swing like your life depends on it. Although it doesn't beat a good old sword and shield, if in need, you can wield many different items you find scattered amongst the debris as a weapon.
The armour system is incredibly modular with a tonne of combinations of equipment you could wear  on top of eachother. Having a thick coat on top of your shirt could provide you with that little extra padding that could determine whether the next blow to the ribs is your last or just a slight bruising. Then on top of that, find yourself some chainmail, a breast plate, some shoulder pads, gloves, vambraces and you could turn devastating hits into simply minor blows.
The combat system is very different to most other games, so it may take a while to get the hang of and considerably longer to master. Combat is highly dependent on how you move your character as your movement, momentum, speed and angle of attack all have an impact on the damage you deal. Stepping into an attack and landing a blow with the head of your axe and then following through with the swing will do considerably more damage than simply standing still and clicking or smacking someone with the haft of your axe. However, due to the nature of the physics based engine, it will initially look like a drunkards fight as you flail around stepping all over the place trying to understand how your limbs work together.
I thorougly enjoyed every hour of this game, even after initially dying multiple times, it draws be back in to try again. I've learnt to handle the combat like second nature and it has become an incredibly enjoyable experience to feel the weight behind my blows, to hear the dink of a sword glancing off my helmet as I slam a war hammer into someones ribs and send them sprawling across the floor.
That being said, it's still an early access game and has plenty more in development before it reaches the developers vision. So it is up to you if you want to wait for a more completed version. However, I must say that even in it's current state, it is well worth the $15, with plenty of content to keep you busy for atleast 6 hours as you learn the game and run through the first 5 levels of the dungeon as well as an arena mode to hone your skills. Many more levels and features are planned so keep an eye out :)

Truly magnificent art, a perfect blend of 2D and 3D with astounding colours, lends a lot of authentic personality to the world of Silence. Every scene is a sight to behold, with gigantic statues and majestic structures set among impressive natural landscapes, and even a few unexpected hallucinogen-induced sequences. Absolutely fantastic work.
On the surface, Silence looks sufficiently different from
to feel like an entirely new universe, but it is indeed a proper sequel.
It eases transition into this new story by briefly retelling the accounts of the first game. The small cast of genuinely interesting characters is nicely designed with slightly oversized proportions, some of them returning in improved forms, plus original new villain creatures called the Seekers.
Gameplay alternates half and half between siblings Noah and Renie, plus a few short segments where their sentient metamorphic caterpillar pet Spot goes solo. The parts featuring the charming young lady are by far the more compelling, with the game being arguably entirely about her.
While vastly improved over the original Sadwick, Noah is still not the most likable protagonist, especially after a particularly revealing plot twist. I hold almost exclusively bad memories of this game's predecessor because of its insupportable main character, a collection of bad to worse design decisions.
Manipulating metamorphic Spot offers effortless solutions and still feels a bit of a cheap catch-all device. At least he now looks cuddly in this incarnation.
The game's extremely simplified point and click system is possibly its most contentious design decision, an effort to render the game more accessible at the detriment of proper puzzle-solving.
Many actions that require dragging an arrow in the intended direction become at once innovative and annoying. In the best cases it lends weight to your movement, but it also leads to a repetitive balancing mini game, plus rare situations where the mouse input does not always register properly.
Inventory management is replaced by contextual actions where the game essentially reveals its solutions, and the very few actual puzzles that require a bit of reflection can be skipped.
Minimalist dialog options bring light flavour to conversations in the form of inconsequential binary decisions. The game proposes two equally melancholy endings entirely determined by a single crucial choice at the very end, which is really the only agency afforded. The autosave feature lets you see both endings easily.
I would have liked to spend more time exploring Silence's unique world and characters. Quite a fair amount of planned content is absent from the game, evidenced by full backgrounds revealed as bonus materials at the end. Slight jumps in the story don't feel entirely intentional and other completely unused areas such as the locked bridal shop also convey the sense that the developers lacked funds or time to fully realise their vision.
What's here is nonetheless breathtaking for players looking to be told a dreamy story more than stretching their intellectual muscles.

The game without a target audience.
While the user tags prominently sprout a Point & Click tag, this game is not point and click. The suggested control method is with a gamepad (not sure if there even is a point and click input option. I never checked since it would be - hah - pointless). A huge plus for me since I don't much enjoy neither pixelhunt nor the training wheels of show-me-the-hotspots.
You don't have a magic inventory where you keep your piece of coal, a piano, a birthday cake and two rabid rodents. Items are picked up and either dropped or used right after. I like the idea a lot since most games annoy me a lot by turning you into a walking warehouse (I am looking at you Everything-from-Bethesda). I also gets rid of the cheap lategame point&click timewaste were the solution to a puzzle might be one of the 50 items you still carry around from the first scene
Most puzzles make sense. That in turn makes them easy. Since I don't derive much satisfaction if solving puzzles by just randomly doing stuff that again is fine with me.
Put all of the above together and you don't get a Point and Click. I'd go with casual interactive storybook. If you don't do in with a wrong expectations (not created by the developer, but by user shoehorning the game into a category it does not fit). There are some reviews that complain about exactly that "This is supposed to be a Point and Click but its not". Want me to tag it as a FPS or MOBA? Enough random ranting.
Why did I call a game without an audience?
Visuals are gorgeous, voice acting is solid (played it in english although I am german since something rubs me wrong about the delivery in every german voiceover, but YMMV) and I already called it a casual interactive storybook. I want to wholeheartedly endorse the game for parents playing with their kids, however that might require you to explain to your kids the reality of war where being a protagonist does not automatically mean you get a perfect happy end.
Too dark for kids; too casual for experienced gamers; too cute for the cool kids; too short for the 'must get X hours per $' faction;
Still it is a great game, especially if you value quality or quantity and are willing to take the game for what it is and not for what some entitloid tagged it with

Silence is a point and click adventure game that focuses greatly on the story rather than puzzles. It is the sequel to 'The Whispered World' another point and click adventure by Daedalic Entertainment.
While Silence uses part of the story laid on The Whispered World, it is not required for you to have played it, as the characters will reveal important information on various occasions, familiarising you with what it is all about.
You will follow a brother and sister, Noah and Renie, in their adventure through the world of Silence, a world that is more that it seems, with memorable characters and surprises. It was quite hard to choose what I'll mention in this review, mainly to avoid any spoilers or surprises.
Visually the game merges 3D character models with hand drawn backgrounds. At the beginning, I was sceptical as characters seemed to 'not perfectly fit' with the rest of the environment. Fitting a 3D model, that makes depth noticeable, on a 2D environment felt weird, the way Daedalic fixes this, is by making every environment have multiple layers, thus creating a pseudo 3D or 2,5D if you prefer. That being said, I quickly dropped my objections as their animations, especially on how the characters interact with several objects, towards the depth of each area are well made. Additionally, the voice acting is on point and will make the characters noticeably more believable.
To my surprise, unlike the majority of point and click adventure games, silence does puzzles poorly. Meaning that there is little to no challenge for experienced adventure players, but that doesn't make the game bad, as it is the most friendly game to introduce this genre to non-fans. Additionally, the game offers a variety of options towards how much help you need, from outlines to intractable items and even tips, meaning that the game is made to by beaten while offering some difficulty options, should you wish it. However, even without the traditional puzzles, Silence has some quality enjoyment to offer, as everytime I had a puzzle involving Spot, I was always pleasantly surprised!
That being said, to compensate for the lack of puzzles, you will have several choices to make during your playthrough, others will have little to no effect on what comes next, while others may even alter where you 'll go next! Due to the game's autosave system, you'll have to replay the game should you want to explore all the other options, thus offering the game some replayability in time. Additionally, the majority of the achievements will reward the choice you made and offer completionists a bigger reason to replay the game!
The music is a solid 10/10 as it fits the game's theme in every perspective!
Finally, two features I really enjoyed. Firstly, at certain points you can choose if you want to continue your current area or swap characters, it certainly helps if you get swamped but still want to play! Secondly, I was surprised at the support of controller, yes you can actually play the entire game with a controller with no issue at all!
On the opposite side of the coin, the game has some weird bugs or inconsistencies. I'm my playthrough I've encountered a dead end, where I could not change area because the correct exit was not intractable. This was caused by me, choosing a specific voice option on the dialogue before, while choosing the other resolved the issue and I could proceed normally. Sadly due to the 1 autosave feature of the game, I could not roll further back and check if previous choices would affect that. In addition to that, a paradox, where some dialogue options may not provide certain information the other choice would have.
As a final negative I will further point out that Silence, it's not a game for gamers that want the classic Point and Click adventure, as it lacks puzzles where you combine items, require inventory screens, take notes or have any special logical interaction.
To sum up, I believe Silence does not worth its full price, but it can offer quite an enjoyable time. I would recommend grabbing it with on a 50% sale if you want a nice story or want to introduce someone to the genre. I give it 6,5/10 not because it is a bad game, or the negatives make it so, but because I have much higher standards for adventure games from Daedalic Entertainment. Silence does features both steam trading cards and steam achievements. Alternatively, should you want something more, it's prequel 'The Whispered World' follows the more classic features of the genre.

It's so refreshing to see a sports game developed by people who put their heart and soul (you can really tell) into it because they love the game.  Can't say the same about the big name sports titles that get regurgitated every year by corporate drones.
On the surface, this game harkens back to RBI Baseball, Baseball Stars, and Ken Griffey Jr baseball.  Beneath the surface, though, is where it really shines.  The physics are remarkably accurate and repeatable, and the team management system is almost as fun as the gameplay in terms of balancing strengths/weaknesses and deciding exactly what kind of team you want to take the field.  Difficulty is user-managed by the EGO system (1-99), which determines not only how well the CPU will play but also how good your joystick skills will need to be to pitch/hit your way to victory.
I can't recommend this game enough for baseball fans of all types.  It isn't just for older fans of the aforementioned games.  Rather, it should appeal to fans of almost any age or gaming desire other than hardcore simulation.
