It's not a walking simulator. In terms of gameplay, this is very decidedly a third person platformer. You'll be hopping from surface to surface, sometimes making mistakes, sometimes dying. You will jetpack. You'll roll rocks. You'll use a hydraulic manipulation arm. You'll solve some simple puzzles. And yes, you'll walk and look and listen, so it has a bit of the "walking simulator" in it, but it's very much a game with game mechanics.
The Steam description for the game already tells some details from the story so I won't worry about spoiling: you're an astronaut exploring a lifeless planet, yet finding remnants of a Soviet base, and then a figure in the distance who might be friend or foe.
The game's backstory is told in bits and pieces, as you travel through setpieces on this foreboding planet. There are themes of fear, sadness, hubris, and exploitation.
It's a lower budget game, evident from the models, the terrain, the quality of the cutscenes and animations. And I think they did an excellent job working within these constraints. Even with these limits, the game manages to be engrossing, even creepy at times.
I can say I loved this game. If you want a semi-casual single player platforming linear experience, with a simple but engaging story, I say go for it.

Video Review:
Massive Chalice is a turn based strategy game that’s really honestly very unique, but not nearly as complex as its official description might lead you to believe.
So in this game you play as an immortal strategist essentially. You and your talking chalice work together to run a kingdom that’s under invasion by the cadence which is essentially a mist that spawns enemies and consumes territory if it manages to corrupt it enough. You can create keeps and assign your heroes there to rule it. They will produce new heroes, the class and traits of which being influenced by the regent’s traits and class along with that of his or her spouse. You can research technologies except not really. Research is used to build and craft new items and buildings like keeps, guilds that increase research speed, and crucibles that help train your heroes to higher levels. Higher level parents also create higher level heroes, but if you assign all your high levels to rule then you won’t be able to fight with them. As awesome as that entire strategic layer sounds you have to realize that’s all there is to it. You have a very limited space to build and engineering your bloodlines turns into more of a chore with the more keeps you get. Your time out of battles will be almost entirely spent replacing dead heroes in non combat roles and just repeating the same drudgerous tasks over and over again. And that gets old fast.
There are special events that pop up as well on that strategic layer that allows you to make a choice of how to handle situations. These situations can either lead to you gaining or losing a hero or maybe even suffering an invasion in a critical location in your kingdom because you thought opening what was essentially pandora’s box was a good idea. As bad as they tended to ♥♥♥♥ me over I really did enjoy their presence. They helped add some variety and extra challenge to an otherwise bland and repetitive premise.
The combat works amazingly similar to XCOM. It seems directly inspired by it, in fact. Though it does lack a meaningful cover system. You move your heroes around and can use items, abilities, and basic attacks. There’s a stealth mechanic built in for a few hunter-based classes, but it’s really rather useless since range doesn’t affect the accuracy of that class’ attacks. You venture through an area and open up the fog and then spot new enemies and try to deal with them. You can also have a keep or something be attacked, in which case all the enemies run out of the fog and try to overwhelm and destroy you. The enemies scale up in level over time to make the game more and more challenging.
That’s another good thing to note is that this game is played on a timer. You have to survive about 300 years or so in game. As time goes on and enemies scale up in level, you will also find new types of enemies. Always much stronger than the last. There’s typically a trick to fighting all of them, but these enemy types are really brutal. One of the early on enemies drains the experience of your heroes with every hit. This can cause them to even lose a level, a skill, and stats as a result. Another one advances the age of your heroes with every hit. I’ve literally had one of my heroes die of old age in combat because they were hit by one of these things. Then there are plenty of generic ones as well with their own twists like these kamikaze ones called ruptures that rush in, blow up, and basically consume your heroes in a pit of acidic goo. The variation and challenge in the enemies is fantastic really. It’s so painful to watch a hero you’ve trained up die of old age as they’re rushed by two age-advancing enemies, but it’s so much fun to get stronger and kill them before they get a chance to attack.
The graphics of Massive Chalice are cartoony. They’re nothing to brag about and the sounds are alright as well. They certainly weren’t revolutionary for when the game released, but at the same time it’s not like they’re ancient now.
Overall Massive Chalice is actually a really fun concept and it has some really good things about it. Unfortunately the gameplay itself is very repetitive as there’s only really two aspects to it and you switch between them a lot. After your first 50 in-game years you’ll feel the repetition becaue within that time you’ve already experienced everything the game has to offer. All you have to look forward to is a scaling difficulty and a race against the clock. Part of the challenge of surviving 300 years in Massive Chalice is trying not to get bored in that time. It was a really fun game...for a very short amount of time. I got it for $2 on a sale and let me tell you, there’s a reason it was $2. You might as well just play XCOM instead. Any of them. Even spinoffs of it. They all have more depth than this.
Massive Chalice gets a 4/10 from me. It has some really refreshing and underused concepts in it, but it’s just too bland and lacking to really justify its full price of $20. Even paying $2 I don’t feel like I got my money’s worth because I was frustrated with boredom for most of the time I played it. I’d avoid this one if I were you. It’s very short, very simple, and very boring.

I ran into this game shortly after release having heard nothing about it but being intrigued by the premise.
I want to enjoy the game. It has a lot going for it...but there are just too many cracks to give it a strong positive recommendation.
Time is supposed to be your enemy in the game; your heroes age and die, the Cadence creep closer and closer with each year, research takes decades, etc. The problem is, at least with your heroes, time moves far too quickly. Often heroes are in their 50's or 60's before ever taking the battlefield and while you can sometimes find yourself with a plethora of heroes, distributing them to various positions throughout your kingdom leaves you one good TPK away from having either no heroes or being stuck with a pack of newbies who die off at an impressive rate.
By the time heroes are strong enough that you don't have to worry about them dropping dead every battle, they die of old age and are useless.
The mechanic isn't necessarily bad but after a while all the heroes and houses just blur together because they're being born and dying so quickly. Any sense of individuality or attachment that you get to characters in these kinds of games is blown away because your roster changes so frequently.
Most other mechanics in the game have been done by other games and frankly done better.
This was a great attempt and it really has the seed of something wonderful in it but overall it just falls short. Too short for me to recommend it.

A unique take on dungeon crawlers. Exanima features impressively detailed combat controls focused entirely on player skill.
It's one of the few early access games I recommend. On it's own, even in its unfinished state, I have put in many hours and really enjoy the combat in this game.
The graphics and sounds are also impressive.
The controls are awkward at first, and I could see it turning new players away, but I'd say to stick with it. It's more intuitive than it seems and results in swordplay that gives you total control.
The game features great ragdoll technology that reacts to forces, and characters who have a sense of balance. This creates very dynamic battles where you can lose balance, and even fall over.
My only real complain is the overall slow pace of combat. A single swing fields like a cumbersome, tiring action, as if the fighter is totally out of stamina. And a nitpick about how stabs are handled.
I cant wait to see where this game goes, and I hope to see multiplayer combat added in soon!

I put this game in my wishlist and eventually bought it for 2 reasons.  Reason 1 being that it looked incredible.  To this extent the game delivered flawlessly.  From tables to barrels and even enemys the graphics were high quality.   The feel of walking through a damp, dark, and mysterious dungeon was perfectly captivated.  The second reason I bought this game was for the combat.  It from the videos shown I saw the characters locked into fights that mimicked real swordplay.  It actually looked like fun.  Oh how wrong I was.  In actuallity the combat that looked so fluid and fun in the screenshots and videos was somehting akin to two drunk ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ trying to bash each other's heads in with sticks.  More than once I found my character hugging the enemy, or I found my weapon being held behind my back as if I were being pinned by some invisible force.  The way the game describes how to perform combat makes little sense and resulted in me clicking and swinging my mouse around like a fool to no avail.
In summary, if you are looking for a hard game to play, don't get this one.  Get something like darksouls.  This game trys to be "hard" through broken combat mechanics and overpowered mobs that will bash your skull in before you can even figure out what is happening.  I can honestly say that I had high hopes for this game, but it failed to deliver on its main selling point of a "physics based combat system".

This game has a fairly steep/long (and possibly frustrating) learning curve, but if you give it a chance and stick at it long enough to become even slightly proficient, you won't regret it. It's a unique and hugely satisfying experience.

This little gem has me itching with impatience for the long-awaited release of a playable Sui Generis.

I played the first level until the first boss, and I have to say, I feel like this is a poorly designed game.  It is true, I didn't give it much time for it to develop, but I couldn't help but notice some design attributes to this game that really set me off.  First, there is no health potion in the first level, and it is understood for the most part, considering it is your first time playing the game, to die, and then respawn with full health at a check point.  I was concerned this would be the way things are done.  Second, I found the restricted area of fighting to be quite annoying.  And I get that maybe the ideal distance to fight, then I would argue put less stuff on the map at the same time.  I get it that the game is trying to be more challenging, and this comes to my other point, it wasn't challenging, it was annoying.  It wasn't fun.  There are these head guys that float in the air while you fight on the ground, and it just takes away from the experience.  I would rather fight without some head thing dangling above my head forcing me to dash and sometimes take damage, even if that means it is easier.  Third, on the first boss, these head things use a red laser to tell you the trajectory that they are going to fire.  Well, the background is a fire, and you can't really see where they are going to fire.  This I think is poor design, and they should of had that laser be blue or something.
I also understand that it is the beginning of the game, and maybe there is a level up system, but the combos were insanely easy to pull off.  I feel like what would of been a better alternative, is get rid of the heads, and force people to kill opponents quicker by using the combos given to the player at that time.
Not to mention the environment progression, albeit it is the first level, is just left to right.  There's no secrets, no multiple levels, annoying as hell fighting, and no health potions, it just isn't a game for me.  Oh yeah, insanely easy combos.  Usually what games do if they have easy combos, is they introduce a fatality sequence.  This wasn't presented to me when I played it.
I make quick decisions when it comes to my game selection, simply because there are so many games to play.

Onikira’s painted pseudo-fuedal-Japan is absolutely beautiful, with careful use of depth of field and parallax often creating the impression of playing through a painting.
Mechanically indebted to Shank and the latest DmC, Onikira’s world is populated with imaginative, aggressive enemies - forcing you to plan your engagements quickly, shift your tactics to match your situation and fight like hell in search of that SSS rating.
SFX is crisp and effective, and the music mostly eschews evoking the period in favour of effectively ratcheting up tension and excitement - the correct choice for this genre. There are a few collision errors and typos, but nothing to obscure the delightful blood frenzy that beats in the chest of Onikira!

Onikira has a LONG way from being in the same league as games like Shank 2, The Dishwasher, or Dust: An Elysian Tale.

Let me preface this review by stating that I am a baseball fanatic. In fact, I believe I am the only person in the United States that follows baseball and no other sport. I am a student of the history of the game - especially the Dead Ball Era. As such, I have played every "serious" baseball sim with mainstays being OOTP and Baseball Mogul.
I've been looking for a fun arcade type baseball game. In the glory days of the C64 and Amiga it was Hardball, MicroLeague Baseball and Earl Weaver baseball - the latter a decent strategy sim. My best friend and I used to stay up all night playing Hardball on the C64. I tried other arcade titles such as Star League Baseball, and The Show. None of these could touch the sheer fun of the first iteration of Hardball - until now.
Super Mega Baseball Extra Innings - known for the rest of this review as SMBEI - has completely captivated me. There are no trades, the longest season is only 40 games, there are limited substitutions, and the game looks like a nice little game forkids. But, don't be misled by these observations. SMBEI is a well done representation of baseball in an arcade format. Developer Metalhead have put a lot of love into this game and it shows. The game plays very well with KB and mouse even though the devs recommend a controller.
There is a visceral feeling to hitting the ball and pitching is a blast. The cartoon aesthetic may put some potential gamers off but, this is really quite a serious baseball game. The parks look fantastic, the fans are hilarious, and the cusomization is pretty good.
Difficulty level is determined by a mechanism nown as "ego." The higher the number, the more challenging the game is. And I would strongly suggest that after a few games to ratchet up the ego rating for a real challenge.
All of that said, there isn't complete joy in Mudville.You cannot create your own teams, bench and bullpen are very limited and while replayability is good, it could be better with more teams as well as an option to import stats from the free Sean Lahman Baseball Database.
It's the perfect baseball game to play when you aren' feeling up to the intricacies of games like Baseball Mogul and OOTP. Hardball has been dethroned; SMBEI is the new king. Long live the kin!

I have tried a few baseball games over the past few years, and none of them can be actually titled a good baseball game. The only option available out there was OOTP, which isn't really my thing.
A good experience I remember having was back in 2007-2008, when Ulltimate Baseball Online (aka Real Baseball Online) was around, which then became inaccessible. Different attempts to bring it back by other parties also didn't go well.
Then I saw this game. I didn't expect much from it by simply looking at the pictures. Yet I gave it a try and playing the game is a whole different story. It's "arcadey" and all but has everything covered.
I am not really that versed with rules of baseball, and can't really say what the game misses, therefore I think it's a nice game that anyone can pick up, even without having prior experience/knowledge about baseball as a sport.
Apart from being able to play a full baseball game, the game also offers ability for players to assign their team members with new skills and traits that can be applied in a game. Those skills are gained at the end of games based on performance which is calculated with points.
Players also have the freedom to set the difficulty of games using "ego" which decides how much control a player needs to put on the team members. The higher the "ego" the more attention a player needs to put into controls and depend less on the AI aspect.
In addition to that, the customisation of team members in terms of looks is also possible. It has a wide variety of funny looking faces and hair styles that don't really reduce the game quality but instead add to it a fun and less serious atmosphere. Don't let this stop you from enjoying the game.
Not to forget the funny remarks that the umpire throws in his voice.
So it doesn't matter if you're a baseball fan or simply wanting to start getting into the game, then this game isn't a bad choice.

Just Cause will evoke strong love-it or hate-it reactions from people for a lot of reasons. The game's amoral stance on the complicated issues surrounding US-sponsored regime changes in the third-world countries will rub some people the wrong way, while others will be annoyed by its fast-and-loose approach to basic physics.

I admit, I went into this expecting the original with some graphical and audio tweaks ala HDTP.
I was wrong, and am so glad for it.  The levels are subtly different - better, I'd contend, in layout and AI placement.  The extra RPG elements from the Shifter mode are very much appreciated, making each kill (or knock-out) or hack or lock-picking contribute to your increasing abilitites.
The ability to pick up multiple items of the same type is ... novel.  Not sure why I need two sniper rifles - there's no apparent weapon degradation mechanism.

Stealth AI feels broken (ex: been detected behind cover, enemies can "hear" you standing up, an action that is completely silent.) Playing on realistic difficulty leads to a lot of cheap deaths that didn't exist in the original. I want to like this but I feel that a lot of the changes are for the worse and not the better...

Optional stuff this mod does:
Shifter and Bimod integration (I recommend Biomod, even for a first playthrough)
New soundtrack
New models for certain characters (basically the PS2 models. Kiiiiiiiinda creepy)
Just to emphasize - these parts are optional, and I won't bother reviewing their quality one way or the other. You may freely turn them on or off should they affect your enjoyment of the mod. The actual substance of the mod consists of:
New textures
Occasional different item and enemy placement (more enemies in general)
A number of expanded or remodeled areas.
The textures are a marked improvement. The new item and enemy locations keep things fresh (assuming you're not playing Deus Ex for the first time using this mod. Not saying that would be the wrong thing to do, just that it's a bit unlikely). The new areas range from somewhat superfluous (Hong Kong) through acceptable if not terribly interesting (Hell's Kitchen) through a definite improvement in that makes Paris look like a real city (the moon base. Just kidding, Paris, obviously) or greatly expand upon a cramped and tiny original level (the surface area of the Missile Base, Area 51).
Overall, I thought the main content of the mod ranged from adequate to exceptionally good, and the optional changes were wisely left optional. I recommend it for any replays, and don't think using it during your first playthrough would be particularly wrong.

Deus Ex is one of my all-time favorite games and I've probably played it a dozen times since 2000.  I still love the game but know it so well that playing it has become routine: through the door, kill the 2 greasels on the left, wait for the baby karkians to come out, then send a wp rocket into the office to polish off the daddy karkian . . . I figured I'd played it for the last time. But then I saw that Steam was offering Revision. I downloaded it to see what the game would look like in 1920x1080. But Revision is So. Much. More.
Liberty Island. There are more NSF. I go to open up the container where the med bot is hidden. It's not there. The sniper is up on a perch where he actually has a field of view. He kills me with a headshot. The dynamite that was so handily lying about so I could dispose of the bot is gone. I can no longer fall back on the same old solutions. Every area is fresh.
Unatco HQ. Paul has an office? Of course he does! Why wouldn't he?  Gunter and Anna have their own offices too. Alex's computer center actually looks like a server hub. Everywhere you look there are changes and the amazing thing is that they are all absolutely right on.  Manderley's office befits the head of Unatco.  The NSF in the Ton Hotel have set up laser alarms on the stairs and when I try to go up the elevator shaft as I have the last 12 times . . . well let's just say that doesn't work anymore either. It's like playing for the first time again. I can't wait to see what they've done to Hong Kong.
If you've played Deus Ex before you really owe it to yourself to play Revision.  You'll find yourself saying over and over again: "This is the way it always should have been!" If you're new to Deus EX, Revision is the version you want to play. And you really should play it. See why so many of us old-timers still have it on our all-time greatest games lists.
To the people who produced Revision: Thank you. What you've done is amazing!

Just finished it.
I liked every second of it; this revamp, breathes new life into an old game; optimised level design, better graphics and a new soundtrack to boot!
Gameplay:
It plays the same; some changes to the augmentations, like the power regulator, that now activates with some high energy use augs, are very neat.
Changes to map design, have also improved the gameplay, enviroments feel easier/harder to traverse. areas that were easy in the old game have been made harder, while the general navigation feel much easier, always making sure that youre on the right track.
SABOT (shotguns), Willy Pete (GEP), Darts and Flare Darts (Crossbow), EMP and Scramblers, are more frequent, meaning that you can actually start to use those types of ammo more frequently, one of the few things i disliked about the old game.
The mission areas, are well done and allow for great combat and stealth, meaning that the original pillars of the game have been improved.
Sound:
Some gun sounds have been reworked; like the silenced AR. It no longer shoots a single silenced shot, but an actual burst, which is great.
Weather effects like rain, sound really good, other ambient noises are great, especially in the city hubs, all make the game feel way more alive.
The biggest thing however, is the addition of a remixed soundtrack. The soundtrack is good, and i applaud their efforts, the only one i didnt like was the Hong Kong theme, but fear not! you can easily turn it off in the options menu, and play with the old soundtrack.
Graphics:
Huge improvement, with very few downsides. Hub areas have been reworked, and look beautiful (compared to the old game); they look like real places that ppl live, with apartments, that you can peek into, glass doors etc. Streets look like streets, and offices look like offices. There's more nook's and crannies to explore, and all the old secrets of the game, are still there, many, accessible trough new ways. In short, Hub areas and Mission areas, are greatly designed.
Posters, advertisements, clutter, garbage, all add to the feel of the hub's (much like the DX:HR style, but with an older engines limitations). The additions never really feel overdone, despite being very ambitious and large. Also, they really did a number on the light effects on the game; pretty much all look great.
However, you might want to ramp up the brightness a little, as the game is somewhat darker.
Weapons now have great models, where the weapon mods actually show on them; so you can see the laser pointer, the scopes, supressor etc. As far as i know, all weapons have new models, all which look great.
The only thing i didnt like was the new character models, damn they are fugly, but no problems, you can switch them off in th Options menu, so not really a problem.
All in all 9/11 would bomb the statue of liberty.

This is a $5 game, as it plays like a mini game in a larger game that doesn't exist.

It's a game about eugenics, I guess.  One of your main goals is to improve the bloodlines of your noble houses over the years so that they produce ideal soldiers.  There's more to the game than that, but that's the gameplay element that makes Massive Chalice stand out from other tactical RPGs.
It also has nontraditional music for a fantasy game, with themes of Rock and Metal, which I appreciated.
Finally, the voicework is charming.  In Massive Chalice, you are joined in your three-century task by a giant talking goblet.  Drawn in the negative space of either side of the Chalice are two faces, and they both have their own personality and history.  One is a meticulous old British man, the other is a spunky American woman.  They don't share their names with you, but you'll get to know them pretty well over the course of your career.  I grew to like them both.
I'm not going to give you any strategic tips, because the truth is I'm not that good at the game.  I always seem to fail at the final battle.  I still enjoy playing it, though.  Something something the journey is better than the destination blah blah blah.
Fair Warning:  If you have a problem with simplicity of design, don't get this game.  If you can't handle only three playable classes and seven kinds of enemies, just don't expect to like Massive Chalice.  There's some variety beyond that, but not enough to satisfy some of you.  They were going for elegance through simplicity.  Whether that's a good thing or a bad thing just depends on your tastes, okay?

:: How I come to Hexels ::
I tend to use Photoshop / Illustrator for daily designer-related tasks and GameMaker Image Editor for in-game assets sometimes. But yes, I come to Hexels because they have all-in-one toolset from making grid-based pixel art asset/concept to animating them. Even that I use the cracked version 2.03 quite a long time ago before actually bought Hexels 3 on Steam (since trial time wasn't enough when I forgot to use it) just to make sure  it's getting better right now ( and indeed, it's ).
:: Rating ::
My experience with Hexels 3 was quite good, although I haven't used much.
:: Pros ::
+ The toolset was very simple and easy to use.
+ Kinda light-weight  and light-performance  on usage.
+ Animation was pretty comfortable to use.
+ GLOW :
special feature to glow your pixel art like HDR.
+ Flexible Brush setting and sizing the same to Photoshop.
+ Selection / Scaling / Photoshop basic tool-like... are all included !
+ Good Layer functionality :
alike to photoshop, including blending mode.
+ Many Grid Modes :
Square / Hex / Trixel .... this actually what made Hexel unique.
:: Cons ::
- BUG:
I still see crashing on first saving ( if I move or change the UI )
- COLOR PICKER :
For now, only 2 modes are included, which I don't like much.
I expect a more useful color picker, like Photoshop's CMYK or a Hexagram of dimming color.
- Not yet Flexible UI :
as you can't really "Dock" Color panel to the left ( I'm left hander ! )
and main toolset UI bar is fixed to the left.
-  A bit expensive at some regions :
50$ ? are you kidding me ?
Also I bought during sale :)
- STEAM ONLY : stick to Steam license and you can't link to use standalone.
:: Verdict ::
I recommend this great tool to any indie artists,
who is struggling with Photoshop complicated Timeline
or just want a compact too specially made for pixel art !
* P/S to developers :
I really hope you guys improve features and stable performance in the future release :)

Of all the games of this type I've played, it is most similar to the XCOM reboots. The setting/tone/flavour are all very different, but a lot of the core gameplay elements are similar.
A few caveats follow:
Massive Chalice is simpler than XCOM:EU/EW and XCOM2 in most ways. This seems to be both a deliberate design choice and also the result of working with a much team and budget. The game feels polished and well-made, but a little bit sparse. In particular there isn't much variety in the tactical game. For me there was just enough present to keep things interesting during the 14 hours that it took to finish my first playthrough, but I think I'll struggle to enjoy replaying it.
The visual style is charming, and the maps and enemies in particular are very pretty. However, the people all look very similar and are chiefly differentiated by changes in hair style and hair colour. That would be a real downside regardless, but it's particularly glaring given the way that almost all of the strategic gameplay revolves around deciding where to situate the various people and what they will do.
The ageing mechanic and all the associated people-wrangling is a very clever idea. It works okay in implementation too, although I think the pacing is a bit off - the people age (and have children) too quickly relative to most game events, which often felt like it reduced the circumstances where I got to make really impactful or difficult choices about them. Combined with the homogenous representation I mentioned previously, the effect was rather distancing.

This is definately an interesting game and I enjoy it very much but it is not for everyone. If you came here from Kerbal Space Program you may be dissapointed in the gameplay, but that is because rather than being a sandbox game that you fly your own rockets, in this game you play as the director of the space program.
You manage all aspects from how many astronauts and flight controllers to hire, and how much to pay them for their services all the way to what rocket and payload programs to implement. Want to do a Gemini lunar mission, you can do it here. Want to put an Apollo capsule on a russian rocket... yep you cna do that too. Of course dont expect the game to always depict your rocket properly as the graphics havent accounted for what it looks like to say put a Mercury capsule on a Proton launch vehicle and many other possible configurations.
This game is somewhat like Kerbal Space Program in one respect. It has a steep initial learning curve that gradually gets much easier. It can also be frustrating at times to have a spacecraft with 99.9% reliability decide to suddenly blow up at random (sadly you dont get to see the explosion though). Keeping up with all the training and amangement of personnel can also be a chore, especially early on in the game, but if you do it correctly the gmae gets more fun as you go along and your equipment and personnel beocme ready for use. Your first several seasons will likely be without any launches, but as you get closer to that ultimate goal of landing on the Moon, you will find the mission launches become much more frequent.
This game is somewhat sandboxy in that it doesnt hold your hand and tell you what to do (other than perhaps your goal of landing on the Moon) but it also has its limitations.
Overall, this is more of a management type game than an arcade type game and it certainly isn't for everyone.  With that caveat, I will recommend this game.

This one ain't Kerbal Space program so if you are looking something similar to KSP this isn't it. This is a pure management sim where you take over the responsibility of running a space agency. You can either play the historical ara NASA, The Soviets Agency or a neutral global space agency which allows you to run program from both sides.
So how does it hold up? Suprisingly well there is fun in this one if you like space exploration in particular the golden age of it and a rather simplistic management system, At least that is once you pass the initial hurtle but it isn't flawless by any means.
A couple of things that annoy me:
1.) Even though you can skip through the little videos of the mission sequence (and you really would like to after seeing the same launch sequence for the 10th time more variety would be nice) but it is not adviced to do so simply because you don't have any means to interact when something goes wrong in one of the stages no means to hire a more experienced team that might just push the odds over to success. When you skip your most likely to fail. So you can only do that when the odds of success in each stage are extremely high (like >95%). Some way to speed this whole process up would be nice.
2.) The space probes barely make an impact and a far more an distraction as you really need only one or two to succeed in the game.  A better balance between manned and unmanned missions would be nice. Especially considering than unmanned missions dominate the space ara post 1980s
3.) A pitty the game basically stops right now at 1970s. You can play on but there is basically zero motivation to do so as by the time you have reached the Moon you probably already have exceeded all the other mission options as well and it doesn't really make sense to go back to any of the previous ones. This is when you play GSA.
4.) Some of the menu structures could be streamlined especially in the mission planner
Overall I would give it a thumbs up but than I got it in a reduction offer would I have paid the full price frankly probably not!

First off let me tell you that I love this games concept.  the turret deffense along with leaderboards and other things make for a rather interesting game.
some key things I have to dissagree with on the concepts.
1) leaderboards are broken.  how can you beat a level in less than a min.  it takes more time for your orbitals to land than some of these people took to beat the levels.  I call foul.
2) Campaign - It seems choppy at best, and broken as worst.  sure I was able to beat it.  but most of the items you have at your disposal and the fact that even two ore harvesters cannot support one single ore spitter for continuious fire is sad.  then there are the titans.  Useless in ever case.  even on the missions you may want them they take too long to fire, the creep comes back too fast even on 1x speed to do anything tactical with them, and the last one is only for the end mission, you don't even get to use it on special missions after you unlock it.
now for the reason that this game is great!
1) it has user/mod like interface.  looks to me (haven't finnished all bonus sectors yet) that you get to make and share with other players in these maps.  maybe they just modify/test them first to make sure you don't screw over the comunity, but this is a rather interesting idea.
2) the story is actually decent.  Sure it may seem obvious at times, and others down right boring.  However, if you decide to read it all (storyline) you get an interesting story.  one worth talking about to friends and family.  Just like when you read a good book, or new article.

Just wish they had some kind of RPG element sector where you gather things/currency and use them to improve/unlock different items to use in the next mission (like if you could boost yourself with a starting ammount of energy or something)  of course this would destroy the leaderboards in that sector, but that would be something like score rather than just time (like -points per sec and +points for builds and kills.  Also give you a point handycap for bonuses, and a point bonus for detriments)

Skill based combat.
Physics engine.
Interesting, different fighting that isn't just spamming one thing but relying on the player's actions.
Exanima is a skill based fighting game in which you'll actually learn things over time based on what YOU find, rather than the game.
The steep learning curve frightens many players and bores others. Do not let it get to you. Your first few hours will be struggling with even learning how to move. The next will be learning to try and block, dodge and swing.
Finally, you'll try to learn how YOU play. Whether it's making your character extremely tall and slim, allowing them to swing headshots and have a long, dangerous range, or having a stocky character which can trip enemies and can get close and personal.
It takes time and practise, but as soon as you learn how to do the universal movements, and you begin to play with your own style, it gets good.
Practise makes perfect.

Imagine a game based on medieval one on one combat, but you have no control over whether or not your character is hit or your character hits your enemy. That's this game.
So the developers claim that all the combat is based around complex physics calculations and the velocity and location of your and your enemies hits, but that's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. What the combat is based around is your character's AI and their complete and utter ineptitude, and though the developers claim there are no hitboxes, there are some very shoddy hitboxes. There's a lot of "tends to" and "tends not to" in this game's combat. Your enemies attacks tend to hit your character if you're in range of them, but every once in a while the AI will function properly and your character will block an incoming attack. Yes, you, the player, have zero agency over whether an attack is blocked successfully or not, instead it's up to your character's half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥artificial intelligence. Your attacks tend to have a very minor relation to the way you move your mouse after clicking/holding it down. Every couple of hits you'll notice a very slight correlation between the way you moved the mouse and the way the character attacked, if they decide to attack at all, since even attacking is up to your character's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI. More often than not your character decides not to attack and will stop their weapon just short of a blow, only to receive many blows that they decide not to block. Enemies tend to block your attacks and attack at the times and places that are most damaging to you, because the enemy AI is much better than the player character AI.
Don't buy it. It's not fun. It's just broken.

I like this, but I have to lodge a few complaints. I know this is a work in progress, so I hope some of this criticism is constructive and not just ♥♥♥♥♥ing.
Although this makes for a more interesting replay, I have to admit that I don't like some of the changes, e.g. removal of many of the augmentation upgrade canisters. There weren't enough aug upgrades in the game in the first place, why the hell would you take some out? The damage done by darts is also significantly lower (12 now vs. 25 in original, I think), and for what? I don't understand that change, you effectively made the lethal darts almost useless. It seems like there aren't as many bioelectric recharge robots, too. Again, why? It's just annoying to have to use BE cells just to have access to a GD flashlight.
Also, some of the problems with the original are still there. For example, if you have a target incapacitated with a gas grenade, and you shoot them in the leg with a gun, they look up and place a well-aimed shot on you for a moment before rubbing their eyes again. That was ALWAYS a stupid and annoying bug in the original. Worst of all, the inventory problem is still pervasive and very limiting to playstyle. If I want to use all 3 heavy weapons, I effectively occupy 80% of my inventory, and the remaining slots are mostly mandatory items (lockpicks, multitools, BE cells, melee).
Anyway. I like it, and I hope it keeps improving. The details that were added to this are really nice.

Pregnancy is a game about leading a character through a dark and terrible situation by making choices and watching how the different options affect the world. However, this game differentiates itself from all the others that might fall under the same description by putting the player into the role of a literal voice in the protagonist's head, rather than controlling them directly. This allows the player to converse with the character, discuss the different choices they encounter and become a character in their own right.
The ability of the protagonist to choose their own path despite the player's input is a core component of the game, giving them free reign to argue against decisions and question the player's motives and competency. The capacity exists to become friends or enemies with the main character and the relationship between the protagonist and the player is one I wish would have been explored more, had the game been longer.
I played through once, which took twenty minutes.
I did wish there were more dialogue options, sometimes, but I'm always happy to pay £1.59 for a unique, interesting experience that makes me think.

Onikira: Demon Killer
2D Hack'n'slash
Digital Furnace Games
Merge Games, Headup Games
is a side-scrolling hack'n'slash developed by Digital Furnace Games and published by Merge Games and Headup Games. While the game is in Early Access, this is the review of the final product that will be released the 27th of August.
The story is your typical "feudal japan fantasy" featured in so many movies: demons come to the earth, someone with magic slays the demons, they come back stronger than ever centuries later, the player starts a journey to slay them.
To be fair, there is very little story in the game, told through animated cutscenes or small dialogues during the game. It is very basic, but lacks anything to make you care about your quest. But lets be honest: you are here to kill demons in cool ways.
The game looks gorgeous: the hand-drawn sprites are very polished and the animations are fluid. But the real star is the background: god rays, cities burning to the ground, beautiful trees and gigantic demons are just some of the things that really made my jaw drop while playing this game. Fans of this art style will have a lot to stare at.
The game is a mixture between Devil May Cry and Guacamelee: you have a style system which rewards you for beating enemies using various combos and weapons, and sometimes you will fight enemies that require you to destroy their shield with a certain weapon in order to defeat them. There are also some fairly easy platforming sections, that usually lead to secrets and hidden upgrades.
In the years I grew tired of hack'n'slash games, but Onikira felt fresh to me: maybe it was the use of 2D, maybe it was the art style, maybe it was the setting, but I rarely got tired while slaying demons through the 7 levels of the game. If you are a fan of the genre, there is enough variety here to satisfy your hunger for non-stop action.
The game isn't all that hard: your only way to avoid getting hit is dodging, but sometimes that is not all that easy because of the huge number of enemies on the screen that make it impossible to see who's doing what. That wouldn't be a problem if the health that the enemies dropped didn't heal you. Also, some of the bosses are so big and slow that they are easier to beat than a group of standard demons. The really challenging part is the Combat Arena: multiple levels a-la God of War challenges that require all your skills and reflexes, resulting in some very frustrating rage quits.
Both the sound effects and the soundtrack do their job: nothing memorable. The soundtrack will easily appeal to fans of japanese movies.
There are a total of 7 levels (each between 30 to 40 minutes long), plus Combat Arena, hidden secrets and 45 Steam achievements make for a game that, if enjoyed, will make you stay for more content.
Overall, fans of hack'n'slash and action will have a blast playing this game. However, if you are looking for a game with variety or more depth, you won't be satisfied.

It’s not like Pregnancy doesn't have some interesting ideas, like how it wants to introduce the player as some mind hitchhiker rather than just a disembodied voice dishing out advise. It wants to establish you as an outside personality -- you have to supply a name, and are questioned on possible shared interests and the state of your life outside the confines of the girl’s head. Again, though, it’s an idea that never reaches fruition due to the title’s brevity, and all the interesting quirks about being your own person talking to a girl in crisis seems like it could have been better spent, you know, learning about the girl in crisis. Everything is condensed down into a tale far too rapid fire to deal with the complexities of the ordeals it seeks to talk about.

This is the gaming equivalent of a sophist argument, it looks cool, and the controls feel good at first, but the flaws are evident when examined under a watchful eye
Well, some flaws are evident even if you aren't a beat em up enthusiast like i am, there are many bugs that have been around since day one, and persist to this day after various patches, for example, your character randomly dashes after certain attacks even if you don't input a dash
I've seen some other negative reviews that talk about those issues, but miss(and even praise!) the biggest one, that is in fact the core of the game, the combat
TLDR-it's a bad copy of DmC, the Ninja Theory one, the shakespearean, redheaded stepson of the family
There are many attacks that were blatantly ripped off Dmc:DmC, the Scythe air to ground launcher makes an appearance, the Scythe's ground spinning launcher(i think it was called Shredder or something) also makes an appearance, the grappling hook is also there
And these aren't even well executed, the Shredder launcher can be held to do some extra hits, but the first hit launches the enemy higher than the additional hits, so you have to until the enemy falls, which is really annoying
Which ties into another of the game's problems, there is little move diversity, there are 2 attack buttons, 4 weapons, and 2 sets of moves(ground and air), that's around 20 moves in total, since there aren't many command moves, that's not bad in itself, but the game makes very bad use of its moveset
There are about 4 hit effects, simple stagger, Upward launches, Downward launches, and horizontal launches, so a lot of moves cover the same uses
All weapons have a simple attack chain(on the air too), and a ground launcher, as far as i've noticed, both of these moves do the same thing with each weapon, the attack chain sends the enemy flying on a 45 degree angle, and the launcher sends them straight up
This raises several questions, why aren't there simply command moves, like up +attack, down + attack, etc, this way, the game wouldn't waste a button on a launcher, and that button could be used for different moves
What is the point of weapon switching?, if the 4 weapons dont do different things
If the weapon switch is so quick, why don't the other moves cover options the sword doesn't already cover?
I could go on, but just trust me when i say this game is badly designed

This fun factor is best supported by its solid  and mostly intuitive control mechanics and vibrant atmosphere.  This is the first baseball game that didnt compel me to go out and buy a brand new baseball bat and break it over my knee because the mechanics and flow of the game were so infuriating.
The cons for some (which in my opinion are strengths as it contributes to its charm) are no mlb licencing (which is fine because I dont want to pay for that) and limmited teams and field choice (again acceptable as sometimes less is more as I find i spend more time looking at the options rather than playing).  As many pointed out, the running system is a little unintuitive.
Bottom line: a fun engaging wieldly game that doesnt take it self too seriously but offers the player enough depth to play a casual arcade slugfest and/or manage, customize and play a team throughout a season.  Very pleased with this game!

This game is absolutely amazing! I simply love these kinds of strategic city builder games that require planning ahead to create vast cities! If you've played games like Banished or Forest Village, you will love this game! However, unlike Banished and Forest Village, this game is FAR more simplistic! It is very forgiving, resource gathering is quick and efficient, food production is very high and it's nearly impossible to have starving citizens. The Advisors are wonderful and add a lot of character! And to top it all off, this game has a very cute minimalistic style. This game is very much worth it's price! Good job Lion Shield!
PROS:
\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\
> Worlds are randomly generated to add variety
> You can choose anywhere on the land to start your kingdom which is absolutely fantastic!
> Resources are easily and quickly gathered in large quantities
> Food production is very forgiving and can easily be expanded
> Expanding your kingdom is easy and can be done quickly
> Very easy to learn and pick up
> Automatic roles (citizens are automatically assigned to tasks when they are avalible. This is a great feature for anyone who knows how annoying assinging roles can be for games like Banished and Forest Village)
> Peaceful mode is avalible if you don't want to deal with vikings and dragons burning down your kingdom
> Very lovely art style
> Music is great and varies
> Sound design is good and seems to be procedural in some areas
> Citizens VERY quickly fill up avalible beds (I LOVE THIS SO MUCH!! It's brutal waiting 30+ minutes for babies to grow up in Banished or Forest Village just to have them die from starvation)
\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\
Lion Shield took the strategic city builder genre from Banished and Forest Village and made it easier in all the best ways! However, this game is not perfect; there are glitches and strange design choices in the game.
CONS:
\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\
> The worlds are TINY! You will very quickly find yourself running out of room to expand your kingdom
> Some buildings require far too many workers (*cough* 10 WORKERS STOCKPILE! *cough* this also blends into the next point)
> Stockpile storage is far too small for how many workers they require. You produce a lot of resources (which is good!) but you need a TON of workers to actually store all these resources.
> AI is pretty bad. Vikings will invade and will either burn everything they come near or literally do nothing. Dragons are pretty sad, like they're supposed to be this "oh god, a dragon!! run for your lives!!" but all they do is hover over a building and burn them one at a time.
> You need wells EVERYWHERE! You need to pepper wells all over your kingdom just to make sure it doesn't burn down, if you want total protection you need a well almost every 6 tiles.
> You are required to place farms on fertile soil, which makes sense; but as you near filling up the world and need more farms to feed citizens, farms can become an issue and can mess up a lot of design or functionality. (it would be amazing if there was a building you could create that would allow you to build farms anywhere, like the pier in a way.)
\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\
I'm sure Lion Shield will continue development for their game and improve a lot of these cons I have listed. But besides that, this game is VERY fun! I highly recommend you buy it!

One of the tags on the store page for Lifeless Planet is "Walking Simulator".  Now I don't enjoy walking simulators and I'm unsure if this is one or not.  It does involve quite a bit of walking, but also a generous amount of jumping, jet-packing and puzzle-solving.  I'd say it is as much a 3D platformer as a walking simulator.
I found the jet-packing segments to be the most fun.  Our hero doesn't always have access to the full abilities of his jet-pack due to a lack of fuel.  The fuel is storyboarded to run out at certain sections of the game, it's not some resource that you can carefully manage to make other parts of the game easier.  It's designed so you can jump higher and further on the platform-type parts of the game and afterwards it becomes depleted.
The puzzle difficulty isn't too perplexing.  The couple of puzzles that had me stuck meant that I just needed to explore the area a bit further until I found an item or a switch that created part of the solution.
Due to the game not having a great difficulty level it's a fairly relaxing affair, I found myself playing the game last thing at night to unwind a little.  There's a great atmosphere in the game backed up with some really nice ambient sound effects that demand the volume be dialled up a notch or two.
The graphics are pretty nice looking with the exception that a lot of the textures for the surroundings are fairly low-res.  This becomes apparent when the camera is close up to them, from afar the world looks quite impressive.  The hero is really nicely detailed, especially the reflection from the visor on his space helmet.
It took me about seven hours to complete the game at a leisurely pace.  I found myself picking it up and playing it for about an hour at a time.  The game holds a couple of achievements that increase the replayabity somewhat.  One is to complete the game under four hours and the other is to complete the game without dying.  I'll probably attempt these soon.  I'm not sure how I will fair!

6 out of 6 stars (please ignore my hour-in-game count, as I played countless hours outside of steam including beta)
This is a very good game. A worthy successor to the classic game "Buzz Aldrin's Race into space". Its not just a modern version of that game with better graphics, it has been improved and expanded in a very positive way.
Now you can play one of three agencies:
1. NASA, with its historical programs as well as a few speculative ones and alternative variants. You can for example make  amanned lunar direct ascent landing with the Gemini.
2. Soviet Space program. Again, historical programs (including a few obscure probe missions) are present. You can also try to make a lunar landing with the N1-LOK as the sovits historicaly planned, ior you can engage in a very interesting variant with the UR-700 megarocket.
3. Global Space Agency, which functions as an open-ended speculative campaign where you can use both US andSoviet hardware (and mix and match both!).
Each agency can also be played in sandbox mode in addition to the campaign mode.
The sounds and music are very nice and atmospheric, not something one would expect from this sort of strategy game. Graphics are crips and pleasing.
Overall I strongly reccomend this game to anyone who enjoyed "Buzz Aldrin's Race into space" or someone who would like to play a well-researched strategy game about the Cold War space race.
NOTE: this is primarily a strategy game, focusng on planning, managing the space program, its technology, human resources and finances. If you expect something like Kerbal, please watch some youtube playthrough of this game to make sure what this game is all about, as its quite different from kerbal.

The original Buzz Aldrin's Race to Space game is one of my all-time favorites, right up there with Master of Orion II. The new BASPM goes a bit farther in space exploration than BARIS did. I enjoy have so many different satellite and rocket programs to research. It is also nice to see so much research flowing into similar programs on future programs. I do miss the videos from BARIS still, but I like that there aren’t bad CGI mixed in for Russian events that never happened and the graphics have continuity at least.
Please add some flavor text for the failures that happen on missions, this is something I enjoyed in BARIS and really find lacking, when I get an Astronaut/Cosmonaut killed I deserve to know how/why. As other commented partial success/partial failures should be added with the ability to scrub/abort on some warnings. Maybe you could even allow the player to choose abort/scrub during the mission based on the issue or continue with penalty/risk might be a bit too late for that though.

So when you swing the mouse around, the character does VERY limited combat swings. (I think these get more numerous as you level up.)
Sounds interesting.?... The problem comes from a few really irritating factors.
🌌  1, As you swing wildly around, your character lurches about as well. (I have even read veterans who have played it for hundreds of hours, and forum posts) call it "the drunken combat style."
🌌  1a, The combat as well as happening with swipes of the mouse, also happens with mouse button clicks. Which makes no sense, and defeats the whole "mouse swing mechanic."
🌌  2, The camera randomly changes its position, and angle, as you pan near walls, and run uncontrollably round, so you have to keep correcting it.
🌌  3, The mouse has no option for inverting the Y axis. (and even numerous forum requests for this universal option, fell completely on deaf dev ears. with a complete ignoring of the thread.
🌌  4, you have to switch into combat stance with the "tab" key, which is utterly frustrating. As when you are being owned by any number of mobs, running away is possible but (again) very difficult.
Meaning you have to keep switching back and forth into and out of combat stance. As well as the mobs chasing you literally all round the dungeon.. on.... and on... and on... until they catch you... and defeat you AGAIN, and then stand by, or near  you... sigh.
🌌 5,   When you are "defeated" you loose your weapons on the floor, which takes a few seconds to pick up and drag to your inventory again to equip.
The only, and HUGE problem is 9 times out of 10, the mob who just kicked you backside is standing right besides you, and you have utterly no chance to re-equip, or even palm a weapon from existing inventory items, because he/she they, are beating you back to the ground.
🌌6  ,The camera does not follow the direction your character faces, so you have to keep hitting space to turn literally every five seconds.. This does not matter in games like Titan Quest. Or DOS, or Pillars etc..
But when you can only see 10 feet all around you, or there are walls blocking your sight...
....IT REALLY DOES.
All this absurdity, and making the controls, and "combat system" as odd, and awkward, and difficult for the sake of it.
Is explained away by both the none- replying devs, and the hard-line zealots,--
(And forgive me zealots 😉 I know a couple of you guys tried to help on the forums, even though the devs did not.)
--As... "This is what makes it great, it takes practice. Keep at it for a hundred hours and...
• You will learn... "The "drunken style.
• You will learn how to keep hitting button after button just to keep the camera aligned, and see what's happening.
• You will learn to fight with a lurching, "drunken marionette puppet."
• And (and this makes me laugh)... You will learn how to cope with the camera Y axis not being how you play in every other game.
Again... This could be a cool dungeon crawler with some great exploration.
But the "uncontrollable 100 hours practice just to run around and hit stuff control scheme."
As well as the devs obvious indifference, to at least offering "the norm, of what is expected in an enjoyable isometric game," completely ruins it.
Yes I know there are gamers that either like it. Or put up with it in almost masochistic "I'm going to get used to it... I am..! frame of mind.
But I actually like to enjoy games I play. And not play a grindfest just to be abe to play. ✨
EDIT. I finally just saw a reply from one of the devs, and it was about as helpful as the fighting is intuetive.
"The reason this thread isn't getting much attention is because the controls have already been discussed numerous times both here and on the official BM forum so it'd just be rehashing the same thing over again.
There are valid and legitimate reasons for why the controls are the way they are and it's not for the sake of being difficult. If you'd like to know more I'd suggest looking up the dozens of responses already given by the devs/mods on this topic."

I started out really enjoying this game, but after a couple hours realized it's about 2-3 patches away from becoming a game worth sinking time into. Unfortunately, it's not going to see those updates.
The game attempts to carry out the base building, recruits and team structure, and combat of X-Com. At first, it seems fairly interesting. Percentages and damage potential for attacks, heroes can die and require either raising children or recruiting more, etc. Enemies will wreck your team if you rush out and don't play to their weaknesses, but hanging back and taking a strategic approach to the combat situations helps avoid too many losses.
The problem comes mid-game. Similar to X-Com, there's a difficulty ramp mid-game with new, tougher enemies. The problem is that the combat situations and maps are poorly tuned to the point of being garbage. X-Com punishes you for poor strategy. Massive Chalice punishes you for literally standing in one place.
First, the mid-game difficulty ramp places 6-7 of the tough enemies (that are capable of one shotting your heroes) in the same map area, outnumbering your squad in a single encounter and ensuring the death of at least one hero. That's not making a game strategically difficult. It's making it garbage and unfair. If you're going to, guaranteed, lose 1-2 heroes on the map, what's the point? At that point, the player has no ability to strategize and plan, which is the entire point of the game.
And if you think, "oh, just take it slow and easy and only reveal 1-2 at a time", you're going to get bit with that line of thinking. Because there's no real consistency at all to the fog of war and sight of your heroes. In one map, you may reveal enemies at a certain distance. In a different situation, the enemies will be revealed randomly after your turn is already over. What's the point of that? If the map is going to be revealed based on the scripting of the situation, then there's no strategic element to the movement of your team in that way, either.
To round out the theme of inconsistency and no real strategic planning, damage chances seems completely random as well. For example, a long-range hunter may have a 50% chance of hitting an enemy when they're 10 tiles away. If they're 5 tiles away, the hit percentage stays at 50%. That's strange, because they're closer. On the next map, the same hunter may have a 70% of hitting them at 10 tiles away and 100% at 5 tiles away. So yet again, there's no point in thinking strategically about the combat. Just click "attack" until all the things are dead. Because placement doesn't matter.
And no, cover makes little to no difference here (at least I never noticed) other than an enemy has no line of sight if a hero is behind cover. But partial cover doesn't seem to do much if at all.
This game needs serious tuning by someone who understands strategy games. That's the major crux of the problem with Massive Chalice and with Double Fine in general right now. They continue to make games that they don't really understand, and those games end up poorly designed and not as great as they could. The rest of Massive Chalice is dull but inoffensive. It's mostly just clicking on research goals you haven't done yet and making sure that keeps have heroes assigned to them. The only real thing to strategize and stay engaged with is the combat, and it's poorly designed and just a bad X-Com knockoff that tries too hard to copy a formula it doesn't even understand.
If this game could get some TLC in a patch (I.E. balance some of the encounters to give the player a chance, tune the line of sight/fog of war and hit probability algorithms, that would be enough to make the combat interesting. As an unbalanced mess that it's currently in, it's impossible to play through a combat situation and strategize well enough to come out ahead of the AI. There's no point in trying, because the game is going to use poor balance and tuning to rip heroes away from you. At that point, it takes the "Strategy" out of the "strategy game".

A Hole New World is one of the best retro platformers you can currently get your hands on via steam!
The game has a basic story to explain what is happening and why you, the potion master, have to prevail against the forces of chaos. This is shown via the quick intro that leads you into the game where you just start playing, with no help or hints. Don't worry the controls, besides that they feel responsive, are quite basic and easy to grasp and whenever there is a new mechanic, the game will show you how to use it and in most cases, it will have some use immediately! It starts at a quite basic and chill difficulty level and quickly ramps up with every boss fight!
It delivers the 'classic feel' from games like MegaMan, both with its mechanics and its visual and sounds! The visuals consist of pixelated models, effects and backgrounds, all well made and unique so you can easily distinguish each. The 8bit music further complements the retro theme along with the various sound effects that help you understand what is happening.
The main feature of the game is that you can swap between 2 worlds, cleverly named Versee and ReVersee. This allows certain precision challenges to be created, along with the marvellous boss fights, that each has unique tactics and rewards you with an upgrade. In addition, there are secret areas that you need to explore in order to find, along with other areas, that while they are hidden there is a visual hint that something is there! Thus your observation is rewarded with more upgrades! Finally, the game features a game+, boss rush and challenge mode, available after you beat the game once, and, to my big surprise, multiple endings! For completionists, the achievements can provide an additional challenge, as there are various tasks, from do not take any damage in a boss fight to kill all enemies or even don't kill any enemies ones!
You can easily play with both controller or keyboard, with the latter being customizable. The only negative I can think for this jewel, is quite minor, that if you want to play fullscreen you may get tired to the relatively big pixels.
A Hole New World easily scores 8/10 not only because it offers this retro gameplay but it also offers it so well. You can easily tell that the game was made with love! As a final note, the game besides achievements features steam trading cards.

Enjoy Deus Ex: Revision for what it is, for that is the very best thing about it. Don't play this game with a purist's mindset and complain about every single deviance from the original game's level design like many of those who thumbed this mod down. If you're not willing to embrace new ideas or changes, I don't know why you would even bother playing a revision mod of, well... anything. These folks put in 7 years of hard work to create this mod, and in my opinion they nailed it.
Revision makes me want to explore the Deus Ex world all over again with its revised and expanded environments. Essentially, it's still the same game with a fresh coat of paint. If you played the original Deus Ex, much of the original game's level design remains in this mod. Environments and map layouts will still be, for the most part, very familiar. New and expanded areas provide new approaches and variety in gameplay and exploration. Whether you're new to the original Deus Ex or you're a veteran gearing up for yet another playthrough, Deus Ex: Revision offers a new experience to all players that remains true to the original game.
Is it a perfect mod? No. It has its share of glitches and bugs that are still being fixed, and the Revision soundtrack is arguably hit or miss (The Synapse, no one can replace you). Still, there is absolutely nothing about this mod which I'd consider thumbing it down for. It's a truly passionate addition to Deus Ex.
Kudos to the developers of Deus Ex: Revision for their hard work. This free mod certainly is a treat for us old Deus Ex fans and newcomes alike.

This review is going to be long so if you are not interested in the 'wall of text' then look at the bottom of this for the TL;DR summary...Now with that said and done, from my mountain stronghold I write this with no fear of retaliation!
Deus Ex: Revision is as the title suggests, a revision of Deus Ex's graphics, the game is the same but it looks much more polished, the gameplay is as solid as ever and while the remade music CAN put some people off, I don't have issue with it as it manages to maintain, if not at times, IMPROVE that feeling that you want in a Cyberpunk Game.
It has flaws, the aforementioned soundtrack being offputting to others, the fact that there is added bits in levels CAN lead to some serious confusion, I almost never found the crowbar you could find early until I saw the hut they placed. And that's about it with flaws for me...I may not be all that qualified to say flaws given my time with it but just letting that out for ya.

In its current state, Kingdoms and Castles is more of a sandbox than a city sim, city builder etc. This is because the game doesn't offer much in terms of enemies and a challenge - the fun comes from creating the city, trying different designs in new worlds and finding the most efficient way to thrive. Although there are two enemies, vikings and dragons, which attack independently of one another at any random time, they can simply be avoided on the hardest difficulty and just reparing the damage after they inevitably leave. The game claims you can also lose if your city's too unhappy, however this hasn't happened to me on many playthroughs and you're given plenty of warning in advance.
Despite this, the game is still enjoyable and relaxing to play and very accessible due to its simplicity as there are only two things that need to be maintained, food and happiness (individual houses and peasants will tell you how to improve their happiness). However, players must create their own challenges to be able to get any replayability out of this game. But I'd recommend getting this game whilst it's still cheap because the few developers behind this game seem keen keep working on it!

Pros:
+ Very pleasing visual design
+ Replay value from random maps
Cons:
- This game does not fit the mold of any other City Builder -- it is unclear what the goal of this game is:
-- its not balancing the economy (there's very few things to build, and no need to balance ratio of buildings)
-- its not city management (no penalty for idle workers, no need to place certain buildings in close proximity, buildings like churches have no "capacity")
-- its not trade (there is no trade, and every island can build everything it needs)
-- its sort of military (dragons and vikings force you to build defenses, but you can play over an hour without an attack)
-- balancing happiness is very minimal as building churches / pubs / libraries has no long term cost you can build as many as you want
- after hitting 250 workers you begin to wonder why you're still playing. You've built everything there is and there's no motivation to continue. Furthermore, there's no practical way to provide employment for everyone once you hit 500 workers
- Game feels very incomplete, and devs are still adding major features (as of this writing game is slated to get Merchants in the next update)
Conclusion:
This game still feels like Early Access. I recommend waiting until all major features are there.

After about 5 hours, I feel like I'm done. Sure there is more I could do, with achievements, min-maxing city development, trying different city designs, setting personal goals, etc. If that's your thing you'll get more mileage out of this than I did.
But I was expecting more. Some reviews mention that the game feels unfinished. I wouldn't go that far, but the game feels much less than it could be. If the developers were still developing or communicating about the future of the game, I'd be a bit more excited about it.
Pros:
• Building a town is fast and fun.
• The game's got great ambiance. Clouds, music, and art design work well together. I found it calming to play.
• Good balancing and mechanics with regards to city building.
• Fun little details like citizen names and skill levels.
Cons:
• The "tower defense" element of the game is too easy. Enemies are wusses. I played on hard, and once I build a few tall towers, I quashed enemy raids like annoying mosquitoes. Before I had defenses, vikings and dragons completely overran my town, but you can recover from the damage in just a few minutes.
• Shallow city improvement model. I thought more things would appear and unlock as I played more, but pretty much the development tree you see at the beginning of the game is what you get. After a couple of hours, I'd basically unlocked everything.
So recommend or not recommend? I'm right on the fence, but at the moment, I give this a thumbs down. For the current price, I feel a bit disappointed, considering how much gameplay $10 can get elsewhere on Steam. If you can get this for a couple of bucks, however, I'd grab it.
If the developers rework the tower defense element of the game and add more stuff to build, I'd consider revising this. With more depth to city development and a robust tower defense mode, this could be a ton more fun.

EDIT: Added a list of game mechanics I enjoy.
Friendly visuals combined with its arcadey gameplay make this an extremely accessible baseball game on the PC!
But don't let the skin of the ball fool you, this game has meat! There's much more depth here than you may expect. A ton of super-solid game mechanics with the right amount of control to satisfy those of us who want to jump in and play but also feel like we're mastering a game and crave the feeling of progression.
Some of the solid game mechanics I enjoy:
BATTING - has both tap button swing and power swing (hold the button to build up power and release at the right moment) all the while moving your mouse/controller to position the bat. Increasing the EGO (difficulty) will make positioning the bat more important!
PITCHING - similar to batting, has a tap button pitch or power pitch by holding the button and aiming with the controller (or mouse).
FIELDING - while simple, the options to jump, dive, and wall jump all exist. On higher EGO ratings, you will need to guide your fielders more towards the ball.
BASE RUNNING - a nice feature here is you can tell all players to run at the same time OR you can control individual players (want 2nd base to run to third but 1st base to stay put? No problem).
EGO (difficulty settings) - It has a difficulty system that allows you to fine tune the AI to provide you with the pefect non-frustrating balance of challenge (the values range from 0-99!), it's really quite incredible. This allows you to tweak the game's difficulty as you get better but keep it from being frustratingly difficult, unless you want it to be.
To put it simply, Super Mega Baseball is brilliant and an absolute joy to play.
My only con: multiplayer is local only.
Super Mega Baseball came out of left field for me and seriously hits it out of the park!
Highly recommended.

This game plays on Windows 10. I couldn't find any reviews or information as to whether SMB would play on this latest OS from MS (although by the time I write this they will probably have come out with another wallet sucking venture). As a result I was reluctant to purchase this game. However, I decided at the price, what the heck... I would give it a try.
What a beautiful game. So happy that it runs smoothly with Windows 10. Don't let the arcade style cartoonish baseball players fool you. It is still baseball and so much fun in its simplicity. The EGO system is a stroke of genius. There is still enough tweaking that can be done to keep it interesting. Re-naming player names to Actors names was a hoot. It is a wee bit confusing at first, but within a few hours and some experimenting you will get the hang of it. If you want to micro-manage every little aspect, then don't waste your time. This game is visually stunning. The colours are vibrant and pop right out. The different ballparks are amazing. Please take note; the teams are not "linked" to any particular ballpark as there are more teams than ballparks. My understanding since joining the forum at
is that it takes time to create the ballparks and there will likely be more added in the future. The ones they have now are fantastic. The stands are full of cheering throngs of cartoon fans. The atmosphere is electric at times and you really get the feel of playing at a packed stadium. The cut scenes in between innings are outstanding. What a gem of a game. The streets outside the ballpark, full of traffic. Sparks flying off hydro poles. Subway cars, birds dive bombing the field, ferry boats... the detail put into this is absolutely amazing.
