If QWOP and Goat Simulator had a baby, and Die By The Sword and Dark Souls had a baby, and those two babies had a baby, you'd have Exanima.
While this game was fun for the 1 hour 11 minutes I gave it, my long term concern is for the combat. You press one button to attack, and the character will swing their weapon, and the animation of that swing will be procedurally determined by the computer. It's up to the player to side step into or with the attack to increase damage ("physics".)
The biggest problem is that alot of weapons are missing viable attack animations. The first weapon the player gets is a dagger length sharpened spike. Great stabby weapon, right? Well, the only attacks I could get out of it were rather wide left and right swings. While workable animations for sword length weapons, the short range of the spike made it really hard to judge distances, every attack either missing or turning into a bear hug.
The overall lack of stabs and overhead swings for single handed weapons (strange, considering the trailer had a two handed sword with an overhead attack,) means that every combat is a clusterf*** of either the player or the enemy's sword arm getting stuck in door frames or random furniture. Since the animations seem to be procedurally generated, there are also physics glitches where the player's sword arm will get stuck behind their back, requiring entering an exiting the combat stance mid battle to 'reset' animations.
For the game to be worth playing in the long term, either the engine that picks attacks needs to be refined to the point where it doesn't choose swings that will get stuck in a random bit of environment, or the player needs to be able to influence which attack the character makes (forward + attack = thrust, for example.) The current system is 'different,' but it isn't an improvement over current gaming systems, placing it well within gimmick territory.
For the most part this game can be fun, watching your character trip over furniture during a melee, or dodging an enemy attack, having the enemy hit a bybstander by accident, and watching the bystander kill the enemy for you was fun, but I just couldn't be convinced that what was there will be refined into a worthwhile game.

Overall, its a nice look at history and the perilous advenntures of the space race, but it is not something i'm gonna outright recommend to anyone not seriously interested in history or simulations.

This game has been sitting in my library for... Some time. And now I got around to playing it. I recommend this game, however for statistical purposes I'm giving it a bad review. If you will indulge me, I can justify my reasoning.
The game has an "inde" cell shader aesthetic with fairly saturated colors. It's base mechanics are similar to any other turn based strategy with an isometric map, but there is a twist. Your units are pooled from bloodlines. Quasi RNG breeding to get new units, or spending your time resource to recruit new random units. This game was apparently a crowdfunded game, and for what it is I will not be too harsh. But there are issues that you may want to be aware of.
The UI is very bad. At first I assumed it's because I don't know how to play. No. The UI is cluttered and lacking quality of life behavior at the same time. For example. In combat, you have the option to use keystrokes and mouse clicks to execute actions. However, you are also presented with on screen buttons to use forgoing the keyboard. The hit boxes are not correct for said buttons. If you click on an ability, and then confirm. Unless it's in exactly the right spot it will select the ability instead of confirming your action. Additionally, MOVE AND ATTACK ARE THE SAME BUTTON. You are not able to check your attack range for archers. Which has frequently moved my unit instead of attacking, in my first few hours.
The environment designs are minimalist, and cell shaded. Which isn't necessarily bad. But the camera is isometric for no reason. Which causes issues with walls and tall objects in the maps, as well as the map borders. Games like Xcom suffer from this issue as well, but at least in Xcom, walls fade out intelligently so you are able to see movement options. There is a decent soundtrack in the game, but if you take more than 5 minutes per combat. Be prepared to spend most of that time in dead silence.
The bloodline system is interesting, and I would like it if it were a bit more consistent. Each unit has inborn attributes, and personality traits. Personality traits can sometimes be gained or lost due to events and units influence on each other. However, even if you do find a good unit to continue your bloodline. The children have a fairly high degree of randomness to their stats, even with both parents having favorable modifiers. Such as a pair of fast intelligent long living parents birthing a dimwitted slow child who is nervous and flinches. The equivalent of a 0 IV Pokemon, literally trash. With most units living until about 60, the breeding system always feels like it's rushing you to make more inbreed garbage. Instead of elite houses that produce fine soldiers.
However, the classes and the way they interact with the breeding system is quite superb. I even find myself becoming sentimental about some of them after they died. In combat or of old age. There are three base classes, a brawler, an archer, and a dude that throws bottles. However, each of these classes have two sub classes that modify the archetypal class in some way. Such as a brawler that can stealth like an archer. ECT. They all seem to be fairly well balanced, now that the game has been released and is no longer supported. Which brings me to the last point.
Game balance. Sometimes, it's fun. Sometimes. The game literally cheats. It can cheat by making mobs "RANDOMLY" wander right next to your hidden unit. From over in China. Right next to screwedmyplanistan. Sometimes, on some maps your units will be paired off in two groups of two and one all by itself. You can have a maximum of five units in combat. [Aside from special missions.] And getting a spawn that splits up your entire squad is almost like the game has decided that you need units to die turn two. Some times, mobs will spawn all around you instantly seeing you. Then proceeding to fight a very costly battle, clostly for you that is.
Modding. The game not only doesn't support modding. It also appears to be written to prevent any modification at all. No community patches to fix game balance, no patches to fix the UI. No way to choose where your units start. Can't even use the soundtrack DLC to make the music loop a few times. No ability to make your own bloodline without the cringy memes. Nothing.
All and all. The game is very novel. I enjoy it, and will keep making new saves until I beat it brutal difficulty iron mode. Because I come to try hard or uninstall. I very much think the game needs more polish and feel it's an example of why crowdfunding is awful. That said, if it's five or six bucks. You might enjoy it, I'm recommending it. Even considering the lack of polish.

I'm not sure how I originally found out about this game, but I liked what I saw and have been following the developers on Facebook. I generally liked the aesthetic, the upside-down-world aspect (which kind of reminded me of Battle of Olympus) and the gameplay that looked like an interesting take on Mega Man.
Overall, I've been happy with the game. It controls quite well, even in the upside-down-segments (which I tend to have a lot of trouble with it games). The level design is interesting -- it is obviously planned out, but also has kind of a random-feeling quality to it. Some levels are fairly straightforward left-to-right affairs, while others require some backtracking. I've enjoyed the weapon system too -- you get new abilities by beating bosses and can switch on the fly, ala Mega Man. Unlike Mega Man, there's no weapon charge meter, so you can use them to your heart's content. I've actually found the 4 I've found to be different enough to be worth switching between fairly consistently, it's not just a matter of picking the right thing for a boss.
On that point, the bosses have all been pretty cool. They have patterns, but there is a lot of variety in those patterns. So I've found them to be challenging and largely fair. I am stuck on one boss now, but I know with some time I'll overcome it. This is made a lot less frustrating because while the game is difficult, it does have checkpoints -- I can keep retrying a boss easily, the main loss is that my score resets to zero (my impression is that this also affects the ending?).
There are some things I don't love about it. The early stages, in particular, have some fairly busy backgrounds that are of a similar tone to the foreground -- so I've had a hard time differentiating between things. This was especially hard for me in a forest area where I was dealing with spiders jumping in and out of the underground world because I could barely tell where they were. I was glad to find this to be less of an issue later in the game.
There are also situations where you just feel overwhelmed with enemies. It's certainly possible to overcome them, but having 10 clouds shooting icicles at you while dodging two other things is a bit much. That said, the fact that enemies don't instantly respawn offscreen makes this a LOT more managable than it would have been in the NES days. In fact, they don't respawn at all: there are a couple of achievements revolving around killing every monster in the stages.
In the end though, I've enjoyed what I've played of the game and think it's a good example of its genre. The main game looks to be about 90 to 120 minutes if you blast through it, but there are items to collect and other modes that round out the package. So I feel like it's worth the $10. Looking forward to finishing it and checking out the New Game+ option.

Revision is a mod that updates and polishes the original Deus Ex both technically and artistically with new textures, music, enviroments and game settings while keeping the original gameplay and story of Deus Ex intact. I'm happy to report that with few exceptions Revision succeeds!
With Revision's new high resolution textures, much improved lighting and larger, more detailed enviroments, Deus Ex is so appealing on the eye that I actually forgot that I was playing a game whos engine is almost 20 years old! Revision is in this sense a testament to how almost anything can be accoplished in modding with enough dedication and talent.
The new soundtrack is also really solid and for many tracks I actually prefer it over the original. The reason why is because the original soundtrack sometimes felt a little bit too upbeat to fit in with Deus Ex's grim and apocalyptic setting. Some of the new tracks just do a better job fitting in with the game's atmophere by being more moody and slow paced.
Another great positive with Revision is how easy it is to install. No need for any external game launchers or messing about with folders in the game directory and the new game settings such as the FOV changer are just a god send.
Now we get to some of the negatives about Revision:
Well first of all there are some bugs in the game, I won't list all of them because that would be tedious but one thing in particular that annoyed me is that some of the sounds such as alarms don't seem to correctly eminate their sound. It's like the sound is coming from a location different then from where it ought to come from. I'm not sure what this could be the result of but it needs to be fixed, it's important in a stealth/action game that the sounds are working properly.
The bigger and more ambitious enviroments of Revision capture the feel and look of the original but could be criticized for being style over substance. Yes, they look amazing, pure eye candy but how functional and interesting are they really to play? Well it varies from map to map but some of the maps in Hong Kong are especially needlessly large. The map where you go to the temple to meet the triads is massive in scale but other then the temple there really isn't much of interest to explore or loot.
The result of having needlessly big enviroments in some places, is to screw up the tempo of the game and that's a big problem when you consider just how great the tempo of the original Deus Ex was paced.
Another minor problem with the new enviroments is that they sometimes fool you into thinking you can explore certain areas that aren't actually explorable. You spend time platforming up a builing trying to jump inside an open window with a clearly explorable room only to find that there is a invisible wall that makes it impossible to get inside.
Despite the critisism I've brought up, I loved my playthrough of Deus Ex with Revision and I highly recommend it to both Deus Ex vets and first time players. I give Revision 8 out of 10.
In case anyone wonders, I also posted this same review on moddb.

This mod improves my all time favorite classic, with better textures, models, level design, audio as well as Direct3D 9 rendering, widescreen resolution support and much more. Of course this mod uses many elements made by different members of Deus Ex modding communities, that said mod authors did great job implementing them all into the game with ease.
I always thought that Deus Ex had amazing story for it's time, very deep and non linear, with choices and consequences, fully voiced dialogues which wasn't that common in 2000, but what this game lacked back then was visuals, and Revision adds just that. So now to me, it feels like complete game.
I like everything this mod does, from improved intro and Deus Ex themed in game music, to improved environment elements, additional placement of props and decorations, as well as completely reworked areas and new character models. I know that many fans love original game and prefer the game how it was made back in the day. But this mod is closest to Deus Ex remake you will get in a while unless devs or someone tries to make it similar to DE:HR, which is not that likely. Game feels more atmospheric, with detailed environments filled with new props that make levels richer and not as plain, empty and boring as before.
This mod is for those who want to replay the game with "fresh coat of paint", a game that looks "newer" yet keeps all the feel and charm of the original. You can disable some features of the mod if you prefer old character models and music, but honestly if you don't like what this mod does, just play the original. I've spent 9 hours on it, finished the 2nd mission and I'm having a blast, it's so much better now and there's even more to do and explore now, which is awesome.
I didn't want to and/or was bored while trying to replay the Deus Ex, but with Revision I jumped right in with no second thoughts and I'm enjoying the game. Story is the same it's just so much more enjoyable to the eye, so don't be hating on work of love that the modding community has given us.
I recommend this mod for those who want more richer visual experience, with the same old Deus Ex story, gameplay under the hood. Full playthrough took me roughly 40 hours, and it was a blast.

I don't regret buying the game, cause it's beautiful and even in it's short playtime quite emotional.
Would this game stand for its own, I wouldn't moan.
But it's a sequel. To a game that does absolutely
better. (Except for the graphics)
And that's sad. Cause when you play
game you always remember how beautiful the first one was... and how downgraded everything in the second one is.
It's supposed to be a point and click adventure. But there isn't much left from the idea behind such a game. There is no inventory at all. Every object you find has to be used on the same screen. And most of the time you just have to klick on things in the right order. No thinking involved, no puzzlesolving, no crazy item combinations.
There are equally as may cutscenes (if not more) than playable passages. And here is where you get the most dialogue in the game. A few sentences here, a few there... and that's all. Every character stays a blank paper without much depth.
In the first game you had lots of dialogue options for every NPC and everyone of them was very well written.
The result is that you can't build up any kind of emotional relationship to
of the NPCs. And as things get bad... you just don't care.
The first time I played The Whispered World I needed something around 12 hours to finish the game.
For Silence it took me... 6.
Why is this bad? A short game can be very great as well! And that's true.
But the short playtime is the result of:
- having very few locations you can actually
something in.
- having nearly no gameplay there at all
- having no real puzzles to solve
- having nearly no additional dialogues with NPCs
And the last thing....
I don't mind paying 30€ for a 6 hours game.
But I mind paying 10€
for a game that lacks absolutely
it's predecessor (and actually every other Daedalic adventure) does better! And all the other adventures cost 20€ at release.
So to summ it up. You pay more and get less of everything.
And that's just... sad.
And brings me to give this game a thumbs down despite the fact that I enjoied it. Cause it really makes me sad to
that Daedalic is
to do it so much better!
All that is left to say is... I hope they don't stop making the great adventures they are able to make. Let's see what the future may hold.

I finished the game purely because I wanted to know where the story was going, but the amount of time it took to get there was not worth the value. You spend enormous amounts of time just walking across completely drab landscapes of rock. Occasionally you find actual structures and signs of settlement, but with nothing connected to them. If you were to compress a walkthrough down to just the story bits, there's maybe 15-20 minutes worth of plot to this game.
All story is told through notes and audio recordings, and to its credit the sparse amount of voice acting in the game was good (at least, the parts that were in english). I just wish there had been more of it.  You could fit the main character's dialog on to two sheets of paper.
The visuals are drab and uninteresting, 80% of the time consisting of the same rock texture overlayed with a few greens and reds. Things did get more visually stimulating when you reach the volcano, but then its back to more boring rock. The character and building models feel straight out of the late 90s, and if it wasn't made in a modern game engine then I'd think they made this 15 years ago.
The biggest flaw in the game is that most of the time the only clue you have about what direction you're supposed to trek in is a slight green tint to the ground texture, or a sheen on the terrain that's only visible when facing a certain direction.  When those indicators fail you basically navigate by spotting land forms that clearly are lined up in a linear direction. Level design was not only boring, but almost cliche with its uninspiring platforming challenges.
All in all the entire game just feels really cheap and not very fleshed out.

I started following this a while back purely out of the excitement of the physics and collision driven mechanics I saw in early demos.  I bought it one sale, and then put almost no time into it.  I started playing it only recently, and I cannot believe this game is still Early Access.
With 25 hours in, I've played almost zero of the campaign/story.  I've only played the Arena, because I think it's super helpful to get your mechnics, movement, and combat down.  I'm only halfway through what I intend to accomplish in the Arena (fully built out group of 3), so I expect I'll get about 50 hours purely from the Arena mode (assuming no further content updates there).  Then factor in that I'll eventually play the story mode, and I"m expecting to get 75 hours out of this game.  I cannot say that about a lot of AAA titles I've played in recent years, honestly.
This game is an exciting and rewarding play experience.  I really enjoy that "learning" the combat is not purely numbers and stats driven - your character gets better because you literally learn to control him and his movements better.  That makes dominating combat hugely satisfying (I'm talking, laughing out loud and chuckling like an idiot when I land solid blows and combos).
I would love to build a rull RPG experience leveraging the combat mechanics of this game.  Very pleased with this purchase.

Exanima has a very, VERY steep learning curve. It takes many hours of practice before you start to get a grip on the basics, but thanks to the physics-based combat (no pre-made animations, everything that happens is a physics calculation) the skill-cap is incredibly high.
Replayability in the story mode is low, because every level is constant and does not change. However, the arena mode is amazing. It generates matches and opponents for you to fight, it never gets old. There's also a practice mode, which lets you fight increasingly difficult opponents, and is reset when you close the game, so there's no consequences. I recommend that beginners play the practice mode a lot.
There isn't much of a tutorial at the moment, so be sure to look up the controls.

A true indie gem.  The tags say this is a tower defense game, but it is really it's own thing.  I suppose tower defense is the closest thing to what it is but it is a bit misleading.
So what it is?  The premise is you have to fight back the creeper, which behaves pretty much like water pouring out of a spout (or more than one most of the time).  It slowly spreads from it's source, and is stopped by walls and higher ground until it fills up the area below and reaches the correct height.  To fight this, you build cannons, mortors, flying craft, anti-creeper producers (your beneficial creeper than cancels out the other creeper) and a few other weapons.  These are your "towers" but they are all mobile and can be placed anywhere they fit.  To support them you need to produce energy, which comes from nodes that cover the ground and reactors.  The nodes link up to others and need to link back to your base to produce energy and supply your troops.  Reactors don't need any ground to cover and produce more.  Troops out of supply will soon use up there reserves and will no longer be able to use their abilities.
So for gameplay you will slowly spread out over the map, extenting your network and fighting back the creeper until you reach the sources and take them out with special weapons.  That's the basics but there is more.  There is a scripting language for the maps that lets them bend the rules.  There is one, non-story level where you control a man through a maze who shoots and finds keys for instance.  To top it all off, there are literally thousands of maps (most likely, I didn't count).  The main story is only a very small part of the game.  After completing parts of it other areas open up, which are basically user created maps, beta testing maps and challenging maps.  If you like the game enough you could spend thousands of hours on it, I'm sure.  I was content with just the main story and a few other maps though.
If this looks at all interesting to you, do yourself a favor and pick it up.  It isn't even expensive.

Pros :
+ Space game. There is a serious lack of space games today.
+ Good management aspects. This game is not about building the perfect rocket, but how the agency manages between launching less-important mission to get some funding and launching important mission for the moon landing. Also a juggle between the risk of launching a risky mission now to get some big funding for the next 4 years. Most of the game dillema revolves around this thing. If I launches this mission now, I may get huge funding for 4 years, but the reliability is still low, and I can lose my craft and my money, etc.
+ Different animation between NASA and the Soviet space program.
+ Lots of space program available : Mars probe, Sun probe, Saturn probe, Space plane, etc.
+ Lots of ways to achieve the final objectives (the Moon). You can use 2 man craft, or 3 man craft, using lunar rendezvous or direct ascent, a lot of choices.
+ The mechanics of research that gives penalty if we attempt something "too foolish", or try to research for "too advanced" systems.
Cons :
- Mission is too limited, only limited to Moon landing. How about space stations? Mission to Mars? This is a serious problem.
- UI at times is clunky, especially when managing your researchers.
- No animation on destroyed/failed mission
- You can't take any decision when mission is already a go. Success and failure is only a dice roll away.
- "Rocket" research is useless, only useful in opening stage of the game.
- Failure in the opening of the game to secure big funding may make you fail for the rest of the game.
- The competition between space agencies is not developed enough. We only know that the Soviets/NASA has done this and that, without knowing what technology they have used. For example NASA has completed an Earth orbit flight. As a Soviet player, I think it's important to know whether the NASA uses Gemini program, Mercury program, or Apollo program. Maybe I should also know the type of booster rocket used. That's what intelligence is for.
For gamers that don't have specific liking to space and aeronautics, you better stay away because most of the "management" in this game is limited to human resources management only, and there are lack of anything else. For gamers that love space and aeronautics, this game have a lot to offer, and a must buy.

When I heard that this game was coming out I immediately remembered playing the predecessor game in the 90s Buzz Aldrin's Race into Space (BARIS) and while there are a few areas where I think the original was better I think that this game is a large improvement overall.  The launch animations aren't exactly impressive for what they could have done, but the fun in a management game like this is in reaching objectives not so much the graphics.  That being said I kinda wish that they used some video clips here and there like they did in BARIS.  I actually kinda liked the video clips even if by modern standards those in BARIS were very grainy.  Much like the original a poorly executed mission can massively derail your program, but on the easy level I've noticed that people don't die as easily as they did in the old game.
Now there are countless diverse missions from the X-15 to orbiting satellites to lunar impact probes that allow you to pursue numerous programs that NASA and Soviet Space Program pursued in the 50s and 60s.  The only area I see some regression from the old game whereas mission options is that BARIS allowed you to take a Direct Ascent or a Minishuttle (e.g. DynaSoar) mission to the Moon.  Considering I never really considered Direct Ascent a practical means of getting to the Moon compared to EOR or  LOR I don't really consider that a big loss.
Whereas the original game you could only really customize the skills of Astronauts/Cosmonauts the new game let's you develop the skills of your Scientists/Engineers and mission controllers.  This has added an entirely different dynamic to the game.
Whereas Astronaut names other than Buzz Aldrin I don't see too many original names in the Astronaut rosters.  I'm not sure whether unlike BARIS they had issues with using the real names for the game or their legal dept was just paranoid.  Not a big distraction, but wish that their roster had more historical names.  IDK whether I really care for micromanaging the skills of mission controllers, but it adds more things for you to manage.
One area that I think I don't care so much for is that when a mission fails you lose prestige points even if the failure isn't catastrophe.  (i.e. Apollo 13 would hurt your prestige as much as a Challenger accident, which doesn't make sense imho)  In BARIS you had the opportunity for a partial success where you met some of your goals (e.g. you do a duration and the crew gets sick you may get credit for the duration that you didn't cut short) and I hope a future patch will resolve this bug in gameplay.
Unlike the old game where a hit in prestige would immediately hurt your funding the next year funding is only calculated every 4 years.  This can be a bit of a mixed blessing though.  When you are doing great in prestige sometimes you can actually far exceed prestige goals and be assured of a huge raise in funding at next review in several seasons away, but your current funding hand ties you to how fast you can proceed even if all your missions are successes.  It seems like in real life if you are scoring huge prestige points that the government wouldn't wait 2-3 years to reward you with some more money.  The 4 year funding review if you hit a bad failure right before review might get you locked into a funding problem that you may never be able to get out of before the other side flies past you and wins the game.  I think this often discourages you from taking a big mission right before funding reviews because near the start of the 4 years you have time to rebound, but otherwise you get stuck with poor funding that will kill your program.  Unlike the original BARIS I haven't seen a lot of random events where you get money or lose money.  This makes the game a bit more about your skills than luck, but I think it might reduce the replay value a bit.  Sometimes half off discounts off new hardware/programs could really help in BARIS.  I think that was an incredibly unbalanced random event, but private sector R&D contributions here and there aren't outside believable.
Unlike the original BARIS money management is a lot bigger role in this game.  You have recurring costs for salary for Astronauts/Scientists/Mission Control and even the programs themselves.  The first time I played this game I lost because I ran out of money because I wasn't paying close enough attention to recurring costs.  If you fall into the red you get fired as director so you really need to manage your funds carefully.
I do think that the UI was confusing at times.  There are certain times where I was didn't immediately see how to leave a window.  It isn't horrible, but I think the UI could be a bit more clean at times.
I've planned the game 3 times now.  The first time I ran out of money.  The second time I lost after a series of mission failures made it difficult to catch back up.  The third time I won.  I haven't really played with the sandbox mode yet, but I see a lot of potential fun in this game despite some flaws.  Considering the lack of expensive complex animations or videos to license I'm not sure that this should be $30, maybe more like $20, but for fans of BARIS this game looks like the successor that many of us were looking for.  There aren't many games in the space program manager genre, but this is probably the best I have seen so far.

This is a brilliant game for anyone intersted in the space race or spaceflight history in general. Space programs include all the major ones like Gemini and Apollo but also ones that werent followed like the Gemini direct ascent mission to land on the moon. Each mission is carried out ina  lovely set of cutscenes that are really evocative of the historical mission and are animated, as well as being very accurately protrayed.
As you progress towards the moon landing you can have setbacks and it can get very nerve wracking as you start getting short on money, or failing important flight tests. Its very satisfying if you make a moon landing before the historical date.
This is the first of two other parts to this series, the next one should cover the shuttle/space station era and the final part should hopefully cover a Mars landing. If theya re all done it will be a superb game covering the whole of the space flight era including practically all the various space programs and technologies - what a fantastic undertaking and what a marvelous tribute to the bravery and hard work of all the people involved in the endeavour to explore space.
Definitely highly recommended as a beautiful, engaging recreation of the space race and early space exploration era.

Very interesting game that will reliably give you a really fun 20 hours gameplay (the length of a single playthrough) if not more. It's XCom meets Game of Thrones!
This review is mainly for people, like me who are are fans of XCom, but need something different to give us our "fix".
Massive Chalice (MC) takes the basics of XCom - the turn based tactical gameplay and the overarching strategy of building a squad and base to survive an invasion, and then adds its own little twists.
Most importantly, it tries to fix one of the main problems of XCom, where once you build up a strong base and squad, the game ceases to be difficult. MC does this with the somewhat inspired "generations" mechanic, whereby your heroes will decline with old age, eventually die, and their children and grandchildren have to take up the fight. This helps prevent the game from getting stale, and keeps it interesting and challenging right to the end.
There are some bad points. Elements of the game just aren't quite balanced. The tactical gameplay is messy. The cover mechanic doesn't make a whole lot of sense, it's unclear when your troops can and can't be hit. And counter to that, it's a bit counterintuitive as to why proximity to the target doesn't affect the accuracy or damage of archers, but is critical to people throwing explosive flasks (for accuracy sure, but damage also increasing with proximity!?!).
In terms of strategy, the generational breeding is a great concept, but I feel may have been, understandable, held back by not wanting to go too far down lines of either eugenics or gender stereotyping. It's never entirely clear, for instance, at what age your heroes can stop having children.
The good points definitely outweigh the bad. Definitely worth the purchase.

This game is simple - you take X-COM (except without the RNG that's programed to hate all terrestrial life with an undying passion) and you combine it with one of those management games, you know, Canadian Curling Manager Xtreme or whatever.
At its core, MC a third-person tactical; you go a number of squares, you have a number of actions, the monsters get increasingly wierd and powerful.  Its when you're not figting that makes this game unique - because it happens in a timescale much greater than a human life, not only do you get to watch your heroes grow old and die, you have to build dynastic houses to keep certain hero classes going from generation to generation.   Is this character more valuable on the battlefield, or is she more valuable spawning the next generation to keep the fantasy alien menace at bay?  And oh, her husband isnt too thrilled to be part of this arranged marriage, so go king it up and try to get them to get along again.  Do I research that nifty suit of armor, or do I scour the kingdom for new talent?
Play is smooth, graphics are blocky but this doesnt detract.  Voice actors for the two advisors are charming without being grating.  I suspect a decent level of replay value, as there is enough built-in threat that victory is not inevitable (hard choices: loose the area with the Crucible, or the one with the Keep), and enough randomness in the character generation that you wont have the same game twice.

There's a lot to be said about the fact that a Deus Ex mod being released in 2015 garnered publication on some major blogs. Deus Ex still stands as one of the hallmarks of the RPG/FPS genre. It's an excellent game with a well written plot, superb music and great use of multiple choice solutions for players.
Certain aspects of it may not have aged gracefully (those graphics were never good), but the game is wholly unique and hasn't really been replicated since. Even it's own sequels fail to live up to the original (though Human Revolution was a damn good game).
So instead of looking to the future, mod team Caustic Creative tweaked the past. With Deus Ex: Revision, we're given a new look at an old classic. Let me emphasize that last part; this is a new look, not a good one.
I sadly can't get on board with a lot of the changes made to the base Deus Ex game. I don't mind the graphical upgrades (as I've used a few of the mods contained in here) and even the new music can be cool (you can also revert to the original soundtrack), but the level design takes a tremendous nose dive after the third mission and never recovers.
When the description boasts, "new world-building detail," I didn't expect them to mean that literally. Most of the maps have been expanded in a way that adds more frivolous items instead of anything concrete to the flow of the game. At best, it's superfluous, at worst, it destroys some of the freedom the original game offered.
Certain parts later in the game are boiled down to a linear path and others are obscurely hidden behind walls and grates that a regular player wouldn't find. There is no other point in the game which requires me to break open a wall, so why hide the exit to a level behind that?
Worse still, when the options are stripped away, the game just feels like a typical sci-fi shooter. That is something the original Deus Ex never felt like. While not every level was brimming with hundreds of choices, you always had an alternative to progress.
Then there are the maps that characters hand out to you. It's fine if you want to make some changes to alter layouts, but at least update the image files. Walking around the catacombs aimlessly to find a pathway not marked on the map is frustrating as all hell, but even other areas refer to places that no longer exist due to the revised map structures.
It sours what is otherwise a great update. Some of the balance tweaks to the guns are appreciated and I like the AI being generally smarter, but that even brings up issues with the new level designs. The enemies are so intent on killing you that they will often unlock doors and grant you access without having to deal with lockpicking or finding passcodes. It robs you of yet another choice that Deus Ex thrives on.
At least if you could revert back to the standard game with this, but that option is absent. If you've never experienced the original game, don't even bother installing this. Look for a guide about texture mods and go from there. The classic game has so much more nuance and versatility then this.
That basically leaves Revision for veterans of the Deus Ex experience. For them, I guess this is okay. I kept getting lost and lacking any real hints from maps or in-game dialog. It's hard to navigate when an area just isn't where a character states.
I will commend Caustic on making this a free mod and going through the lengths to get each individual piece installed seamlessly. I just wish they had more options to let me experience simply the graphics and rearranged music instead of going with their version of the Deus Ex mythos.
As it stands, I'd just say skip this. It's exciting to still be talking about the OG Deus Ex, but the game is a classic for a reason. To tinker with it just feels nasty.

Lifeless Planet sells itself as an action adventure tribute to Cold War era science fiction. What’s clear from the very beginning of the game is its dedication to creating a rich atmosphere and an engaging plot, but its gameplay may be unable to keep up with the elements surrounding it.
It starts with an international space mission’s crash landing on a planet that was supposed to be covered with a blanket of life. Of course, when the unnamed astronaut the player controls wakes up, they find their crew missing and the planet lifeless – just as the game’s name suggests.  The astronaut must explore a barren landscape to find his crew and figure out why the planet has turned to waste.
The astronaut provides commentary and occasional flashbacks to reveal a character left troublingly lonesome after the loss of his wife. The fair voice performances and writing are enough for the clichéd premise to be convincing and successfully instill loneliness to the player. What really makes it work is the raw isolationist tone emanating from the very composition of the environment. Grand expanses of seemingly endless nothing stretch out towards the horizons. Massive cliffs, rocks, and mountains dot the landscape to remind the player just how small we humans are. The camera itself is positioned purposefully distant from the player to compound the humbling effect. The astronaut is small, lost, and alone. The player feels small lost and alone.
As the game progresses, the mood evolves with it. The environments become increasingly hostile and sinister in appearance. Horror elements are sprinkled in adding an effective sensation of uneasiness. It’s not terrifying, but it does venture into unnerving areas to evoke the frightening nature of space exploration.
Regardless, the astronaut keeps going. According to the occasional loading screen, it’s what his wife would have wanted. He eventually comes across the ruins of a Soviet colony, adding new elements to the mystery. Why are the Soviets here, how did they get here, and what happened to them?
Logs from the colony’s leader can be discovered providing clues into the planets colonization and destruction. It’s no surprise the story’s themes play heavily with the environmental consequences of man’s hubris, but the game trickles out new information and insights at a satisfying rate. New ideas are consistently unveiled, often altering previously formed understandings of the plot. It successfully provides answers leading to more and more questions. While the outcome likely won’t take anyone by surprise, the long and twisted road to get there is a deeply fulfilling mystery.
Unfortunately, the quest for understanding might as well be the sole driving force of Lifeless Planet as its gameplay leaves much to be desired. For the most part, there isn’t much to do other than walk from clue to clue while admiring the game’s rustic beauty along the way. It’s almost enough to work as an endearing walking sim, but it adds clumsy mechanics on top of what could have been a purely explorative adventure.
The most common obstacle is basic platforming, but the game lacks tight enough controls to be anything more than frustrating. It requires the mastery of managing forward based momentum over precision jumping. This direction makes thematic sense with the planets low gravity and generally large settings, but it ends up feeling as though the player can lose control at any moment. The problem is made more evident when the player comes across special jetpack fuel allowing for multiple bursts. With triumphant music accompanying the new ability, these moments are presented as empowering, but the sight of fuel canisters often produces dread. More boosts means longer jumps, and longer jumps provide more opportunity for failure. The particulars of the game’s physics can be learned over time, but successfully landing a jump never feels skillful. Getting past a platforming segment should feel like an accomplishment, not a relief.
Occasionally a lite puzzle will block the way, but calling them lite puzzles feels a tad gracious. Solutions are always obvious and are never far away. More often than not, they only require a peculiar sphere to be placed inside an equally peculiar obelisk providing power to doors or elevators. A cool mechanical arm is sometimes required, but it isn’t used for anything remarkable. It’s just conceptually intriguing and nothing more. The puzzles never give an intellectual challenge, but do succeed in managing the games pacing while occasionally triggering neat visual treats.
While lacking in enjoyable gameplay, the game’s mysteries and environments are enough to carry the game to its conclusion. Lifeless Planet is occasionally frustrating and often vapid, but still manages to be engaging and beautiful.

I'm of two minds about this game. I really enjoy the batting and pitching mechanics, which are essential to a good baseball game, but everything needs some work. The fielding and baserunning are just ok. Both are too slow for my liking, even in season mode after you train and upgrade players. The difficulty curve is a little odd as well. The game has a Ego curve that goes from 1-100. I can absolutely crush CPU teams all the way up to EGO 60. Moving up to 65 to add more challenge just seems to make the game more unfair. CPU batters hit balls out of the zone off the tip of their bat a bajillion feet into the stands, CPU Pitchers get ridiculous strike calls.
Batting is incredibly fun, except when it isn't. I think making contact with the ball and managing your power swings are done well, but I feel like you ending up hitting the ball directly to a fielding CPU player far too often. I once played a game where I went 8 innings just crushing the ball, and I bet the fielders in the had moved a combined 20 feet to gather them all up.
I wish I could find a difficulty level that really hit the sweet spot. The core mechanics of the game are solid and worth a shot.

Great play mechanics. Pitching is really fun and the control over location is really tight. Equally as fun is the batting which has a very intuitive/visceral feel to it.  Baserunning is a little tricky, but you get the hang of it. Fielding is pretty much automated but diving, jumping and throwing give you more control. A surprising amount of depth once you start adjusting the difficulty setting called "Ego". The cartoon characters have great variety and include male/female. This is by far the best arcade style baseball game. Strongly recommend it.

Oh boy...OMD 2...or the game that's clearly not been designed around single player.
With OMD 1 and its mini expansion I spent about 8 hours on the medium difficulty. I had to restart some levels, readjust strategy, etc. But overall, the levels were pretty fair and you got around via portals quickly. In OMD 2 this has been - for the most part - completely scrapped. Pretty much every map has been specifically designed around 2 player co-op. Even the first few levels you start having problems on the normal difficulty when you're on your own, since your characters are mean killing machines, contributing a ton to the actual damage dealt. From what I've heard, later levels are supposedly next to impossible on higher difficulties. The DLC packs are "a bit" better in that regard, but suffer from the same problems. This also results in later levels not being able to complete the "par times" for a map, which in turn results in less skulls, which in turn means you have to play more to earn enough to unlock new stuff or upgrade existing stuff. And due to the map layouts it's almost impossible to cover all "lanes" and build new traps, because you only have 10 seconds between each wave on normal, until you get a respite every 3 or so levels, but then again, it takes so much time just to MOVE to the other side of the map that you can't keep under par. Even on easy I'm like 4-5 minutes above them at times. Never had a problem in OMD 1 on normal 0o. More on that later. I think the maps are fine for co-op, but if you just want to murder some Orcs, stick to OMD 1. (Apparently Orcs Unchained is even worse).
Unlocks: In OMD 1 you got a new trap after every level you beat in the campaign. That system wasn't flawless, but it kept you going. In OMD 2 I unlocked not a whole lot by playing, but by paying instead. You get skulls for beating a level (up to 5) and bonus skulls for...I don't even know. Sometimes enemies drop them. Maybe it's for achievements like total number of career kills or something. While you can get a lot of skulls early on, obviously it becomes more difficult later and the unlocks themselves are very expensive, since there are 3 tiers for each trap + a special ability to unlock (that was 1 unlock in OMD 1, albeit a more expensive upfront cost). Since there are no damage numbers in the game, you can't even verify what the improvement is. Most higher level traps also have to be unlocked via skulls in the first place (I'd say more than half of the traps available in the game). The only good part about it is that you can refund all of your skulls at any given point and are able to redistribute them. However, it would have been better if you were able to downgrade individual traps instead. But it's better than the permanent system in OMD 1. To earn more skulls the game constantly reminds you to do maps on endless mode. Not very interesting if you ask me.
Your lovely idiot from the first game is now being accompanied by the "evil" female apprentice. I initially wanted to play the game with her, until I noticed that her starting weapon does pretty much nothing on its own. Damage is low, stopping power is low and somehow headshots have either been taken out of the game or are very obscure and very hard to achieve. The idiot however starts not with his trusty crossbow for some reason (which can be unlocked for skulls, but is totally pointless, since it deals less damage, has less stopping power and is so terribly inaccurate that it hurts compared to his main weapon), but with a shotgun. I have to say it kinda grew on me later on. It has pros and cons, obviously. A con is definitely that you can't reliably get headshots (if they are even in the game. Like I said, I didn't really notice, but it seemed that hits to the head DID more damage, but with a shotgun...yeah, difficult from anything but closest range). The pro, however, is that it can be upgraded to knock over most heavy monsters. That means you can single handedly defeat an ogre without it even touching you, since you can just constantly knock it to the ground...very boring. Even 2 ogres can be soloed this way. 3 or more are a problem...and boy the game throws a lot at you later on. I think only some DLC monsters are knockdown immune like the Ball and Chain for example. The shotty also has a mana reliant grenade, which does splash damage and can knock enemies into chasms. It's neat, but it lacks "oomph". I would have liked a much higher cost with a much higher impact. All in all, pretty disappointing. I guess the witch is only useful as a support character in co-op, but she just seems to be the weaker of the two characters, period.
They've included some new monsters, but most of the more interesting ones come in the 3 mini DLC packs. Sappers are even more obnoxious now. And the basic orc models look kinda dumb and weird.
If you like co-op with friends (because there is no matchmaking), you may give it a try, but I personally don't see the appeal in endlessly farming maps for skulls to unlock and upgrade everything. There's only so much variation in a map you can possibly test out. If you only want it for a quick SP stomp, I'd avoid it.

Hexels 2 is amazing, it is very easy to learn and one of the pros for game devs is that you can quickly prototype some art for your game. The grid can be seen as a limitation or a con of this software, but in my opinion it helps you create art faster and make it look nicer. The last part is mostly for people that have struggles with traditional art tools. If you can get this software for a good price I would definitely try it.

Awesome little art program. Thumbs up, even at it's full price. It's arguably more fun than Black Ink which I like (don't fully understand it, but I'm trying :P) and certainly more usable for certain styles, and for a lower price.
I got it as part of a humble bundle (which I mainly bought for Spriter Pro, this was an added bonus), so I don't know if I'd have made the purchase at full price first off, but after having used it for a couple of hours (which you can do as part of their trial version) I already know I'll get loads of fun out of this program, and so if I'd gone the trial route I'd probably have bought it soon after anyway.
All I've done so far is made a couple of quick animated GIFs with the software, and I can see that it's really suited to that, as well as still pieces. Though I'm having loads of fun with the animation as it's the first ever art software I enjoy animating within. I'll get back to doing still pieces with it in the future and maybe re-review it then.
I could see someone who spent long hours working with this be able to create insanely intricate scenes and animations. And there's no real learning curve for a beginner, even if I do come from a digital art background (I mainly use Krita and Black Ink), I could see it being a fun program for a non traditional artist to excell in (though I'd be interested to see what the traditional artist could make with it.)
For those of you who think it doesn't look versatile, it can do a lot more than you might think at first glance. In fact you can make pieces so smooth they don't look like they were even painted with hexels or trixels (the main painting mode). It also has a well developed pixel art mode. It also has a user customisable shape mode where you can make the most insane looking paintings known to mankind.
Animation is super easy. Compared to many tools with animation options (such as krita 3 which I love for still art but abhor for animation) the process of learning how to make somewhat decent animations is very fast. My first piece was a minecraft/fez style isometric block world with a working day night cycle, my second, a dragon breathing fire down onto a warrior, who backs up and raises their shield. Other than watching a couple of artists videos for inspiration the night before, I worked through zero tutorials.
I use a pen monitor (Ugee 1910b) with it, though many awesome artists (including Mark Knight who I mention later) use just a mouse to draw their creations, which makes this program especially suited to a beginner digital artist who may not own or want to buy even a cheap drawing tablet.
If you want to see some awesome artworks made entirely in this software I reccomend you check out Mark Knight's Hexels youtube channel
and Tumblr page. He's the reason I decided to give it a go. He makes amazing art based on film and video game scenes, objects and characters.
Hope my review was somewhat helpful, and if you buy Hexels that you get as much enjoyment out of it the first few hours as I have :D

Pros:
+Basic combat mechanics and controls are awesome, it's basically DMC but you can change weapons on the fly really easily, making fighting very varied and fast paced (the claw grapple and halberd hook are really cool for movement and crowd control), and the super-sword slash thing is cool but I have literally no idea how to make it happen
+Visuals are pretty cool, some very nice background effects
+It's basically a potentially awesome 2D DMC
+Enemy design is pretty cool; though the art style isn't to my taste it is stylised and holds well to its aesthetic
Cons:
-I wouldn't call this early access, it's still development, I got stuck in menus multiple times and lots of the UI looks out of place and unpolished, with menu items disappearing and typos galore
-Combat still needs refining, the range of moves is good but the feel of it is very bland, gravity needs to be much stronger for one
-I don't have a monster PC but even running this at 1080p took it's toll, lots of stuttering, which I'd attribute to the atmospheric effects which are a little overdone here and there
-The level I played was pretty bland, and you get four new weapons in the space of about 2 minutes, I'd say it'd be more fun if you introduced them a little more slowly, but then you lose the main saving grace of the game until they're available
Overall I'd say it's a promising looking game, a pretty solid adaptation of DMC in 2D and the aforementioned combat mechanics using the triggers for different weapons are very cool. Maybe chill out on the effects and make combat quick and fluid, with the moves having a distinct heft to them. And phase the weapons in, as DMC does (not to encourage more DMC inspiration but it is a good system), because you have literally no time to learn how to really use the sword, claws and halberd before another new weapon comes along and makes it so much more complicated.
Other than that, the storyline sets out with a pretty cool premise but there is basically no introduction to the character you play as. And I never really liked the "trap the player and open portals" thing from DMC, which had similarly bland level design but redeemed itself with detail and layout. But then that might be personal taste.
It's a game to look out for in the future, but there's still a long way to go. I can't recommend it yet as it's frustrating getting trapped in menus (in-game pause menu is also blank for me every time I open it), it's unpolished and the combat feels too fluffy and mushy.

Early Access Examination -
Beat em ups usually fall into one of two categories, button bashers and combo based. In Onikira you can do both, you could just about get along by button bashing although you'd have to be pretty prepared to die on a regular basis. I like beat em ups that have combo's, if done well it gives combat more depth. Onikira thankfully pulls of combos well, you can pull of ground and aerial combo's easily. Your able to seamlessly transition between weapons in battle allowing you not only to pull of great combos for example slicing the enemy up on the ground with the katana then lifting and slaughtering them airborne with a nagita, then hammering back down to the floor with the dual blades.
Each weapon has different attack combos and more can be purchased by using souls at the store that comes along every now and again. As you build up combos you will gain a rank that will which will effect the amount of souls you collect to spend on combos. Throughout the levels you'll come across dragon-blood shards that once you have collected three you'll gain a permanent increase to your health.
The enemy variety in the game is pretty good, there's a selection of both airborne and ground enemies and each has different attack mechanics that can either be dodged or is some cases countered like the bomb throwing demon samurai where you can hit the bomb back at them. There are several boss battles throughout, each requiring different tactics to win. The bosses look pretty cool like the giant demon samurai.
One thing I personally didn't like was that there is no block which means that you must rely on your dodge. The main problem with this is particularly against bosses and tougher enemies is that often you can't dodge their attacks due to their attack radius being so large. It can become quite frustrating, that being said with enough skill and making sure you dodge well and stay airborne quite frequently you'll manage to avoid most attacks.
There's is also some platforming elements in the game, these usually entail wall jumping or running away from something such as fire for part of the level. The platforming sequences are not usually long and can provide a nice break after a tough fight. There are quite a few secret areas where you'll find the dragonblood fragments as well as bonus souls so keep on the look out for areas to explore.
Graphically the game is not bad, like I said I like the art style though I would have liked everything to look a lot sharper so that everything stands out a bit more, everything is has almost a blur effect over it. The game currently does have a few bugs but nothing game breaking has happened to me quite yet but that's the nature of early access games. As long as it doesn't translate into a buggy full release I'll hold off the scorn for now.
In terms of actual playable content you can only access a few levels at the moment with more on the way. Levels are a decent length and tend to be pretty well paced. As the developers add levels they do intend to add more enemies too. I think that for $10 its not a bad price for the game if you want to play it in its limited early access form. I like Onikira it's a solid beat em up that will entertain and for $10 its well worth it when it comes to full release.

While i can see some potential,  I don't recomend a current purchase for the current price.  This was picked up as part of a bundle.
While the game itself is really quite fun, the graphical style is quite charming and runs (For the most part) quite smoothly, There are still some clear signs this is an early development build.
The game itself plays a lot like a 2D version of the most recent Devil May Cry. The combos and weapon switching plays very well and can be strung together to make some quite satisfyingly flashy combos, although there's a bit of a lack of depth beyond the basic attacks you do have with each weapon. The main problem is that frankly a lot of the enemies behave the same and can delt with fairly quickly by just mashing attacks. There's no real technique other than hammer away and occasionally dodge (or even just walk) out of the way when an attack comes near. There's no real need to switch weapons beyond your own amusement. No enemies take advantage of the different styles to make you change the way you play. To compare again against DMC. Where as heavy enemies would requite you to break through shields or land attacks with your stronger weapons to stun to be able to get an in for your regular attacks. From what i've played so far (Admittedly not much since the game glitched out a few times after the first boss) there doesnt seem to be any real need to change tactic.
While i can see it being fun in short bursts, overall it's too simple to be played for too long without getting bored. The fights themselves are repetative, Hopefully in later updates (Or later levels, again cant get past the first boss yet for some reason.)  This can be expanded on.
Other minor issues mostly relating to the fact of early development:
-Not enough feedback or impact that you've been hit.
-No real detriment to losing a life apart from just restarting a section.
-Stuttering and skips on occasion.
-The letter F refuses to cooperate with words in the font.
For an early alpha you could get some fun out of it in it's current state, but It's clear some work is yet to be done for it to be truely great.

Fun city management game with lots of potential. Some people feel the game is too short, I found the real endgame to be getting the "Kingdom of Gods" achievement on the hardest difficulty. With the current map size, you are limited to how many production facilities, farms, buildings, and homes you are allowed to place while defending against giant viking raids that come by occasionally, it becomes a challenge of making everything work together.
Pros:
- Replayability is very high
- Mechanics are simple and easy to understand
- Visually appealing
Cons:
- FPS will drop dramatically as your kingdom begins to take up the whole map. Running a i5 CPU and GTX 960 GPU I got an average of 13 - 30 FPS on the lowest possible settings at around 2,500+ population
- Map is currently very limiting if you want to achieve 5,000+ population however, devs did mention a bigger map size is in the works.
- Dragons are very weak, I had a tower in the middle of the kingdom with 4 ballistae (ballista) in range of the entire map and I never saw the dragon again. Each time it spawned, it died immediately.
- Even on the hardest difficulty viking raids rarely spawn.
- The hero and footmen are useless compared to having towers or walls with achery stations/ballistae on them for defense.
Potential Improvements that can be made:
- Increased difficulty; while the current difficulty spawns large viking raids, they are easily delt with once you build a wall with a few archery stations/ballisate on top. Early game they put up a challenge. However, late game I never bothered worrying about viking attacks. Multiple viking attacks on multiple fronts would be nice.
- More variety of enemies; maybe a bigger dragon considering the current dragons are so underwhelming. Mages, bandits, cults, trolls, goblin raids could also be viable.
- Increased usefulness of the hero and footmen; I had these guys idle next to the keep the whole game never did I find a use for them.
Overall a very enjoyable game thats worth its cost with alot of potential for improvement and further development.

I'll keep it short and sweet- this is a very simple and entertaining game. It's like a simplified Civ with castles and Sims graphics. It still presents a bit of a challenge, though, between balancing population, food production, and the variety of jobs available. Not to mention the occassional dragon or viking attack! So far, my main complaints are minor ones about the UI. For one, the text is very pixly and hard to read, even at higher resolutions. Maybe make the text just a tad bolder so it's easier to read? That might just be my machine though. Also, the mouse controls are a little tricky to get used to. I wish my advisors' advice would just pop up instead of having me click on the castle just to close out the window every single time. Or even better, keep the advisors on the bottom.
Also just a suggestion: maybe make the passage of time a little bit slower? Like make seasons slightly longer so I have sufficient time to prepare for them. Also, it would be nice if there was a visible calendar so I could actually see how many days and years are passing.
Otherwise, this is a fun game.
Pros:
+ Simple and fun graphics
+ Presents a good challenge
+ Well balanced
Cons:
- Somewhat difficult to use UI
- Hard to anticipate problems without a visible measure of time.
Overall, 8/10. Would recommend. Keep it up, Lion Shield.

I love Silence. Unfortunately I have not played The Whispered World (yet!) but now I intend on doing so. I have to say, I personally prefer the classic point and click adventure style, with proper inventory, tons of riddles and a good deal of playtime. Like, let's say, the Book of Unwritten Tales, or the Deponia-Franchise. I totally understand that the developers of Silence wanted to avoid long breaks in the cinematic game flow, that they wanted to keep the story progressing for the player without overly heavy challenges where players get stuck for hours. But Silence is just so... sooo beautiful that I would have loved twice the number of scenes (and playtime). So in strict catergories of point-and-click-adventures, Silence can't keep up with Daedalics other great adventures. But in each second of playing Silence, you can feel the love and heart warmth that the developers have put into it.I admit I watched the trailer many times and even after the first time I knew I had to play this game. Each time I watched the trailer I had to blink a tear away. The backgrounds, the characters, animations, the soundtrack, even the voice acting - it all fits. My highest compliments to the artists!  Silence is naturally not the perfect adventure game, but it's an utterly beautiful experience. Next to more content and back-to-the-roots-adventure-mechanics, I'd be wishing for more alternative text lines when clicking the same spot twice, so Noah or Renie don't always say the same. Oh, and I'd love a super-extended version of the "And then there was light" track! I'm loving it!

This game is excellent - as a remake of an early 1990's game, it captures the feel of difficulty and consequences that were the hallmarks of so many games from that time period. Playing campaigns on Hard, I've been beaten every single time by the competent AI - some because I was too aggressive in my actions, and some because I wasn't aggressive enough.
Killing astronauts isn't something you're going to get away with in this game. A single poorly planned mission can cripple your agency and destroy your chances of getting to the moon before your opponent. That said, when a gamble pays off and you secure a enough prestige on the last turn of a phase, and secure a much larger budget for your next phase, it's very rewarding.
This isn't the best looking game, as others have pointed out, but you don't buy a management simulation for graphics. If long-term and short-term planning, with a healthy mix of personnel and budget balancing is your kind of thing, you're probably not going to find one much more fun (or educational!) than Space Program Manager.

A surprisingly addicting strategy game. No frills, no fuss, just "here is your space agency, now go." The game is simple and complex at the same time.
The UI and graphcs are the simple part. You have a list of employees, they are all blank silhouettes with statistics. This is a somewhat cold game of numbers. The graphics are two dimnesional moving "collages", if you choose to follow the launch of your next project, rather than skip to the outcome, with recorded sounds and voices from the time when the space race happened. It might not be the most eye-candy game, but just having that is enough. "We have a lift off" never seems to get old.
But the game itself, while it works in fairly simple principles, is hard. It's a challenge, and like I said, extremely addicting especially if you ever dreamed in Armstrong's shoes, or well, EVA suit.
The UI could do with some improvements. I would love less clicks in some places without having to sift through several screens to figure out where everything is at and what works with what.
If you are doing the Global Space Agency campaign for example, you get given goals to achieve, yet there is no simple way to see a list of goals and which program allow you to achieve them, apparently without opening the program category first. It is also hard to figure out which rocket goes with what payload without having to click through a number of menus. It just seems a little too laboured at the moment.
Other than that, I spent more hours in 1 1/2 day of playing this game, than I did playing some hotshot with next gen graphics that have recently come out. I definitely recommend it.

Since there are already a couple of reviews out for this, I will focus my review on the following three things:
- How it compares with the original Buzz Aldrin's Race Into Space (BARIS)
- Interface and gameplay
- Price
1) Buzz Aldrin's Space Program Manager vs original BARIS
I loved the original BARIS, but for me it was flawed in two fundamental ways: Firstly, it was very difficult to compete with your rival nation (be it Russia or USA depending on who you were playing with). Secondly, if you hired astronauts without sending them into space, the left the program after a few years, which made the game even harder. In the present Buzz Aldrin's Space Program Manager both of these issues have been resolved, in addition to a number of other small issues. If you liked the original BARIS you will probably like this game too.
2) Interface and Gameplay
I've seen several reviews complaining about the interface of this game, and I do agree that it could be better. That said, once you get into the game and start getting use to the interface it works pretty well. It is still a management game and I don't think it is intented to be too easy. I do tend to juggle multiple programs at the same time, and you do have to think about who should be doing what in terms of training and assignments between the different groups (engineers, flight controllers, and astronauts), but it is a nice challenge if you are into management games.
Regarding the gameplay: The radio chatter, sound effects, and animations do a great job of immersing you in the missions and there is a nice feeling of tension and exitement as you try reaching new goals in increasingly ambitious missions. It is a little bit annoying that you lose the same amount of prestige for a given mission irrespective of what the failure was, and it would be nice if the developers included different levels of success for each mission.
With all that it mind, it should be said that if you are new to management games and have little knowledge about the historical space race, this game will have a steep learning curve for you.
3) Price
In my opinion 30 US$ is a bit steep, if only because you can buy Kerbal Space Program (KSP) for the same price right now. The games do offer different experiences, but in terms of space simulators KSP is more fun and you will probably get more hours out of it. Buy it at full price if you really like this kind of game, but otherwise rather wait and get it on sale.

Not bad but not amazing either.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is a combination of sliding tile puzzles and point and click adventure games. You have different tiles which can slide around a field. Each one, however, has unique items such as keys, candles, or phones which allow you to have certain abilities like teleport or opening doors. You have to combine them in a way to reach the end. It seems simple but there are a lot of items and elements that come into play. Progression is split into 4 “worlds” so each world tends to introduce 2-3 elements that are usually used until the end of the level. Overall, it’s OK.
There is also a “hub world” (3 doors) that include more of a traditional point and click section where you need to use items in order to get puzzle pieces. This part of the game seems very unnecessary and rushed. You only have like 10 objects which defeats the point of having a limited inventory and seems like they made it for the sake of having it.
Story
You’re a dude that’s been trapped in a world where you have to solve puzzles… It’s not really much of a story and it seems contrived. In reality, there isn’t anything important here.
Graphics/Performance
The game has an element of FMV in it and it looks different but it lacks good resolution options and level detail. Overall, it’s passable but only barely so. The game ran fine but you would hardly notice with the lackluster presentation.
Final Thoughts
It’s OK. The game was always accessible to me and was unique which is good. However, if the game was any longer, I would just give up on it. Play it if you really like puzzle games. Otherwise, leave it.

Basically X:COM, where heroes are born from other heroes to die on the battlefield or from the old age, your territory slowly dwindle and you need to stay alive 300 years. Beside that there is simple base management, simple character classes, that can be mixed to create other classes, simple inventory management and simple researching.
I used word "simple" a lot and I think it sums up this game quite well. You can create building, but only three types and there are no upgrades. You can mix classes, but there are only three base ones, and mixeds one are not that interesting or usefull. Their abilities trees are a bit different, but a lot of heroes skills are not usefull either. You can research stuff, but most of them would not be used or available in some scenarios. Your only real resources are your heroes and you can have an abundance of them, to the point when most of them can die without single battle. Especially when there is almost nothing to do on the world map, except of clicking "move time faster" button. Technically you can call corpses of your enemies a resource, but apart from gathering them to fuel some research there are no uses for them. You do not create equipment and you do not need to repair it. You researched new armor? Great, here is infinite supply of it.
The combat is also very simple. There is no cover system, no overwatch for heroes without better things to do, no armor stat other than modifier to decrease damage, no enemies - with one or maybe two exception, and those are easy to counter - with interesting abilities (no taking control of characters, no temporary shields, no illusions, no solid debuffs), no higher or lower ground, no missions other than kill everything ("before they destroy the thing" in one instance), no ammo conservation beside explosives, no in battle activities or interesting choices, no loot from battle, no post battle penalty for taking damage. You go in, you kill all that moves, gather experience and go back, over and over again. On top of that AI is pathetic and close combat classes are useless most of the time. With ranged weapons you can easily win most of the battles, especially when you heroes can detect enemies hidden in the fog of war. Explosives are simply overpowered and if you know how to stun enemies, then the game became a great snorefest.
Oh and there are some weird UI choices, like separate button to decide where your hero will stand before performing melee attack. Or in the battle you need to click hero flag to see his stats, but you can easily click other hero flag, cause all of them are very close together. Or that you need to use separate menu to understand what mechanical implications character personality traits have. Or that some of the ugrades don't have even the simpliest descriptions. Or that you can't see the movement or attack range of the enemies. Or that your hero need to shout his house motto every time he killed an enemy. Or that when your hero kill multiple enemies you need to see XP reward for all of them separately.
There are random events, some lighthearted humour, worldbuilding attempts and nice aestetics, but overall this game is just too basic and too dull to be played more than once. Mods could save it but sadly there are zero. Good deal for 5 dollars or less or if you are really hungry for some turn based strategy game.

The impending doom that plagued your land is just a motivation for you. The game revolves around marrying your heroes to get the best heir possible, it's the game biggest, and most fun feature. The combat part is where you test whether your pedigree is of the top quality or should be put in the trash can (AKA science building). Your chance to beat Massive Chalice depends heavily on the success of your breeding method.
The combat itself plays out almost exactly like XCOM. You start from faraway and you progress through the map to finish your objective, which mostly revolves around kill all the enemies. It's fun, I love turn-based tactics, but Massive Chalice could be repetitive after a while.
The low cost low-poly approach in art direction is charming and I like it. Music could be better. I could pick either mediocre or average to describe it. Both have similar meaning with different connotation. For Massive Chalice, I chose average. As in it's not memorable, but at least it doesn't detract me from the experience.
One feature that I sorely missed from this type of games is being able to create custom clan. There's no customization whatsoever with Massive Chalice and I say it's a shame. A missed opportunity.
I give this game a thumbs up for offering me a chance to play a selective breeding simulation, a definitely controversial topic, but unique nonetheless; and giving me hours of entertainment at a bargain.
