To give some perspective, I have been playing this game since the very first combat alpha release and have over 2500hrs of play time.
Let's start with the combat.
After so many hours i am not even close to bored with it. All the time things i have never seen before happen. I feel i still have tonnes of room to grow and become better at it. This will likely increase further significantly after more skills, maneouvers and stances are added.
The seemingly perfectly accurate collisions(no hitboxes etc.), the physics simulation and control system create by far the closest to real life combat i have experienced in a game. Judging and utilizing distance in various ways, timing, rhythm, foot work all matter greatly and can be used as you would logically expect(Fot example stepping in close to your opponent where he cannot effectively strike you when you are unable to dodge a strike). You can translate real life combat understanding into your gameplay.
It is very dynamic and you can do quite a lot with it. The physics in Exanima are innovative, never done in another game. Very complex and integral to the gameplay and the game as a whole. Characters have 100-200 simulated muscles, things happen in real time and there are no pre-canned animations.
So, the combat is incredibly satisfying, skillfull and fun(well, may be frustrating to some while learning ;d). You can feel the weight behind the blows and movements. It can also be quite elegant and fluid. With all this it is very organic and flowing, especially when you are good at it. I can keep going but you get the point.
The screams you and your enemies produce when struck, and the sounds of the weapons and armor clashing are note worthy as well.
It can be difficult to learn for some. However, compared to early releases it is much easier nowadays.
While the combat is incredibly awesome it is not the main focus. It is not a game where you just go and kill stuff for some random reason.
There are 3 modes. A campaign/story mode, a full blown arena mode with progression and a practice mode.. for practice ;d
The arena mode is great, i have spent a great deal of time in it awaiting more story content ;d You can hire fighters, progress up the ranks, earn gold to buy better armor and weapons etc. There are many different match types, it will take too long to explain them all here. Still many features and improvements to be added here.
Now, the main thing. The story mode.
It is often referred to as a dungeon crawl though that can be a bit deceptive. It can't really be compared all that much to your average dungeon crawl game.
You are not in a dungeon, you are in a underground city like environment. The world is carefully crafted to be realistic. You can see how this place could have functioned before being abandoned. It is evident people used to live there and function as a society. There is a huge amount of objects and "props" around, all of which you can interact with.
I don't want to say much about it because i don't want to skew anyones' experience in any way. I will say if you search to immerse yourself in a world, take your time and soak everything in, you will love it to bits.
Just know it is not a hack and slash or anything of the sort, it is not about mindlessly slaughtering things.
Few other things i would like mention..
The armor system is also very  realistic and well done. You can layer many pieces of gear, for example - gambeson+tunic+chain shirt+plate armor/ arming cap+chain coif+plate helm etc.  Armor is very protective and important if you want to survive for long.

This game was not in the least bit what I expected. With selling points like "Look for love in extremely wrong places!" I thought I was getting into a highly excentric and humourous tale-- instead I got a political and stressful hot mess. Don't get me wrong, I actually really enjoyed this game. But damn. I was not prepared for some of those choices. Would you rather save your city from a drought at the price of displacing a whole farming community or see prices sky-rocket causing economic destruction to defend the land-rights of a small village? Even if the choice is easy at first, characters will spend the rest of the game guilting you about whatever you chose and telling you how wrong you are. Unless you adapt a pure evil attitude, the decisions you make will not come easily. The game does well with giving situations that are not black and white, but rather have both rewards and consequences. The plot and characters are interesting; you are sometimes thrust into relationships and sometimes have them grow slowly. Your integity is constantly tested, and it seems impossible to remain humble.
Now I do have a few qualms with the game-- the story doesn't always flow easily. Certain situations feel disjointed and take you a while to understand because you didn't choose the option that gave the thourough explanation. The politics of this fictional society can be outright confusing, and the game won't always spell it out-- so occationally you make choices based on what you *think* is happening, simply because you don't quite understand. Despite this, I still enjoyed the story. The second problem I have is that the stat system seems rather pointless-- perhaps you see more benefit with it with multiple playthroughs, but otherwise it doesn't seem to do much. (Update: several playthroughs later, I still do not see the point of the stat system. I think it's just for show.)
All in all, I think it's fun. Well worth its low asking price. It took me nearly three hours to get through it. It can be very funny at points, it's quite engaging and definitely makes you think.

The interesting part about this game is that you are suppose to manage bloodlines, breed desirable traits and weed out bad traits. The problem with the game is that you never get the feeling that a blood line is distinctive, like for example most heros from this blood line has high strength but are sickly and prone to die early.
The reason is because, within a few generations the bloodline's trait might change wildly into something completely different from the start. Although this means that it is easy to get rid of bad traits, it means that those bad traits keep coming back. It also means that good traits does not stick and you are left hoping that RNG favours you and generate children who have the good traits but not the bad ones. Every generation you must play this RNG again and sooner or later you are going to lose and drop back to square one.
What they should have done is instead of having binary on/off states for the traits, the traits should be a gradient. For example the quick study and slow learner traits should be combines into a single trait that give +/- exp modifier. Every children will inherit a slightly different modifier. Small changes should be more common than large changes so that you cannot breed good learning within a few generations. At the sametime you can't lose it easily in a single generation if the RNG goes against you.
The game fails at its most unique aspect, which is a shame because with some tweaks it could have worked much better.

So I waited a bit to review this game, I tried very hard to put my best foot forward and give it a good once over before I made my judgement. I’m a big fan of storytelling, whether it is being told to me (JRPG Types) or I am making as we go (Western RPGS). This is an odd mix of both, but I suppose it is more of a story being told to me. Let me explain-
You’re the boss, doesn’t matter what you pick for most part. You get some options in the beginning as to how you came to the states, but none of that matters except for starting stats. And while you can pick what jobs and other criminal activities you do but in the end you are walking through the story.
So kinda of pick your own adventure, I guess?
Gameplay-
Well here’s were we complicated, there are two modes effectively. City mode and combat mode, both very different, well as it should be truth be told. So City, is a resource management, time management kind of thing. So buy low, sell high, have enough people available to get your jobs done, but there is a little twist which is nice at the start but you begin to expect it as you go. Certain characters give you chances to buy more, or give less money, or the occasional combat mission. It can make or break the deal with some people. Over all you have some options, can run legal and illegal types of business, run errands around the city, and have a Liked and Feared Rating. Both give bonuses to different things, and unless you want to fork over tons of cash or a stockpile of resources you can make people talk and find out about things going on in your part of the city.
Now combat…(deep sigh). Well here is where the game falls flat (on it’s face and rolls down a ditch.) Now I really enjoy turn based combat, Fallout (classic), Xcom, so on. So I tried, really hard to get into it, but it’s hard, plan and simple. Cover is kind of crap, weapons aren’t great, and you can easily shoot your own people…. Which sucks, let me tell you. Thankfully most of the time you can forgo combat, with auto-resolve and a support option, which certain characters are better at it than others. Sadly there are times you have to fight it out, and the AI is less than great, since it knows the game better than you, you’ll be a disadvantage, period. Of course the combat isn’t great so you can just muscle your way through it. You can make your gang better with weapons through perks and what not, so not all is lost.
On the plus side you get to shoot KKK members, which is always good.
So after reading this I’m sure you thinking “Well is it a game I’m willing to spend money on?” Or “Is he recommending this game?” The short answer is yes, but it’s not for everyone. I’m giving it a thumbs up over all, interesting enough to keep me coming back, I need to finish it just cause I want to. It has its ups and downs, but if you can look past a few things it’s a fine game. I’m hoping for a second one where they learn the lessons from this game and make a much better one.

Swarm Arena is a great concept for a simple 1-on-1 battle arena game that is rather unique. You control a swarm of flying pixel thingies that when in range of your ship can be used defensively or offensively. Defense, forces the swarm to hold its position, providing you with some cover against incoming attacks, where Offensive has a number of modes (shoot, circle) used to push your swarm out to attack your opponent. The first person to hit the other ship wins.
The biggest issue I have is the lack of control you feel over your swarm. Despite any tactics you may try, such as seeing an opening to quickly attack your foe, your swarm doesn't move in to attack as you may expect making your chance to hit seem very random. Wrongly timed attacks can result in almost instant loss of your entire swarm leaving you very frustrated and likely to loose the round.
There are only a few different game modes to play, and with the age of this title now there is no-one playing online anymore. Unless you have friends who want to play you are stuck with the AI or score challenge modes. Talking AI, this has to be a strong point of the game. AI is tough (very tough!) and smart which is rare to find in a Triple-A title let alone a small indie game, but again due to the poor control system over your swarm this ultimately turns to frustration and not a legitimate challenge. This had great potential but simply doesn't pull it off!

Beautiful piece of sci fi storytelling.
Given that this is a game where all you really do is walk/jump around and read, I was somewhat surprised to find myself completely hooked from the get go. It's an atmospheric mystery with classic old school sci fi elements. While the themes of the story such as technological progress vs ecological balance, the potential for both horror and wonder to come from science, and the pratfalls of colonialism (space based or otherwise) are well worn territory, this game never makes them feel like tropes.
While the gameplay is very straightforward and you pretty much always know exactly what to do, the feeling that you are walking through the final chapter of a fantastic and intricate story, uncovering the earlier chapters as you progress makes for a very compelling experience. I found myself very quickly drawn in to the lore and the environment and the game's central narrative device of the mysterious woman you're following quickly became an obsession, in a good way. While there are occasional moments where something feels incomplete (why am I over here now, why can't I land in that spot where I clearly need to go, etc...) I found myself instantly forgiving most of these small mis steps and almost never found them immersion breaking.
In addition, the physical world itself is absolutely beautiful, well accented by the minimal UI and solid camera work. I found myself taking a lot of screenshots as I played certain levels.
Overall, this felt like a chance to go explore an excellent and compelling philosophical science fiction story (Aelita and Solaris are both major influences on story and tone) and one that I thouroughly enjoyed. While the gameplay is mostly linear and easy, the atmosphere (both thematic and visual) kept me thouroughly engrossed and this is a game I'm very very glad I had a chance to play.

The decision if I will recommend this game or not was pretty even.
Running around in on a space planet without much additional sound effects and a leading voice was quite good. Most of the time you had just the background music and nothing else – this created a good atmosphere. Spacesuit, surrounding objects and the jump and run appear fitting for this game and planet.
In my opinion you are very limited in your choices to run and interact on this huge planet. A lot of empty areas and little areas with exploring for achievements. Upgrades are only available, as long as you need them to proceed during the story. (Example: You receive a jet-pack fuel to jump higher. This is available an unlimited time and unlimited uses until you reach point X and it is immediately depleted). The chapters start and ending is also quite abrupt. No cut scene or a link to the previous chapter. You are running over a bridge and – bam – you are standing on a hill, no bridge or something in sight.
I would like to vote ‘meh’ but it is not available.
If you like such ‘running and jumping around accompanied by a little story’ – go for it.
Atrocious platforming mechanics and awful pacing ruin an otherwise good idea.

The game Lifeless Planet is one that feels like it has potential, but ultimately falls short.
The story seems like it could be fascinating, but unless you take the time to go out of your way to search out every single tape in the game you are left with something that feels fairly generic at best.
The game mechanics that are presented seem to work fairly well, but they're all things we've seen a thousand times before (with the possible exception of the robotic arm which was terribly under utilized). They really start to quickly feel samey.
There are moments when you need to refill your oxygen tanks or top off your jetpack for some jumping puzzles which I felt were kind of hit-and-miss in their appeal. However, there isn't any kind of gauge or timer for either tank. You only need to bother with oxygen when the creators felt like having you worry about it at seemingly random points in the story. The jetpack also lacks any kind of gauge or limitation on it's longevity. You can try the puzzle and use as many boosts as you feel like all day long. But, no matter how quickly or slowly you solve a challenge, the jetpack's fuel level mysteriously goes low again a short distance away.
The game feels like it has so much wasted potential. It's entertaining for a while, but quickly becomes dull and repetitive.
If you want to try this game out, by all means do so. Just wait until it's steeply discounted in a sale.

If you're a fan of the
series or Andrei Tarkovsky's oeuvre you might enjoy this... or you might come away from it feeling like the developer shot for
(1972) and came up
(2002), patching the cracks with a narrative epoxy derived from the bargain bin of
(2004) instead of the deeper and more consistent Eastern European science fiction referenced throughout.
Early visual teases evoking Pink Floyd's
set a misleading supernatural tone that undermines the science fiction bedrock of the narrative.  Key gameplay elements function as foreshadowing - if you see an oxygen drop in the distance you'll learn you have just enough time to beeline for it before you die; when you find jetpack fuel you know it'll run out as soon as you've cleared the jumping puzzle that it portends.  Air and propellant are otherwise infinite, which neatly avoids the tedium of "survival" resource management.  Jump cuts between levels are frequently immersion-breaking and serve as reminders that despite a very Open World feel,
is a linear platformer with few, if any, rewards for exploration beyond the path set by the narrative.
Pretty, minimal, and functional, with very low replay value -
is a short game and a short
.  The brief runtime (or rather, walktime) combined with shallow gameplay and a personal distaste for certain elements of the narrative lead me to
recommend the game at the list price, though I certainly recommend checking it out it when it's on sale.

I saw the word "Creeper" in the name and was curious if some kind of Minecraft ripoff had made its way onto Steam.  What I found was a highly addictive and unique stragegy game.
You face the creeper: a flood, literally, a fluid enemy pouring across the battlefield from emitters.  Later encountering corrupted machines and other new threats and rule-bending forces.  Your typical mission begins by dropping your HQ either far enough away or on defensible enough terrain to build up your economy and weapons to begin pushing back.  Branching out your energy network to lands secured by weapons fire (or other interesting units and abilities) to allow units to operate further and further afield, advancing step by step, until close enough to set up a special unit to destroy its source.
The games many maps are very diverse.  Fighting on all sorts of mundane and exotic planet surfaces, fragmented worlds, moons, asteroids, vast artificial structures etc.
Your economy is energy.  You recieve a constant income of energy from collectors and reactors, which require either plenty of creeper-free land or large investments of energy.  Energy functions as the building material for units and their ammo.  Losing a chunk of your income, or a link in your network of collector and relay nodes, or just spend it on doing too much at once and your weapons will have only several seconds worth of stored energy before that wall of firepower becomes a trickle, or nothing at all.
The main con with this game I think is that, with the exception of a few time sensitive missions, you are very unlikely to lose once you have built a decent defense early in the mission.  Once that is accomplished, a player be as slow and patient as they like, lazily inching things forward one at a time as much as terrain allowed.
I might have played CW3 that way, and been left with a feeling I wasn't challenged, and that there weren't many important strategic decisions to make... if not for one simple feature: leaderboards for best completion times.  This is one of the few games that have managed to interest me trying to get into the Top-Whatever ammount.  I recommend doing so, it greatly enhances CW3's challenge and replayability.
Unfortunately, the leaderboards are polluted with illegitimate scores, particularly in the main campaign and most popular other maps.  I mean times well below what it takes to build, charge and fire a single nullifier even in the best conditions filling the Top 10's and 20's; with legitimate champs finding themselves in around the Top 30's... so at least it's still meaningful to be in the Top 100's.

First off, I don't like "hardcore games." I've never played Dark Souls and honestly I don't really feel like I want to. But my roommates tell me Exanima looks like "top down Dark Souls," and they might as well be right.
Secondly, the phrase "dungeon crawler" turns me away. It makes me think of something with barely a story, a samey enviroment, and a run of the mill combat system. Even the man in charge of Exanima admits to both disliking the term dungeon crawler, and Exanima being one.
So listen to me here; Exanima is one of the best games I've ever played. I took a risk buying it, as I don't like all the terms generally associated with it. It was the physics-based combat system that lured me in, and boy did it pay off. I've never seen anything like it, because there is nothing like it. There are games that say you can only get better by playing and practicing, and there is no better example than Exanima. I almost quit after I first got it because I found it so challenging, but something pulled me back in fast. Now I can see myself getting better and better at it, noting the strengths and weaknesses of different enemies and different weapons, coming up with and testing out strategies to get around them. You learn something new everyday.
I'll admit, it may be a rather niche game, and I wouldn't mind an easy option to play. But, if you're willing to risk a few dollars, you might be surprised to find that you're in that niche. And if not, wait for Sui Generis to release.

Note: This review aims to be as spoiler-free as possible.
This is a mod I have been following for close to... say, 7 years now, since their original few alpha/beta releases on ModDB in the late 2000s. Imagine my surprise waking up this morning to this being on Steam. So far, I've only had the pleasure of playing through the first few levels up till the warehouse.
I must say - while I appreciate the extremely hard work in attempting to re-create the Deus Ex experience, this mod has been a total let-down. Perhaps the largest issue I see with this (which it was not supposed to) - is the fact that the entire soundtrack composed for the game by Alexander Brandon in the late 1990s. There is just this certain vibe that stuck with me playing through the game while I was young still - while the new soundtrack definitely is of a higher-quality, it does not bring back the vibe that stuck with me playing through the original. EDIT: As noted by Panopticon, there is actually the option of sticking with the original soundtrack under Settings -> Sound.
Secondly, the level design adds WAY too much clutter into the game that was never there in the original. Take Liberty Island, the very first level for instance. Not only are many spots horribly illuminated, but a lot of fluff and unnecessary objects end up on the level - making it a chore to go through the game, not because of exploration challenges - but because there are items which make absolutely no sense to have there.
Finally, the alteration of several scenes has removed a lot of symbolism around these objects in the original. In the Into sequence, the globe-hand was removed to make it somewhat like the PlayStation intro, but it never makes an appearance in this version compared to the PS version which at least included it.
I think players who have played through the existing DX may have some fun getting through this version, but for those new to the original which has been ranked one of the best games of all-time, I recommend just:
1) Downloading Kentie's custom DeusExe launcher
UPDATE: Kentie's DeusExe had an update in it's August 2015 release that "Added native UI scaling fix that no longer requires OTP patch. Has a manual scaling setting, and properly deals with resizing of the game window."
3) The Direct3D9/10 renderers (also can be found on Kentie's website)
EDIT: 4) New Vision texture pack as noted by Hyperion in the comments! Replaces some of the textures in-game with updated ones that are of higher resolution, etc.
and just playing through the original. It has an amazing storyline and soundtrack. Afterwards, perhaps try The Nameless Mod (which is a total conversion modification released for the game, winning ModDB's Editor Choice when it released in 2009 - introducing a new storyline [and of course, also a wonderful soundtrack]).
In conclusion: While I don't doubt the many years of hard work that has went into this (and for something released free!) - it's just not my cup of tea. It may or may not be yours, but I just had to point out the things I took issue with ;)

Grass Simulator looks like the result of somebody wanting to celebrate creating their first terrain map by putting a model of a grazing cow on it and trying to monetise it.  The maps use only a few different tree models and they are all placed in the same orientation, i.e. they haven't even been rotated.
You'll have to take the developers' word for the protagonist's moustache and cliché 80's mullet because the game uses a first person perspective and there are no reflective surfaces.  However, I wouldn't put too much stock in this, as their claim in the same sentence that his only other equipment is a magnum revolver is disproved in the screenshots showing him holding a submachine gun and a semi-automatic pistol.
The game aspect appears to be limited to traversing the map and shooting the cows, which do not react at all until they are shot enough times to disappear in a Hollywood special effects style explosion (smoky fireball) for a few seconds before returning.  Weapon selection is via the Q or E key, something that the key map on the Game Launcher "Inputs" tab fails to mention.  It does identify a reload key, but the guns do not need to be reloaded.  There is a mace/morning star, but striking the cattle with it has no effect.  It is an extreme stretch to call this a simulator, as the grass doesn't grow, get grazed down, die, or even move in response to the explosions.  You cannot shoot the cows in the head.
Despite what the game description says, there is no looting.  There is a token that slows time for a while, as if it wasn’t already interminable, and another that accelerates time, although I found it unreachable in the Classic Mode.  The Snowfall Mode is essentially similar to the Classic Mode but on a map with different weather.  You can ignore the warning about blowing your foot off in the Shooting Range in the game description:  you only have a disembodied weapon hand.  Apart from making everything except your hand red and yellow, Hell Fire Mode removes the detonation sound of your gun ammunition, but not the cattle explosions.  Bad Disco Mode includes some grossly abnormal physics to continuously move the cow models around the map, obliviously grazing all the while.  Dubstep Mode potentially adds some interest to a select audience, with some graphical effects such as skybox movement that might be compatible with psychedelic drug use.  I also thought the music was pretty good.  Dubstep Mode is, however, a rather passive experience, with the weapons inaccessible and movement confined to a small paddock.    Annoyingly, all of the cattle continuously rotate at high speed (about 120 rpm) in an anticlockwise direction, with their orientations perfectly aligned in synchronisation.   For sober and unimpaired minds, the novelty of Dubstep Mode wears off after a couple of minutes.  Online Mode is apparently a multiplayer game, somewhat like Counter Strike, but nobody was online the few times I tried it.  The cattle cannot be shot in this mode.  I had a ping latency of almost 400 ms in the rooms I created, and I think I’ve seen all I need to of this.  There appears to be no way to exit Online Mode other than killing the window via your OS.
Just go outside and sit on some real grass.  You will find it far more interesting.

MASSIVE CHALICE has likely flown under your radar, and for a certain (possibly large) percentage of you, that's totally OK.  But for the remaining 5%(?) of us out there that thoroughly enjoy turn-based tactical games, regardless of whether they're a bit bloated (XCOM2) or trimmed down (MASSIVE CHALICE), this is a great find and I encourage you to buy it.
What makes it an engaging experience?  Well, I'd say that the designers succeed at their primary goal of marrying short-term tactical battles with a LONG-term strategic agenda.  The tactical battles will seem familiar, and to be honest, they are less satisfying than those of XCOM.  However, there's more depth in the classes that you may originally perceive.  At first, it seems like you have a choice between:  melee tank, AOE bomber, and ranged striker.  But these primary ones can be mixed to create hybrids through family manipulation.  In truth, there are actually 9 different classes and significant variability in how your individual heroes will operate.
And that's where MASSIVE CHALICE breaks new ground.  The long-term strategic elements are primarily two-fold.  First, there's a relatively simplistic tech system that will allow you to research stronger weapons, better armor, and useful items.  These will be vital to your success in the late-game, and satisfyingly, you won't be able to research them all.  Thus, you'll have some tough and interesting decisions ahead of you.
Second, and more importantly, you will be maintaining a kingdom of important families (vassals, if you will).  You will decide who marries who, and indirectly, what their children will be like.  Not only will the children have a class determined by their parents, they'll also have a set of traits - both good and bad, which will influence their utilty in combat.  You may have a 16-year old Caberjack (the primary melee class) who possesses Bear Strength (giving her attacks bonus damage), but who is also Sickly (fewer HP).  On top of this, every child develops a personality, perhaps Cocky, or Valiant, or even Passionless. Traits can be passed down through multiple generations, so if you're not careful, you might create an entire line of Caberjacks who possess serious genetic shortcomings.
It's fascinating stuff, actually.  On my first playthrough, I mostly made random (or near random) decisions when it came to marriages and such, focusing primarily on success in combat.  But if you don't manage your families well, keep their children trained, and equip your heroes with solid items, the advanced aliens (sorry, "Cadence") are going to wipe the floor with you.  As such, the two threads of the game - tactical combat and family dynamics - are interwoven quite effectively.
MASSIVE CHALICE is easy to learn, difficult to master, and is nearly constantly revealing new ideas that surprise and delight.  You'll likely want to play at least 2 complete games - one on Easy to learn the ropes, and one on Hard once you understand the genetic intricacies.  Winning is thoroughly satisfying and certainly not guarenteed.

Short version: A pokemon'esque game done better than the actual pokemon. 10/10
Slightly longer version: This game is a relic of the long forgotten mythical epoch when the games were made to be fun and entertaining rather than to squEAze your wallet dry. One of my favourite games back in the beginning of 00's and when i have replayed it recently i still found it amazing, so Zanzarah definetly passed the trial of time, even despite somewhat obsolete graphics. Dissecting the game itself and describing the components is meaningless, because this game contains Magic(tm) which cannot be described on the paper - only felt firsthandedly. If you happen to play the game and find it awful - than i have a bad news for you - your heart is not capable of feeling the Magic(tm) hence you woun't be able to see any fairies. Sucks to be you.

Zanzarah is one of the games which truly deserves a proper sequel or at least decent enhanced edition. A beatiful fairy (pun intended) tale world designed in classic, but light-Castlevania style with blocked paths and levels until you get proper abilities, it is built on a foundation of creature evolving pokemon battles taking place on merciless Quake-like arenas. Playing as cute heroine Amy, a girl from smoke covered London suddenly teleported into a picturesque fantasy world, you capture and evolve during battles magical fairies, who range from beautiful creatures of nature, oceans and light to funny grunts of earth, screeching metal constructs and devil-like habitants of shadowy crypts. The NPCs are just as adorable, from elves witht heir pointy heads speaking some sort of french-inspired gibberish to dwarves and dark elves challenging you to battles.
Oddly enough, Zanzarah is not an easy game, and the further you go the more important it becomes to have balanced deck of fairies to pierce enemy resistances and not get one-shotted by enemies. Some fairies and battles are so hard to get in fact (like a properly evolved Light fairy) that you should either be pretty quick in arenas or conserve resources to evolve them, or grind like hell. If you focus on a few different fairies from the getgo though, like leveling up at least one Nature and one Water fairy, you should't get too many problems.
The game features hauntingly beautiful main theme and overall exceptional soundtrack, catchy creature voices and item sounds. It also has a surprisingly cool backstory and satisfying conclusion.
It's a truly unique game, and I recommend it to anyone who wants something made of light and bunnies, yet also has captivating gameplay and sometimes bunnies want to eat your face while still looking cute.

At first I was frustrated with this game to the point I was going to uninstall it.  But once I got used to the combat I became addicted to it and put over 100 hours into it with all the DLC. There was more than one time where I was close to killing all of my enemies or reaching the exit and it would hang even if I waited a while before ending my turn.

The game has some flaws, but I have enjoyed my playtime with it. It has a bit of a learning curve, especially since the game has combined city building and development with tactics style combat and both have some nuances, but it's not an especially steep learning curve. Mostly, it's learning what buildings are effective and what actions and abilities "gang members" can do. Just about anyone who has played a city building/development game like Tropico should be able to figure their way around. Same goes with the tactics style combat, which plays a bit like X-COM. The game does reward playing each well, as the city building can make your combats easier through weapon upgrades and buildings that can provide reinforcements, and combats can keep you from having to spend money to progress. The pacing is a bit slow to start, but the early stages of the game go by quickly once you figure out what you need to do.
The campaign missions and story, while nothing spectacular, are well connected and coherent. The story provides context and fleshes out the setting, giving you a nice backdrop for the game itself. You start off as a low level don and begin building your criminal empire. As a bonus, just about all the dialogue has voice acting, and the voice acting is quite good, especially for how much there is.
Overall, the game is a laid back game, occasionally punctuated by combats, which can be very easy or extremely challenging, depending on the difficulty you choose. I would recommend this game for people who enjoy games like Tropico and X-COM. While neither the city building or tactics combat is as polished or heavily detailed as those games, the interplay between the building and combat is interesting is an overall enjoyable experience.

I got this on sale for 0.78, and it's awesome. The bulk of the negative reviews are due to this being an old game (2002) and simply not running on newer systems. The only issue I had was cursor lag, and that was fixed by switching the game's resolution from 16 to 32 bit. The rest of this review will assume you too can run the game:
Graphics
This game is pure ps2 era glory and the graphics are true to form. Just look at some screenshots to see if the graphics are something you're ok with.
Gameplay
The premise is basically pokemon with fairies. You capture fairies of different elements with different skills and pit them against each other. When you're not fighting wild fairies or other "Fairy Masters" you're exploring each area for items and directions to your next destination.
Combat
Small arena fps with fairies. Seriously. You take control of a fairy in first person and lob magic missiles at the opposing fairy. It's bizarre but it works so well.
Story
Pretty basic fare of "defeat the evil and save the world" with the added allure of the "gotta catch them all" fairy collecting.
Overall I find it to be simple but satisfying, a fun romp through a game that sucessfully mixes familiar systems into something unique.

I bought this quite a while ago and enjoyed the novelty for a few hours before getting frustrated and forgetting about it. I recently came back and gave it another try, and the improvements made are substantial.
The animations, particularly for movement, are still a bit wonky, but it's definitely looking and feeling more natural as development continues. The improvements to combat have made fighting generally more managable and predictable while retaining the ultra satisfying kinetic feeling. When you play your cards right and land a solid hit, it really does feel satisfying in a way non-physics based combat rarely does. Also, the visuals, optimization and sound are stellar too.
As the description states, this game really is different. I struggle comparing it to anything but Hammerfight, and that's a stretch at best. If you're into the idea of trying something genuinely new, and aren't scared of a learning curve, pick it up and support the guys at Bare Mettle. They deserve it.
Update: After getting a few maps deeper and making a fair bit of progress, I really feel like there should be some form of navigational map, regardless of how it's implemented (possibly a different game mode?). The areas, while very immersive and well styled/designed, are laregely devoid of landmarks or other things to help orient you in the world. Unless you're paying very close attention to your compass, assuming you found it, it is extremely easy to get lost and turned around, especially after combat encounters. Even WITH the compass I spend quite a bit of time trudging back and forth trying to remember where I've been and where I've not.
I'd just like to point out that I do have a pretty good sense of direction, and I have no trouble navigating other mapless games like the Souls games.
I'm aware this could be a by-product of missing content, but there's not enough to go on visually to really give me a sense of direction and getting lost or trying to find specific rooms again after you've moved past them is becoming quite frustrating.

For what is mostly a side game to the main upcoming title, Sui Generis, Exanima stands quite well on its own.
There are two modes of play, Arena and Story.
Arena lets you build a Gladiator-like guild where you hire recruits, fight different types of matches and slowly raise your experience and gold.
Story mode takes you on a journey through many levels of a dungeon whose history and events you discover as you delve deeper.
Combat-wise is where this game shines, very few games have anything like it. Although it can be quite hard to get the hang of at first, once you have figured out how to fight, it becomes very rewarding.
The setting is a very dark low fantasy world, there is no hand holding, and this is why the game is great.

It does take a bit of time to learn combat (a little over 2hours to get comfortable for me and I'm sure I can still improve greatly) But overall it's fantastic even at this stage. The combat is dynamic and fun. Every encounter could be the death of you, you're one mistake away from death. This game is 90% skill 10% luck. For those that love a challange, this game is perfect.

Havent finished the main campaign but the arena is the most you will get out of this game in its current state (0.6.5.4). The Dungeon crawling is creepy yet atmospheric with a sense of mystery and dread when exploring a new room or sector. The combat has a steep learning curve, its extremely unique with some rough edges that can be evened out in the future. Each hit that lands properly will be satisfying, with the sound and graphical feedback to make you feel the pyhsics of the characters.
My real love for this game is the arena mode, it can be a bit "grindy" when reaching higher leveled characters (and the AI companion), the feeling of winning duels and fights with the characters you made is special. The feeling of getting a 1 hit KO on an enemy is exilirating. Having a character you had from the beginning get killed is always saddening and sometimes hilarious. the various gamemodes that pit you against multiple enemies with AI companions to help, as well as duels and the occassional beast fight make the gamemodes for a secondary gametype in its infancy feel like its more than it is.
8/10, combat after learning curve is great fun.

So I've been playing Kingdoms and Castles for a couple days straight, no other game in between. I have to say it's a solid game, runs extremely well on an i5 8GB RAM system with an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB graphics card. The concept is basically the same as any other builder, but the cell-shaded graphics make it different from games like Stronghold or Age of Empires. It's cute and fun! The controls are almost seemless. Sometimes the pan and zoom will annoy you, but for the most part you can expect an easy interface to interact with.
Surviving is fairly straightforward, and once you find the balance between growing your population and managing your food supply, expansion becomes much easier. I enjoyed the first 15 or so hours very much. However, once you get further into the game, everything starts feeling very repetitive. I'll talk about that in a minute.
There are a couple issues and bugs, but nothing that can't be solved with a quick quit & save, then rebooting the game. Mostly these issues are aesthetic, with the green/yellow/red highlight button for houses sometimes not working and leaving a few houses colored while the option is turned off. Sometimes forestors regrow trees on a cell you don't want them to, but you can't click on it to cut it down, so you have to save and quit and come back. However, most issues are gameplay related.
The main issues I encountered have to do with NPC intelligence. Some workers would not do their jobs no matter how closely I placed materials next to their buildings. The only way to fix this kind of issue was starting a new game. It mainly occurred with charcoal buildings. I advise you to make sure charcoal makers work on your game state before continuing in earnest.
Another thing (which is common with most games of this type) is that workers will not go to the closest source of building materials and will instead walk all the way to the other side of the map just to grab something. This slows the building process immensely. They also fail to walk on the roads you build and instead go diagonally across forest or water. It's very frustrating.
A small gameplay mechanic that also bugged me was the necessity for a well when the buildings that are experiencing "fire danger" are built directly on top of a pier and next to open water. It also makes no technical sense to put a well on a pier. I would either like a different kind of item to prevent fires for buildings built on piers or an alternative of some type that doesn't require an object.
The biggest issue with the game is its longevity. It's fairly new, so I hope more content is coming in the future, but the lack of buildings, aesthetic objects, combat mechanics, and difficulty in late game is a definite deterrent. I read an update that the maps will be getting larger. I propose that users have an option to change map size when starting a new game, and also that realism be introduced in the game so that your kingdom isn't just an island in the middle of no where. This is just an aesthetic issue, however.
The main issue is gameplay-related. There is no point to keep playing once you've built a three-level deep wall all around your tiny island. Any invaders quickly die and dragons drop dead before they can get past the walls. You can't expand any more once you've conquered your small plot of land unless you build piers, but in order to build piers, you need wood. In order to gain more wood, you need more forests. In order to have forests, you have to not cut them down in order to make more food. You can't put too many foresters in the same area or you get deforestation. You also have to have enough wood for charcoal makers to make charcoal. You're stuck in a loop with no possible way of expanding realistically, and so the game ends without any clear resolution.
Overall I would recommend this game, but only for its discount price. The 15 to 20 hours of fun gameplay is worth it, but not at full sale. Don't expect to conquer any other settlements or face any difficult challenges later in the game though. Unless the devs address this, I wouldn't recommend buying it for full price. I don't expect a storyline or narrative in a game like this, but I would like some kind of ending or never-ending potential. With the current state of things, the only ending you receive is resigned stagnation while your advisors continue to berate you for not having enough houses for "visiting" people.

Overall a really great game but the last mission was bugged for me.
There are two bugs that kept me from entering the final battle and made mme spent at least an hour and a half trying to get past these bugs. Slight spoilers ahead. The first one was where if Spock doesn't inspect the torpedo/weapons system then there's a chance you'll never be able to complete the game and wait for your death. The second bug was after getting everything ready for your surprise attack against the priates, and successfully blowing up the pirates, the game suddenly says the pirates boarded and it's game over. I had to replay the last part at least 10 times because I would randomly get a game over because the pirates board but yet they just been disabled. I just got lucky once and managed to get into the final battle sequence of the game.
Now the final battle is hard in this game. I would say the difficulity is surprising because up to the last point in the game you don't really have that much practice with battling with your enterprise ship. You might not be prepared for it and sometimes you have to get lucky. My tip to new players is that you should save, save, save! What I did was destroyed the first two pirate ships first, then I saved with the last remaining ship on there. Now the final ship (which I can't spoil but you'll know it's very unique) is very elusive. The trick I found is to go in reverse and try to go the opposite direction rather than following it on your radar. So basically you follow opposite, hit reverse, then you get a clear straight sight. Another trick is if your ship is badly damanged from the two pirate ships, you can heal/repair the ship by simply going really fast and constantly trying to actually "follow" the ship on radar rather than going in the opposite direction. Wait until you're fully repaired, then engage the target. Just remember to save at least once so that if you mess up you can reload and not have to destroy the other ships.

Super Mega Baseball strikes a strong balance between the action and presentation of an arcade game and the depth of a sim. The offensive side of things is pretty standard stuff, but it's the pitching that has a surprising amount of meat on its bones. Lots of pitch types, a twitch-based cursor-and-target system, needing to mix things up to keep the hitter guessing - it's a wonderful system once you get the hang of it. Fielding is somewhat CPU-assisted (less so at higher difficulty levels) although you can still take manual control of your fielders to chase down fly balls, leap for line drives and dive for ground balls. All of these mechanics are layed out via a helpful in-game tutorial system that works quite well.
I really like how the "Ego" difficulty system is implemented. It allows you to ease yourself in and gradually increase or decrease the challenge until you find your sweet spot. And I'm very satisfied with the quality of the port - Runs smoothly on my 7870 and has settings for AA (up to 16x), AF and shadow quality as well as Windowed Fullscreen support.
SMB is lacking when it comes to varying modes, unfortunately. Exhibition and Season mode is it. Something like a HR Derby or the option to jump right into a playoff tournament would've been nice. There are also only six ballparks, though all six are well designed and full of life. Baserunning controls feel a little awkward at first but I'm certain it's something that will only require a bit of practice. And while there is local co-op, the absence of online multiplayer is disappointing.
Despite its shortcomings, SMB's finely-tuned gameplay and charming personality make it a joy to play. Easily the best non-OOTP baseball game on PC since MVP 05, and recommended for both casual and devoted fans of the sport.

The strength of Lifeless Planet is in the Exploration. The curiosity that move us to  look at new horizons, take interest in details and discover what happened to this puzzling place.
It would be dull for a person to watch someone else play this game, but not dull for the one playing. If the idea of exploration is not enough, the Story sure helps. It's not gonna blow your mind, but has it's interesting twists and a satisfying end. Not to mention that it goes hand-in-hand with the Exploration; the more you explore, the more details you get to understand the mystery.
If you don't get minimally excited with this idea, just go to another game.

Reviewed in 2014:

This is a playthrough review of the original game, not the "Premiere Edition."
Lifeless Planet is a sort of platformer/adventure game with a story about an astronaut who has landed on a remote world 20 light years away, on a one-way trip with two other astronauts to explore the first known habitable world. However, things go wrong and on arrival the ship crashes, the planet turns out to be barren and then mysteries begin to appear. If you've heard anything at all about this game then you know the (SPOILER ALERT) key premise of the mystery is that your astronaut stumbles across what looks like a remote Soviet-era town, leading to many more questions about how this could have happened, if it's even really an alien planet, and so forth. There's a lot more to it than that....but the core conceit drives much of the mystery.
Unlike many adventure games of this sort the core gameplay is driven by platforming...which means lots and lots of jumping. It's not overwhelmingly all about jumping, but there's enough of it that if you're playing the game for the story and mystery it can get a bit tedious. If you're playing for the platforming elements first and foremost you'll probably find this to be below-par for your average dedicated platformer ...but don't take my word for it; I'm not a platformer kind of guy, and I definitely played this for the story.
Graphically the game was designed by one man and it does show a bit. The game would have looked stunning a decade ago; now it looks and feels like a genuine above-average indie game. I am not easily impressed by indie titles, by the way....I find few of them grab me or offer more than a moment's distraction before becoming tedious, but Lifeless Planet manages to keep you going with a decent mixture of story, ambiance, mystery and discovery.
A few items to note: there is no violence as such in this game beyond the risk of death from exploring a sometimes hostile alien world. There's a certain sense of dread at times but it is not a horror title, either. This is a solid straight SF tale through and through. There are some "huh?" moments in the plot, but it's more fun to let you see if you can find them. I'll just say this much....as you find each of your fellow astronauts, think carefully about how they came to be where they were, and what exactly happened to them. They were clearly experiencing a more terrifying game than our protagonist!
All told it takes roughly 5 hours to complete the game and the experience was fun. If you like adventure games like this and can tolerate a little jumping around you will likely find this worth your time. I suggest you play with a controller, as there are some exercises in the game that are just easier with a controller setup than a keyboard.
Addendum: I ca't say this was a $20 purchase, but if you can find it for $12 or less I think it's worthwile.

Word of warning, however, unless you're playing in the peaceful mode (sans combat), there is quite a drastic difficulty curve a fair ways into the game. You have more than enough time to prepare for it. Even with it being my first playthrough, I caught onto the mechanics very quickly and followed the advisor's advice and managed to fend off the worst of the attacks for quite a while. I eventually succumbed to a fleet (~7 ships) of viking raiders, who burned my village to the ground.
It still wasn't technically game over as they left enough of my castle to rebuild if I felt like it, but I decided it was time to take a breather.

I love it. The artwork is perfect and although it's much simpler than many other city builder games, there's no shortage of things to do. I'm currently trying to build enough city walls and ballistas to keep the ogres out...

I really wanted to like this game, but in the end I did not.
Family simulator 2015, the real meat of the game is not the battles, which are repetitive, easy and boring, but in marrying off families to the various thrones you set up.  Different men and women will have different traits listed.... but as there is no actual interaction the personalities of each person is just words on the screen.  Personality traits don't even matter in the handful of grab bag random events... which like the banner saga have unpredictable outcomes no matter what is chosen (making them random events where you have the illusion of choice.)
Now as a strategy game where you pair off families and breed lots of children it works well.  But nothing can be customized so you never have any sort of investment in the dynastys you are building.  Plus, if you are any good at the game you will have so many children in each line that it doesn't really matter what happens to any individual.
The soldiers you take in will only fight for a few battles before they will grow old and die, so you will never become attached to them.  In addition, every person you manage is so interchangeable it doesn't even really matter if a bunch of them die in a mission, there are a legion of bland replacements ready to fill in.  In addition, while the game has 9 "classes" which do have some slight variation, you are really just dealing with three... hand to hand single target, ranged single target, or ranged aoe.  The broad archetypes of which set of three classes a family has access to is set by the class of the founder of the family hundreds of years ago.
Now, even with the boring battles, the fun of breeding families might in itself have made a fun game.... except for one major problem.  Like the latest XCom, the designers seem to think that interrupting you every few seconds makes for an exciting experience.  You have to make it through 300 years, but it felt like every few days I was being bothered with the death of someone, the finishing of research, a new useless invasion, etc.  Never did I really just get to let the clock run and watch the dynastys play out.  I loved XCom, but hated that the strategy map interrupts you constantly, and this game is even worse in this regard.
It has some strong points.  The narration in particular is inspired.  And it CAN be fun to match up that 55 year old war hero with a 16 year old bride and see if they manage to breed.  But overall the experience was just an annoying slog filled with unrealized potential.  Without interaction between the people of any kind, all of the personalities and dynasties meant nothing more than ticks on a spreadsheet.  Maybe that is all life is in the end.

Zanzarah is a great game. I mean it! It's basically one of the only creature-raising games on PC, and even if it's quite old, it's still worth playing for that function alone.
So then, why don't I recommend this game?
Because for some people, this game runs flawlessly out of the box, and for others you're going to have to fight to get it running -- and unfortunately, you won't know where you stand until you already have the game. Depending on the luck of the draw, the hoops you have to jump through to get Zanzarah in a playable state aren't worth it for most players -- this game is a mess.
Pick up Borderless Gaming, folks... you're gonna need it, because if you get the screen flickering issue, the only way to fix it is windowing the game (alt+enter won't work, append -windowed to the .BAT in the game folder.) But take heed -- if your cursor leaves the game window, the game will restart. It's not even a crash -- it seems to be some sort of intentional function (which is horrifying.) If this happens in the middle of something important it means backtracking and rebattles. Not fun. Plus, those with a nvidia card better grab the legacy PhysX drivers, or get used to excessive mouse lag in menus -- in addition to the worst screen flicker I've seen since Circus Tycoon.
Thus, BG comes into play -- you can pseudo-constrain the mouse to the window this way. It's not a perfect fix, but it's better than setting your system resolution to the game's native res.
Of course, this is just my own personal experience of trying to get the steam version to work -- the disc version was unplayable for me on a modern OS, with abstract broken polygons stretching in all directions... from what I understand, this is also a problem people may face with this release as well. I'm not sure if compatability mode will help, as when I've tried launching it with that setup, it just endlessly loops the loading screen... getting this game running was not an insignificant amount of effort, I can say that much.
And on the matter of screens -- constrain the maximum prerendered frames to one and get used to black borders, because this game's maximum resolution is 1024x768x32 -- oh yes, there are 16-bit color options. Just in case you want them! Folks with 4k monitors -- my sympathy for your plight. It's not going to look that great in any setup, but for it's age, I can forgive that... now that I've solved the fact that I couldn't see much at all due to the graphical errors.
Zanzarah really is a good game. It's fun, it scratches that creature-raising itch while you wait for certain other titles to release, and if you've nostalgia for it, it's still as lovely as it always was. But it's a flawed game, and it has aged wretchedly as far as compatability stands. I can't recommend it be bought in this state, not when it's significantly likely to be unplayable without a lot of fiddling -- not when much of it requires more work than the average computer novice could put into it. I got it working without too much trouble, but I know friends of mine would be utterly lost -- and for that, I cannot recommend this game without saying "caveat emptor."
If you still want to play it, by all means. It's not a bad game! It's just so risky to spend money on something that might not work -- so if I do have one suggestion to impart, it's this:
If you want to take a shot in the dark about whether Zanzarah will run on your system or not, get this game on sale. Heavily on sale. I'd pay the asking price for it if it was at least moderately updated to be stable, because I hold that the game offers that much enjoyment for me. But like this, don't waste your money. Don't pay more than a few dollars for this game unless it gets some serious updates to fix the compatability, because it's likely you'll spend more than two hours troubleshooting it -- and then you're stuck with a game you might not be able to play at all.
TL;DR: Zanzarah is a good game marred by significant instability and graphical errors that render it nigh-unplayable for many (especially those with nvidia cards,) and therefore despite it's good points, I cannot recommend it to the average player -- and caution anyone interested to pick it up on sale at the least.

This game unfortunately seems to divide reviewers, mostly due to its steep learning curve.
If you like a challenge, and don't mind getting frustrated at your own initial ineptitude, then this is probably the best 'medieval style' combat simulator available. Combat is all physics based, so your footwork and bodyweight matters in getting effective blows in, with whichever weapon you choose, as well as hitting with the appropriate part of the weapon: ie. the head of a glaive rather than the haft.
If you stick it out you will get good, you'll get immensely satifying kills, and a real sense of accomplishment, but only if you don't rage and give up after being utterly destroyed, and losing everything, for a good few playthroughs.
It draws obvious favourable comparisons to dark souls in terms of available weapons and armour, along with the dark, ominous and oppressive atmosphere that is so perfectly cultivated. The level design is vast and sprawling, and the attention to detail in the environment is staggering.
I would highly recommend this game if you like a challenge and, if you can stick it out, you'll have an extremely rewarding experience.

I feel like this game deserves more positive reviews so here we go!
The only real reason I've seen for negative reviews for this game is that it's not optimised for modern systems, which is true, it's pretty much unchanged from the original release version of the game. Hovewer I did not expierence any glitches or crashes yet on Win 10 so I guess I've been lucky.
Pros of the game:
- Great music
- Great graphics, especially for the time it came out (even if you're not a fan of older games, you gotta appreciate the designs)
- A world that is fun to explore, a lot of secrets and little extra details here and there
- Two types of gameplay - one is more exploration/adventure style with simple puzzles, another is a first-person "shooter" on small arenas
- Collecting fairies is fun! Training them, building up your team, managing and making strategies, it's pretty hard not to get invested
- Yes, a lot was taken from pokemon, but instead of mindlessly copying, the developers only took the basic idea and made their own thing out of it, it's pretty obvious that a lot of effort went into the game
Cons:
- Possible problems with controls and glitches or making it run at all
- A lot of things are unbalanced. It feels like some fairies are more useful than others, I've been able to play through the whole game with 3 water fairies on my team and it felt like a way to go. I know everyone can make their own teams however they want, but many enemies use the same types of fairies so you don't really need to struggle with making your team well balanced unless you want to. Some of the coolest looking fairies only appear closer to the end of the game and unless you want to spend a lot of time training them from scratch, there is no reason to make any changes in your already established team.
- If you've already played the game and seen everything the world might seem a bit small, some areas look pretty but lack actual content.
It general though, the game is a gem and deserved way more recognition! One of the greatest dissapointment of my childhood was when I learned that the sequel to the game was cancelled due to poor sales. There are some fans now who are still trying to create a sequel on their own, that's dedication! After finishing the game I felt sad that there wasn't more of it, and that's barely a flaw. I'm sure everyone who can make this game run on their computer is going to have a good time with it.

Just Cause is a cool open world game set in the fictional country of San Esperito. The story is like what you'd expect from an action movie: you play as a secret agent working to overthrow the dictatorship of Salvador Mendoza, and there's tons of explosions and stuff in the process.
As far as gameplay goes, well, it's mostly fun, but there are several problems in my opinion, one of the most important ones being the driving. Driving anything in this game is pretty much impossible, as you'll soon find your vehicle going everywhere except where you want it to go. On the other hand, flying seems to be a pretty good way of getting around, as helicopters are pretty easy to use, and you can jump out of them and use a parachute to land safely. You also have a grappling hook, but using it is somewhat difficult.
Besides the main story, the game also offers a few types of sidemissions, including races, side quests, and liberation missions, and there's two factions which you help during the course of the game, the Guerrila, opposed to Mendoza's government, and the Rioja Cartel, which supports the Guerrilla. Races are pretty straightforward, you only have to reach the checkpoints before the time ends; what's interesting is that you can use practically any vehicle, so if you're having difficulty with one, you can just grab a helicopter and fly around the track. Liberation missions are divided into Guerrilla missions and Rioja missions, and they consist of fighting against the government troops (in the case of the Guerrilla) or the Montano Cartel (in the case of the Rioja) in order to liberate a settlement. They all play out the same, however, with you having to kill a certain number of enemies before the next objective becomes available. As for sidequests, once again, both the Guerrilla and the Rioja offer them, but they're really repetitive, and the faction relation system is somewhat unbalanced, as it requires a lot of points, and most missions only give you 30 points.
The game world is huge, with tons of towns, cities, and small villages, and plenty of jungles (maybe too many jungles) here and there. Even though there's not lots of things to see, as it gets somewhat repetitive, it's still nice to simply grab a helicopter and fly around, seeing the island below you, while the Sun sets on the horizon.
The soundtrack is pretty good, adding a lot to the atmosphere during those high speed chases. As for the dialogue, well, not so much. I wouldn't say it's outright bad, but there's a few details here and there when it comes to characters speaking in Spanish.
Even then, with all its flaws (including some funny glitches here and there, and a huge difficulty spike in the last story missions), I'd say Just Cause is a pretty fun game, so I can recommend it.

An awesome game for fans of defense, strategy, and single-player RTS games.  Near infinite replayability beyond the campaign levels with extra-hard levels/custom-created maps (the game has its own scripting language that diehard fans are exploring tremendously).
Pros:
-The liquid-based enemy of the Creeper is totally unique
-Satisfying "combat" and a real feeling of accomplishment that is visually rewarded when overcoming an obstacle (Your energy grid and supply lines grant amazing visual feedback)
-Surprisingly deep decision making for some of the harder maps, but everything is always fair - no cheap shots or surprises
-Play at your own pace, pausing to build or plan ahead, and saving/loading whenever you want (You can play a mission slowly and safely and eventually overcome anything, or push yourself to the limit and try to beat them even faster or more efficiently)
-Low cost for the amount of replayability offered
-Highly customizable - Sound, controls, visibility/colors of elements on the game screen
Cons:
-There's a definite learning curve beyond the main missions that may seem off-putting at first - complexity of units, resources, mechanics, terminology
-Fans of defense games with direct player combat/intervention (FPS controls or special abilities) may not like the nearly fully automated weapons/enemy
-The art style is a bit simplistic, even if you're a fan of pixel art-y or tiny models, and can cause the visuals to blend together for new players
-Some of the sound design can get repetitive, especially when you've got large scale bases and battles

TL;DR: You can tell that every ♥♥♥♥ing part of the game is made with a love of baseball
I have been wanting a baseball game on PC for years, and it's no secret to PC gamers who are also huge baseball lovers that there is a huge lack of games for us. Sure, we have OOTP Baseball, but it's not a baseball game. I love it as much as the next sabermetric fan, but I wanted a game to actually play baseball. And then we had RBI Baseball, which was a letdown. So naturally, I was excited when Super Mega Baseball: Extra Innings was announced. And now that it's finally here, it feels like after years of being deprived of a good baseball game has finally come to an end.
Now, I only really have three complaints about the game, but they're sort of not even complaints at all. More like a couple of things I want added to the game in future updates.
Let's get those CONS out of the way first:
- Lack of sabermetric stats
Baseball fans LOVE stats. We love OPS, WHIP, AVG, and ERA, and I'm glad those ones are in the game, but over the years, baseball has evolved to embrace much more in depth stats. I want to know the WAR, BB/K, ISOP, BB/PA, RC27, and G/F of my players.
- Lack of customizing options
I want some of those Chris Archer stirrups. I want my player to look like that 20-something Jaden Smith-looking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. My nasty slider needs the player look to match.
- Lack of online multiplayer
I want to have my Harry Butts dominate another man's bat. I mean, he has a 1.45 ERA, 11.4 K/9, and .122 OPP AVG. Let me show him off.
And now we get to the PROS list:
-The game is beautiful
The player models are clean and fun. the graphics are vibrant. And the stadiums. Oh the stadiums are gorgeous.
- The gameplay is fun
IT'S BASEBALL. IT'S INSANELY FUN.
- There are no special pitches or swings
Take notes, Backyard Sports. Nobody likes to play against a pitcher who makes the ball corkscrew while it digs underground and pop up only to burst into flames and then into the batter's♥♥♥♥♥ Super Mega Baseball is cartoony, but it's never cartoony in an unfair way.
- Ego difficulty slider
I love this. You don't have an option of easy, medium, and hard difficulties to play on. You have an actual slider that sets the difficulty in small amounts.
- The names of the players
You know the names you think of when you think of baseball? Babe Ruth, Clayton Kershaw, Sandy Koufax, Wade Boggs, Joe Dimaggio, Mickey Mantle, Rollie Fingers, Gaylord Perry etc. They're baseball names. Their parents looked at them and thought, "Bob doesn't sound like a name for a future Hall of Fame catcher. Let's name him Buster." Well, in this game EVERY player has a baseball-sounding name. It's awesome.

While I do appreciate the work that went into this mod. I really feel the heart of the developer was in the wrong place.
Deus Ex Revision is a mod that ups the visual quality of the original Deus Ex. Mostly in terms of textures and characters, as well as replacing models for things like weapons.
The environment replacements are the biggest appeal to this mod. Some of the environments look extremely good with the higher quality texture replacements. Likewise the tweaks to things like the UI and Direct X 9 support out of the box is very welcome.
However, all of the characters look terrible. The hidden valley is everywhere. And the art style clashes heavily with the original. It makes it feel like a very low budget PS2 game and it's something I dislike a lot. It feels very unnecessary and like the devs desperately wanted to make a charming low poly game into a disturbing high poly one. There's also no new content added in the form of weapons or extra areas. And ontop of this it
the Steam release of the game. Which is pointless and alienates a great deal of players for no reason. A lot of the models are also still vanilla. So it's extremely jarring to have a high poly Walton Simons talking to a low poly Bob Page.
I think Deus Ex would go great if it was remade. But at this point I think it would require more than just tweaking the original game. I'd much rather see a modding attempt to remake Deus Ex on an entirely different engine than something like this.

. It has been 16 years since I have last played this game and I have missed it! Aka ‘the one where a talking planet joins your party.’ Sure, Deus Ex gets all the Ion Storm cred, but let’s not forget that the other half of the John Romero-founded outfit also pulled off something pretty special, with gonzo role-playing adventure Anachronox. Robo-chums, malignant aliens and interplanetary detective-work might be the superficial appeal, but it’s the strength of ideas, wit and cheerful weirdness that keeps it an essential part of the PC back catalogue. The combat’s a chore admittedly, but it’s the cast that really makes Anachranox – the aforementioned planet; the old geezer who defeats foes with endless, tedious anecdotes; a woman who ‘lives’ inside your mouse cursor – but its regular diversions into unexpected settings or unexpectedly detailed explorations of ideas are glorious too. Anachronox isn’t forgotten, as such, but it certainly didn’t get the audience it deserved. It’s never too late! If you enjoy nostalgic games then I highly recommend you play this game! All in all, Anachronox is a long, rich, elegant, worthwhile, and above all satisfying gaming experience. The characters, story, and quests are really loads of fun... even with with the weird walking glitches that makes it look as though everyone is sliding around instead of walking LMAO!
This game was ahead of it's time in 2001! It's a shame that there hasn't been a sequel 16 years later.

"Anachronox" is a comedy, sci-fi noir RPG brought to you by the creative genius Tom Hall (of DOOM and Commander Keen fame) and was developed and released by "Ion Storm" in  2001.
Basically what you've got here is "Blade Runner" meets "The Fifth Element". Some seriously cool and thought provoking sci-fi infused with a quirky (and at times, downright strange) sense of humour on the backdrop of a sleuth story.
Although I thoroughly enjoyed this game, it certainly suffers from a few issues. Mechanically speaking it's not a great turn-based RPG, the game has some bugs that can result in crashes, and the story was left unfinished (due to Ion Storm's dissolution shortly following the game's release).
The game's creative director Tom Hall has lamented the loss of the IP to SquareEnix in Ion Storm's disolvement, and wishes to one day complete his work on the series (be it in the form of another game, or publishing the completed plot online).
For an old game it still gives me joy to play this. The quirky characters and lame jokes still stand up to today's standards and I would recommend this to anyone who has not yet played it.

Fun casual game.  I quite like the "empire" building, and the planning required to spend your money wisely, build income while keeping the cops at bay, and acquiring unique weapons to sell on later levels.  That half of the game is more like a strategic economics game.
The other half of the game is turn based combat.  I work with numbers, so I wished they used anything other than numbers for their combat system.  The probabilities clearly skew depending on environmental factors, but the hit probabilities they show don't reflect all those factors.  But once you get used to it, the combat becomes much more enjoyable, especially as you upgrade skills and weapons.  Melee combat was more frustrating than using guns, yet way more fun.  (Try making a melee boss.)
The Japan DLC is FAR better than the base game because of the full character roster and competing gangs constantly jacking your businesses.  The difficulty skyrockets, and the base game seems like a tutorial.  I thought the story was extra cheesy with a side of cheese, but it was a satisfying challenge.  The DLC also lets you shoot Klansmen!  We need more games where we kill Klansmen.  Though the game didn't show the details, there's something very satisfying about making a Klansman bleed on his fancy white dress.
What stood out most in this game is the design aspects that gave me an old timey feeling, which is really nice after a long day of work.  I eventually had to kill the music, which I enjoyed, because the trumpets sometimes sounded like sirens.  I'm also a fan of mafia fiction, so the setting won me over easily.
I'd gladly buy more DLC along the lines of the Japan story but won't be disappointed if nothing more comes of this game.

I bought this game after binge watching Boardwalk Empire and suffering from withdrawl. It immediately made me feel better. Omerta captures the atmosphere with the music, maps and characters perfectly.
The henchmen and NPC contacts have distinct personalities, despite (mostly) only having a few voiced catchphrases. There is a good selection of henchmen with different talents and abilities; some vastly better than others. There is also weapon variety, from brass knuckles to sniper rifles, and a cheap respec option that makes new builds and switching to new weapons easy. The story is engaging and most henchmen are introduced through it. When they are not and just unlock silently after completing a map, it does feel a bit disappointing though.
Though the basics to get the business running on a new map are a bit repetitive, it doesn't bore me to tears. Neither does the tactical combat, in which skills and team composition matter a lot. It is true that you start out as the world's worst gunman, but as you level and gain new abilities, that can change. I say "can" because the popular approach of just giving everyone a tommygun and thinking it's the pinnacle of strategy won't work. It may not be the deepest combat system, but it does require some thought to get a capable gang running.
The DLC adds new missions and henchmen, some of which belong to the best you can hire (specifically Jan Koloff from Bulgarian Colossus, who can become a near immortal marathon running tank), so I definitely recommend picking up the Gold Edition.
I have nothing but praise for the single player mission, but the multiplayer component is a massive let down. You do not get to play on the strategic city map and take on a rival player's gang. All you get is the tactical combat, where you have to unlock and level henchmen and weapons, painfully, one by one, and the co-op mode has no in-game chat to coordinate with the other player either. The entire multiplayer option feels tacked on and unfinished. If you are looking for a fun single player experience, I can't recommend this enough. But if you are looking for something to play against friends, look elsewhere.
