Solforge was put on the chopping block for a while, but the axe never quite fell, and now (as of July '17) it's back (supposedly to stay), so if you've been hesitating on this one, dig in! We need more players.
This may be the single best (and best-looking) battle-card style game in the genre -- it has an addictive strategic depth between its four factions and wide variety of card types, but is fairly easy to learn and comes loaded with a set of helpful campaigns which serve as tutorials to the four factions and their various strengths. The campaigns are challenging initially as you learn the ropes, but fairly quick to complete overall, and from there you'll be experimenting with your own 30 card deck builds and playing in daily ranked/unranked matches and tournaments.
Two faction types are allowed in a deck build, and each faction has a vast array of creatures and spells, so you'll be experimenting with mixing and matching the unique faction strengths in a variety of combinations. There is a LOT of room to experiment with deck types. You'll earn silver through tournament matches and various daily rewards, with which you can buy new cards and gradually build up your collection. There are hundreds of cards, and periodically new releases. You can also speed up the card-collection process by spending actual cash, as earning silver is a somewhat stingy process, but doing so is not essential.
The biggest thing Solforge currently lacks is a healthy breadth of new players. Even a fairly experienced player like me gets tired of going up against the same old veterans who have the maximum allowable # of the most unbalanced, powerful legendary cards. Still, finding both Unranked and Ranked matches is usually pretty quick (sometimes immediate) and there are enough of a variety of playstyles to keep things consistently interesting. You find yourself consantly getting ideas for new deck builds to experiment with, once you have a few cards and a little experience. I'm still finding interesting new combinations after more than a year of play.
My biggest gripe in terms of game balance are with the cards Apex Predator, Chrogias, Iron Maiden ... mainly those 3. Once players have 3x of those with some healthy Alloyin level-jumping supplements, it is very, very difficult to survive matches against them without a similarly built deck. The new developers should make a few tweaks to some of the overpowered and most commonly hoarded Legendaries. I also think they should explore or revisit the 3x per card type rule for deck-building -- make stacking a custom deck to the gills with Legendaries the exception style of play, optional -- for standard matches, nobody should have 3x Apex, Predator, 3x Chrogias, 3x Oros, 3x Sharkplate Toxoid, etc. -- unless their opponent has the same kind of deck or has opted for that level of challenge.
That aside, if you have even a vague inkling of interest in this game, I highly recommend you try it out. It has a lot of variety, tactical depth, and staying power, and can be very hard to put down.

I put my old review in a Google Doc, for those who want to see how much of an idiot I am:

Exanima is a low fantasy RPG with real physics and permadeath. There are two types of damage your character can take: Yellow and Red. Yellow(stamina) heals over time but Red damage is permanent. With full red,its permadeath and time to make new character.
There is Global experience that is shared between your characters,so the dead one's aren't useless,their exp will give your next character new skills to start with. Red damage can be healed with potions,but there aren't many of them. Later on there is a Magic Mask that can heal your Red damage too,provided that you find crystals to power it.
Their combat system is unique and takes some time to master even halfway decently. Physics affect all your swings and your balance, allowing you to use movement to put more power in your attacks. For example, you can just stand and hold LMB to keep swinging,but if you move your mouse in sync with the swing, you can hit far more deadly strikes. Then add in movement and momentum of your character to pack up even more power in your strike.
You can also trip yourself easy or get your weapons in weird positions if your mouse flies around too wildly, as it turns your character and he has actual balance. This also naturally makes attacking harder since you are offbalance.
You will also aim at different bodyparts with your mouse while swinging and it makes another big difference where you hit at. Powerful blow to the head and enemy goes flying down on the ground,allowing for easy overhead attack. Or hit them in the knee to trip them.
Blocking and parrying are automatic,as long as you aren't attacking and holding the mouse button down and facing the right way. You can't block to your back.
Small weapons are fast and short,big weapons take bit more time to recover from missed swing just like in real life. A Sledgehammer is slower than an 2h-axe,but when it lands a hit,it will always hurt.
It also matters what part of weapon you hit with, a big poleaxe really only does damage with the blade at its tip,not with the shaft.
This allows for even more tactics,as you can simply wield a 1-hander and shield and stay close to 2-hander fighters,denying them the range to actually use their weapon effectivly.
There is even Dual wielding now in the game,ranged combat is also coming in.
In essence,the combat system truly achieves the feeling of chaotic medieval fighting and when landing that big hit, it always feels earned after trading blows and parrying and blocking.
Physics also extend to the world. You can move and turn around almost any object in the game. Create barricades, drop a load of chairs on the corridor to trip your enemies, stash boxes to block a door, you can even trap enemies hands between doors.
Levers can be blocked down too! See a pit and have no idea how to close it? No worries,build a bridge out of the planks and other stuff in the dungeon!
Want to throw that wooden box on enemy's head? Go ahead!
Drop that ladder in their feet? Sure!
Make new armor fashion by wearing a chair on your back and a bucket on your head? Absolutely!
Armor system is also rather unique, layered armor starting from shirts to vests to jackets to brigandines/cuisses/plate armors. It also slows you down the heavier armor you put on. Pieces of armor have different coverage too, so using a breastplate leaves your waist open,while a full plate armor protects that part. About every single bodypart is used in armors.
Skill system is good too,there are no real "stats" on the character,rather the skills open up new techniques for fighting and defending,providing really good feeling of progress.
From basic attack skills you can choose to take fend,feint, left-to-right swings, from armors better coverage to exposed parts for parry/block,reduce encumbarance,from shields attacking right after block,continuing to attack while blocking,getting more staming to shield arm for blocks, just to name a few.
Thaumaturgy and ranged skills are also coming at some point.
Currently the game has 5 levels of story mode and endless arena-mode to create a team of fighters and equip them.
Story mode is rather hard,since you start without any armor or healing items and even a single hit can hurt a lot. Finding the first good pieces of armor and a good weapon feels great once you get that far. Even the simplest enemies must be taken with care.
This game has a really good feeling of succession in what you do, because death comes swift and fast. It really makes you avoid those hits because the price for them is high.
Later with good armors and weapons,you start to take less red damage,but take a fight too relaxed and see the red bar growing fast. :)
Devs also stay in contact well on the games forum and regularly update the game with more levels and equipment.
The game is also very stable and haven't found any game breaking bugs. Couple really minor one's that get fixed fast.
Story is also well made. You piece it together from old parchments,the environment and books. Everything tells a little story. It really keeps it more interesting than just simply telling everything straight out. The dungeon actually feels like its really,really old. Everything is mostly rusted and useless,as you would expect from a place overrun with undead.
If you want an rpg with some real challenge and actual,real physics,try this game. It will reward your patience and training.

If you are a fan of those games (or even one of them), Massive Chalice is worth a playthrough. XCOM was already a streamlined remake of X-COM, so you might wonder how it could be further simplified. The solution is reducing resources that need to be managed to just bloodlines, territory and "Research". The later can be used to get new technology, build out infrastructure and aquire new heros. Instead of the slightly complicated system of engineers, scientists and money, you can build one project at a time and speed it up by dedicating heroes to become lifetime "Sagewrights". They can't fight for you anymore, which is always the tradeoff when assigning heroes to special positions.
It's a similar situation with expanding your bloodlines: dedicate heroes to become "Regents" and marry them to start having children. This part of the game take the primary decisions in CKII (arraigning marriages) and removes minor (and fiddly) decisions like assigning counsel duties and building structures in each county. The overworld game operates on a puasable realtime system, but unlike other games you don't spend much time waiting around.
It helps that there's a steady diet of random events such as deciding whether to punish heroes who have children out of wedlock. While I enjoy these bits of story, I can see how they can be frusterating for people who enjoy strategy. The results seem to be random even when you see the same event in a later playthrough. Sometimes forgiving the couple gives them a positive personality stat and othertimes a negative one. It's never possible to make a perfect decision. For me, however, this is just the right level of chrome.
XCOM fans might be disappointed that heroes age and die off whether you play well or not. Massive Chalice seems to want players to be invested in bloodlines (AKA, dynasties in CKII) rather than individuals. Parents randomly pass genetic traits to children and also determine the hero class. Bloodlines specialize in one of three base classes: ranged, melee and area damage. These classes can be combined by marriage to create interesting dual-classed heroes. Once you get the concept of managing families rather than a team of individuals, the game will be less frustering.
The tactical game starts fairly slowly, but as you develop technologies and bloodlines your tactics change. Meanwhile enemy forces bring new powers to the fight. The forces of chaos invading your nation are called "Cadence". Appropriately, their sortees come at regular intervals for 300 in-game-years. Fighting isn't too different from XCOM in terms of feel, but heroes start with fewer options. As you develop your bloodlines and technology, new and surprising tactics are opened up. Because of the bloodline mechanism, it'll take several playthroughs to see all the possibliites.
Unfortunately, the tactical maps start to feel samey after a few battles in the same regions. If they are proceedurally generated, the just isn't enough variablity. (I have the same problem with XCOM, which is odd considering X-COM (1994) largely avoids the problem.) Other then the occational base defense missions, most fights settle into careful seek-and-destroy excersises. Cranking up the difficulty helped a bit.
I tend to play these games in Ironman mode as it remove the tempation to break immersion by save scumming. This worked great until the final showdown when I accidently
. With no option to restart the mission, I was stuck starting the entire game from scratch. I'll probably want to do this at some point, but I don't think it'll happen until I've mostly forgotten the slow start.
In summary, Massive Chalice does a great job of feeding the player with a steady diet of meaty decisions. But there isn't quite enough spice to sustain the mulitiple playthroughs needed to explore all the choices. A faster start and more variety in tactical maps would have helped.

TL;DR - The mod is a great facelift to an already nigh-on perfect game, despite its age. I couldn't recommend it enough. If you own DX GOTY, try this for yourself.
The Basics: Deus Ex - Revision is a overhaul mod for the original Deus Ex released in 2000, which was followed up by the games Deus Ex: Invisible War and Deus Ex: Human Revolution (Both games, I would say, are great. See my review of IW for more) The aim of the mod is to provide graphical enhancements, and to bring the game to a modern level design wise (Pro tip: Ignore the old fossils who seem to think that "Modern Gamers" are bringing the industry down)
Deus Ex was released to critical acclaim, and is hailed to be one of the greatest games ever, and I would completely agree with that assertion. The game just works, from the Music, to the story, to the gameplay.
Having beat the base game a few times over, the first thing I noticed off the bat was the change in level design with additions or changes to certain things (For Example: When you start at Liberty Island, there is now a shack containing some supplies, instead of having them strewn throughout the boardwalk like in the original) Some may view this as a bad thing, more-than-likely caused by a fear of change. It's hit or miss to change any major detail of a game this famous, but I think the people at Caustic Creative have done it well. Another example is the change in layout to Liberty Island proper, with added light posts and foliage to more live up to how it looks in real life, which I approve of.
The next thing I'd noticed, was of course, the Graphical upgrades. DX: Revision comes bundled with the HDTP (Upgraded character models) and New Vision (Better Textures) mods. The game looks nothing short of stunning with this mod. The textures are crisp and clear which I adore, and the Lighting feels so much better compared to the original. I heard complaints of Lens Flares, but I haven't yet to see that, so I'll update this section should I come across them later on.
Next, you'll notice the remade music. If you didn't know, CC had someone completely recreate the sound track to the game. I don't have a particular opinion of this for better or for worse, I think both are OK.
So far, the only negative thing I have to say about the Mod is how CC went about releasing it, by which I mean making it Steam only. Now, I already owned Deus Ex GOTY over Steam so I was all set to download and play. However, not everyone owns it through Steam, and not everyone even likes Steam to begin with, and I can understand them being put off by having to buy the game again (sale or no sale) when they might already own it via GOG (Good Old Games) or even still own the original retail version.
All that being said: Deus Ex as it is perfect, as I've already stated earlier in the wall of text. That doesn't mean that this mod doesn't make it even better than it was before.
Recommended. I hope this review is more helpful than some others who choose to write things condescendingly like they could do better.

I spent over twenty hours in the world of Anachronox, and I didn't enjoy most of them. The game has a fairly small but utterly devoted following among fans of the sci-fi RPG genre. These people seem to really be the only ones talking about Anachronox in 2017, which is probably why I could find nothing but abundant praise for the game on various message boards and gaming sites. The combat offers no fun whatsoever, and the exploration is both unrewarding and very limited. The main characters are quite likeable, but the minor NPCs often seem to just be a vehicle for the writers' comedy.  The cutscenes are generally entertaining, and I think they're my favourite part of Anachronox. They're too thinly-spread to motivate me to persist with it, though. This definitely isn't the worst game I've ever played, but I personally regard it as one of the most overrated.

Alright, so I've nearly finished this game and all it's DLC mission addons (3 of them) in about 14 hours; and I play games VERY slowly. I didn't just do all the side missions, I also upgraded the main HQ each time to full stats, and bought cars for everyone, bribed everyone on the block, and bought up most of the private homes around the map before I'd go to the next level.
So this game is very short, but I still had fun playing it. The graphics are great, and I spent ages zooming in and looking at the details of houses and roadways and such while I was waiting for money to accumulate etc. The voice overs are great, and there are a lot of details in the cities and menus etc. that I loved.I liked the economy feature of being able to smuggle things, or to buy or sell on the larger 'cities map' to other gangsters, and I liked all the different 'building' types to serve different needs.
I played the **** out of "Gangsters 2" back in the day, and this reminded me a lot of that. Economic strength is the best way to go, but the economy system in this game didn't quite have enough elements in it to keep it challenging, or non-repetitive. The 'police heat' system is rubbish, it just slowly accumulates if you're not doing anything, or it accumulates quickly if you're active. Each time you can bribe your way out anyway, so not great.
You can't control your henchmen directly in "street view", and you can't hire thugs to protect your person in the street - not that you need to because all the action (even driveby shootouts!) happen inside buildings where you can't control or see them.
There is no tutorial to speak of, or at least a lot of elements aren't explained properly. I learnt a lot from watching Youtube vids of people playing; and I was often like "oh that's how you get bigger guns!"; and then I've have to go back and start the game again to get them all (there are only a few select guns on each level).
The turn-based "XCOM" style combat system is terrible, and should be abolished completely. It is incredibly unbalanced, and there are just too many complaints about it here from others (and for good reason). I would recommend going back to direct "street view" control with moveable units, hireable henchmen to protect the main character, and live fighting; like in the incredibly successful Gangsters 2 game of old. It really worked there, and to me it makes no sense to go from a live "street view" system to turn-based fighting, even if it was well balanced.
All-in-all, a fun game for a few hours, but buy it on sale as it's not amazing. If the devs are reading this, please release a second one, and listen to the feedback from your customers before you start making it!

Introduction:
I'll get some of the more objective stuff out of the way. The game is a linear platformer with some puzzles thrown in for kicks. The term "walking simulator" is a very apt one as that is essentially the core of what you'll be doing in this game. Most of the game involves walking from place to place, discovering message and data pads that slowly reveal what happened to the colony that was previously living on this planet. The only real challenge that comes from this game are the platforming sections where you'll be jumping, frequently with the assistance of a jet pack boost, from rock to rock in an attempt to get to the next location. Puzzles are also a component in this game. They all involve either figuring out how to get a glowing green power core into a monolith or pushing rocks and barrels around to divert liquid or give yourself a higher place from which to jump. There is no combat in this game. The only collectables in the game are the documents which tell you a great deal of the story and samples of rock which allude to volcanic activity on the planet.
The Good:
1. This game has a really good soundtrack. It is a mix of atmospheric, space ambient, and synth. While the soundtrack is very sparsely played, when it gets going, it has a power to it and I found myself standing, admiring the view while it played.
2. There are a ton of beautiful vistas in this game, many of which I took screenshots of an uploaded if you want to see them. While the graphics aren't exactly what I'd call stellar, Stage 2 Studios manage to work with what they have and make an environment that captivates the senses.
3. Atmosphere is one of the game's strengths. This planet truly feels dead. From the scorching deserts and abandoned bunkers to the fiery volcanoes and haunted dead forest, it truly does seem like all life is gone from this world.
4. The story was quite good. You are an astronaut (I never caught a name if he has one) who has just crash landed on a planet which you were told was filled with life. You quickly discover that the other members of your crew have left the crash site and headed out into the wild. You follow and quickly learn that something happened on this planet to cause all life to vanish. Not all is as it seems. I can't go into anything else without spoiling the story. They story is told through both voice acting and documents you find. The main character gives the bulk of the dialogue, only broken up by a man speaking Russian in the documents and a couple of mysterious voices as your character hallucinates.
5. For me, this game was the perfect length. I beat it in about four hours and feel that if it had gone on much longer, it would have gotten tiresome.
The Bad:
1. The camera in this game annoyed me. While running, you can't rotate the camera around your character with turning the character and making the camera spaz out.
2. Character movement is very clunky. This is particularly noticeable during the platforming sections. You essentially can't turn your character in midair and he slips and slides a lot while running, which caused me to slide off the rocks several times.
3. I encountered several bugs while playing though none of them were unfixable. There are multiple times where I fell through the landscape and clipped through terrain to my immediate demise. I encountered a bug during a puzzle during the Ancients chapter where you have to push four stone blocks out of the way so that you can move a semicircle down a little strip to another semicircle. Due to the clunky characters movement, I accidently pushed the semicircle out of the strip so that it was floating in mid-air and I couldn't push it back in. I was able to fix this by quitting out of the game, load back in, and repeat about five minutes of walking.
4. The save system in this game could use a little work. In some areas, it works fine. If you die, you won't have to repeat much to get back to where you were. There are several areas though where I had to repeat ten minute chunks repeatedly because the game didn't have any saves close by.
5. Exploration in this game frequently doesn't lead to any rewards. There are a lot of giant flat areas with paths that seemingly lead somewhere but ultimately end in a dead end. There is nothing which tells you your objective so often you can be left wandering around until you figure out what to do. I found navigation in the Chasm and Inferno levels to be frustrating because I didn't know which direction in which to head.
The Ugly:
1. Some of the textures in this game look like they're from the early '90s. I particularly noticed this during the Chasm chapter. Many of the texture are smeared and stretched so that they are just a giant blur.
2. The framerate frequently dipped below 60 for me. I have 2 GTX 970s, both of which had no problem running poorly optimized games (as of the time of this review) like Arkham Knight at above 60FPS. I noticed the frame drop most prominently in the chapter called Ancients. According to the frame counter that was introduced in a beta client of Steam, I was getting anywhere from 15-40 frames in that section unless I was looking directly at the sky or ground. This shouldn't be much of a deterrent as there are only a few spots like that in the game. Most of the game ran at or around 60 frames per second.
Summary: This game is good little game if not a bit rough around the edges. Most of the negatives can be overlooked and some people may not even have a problem with them. I would definitely buy this when it is on sale, around $10.00. It offers a good little story and some beautiful vistas and some a few interesting platforming sections.
What an experience of a game and a fine story, some may see this as a bore of jump and explore but keep with the game and enjoy it with its fine music.

Zanzarah is a fantastic game, a real hidden gem that has been criminally overlooked. However, this Steam release is not the best way to experience the game.
Now for the record I love this game. Imagine Pokemon but when you get into fights, it becomes a FPS like Quake or Unreal Tournament. It's got a great fantasy world with some clever and witty writing, the storyline is pretty neat and the graphics still hold up today due to the artstyle and art direction.
Zanzarah is my definition of a hidden gem; that being said, the Steam release is pretty pathetic.
For whatever reason, whenever text or a text box is present on screen, the game slows to a speed that could be compared to a crawl. It lags to the point of completely unplayablity and at one point reached such an absymally low framerate that the game just gave up and crashed. There are graphical issues, slowdown, hitching, framerate that goes out of control. Navigating the menus by the way is almost impossible - remember, menus are text? You can sit there and watch your mouse move through menus like a pig in mud. It's really something.
A lot of this has to do with old games being incompatible with newer tech, I get that, and if you read through the Discussion Forums below you can find some solutions that MIGHT work for you. Something to do with dgVoodoo wrappers and stuff. Maybe something might work for you?
But the fact of the matter is that the troubleshooting/patching work shouldn't be on you, the consumer, to fix your broken purchase. This game should be playable from the minute you buy it. A company can't just dump a 13/14/15 year old game on Steam and do little-to-no work to fix it.
It pains me to have to give this great game a 'NO' recommendation but I can't recommend this version. I can recommend you going on Ebay and buying an old copy or hell, even searching the web for an 'alternate download'. Play Zanzarah, just not like this.

.

By today's standards this game looks very basic. It belongs to the era of video games in which far less pixels were used to render the graphics. No one who plays HD games could take a title from this era very seriously at first glance. For those who have played it, like me, the gameplay far outshines the minimalist appearance. Full of authentic gadgets, weapons, alien technology and races faithful to the OS of Star Trek, the 25th Anniversary is a masterpieces of discovery and action. The battles with the Elasi pirates, the unveiling of an ancient and advanced civilization beneath the surface of a Federation Colony, to the Klingon trial and the conspiracy to build duplicate ships Enterprise, all combine to create what I believe to be an admirable extension of the series. What could have been filmed became part of a game that nicely implemented space combat, ground fighting and real time puzzle solving. Broken Sword owes its existence to this product. It put point and click games on the map and showed fans of Star Trek that simplicity can't get in the way of a good experience.

I would highly recommend this game to any hardcore Star Trek fans as every level plays out like an episode from the series. Ok. Creeper World 3 is an amazing RTS. You need to build your base, collect resources and build defences to protect yourself against the overwhelming enemy that quickly grows in power and takes over the whole map. When you grow strong enough, you start pushing back, shooting your way through the enemy forces. You need to make sure that your assault is well covered, is connected to the supply line and that you won't run out of resources at a critical moment.
You shoot down air units and lauch air assaults and bombarding deep in enemy territory. Oh, and NEVER forget about defending your land. A small mistake can be enough to screw up your plans.
It's extremely satisfying when you capture land and push further into the enemy territory, and destroy they structures. The game combines moments of despair, heroism and triumph. But there's one important detail.
You don't fight humans, but blue alien mass that spreads extremely fast and destroys everything in it's path. But despite this you still feel like you fight a war against a much stronger enemy.
The amount of different things you need to keep track off, the gameplay focused on tactical planning, the awesome music that's both dramatic and badass...
Oh, and did I mention the crazy amount of content? There are thousands of maps you can fight on in the official campaigns, and there's also a level editor and a random level generator.
In short: great RTS with a truckload of content. Buy it now.

As soon as I saw this, I pretty much bought it instantly (damn you Steam for being so convenient).  After sinking a couple hours into it so far, here are my thoughts.
Pros:

- Fantastic voice acting and writing - The original cast is present in all their glory.
- Great writing - The episodic storyline feels like an authentic piece of the series.
- Good dosbox tweaks - While it's clear that Interplay didn't put a lot of effort into porting this one (basically just bundling it with Dosbox and auto-launching), I do have to give them credit for customizing the dosbox settings for relatively smooth playback.   The resulting experience is the way it SHOULD be played.
- Creative puzzles - There are some great puzzles to solve here (which is a critical part of any adventure game right?).

Neutral:
- Very minor bugs - There are some extremely subtle bugs (for example num pad keys not typing text until numlock key is hit twice).  Nothing that significantly impacts gameplay.
- Nothing new - I get it. It's a port of a classic adventure game and  Interplay wants to maximize profits by re-introducing it.   That's fine.  If you've already played it though, don't expect any major (or minor) differences.
Admittedly, I think I'm experiencing this with rose-tinted glasses. Still, if you'd a child of the 90's like me and grew up with this, it's an easy buy.

This remarkable physics-based medieval combat game keeps getting better and better. While it's still in early access, it's been receiving continual improvements throughout development - with the recent addition of two outdoor, variable daylight, variable weather maps (intermittent rain is particularly impressive).
The core of the game is split into two modes - the story mode, in which you play as a warrior stuck in a dungeon full of zombie-like monsters, and the arena. While both modes are great and well polished, the arena mode, features team recruitment and management, a weapons and clothing store, as well as a practice mode. There's also a skill-based progression system where you can tailor your fighting style.
The most important, and impressive element of Exanima, besides the photoreal environments, is the combat - every weapon, every thrust and block, has weight and feels solid. Fighting, especially after the latest update, is always a matter of skill, rather than luck. The gameplay style does have a steep learning curve, but it's worth it.
I highy recommend this game.

One of the better online co-op games out there, Orcs Must Die! 2 is a tower defence with a controllable character. The first thing I noticed was how the graphics and overall cosmetic design resembles of World of Warcraft (cartoonish style, creatures with a touch of humor). At the beginning of each mission, you choose from a wide selection of traps and set them to stop the flow of enemies such as orcs, gnolls, trolls etc. You also have your own weapon, making Orcs Must Die basically a tower defense – FPS hybrid. Traps, hazards and weapons are funny, interesting and useful enough to encourage you to try different selections.
Not having a partial refund of traps option was a design choice from developers that I have found a bit annoying. Instead of being able to refund some skill points you have distributed to specific traps, the game forces you to refund everything and start from scratch which slows down the pace, especially since you are most likely playing this co-op with a friend.
I would definitely suggest playing this in “nightmare” difficulty, since normal difficulty is too easy and thus, does not require building any strategy. On the other hand, you need to complete the normal difficulty first in order to unlock “nightmare”.  This, in my case, meant a lot of wasted hours because I wouldn’t have played the scenario twice otherwise.
Orcs Must Die! 2 is a great choice for anyone looking for an online co-op game. Remember to try the harder difficulty before you judge it.

Scratches the tactical game itch. Having the game take place over a period of 300 years and having the player essentially breed their army over several generations was an interesting way to handle resource management inbetween combat encounters instead of just using the XCOM-style base management.
There may be some balance issues between the unit classes you have, and some may not like having most of the classes be permutations on three main classes, but it didn't get repetitive over my playthrough. Massive Chalice may not be a great game for repeated playthroughs, but it was fantastic for a one-off. I love eet.

Not the most complicated strategy game, but the interlocking pieces of the game make you want to keep going through the next battle, to the next piece of research, to see the next trainee. It never seems to give you too difficult a puzzle but there's enough nuggets of complexity to keep you going.

I'm having a surprisingly good time with this game.  There's not a lot of depth here, but the core mechanics and presentation are fresh and interesting.  Breed, train and upgrade your heroes for turn based xcom lite battles.  Feels polished.  Looks like a Double Fine game. Has replay value, well worth the sale price.

It is  tactical battle and a unique game of strategy. It was good but could have been much better. The strategy seciotn was primarily breeding your next generation of warriors and scholars using sires which were imperfect. You had to decide which defects to live with. The list of characteristics was relatively few and it was often hard to tell how choices affected the outcome in battle.  For instance, I never could tell what effect "drrunk" had on performance.  Another frustrating thing about the stategy section was the random events which were relatively few in number and the best answer wasn't logical - just random.  It would have been much better if all actions had positive and negative consequences which had to be weighed without knowing the severity of the impact.
The tactical game was good.  I recently went back to play xcom, but the tactical battles were clunky and the time  limitation frustrating. In this game, you always knew how far you could move and still attack. The management was smooth.  One unfortunate thing was that distance made very little impact on accuracy of archers - it was mostly warrier level and skill rating. It was also hard to tell when you were lined up with enemies to hit multiple with one shoot.  I would have to wait several years before enjoying a replay.

The simplest way to characterize this game is an X-Com Lite. You build your kingdom, research upgrades, recruit heroes and try and defend against an endless assault of enemies. You win while if you survive a set number of years. Now if this was all that was to it then I would not recommend this game.
Instead the story of the kingdom comes together over the years, you get to know the bloodlines of you empire, you make decisions that have repercusions later down the road. I for one didn't establish an alchemist bloodline and later down the road all my alchemists died of old age, I had no alchemists for more than 100 years, but I still won battles because I chose strong heroes to train future generations.
I had one of my strongest bloodline of front line warriors die out because the matriarch of the clan had low fertility and a long life so her sons and daugthers died in battle before they could foster children of their own.
I lost a whole region to corruption because my only alchemist was a drunk and a stray grenade killed two of my best archers.
I also won against great odds against me because of a combination of strategic thinking, good recruits and knowing my enemies' abilities. And on this I would like to note the classes and enemies in this game are very original.
Also a big plus to the game's music and voice acting.

I wasn't excpecting to like Massive Chalice as much as I did.
The game has a lot to like about it, it's got a decent amount of combat depth and can be played casually through or with more of a challenge on the higher difficulty raitings.
The overarching generational breeding and house management game is what really kept me playing.
I also enjoyed the dialog as it did build some good character chemistry between the two halves of the chalice, though after a few playthroughs, it can get a little repetitive.
If you see it on sale for a low price, or in a bundle, get it and give it a go.

Caustic, you have done an amazing job and have done an amazing service to the fans of a great game.

While a graphical update is much appreciated in theory, this particular version took a lot of liberties with the new design. Some iconic scenes are missing, like the intro hand sculpture. Some areas don't feel designed as well, just cramped full of detail. Lighting completely changed in tone for some places. Same goes for the great 90s-UT soundtrack on the original.
Additionally the added detail can not completely eliminate the jarring difference between brush geometry and a bit too high res textures (and models, for some props). That bothered me with earlier high definition mods on the orgininal game as well.
So, should you play this?
If you wouldn't play the original but the looks of this one help your suspension of disbelief, then go ahead and enjoy it.
If you already know the game and want to give the included gameplay mods a shot, do it.
Someone who is playing Deus Ex for the first time might want to stick to the original game for the most rewarding experience.
The basic mods to make that play nice on modern hardware for an overall better experience would be:
1. Look for Chris Dohnals utglr page and get the latest dxglr dll. (important - widescreen etc)
2. Get the "Deus Ex Maps Patch" which restores some patched map files available in a patch before GotY. (nice to have)
Yes, it's a bit ugly, but consistently so.
The overall negative recommendation on this mod is based on the fact that I wouldn't recommend this to a newcomer and dislike many design choices I spot on the graphical update.
The gameplay mods and new balancing of the levels is a different issue.

This takes the point from perfection, since it IS a♥♥♥♥♥♥move, especially since it hasn't been said prior to release. Whose idea it was does not matter, since many people are sour over it regardless of who is to blame. I, however, won't spam thumbs down just out of spite. was undoubtedly one of the best foundations for a succesful storyline, trilogy to be precise. It gave a simple development of the Agency characters which is then later advanced in future games, which was a very good judgement on The Studio's behalf. However, in JC3,
I really did enjoy the gang aspect of the Just Cause Franchise, JC2 had a good selection, but
I loved the fact that in JC1, conflicting Gangs like the Riojas and The Montanos would start to fight in the streets because they saw each other, but the uncalledfor attacks by the other gangs when you are driving a school bus at 30mph are not really helpful...
The Gang AI is quite clever, they kind of adapt to your actions, but nothing like MGSV:TPP, when they overdo that AI aspect slightly too much. The Government forces are quite odd because you can hear them shouting
when, yet again, you are going 30mph in a school bus! In effect, the AI could have been more well done.
Since this is a Just Cause title, you would expect the graphics to outperform any other competing game in the market at that time. And so it did. The graphics were absolutely insane - the sunsets can be absolutely phenomenal and the sea, oh wow! Summing up, JC titles will always grab that no.1 spot for "the insane graphics award".
This is where JC1 kind of fell down. The driving did not feel as realistic as it should be, but that mistake was rectified in JC2. The grapple gun was a weak invention, but deep down, the main motif in the JC saga is the evolution of the grappling device, and that is supposed to sybolise some deep s**t.
The best part of JC1 is, by far, the soundtrack. I always loved, and still love, listening to the Hispanic Music everytime you completed a mission, however, the music does get a little excessive when you get in a helicopter and, this is an XBOX 360 example, press RT on the controller, suddenly some inspiring music starts to play and you end up crashign down to the ground because it caught you off guard. Yep, That's JC1 for you. But in JC2, that mistake was rectified
To conclude for this section, I would say that the soundtrack was well composed, but the timing could have been an improvement.

It's like Grand Theft Auto but on an Island, with a grappling gun, and can eject yourself from moving vehicles and skydive and use a parachute. There's also a lot of trees.
Enemies appear out of nowhere and disappear in front of your eyes on occasions.
You can steal a car and have the whole islands army on your♥♥♥♥♥with no stars to indicate when the assault on you will ever end. (It won't). They will gun you down to the end of the earth or until you reach your objective and then it's mission complete.
Cars stick to you when they are chasing and ramming you, can be a pain to shake off and driving uphill is a struggle.
But then, when you can climb out of your vehicle and jump in to another. Who cares about the bad things.
I drive my pickup and then climb out on to the roof and jump in to a sports car alongside me. Then I race to the edge of a cliff and surf on roof, leaping from it just as it goes over the edge. Free falling for a moment and then releasing my parachute, I float down to the sea, hop in a boat and speed off to another island, and on my way, spot a plane that takes my fancy.
Very short game if you only do the main missions, which is what I did. There are side missions which are like Assassins Creed or Far Cry where you take over the area by destroying blockades with your team of rebels and then eventually once enough damage has been made change the flag in the town centre. I didn't really care for these as they are very repetitive.
A nice feature which helped to navigate the map easier and a lot quicker was the extraction option that is in the PDA menu, which can be used at any time (even whilst on a mission) as long as you are not under attack. Where a helicopter will pick you up and take you where ever you want to go, be it to a new mission briefing or just to one of your safe houses. You can also have vehicles dropped off to you using heavy drop from the PDA.
Kind of hard to say if I should recommend this or not.
It has some very good positives and being an open world game has the ability to bring a lot of hours of game time just roaming the island and getting up to mischief. However there isn't a massive amount of vehicles and all of the terrain is pretty much the same (lots of dirt roads, few tarmac ones, trees. mountains) and not much going on the street in general unless the army are after you (which is kind of all the time)
The game is a bit of a bad port from (what I've read) the XBOX (not 360)/PS2 version of the game. When in the menu there is no mouse cursor to select options and navigating must be done from the directional buttons on keyboard and return and No controller support (although I didn't try).
The games display aspect ratio is 4:3 at 1024x768 with no support for widescreen monitors by default.
(To allow the use of 1920x1080 16:9 you need can get a universal resolution changer file from WideScreen Gaming Forum which is easy enough to add to the games install directory in order to change this -
Although this does stretch the HUD, PDA and map screens noticeably and the cut scenes more so.
I played at 5760x1080 res using this fix and in game the resolution was fine.
If you see this game on sale grab it. I got Just Cause and Just Cause 2 with DLC for £3.24 in the sales. For that price I would recommend this game all day. Even if it has got a few flaws, its still a fine game with around 21 missions, lots more side missions and being an open world game is more what you make of it when not doing these.

A couple things to keep in mind before you let this review persuade you not to buy.
- First, check the date on this review, make sure the issues I highlight are still a problem.
-Second, early access is intended to allow people to assist the devs, both in bugfinding and also by funding further development.
Having said that, this game is currently non functional.
Extra stockpiles do not work, and you can destroy your beginning stockpile if you wanted to resize it.
Filling the stockpile can cause your dwarves to lose the ability to queue tasks correctly. Occasional clipping behaviour issues (dwarves sinking half-way into a layer, or dropping four layers into solid stone)
FPS issues if you have the game running for very long. Many crashes, most of which appear to manifest by interrupting the behaviour programming of your dwarves- ruining the save file.
Currently there is no/next to no community support around this game in the form of Wiki or Forum that I can find, which makes troubleshooting these issues difficult.
I don't recommend it generally.
But, if you feel like you'd very likely buy this game (once complete) and you don't mind being part of the development of a currently non-functional game, then maybe I would recommend it to you.
The core of this game seems to be a really nice collection of influences, Rimworld and Dwarf fortress being the most obvious.
And I think we need more games like that. Especially a game that really fulfills the Dungeon-sim niches of old, which this game seems able to do with it's tricky-but-clever UI/Slicing system, vibrant personality and bright artwork/audio.
tl;dr
game currently non functional- do not buy without knowing what you're signing up for but get it if you want to be part of the process that helps make this game grow.

An inter-galactic evil threatens to destroy the multiverse and only this universe’s B-Team stands in its way in Anachronox, a sci-fi RPG with an unlikely cast of characters including a washed up detective, a snarky robot, a miniaturized planet, and a former superhero. Their adventures take place inside Sender One, a humongous space sphere containing numerous planets inside of it and which is also the means of transport between them using FTL devices called sender spikes.
One of the things I really liked about this game was how it didn’t take itself too seriously. Many other space-opera games like Mass Effect typically have a constantly sobering or depressing doom hanging over everyone’s head and light moments of humor often come off as sarcastic. Instead, Anachronox presents a theme that could have been pulled straight out of the Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, rife with random quirky and satirical humor.  Even your crew is ridiculously assembled with each member getting their own unique mini-game ranging from telling miniature council members to shut up or pressing the right buttons to fill a character’s lungs with air so they can move people aside via long-winded arguments.
Combat in this game features a Chrono Trigger style encounter system where you see the baddies in exploration mode before you encounter them at which time everyone moves into place for turn-based combat. Speaking of placement, you can move freely across empty grid points to get line of sight to a target or to close the distance for a melee attack. There are also sometimes environmental switches that players can activate as a means of blocking routes or damaging enemies. Eventually you unlock a kind of equip-able magic similar to Final Fantasy 7’s material system except with each character having a unique affinity allowing them to cast higher levels of specific elements while still being able to use lesser-attuned magic if desired, albeit at lower levels.
Of course even an AAA production like Anachronox has its faults. At its release date in 2001 the graphics were a bit dated with blocky character design that has gotten even worse with age. The music is often repetitive and level design feels empty with many long vacant hallways and sparsely populated cityscapes. Thankfully, most of the annoyances are mitigated by a patched-in taxi system and fast forward option. Pressing the backslash key at any point in time produces an effect similar to increasing speed in a console emulator on PC. Boring long corridors? Fast forward. Slow Elevator? Fast forward. Spell animation taking too long? Fast forward. The ability to fast forward at almost any time allows you to cut out all the “filler content” in this game so you can get right to the good stuff, something I wish I could do in many other PC games.
Anachronox is a welcome change from your typical cookie-cutter RPG and despite its age I still found myself enjoying brief moments of amazement and amusement. My only real gripe is that the game’s ending leaves it open for a sequel that was never made due to the dev team closing shop before it could be completed. One can only hope that this would-be series catches the eye of a new developer capable of treating the IP with the respect it deserves.

I'm writing this review with only a few hours playing because I think in my profession it is important to save people from undue psychological stress.  Anachronox is a stressor to the Nth degree.  However well the developers made the game they wanted to, however well the outcome came for them, however on time and on budget it was; the game still will kill someone with certain somatic disorders because of its execution.
In Anachronox you move a few characters around to interact different ways with the 3rd person explorable world.   This world you move in is guaranteed to give a heart condition to someone who already has a marginally stressful job.  While exploring you will be met with transition event after transition event, and a quest every step of the way that will bring you back through every event you saw while getting to the point you were supposed to be at.  Does the way I explain it sound confusing?  It is and it isn't.  You will remember how to get around, but will you like getting around? Maybe if you're a kid without any problems in the world or someone who was able to retire sitting on enough money to never worry about being a member of the working poor you would be such a person to like venturing around in Anachronox.  When it comes to someone like me (and most likely someone like you) “no” you will not like venturing around the city planet that is Anachronox despite it having all charm of 90s cartoonary or a JRPG interface with many colorful party members.
Skip this game and save your blood pressure medication for something else more important in life than a videogame.  Anachronox will drive you nuts.

This mission pack is terrible. Let's break down the individual components and assess why each one is good or bad.
The most omportant one is probably the new levels. They are even harder to navigate than the original Quake 2. There is MORE backtracking, more opportunities to get lost, and I found myself opening up a walkthrough a few times. Pretty poor level design. Also the turret placement... wtf guys. Also the machine gun / grnade launcher guys are around every corner, and on every ledge above you. Really slows the pace of the game to a crawl as you have to peek around corners for an instant to land a rocket or rail on them.
This leads me to a new enemy... The turret. There are rocket and cell-firing varieties. They have mild predictive aim. They lead you if you are moving. They take 2 direct rockets or rails to kill. They are small. They are place directly above doorways, around corners, and just generally all over the ♥♥♥♥ing place. They are the worst part of this xpac by far. Once again, peeking around corners for a split second 3 - 4 times in a row to land / miss rails is not fun. And when you decide this is boring af, you and take another approach, you just ♥♥♥♥ing die.
Another enemy.. They spider thingies. They arent too hard. Although they do 20 dmg per shot, and lead you, and jump up and down repeatedly. They take a while to learn how to handle them, but still they really don't add a whole lot of value. They are like the lick-a-tongue dog things but ♥♥♥♥♥ier and more trappy. Traps. This game is all about trapping the player.
Also there is a shielded icarus. It's fine, it just takes like 5 or 6 rails to kill one if you commit to picking them off from afar.
So, on to new weapons, there is a ETF rifle, that sort of behaves as a nailgun, or a ♥♥♥♥♥ier hyperblaster. It's kinda weak, is easy to miss with but looks cool. Not that great, and has a lot of overlap with existing weapons.
The proxmide launcher is garbage. It's barely useful, and I just end up killing myself more often than not, as the hit detection for what it sticks to is ♥♥♥♥♥♥.
There is also a plasma beam. The only legitimately good addition, although it uses cells. So great, an excuse not to use the hyperblaster and bfg, both of which are sweet guns that control great. This gun is essentially just a perfectly hitscan lightning gun.
Next is the Chanfist (it's a 1 handed chainsaw). Hot trash. Does terrible damage, and there are no real opportunities to use it. (sepaking of bad level design, they give you this then immediately bombard you with flying and ranged enemies....)
So there you have it. A bunch of half-baked additions, poor level design, and some legitimately bad game design choices that are leaned on time and time again to result in a frustrating mess of a mission pack. Play this only if you really want to. It is not fun.

I can't help myself but when I'm looking at Omerta - City of Gangsters I see that legendary game called Chicago 1930. Is it atmosphere? Top-down camera? Visuals? Gameplay experience? Most probably one of each. Anyway, Omerta is coming from creators of popular series Tropico and yes, we can feel their signature over here.
It's been said many times and I have to say it too. This game features two basic elements which aren't near their maximum potential. One is combat system and second is economy and managment. Both of them are important part of game. Thing is, or let's say speculation, that if Omerta's main element was either combat or economy & managment made to its maximum it'd be truly awesome creation. But it is what it is. We have two features that are not reaching their top and they're not created the best way they could be.
I've liked that turn-based combat system I must admit, it was more gripping than I've expected. Fights are mediocre, sometimes too easy and sometimes pain in the butt. However fact is that AI is terrible. Rival gangs in combat and outside are really bad. Some just run straight to you where you have 4 of your soldiers so you can kill them with ease. Every member of your team have its own bonus, and each is good at something so you can plan out some strategy or think in advance. You can upgrade them, deploy them, release them, they're all yours.
The economy & managment will be kinda average for players that came here from Tropico series. It's like its weaker brother. But it's fun for a while. Building your imperium and taking over cities of America, starting from scratch and reach the top. You can set up different buildings to work for you, you can upgrade them, raise their efficiency, you can buy out joints, frame other gangs, heist their warehouses, bribe officials, steal cars, and much much more and it might be pleasurable for few hours.
Game will last you around 20 hours and less, MP or CO-OP is not helping that much. Every DLC except Japanese Incentive will give you just one level so it's not really great deal as you can imagine. But Japanese Incentive will give you 12 so it can boost up your gameplay time by 8/9 hours easily, but in the end it's just how you play it, fast or enjoyable. Hours may vary.
Game can run pretty smooth even on old machines, it doesn't really look that well and sound is not great too either. It all depends on how you feel with the game, but chances are it will get repetetive after 3/4 levels. When you upgrade your mansion to the max, and go to new level, guess what, your mansion is gone. So as I said you're starting from scratch. Both combat and economy is not deep at all, half of potential for both is used.
It's not that bad and it's not really good either. Solid average maybe little bit above. With the Demo available you can try it out yourself before spending money.

Put simply, this game has been a chill and enjoyable experience to play; it's easy to pick up on, it's addicting, and it's really quite fun. If you're looking for something that'll keep you occupied and happy, this is the game for you. But while I'd recommend this game from a surface standpoint and a fair price, there are definitely some things I'd critique on a more technical level.
Yes, it does feel unfinished, but not just in the sense that it lacks content.
There are ideas in this game that just aren't adding up and aren't being used to the best of their ability, concepts that seem arbitrary, mechanics that are either far too easy or far too challenging.
At a certain point you can build yourself a treasury to start taxing your citizens for money; it starts you off at a base of 2 gold per person, which will add up to a certain amount each household will pay depending on how many people live there, and lets you collect up to 1000 gold per treasury. Citizens pay taxes each year... which last about five minutes. Coinsidering how little money is actually spent, the whole thing just seems unnecessary. Sure you have to pay some establishments salary each year, and there are some structures that require money to be built, but what else? I have three treasuries right now and I've never seen my gold go below 2800 at a time, because people pay their taxes so soon. And while there's an option to raise taxes, why would you? The base number is more than enough to comfortably sustain you.
I've had a similar issue with armaments and tools. I had my 2 blacksmiths pumping them out as quickly as possible, considering I had very little of either one towards the beginning, but now they're pumping them out far quicker than I can use them. The only thing you can use armaments for is to train soldiers, which is something you have to do one at a time and manually, and the only use I've found tools for is to make rock removers, which I've never had to make more than 10 of the whole game. Now I have almost 400 of each just taking up space. I could tell them to stop producing them, but then what's the point of having a blacksmith? Maybe the blacksmith could produce other products? Or the products they DO produce could have more use?
The happiness mechanic seems gimicky, too. Houses' happiness are affected by what's around their enviornment, and it effects how many people decide to come live in your city, or even leave it. In game you're encouraged to build a church or a library near homes to keep their happiness up. But doesn't building a church or a library every two blocks seem silly? I have two houses in the woods where I established my wood production, but I need to have a library there with them to keep them happy? And sometimes it doesn't even matter! Houses will continue to be even barely placate despite being surrounded by EVERYTHING that could make them happy. Maybe adding more structures that affect this status, like universities or gardens or something along those lines, and making them each unique in that they effect the community in some way besides "make people happy", like how hospitals are made to help people when plague breaks out, would be a nice way to spice things up?
And the citizens seem to have stats that depict what skills they're good at... so why can jobs be specifically assigned? Sometimes citizens take on a job that has far less priority than anything else that needs to be done, and a tree I wanted cut down 15 minutes ago still hasn't been touched. I open up a quarry and instead of the gradmaster of stonecutting I saw waltzing around going to work there, a grandmaster agriculturist takes the job. And when you close an establishment to give something else more priority, the crew you had working there will disperse and won't come back when you reopen; a whole new set of random people who are close by take the job instead. It just seems like this whole system is disjointed and inneficient.
Even the enimies seem unpolished; with only two types (dragons and vikings) there isn't a whole lot of variety to how combat will go. Balista towers beat dragons when you have enough, and citizens will, more often than not, put out any fires they cause what with all the wells you build to keep happiness up. The viking ogres are a real challenge, but the actual vikings are a cakewalk to beat if you have a general with a handful of soldiers. There's just too thin of a line between insanely easy and insanely hard with the combat.
I'll try not to let a lack of content get under my skin too much though.
With an infrastructure update having been added a few months ago and a merchants and ports one coming soon, I doubt content will be a main concern for much longer. This game has more and more potential the more I think about it, and with some fine-tuning around the aspects of each mechanic (AI, resource management, diversity in building, ect), I can see this game easily becoming my favorite to start up and get lost in.
Overall I think it's well worth the $10 to experience the hours of fun and replayability it can provide, and I really look forward to seeing what the developers can do to build upon this awesome game.

Taking place during the same timeline represented in Quake II and The Reckoning, Ground Zero casts the player as a marine known as Stepchild, who is part of the first wave of attackers sent to planet Stroggos.
The structure of Ground Zero's single-player campaign does not deviate overmuch from that of previous Quake II releases. It is organized around several mission-based hubs, or units, each with a single primary objective and many secondary objectives.
Aside from new weapons and enemies, the biggest addition made to Quake II in Ground Zero is enhanced enemy AI, which affects both new and returning foes. This change manifests in many aspects of enemy behavior. Strogg will attempt to sidestep incoming fire, blind fire at a player's last known position, and will also make a more concerted effort to track down an evasive player.

I would recommend playing this if you feel like you haven’t had enough Quake2, but it’s not a high recommendation. Ground Zero is okay, but not great. I think the new weapons are gimmicky at best as they deal too low damage or waste too much ammo, not a single one I found particularly useful and stuck with default Quake2 weapons most of the time. It wouldn’t take much for someone to buff damage of the new weapons and make them more applicable, it’s just unfortunate they weren’t more functional to begin with.
It also has a bunch of escape to survive scenarios which are rather annoying. The backtracking element of the map design isn’t my cup of tea, but the level design itself is interesting, stronger in some parts than other. The story is once again near identical to Quake2 and the first mission pack, I think they should of done something more original.
I liked most of the new enemies except the turret/sentries, they are more annoying than anything and keep reappearing even after you cleared an area. The two new bosses are a decent addition and seem to fit well with the Quake2 universe. Overall recommended, but don’t expect anything mind blowing.
Steam version of Quake2/Mission Packs do not include the original Quake2 soundtrack, for best experience you will need a more modern single player client like Yamagi and to download the soundtrack elsewhere in OGG format. Launching the Reckoning/Ground Zero Quake2 expansion packs from Steam is possibly broken with a custom client, but you can launch it via shortcut or bat file however.

The idea behind this game is fascinating, the idea of a squad based tactic Mafia game makes all kinds of sense, and the idea of packaging into a kind of business management system makes all kinds of sense too. Layer a coherent gangster story on top of that, it really should have been a great game.
It really isn't a great game.
I think this game is a perfect case of spreading yourself too thin. If the combat was better, or if the management was better, this would be an easy sell, but everything just feels a bit lacking. I'm going to focus my complaints mainly at the combat because frankly, it's made by the same people as Tropico from 3 onwards, if you've ever played any of those games you already kind of know to expect theme over depth. It's what they do, I'm no big fan of it but it is what it is.
The combat however was really just heartbreaking, because even if the combat wasn't great, they could have gotten it feel to thematically pleasing. And when I say this I mean like the classic scene of cops vs gansters in a fancy dining room, overturned tables, firing accross the room at each other. Instead what we get is dude hiding behind a table, other dude runs around the table with no supressing fire, pressing his double pistols into the first dudes back, missing both shots. Original dude runs around to side of the table, fires into the air and misses. Rinse and repeat for 5 rounds. It's not even that the RNG misses are BS(and it is, 70% to hit with a shotgun point blank, really?), it just feels completely unimmersive while playing it. The fact that there really isn't any surpesssing fire during enemy movement just breaks it completely, both mechanically and thematically.
I really wish they'd look into a sequel with this game where they flesh out everything, because if it were done properly, it would be an instant classic. This game though, sadly, was a big swing and a miss.

So this is the weaker expansion for Quake II (and IMO, the weakest Quake Expansion).  The Reckoning is much better paced and much more fun to play.
Basically, due to poor enemy design, the game is much slower. You can't just "run n gun" through the game thanks to extremely tanky enemies and the sentry turrets.
Especially on the harder difficulties, it's a slow and tedious crawl as you check EVERY corner for a turret, because:
A) The turrets do ludicrous amounts of damage (a fifth of your HP per shot for the WEAKEST ones, half or more for the rocket/rail sentries)
B) The turrets are usually in blind spots. Walk into room, get shot in the back. Beginning of level, get shredded by two hidden rocket turrets.
C) About 15-20% of enemies are turrets. Yes, they're that common.
And to top it off, the game is stingy with ammo. Like, I was often out of shotgun shells. That's ridiculous in a Quake game. Of course, it doesn't help that they added a massively tanky enemy that spawns mobs en masse indefinitely.
The bosses are ridiculous. It's basically a giant room fight with no cover. You're expected to have saved a ton of OP stuff, which means you're SOL if you didn't.
I did not enjoy this one. I was spending way too long creeping along corners sniping turrets with the default blaster just to save ammo and not enough time running around. I ended up just using godmode towards the end and I had a much better time. Perhaps it was because I was playing on Hard+, but "The Reckoning" was much more fun, even on Hard+.
Very addictive game, just some spelling mistakes here and there.

Rating: four scary pizzas out of ten.
Don't let the nasty red thumbs-down fool you; I did enjoy my time in this game. I just don't think I'd ever actually recommend it to anyone for any particular reason, and, well, that's what the rating is for. I'm also blatantly not the target audience. But here's how I spent my time as a wannabe pacifist in the city of gangsters.
The Boss arrived in Atlantic City with a few simple aims: to provide food and medicine to the downtrodden, to make boatloads of money, to sell the scariest pizzas in town, and to be loved. Within minutes of meeting him, I could tell that the Boss was a somewhat insecure man, desperate to assert his importance as he made his mark. "There's a reason I'm the boss," said the only worker in the entire organisation to himself. "A real boss isn't afraid of grunt work," he said to the zero other people available to do grunt work for him.
Sadly, soon after settling into Virginia Avenue, it became clear there was a local criminal gang involved in all sorts of foul business, and so, though he was ultimately a man of peace ,happiness, and pizza, the Boss realised he would have to either perish, or take out the gang first by striking at their hideout. The trouble was, he had to find it first.
Hmm, he thought, looking around the area. Maybe – just maybe – it's that building there, diametrically opposite my hideout, that looks exactly the same as my hideout? To make sure, he still needed to ask a guy who to ask about someone who'd know who to ask about whether that was the place he thought it was, but it wasn't long before his hunch was proven true.
With a collection of guns people had handed in at his new pawn shops, and a bunch more that that nice man from the army had going spare, he got ready to storm the enemy hideout. But this plan would need friends to work, so he put together a team of allies the same way any sane employer would: by seeing who had the most tragic backstories. That ruled out a lot of nasty stabby people, but there were enough left over after that. Squiggs and Happy were clearly victims of their circumstances. The haunted former doctor O'Connell and jazz-loving Walker Johnson – both brought a tear to the eye. Brigitte's backstory wasn't that tragic to be honest, but she STOLE HER OWN BIPLANE and STILL USES IT FOR STUFF so she was invited anyway, in the offchance that the Boss could have a shot in it.
The assault began. They won! Somehow, nobody, not even on the other side, died. "Well done, friends!" the Boss probably said, "But now we're broke, so you're all fired."
And so the Boss got back to work. The enemy gang gone, several vacant properties to build in, but only about nine dollars to his name. He took out a loan, started earning small amounts of money, and carried on.
In the new-found peace around Virginia Avenue, he slowly and without fuss made his way back up to a position of power. As soon as he had enough capital, the Boss opened a soup kitchen to feed the locals. He felt guilty about firing all his friends, so re-hired them despite not desperately needing them. Property was purchased. More soup kitchens appeared. He opened a pizzeria, which apparently people found intimidating. Rather enjoying the scary reputation that the pizzas gave him, the Boss bumped up his dark image even further, exclusively by paying a drunk national stereotype to sing songs about how scary he was. Eventually, the Boss sent O'Connell, who had long ago departed from his medical career after failing to save a child's life, and had him establish a clinic for the locals, thinking it might help reconnect the poor doctor with his old ideals. "Worth going to hell for," said the proud doctor as he opened the clinic.
The Boss's remaining days in Virginia Avenue were spent compulsively buying up property, and repeatedly redecorating his home with nicer and nicer rooms and flowers. If only I could do this more often and with more control, he thought, and then he went to play the Sims. The End.

Was a big fan of the first game, enjoyed it a lot, and while this game has new content in the way of enemies, traps, items, and of course levels and multiplayer along with new modes. Despite all that, nearing the end of the game I'm finding it a big slog.  Traps and Items have too many upgrades, each with at least 5, and by the end of the game I find myself with only about half the traps unlocked and maybe 3 traps fully upgraded.  And because it seems more effective to upgrade traps instead of unlocking new ones, you end up playing with the same smaller pool of traps throughout the game.
Part of OMD1's charm was having a lot of different trap types and experimenting in different scenarios, with only one upgrade per trap, each was not a huge investment and you had a lot of variety at the end.  But this game it seems you need to play endless mode to unlock skulls in order to unlock more gear.  The weakness shows when you start seeing something like a Frost Ogre and you have no fire items, instead shooting the guy literally 40-50 times in the head before he goes down.
I also find the map design underwhelming. The game also has an annoying tendency to introduce a map which seems like it needs a certain strategy to be effective, and then they throw in enemies to stop that strategy. Like barricade-dependent maps get tons of sappers who blow them up, or maps that require guardians get gnoll hunters to take them out, some maps have environmental hazards but they take too many shots to activate.  And the levels are too long, the later levels seem to all have 12 waves! Just goes on and on and on. I do suspect that some levels are designed for co-op because geographically, some levels are just so spread out that it's impossible to put down all the new traps you want in the 15 seconds or so between waves and there are not enough teleports.
In closing I find this game's biggest problem is the attempt to extend gameplay through unnecessary unlocks. To give more value, or more content, they add a bunch of unlocks so you need to play multiple times to get all the traps and gear and items or new costumes that cost 50 skulls!  And to be honest I have more money than time so when I play a game I want to play it once and be done, games that extend their play time in this manner just give me a subpar experience.  Sometimes I'll put 50 or 100 hours into a big AAA game, but I don't want to put that amount of time into an Indie or a game like Orcs Must Die

Exanima. A game which defies conventions and escapes pigeonholing. Easy to learn, difficult to master. Frustrating but rewarding at the same time.
It is a dungeon crawler in its purest form, but one that also harks back to the hallowed times of old-school RPG games, where maps were drawn by the player in pencil on checkered paper and in-game written sources were re-read several times to make sure no details had been overlooked. Patience, thoroughness and attention to detail are essential.
For those more action-oriented, the game offers the 'Arena' mode, where one nurses a team of 'gladiators' to mastery by participating in bouts and buhurts. It has endless replayability (partially for reasons outlined below) and offers scaleable challenge fit for rookies and masters alike.
Main focus however is the 'story' mode, currently unfinished, which tells a story of a single character exploring dilapitated outpost / dungeon in search of... answers to a question that was never asked.
This basically means, in meta-talk, no quests, no journal entries apart from the ones you write yourself, no cryptic musings of an old man etc. The entire weight of piecing the story together is on you. And the story (so far) is rich, detailed, handcrafted and very highly polished. Each creature you encounter on your way is unique, not randomly spawned mob, but a character with attached story and purpose. With some imagination the story Exanima tells is compelling.
The game engine helps with immersion. It's designed around rather dull colour palette and complete darkness. This creates ambience and believable, grim atmosphere, allows for shadows cast by the light of a flickering torch - oft the only light source - and makes the player think twice about rushing headlong into the unknown. Many a time a sudden appearance of an axe wielding denizen made me jump and scramble for the shield or press the wrong button in panic. I haven't had that experience since, I don't know, "Perihelion: The Prophecy"?...
Which brings me to another crown jewel of Exanima - the combat system. The word limit doesn't allow me to write all the positives here, but in essence it's superiorly refined Die By The Sword with infinitely more realistic damage model and easier controls. All this is possible because of realistic physics engine, which calculates momentum and impact of every blow, considering things like weight, balance and type of the weapon, and also mass and footwork of the character wielding it. There is no arbitrary damage value attached to a sword which is then modified by special abilities, auras etc. No. You get a glancing blow not because your stamina bar depleted but because you've mistimed the swing and employed rubbish footwork. The combat is devilishly hard to master, as practically every weapon is slightly different and requires practice to work out the nuances - this also adds to replayability. Any other action RPG or combat game will feel shallow after you taste Exanima.
The next thing to recommend is the equipment system - and your paperdoll. There are no slots. Correction: there are slots, but instead of 5-6 you get... hundreds? The armour / clothing is used in a realistic and believable way. A gambeson fits under your maille shirt and a breastplate over it. High, thick boots will not be compatible with plate greaves. Arming cap fits under the bascinet, etc. ad infinitum.
The game difficulty is punishing - at first of course. Couple the steep learning curve with unforgiving, roguelike-style save system and the result is frustrating to say the least. I have had several ragequit moments myself until I got to grips with the combat, some dozen re-starts later.
The game is obviously still in beta and some essential scripts and mechanics are not implemented yet. The developers apply high gloss finish to everything they do and therefore the update cycle is fairly slow. Bear that in mind. It is also a shorter, smaller scale, standalone sister title to the open-world RPG called 'Sui Generis' which is being developed concurrently, and - as far as I know - helps funding the said upcoming title.
I wholeheartedly recommend Exanima if you like slow, meticulous exploration and deep, rich, tactical combat. It will give you more than you ask for, but it requires patience in learning the ropes.
