Before we begin, I would like to state that I have only played about 2.5 hours of the game so far. I will also not be including any bugs/crashes/technical issues in my review as this game is in Early Access. It is in a unfinished and "In Development" state. Please be aware that there are some game breaking bugs in the game, but I do feel the developers will be working hard to Flush them out and stomp them with their dwarven beards.
So, Had a friend of mine see this game, and say "Hey! check this out!" so I did. As someone who has loved his hundreds of hours in Gnomoria, this looked like a game with potential to keep up with that. I have found it interesting if not slightly lacking in content in its current state *I want it to be known I know more is coming so this review will be updated or completely rewritten as needed*
Graphics: 4/5 - Mix of 2D sprites with rotation 3D enviroments that give a very ps1 era feel. Think Final Fantasy tactics or Thousand arms. A little clipping here and there but nothing major. Changing Graphic settings did little to harm my resource usage and seems to be stable. They give a very nastalgic feel for me, and cant wait to see just how far they will go with this.
Sound: 3/5 - A bit... Normal. The music is good and gives decent ambiance but lacks Originality (sorry devs) Im sure there will be changes or as more music is added, that view will change but it is as it is. as for sound effects, it once again falls to "normal". There are no sound bugs or issues outside of the fact you might wanna turn down the sound effects when you first start your game, but they dont jump out and pop. but not so bad you dont know what they mean. the sound express exactly what is needed but nothing more. Main reason it still maintains a normal rating
Gamplay: 3.5/5 - From what I have experienced so far, the game is very similiar to most colony survival games. You farm, dig, mine, craft, and keep your people alive. The trade system though brings it up a notch. Now you need to earn money, make allies, war, and be profitable. This system has alot of promise to make a real stand out for this game. Currently that system is very Basic but I hope that it gets more development added to it (along with more reasons to trade/war and random events that push you into a corner) .
Overall score: 3.5/5 - The potential is there, the idea is solid, and the feelings go with it. Though, I can;t recommend this game for anyone looking for a replacement to their Gnomoria or Dwarf Fortress play, or for anyone looking for a game that feels and deliver complete. I can and will recommend this game though. Yes, bugs need squashing, yes content needs growing. YES, THE BEARDS OF THE WOMEN ARE MAGNIFICENT! But it needs time to grow. It needs players who will enjoy it, test it, report bugs, and help.
If you are one of those players who doesnt care about a bug or 2, and is willing to play a trade/colony building game, this is the game for you!

I REALLY want to give this game a good review, but...
I just can't.
Good:
- The mechanics of the game overall are fun and easy to understand
- The single player campaign helps learn how to play and provides cards to help make decks
- The columns mechanic and the overall number of different mechanics in the game are fun and varied, allowing multiple playstyles
- The game also has a fairly helpful and welcoming community.
Meh:
- The daily quests are helpful for getting some cards and tickets, but there's no variation at all in daily objectives. Might help to have some easier ones for new players (the 1 and 3 win ones can be nigh impossible for new players)
- No trading (At least that I've seen). Makes collecting cards to make a half-decent deck to play with regularly that much harder and slower
- Weekend events help with gaining cards, but still are heavily geared toward those with a vast library. It seems only 1 out of 3 events is one allowing the player to use cards they don't own
Bad:
- The curve to get into playing the game is steep. Unless you just don't mind taking your lumps getting beat a lot for a while until you can get some cards in your collection (like 6mo+ of it), expect to spend a fair amount
- Their customer service is atrocious. I submitted a ticket about a problem with my account 2 months ago and heard back once about 3 weeks after. When I replied to the response, I've had no response since. Brough it up on their FB page and had the same response there. One person from there replied and been weeks since I've heard from them. Certainly makes me not want to spend any further time or money on the game
- In a similar vein, it seems like there's very little contact from the company with the community (at least that I've seen). I get it's a smaller company, but nowadays, there's zero excuse not to have a community and/or social media manager to interact with the community.
As much as I find the mechanics fun and different, I just can't recommend this game to new players until the company pays more attention to the customers and they can lower the overwhelming curve it takes to get into the game for new players.

Earlier this year, Stone Blade Entertainment rolled out a new client for this game, and it was pretty unstable during the launch period. This upset a lot of people and led to a lot of negative reviews on here, which I don't think is particularly fair considering most online games have rocky launches. While the new client does have some annoying bugs, it is way more stable than the previous version, so take those comparisons with a grain of salt.
Gameplay wise this game is like a combination of dominion and MTG. I love the core gameplay, although I don't always agree with their balancing decisions. Generally cards have less RNG than card games like duelyst or hearstone, although it still is used occasionally. The monitization model is one of the most ethical I have seen, compared to other online tcg's solforge practically hands out cards.  It's very possible to build a solid collection without spending any money, although it's definately faster if you are willing to spend some cash.
The meta is pretty healthy with a lot of variety amongst the tier one decks, and drafting is extremely fun and accesible for new players. If you like TCGs but don't like the monetization model of something like hearthstone, this is a solid alternative and is imo the best online tcg availible.

Every bit as fun as I remember it on the 360, where I played it several times.  As nice as it is to have all the new special features like challenge packs and camera filters, I only picked this up for nostalgia's sake.  I honestly can't see myself spending the time with it to get every achievement.
That being said, if you have never played Shadow Complex before, this is a game you will thoroughly enjoy.  Everyone I have told to pick it up always come back surprised at just how fun it is.  It's a Metroid-style game wonderfully crafted by Chair, who have been REALLY bad about following this game up.  The progression and level design really hits that sweet spot where backtracking doesn't feel like a chore.  If you're thorough, however, the challenge level will steadily decrease as you progress as you will ultimately become an invincible killing machine (which makes the ending ridiculous).
While this was supposed to be some part of some unrealized multimedia franchise by Orson Scott Card (author of Ender's Game), it never really took off because the other projects didn't quite work, but Shadow Complex was the one beloved child of the abortive project.  The story is dumb and useless and will ultimately lead nowhere because the project collapsed (possibly due to hubris), but this is a pure adventure with lots of action and great platforming, a bajillion secrets to discover, etc.  More importantly, the harder your difficulty, the less the game helps you out.  At normal or whatever it's called, everything will inevitably be marked for you - if you want to discover everything yourself, bump up the difficulty (don't worry, the game is never that hard).
Anyways, highly recommended to those who have never played it.  For veterans, eh, it really depends on how badly you want to play this again.  It's still as fun as ever.

Shadow Complex is really fun, but it's stupid fun. The game begins with a man named Jason and his girlfriend going on an afternoon hike in the verdant Uncanny Valley, when they basically trip over a huge terrorist complex where which Jason proceeds to MURDER EVERYTHING in sight. Jason spouts dreadful lines like "Huh, the killing is getting easier, I wonder if that's a good thing. Yeahh... That's a good thing" as my suspension of disbelief is busy jumping over a sharknado at the rest of the story's happenings. I found the game's narrative hilariously "So bad it's good", but it's only right on the edge of the kind of stupidity that could make it a "Great" SBIG thing.
I say that possibly because the gameplay is a mixed bag. On the one hand the level design, up until the final chapter of the game, is actually pretty well laid out. It's fun to explore around and collect things, and for better or worse your next objective path is laid out for you, meaning that unless you're being OCD about power-ups you skipped, the backtracking is relatively minimal. It does kind of lose that value in the late game however when you've revealed a majority of the map and you're told to go collect the last most-important items you missed. You're locked out of acquiring the items except by specific entry points for no other reason than "The door is apparently stuck". which felt unnecessarily restrictive. Jason moves fast, and while he's a little wonky, I thought it was fun to navigate the passageways with him overall.
However, the combat just sucks - which makes it a great thing that it's usually pretty short. They tried to do this 2.5D thing where enemies come at you from the background layer, but since you control your character on a 2D plain you basically have to spray and pray to target enemies in that layer.  There may be some nuance to it I just didn't get in this playthrough, but I can't imagine having a lot of fun on the harder difficulties messing around with aiming. What they could have done is had the right analog control a cross hair for more accurate shooting, but I doubt that would have improved it all that much. Bosses were just boring; almost every single one could be defeated by finding a safe distance and then casually tapping the grenade button over and over again until it's dead.
In spite of these problems though, I enjoyed my time with Shadow Complex. I wouldn't call it a "Great" by any means, but for a game I probably got for free it wasn't the worst way to spend 5 hours of time. I ended up getting 62%ish of the game's collectables and completed 80% of the power armor.

Ask yourself these questions: Do you like fantasy lore, RPG's, FPS, Pokemon, beautiful visuals, great soundtrack, a captivating story and more all that in a beautiful, large and very diverse semi-open world? If any of these are a YES, then go and buy Zanzarah. You will not regret it.
I've been playing this game on and off since it came out (I just recently got it on Steam but I have a lot of hours with my CD). It is in my top 10 games ever, and I've played a lot of games.
You play as Amy, a eighteen year old girl from London, UK. At the start of the game your house is visited by a swamp goblin Rafi, and he places a magical rune in your attic. Investigating the rune you are transported to the world of Zanzarah — a different realm. A realm of magic and faeries, strange creatures and odd landscapes. But you are transported there for a reason — you are the Chosen One, from the old legends which speak of a human girl to save the world of Zanzarah from an threat and unite Zanzarah with the human world. The story later further reveals that Zanzarah, Earth and the realm of Faeries was the same world and humans, faeries, dwarves, elves, goblins lived in peace. But humans became corrupted and the human world had to be cut off from the magical realms.
The gameplay consists of two main areas, the first is the RPG in which you play as Amy and navigate through the world talking to NPC's and solving platform elements. Amy mostly serves as a faery bag to be honest. The second is the FPS where you take part in faerie battles.
Playing as Amy you can talk to NPC's, collect items, pixies, and most importantly explore the world and capture faeries. Amy can also partake in a
few minigames and puzzles hidden around the world. Capturing faeries is the most important aspect. There are 77 different faeries, divided into twelve elements, each having advantages and weaknesses against eachother. You can only have five faeries in your deck, however you can go back to your house in London anytime in oder to change them. Faeries are usually caught at a low level, and then you have to train them against faeries of their own level in the wilderness (the world is divided into element and level areas) or at several trainers which costs money. Most faeries can evolve upon reaching a certain level into their other, which means they get new stats, look and spell possibilites. The maximum level for faeries is 60, and leveling and catching all faeries will take time and effort. Each faery can have four spells, two offensive and two defensive. Your faery can also gain a joker spell slot which means you can put a spell of a different or any element for it to use. I shall be making a Guide covering most of the game mechanics and good builds and decks.
The combat only exists inside the Faery battles, and takes form of a FPS in a arena where you can move, fly around and hide. You have two sets of spells, and each has one offensive and one defensive. You can swap these around when not in a battle, and theres a bunch of different spells each changing the way you battle. Mana is limted, and spells can be charged for more damage (which should be done almost always). You can also swap between the five faeries in your deck at anytime, because some faery types do more damage against others. There is a certain tactical feel to it if you look at it at a certain angle, especially for some very difficult battles. The combat is very fun!
The graphics are outdated, but still beautiful. The game runs on DirectX 8.1, so it can be a problem streaming using OBS (personal experience). There are no HD resolutions, and it would be nice from Daedalic to update the DirectX and add more resolution options, as well as a windowed option. Apart from the technical stuff, the game still looks very pretty, the world is diverse, and tastefully made. The menus work and look very good.
The music is fantastic, especially the main theme sung by Kariina Gretere, similar to Enya. The other sound effects are fitting and of great studio quality, however some sounds can very, very, rarely sound too loud.
The game has some form of TCP/IP LAN multiplayer where you can use your gamesave deck and fight with your friends. You can use third-party programs like Game Ranger or Hamachi to play with your friends. Remember, this is a game from 2002 so don't expect any servers.
Zanzarah: The Hidden Portal is a fantastic game that you are sure to love and play for a long time. It might be hard at start to get used to all the faery stuff, but the learning curve isn't very steep. The game has some very difficult sections, which require careful deck planning and leveling of faeries. The story can be speed-run in some fifteenish hours, mostly because you need to level up faeries in order to defeat certain enemies blocking passage or to progress the story. However it will surely take you double that much hours to finish the game with a normal tempo, and this just means finishing the main storyline without getting all the faeries or leveling them up, or even trying to collect  everything. To do that it will take at least 100 hours of gameplay if you are fast.
The only real negative sides of the game is the use of DirectX 8.1 if you're streaming, the resolution, and the biggest break is that after you finish the game, there is no save just a cutscene and then the game reloads to the last checkpoint. You can still go back and do whatever you want, just there isn't anything after the "ending".
But even with that taken in consideration, this is a gem not to be missed, and is worth more then its price, even when it's not on sale.

I saw a group for this game while in development stating that a giveaway of keys would take place on we had enough members or something. I joined up because the premise was silly as hell. With all of the "simulation" genre taking off, it appeared a good goof was in order.
That's what this game is, an elaborate joke that will cost other people money to be in on it. I know other simulators were around that goofed (Surgeon Sim, Goat Sim) and were great to play. This game was limited in scope and touted the "best" level as a bunch of cows spinning and flying to dubstep.
Have there been updates? Yes. Not many, not a lot of content aside from different dubstep and tree textures.
Is this a game? No. You can't add a gun and leave out story/objective and be a game.
Is it a simulator? I'd say yes, if the mechanic was really a zen environment where you sat around as grass and blew in the wind, like a paid for screensaver/sound machine.
Is it fun? No. Shooting cows with limited ammo and watching them explode on death is a lot like adding god mode to a game and skipping cutscenes and dialogue. There is no fun to be had when the fun is limited to "stand still, listen to dubstep, shoot exploding cows if you feel like it, whatever. we don't care."
I would recommend buying this for a gag gift, but you'd probably have more fun with a fake lottery ticket.

I was intrigued by this game, but didn't think I would be really into it at, and just tried it to see. Well now I know I really like it! The game reminds me of the HOMM games, with many differences of course.
My first playthrough, I played without paying much attention and dropped it after about 50 years, I was doomed...
I cleared the game with my 2nd playthrough, and I still did so many bad things in it... (normal difficulty).
Pros:
- Interesting bloodline thematic, I don't remember having that in another game. It was nice though I wish I knew earlier than once you place a bloodline in a keep you're stuck with them forever.
- The mini question games that popped up every now and then, that was amusing and quick, I kept waiting for a new one to pop.
- The voice actors are great!
- I liked the only one mission for the whole game thing, so if you mess up, you got to restart from scratch, it's quite refreshing (though I probably wouldn't feel that way if I failed around year 280 ;) )
- Following above, being strong at one point doesn't mean that you'll stay this way, things happen and if you don't pay attention you're back to having weak heroes again.
- The mixing of classes to create new classes was fun!
- The various attributes for a heroes and the random traits and personalities.
- Various details like a feud can occur between families, which will decrease their efficiency if together in battle.
- Since the game is randomized the replay value is pretty good.
Neutral:
- Somehow I wasn't a huge fan of the battles, and skipped the one before the last since I could afford it,
- I got a bit annoyed at having so many sages dying in a row, till I figured out making young ones sage would bypass this issue :)
Cons:
- The voices get old quickly as they keep repeating the same stuff over and over again... I understand the game is randomized so they cannot have fresh voices for everything, but more variety would have been nice.
- There's pretty much no story told, all we know is that there's an evil corrupting the land and it will take 300 years for the chalice to be able to clean it up... strong storytelling!
- Not enough upgrades in the end: I used mostly hunters and had plenty of heroes all around, so around 200 years I maxed out all I care for and ended up doing the heroes and alchemist upgrades just because I had to do something... I wish I would have looked forward to upgrades during the whole game. (it's not a big issue of course).

All in all i would recommend this game for people that just want to sit down and relax and have a lot of fun killing orcs in very funny and fascinating ways.
PROS:
Story is good but short (Can be a CON to some)
Co-op is well placed and developed making it fun with a friend.
New traps and other items to help progress threw the game.
Now has survival unlike the first one which adds more content.
New types of deadly orcs, Although some was just copy and pasted with the same attacks and animations
Game offers great rewards and challanges and can be fun solo or with a friend.
The skull system is really good with unlimited respecs to allow for more diverse play styles
Has nice unique armor sets that make the character look good but offer no bonuses (can be a CON)
Offers a lot of new unique maps for the story and even endless mode which offers new advantages and disadvantages
CON:
Some of the orc units are copy and paste

Biggest complaint I hear about this game is that you only get to use your heroes once or twice, meaning you have to keep going back to square one. This is a misguided conclusion. Heroes with high xp are the ones you breed, making their children start off with higher xp.
Over the course of the entire campaign, you will work with heroes that slowly have more and more beginning experience and levels. It also sidesteps the problem that often comes with XCOM: losing a hero means restarting the leveling up process or restarting the level. In fact, losing a hero is often fine, so long as you have more in backup. They all will likely be the same general level, so the ones you use in battle are the ones you want to eventually take out of battle for breeding.
It's all about planning for the future, and the new types of heroes you get from mixing class types makes for an interesting experience as you try to maintain bloodlines, level up families, relics, and research.
And remember which enemies to use your Wunderpants against.
I can safely say I've had more fun with this game than with xcom, and while parts of it are simpler, that doesn't mean it's less fun. It's easily more focused, and removes frustrations with the format cleverly.

I have to recommend this game.  I've been watching Let's Play videos and then embarked on my own playthrough, and it was a glorious, addictive session.  After loving X-Com and being perturbed by X-Com 2's failure to improve/grow significantly, Massive Chalice gave me that X-Com, can't put it down, strategizing, permadeath-fearing warm and fuzzy feeling.
First, the negatives:
I don't like the art style, or the alien self-contained culture (caberjack??  what??).  I don't like being confined to your set of zones, having some be 3x the area of others, no ability to ever take back lost areas or expand your reach, and the mind-numbing "you can only fight one battle!" mechanic taken right from X-Com.  I don't like marrying a 71 year old dude to a 16 year old girl, something about that being allowed makes me feel dirty, but hey that's the game.  I don't like that you have to immediately replace a dead regent with their offspring, even if they are in the cradle, that's weird.  And I don't like that some of the AI monsters run in circles or act incoherent.
I STILL have an awesome time playing the game.  Time and lives are your only resources - no need to horde gold or decide what to spend on equipment.  You focus on spending two things - time, to find heroes or research or build keeps - and your heroes.  Do you keep this one around for battle, or set him as Regent to sire children for your future army?  Useless characters can find a home at the Sagewright's guild, and your amazing, infertile warrior can teach others as the Standard.
Balancing bloodlines and classes, working all 3 main classes and their subsets to get a good mix while growing more powerful and staving off invasion, it's a brilliant challenge.  Having to decide which of the best 3 sons will continue the bloodline, leaving the others to become Standards or just keep fighting.  Becoming enamored with a character that lasts 3 battles (~45 years), and then seeing their offspring inherit their Relic.
The random events are a little lacking - too often they are minor with no impact, or suddenly take away two of your most valuable characters.  Middle ground seems to be missing.  But sometimes, when your 48 year old veteran asks to go out by competing in the Lash tournament, you grant them their wish.
This game drives home the shortness of existence like few others can - Civilization doesn't show you individual people after all, and X-Com has everyone going from scrub to uber soldier in 3 or 4 months.  In this game you can see your heroes, from the cradle, to 15 year old recruit, to bearded prime-age warrior, to aged veteran, to elderly scholar, growing and changing over time.  It's definitely not a connection like other games - you can't have anyone around more than a quarter of the game, and only that much if you are extremely lucky (and they are only useful for a portion of that).  Your connection will be with 3 or 4 family names that persist over time, if you are lucky, and the relics and experience and traits they pass on.
Different, interesting, very X-Com but with enough of its own mechanics to make it shine.

Anachronox is an active time battle sifi CRPG.
The plot of the game is simple enough to understand, The main character, Sylvester "Sly Boots" Bucelli, is a run down drunken private detective living in the gutter. Until one day he decides to get his♥♥♥♥♥in gear and actually take a job from someone, that person being grumpos, a crazy old coot with an obsession with mystech. From there, they follow the mysteries of mystech and gain a number of weird companions along the way as they try to solve its meaning, all while space time itself begins to distort and warp around them.
Gameplay is split into two parts, combat and exploration. The exploration is simple enough, you can only have three characters in the party at any given time, each one being able to have unique interactions with the world and use special abilities which allow them to access items and areas otherwise impossible to get to. You mainly run around areas talking to NPC's until you move on with the story. While exploring, its possible to unlock your characters personal abilities by doing certain actions, or obtaining certain objects. You can also shop for mystech and other items, or try to collect random items for a completion bonus.
Combat is similar to the final fantasy series in that every character has a gauge which fills up, eventually allowing them to take one of several actions.  Attack (which is modifed not only in damage, but range, depending on the weapon equipped), use item (pretty obvious), use ability (each character having access to several unique ones which use bars of a special gauge, which fills over the course of the battle), move and use mystech (each mystech has a special effect and can be cast as if you were using a spell, with upgraded versions of the same spell costing more power to cast. power is a static number, only recharged by sleeping or using an item).
Each battle takes place on a grid, with nodes on it that can only be occupied by one unit at a time. This allows you to position units between another and an enemy, preventing that enemy from targeting them, at the risk of putting the one inbetween in danger and so on. However, moving is a single action, so you could waste a chance to get a good hit in.
Now, this game is deeply flawed, on many levels. It runs perfectly fine, but everything is so slow, not due to the engine or performance, just because of how it was designed. Battles take an extremely long time, even short ones, to the point where you will be spending about two or three minutes just going through one encounter, with very little actually happening. Walking around the world is also painfully slow, it takes forever to get anywhere at all, making a simple trip to the shops, from one area over, a real pain. There are also needlessly long cutscenes, not like metal gear solid where its all talking, just long pauses of silence as you go up and down a lift, or through a door, and they happen every time you use them. The only reason i didn't put this game down was because i found a mod that allowed me to speed everything up by holding down a button, which makes the game bearable.
It also has an extremely confusing system with mystech. At first you just get simple lumps, which are fine, but later on you get these multi mystech objects that require you to slot bugs into grooves, feed these bugs flower petals and try to figure out a good combination. It does try to explain this system, but it was so utterly confusing that i had to look up how to even get it to work properly. The mechanic isn't broken, just very badly designed. The thing is, if you do crack it, you've won the game, its very easy to make really powerful mystech spells with this system and spam them repeatedly, just by stocking up on items to restore your power.
Then there is the side quests and collecting random objects for a big reward near the end. alot of them are very easy to miss, as are the items that grant your characters new powers, unless you have a walkthrough, you are not going to be able to get half of the abilities and weapons in this game, because some of these could only be found by talking to every NPC as every character and stumbling upon the things. You also cannot go back to many areas in the game, meaning that if you missed that one ability earlier on, you can never get it again, even if you do return to the area, it'll have changed, so that NPC you needed to meet is now gone.
The game is also meant to be very funny, but i can only think of one or two times where i actually laughed. Its humor is really simple and often times just really weak, alot of the time its too childish for my tastes as well, and at its worst, totally brings me out of the game and just makes me want to do anything else but keep listening.
The game looks nice enough for the time when it came out, and with the mod that allows you to speed things up, its an enjoyable sit, but there are many other titles that are far better than this, each one worth your time more than anachronox. If you are a fan of Ion storm and its very off the wall humor, you may like this, and final fantasy fans might find something to enjoy from the battle system, but beyond that i can't see too many people getting through this without a guide.

Truly Extraordinary.
I expected, going in, a random journey. You would click on tiles, and get a random monster, and the, uh, "AI," would also select a random monster. This part works well.
What does not work, on any level other than "Garden" is really anything else.
It loads in the models of the monsters, gives them both the same stats, and then plays an animation and attack sound over and over again, evidently to no effect. You have to press the escape key to get back to the main menu, so that you can go back to playing "Garden."
"Garden" has its own set of problems. You would think that designing random creatures with varying stats would be within the skills of any developer. This is not the case. I have "played" "Garden" "extensively" and have found that three of the animals have different amounts of health. What this means that if you get the pig, which has 4 health and no attack, your opponent's creature will attack the pig until it is dead, which could take up to--stay with me here--4 attacks. What this means is that the field mouse, with 1 health and also no attack, is preferable, because you die faster. While you are playing this game, dying quickly is really the best you can hope for. I am not making a suicide joke here: even if your creature wins, there is no reward. More on this later.
"Garden" has one round, which means that you get to see one fight take place. If you are very lucky, you may have either you or your opponent select a blank tile, which means that you get to skip a round, and you get to see an extra creature. Or both you and your opponent might select creatures with 0 attack, in which case their models pop in and them puff away, which is probably the most excitement that can be had in this game.
I have also experienced one other fascinating glitch. I loaded up the "Arctic" level, and tried to take a look at the scoreboard to see how many rounds this one has. I could not move my camera far enough to see the whole scoreboard, which was strange. I then tried going around the other way, and found that I was locked in that direction too. So I turned my view all the way back, and found that I could no longer see even part of the scoreboard. I repeated this process and found my view stuck in such a way that I could not select the tiles. I had to go a full three-hundred-and-sixty degrees to, uh, attempt to play the game. Naturally, my polar bear got stuck in an attack loop on the frost knight, and I had to press the escape key again.
Also, two of my friends own this game (at the time of this writing, you can get 9 games, some of which are from the same developer as this one, for a dollar on BundleStars in the "Nova" bundle. I do not recommend that you make this purchase.). Anyway, the only extra stages we "unlocked" through the coin-gambling system (which does work: you can unlock 2 monsters: Dragonite and Fat Worm and three stages: Arctic, Swamp, and Canyon, all of which are broken in the same way.) I believe that there are no other stages, because two of us "unlocked" each of these stages multiple times in the gambling process.
Also note that you can win more coins to gamble to unlock things by winning (think loot boxes from f2p games). You start off with 100 coins, or three free rolls. Please note that you cannot use your 100 coins on the "Dragon Cave" level, which purportedly costs 100 coins. Since you can only win in "Garden," and Garden does not award any coins (despite claiming that it does), once you run out of your starting coins, you are out of luck.

Quake 2 Ground Zero is a second mission pack that has been released for the official game. I shall reveal it!
The pack gives you some new weapons such as the powerful ETF Rifle that acts like a Nailgun from Quake 1 with the ability to penetrate the shields or a Tesla Mine which shoots lightning to anyone except you at the very short range with less damage, commonly used to distract or lure the enemy for a better shot. There are also other weapons you can find but i ain't gonna spoil the fun in here other than the fact that this expansion has more new weapons than the previous one.
Like The Reckoning, you have new enemies to deal with, although less than the 1st expansion but it is compensated by their health and their abilities. Such as the sneaky Stalker that attack from unexpected way, DESPICABLE turrets that shoots their chosen ammo such as rockets, blaster or railgun which are extremely smart and more.
Speaking of the smart enemies, Rogue Entertainment has updated the AI for all of the older enemies as well like: Enforcer won't load his chaingun to shoot, Gunners' grenades are more accurate and worst of all, Tanks are even bigger ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s as they will
shoot rockets at you once you leave the cover which turns them into the most annoying and worst enemy to deal with (Yet ONE new enemy will give you even hard time to kill him than the Tank itself).
As hard as it looks like, the Ground Zero brings more new powerups such as the downgraded Quad Damage which is more common to find called "Double Damage", Defender Sphere which reduces your damage you recieve and attacks the enemy etc. Although the multiplayer lets you use even more new powerups than the single player. Oh and no Invulnerability powerup, as it has been replaced with one of the powerups.
Onverall, this expansion will offer you the biggest challenge of all Quake's mission packs giving you new powerups and weapons to play along with new enemies to deal with. Hope your skill is high....as you will need it.

TL;DR
The game has a high learning curve and it is really fun for those who like challenging and yet unique gaming experience, beware of slow updates though, it is totally worth if you are patient enough.
Long version.
Physics based mechanics does really add challenging and fun gaming experience, lower tier enemies could still be a thread and can take players down if you make mistakes, so fights are always intense and it is up to players to achieve success.
While it is not a simulation, developers did a great job keeping the game to be authentic and fun at the same time.
The good:
+Physics based fighting mechanics does really add a lot of fun (sometimes it looks like real people fighting).
+High learning curve.
+A.I. is really good.
+Interactive objects (meaning you can hold and move objects such as doors, chairs, etc. can be used to trick enemies or even make obstacles to slow them down).
+Different game modes including practice mode.
+Character customization.
+Good variety of weapons/armors.
+Good graphics and a lot of graphical options.
+Medieval theme is very well done.
+Soundtracks and music are nice.
Neutral:
~No modding support or workshop yet, and it is not clear if there will be modding support in future.

If Diablo had a child with Dark Souls, they would probably call it Exanima.
This game is very hard, but in it's hardness it is very similar to my beloved Dark Souls (played only DS2:SOTFS). What I mean is both are very hard games, until... you learn how to play. A game can be hard in different ways- player could have low health, monster could swarm the player, deal massive damage, etc., etc., but these are artificial types of making game hard. Exanima has nothing of this. Exanima is hard because at the beginning you have no idea how to fight properly! You need to figure out the controls, and then spend some time practicing in the arena, practicing your moves, swinging your weapon. Also, every weapon acts differently, so when you finally learn how to use a sword properly, it doesn't mean you'll be instantly proficient with maces, or sledgehammer.
As you progress, your character starts to move less than a drunkard, and more like a real knight (or whatever you want him to be). Your skill really matters in this game, so you'll better spend some time practicing, because that's what will make you a better player.
The greatest feature of the game is of course physics based world with which you can fully interact. You can pick up things like in Skyrim, you can even drag bodies the same way. When you drop them, they would behave exactly like you would expect them to behave- falling to the ground naturally.
Physics based world means physics based combat. If you've ever heard of Overgrowth, you'll know what I mean. Animations are procedurally generated, so every fight feels fresh and gives enjoyment. The only thing about animations I don't like at the moment, is how the character moves- it looks like it's sliding on the rink. Keep in mind it's still in beta though, so things will improve hopefully.
What do I miss in Exanima, is cutting limbs off. Call me sadist, but in this game, where blood is spilled in liters, this is a very wanted feature.
At the time of writing this review, Exanima has few playing modes available:
-Practice arena (novice/expert), where you duel 8 enemies one by one, each being harder/having better equipment than the previous one. Health lost in a duel is carried over to the next duel- you'll regain only small portion of lost health before every fight. Beating novice arena unlocks expert.
-Arena, where you start with nothing, and can participate in different types of fights, where you choose which one you want to participate in. In this mode you can earn money by winning the fights, and you can then spend earned money to buy equipment for you character, to increase his survivability.
-Story, where you start in an unkown dungeon, trying to find out what's going on. There are currently 4 complex levels, allowing for good few hours of playing, and there are few more levels to be added.
One thing to know is that Exanima will be just a "Demo", even when released. What I mean, is developers are working on the second game simultaneously, it's called Sui Generis. While Exanima is being played in a dark dungeon, Sui Generis will offer a fully explorable open world, when you decide what to do and where to go. Treat Exanima as a game which shows you what to expect from Sui Generis, as it's more than likely they will share most of the mechanics seen in Exanima.
Exanima is currently in beta, but for me it's totally worth the price (15 EUR), I've spent 90 hours on Steam, and some more before I purchased the game.
If you're not convinced yet, you may want to check my miniseries on YouTube!

I originally bought this game, thinking it would be like a mix of Gangsters: Organized Crime with a bit of X-Com-lite turned based game, and have to say I'm disappointed.
Pros: It looks nice, the interface is easy to play with and it does invoke the era you're playing in and the base building is actually a nice litte touch that gives the players a sense of progress beyond watching the numbers go up.
Cons:
As many reviews noted, the combat system heavily favors the AI - your henchmen can't hit for beans, and statuses such as bleeding seem to proc way more often when the computer is using it. It is challenging, but not in a way that feels fair. Add to the limited amount of maps you play on, the fights become grueling slogs of same old same old.
The sim section is incredibly easy, especially if you played other management or sim games before and there is not a whole lot of variety - you're basically almost entirely doing some form of rumrunning. In the aforementioned Gangsters (A game released in the 90s), you had a much larger variety of illegal activity such as gambling, teamsters, and smuggling and pairing appropriate fronts with illegal activities for maximum profit and minimum visibility is part of the game play. In Omerta, you know exactly where these things are placed, it's just a matter of buying and pumping money in to run errands.
I had very little issues with rising heat, as bribery is too easy a fix for it and as I found combat frustrating and sloggish, I don't actively seek out extras (which is the main source of heat).
There's stages where I've literally bought illegal enterprise, maxed out the safe house, and did all the story objectives so it ends up being a matter of waiting for my cash flow to hit the goal.
And the stages all have the same general flow: Fight some rival mobs > Buy some distilleries and Speakeases > run errands  > couple more combat maps > buy more land, maybe bribe someone > wait for money.
It's not a terrible game, but a very repetitive one that isn't worth $20 (And as people stated, the DLCs are not worth $5), if   you're still curious, I would highly recommend getting it on sale.

I have been playing this game since the beta and first was amazed by the graphics and sleek design.

Now, that is not necessarily a bad thing.
I could tell you about over-powered cards now that can dominate a whole game but let me assume that every strategy game has at least one of these.
Instead let me tell you what I have noted as a casual and none-paying gamer:
You start the game off with (naturally) weak cards and are being pointed to the campaigns that serve as tutorials and also offer stronger cards as rewards for completing them.
So after you have mastered the first, let's say, four of them you might feel the urge to test your cards on the field against real players.
Now this is where it goes wrong for me. No matter if you choose a ranked or un-ranked game, the opponent you face will have stronger cards than you. The change to win any game with just a handful of compaigns completed is about 1/10 if you are lucky.
There are a couple of ways to get cards beside through the (limited) campains though:
1. buy with real cash (easiest and most promoted as this is how this game is financed)
2. complete quests (win 1 online game, play 4 games etc) to get game gold or random cards
2.1. forge cards (requires game gold)
Attention: I do not consider the tournaments here since I have not entered any. Reasons to be found all over the review.
Now here is the funny part:
You either have money to pay for cards and win (the greatest deal of) games against non-paying players resulting in more cards and game gold to forge and/or buy better cards
OR
You do not have the money to pay yourself to victory and a strong deck. This means you have to play. A. Lot!
This way you can at least get the daily quantity quest completed (play 4 games). Let's say one game takes half an hour and you only play 4 per day to get one rewards which is either 6 cards or a bit of game gold (of which you need 3 to 4 portions to buy 6 random cards). In each random card deck you get the chance at two higher ranked cards. To get there you need to put in two hours per day considered you do not get lucky and do win a game.
Are you doing the math?
If you are a hard-core player or one with a great budget, then this game could be something for you.
The decision is all yours!

Bitesize Review - Shadow Complex Remastered
The Good:
- Setting/mechanics for the game
- Metroidvania Style of game
- Satisfying to unlock gadgets and weapons
The Bad:
- The PC controls can cause your character to mis-aim sometimes
- The graphics are blurry in some spots
- The FPSs drop and the game does freeze up for a second or two while the next level loads in the background
- You play as the most sterotypical white man in the world
- You are trying to rescue the most white girl in the world (who you just met!)
- The badguy is a bargin bin Cobra Commander
- The last 3 points add up to the story is pretty cringy all things considered
The Verdict:
I had heard so many good things about this game way back when it was first released. I was excited to finally start playing it a few days ago. What I ended up experiencing was kind of a blurry, technically iffy game with a very sterotypical story.
You start the game as a Nathan Drake type white dude who's going on a hike with a girl he met at a bar. She decides to go on ahead of you and before you know it she is dragged off by two armoured soliders. You start with a flashlight and end up getting better and better gear to help you get deeper into the complex. As you play you see doors and stuff you can not get past until you get the appropriate gear (guns, grenades, missiles, grappling hooks, and a foam gun). The game is very metroidvania style in the sense that you'll be going back and forth through the complex using your new gear to get to new places as the story progresses. This all sounds good but then a few things ruined my experience with this game.
The graphics were blurry, which was to be expected with an older game, but when the game had cutscenes it was clear but when it zoomed out for gameplay it was blurry. Also the game very often stuttered as you moved from room to room due to (what I assume) the game is loading levels in the background. And on top of this the story really is so vanilla - Joe america must save the also white girl and save america. There's nothing wrong with a white dude saving the day but dude - this is the whitess dude and it just made me put my hand over my face when he or the girl spoke!
Anyways if the game did not have the technical issues I would probably recommend it - it was a fun little game when it worked. But with those issues and the story the way it is, I kind of feel like you should give this a pass to be honest.

Map making: Ditch the obscure scripting language for javascript or similar. Allow multiple map campaigns that allows some progression. Where the outcome in one map can affect following maps. I bought this game when it was originally released and it instantly captured me.
Where to begin?
In this lovely game you play Amy, a teenage girl who gets drawn into the world of Zanzarah. In this magical Land where dwarves, swamp goblins and elves inhabit the world, everything revolves around Fairies. These creatures exist in the astral plane , where they often battle each other.
FIrst you defend yourself against rogue fairies who lurk in trees, stones, lakes... Later on you are able to collect them. The omnipresent rock-scissors-paper principle grants interesting battles. Its a constant challenge to set up your 5 member fairy team against current obstacles, like getting through a psi-fairy ridden cave. Should you at any point be at a loss which fairy is effective against the one youre battling, simply press f1 and keep scrolling till you can see the effectivness chart.
As the story continues you begin to realize into what you have been drawn into. While it starts quite peaceful you soon uncover that Zanzarah is in peril and its up to you to save it. As you get more and more powerful (or better put your fairies) you will be able to get to Areas which were previously inaccessible. There are not many games around which give you this feeling of accomplishment / progress. Which is even more true to the rune system: You are able to fast travel to many locations, which means (too) long walks arent necessary.
While today it may seemed dated (but still very nice to look at), back in the day the graphics were simply breathtaking. Lush green forests, mountan landscapes, swamplands... you surely get around in zanzarah. And every Area is so detailed, you can feel the love to detail that ran into their design.
Zanzarah can be compared with a certain asian game where red and white balls with little creatures in them play a big part ;)
In short: Get the game, immerse into the magical world of zanzarah, have fun :D

I rate the game Just Cause 4/5. Overall this is a Good game. It is a fun but flawed, third-person perspective, grand-theft-auto style, open-world adventure game. It has aged relatively well for a 10 year old game.
Incredibly ambitious but terribly flawed, this game is still quite a bit of fun to play and features some very pretty tropical landscapes which shine through despite what are, by today's standards, generally mediocre and somewhat buggy graphics. For the current price of 7 dollars or so, this game gives you a lot of fun for your money.
+Good graphics which adequately depicted the heat and humidity of the game's tropical setting. The colors used by this game were bright, hot and at times, even muggy but consistently beautiful. The graphics were always very cartoony however but perfectly matched the game's silly sense of humor and ludicrous stunts and physics.
+This game gives you tremendous freedom and the landmass of the area you get to explore is truly humongous. No spatial compression here (like in Skyrim where the place looks larger than it actually is), unlike in Skyrim, this game really is as huge as it looks and you will usually need a helicopter or airplane to get around from place to place in a timely fashion (which gives you the most beautiful views of the game anyhow). Unfortunately, there isn't much to do in the big environments you have available to you.
+Trying out all the vehicles and zipping all over the island and off of cliffs is a LOT of fun. Finally getting into a helicopter and flying around is even more fun especially since the game becomes even more beautiful at that altitude (fewer visual bugs caught my eye at high altitudes). The vehicle stunts were fun (but the grappling hook gun thing was always cumbersome). This game has great controls and makes it easy to reconfigure those controls to suit your personal taste once you figure out how the control menu works (and that its perfectly ok to have key conflicts).
+/-Severely buggy. Physics bugs are particularly prevalent. Doors of cars fly off and into the distance at tremendous velocities when you open them. Traversing a turret on an armored car causes the car somersault crazily up into the air. Rotor blades ignore tree branches as if they aren't even there. The physics engine isn't remotely realistic and in many ways seems more similar to the physics in loony tunes or something than to real life. Rather than causing frustration however the bad physics leads to a lot of laughter and unexpected funny moments wherein stuff that should not possibly happen, happened. Mostly (except for the problem with traversing turrets) the physics problems actually make this already easy game even easier.
+/-This is a very easy game and there are few missions which will prove challenging. Unfortunately the final mission is much, much harder than the rest of the game (I had to try if about 7 times or more before I got through it). For the most part though the game will seem too easy rather than too hard.
+/- Merely adequate sound effects and mediocre (at best) music which quickly becomes repetitive given the potential length of the game. The voice acting is good (your character looks and sounds like Antonio Banderas, but he repeats his little taunts too often. Enemy taunts and voices are repeated too often also. There is no GTA style fake radio and you cannot apparently insert your own music into this game making for a very boring soundscape throughout. This meant I turned the volume down pretty far most of the time making this a very quiet game for me to play. The sound effects aren't that great when turned up far anyhow.
+/- The game's main plot/story isn't totally boring but it's not nearly as interesting as it could have been. The major problem is that none of the characters explained in any great detail nor is the overall situation. Maybe there's more background information in an instruction manual somewhere which I didn't bother to read.
-The side missions are generally repetitive and boring. The best thing about them is that they are entirely optional. You don't have to do them at all in order to play the game and the rewards they yield don't hardly make them worth the effort of doing them anyhow.
-The enemy AI is about as good as it was in GTA III. That's not so good, which makes the game even easier. Enemy soldiers run around fighting for themselves with no squad-based tactics like a senseless mob. This helps make battles feel chaotic (because this way they actually are) but they don't feel remotely real.
-You can explore but the HUGE tropical island environments are ultimately mostly uniform and boring and not very interactive. The civilian population is not very interactive either. You can hit them with cars or not or whatever but it makes no difference. You can't have sex with them or anything like that (like in GTA III). There's no sense of morality and no consequences for wantonly killing bystanders. There's no multiple ending structure to this game either. The island population is just there as random bystanders and to provide you with ample vehicles to hijack. Asides from tooling around in various vehicles and doing repetitive side missions or the games relatively few main-plot missions there just isn't much to do given the truly massive amount of geographic territory the game gives you access to. This is Just Cause's biggest, most critical flaw.
-Given how remote many of the locations in the game look the tropical nation's dirt and non-dirt roads alike are all too packed with traffic. There is almost an inner-city level traffic almost everywhere you go no matter how deep in the countryside you are which always seemed really weird.

Hmm, the question "Do you recommend this game?" is answered in my mind with a "maybe". I liked the story of it, but there were quite a few moments of gameplay that I did not like.
Probably the biggest downfall of the game is two achievements that are supposed to only be obtainable on the very first playthrough - meaning if you screw up, you shouldn't be able to get them. I believe there's a FAQ by the developer on how to reset the saves so you can get these achievements, but considering that's how they were initially put in I still find it rather stupid. Who the heck plays a game perfectly the first time?
The other part about the achievements I do not like would be time related ones - while Rocketeer is rather easy to get (finish game in 4 hours first time), having an achievement about playing the game for x amount of hours total is not really that good of a idea in my opinion. Some games I expect to rack up 300+ hours playing - this type of game I would be suprised if I have more than 8hrs trying to get all the achievement (except for the one about how much time to play). Thankfully it's only 10hrs, so I should be able to manage to muddle through it in the end - but I hate this type of achievement.
Moving on to whether you should get this game or not. I do not recommend this game at the full price of $19.99. To be quite frank, it's not worth that much. It's barely worth paying $5 for, but I would recommend it if you can find it at $5 or cheaper.

Massive Chalice is a turn-based tactics game with a rather unique strategic management layer. The game takes place over time period of 300 years, so in addition to individual heroes you also need to manage their bloodlines.
The strategic layer is for the most part rather simple, as you only have access to three different building types. Rather annoyingly once a hero is assigned to a building they are stuck there forever and can never return to active duty.
The main complication is the bloodline management at the keeps. Picking the right regent/partner is rather important, as both the class and the traits of the children are partially determined by their parents. The game doesn't do a great job displaying this info, however, and it can take a long time finding the perfect parents.
The turn-based battles are passable, but shallow affairs. Double Fine more or less copied the two action point XCOM model but ignored all the advanced features such as height variations or overwatch. As it is, the combat is rather boring and gets repetitive quickly.
The time also passes too quickly for you to really grow attached to any of your heroes or their bloodlines. Even the most long-lived heroes will only participate in a few battles before they either die or are retired to a few more productive years of service in the crucibles or the guilds.
Like many of Double Fine's recent games, Massive Chalice has some unique ideas but is too deeply flawed to be truly enjoyable. There are just too many annoyances for me to recommend this. I ended up giving up around the year 200 as I wasn't really having much fun with the game.
The good:
- Bloodline management is a great concept
The bad:
- The tactical combat lacks depth
- Repetitive after a while
- Annoying enemy designs
- Poor writing
- Ugly art style, especially the characters
- Some UI issues
- Random event choices feel more random than meaningful

Massive Chalice can at first seem a little one dimensional especially on the combat side. However, there are some very good ideas here especially with the way you have to breed better fighters through complex "bloodlines" where traits are passed down the line and you attempt to engineer superior characters. There is also the crucible where you can retire your finest middle-aged fighters to help with training up the next generation. I say middle aged because if you wait until they are too old then they will die of illness or old age before they actually have time to have an influence. Also, combat improves via new skill traits and better equipment invention giving your characters a multitude of new skills. Time passes very quickly though and you shouldn't go into this game expecting to hold onto some "super-soldier" for too long. The real idea is to BREED a sustainable influx of stronger characters rather than just pumping up lone figures. The learning curve is slow and you wont have seen much of how the game REALLY works until after at least your first 100 game years or so.
There are many other nice touches that contribute to the variety of tactics when looking to sustain your nation but they are just too many to discuss in a short review. But I will add that a single campaign can take around 20 hours or so and no two will ever be the same due to the nature of the breeding system so there is plenty of replay value here.

So to sum up, MC is a game which appears a lot more simplistic than it actually is because underneath its seemingly shallow surface is a very deep and original game - and one that I highly recommend to those of a persevering nature. If you can just keep in mind that it is a "slow burner" then you will have many enjoyable hours with it.

Overall a fun game and well worth the money.

Do I recommend this game? - Absolutely!
Even though it is not yet completely finished, Exanima became one of my favorite games. But if anyone is reading this, they are wondering if it is worth buying for them. I have huge interest in history and thus my taste in games are a bit different (my #1 fav game is EU 4 for example), so let me start from few cons to throw you off.
Cons:
1) High learning curve. You won't be able to jump into the game and do spectacular moves with any weapon right away. It might take a while and it will feel like game is very unintuitive. I was about to leave a negative feedback on this game after an hour of gameplay but I'm glad I didn't, because after few hours you get the hang of game's mechanics and from there, fun of it grows exponentially every minute. ~5+ hours in, you will be comfortable with camera and character movement and from that point combat will start to feel very natural. There are few gifs and videos in community hub where people show off what type of moves you can pull off. At first, it might apear that it is almost impossible and only in rare instances of luck you can do such things, but after a while you'll be doing them left and right yourself and feel like real badass.
2) Even after some time, you will trip and fall with your character and it can get on your nerves when it happens in the middle of a fight or when you when you run away from certain enemies deeper in the dungeons (he got a name - Sir. When you'll meet him you'll understand :) ). But also it can be very amusing to see how hilariously your character trips and falls when you rush full speed an empty area and some random chair gets in your way.
3) Game's main campaign doesn't have difficulty levels (unless you consider starting character differences as a difficulty level) so at first game might appear as too hardcore, when even one dumb enemy with chair leg can beat you down. But after a while this view will flip and it will seem as if game is too easy, especially if you'll try to go clear first floor naked, fighting only with your fists. But don't worry, at about 4th floor it will become challenging again.
4) You will only play in dark grimy places. From time to time you might want to see wide open areas with sun high in the sky so you could run around with that two-handed poleaxe in your arms, yet you'll be forced to stick to your torch and switch it when fight about to happen because otherwise you won't be able to see anything. But do mind that this is only prelude to another game Sui Generis and it was intended to be locked to "underworld" while SG will have lots of open areas. As for myself, I don't even consider this as a bad thing since I like the tension this game can create while wandering in dark dungeons without that artificial light you are forced to stuck with in other games. I mean did you see unmodded Skyrim's dungeons - why even bother with torch.
And now for the good stuff. I won't number them, since there are too many of them. I'll try to summarize some of the reasons why this game is a real gem and bear in mind that these are not the only reasons.
As I mentioned, this game has high learning curve but it also is type of game with high reward. If you want grand strategy game you can choose Civ series and after an hour you'll know all bits of that game, or you can choose Paradox's grand strategy games like EU4 and after a month you will still be newbie but one who looks at Civ as kid zone game. Same with Exanima, you can choose something like path of exile and leave it at that or you can invest time into this gem and be glued to it instead of aimlessly clicking on stuff to kill them with whole rainbow of explosions.
Exanima offers dark and grimy world which will create tension and make you feel like this is how true RPG should look like. Every hit can make you crippled, so even if you feel like you are way superior to those stupid enemies at the beginning, one unfortunate hit can make even the start of a game true hell. You will ROLEPLAY this game and the role is your character's life. There won't be potions in every enemy you kill, there won't be fresh food to regenerate life so every bit of your character's lifebar is vital and can change game drastically. You will learn to appreciate "just run" tactic as if you yourself are wandering those dark hallways. And when you do find item that can heal your severe wounds it will feel like you've just found a diamond (by the way, there are only few of mentioned items in the entire game).
There won't be map or flying arrows to show you the way in these dungeons. In fact, if you take a piece of checkered paper and draw map yourself as you explore, it will make roleplaying part even more fun (of course you can google dungeon maps but I highly recommend to take your time and make them yourself).
And finally, the combat. That feeling when you pull off combo of moves with excellent timing and see poor soul crumbling to the ground - ooohhh, that is soooo priceless. I can't even describe the feeling when you wreck your opponent even more so if that opponent is higher level with way better AI than in campaign's first floor. If they have a shield, they will actually use it, if they use two handed weapon, they will use their distance advantage and doge your dumb swings countering them with their own attacks. But the best feeling will come when you'll acquire full plate armor for the first time and meet opponent with same gear - those "can opening" sounds will be music to your ears. You might have used sword to thrust it to enemy's, who forgot his helmet, face but when AI use plate all over his body, pull out your war hammer and crack that can open - so satisfying. Sounds in this game are fantastic. Even small bump into a chair wearing chain mail will make natural metal chain sound. Weapons feel realistic and allows you to pull of special moves if you practice enough. For example, good swing with war axe will threw your opponent off balance even if he managed to block your swing so you can then quickly follow with killing blow, if you use something like billhook, with right footwork you'll be able to easily pull your enemy to the ground. Also devs even thought of such details as "halfswording" with two handed swords so you won't see stupid animations when your character use his 1.5m length metal sword  as a poking stick. Though I have to say that I'm a bit disappointed that we still can't "end opponents rightly" by now, well game is still early access so I don't loose my hope yet :)
All in all, this games offers awesome experience for anyone who are willing to feel frustration for first couple of hours while learning game's mechanics just to reach true potential of this game. It would be a sin not to get this game if you like such games like Mount and blade or if you are looking for realistic RPG. For anyone else who just stumbled upon this game and have no particular interest in history, RPGs or realistic medieval combat I'd say try this game for few hours and ask for refund if by then you won't feel that frustration is going down and fun going up. And if you do this, my advice would be to start from practice arena on novice level (just don't forget to double click your defeated opponent to take his gear). Try to concentrate on where you hold your mouse and not on moving camera constantly to always face opponent. And don't forget - this is not a clicker, if you want to swing your weapon hold your mouse button thru-out the animation and move mouse a bit in the same direction following with footsteps in same swing direction to make your attacks as lethal as possible. If in an hour you'll manage to learn how to pull of this kind of move correctly, you'll be ragdolling your opponents left and right and have a good lough at it.

Exanima could be thought of as two games rolled into one.  The first game consists of an isometric RPG dungeon crawler where you must fight enemies, find better weapons and armour and level up your character with a selection of fighting skills.  Doesn't sound like anything new, right?
Wrong.
The combat system, while it takes a little getting used to, is one of the best I've ever come across.  Unlike other games of this genre where it's very often a slashfest to see who can get their opponent's energy bar down the quickest, here the fights actually feel like fights.  Combatants push and scuffle, arms flail, and they even trip over themselves as they try to land that killer blow.  Blades carve satisfyingly through flesh, and maces hit home with a resounding metallic crunch.  It's all very messy, but it's damn realistic.
Which brings me to the second game in Exanima, and the reason why I like this game so much.  You play the head of a guild where you must recruit fighters, equip them and send them into the arena to fight.  Winning fights earns you gold, meaning you can buy your fighters better weapons and armour as they level up.
Fights usually consist of one-on-one encounters, but there are variations.  Some fights involve weapons, but others are fists only.  There's also two-on-two fights, fights against monsters, and even a 'last man standing' round, where multiple fighters compete for the prize.  If fighters are wounded, they will need time to recover from their injuries.  In the worst case scenario they can even die, so it's a good idea to maintain a sizeable roster, money permitting.
Like I said, it's not a game you're going to master overnight, but if you have the patience to get good at this you'll be well-rewarded.  A real gem.

I first played this on the Xbox360. Loved it so much, I finished it over just a handful of sessions across 2 days. I really missed it when my console died on me and always wished a PC edition was available. Surprisingly, I wasn't aware of a PC 'Remastered' edition all this while until the recent Steam Sale. Double combo!!!
Don't go in expecting an Oscar-winning story; the book it was based on is probably way more interesting. It is engaging enough to make you want to move it along, especially when the game seamlessly transitions to in-game scripted scenes. There is also a mild hint of parody at spy or action movies by way of how the script was written.
What do I enjoy about it? Simplicity.
The power armor is over-the-top powerful by end game, it is such a refreshing experience to feel godly after all the effort pumped in to the game. The game is short, but highly replayable, with or without your upgraded armor. Want some challenge? Replay it and DON'T go for all upgrades and secrets. Want to squash your enemies like the ragdolls they are? This is the perfect game for it!
The level design is coherent and, even for a small game, gives a sense of continuity and size. The whole game world is seamlessly connected, and there is even a full game map provided as you explore. Imagine having that in Mario! The map even hints at hidden secrets in a location in case you missed any visual cues on the scene. Some may find this less challenging, but I don't believe the game was designed to be a grind. It has the right balance of challenge because some of the secrets are SO obvious in their location but takes either motion agility or some smart thinking to reach them.
The only real downside? The game is short. I took my time and still finished it in a few hours. There are achievements to finish the game in 2 and 3 hours respectively. Good thing is the game was never priced with a full AAA pricetag, so it sets the right expectation. If you enjoy a smart, fun platformer, then it is worth more than a few of those so-called big name games.
Highly recommended, with or without the Steam sales. I already owned a copy on a different platform, so the sale price was extra appreciated.

Amazing west made JRPG. WRPG? WMJRPG? ZOMGFBBQWMJRPG?
Whatever you wanna call it, this game is absolutely fantastic, it was made by ION Storm (the Deus Ex team, not the Daikatana team), the story is both depressing and incredibly funny and optimistic at the same time, you meet tons of whacky and unforgettable characters along your journey, for example, your mouse pointer is a small ship housing the AI of your sarcastic dead secretary, and that's just the tip of the iceberg.
Keep in mind though, mechanically speaking, it has quite a few problems that are more outdated stuff than anything.
The graphics is the first thing that comes to mind, personally I don't mind a classic looking 3D game from the late 90's / early 2000's, especially if antialiasing is added through the drivers, but these might be a massive turn off for some, also there's no easy way to run this in widescreen aspect, so unless you look how to unlock widescreen resolutions
, you're mostly stuck with 4:3 aspect resolutions.
This being a JRPG style game, means that the battles are naturally turn based with your party of characters and that's great really, especially because there can be a surprising amount of strategy to kill certain enemies and bosses. The only thing that it could've improved over it's japanese counterparts, is the overly long animation sequences, those can get under your skin if you see the same long animations over and over for a long game like this.
Outside the battes though, it's just a wonderful fully realized massive 3D sci-fi world(s) to explore, it kinda reminds me a lot of Mass Effect for the many friendly (and non-friendly) alien races you get to meet, it also reminds me of a traditional point n' click adventure games, there's a lot of stuff to see, tons of people to talk to, tons of places to explore, it's just good stuff.
So yeah, in conclusion, this is quite a fun west made JRPG with a few problems, but overall, I highly recommend it.

TLDR I am a rabid fan who hasn't dropped a dime on this game in 2.5 years but have a massive collection, play competitively, adore draft, and just earned $40 of in-game gold in competition this past weekend.  I am not the only one.
Let's be frank, I've sunk a lot fo hours into this game--in fact, I play 2-3 hrs daily on my Android phone, so it's very likely my total horus should be around 3000 after 2.5 years of play.  I have loved this game, I have seethed at it, I have quit for months (a brutal constructed meta in SUmmer 2015) and returned.
I don't understand the complaints of the new client's appearance--it is different, and people hate change, but it is easy to read and decipher what is going on and very easy to work with on PC and Android.
Is it buggy--absolutely--the Discard pile can be broken by a key legend that levels cards in it, the ability to open the deck can be blocked by use of another popular legend, and if you don't know the right tricks, you can loose a brand-new deck you've just designed because the game forgot it existed.
So, player beware--it isn't a the most smooth UI in existence.  But, the core of thsi game is fantastic--I played MtG for 15 years and have never looked back.  Yes, you can get "level-screwed" but is honestly less likely to happen than in MtG or Hearthsone and you always have 2 guarenteed plays and only 5 lanes to block, so it can be survived.you're doing.
As to Pay-to-win.  Two thinsg to consider: One, if a player were to drop $100 on MtG and then play in an arena where they are facing vetrans with lots of time and money invested, would we claim it's pay-to-win? Possibly, but we wouldn't assume that if that player had paid $1000 they should have been able to achieve a championship right away either.  This is a game of skill, it has a learning curve, and you are going to lose to people who have played more and have earned up to better cards.
Dailies: At this point, you need to win against an online opponent to gain a booster per day--this is not simple, it was easier when you could just beat the computer for two boosters, but SBE has also made it possible to earn 2 tixkets a day just showing up 8 times (heck, you can even concede).  That means every 2 days you can pay those 4 completely free tixckets to draft 30 new cards, many of which can be new rares and heroics, and play to get new cards and silver to craft even more--and let's be clear, the single pack you earn now has a much higher-rarity drop than those of old.
To cap it off, I have never spent any money on this game--I have been drafting and building and competing for almost 2.5 years, yes, but I run 3 separate accounts and am Platinum or Titanium ranked on each of them, can accrue enough silver to purchase brand new powerful cards on release, and can compete in Elite tournaments to earn valuable in-game gold for free.  I rarely play anything else; I am a rabid fan.  You'll never know if you can be one too, unless you try it for awhile.  And for all that's good, go to
and get to know the friendly and helpful side of our community
