If you're like me, and you like a (relatively) easy strategy game with an engaging story and characters, this really isn't it. If you're not like me, and you're a heretofore unknown deity of strategy games, then you probably don't care what a puny mortal like me has to say anyway.
With that being said, I tend to play most strategy games on what I like to call, "lil' ♥♥♥♥♥ mode" because while I'm terrible at strategy, sometimes it's just fun to manage a group of characters. What can I say? I like playing god.
When I started the game, it hit most of my buttons. Pretty art, cool game mechanic (bloodline management), interesting premise, snarky narrators...And the combat was fun.
I even enjoyed the research, although it did get kind of boring after a while. But I was pretty attached to a couple of my bloodlines so I kept going.
Then, the Chalice started suffering from dementia, because they'd repeat themselves. Over and over and over. Apparently, the dementia was contagious, because the Cadence seemed to catch it and kept attacking the same three sectors. And the random events. My god. I was more scared of them than I was of the Cadence, because while I had a 33.3% chance of an OK outcome, the other two outcomes were invariably bad and terrible, so I actually had a 66.6% chance of one of my heros dying or getting maimed each time. Hm.
Despite the Chalice's mental health issues, I soldiered on and made it to the halfway point. I felt pretty accomplished. I'd been beating back the Cadence, my keeps were doing well, research was progressing, and then
the Sagewright's guild got attacked. And what do I see when I get in there? Advanced Bulwarks. 5 of them. Surrounding my heros. Who all died. I think it only took about 6 turns.
Well ok. Maybe I deserved that after all my successes thus far. Maybe my next battle will go better.
Actually, the next battle was less  "I should be careful so I don't lose any heros" and more "Jesus  H. rollerblading christ i finally killed a bulwark after getting acid all over me from the rupture I missed and now there's 5 more bulwaks, 6 lapses and another rupture?!" Needless to say, it was every hero for themselves after that.  Billy-bob over there who failed to hit the broadside of a bulwark when it was three squares away and dead ahead? Sorry dude. You're going to be rupture bait while the rest of my hunters nope on out with their veil armor.
TL;DR: It's pretty, bloodline management is cool, and it's really fun for the first half when you can actually kick some♥♥♥♥♥ Said♥♥♥♥♥kickery makes up for the repeat dialogue, the extremely slow pace of gameplay, and the god-awful, weighted-against-you (66.6% chance that your day is about to suck, remember?) random events. In the second half of your game, when you're just throwing your heros at the Cadence meat-grinder, the previously bearable annoyances become more like unbearable, i'm-going-to-throw-something-through-the-monitor-if-I-hear-that-line-one-more-time annoyances.
Overall, I don't really recommend it, although I wish there was a "meh" button. if it's deeply discounted or part of a bundle, give it a go, but don't pay full price for it.

You very quickly meet all possible enemy types, and there is both little variation in enemies and in your heroes. Combat starts off interesting but quickly becomes boring and a real chore. Enemies like to hide in corners and the game feels sluggish when you have to spend turn after turn hunting down weak enemies hiding or running from you with no real threat. The enemies themselves might as well be comprised of Nerf and theres little tactical satisfaction from the battles.
Heroes age and die quickly enough that its hard to develop any particular attachment to them or their lineage. Most heroes may be lucky enough to see 2 or 3 engagements if that. If you can feed enough kills to particular heroes, their weapon might turn into a Relic, but again there really isn't any attachment or story or driving force to make me care about slogging my way through the boring combat system.
The game just feels simplistic and empty, and the interesting premise never ends up feeling realized. You wind up investing hours in the game hoping it gets better and it never does- you really do see everything it has to offer within the first hour or two. I kept trudging towards the ending out of obligation more than deriving any fun from it before ultimately shrugging my shoulders.

If you have ever played XCOM: Enemy Unknown, or XCOM 2, and you enjoy fantasy settings with a grand sense of adventure, you will like Smaller Cup- I mean MASSIVE CHALICE.
I have less than an hour into the game, but I can tell you it flows almost identically to modern XCOM. The game appears to have less pressure on the player than XCOM from the get go, but I could see how that could easily change. Much like the way that countries all start support the XCOM project, you can readily have regions in MC be over taken by you enemy. I can't tell you what happens when that occurs, but the game starts out with a given time limit that you have to ensure your survival for, or else the game will end.
The tacical, turn based combat does not use cover or facing unfortunately. Vangaurds start as low leveled fighters and, unlike XCOM, can be turned into research personelle, or kings and queens that run your other supported regions. Thus making a new, and interesting strain on your troops available for combat. You will probably loose if you throw all your Vanguards into R&D, royality, or just into fighting.
Like XCOM, MC forces you to make choices about who to train, what to research when, and prioritise your limited resources. Unlike XCOM it has a wonderful air of not taking it's self too seriously. The little bits of humor thrown in are perfect and over all make you feel not as bad about making poor choices in the game. This is further supported by a semi-cartoonish art style which show cases vibrant colors and original character designs beautifully.
MASSIVE CHALICE is a pretty damn good game that I'd recommend to anyone looking for something as fun as XCOM, or other turn based strategy games, and likes a bit of humor.

I gave up halfway in.
The game is basically a dumbed down version of XCOM.  Less soldiers, less classes, less skills, less mechanics, less.. everything.
The artstyle is fairly unique, but also lacks quite a lot of detail.
What's the main problem with it?
Every single action you perform in combat is held up by an unskippable animation.  Reveal an enemy? Camera moves over to it and it unleashes a battlecry, then moves back to your selected soldier. Attack an enemy? Camera follows the attack then moves back to your soldier. Kill an enemy? Camera moves over to it and it dies, then moves back to your selected soldier to show your soldier's battlecry. (god forbid you multi-kill) Get exp? Camera stays centered on your soldier. Level up? Camera stays centered on your soldier. Used up the action points on a soldier? Camera forcibly moves to another soldier. Etc.
You can't switch soldiers during an action either.  You're forced to sit and wait and watch until they completely finish their action.
There is so much needless waiting that it makes combat take
longer than it should.  This is made even worse by the fact that..
Maybe as a veteran of XCOM (the original and the remake) I have much more skill than the average player, but I just found absolutely no challenge at all.  My soldiers basically one shot everything and I never had anyone die; which leads us to...
Hunters are supposed to do big single target damage.. but they're weaker than Alchemists who one shot groups of enemies.  I found the Caberjacks to be completely useless. They had high damage, but being melee in this game is awful due to Ruptures (explode on death), Lapses (exp loss when hit) and Withers (age gain when hit; extremely bad).  My main group was 3 alchemists and 2 hunters, though a more optimal group seems like 4 alchemists and 1 high accuracy hunter to function as a band-aid for misses on critical targets.
And yes, there are really only 3 character classes.  You can breed different ones together to get hybrids, but they basically function the same, only with a few different skills.  Some of them are objectively worse (ex. Enforcer) due to their skill changes.
The other problem with the game is the management and RNG.  You have a very simplistic map with 10 locations on it.  You pretty much build 1 Sagewright guild, 1 Crucible and the rest are keeps to breed heroes.. and you NEED to build keeps ASAP (see below).  Other than that, you can research some weapon and armor upgrades along with some (mostly) passive items.
Soldiers
all have unique traits and personalities; completely randomized. Some are just flavor text, some are good and some are horrible.. and they're usually horrible.
Soldiers also have ages, and age is a key mechanic of the game.  Your soldiers die from age, and they die frequently as it's usually 20+ years in between combat sessions.
If you do not start breeding your heroes early, you will run out because they all die from old age.  You can hire a group of 5 heroes, but they're usually far worse than ones you can breed due to coming with a lot of negative traits.  For example, the last group of heroes I hired all came with the 'Slow' personality (among other negatives), which meant they moved less tiles in combat.  It may not seem like much, but the default movement is 4, so that's a 25% reduction in how far they can move per turn.  I brought one on a mission and they were left behind everyone; useless.
There's also another very bad one: Heart disease.  The average soldier lifespan seems to be 65.  People with heart disease can die in their 40's.  This makes it almost pointless to even take that soldier into combat, as they'll die far before they get to a higher level. Longevity is the counter to this; those soldiers can last into their 80's, which is extremely useful.
So, this means you
to selectively breed your soldiers if you don't want a ton of useless people.  Traits can get passed down from parent to child.  Personalities however can be gained via the 'Standard', someone you assign to the Crucible to train soldiers (passively as time passes).  They also gain both kinds of stats randomly on birth and while they age.
Pair two good parents together (if you can even get them in the first place), set a good standard and off you go breeding competent soldiers... until someone dies, or the RNG doesn't give them the traits or personality you're raising them with. Hope they're young too, because the older they get, the less they breed.
Oh, and everyone you assign to any of the buildings is forever stationed there until they die.  You cannot take them into combat.  This contradicts the 'Standard' mechanic, since higher level heroes are much better at training.. but what's the point if they just die in a few years?
Between waiting so long for combat, having to manage dozens of soldier deaths every time I wasn't in combat, and the combat taking far longer than it should, I just got so fed up with waiting and needless micromanaging that I stopped playing.
The UI could also use some more work, especially when trying to manage a soldier.  Everything's too big and takes too many clicks to get to or see information you want (the 4 pages of tabs could be consolidated, and there needs to be a 'compact' mode for lists).  There's also no way to sort people by their traits or even search at all, which makes finding specific people a real hassle.
Good voice acting though.  Jennifer Hale and some guy I don't recognize.  Guess all the budget went to them instead of giving the game more depth..
If you can pickup the game when it's cheap (below $5), I'd say go for it. You'll have a bit of fun for a day or so, but if you're expecting something with the intensity of XCOM (or even half of it), then you'll start to get frustrated and bored barely 100 years in.  If we could turn off the time wasting animations, then I'd switch this review over to positive and actually play the game again.

Exanima is a rather interesting game. The setting and story are rather bland, as far as I've seen, but what makes you forget about all of that are the unique physics and controls.
In Exanima you don't simply tell your character to move forwards, you control their forwards movement. It's rather tricky to explain, since I've literally never come across another game that controls in quite the same way. But while the controls are unique, they're still surprsingly intuitive: They feel natural, once you recognise their function.
Basically, you can make your character move forwards, backwards or turn in the classical sense, by using the WASD keys, but doing so will quickly prove itself very clunky. But that's because you can also control your character in deeper detail with the mouse. Basically, your character will move in the direction of where you click with the right mouse button, their speed depending on how far away you click. This feels very natural and is rather simple, so it's easy to learn. The difficult learning part is combat.
By pressing the TAB button, your character will enter a combat stance, and your controls will change drastically. Now your character will immediately turn in the direction where you point your cursor, no clicking required. This might make the right-button movement from before feel clunky, which is where the normal WASD buttons come in. For in combat, the WASD controls will cause your character to make small "leaping" movements, which are quick but requires some time to recover balance; perfect for dodging a blow or rush your opponent, and their distance (and subsequent recovery time) are determined by how long you press down the WASD controls. I might also note that the WASD controls are relative to where your character is currently facing as opposed to the camera, so keep that in mind.
As for using weapons: Your character will block incoming blows automatically, assuming you're facing your opponent and aren't trying to attack at the same time, which makes sense. Using your weapon is interesting however, since its impact will be determined by your movements and whether you hit them with the "appropriate" part of the weapon; meaning that you'll hit harder with a stick the further out on the stick the blow lands and if your body is twisting in the direction you swing, as opposed to hitting closer to your grip whilst just standing there. There's a mechanic for thrusting as well, where you simply hold in the ALT key while performing your attack as usual. There are some different movement required to pull off a good thrust, but it's useful for dealing with armoured opponents or tight spaces. Of course, your opponent will be attacking you and defending themselves as well (assuming they're not zombies in which case they won't defend themselves), so you need to plan out how you're going to deal with them; whether that means quickly overwhelming them with simple brute force or slowly wearing down on them with weak but easily achieved strikes.
All of this is complemented with a physics engine which makes it possible to toss around and get tossed around (by) your opponents, trip on objects and furniture on the ground and get your weapon stuck on both walls and objects around you, so that you have to retain a certain amount of situational awareness at all times to prevent yourself from having mishaps or even gain an advantage in combat.
All of this makes combat feel very realistic and down to earth, something that's very hard to achieve in any game. It might be an early access game, but I can say that even if it were never to be finished, the sheer concept of this game is worth paying a pretty penny for. And it already has enough content to keep you satisfied for a long time. It's a difficult game to learn, but once you've got the hang of the controls you'll feel as though you were in a real fight, with the outcome depending as much on the quality of your equipment as on your skill at using it. Of course, this means that if you're proficient enough you could potentially strike down an armoured knight with nothing but a sturdy stick, but this game does have rogue-lite elements to it, so why take the chance...?
Exanima is already a great game. And when it's finished I predict that it'll become a benchmark for future games looking for realistic combat. And it's why I would like to nominate this game for the first Steam Award in the category of "I Thought This Game Was Cool Before It Won An Award." Without a doubt, this is a game with unrivalled potential and it deserves much more recognition from the gaming community.

Have you ever felt that you had too much control over your character?

Have you ever wanted to cheer wildly when your mostly naked avatar drunkenly throws fists at a dude wearing plate and wielding a halberd but lacking a helmet knocks Mr. High-and-Mighty on his♥♥♥♥♥
Then Exanima is the game for you!
Despite the many difficulties presented by the unique control scheme, they become natural after some practice, and deeply satisfying when mastered. Exanima is a rogue-like isometric dungeon crawler, with brutal difficulty, neat graphics, and my favorite thing of all: loot that matters. This game is heavily skill based and has been described by other reviewers as Demon Souls from a different perspective. That's probably about right.

Unforgiving and satisfying combat. There's quite a bit of learning to do with the combat and combining it with your movement, using your mouse to gain more momentum and force to your weapon, also the how you move during attacks plays a great role.
Lots of different armor pieces that can be layered quite well, they also have weight and different types of protection (slash dmg etc). Weapons also have weight that affects your damage and weapon speed. Should you be using a long polehammer or short dagger, both have equal chances to win if you know how.

I could wait more years until Sui Generis is released.

Anachronox is an enjoyable game where the main positives are that the characters and story are well written. Developed by Iron Storm and underperforming on the market, this game is a hidden gem of the past. It takes the inspirations from JRPGs such as Final Fantasy and gives it witty story telling with some hilarious references and mockery.
Negatives:
1. Poor level design - Levels are designed in a very long linear fashion and often you are required to backtrack several times to complete objectives.
2. Animations are SO slow, especially during combat as it is turn based. Just having the 3 of your party do their attacks can take over 30 seconds.
3.  Unskippable cutscenes
4. The game does a terrible job at describing Mystech effects, skills and several important items such as the Elementor (Main damage dealer requiring specific combinations to deal different types of effects/damage).
*1-3 can be semi-remedied by pressing (\) to fast forward animations.
All in all the game was enjoyable to a degree. It has that old-school feel of classic story telling of likeable characters and a well written plot. I would not replay this game at all due to the problems above though, as it made the game feel like a chore in a majority of playtime. It's great for a single playthrough if you're looking to kill time.

"Hello Forgeborn,
There are only 12 Hours left to get your free 1500 gold! This is something we've never done before and we don't plan to do again. There are no tricks, catches, or caveats. We are literally giving away thousands of dollars in currency just for logging in and playing. Have you gotten yours?"
So I'm like, "why not, I enjoyed the game. I'll login, get a bunch of free money and try it out again, see if I like it." (1500 is a pretty good amount of gold from what I recall)

Tried playing other matches, nothing.
Sent an email to the dev team and got this response three days later, two and a half days after the gold offer expired:
"Hi,
The gold was in the store for purchase at the cost of one silver."
Would have been nice if that was actually explained in the email that prompted me to play the game again. Pretty sure after reading the rest of reviews that this experience can sum up the games changes over the past year and the general feeling that the player base has towards the devs and the changes implemented in the game itself. I played this the day it came out on Xbox 360 however many years ago and finished it up the same day. Never once touched it afterwards, I don't think. I loved it then and it's still a really ♥♥♥♥in good game. Probably one of the best Metroidvanias I've ever played, but I have a lot of mixed feelings about the genre.
And I think it comes back to that common complaint I have about imitation of a winning formula. Most Metroid style games can imitate the basic structure of the game - get some stuff, fight some bosses, wander around a map, find more stuff, go back to places you couldn't go before maybe - but they're missing something. A lot of it is fluid level design. Super Metroid (by far one of the greatest games ever made (and no it's not just nostalgia...that♥♥♥♥♥♥is about as close to a perfect video game as they come)) is beautiful in this regard.
Everything makes sense, your progress is absolutely clear, and if you get stuck, you simply have to fiddle around with all the toys they give you to figure out new ways to move around in the world. (I remember taking for ♥♥♥♥ing ever to make any progress as a kid just because it was so new and so different from anything else I'd ever played up to that point, but I never once got tired of it). Shadow Complex also understands this, and although I think it may hold your hand just a little bit too much, it does a great job at first showing you the entirety of the world, and then letting you run around it collecting♥♥♥♥♥♥that you had to leave behind earlier.
But I think the most important thing is that when you first land on Zebes in Smetroid, you are weak as♥♥♥♥♥♥and you are very aware of that. Every powerup you find is like a weight off your shoulders until eventually you are death personified, literally flying around the planet and laying waste to virtually everything you come across with absolutely no effort. That♥♥♥♥♥♥feels ♥♥♥♥ing awesome, and Shadow Complex nailed that feeling, imo. You start out as a dude with a backpack, but a few hours later, you can punch dudes so hard they fly across the room and literally vaporize them by running past them. It's good and I like this game a lot, but I guess if I had to poke holes in it, I'd say that it's a little bit too easy on the default difficulty

As for the game itself, it's a classic metroidvania with gorgeous graphics, tons of secrets, a well designed world, a surprising amount of plot, and this growing progression from a hiker to what is essentially "hyperspeed robocop" by the end of the game. During the endgame when you're trying to hit 100% completion, it can be a bit tedious trying to get through the lower right side of the map - particularly in some elevator shaft areas - but otherwise it's a fun romp and I highly recommend it.

Got this and it's sequel in a bundle a long time ago, figured it was time to check them out now that #3 has dropped and looks fun.
Observations - not going pro/con as in this case I feel that's a bit subjective:
- Game shows it's age (2006) by not supporting bigger resolutions.
- Map is surprisingly HUGE and not in a good way really. It takes forever to get places, even with a chopper or really fast boat
- Half the time I feel like Superman, the other I'm getting run over and killed by my supporting AI
- Audio is annoying, music from certain areas sometimes sticks with you as you move about
- Random NPC phrases get extremely repetative and annoying in areas of population
- Unlimited pistol ammo, but very limited assult/SMG/etc ammo
- Unlike the Far Cry series which I can in some ways compare this to, the green forrest aren't at all worth visiting are are very boring with zero variety
- Not a lot is explained, each mission will have details but you have to open the menu, then open mission info to learn details
- Voice acting from the very dated CGI cuts scenes is poor, but not terrible for the period
- Buggy with lots of pop-in/drop-out artifacts, mainly cars and enemies. I called in a truck, drove it 200 feet and it died, won't move. Figured ok, got another ride, quit the game later, saving, played again after a while, called in truck, it's still dead, really?
- Map is SO big and it takes you SO long to traverse it on foot that you need vehicles or use the fast travel/agency pick-up system, otherwise it gets BORING wandering around pretty quick.
- Side missions include checkpoint races, fetch quests and kill quests. They never end, so you can do them over and over and that's annoying for completionists like myself. Worse you won't know which you've already done and it's hard to see the benefits until you visit a safehouse.
- Driving physics/controls are comically poor, if you get a flat rear tire on a rear drive vehicle enjoy unbarable oversteer, overall every land/sea vehicle has felt very floaty, getting airborn often gives a lame slow-mo shot, crashing off a cliff and getting the car to roll leads to funny physics.
- The chopper controls are decent, but if you jump out and depoly your parachute it's really hard to gauge how high up your are, so don't let go until you land.
I can see the roots of some cool gameplay elements and features that I suspect have helped define this franchise. However if you make this your first game in the series be preparred to have frustrations. So far for me the frustrations haven't led to rage quits or anything and the difficulty so far has been reasonable - EDIT: essentially rage quit the last time, frustrating difficulty, uninstalling game, updating this review, moving on.
Recommend?
EDIT: I had to change this review. Simply can't recommend this game, it's ENTIRELY TOO HUGE, it takes forever to traverse even with a chopper, forget a car as you almost 100% have to stay on the roads, and F walking, it takes FOREVER - I ended up setting something on my E key to keep moving forward when boringly trying to get somewhere.
Bugs - pull a guy out of a ride and watch his door go flying, get into a APV, get bumped and watch your several ton armored vehicle roll, even fly around, don't walk near a road or get insta-killed by being run over, revive at a safe house only to land inside the structure, stuck.
Difficulty ramped up a TON after I gained control of approximately 50% of the map. When it takes you 5 mins to get from a spawn point/safe house via chopper to your takeover area only to have your mission ramp to level 5 (top threat level) within 30 seconds and have rockets fired at you from God only knows where and die. Then take another 5 mins to get back there to get closer but still die - it's no longer fun and therefore not worth the time, I have way too many other games that I know are better waiting, including hopefully a greatly improved Just Cause 2.
My progress:
My first review was after 7.4 hours in, this update is after over 20 hours. I think I made it around 40-45% through the story missions and I collected around 85% of the pickups while liberating right around 50+% of the map, done several side quests too getting my militia and gang supports up pretty high. I struggled to put aside my completionish mentality and focus on the story, but avoided extra side missons, instead just aiming to liberate all of the locations. After having the difficulty ramp up so much in the last few missions/liberation attempts I just can't see wasting anymore time trying to do really anything else. I tried, but the game defeated me...

From Earth was really surprising, I haven't gotten that far story wise yet, but it seems really well made. There are some rough patches, some areas with terrible FPS, and some crashes. The game is in "beta" though so I am counting on these not being permanent.
In From Earth you crash land on an alien world and are tasked with collecting items you need, completing objectives, communicating and fighting with aliens and all around just surviving. Compared to many, many source mods I feel like From Earth manages to feel like its "own thing", you can still tell its Source engine from the visuals, but style wise I feel like From earth manages to stand out somehow.
What matters most I think is that I am enjoying the game as it is now, and I recommend anyone who might be interested in a game where you dont just have to fight the aliens to progress would like this. There is some thought involved in some encounters and even a few puzzles so if that sounds fun give From Earth a try.
My biggest negatives as of writing this review are as follows.
- Very low FPS when looking at certain glass objects (including the window panes in the opening area)
- Freezes and crashes when interacting with certain objects (like the power cell type item used for the first alien door)
- Glitchy fight training sequence. It took nearly 30 minutes just to complete the part where I have to block blows from my sparring partner, as I was repeatedly sucked inside his model and clipped together with him.
I am assuming these will be fixed at some point in the near future. Otherwise good luck and have fun.

I was looking forward to playing this.  It looked beautiful, and supposedly had a compelling story, complete with mystery and a sci-fi sort of feel to it.
What I got was 8 hours of walking through deserts, and a few notes about how the humans destroyed this planet almost as soon as they arrived.
Gameplay: Walk, run, and occasionally die at the same platform leap every time.  About 5 (very easy) puzzles in the whole game, I don't think I spent even 15 minutes total on puzzles.  Platforming, a few very very VERY tricky jumps but mostly a clear line where there's only one possible path to take, high above everything else so it stands out.  Walk, follow the green track (or footprints), avoid traps that are off to the sides of the footprints.  Walk across dunes. Walk across rocks. Walk up hills.  Walk alongside a canyon.  Walk up to a building. Find a note outside. All the doors are boarded up, so continue walking.
Story: *SPOILERS* (well as much as there is anything to spoil anyway)
I'm on this planet. My crew is missing. Oh there's an abandoned soviet town. Oh my crew is dead.  Oh the soviets are dead. Oh the planet is dead.  The notes say the Soviets killed everything on the planet because they used the sole energy source for power.  Humans kill everything.  Wait, there's one woman! Follow her.  Walk.
Super game breakers:
I might have still enjoyed the game except for the jarring limits placed on me.  Oxygen ALWAYS runs out when there's a refill exactly far enough away that I almost pass out right when I reach it.  Oxygen refills last 8 (in game) hours, or overnight and half of the next day.  Jetpack ALWAYS gets a booster right before I have to make a series of long jumps.  The booster will last until I make the last jump in the set, and run out immediately afterward.  The boosted jetpack was lots of fun, two levels made great use of it's superior platforming abilities.
The world looks HUGE until you realize that there's invisible walls preventing you from getting too far off track.  (With the exception of the forest level where I wandered around in mist for a full hour until I rage quit, looked up a walkthrough, STILL couldn't find the way out, and finally found the answer on a forum here on Steam).  Most of the game felt like the creators were pushing me into one path and saying "Go THAT way! And get there on THIS path! Don't look for shortcuts, we're taking your climbing ability."
The "Save and Quit" function is broken. The only way to quit was ALT/F4 or Task Manager -> End Task.  The save might put you back a level when you restart the game.
In-Game options don't work.
Overall:
Graphics - 9
Platforming - 5 (some levels 0, some levels 8)
Story - 3
Puzzles - 2
Submersion - Nonexistent
Gameplay - 4 (A few good sections boosted it)

MoO2 is known as the king of space 4X. And after 20 years, I still find myself coming back to this game. I have tried other space 4x’s, but they always end up being disappointing.
The interface in MoO2 is bright, colorful, easy to understand and navigate. The game feels like a game, with little bogging it down. You won’t find anything resembling an Excel spread sheet, with confusing icons, and a ugly interface.
MoO2 is turn based, but don’t let that put you off. The strategic elements are very deep. It has very unique racial traits and technologies that aren’t found in other games, that make MoO2 fun and exciting. And best of all, it’s very balanced. At first, certain traits and technologies won’t seem very balanced. But as you become more experienced, you’ll figure out new combos and strategies that are very powerful. And the traits and technologies you once thought were weak, you’ll learn they counter the strategy you just figured out. In multi player games, I had other players laugh at me for the picks I would take. Around turn 100, they weren’t laughing anymore. This is why I keep coming back to MoO2. There is always something new to discover and figure out. Employing a new strategy that no one else has ever seen, and to see it work, is a great feeling!
One of the best parts of MoO2, is ship design and ship combat. This is where turn base outshines real time. You get to decide what technologies, systems, and weapons go into the ship. Then during combat, you decide what each individual technology does, and what each individual weapon targets. For example, a single ship can fire heavy guns at one ship, fire point defense guns at a group of fighters, fire missiles at another ship, then lock tractor beams onto another and engage in ship boarding combat to capture it.
There are three ways to win a game of MoO2. First is to eliminate all other races. Second is to get elected leader of the galaxy. And the final way is to assemble a powerful fleet to defeat an end boss fleet and home world.

A novel take on the tower defense genre.
The campaign is kinda short, but there are TONS of levels beyond those.  Some are user-created, some procedurally made, and a lot of extras from the devs.
Be warned that some of the levels are literally impossible to beat, but most can be done. (All story levels are beatable)

Bringing something new to the tower defense genre, Creeper World is ultimately about logistics. the key to every level involves establishing and expanding a production base of energy and ore, building and defending a transportation network to bring those materiasl to where they are needed, and deploying a variety of defensive systems to repulse a predictable but overwhelmingly endless flow of purple goo.
Graphics are simple yet functional, soundtrack is good but repetitious and the game lacks any voiceovers. In a stricly technical sense, this game belongs in the 90s. However, the excellent design and level of refinement more than make up for the lack of luster and polish.
All in all, it would be a decent buy at the price asked ($15) as of this review, but it's currently (Summer 2016 Sale) $3, which should make this a no brainer for any tower defense fan,

- long game length (300 years) with your heroes being born, raised, send to fight (or some other work) and then dieing from old age (unless they die in fight),

- all enemies (at least those encountered by me so far) have some kind of a twist - seeds suck your life, lapses attacks make heroes lose XP, bulwarks are ranged enemy that will shield itself for one turn after getting hit etc.
- you either build or research stuff,
- you have to permently send some of your heroes to different kind of duty (like research or training others, having children. and stats and level matters, so you can't send anyone).
I liked some of this concepts and decided to give this game a try despite not-so-good reviews.
.
In theory your heroes have everything to make them really interesting: they have traits, that they can pass on to their children, personality that makes them bit unique (both traits and personality give bonus/penalties to stats or some other effects). Their looks and age related status effect changes as years pass. They look different from each other. There are 3 base classes but you can mix partners from different classes so they will train heroes with new classes. There is a simple skill tree with choices to make and skills to choose every few levels. Some of traits even require you to remember them (like trait Optimistic that changes displayed hit chances).
It seems it should be pretty easy to like them, to have your favorite champion, to remember them.
In practice they often take part only in 2-3 battles. You have to sacrafice the best and send them to have children or something. After 5 hours of playing I still had no different loudout to give them.  And they die way too fast. I found it hard to care about them.
Enemies permanently damaging your heroes are also not nice. (if you care about your heroes)
I really liked having my favorite soldiers in Enemy Unknow (with was IMHO inspiration for few things in this game). Getting them slowly maxed out, giving them medals, changing looks. Here your 'heroes' are just cannon fodder - if you start liking one, he will probably die of old age before next battle. Perhaps concept is bad or perhaps this could be done with different time scaling (so you lead your heroes in 7-10 battles instead of 2-3) and with better recognition of their accomplishments (hall of fame or sth).
Battles are turn based. They start with your squad at one point and enemies spread out on map. Map is flat (AFAIK), but contains destructible elements that can be used against your enemy or against you (for example giant berries exploding with aoe after getting hit). Your only goal is to kill all enemies (at least in 5 hours I didn't have any mission with different goal or some kind of a twist).
There are 3 base classes. Hunters with crossbow, alchemists with melee attacks and limited number of thrown aoe grenade like flasks and caberjacks using big logs as melee weapons. In 5 hours of gameplay I haven't seen new kind of weapon or mixed class that would make big difference.
Battles weren't very exciting. Enemies don't seem to look for you and have pretty predictible AI. It's nice though that there is some form of stealth that you can use. Perhaps on higher levels, with heroes having more than 2-3 skills, it gets more interesting and deeper. I don't know and in fact I no longer care - 5 hours of gameplay is more than enough for a game to start being interesting.
Oh, and your heroes have stats that tutorial didn't care to explain. Mouse over didn't help me too. For example I actually don't know if low-dexterity alchemist will have problems with aiming flasks or not (perhaps intelligence is required for this class or perhaps not). It's really stupid, because this game doesn't havy any complex mechanics that would be hard to explain, so it means that devs were... lazy? not aware that their game ideas are not obvious to everyone?
Here you research stuff (including building... since building is part of research in this game). You assign heroes to buildings (regent and his/her partner to a keep - they will have children and train them, sagewriters to their guilds - they speed up research and Standards to crubicle - they will speed up trainging globally). You can also start timeskip that will stop on important events (death of hero assigned to a building or enemy attack).
During first 100 years all attacks looked the same. 2 regions are attacked. You can see what kind of enemies you will face and what reward you will get for victory. You can react only in one region. All regions have corruption meter, if it fills completly, you lose the region (successful defence lowers corruption, successful attack of enemy increases corruption).
There are some interesting choices to make. Should I make my highest level hero a regent so he can train his children to higher level (before they will leave to serve the country)? Should I 'retire' my old hero as a sagewriter or as a standard? What traits I should look for to create interesting bloodline?
Those decision seem somehow less important though when you don't care about losing your heroes and when you are not sure what different stats mean.

I followed this game pretty closely in its early development, then let it go its merry way before finally coming back to it this summer sale. Sadly, it hasnt gone far from where I left it.

The gameplay consists of competent turn based tactical combat and some hero-breeding on the side, with the goal being to keep the monsters out for 300 years while your super weapon charges.
After less than an hour of play and a quick glance at the wiki, I can confidently say that there is nothing more to the game, despire what its name would suggest; the game is small, and basic. It fulfils the original goals of the design document and nothing more,and ultimatly feels more like the product of an indie game jam than a kickstarter project.
Given that turn-based games like this are simpler to make than real time games, the real test of quality is in the execution of unique concepts that go beyond what somebody simply copying XCOM or Tactics Ogre could have produced. This game has no such features to speak of, other than a fairly basic hero-breeding backdrop, and a quirky aesthetic.
Sadly, this game falls behind even things like Banner Saga, which even with its shortcomings is a must play at $10 or less. There is no reason to play Massive Chalice, as once you've read this review you've pretty much played through the entire game. Tell your friends, they'll be so proud!

Anachronox is a cool console-style RPG, made with Quake 2 engine. Borrows heavily from classic JRPGs, such as Chrono Trigger, Final Fantasy 6 and 7, etc. It is very good, but hard to recommend. Here's why:
Pros:
Great story, lots of awesome cutscenes, weird, but loveable characters, decent voice acting, good writing and sense of humor.
Cons:
BUGS! I don't believe you could even finish it after the initial release. Even after several patches, official and fan-made, it is still riddled with bugs. When playing for the first time I got permanently stuck in scenery soon after watching intro animation. Had to restart and watch it again (it is unskippable).
Hyperactive, nauseating camera can be very annoying.
Battles are nearly broken - very awkward interface, long repetitive animations, camera so busy flying around, you can't see what you are going to do. Only hardest skill level is somewhat challenging.
Lots of backtracking. Just to switch characters in your party you have to literally leave the planet, by running through empty locations, going through several elevator animations, many loading screens, and then go back.
The game was obviously rushed, some locations still have crude, unfinished look, some animations don't work. The graphics did not age really well and frequently looks dated even for 2001.
Music is average. Moody, atmosheric synth stuff. Some tunes are good, most are bland and repetitive.
My advice for those who still plan to play:
Launch the game through "Anachronox GCT setup" app(already present in installation folder), DO NOT launch through Steam, otherwise most animations will be broken. Basically, the game will be unplayable.
Use fast-forward button, it is '\' by default, I think. Or you'll go mad. Rebind to more accessible key.
Enable "save anywhere" option and use it. It is not game-breaking and can potentially save you some more time.
Make notes. The game is not able to track side-quests, only the main ones. Remembering side quests, hints and secret locations is up to you.

Yes, it's old. And yes, it's totally worth it. Anachronox was intended as the first chapter of a trilogy (the game has a proper ending, but it's a "chapter" ending, not a "series" ending) and is affected by mild glitches, like falling out of the bounds of the map in some particular places, but nothing game-breaking. Also, you may have problems running it with the more recent systems.
BUT, if you can overlook these minor faults, all that is left is a really good game. It plays like a third-person adventure game with   RPG elements and turn-based combat, with skill-related (like lockpicking) and story-related (and skippable, if it's a hassle for you) minigames. The combat is pretty much the less interesting part of this game, but the story, oh, the story.
Story, setting, writing, character development, dialogues and voiceovers, they're excellent. Lots of humorous moments, the game delivers without being too cheesy. The background music makes a bit of atmosphere, but that's it, nothing really outstanding.
The difficulty levels just define how spongy the enemies are, you can make it through the entire game without grinding levels, controls are ok, plenty of secret bits. You can watch again every cutscene from the main menu, very low replay value. Be sure to install the widescreen fix.
It's also pretty cheap, even cheaper during sales. Definitively recommended.

This game has way more credit than it deserves. At first I was also gonna recommend it, but the longer I played, the more frustrating it became. The last straw was my character instantly dying during the last boss fight because I tried to explore the map and went too far, I guess (and there was no warning like "go back or you'll die").
So, in short, why I don't recommend the game:
- Conrols feel sluggish which is super bad for a platformer.
- The game is in 2.5D, which makes certain passages nearly unnoticeable. Also, it's pretty frustrating to shoot at enemies who are on different planes. There's no way to manually switch between the planes and often the hero shoots not at the right plane.
- The camera is horrible. More often than not I didn't even see where the character was running. And frequently the camera pans so close, you can't see more than 3-4 meters away. Ofc, there's no way to move the camera manually.
- The characters are forgettable, the story is super cheesy and boring.
- Every boss is either a helicopter or a giant robot. However, the story is cheesy, so that's ok. But boss fight are also boring and unimaginative: you simply shoot at the enemy and dodge theire missiles.
- Metroidania aspects of the game are really weak. In total you gain only a few gadgets that make you to get into the previously unaccessible areas.
- The enemies respawn when you go back to the locations you already cleared. Not only that, but the items you destroyed and grates you smashed are back there! That's one magic base that keeps repairing itself in the blink of an eye!
- Despite it being a port of a rather old Xbox 360 game, there're several fps drops on i5@4.3GHz, 8GB RAM, Intel 128 GB SSD and GTX 760. While not a top tier gaming PC, its power should be more than enough for a game like this one.
Overall, while not a bad game, Shadow Complex has a lot of frustrating moments.

Greetings Again!  After beating the original OMD I decided to move immediately to the sequel which is what we have here.  In my opinion this game improves on the original in every way; no we don’t see a graphics update but primarily an update to the mechanics and design.
Even more Orcs:  Not only do we have more types of orcs but also other types of enemies; some of which fundamentally change the way you have to play.  Of course the trap types have improved and you are given a much more in depth advancement system in the ways of spending skulls to improve traps in 3 to 4 ways.  Generally, the first option is just making it more effective but some of the secondary options change the way the traps can be used (such as putting them on ceilings or adding poison).
Crazy Lady Playtime:    In addition to all the improvements the game includes one that I felt was sorely needed; namely co-op.  This also comes with a new character; the sorceress from the first game who actually has some traps and equipment that is unique to her.  Both characters are playable but mechanically I prefer the war mage over the sorceress.  Other than that you get all of the typical things such as leader boards but the main bonus here is co-op.
I’m the Greatest:  The game is great; no doubt about that and definitely an improvement but I try to always level a few areas that I think can be improved upon.  In my time replaying the game I had several crashes; usually at the end of the level (making it even more frustrating); the game usually recorded the win but I ended up having to replay the level in case there was some story I missed.  This happened on the final mission as well which was kind of annoying.  Another improvement is that I’d like some kind of checkpoint or saving option.  Maybe this isn’t needed if I didn’t have to worry about crashing.  I also would have liked some more dynamic levels; especially those that required co-op or those that focused around a specific technique; maybe levels that prevented the use of certain items.
Overall, I still love the game and definitely worth every penny sale or not.  There is some DLC and it is worth a buy but overall I felt a bit meh about it.  I’m a sucker for more storyline (which there is none) and more content but didn’t really grab me like the original game.  Regardless; I’d still recommend the DLC as well.  Enjoy!

(Full disclosure: I rushed through this game's story while doing barely any sidequests or collectible missions, just so I could write this review before I finished Just Cause 3 and wrote its review. Don't worry, I'm going to come back and do some more optional stuff at some point.)
It's interesting to see the progression of the Just Cause series, to watch it come ever closer to what I call the "Just Cause Idea". The Just Cause Idea, for the record, is as follows: In a massive, beautiful, island nation (around 1000 square kilometers) run by a cartoonishly evil dictator, Rico Rodriguez, the world's most physics-defying Hispanic man, must use his huge amounts of mobility and destruction potential to bring down the dictator's rule by breaking everything the dictator owns. And it only gets more fun the more you play it.
The original Just Cause is a fairly generic game, obviously heavily inspired by old-school shooters as well as Grand Theft Autos 3, Vice City, and San Andreas. You run around shooting and driving cars and breaking things and holding an anomalous amount of guns, constantly maintaining a baseline level of fun; enough to keep you occupied but not exactly enthrall you.
However, the first stirrings of the Just Cause Idea are also apparent. You have infinite parachutes; a primitive, vehicles-only version of the later games' hookshot; no regard for civilian lives; a massive island nation run by a cartoonishly evil dictator; and more time spent in freefall than a professional skydiver. And, of course, you're (young) Rico Rodriguez.
In Just Cause 2, the Just Cause Idea is advanced even further, and the game is far better for it. Your grappling hook is no longer a weapon but a permanant staple that changes the game forever, Rico's defiance of physics gets f*cking insane, the shooting becomes merely a placeholder to simply add challenge to all the movement and destruction, the world becomes more diverse, the graphics get prettier (to the point that the atmospheric effects will probably never be outdone), there's more and cooler stuff to destroy in cooler ways, the villain gets even more cartoonish, and the game is overall more engaging, fun, and just...wonderful. The Just Cause Idea proves its worth in this game.
Just Cause 3 is probably the most perfect and complete realization of an idea ever, but I'm saving that for the review.
If I were to use a metaphor to describe the series' progression, it'd probably go as thus: Just Cause 1 is a flower starting to bud, the colorful petals just beginning to show from in between the sepals; Just Cause 2 is that flower in full bloom, its colors open for all to see; and Just Cause 3 is the flower if it were to detach entirely from the plant it budded from, becoming a spherical mass of petals and floating off to live in its own little world of explosions and madness.
Anyway, Just Cause is still a fine game in its own right. Great? Not quite; it's the weakest of the series in my opinion, with its technological limitations and conventionality preventing it from reaching the same dizzying heights as its successors. But it's pretty good, and I guess it's worth buying, especially if you're as invested in the series as I am or if it's on sale.

It's finally time to redo this review. After over three years of having this game positively reviewed, I just can't justify it anymore.
You know those girls that are with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ guys that cheat on them all the time and don't have a job and are basically just terrible people, but the girl talks about how she loves him and she can change him and all her friends tell her she can do better but she just won't listen to them? You know what I'm talking about? Well, I've been in a three year relationship with SolForge and it's been terrible. I kept hoping it would get better. They kept telling me they were going to be better and they were going to fix everything wrong with our relationship. Even now, I'm going back through Kickstarter updates. "Animated Card Preview!" dated February 17th, 2013. "Next Game button!" dated October 1st, 2013. "The future of SolForge including full release this fall" dated May 2015. So many promises, so many hopes. I just kept waiting for it to get better. I wanted to see the light at the end of the tunnel. The pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. And I waited... and I waited.
Well, it came. A few weeks ago, we made it to the end of the rainbow. The new client which was supposed to be developed in a few months and ended up taking over a year dropped. But it wasn't a pot of gold. It was a steaming pot full of festering crap. So poor was the new client release that they basically had to do an "Oops, can't put the rabbit back in the hat, so this week just won't count while we work out our server issues that we 'couldn't have anticipated.'" Turned out to be a couple weeks, but they worked out their server issues and the game is now actually playable.
So what did we get with the new client? Well, I mean I guess it works. A lot of functionality that was in the old client is now gone, such as the next game button, deck sorting when deck building or drafting, the game log now clears if you exit to menu and come back, you can't click on Solbind cards in the card text to see what he solbound card actually does... I mean, I guess the menus look pretty. But the rest is terrible. Like... really terrible. We got a new client that is slightly prettier, but is worse in basically every other way to the old client. Nice.
But let's say that's all fine. Annoying, but fine. What is the actual gameplay like? Well, it too has gotten worse. Much worse. Now, to be perfectly honest, I've had a problem with certain RNG aspects of this game since the very beginning. I mean, it's a CCG so obviously RNG is going to factor into every game, but my problem is that this game frequently hands the game to one player or the other based completely on RNG. Again, I understand that happens sometimes in CCGs, but it seems far too frequent when I look back at a game and realize that there is absolutely nothing I could have done to pull out a win because my opponent drew all his leveled cards and I drew none of mine. Now I said things have gotten worse and everything I've just talked about have been a part of the game since day 1, so what exactly has gotten worse about RNG? Well... it's how many cards are "I win" or "I lose" based purely on RNG. In alpha, there was Everflame Phoenix. It was a very polarizing card due to the pure RNG aspect of it but even then, it wasn't a straight out "I win." Now, there is Othra which features the exact same infuriating mechanic and really, the exact same card design (huge level 1, useless level 2 that can flip on 2.4 into a game-winning level 3) which is like Everflame Phoenix only significantly more powerful. It's the power-creep version of the same card.
The thing is, they keep making more and more cards that are incredibly good based on RNG. In the newest set, Indomitable Fiend is an amazing RNG card. The whole concept of the card is that you can't really direct what lane it ends up in, but it's so powerful you don't really care. In fact, I'm playing an Indomitable Fiend deck right now because it's so powerful, but the thing is I don't really have to play it. The deck plays itself. If I draw Indomitable Fiend into multiple Immortal Echoes, I win. Otherwise, I lose. The actual decision making in the deck is barely a decision most of the time. And the reason I'm playing this braindead deck is that it's actually one of the most powerful decks playable, which I think really gets to the underlying problem with this whole game. For several iterations and several expansions, SolForge is slowly stepping away from decision making and interactivity and more toward purely RNG based games from start to finish. Players have talked about this and written articles about it for a long time, but it doesn't seem like it's by mistake at this point.
And finally there's the power creep. Now you could argue that cards are constantly being rebalanced, new cards are being tuned down and old cards are being tuned up, but the thing is... every new expansion has at least one or two cards that are clearly overpowered. Every time. Sure, after a month or two they tune them down, but I don't think it's a mistake that they come out of the gate overpowered. It encourages players to spend money to buy cards in the new set if they want to be competitive until the obviously overpowered cards are finally tuned down. Coincidentally, it's usually shortly after their forging costs have been reduced.
So after my three year abusive relationship... SolForge... I'm breaking up with you. I'm tired. I'm tired of your crap. I'm tired of your broken promises, broken clients, and broken game. I'm tired of being frustrated about losing games that I never had any chance of winning. I'm tired of winning games that I never actually had to make a decision from start to finish. I'm tired of "alternate art" cards that are just recolored versions of the old cards. I'm tired of a mobile client that hasn't worked in over a year despite it working initially. I'm tired of seeing cards that are stupidly overpowered every single expansion when you can't not realize how overpowered those cards are. I'm over it. I trusted you, I backed you, and you failed me.
Muh.

I haven't finnished the game yet, so I can't speak to the resolve of the story as to whether or not the journey is worth it, but the game design is just poor.  The controls are a bit awkward, you can't strafe, but rather turn in a circle.  The levels are designed with extremely clear paths for you to take.  There are almost no puzzles in the game.  The only puzzles that really exist are jumping puzzles, and that's pretty much the only mechanic.  So if you like Parkour games in Minecraft, you'll love this game, but otherwise you'll find it extremely frustrating.  The terrain is also poorly designed.  There are many places where I just got stuck because the models were just a little too steep in an unsuspecting place.
Thigs in the game are either extremely easy or extremely frustrating.  I don't mind challenging or frustrating games, but when 90% of the game is as easy as following the path, when it finally tries to give you a challenge that is above average in it's level of difficulty, it's extremely frustrating.  Lastly, some things are just kinda broken.  Most recently, I went up an elevator, realized I had to go back down to find something.  On the elvator ride back down, I decided to jump off to save time.  However, when I jumped off the elevator it stopped where it was at!  There was no way for me to get back up.  I couldn't reach it.  And "intentionally" the call button is broken.  So i've had to quit the game.  I hope when I restart the problem fixes itself.
Frustration aside, the story is very intriguing.  I'm still very interested in seeing how this story resolves.  That said, the frequency of details begins to drop off dramatically the more you play the game.  It's nice to be left in the dark for awhile so you can try to piece things together yourself, but the developers have defnitely not mastered the art of witholding information.  If you withold too much your audience will be confused or bored.  If the gameplay was more creative and challenging (in a good, well thought out way) I would forgive the major pauses in story progression.  But it's not fun to put a story on hold simply because I have to follow a path for 10min.

: A game where the developers put in the bare minimum effort.
To start with, I want to say that I purchased this game when it was 80% off (I paid $4) and I feel what I got was worth the price I paid. However, had I paid full price, I'd have felt ripped off.
* There are hundreds, maybe thousands, of bloodlines. (Apparently it was a backer award.) They are all virtually interchangable. They each have a flag, a color scheme, a name and a motto. The first three only matter for identification in the menu, while the motto appears after a member of the bloodline gets a kill. I'm not saying they need a unique perk or anything, but for the sheer volume, they boiled down to class and menu color.
* With only 4 hair colors (including grayed), a handful of hair styles and one skin tone, heroes start to blend together very early. Even the armor colors stop distinguishing heroes once you get Cadence armor types. (And you'll want to use Veil Armor on every hunter.)
* There are 9 classes (3 base, 6 hybrids), but only around ten unique skills. Every hybrid shares the majority of its skills (and armor appearance) with its two base classes. So of the nine classes, there is very little difference in basic function. Heroes will spend the majority of the game being distinguished by which of the three weapon types they use.
* Seven enemy types. Seeds (basic mooks), Ruptures (explode), Lapses (drain exp) and Bulwarks (ranged attackers, take 1 damage from all attacks after the first hit each round) appear early on, joined by Wrinkles (age heroes), Cradles (spawn Seeds) and Twitches (swap positions with heroes) within the first 100 years (of 300). 'Advanced' versions show up around the 150 year mark, which just buffs HP, damage and exp. The only mechanical difference I noticed with any of them was that Advanced Lapses also slowed down cooldowns. Each enemy only has one attack.
* The Chalice duo will occasionally chime in after an enemy or ally is killed, at the end of a battle, or when a random event pops up. By the fourth battle, these lines were already repeating.
* Each zone has one map, with the only major variation each mission being your, and the Cadences', starting positions. Same goes for each structure, when they're directly attacked. (At least the final battle has a unique map, which added a sliver of variety after I had spent the last half of the game just going through the motions.)
* Hunters can stealth, which is essential for scouting. They can also attack at range, and get a double shot that can potentially one-round Bulwarks. They are awesome.
* Alchemists can throw a limited number of flasks (read: grenades) per map and can get an extra item slot. They're useful for dealing with seeds early on, and actually manage to get really powerful with time.
* Caberjacks are melee heroes meant to mitigate damage. The plethora of Ruptures and ranged attackers early on makes them sitting ducks, since they lack the HP or armor to soak any more damage than a hunter early on. In theory, they can knock back enemies to avoid rupture explosions, but their low damage on their first knockback skill means they can only kill a rupture if it's nearly dead, otherwise you need a hunter to off it anyway. Theoretically, they can stun enemies by knocking them into each other or against walls, but again, only if they can close the distance.
* Most hybrids are similar. Shadowjacks are just caberjacks that can scout with stealth. Blastcappers and Boomstrikers don't stand out from their base class much. Brewtalists has the sole distinction of getting a melee version of the hunter's double shot. Enforcers are just hunters that can knockback at range (which is an upgrade over cabers, at least) and are a bit more durable, but durability doesn't matter much when hunters can avoid getting hurt in the first place.
* Trickshots are notable for being an actual interesting hybrid. Their flask arrows sacrifice the ability to be thrown over obstacles and must be aimed at enemies instead of being able to target an empty square, but have longer range.
While the game is sparse on plot, that isn't my issue here. No, what bothers me is the forced and groan inducing 'twist' at the end.

There's a lot of things in the way of liking this game. The gameplay lacks a lot of depth in battle, and out of battle the progression is pretty linear. The enemy variety is nice, but early on it can be a slog. The randomness is also really annoying, especially in Ironman mode.
Still, the premise is great enough that I can get past that. A 300 year war where you have to manage your ruling houses in order to produce soldiers to replace the ones that die of old age is just a really unique concept. It's a stripped down XCOM:EU from a game play standpoint but taking the permadeath aspect of XCOM and twisting it around to be an inevitability that you have to prepare for is really interesting.
If you enjoy XCOM or the 'generations' ideas in games like Fire Emblem: Awakening this game is worth a try. Stings a little bit of wasted potential, but I'm definitely able to look past a lot of its flaws.

Omerta - City of Gansters is a strategy. Or management game. Or at least it combines real-time management, using turn-based combat to settle conflicts. And as you guessed it, it's about running small mafia business, made by Haemimont Games and Kalypso and released in 2013. It also was ported to Xbox 360.
Apparently, this game was release in quite swallow state at first. For examples, from what I know, you couldn't have use cars and there were no enemy gang in sandbox, which will explain to you why the game was recieved negatively. Or maybe there wasn't sandbox at all, I wasn't there. Thankfully, developers actually listened and actually improved the game. Though, I bet that it mostly came by back-porting new stuff introduced in Japanese Incetive expansion pack DLC into base game.
Technically, bugs occasionally pop up. Like, sometimes the game progress in combat will freeze after enemies used fire bomb, making the turn last forever. Or on strategy map my boss avatar on car decided that he can take his sweet time setting Speakeasy and then drove off the map and back. Twice. There were strange lag spikes in sandbox too.
Multiplayer community seems to be completely dead. Nobody in chat, no games to be found. Hm, maybe that's because I don't have Japanese Inciative DLC.
The plot of this game takes during Prohibition Era in USA, as your avatar fled there in a chase after a wild goose that is American Dream. Now your mission is to become a ganster and parasite on society, ruining otherwise good-spirited idea of prohibition. Buying out everything in each part of city and doing it again. And then win. And then prohibition era will end, your business will dissapear, you will end up in jail for tax evasion and you will get heart attack from shaaaame.
No, I didn't beat whole campaign. And obvious Mario references are obvious.
For single-player, here is campaign and sandbox modes. In campaign you have to complete separate levels, the only thing that carries over is your gang and half of Fear and Liked amount. In each mission you have to fulfill a certain objectives to win. And the first half of a game is real-time mangament. And you will see why people compare it to Facebook games - there are no rival gangs. No time speed function, you have to click on character portrait once his order is done, you spend time waiting for things to happen as nothing goes wrong, usually. Wouldn't say that this is Facebook gameplay though, you can still screw up a bit and it doesn't feel as pointless as F games.
You also still have to watch out for police. You will be getting attention if you order something criminal, like burgary, and you will get their attention slowly even if you do nothing. Albeit there are buldings that will reduce this effect. So while criminal things may give you a quick effect, you want to stay as legal as possible. The problem is that in campaign there are no rival gang or anything to pressure you, so sadly there is no real choice and no reason to go dirty.
You just set up even most basic production and then the question from "will I win?" goes to "how soon will I win?".
For handling conflicts, you got turn-based combat. Four of your guys against any number of baddies. It's probably good, there are a lot of good stuff implented. It shows only what your mobs can see. There are useful features like icon which shows who this characters sees. Game shows icon on path that you set which point at spots where enemies can fire at them. Cover system is also neat, but remember that runn out in the open is sometimes a better idea to overwhelm enemy. Or that every enemy has three abilities. Wasting one point for aiming. Melee characters keep movement points after action. Neat stuff, as said.
Though in the end, everybody will be bleeding.
Sadly, they also have very weak presentation here. Visuals and soundtrack here are weak and pretty much no special effects. It's like they don't want you to have a blast on purpose. I am not fanatic of old PC strategies like this to enjoy such approach. Oh, by the way, management side has nice music, I think it consist of licensed tracks.
Sandbox mode on other hand went extreme into another way. You now have a rival gang now and this AI is so agressive, you will keep being dominated. I heard that it was a very late addition in latest patch. I am not sure if AI cheats, but it's probably just way too good, especially when player can't slow down time in management half to issue orders. There is only way to victory - grab money and try to build Security Agency on Construction slots which will automatically generate gangs to defend your buildings, while you also should do "wetworks" missions for crime lord to level your chars and get money. And only after getting Security Agency you will be secured from losing the game and can slowly struggle to take over businesses that surround you from the hands of enemy gang. Until you finally get recources to take on his hideout and get some anti-climax poor fight and be a winner.
Sounds challenging, but having only one way to possibly win isn't too fun either.
As for multiplayer, it was only about turn-based combat. Either coop or versus. I didn't get to play a single match, sadly.
And I am not sure what to think of this game. It's not exactly awful and you can enjoy it slowly. But eh, nothing to excite me. Absolutely nothing. Then again, I am not fan of such genres or settings. Why did I get this game? Oh, right, Tropico 5 pre-order bonus.

I play games of this genre, this game is better than city builder games, which is that you don't need to waste 2 hours for ever 1 hour planning what you are going to build. You have 3 types of building groups joints, premises, and constructions. joints are cash making buildings, premises are production buildings, and constructions are expensive high tier buildings.
Combat is simple and straight forward, take turns, get into position, target, use abilities, and complete the objective. The base game lacks a variety of prison maps, but the Japanese Incentive DLC drastically improves the combat map varieties.
The stats of characters do not impact the performance of characters on the strategic map (moving around the map and building buildings), however character classes DO impact how well they execute their actions. Masterminds finish quests faster, Grifters +populace favor, enforcers +fear, hitmen prevent giving you attention for doing most criminal acts. There's a severe lack of variety in classes, Plenty of characters however.
This game's single player campaign is pretty fun, with a story that is filled with gangster drama, it took me 150 hours to complete all the missions +bonus dlc missions AND the expansion (still a bit heart broken).
Music is very nice, it gives that prohibition era vibe with blues and big bands. What would have made the game nicer is if choice was if the story wasn't linear, because the endings were severely underwhelming after what you accomplish.
The maps are small for a city builder game and this might sound as if it's a terrible idea for a city builder game, until you realize how god painful it is to move scroll from location to location or click on a mini map multiple times.
This game's strategic play will seem dull after you finish the base campaign, but the Japanese Incentive expansion makes it much more fun and intense, where you're up against an AI (playing the game on insane, the AI really knows how to knock you over). Outside the highest aggressiveness the AI will not seem very hard to beat if you're used to playing strategy games. In most scenarios turtling will make you win, but let's be honest that's almost all strategy games.
This game was worth buying at it's current price of this genre.
I don't know of any game that mixes REAL TIME strategic city building and light version of turn based combat seen in games such as Xcom.

Isometric dungeon crawler with an excellent atmosphere and a control scheme that rewards patient practice with exciting and satisfying fights, especially in "Arena" mode - which is essentially medieval European gladiator management.
Physics plays an important role in this game - the shape, size and weight of your character as well as your weapon is important in combat, as is applying proper footwork for balance and to really make a hit count. This WILL take time to learn; don't come into this expecting to lop off heads like a machine, because you'll feel little better than a chronically intoxicated village idiot. If you don't think you can/want to put in time to learn, and I mean really LEARN, how to play a game: please look elsewhere.
The dev team's work is slow but steady - it is safe to assume that you won't see updates for two or three months, but when you do, it's often content combined with behind-the-scenes upgrades to the engine that lays the foundation for more features down the line.

Dear Game Developers, making a metroidvania game shouldn't be an excuse to make a linear platform game where the player needs to traverse the same locations over and over to save on development costs.
This is getting very common, and I think there's a big misunderstanding on what this genre should be about. If you think it's about exploration, at least give us some interesting places to explore, not the same grey boring industrial areas over and over again. If it's about the journey, give us a story to care about. I don't think it's a good sign to start a game with someone yelling about "Saving the vice-president" or some other American cliché. If you think it's about the combat, at least give us interesting and multiple kinds of enemies.
This is pretty much a linear platformer, except it forces you to go through the same locations to give an illusion of an open-world. Other games did the same, like Strider and Guacamelee. But at least the later had awesome combat to make up for it. This one doesn't.

What once was a very impressive little title has now turned into one of the biggest franchises for Square Enix and a Cult Favorite among the fans, so let's see how it all began shall we ?
In Just Cause we play as Rico Rodriguez. He is an agent sent in to the island San Esperito. Our mission is to kill a dictator Mendoza and free the island from his reign.
Back when this game came out I found it quite impressive. The Island is massive, but it doesn't matter cause there is nothing to see there. All of it is just a big jungle which all of it looks the same. There are small villages which act as outposts and you can clear them out.  The city is uninspiring and there's nothing to do there.
The gameplay is by far the weakest third person shooter I have ever seen. The shooting feels clunky and sometimes my shots don't even connect with the enemies, not to mention most guns are weak as hell, and the better weapons have low ammo counts.
The graphics (apart from the CGI cut scenes) are still great. The lush island is awesome and getting a boat and going through the rivers is really fun, but as stated before there's nothing to see, but it's still fun.
The driving controls are some of the worst driving controls I have ever seen, they even top the driving controls in Watch Dogs. Since unlike in Just Cause 2 you can't travel with the grappling hook, so most of the time you will need to use vehicles.
The game also has side quests, but most of them are boring as hell and you can grind them since they never end. So if you want something more with the game after you're done you can do the mundane side quests.
The game took me 6 hours to finish, once the game is finished you can explore the island, but as stated before there's nothing to do there.
The game also has a major spike in difficulty in the final missions, so be prepared to be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off.
Overall even though the game didn't age well, it's still fun to play for a bit, but it's the weakest in the series. In the end I will give this a positive review, but I still suggest playing Just Cause 2 instead.
Final Rating:
6/10 - Okay
