Alright, honestly I'm tired of people giving the new client or the new reward system crap and saying you need hundreds of Legendaries to play the game.
For the New Client: Yes it has bugs, it's a brand new client and a complete overhaul of the GUI, OF COURSE IT HAS BUGS, and SBE is working on fixing them, however they can't do a bunch of small hotfixes because they're working on three platforms, one of which makes updates really difficult, so grouping a bunch of fixes is easier to do for the devs.
For the New Reward system, yes it makes you play against other players which can be a little daunting, but realistically even just getting the ticket for 3 games played is easy as pie and after a week or two of playing and getting cards through draft and what not even the 3 wins isn't that hard. The new reward system drastically increases the ability to get new cards by allowing players to draft every other day. I have played since alpha and can say with certainty that this reward system is sooooo much better than the old stuff.
For all the people who think you need a crapton of legendaries to play online: Having a deck that is one of the top teir meta decks is all well and good, but yes it is very hard to acquire in a FTP account, it isn't impossible however, AND more importantly you don't need a top teir deck to be able to play and get wins, hell you dont even necessarily need Legendaries beyond the great ones you can get through campaign,
I have a Spirit Wanderer deck, it runs 1 legendary: Varna (who you can get in campaign), and 4 heroics: 2 relentless wanderers and 2 rutheless wanderers, and that deck has yet to lose to MonoNekruim hate (A strong deck running a lot of legendaries), Nekruim-anything Fiend (Dont even get me started on this deck), and Stall/Level Chrogias/Iron Maiden (another one of those obnoxious decks that you see a lot of)
I have a Darkforged UT deck, that beats most other decks i've played it against, including a titanium 1 Ignir decklist. How many legendaries does that deck have? Oh... right, it doesn't, I built it for a nonlegendary tournament a couple of my friends where trying to do.
Anyways, sorry for the rant I'm just tired of people being super salty about not being able to build "top Tier" netdecks, and the client update.
TLDR: the game isn't bad, it's quite fun honestly, you don't need a ton of legendaries to make a good deck (you just need to really look at the cards and find synergy) and the new reward system is leagues better for new players than it was in the "good ol days" If nothing else give the game a shot, find a couple friends who are okay with building silly decks and troll around, you might find something that beats the meta ;) and you know what if you hate it go ahead and uninstall, that's fine too, but don't pass the game by just because a bunch of people are being salty.

The game mechanics are fun, the cards are interesting, and the art is very good looking.  I was going to spend some money on this game, and I wish I could recommend it.
Unfortunately, the only way to grow your collection, is to either:
A) Play against other players, 99% of which have hundreds of Legendary cards.
- This gives you a small amount of currency you will collect to have a small chance to get the cards you need.
B) Spend a huge amount of money hoping to get some of these Legendary cards.
- This gives you a variable amount of currency you will use to have a small chance to get the cards you need.
Which means that you are afforded the opportunity to learn how to play the game, and then presented with a wall of people who have either years worth of cards, or have spent $1000+ on being competitive.
After the initial tutorial, you have no way to progress without spending 4+ hours a day trying to collect lucky wins or that rare game where you are matched with someone at your own level.

20 years later this is still the game all other 4X space games try to measure up to (and fail most of the times).
If you like the genre you need to play this game.

Do you like fantasy games? Do you like turn based strategy? Do you enjoy tactical positioning? Are you a fan of leveling systems with customizable skills? Do you enjoy dealing with random chance? Would you like to breed a family of superheroes? Would it be entertaining if their bloodline developed heart disease or alcoholism because they are people too? Would you like to manage the development of a small kingdom that feels like a board game inserted into all of this? Then this game is for you, buy it. If you aren't convinced, wait for it to go on sale ($10 is a great deal for it).
A good friend of mine played this right up to the 300 year marker, but then lost because his heroic bloodlines went infertile around year 250. No one was left for the final confrontation. I got a kick out of that.

TLDR it looks nice, it plays fairly well, and it's unforgiving on the easiest level.  Think niche XCOM.
It's a good game but it is missing a few things that seem to me to be odd ... first off, there is no option for any of the characters to 'hold' their action until something comes into range / sight.  Either you attack it on your turn or you don't at all ... there's no 'overwatch'.  Further, it's not clear what the ranges of various non-melee weapons are, so it's hard to tell if, when you move to a location, whether or not you'll be able to hit something.  Finally, it keeps the camera at a 45 degree angle and rotates 90 degrees from there, but some actions, like Charge, can be performed on all 8 compass points, so it's hard to line things up.  Finally, even on Regular mode, the game is unforgiving and sometimes feels like the RNG gods just have it out for you.
I wish there was more of a choice as to which heroes were involved with which events, so you could send a promising young character out on a quest rather than it seemingly randomly picking a hero for you to use.
Graphically it has a beautiful style, both in combat and between combats, and it doesn't take too long to play through the full 300 year campaign.

This game is an excellent tactics RPG.
The complaint you'll likely see from many negative reviews is that you have to cycle through heroes too much, preventing you from getting attached and preventing meaningful progression. Those people obviously didn't understand the games central mechanic. The hero churn is one of the BEST things about the game. The major form of progression in the game is not individual heroes, but rather their bloodlines. I didn't get attached to any particular heroes, but I can sure tell you that House Thorne and their relic weapon, called Fear, won me many a battle. This game is full of interesting choices about how to best develop your bloodlines, and managing them is where the real meat of the strategy side of the game lies.
The tactics side of the game is fairly simple, but elegant and satisfying. There are three starting classes that mix through the miracle of childbirth to make up to 9 classes. The opposition consists of 7 different types of enemies, and advanced forms of those 7. Most of these enemies have unique gimmicks, some of them playing into the macro-strategy side of the game. Battles happen every 10-20 years, and they remained fun for me all the way through the game.
If there's any real problem with the game, its that it kind of feels repetitive, and it doesn't really build up to its ending. All 300 years feel mostly the same. I feel like the game really wants me to take what I've learned on my first playthrough and apply it to the harder difficulties, but a playthough takes too long for that to really feel reasonable. This game could have really benefitted from each playthrough being shorter, but really I think the game is worth playing anyway.

As I made my way through the 300 years it takes to charge the chalice, I was originally planning to write a cautious positive review. This game deserves some praise for the solid mechanics it demonstrates. They make the game fun, even through plodding self-insert writing, repetitive gameplay, and general lack of refinement in several aspects of the game. I'd planned to say that the game was good, and would have been great, if only polished more. Unfortunately, after finishing, I find myself unable to give this recommendation.
For context, everything in the game builds towards the charging of the chalice. You send crack teams of five controllable heros out to occasional battles, and decide the research, intercourse and economy of an upper class of those 'attuned to the chalice' in a nation beset by a sinister enemy, the Cadence. The rest of the time, you 'sleep'. The game builds the chalice as a mystical power, with dialogue-based time shenanigans and curative powers that spice up the 300 year wait.
These 3 choice dialogues were actually a very necessary respite for the tedium of waiting 300 years, going through battles that because of the mildly varied but still quite limited classes and locations soon became a bit repetitive.
So naturally, I expected something special for the final battle. Perhaps being able to use all of my heros in an epic final stand, or, going off the time shenanigans earlier, being able to choose my heros from all of those who'd passed away as well as those alive. So, I was somewhat disappointed that the selection was made normally. It turned out that there actually was something different about the final battle,
something that actually made it easier. Oh well, I'd been playing on normal, so perhaps it would have been more epic on greater difficulty. Dispatch the last of the enemies and... done!
Only, the ending was a disappointment. A flop on the visual, emotional, and writing level. Not much worse than the starting cutscene, but after 300 years... you expect something a bit more. Drama, a last look at your kingdom, something. There *was* a grand reveal, but so hamhanded that it had very little impact, and didn't make the half-day that playing the game through takes worthwhile.
So I retried the game on brutal hardcore difficulty, though it's worth noting that I never restored from save on my first game. Long story short, my heart was no longer in it. The whole game builds toward the end, and since I now knew that was no great shakes, it was just a slog. I made it maybe 50 years before my alchemists blew up, and even though I very well might persist, I no longer felt it.
TL;DR Brilliant idea, but disappointing.

Double Fine's inventive take on turn-based strategy with rogulike elements is reminiscent of X-COM with a twist in the form of lineage. Players alternate between managing their empire on a broad scale and taking part in tactical battles against a horde of enemies known as the Cadence. Between these skirmishes, players assign researchers to develop new technologies and regents to manage outposts. These regents have families, and depending on the traits of the regent and their spouse, their offspring will exhibit shared traits.
Which is excellent in theory. Each regent will train their offspring in one of three different main classes: Blastcapper, Alchemist, and Hunter. The Blastcapper carries around a wildly practical battering ram, which to their credit can actually do some damage and is useful for breaching doors that don't exist anywhere in the game. Unfortunately, these heroes cease to be useful or practical heroes almost immediately.
In one of the first matches against our eternal foe, the game introduces a new enemy that will run up and gleefully explode next to any of your heroes. Not only that, it leaves behind a toxic residue that saps health and armor at the start of every turn. In every subsequent match except one, this enemy appeared. This wouldn't be a problem if all of my heroes weren't nearsighted inbreds that can barely function on the battlefield. More than half of the enemies I encountered were these blitzing bombers, so doing the sensical thing and trying to lead with the strong melee class was useless since they kept getting hit by explosives.
The second class, the suicide bomber, has an acceptable melee attack but their claim to fame are the explosive flasks they lob at the enemy. Yes, those 5 flasks your bold hero starts off with will serve them well on their journey: two flasks to roast their teammates, two to fling blindly off cliffs or so far away from the enemy as to be useless, and one to hit a single enemy yet fail to kill it. Even if the teamkilling allstar is sitting directly on top of the enemy, they may only have a 70% chance to hit, and chances are they'll just fail and do their lineage a service through self-immolation. Even if they could hit anything, their maximum range is atrocious and as mentioned before, the kingdom is inhabited by a very proud yet blind people so enemies will pop out of the mist and blindside you regularly.
Last but certainly not least, the Hunter. A ranged fighter equipped with a giant crossbow, the only useful class has unlimited ammunition, the largest range, and can use stealth to scout and reveal enemies before striking. The only downside to this class is that the tutorial doesn't expressly mention that once you assign a regent
The other classes appear to have interesting skills further down the line, but your heros are far too frail and inept when faced with the supercharged enemy roster. Aside from the basic enemy minion, each foe has far more unique skills to help them survive than your elite warriors. The first ranged enemy not only deals damage from long range but sucks experience points from your heroes. Those delightful exploding fiends deal heavy damage in an area, and if a hero happens to stand in the residual gunk they suffer huge penalties. There is also a ranged enemy with piercing attacks that can toughen their hide to drastically reduce damage. It feels as though all the really neat abilities are reserved for your enemies, and I couldn't help but start rooting for them after a few matches.
If the thought of watching generations of people grow and produce unique heroes is appealing, Massive Chalice will deliver. The tactical combat feels shallow and frustrating at times, though after slugging through several relentless bouts with inept heroes, who knows; one of them just might hit something.

This is the first game I’ve ever seen on Steam that I used to play a lot as a kid, and I loved it. I could never get past level five, though, because I was missing a key in either level four or five. Once I bought it here, I couldn't wait to dive into it, even though my experience was slightly different, because of the mouse and keyboard controls, and I didn't use cheat codes like I always used to.
So the main objective in this game is to find a bunch of keys to access the different levels in the hub world. There are eight levels altogether, and they all have the exact same mission: Find the keys and leave. The levels aren’t particularly interesting to talk about. You have a jungle, ancient city, ruins, and blah blah blah. The Treetop Village is where I had never gotten to before. You see more cliffs at the start of that level than trees.
Each track from the soundtrack fits perfectly with each level they are in. Some tracks are so upbeat, like in the Jungle level. It actually sounds like a jungle, especially with all the animal sounds. Others can sometimes be quieter, like in a cave. Even going underwater has its own track. 100 gold stars for this composer.
The way the camera moves when you start can be a little disorienting, but luckily, that can be turned off in the "Head Bobbing" options.
If you pick up enough triangles, which I like to call "Doritos", you gain an extra life. You also pick up chronoscepter pieces, weapons, backpacks to carry more ammo, and spiritual invincibility, which is quite useful, since it slows down enemies and makes you invulnerable to their attacks. There is one chronoscepter piece in each level. I won't say much about it, but I will say that if you can get the chronoscepter, good things will happen. I thought the infinity symbols were level 8 keys, but it turns out there aren’t even that many of those keys. Those symbols are actually the chronoscepter pieces. Well, that’s kinda misleading, isn’t it? What is a list of chronoscepter pieces doing in the “Keys” page?
You have a variety of weapons to choose from. You got your old fashioned weapons, like the knife and bow. You’ve also got your military weapons, like the pistol, shotguns, assault rifle, and so on. Some of these weapons become useless due to other weapons using the same ammo, like the pump action rifle, and the pistol. Just use the auto shotgun and assault rifle, they’re much more superior. But there are also plasma weapons. Such colors! Much power!
There are many different kinds of enemies in this game. You start off fighting just regular guys with guns, raptors, leaping lizards, and giant mutant gorillas. But the enemies get tougher in each level, the bosses being the hardest. The boss fights mostly consist of running backwards and just unloading everything you’ve got on them. You will have to do a lot of strafing to avoid being hit by their attacks. Some of the bosses have unavoidable attacks, because that’s totally fair. But oddly enough, those do the least amount of damage, as far as I’ve seen, at least.
There is a lot of puzzle solving you have to do to get goodies. Usually, you will have to look around for a platform to jump from to reach them, or look in all the nooks and crannies for a button, a secret path, a portal, or all of the above to get to those hard to reach places. But there are other secret ways to get goodies too. There are invisible platforms, walls you can walk through, platforms to land on down below, and areas you need to strafe-jump to in order to get to them. There are all sorts of ways to get goodies.
Each level has two bonus areas, in which you have to enter a floating blue portal to get to. You can get some goodies here too, but there is usually an obstacle course or platforming section that you will need to pass in order to get to the good stuff. The goodies don’t respawn, so unless you missed some, or you need to regain health or Doritos, there’s really no point in entering them a second time.

This is perhaps the single most amusing and entertaining old school RPG I have played. If you like tons of humor, including referential humor, and you also like going on a quest to save the galaxy with the most ragtag band of misfits imaginable, then this is the game for you.
The game's story is simultaneously engaging and outrageous. The gameplay is a little clunky but it controls just fine. Mostly my issue with it is it is counterintuitive; to interact with your environment, you have to move the mouse around until a little icon pops up, and you move the camera by mousing to the screen edge. I'd rather play with a gamepad, but it isn't supported. The graphics are really, really, REALLY old school but they get the point across. If graphics are an important thing to you, don't expect much from this game. The sound is surprisingly good for its time; I particularly like that most of the game is fully voiced. I don't find the game to have much replayability, however, although it can be worth it to find what you missed. Irritiating as it is, I recommend playing this game with a guide for all the side quests. Many of the side things you can do in Anachronox do not appear in your quest log, and it is vry easy to miss content. In my case, I probably will play Anachronoc again every two years or so. The story is that worthwhile.
Oh, and don't wprry about leveling up, the game auto levels you to the 'minimum level' when you reach certain areas, which makes a good tactician very unlikely to lose the game. Especially if you keep items on hand for healing and so forth. If you want grinding, exhausting challenge and the need to level up as much as possible, play it on hard.
(Overall 9/10, Story 10/10, Gameplay 9/10, Graphics 4/10, Sound 9/10, Replayability 7/10)

So after many hours I have now finished Anachronox. For anybody on the fence about it, I'd strongly suggest getting it while it's on deal. While the combat is somewhat simplistic, the game is full of humor and charm.
Highs:
The party members are diverse and interesting, for the most part.
Combat system's pretty straightforward, cool attacks/summon.
The game hasn't aged as badly as you'd think at first glance. I was able to get past the quake graphics a lot quicker than I thought I would. It's certainly aged better than FF7.
A fairly wide variety of mini-games.
Really, really funny. There's a lot of humor that works here.
One of your party members is a goddamned planet.
Lows:
A somewhat annoying level of backtracking
You can only change party members in one location.
Some battle animations last way, way too long.
There are a lot of bugs, a few nasty crashes, I had to youtube the ending because the final boss fight crashed on me.
Not entirely sure how to use the spellcrafting mechanic properly.
Overall, absolutely worth your time, especially if you like rpgs.

Full disclosure: old friends of mine from art school worked on this game at ION Dallas back in 2001.  Courtesy of them a few of my jokes made it into this game.
Anachronox was a labor of love for its team, the kind you rarely see today, and it shows in hundreds of small touches.  Unfairly dinged on release for using the aging Quake 2 engine (which didn't keep it from having excellent artwork and level design) and the team's proximity to the high-profile flop Daikatana, it's a vast and beautiful thing, with a tone that manages to encompass both warm, strange humor (Tom Hall is a loveable goofball) and universe-spanning epic seriousness.  We'll probably never know how its cancelled sequel, Anachronox Prime, would have wrapped up the story.
Also one of your party members is a planet. So there's that.

This might actually be my favourite RTS(ish?) game.
The gameplay is only singleplayer and very much oriented around building a defense grid to resist and overcome a stream of Creeper. The Creeper is a liquid like entity that will accumulate and destroy your buildings if your defense isn't up fast enough.
One of the features I think it the coolest about this game is the terrain. Heigh can vary between 1 and 10 and will didctate how the Creeper will flow on the map. It's also possible to terraform it to create things like walls or flatten the place where you want to build.
But walls won't help you forever. Creeper isn't limited to the height of 10 and will accumulate untill you destroy all the spawners.
That's the basic of it. There is also a few more ennemies and you have about 11 buildings to adapt to each scenario.
The main story is cool. The first half will introduce you to new features and the second half will have unique levels to challenge you, especially toward the end. The whole thing is lead by a mysterious sci-fy story.
And the best part is that the story is the small part of the game. After the few hours you need to complete it, you have countless more missions to play and also user-created ones.
Nice defense RTS, tons of content. It might not be for everyone but check it out!

Solforge is a great card game which is different to most of the other games out there.   Most CCG's follow a mana bar pattern where you start off small playing critters, then as your mana increases you play bigger controlling cards, ultimately leading up to your big hitter cards which cost the most mana.     I get bored of this format of playing critters->controlling cards->big hitters.     In Solforge the cards you play in the opening rounds could be the most important plays of the game.
SBE as a company have listened to their player base and have made numerous requested changes to the new client.  In particular you can now earn rewards against the AI again.   This means that casual players, like me, have a method of daily progression.

Solforge is an awesome card game. For anyone new joining in I recommend searching for Kaelari's Ladder on the internet. It's a website we all use to communicate, compete and learn. You can ask literally anything there and our top players will surely help you. There are also guides in the menu there... new players have HUGE advantage if they visit this.
Currently the game is in an awesome state. Fresh start could be hard if you are not properly informed.

The visual overhaul removed a lot of the functional and attractive graphics and smart decisions of the previous interface, and each new set FURTHER nerfs the older sets more than the last release. Do yourself a favor and skip this game. You don't need to nerf old card to make new cards. If you can't avoid power creep that's fine, some cards will just be less good in time, as is the case for all CCG, but there's a cardinal flaw in your design process if you think nerfing player tools is the right answer; make the things that are too weak by comparison a little stronger to make up for it. Thanks for trying Solforge team, your game was fun for a while.

Waited a while for them to fix the glaring problems with this game, to no avail:
-The bias towards higher rarity cards to the point of almost disregarding lower rarity ones (and screwing up the new player experience in the process, together with the recent reduction of daily rewards)
-The excessive accelerated pace of the meta game (spam or die), which wouldn't be such an awful thing if: there was any kind of match making involved on unraked games, and most of the cards needed to counter said meta weren't placed in the upper rarities  (there is something off when you are worrying about countering the meta in casual mode).
-The lack of options regarding buying booster packs of a desired expansion (having only the options of buying the most recent one with cash or an all-in-one pack that dilutes the chances of getting the card your are aiming for quite badly)
Honestly, the lag in the new client and some other technical issues, at least in my eyes, can be waited out and fixed. But the other issues really turn me away from the game.
It is truly an interesting concept for a CCG, with interesting mechanics, but with the glacial pace of the development, the issues that remain unsolved, and a whole world of other CCGs out there, the game ain't worth much of your time just yet. However I would say that you should keep an eye on this one, here's hoping they manage to turn this around.

This used to be a viable, low-cost alternative to titles such as Magic: The Gathering and Hearthstone, which I used to enjoy playing on mobile and occasionally on the computer. It used to have a client which was graphically unimpressive, reminiscent of Hearthstone with almost no graphics other than a background image and card images, but functional. The game used to be very generous, giving you tickets to play in tournaments/draft vs real players and letting you build your collection when playing vs AI. The highlight for me, not having a large collection, was "draft" mode, where you built your deck from a selection of cards, then faced opponents who did the same.
As of June, however, the client and the game have changed dramatically. Client is now full of effects that remind you of the '80s and are unskippable, slowing down gameplay, health ticks down slowly and takes seconds to display accurately. Game is buggy and will seemingly randomly delete your decks. In the three ranked games at the lowest rank I played yesterday, the 1st match was bugged and required me to leave the game, then 2 next matchups were against clearly highly tuned decks full of legendaries that prevented me from doing anything. At the lowest rank. And I've been playing since last November, so I can only imagine how bad it would be for a newbie.
Playing "draft mode" will let you expand your collection without facing overpowered decks, but, unlike previously, to get tickets for it you now have to beat aforementioned highly tuned decks, or pay money. If you do, you can eventually play constructed mode and smack people with lesser collections unless your client bugs out, I guess.
I used to recommend this game, but unfortunately unless things are dramatically rolled back, it's a solid NO.

This game could really go either way in the recommendations department; on one hand, it's an original, indy game that stresses some of the best and possibly most interesting features of an original concept. It's interesting in the same way the "mystery box" of horror or suspense is, and offers some interesting thoughts. I'd love to see more support for indy games, but...
On the other hand, the game failes to follow through on those interesting thoughts. The platforming and controls are absurdedly weak for a game that relies on it. The movement, jetpacking, and other actions get old really fast, and this is for a game that boasts an achievement for completing the game in less than 4 hours on the first playthough. Half the puzzles are exactly the same as previous puzzles, and the other half feel inane and time-wasting. The protaganist is hardly there; rather than telling a story about his wife (as hinted at in the trailer), it becomes the story by lack of any competion, as we learn nothing about her besides her death and his nihlism; he leaves two crewmembers dead without a backward glance, ignoring a story about loss and space (especially in the context of a one-way journey where they likely expected to learn, live, and die together); he ends up following a ridiculously slow genetically altered Russian without ever discovering a way to talk with her and prompt any kind of story.
In all, the game could be worthwhile as part of a bundle (Yay Humble Bundle!) but terrible as an individual game. maybe 1.5/5 stars. Watch the videos on YouTube if you want to learn the "story"; GameKiller346 posted 8 videos that cover the whole thing.

When people try to describe video games as art, I would advise them to include this game as an example.
It has an intriguing story, hauntingly beautiful visuals and solid presentation. The game feels more like an interactive story book, with a protagonist who is faceless enough to act as a simple self-insert, but still has enough depth to give a player interest in his story and situation.
The story and setting give off an eerie vibe and really sells the idea of fearful isolation on a barren world far from Earth, the puzzles are fairly forgiving but challenging enough to not become tedious, and there is lots of room for exploration to find hidden collectibles for achievement hunters.
If there was anything negative to say, I wouldn't play this game if you're looking for a challenge or fast paced action. It's very easy for anybody whose played puzzle games before, and is largely worth playing for the story and setting. If you're not in the mood for trudging a largely barren alien world trying to piece together a mystery, I'd say move on and find something that caters more to a fast paced or action packed style of gameplay.
All in all, I'd give this game a solid 7.5 out of a perfect 10. Definitely recommend for someone in the mood for a great immersive experience.

So I have to say, this is a rather marvelous little indie game.  I feel like the ability for indie devs to create 3-D games like this is sort of a throwback of the early 90's when it suddenly became possibly for indie devs to develop nice looking 2-D games (which were then cutting edge).  It's nice to see a bit of fresh concepts and ideas floating around in the world of 3-D games, which I think is clearly needed.
I will say quickly that at certain times, the controls can be a bit clunky (for instance looking in a direction while you're running, twitchy jumps, occasionally bizarre collision detection, orienting the flash light, etc).  With that said, I personally didn't feel that there was any point where these didn't pail in comparison to the overall enjoyment of the game.  This covers my only problems with the game.
I think the first thing to note about Lifeless Planet is that it's creator's philosophy and artistic style is deeply minimalist, but the implementation is very rich and thoughtfully executed.  Let's start with the gameplay: you can move around, you can jump, and in rare circumstances, you can interact with objects or use your flashlight.  That's it.  All of the puzzles in the game are based around these mechanics.  With these minimalist mechanics, you sort of have to take the sushi chef approach to perfecting the small list of options available to you, which is something I enjoy.  It's not grating though, which a game with the occasional clunky controls could easily have done.  The puzzles aren't mind-bending, often they are straightforward; however, they emphasize the point of the game, which is to explore.  The solution to every puzzle is simply to further explore the environment around you.
This brings me to the artistic style of the game.  In principle, if exploration were required but the scenery wasn't interesting, this game would have failed.  The game, however, has magnificent imagery everywhere you look (and if you're playing the game right, that means simply everywhere).   At some level, the environment (albeit being rendered higher resolution and being better textures) isn't that much more sophisticated than, say, Legend of Zelda: OOT or Rayman 2, and in many ways it feels like a spiritual successor to the era of create N64 games.  A lot of modern games have a lot of sophisticated looking environments, but they sort of look very realistic but at the same time rather drab.  Lifeless Planet uses somewhat repetitive textures, but the textures are used to build very large worlds where the mountains, streams, ponds, sand dunes, etc, all look distinct and have their own character.  Far off into the distance, you can see unique looking mountains and structure that all give the game a certain kind of a character that's lacking in many modern games, and it has to do with the minimal palettes and textures used in the game.
But with that said, you go through many different realms (sand dunes, caves, mountains, hot springs, lava fields, etc), and each realms has a unique character which changes both the game mechanics, which I'll discuss in a moment, and it's own unique artistic flavor.  Looking around, you'll always find yourself mesmerized by the world that's sitting around, enticing you just to explore a little bit further.  So I might imagine that some people might object to this game being linear, since part of the premise of the game is that you're literally following a path that's been laid out for you, level by level.  However, it's precisely because the environment that you stray off the path and find yourself spending 10 minutes just looking at things.  The game rewards you for doing this by letting locate collectibles and achievements this way.
Finally, I'd like to talk about the second major element in Lifeless Planet that makes the gameplay so interesting: The antagonist in the game is the hazardous environment.  As much time as you're spending looking at how pretty it is, you're also spending all of your time making sure not to be killed by it, or how to leverage the environment to your advantage.  To reiterate the first point, there are zombies or wild animals that are coming to get you.  When you die, it's because you weren't paying enough attention to the environment: You fell off of a cliff because the jump was difficult, or you accidentally got burned up by being too close to a lava field, or you weren't paying attention to what violent shrubbery was about you.  And sometimes, you simply run out of oxygen, because the air is entirely CO2 on this planet.  To reiterate the second point, you often have to figure out how to use the environment to your advantage to solve a puzzle.  Do you need to jump higher?  In the hot springs environment, you might need to place boulders on top of water vents, so only one water jet is going and thus radically increases your jump boost.  There are other examples, including using the violent trees to act as walking platforms, but mainly you sort of have to think very logically about what is going on around you, and the answer to how to progress in the game will come naturally.  Again, minimalist gaming mechanics, but thoughtfully executed.
All in all, I found this game extremely satisfying, and I look forward to trying future games from this dev team.

My score: 2/10
I should have known what I would think of the game from my first impression - I couldn't get the main menu to work correctly! I could highlight New Game, but was unable to access the Options menu. After playing the game for a little bit, I would go to the menu and was unable to access the "Save & Quit" option. I basically had to just wait until I got to a save point and then Ctrl+Alt+Delete to the Task Manager and End Task to quit the game... This was only the beginning.
Game Mechanics were a big issue for me, which makes it even more problematic knowing that this is a platformer from start to finish. Timing the jumps is part of the game, but basically missing a jump means dying and dying means restarting, A LOT. But then there are other problems with the game mechanics. There is a part where you have to use geysers to jump from place to place. Although, I was finally able to get through it (simply by luck), I was never able to figure out how the mechanic actually worked to make it happen. Basically, I just kept pushing buttons and after 50 attempts, I'd finally make it. Additional problems are that this was an obvious port from X-Box (still had places to push X or Y buttons), that was badly adapted to a keyboard and mouse. Finally, there were levels that I was able to complete without doing (what I would think are) necessary actibities.  Don't want to spoil the game, but in multiple levels there are these huge machines to turn on to get from one point to another. I went explorting before doing this and managed to reach the end of the level. This is just poor level design. In a game that is all about exploring, I should be able to explore myself out of a level without doing crucial steps.
The puzzles were a bit interesting. The problem was that they were generally the same puzzles time after time after time with very little variation between them. This almost seemed like cheating to me. Pick up stone, use it to power a machine. Walk for five minutes, pick up stone, use it to power another machine. Rinse, lather, repeat about 20 times. Opening doors? Find a code from six buttons. Next door? Same 6 buttons but in a different order. Next door? Guess what? Same 6 buttons but in a different order. This same puzzle for about 6-8 doors.
The most annoying part of the game was all the pointless dying. There were areas where it is difficult to tell where you could and could not go, but if you went to a area you were not supposed to go to, you died. Restart. One level (without giving too much away) sees the player navigating through volcanic activity. This level took me a good 30-45 minutes to navigate because I could not tell what was going to kill me and what wouldn't kill me. By the time I finally got through it, I was so frustrated, I wanted to delete the game. Another part of the game involves plants killing you by coming out of the ground and there was no telling (other than dying) where some of them would appear from. It got annoying because I was frequently not even close to a clump of plants, but still managed to die by getting spiked. Restart.
The story was somewhat interesting. It was the only thing that made me play through the game to the finish. However, it was so anti-climactic that I was disappointed when I finally finished it. Not even the world made want to keep gonig. I did not really find myself once thinking, I wonder what's around that corner, but wondered many times, what is THAT supposed to be? There was one level that (I think) had a glacier or ice on it, but it was so poorly implemented I don't know what it was. The biggest problem with the landscape development was that the rocky outcroppings and "boundaries" of the level were supposed to be stone, but looked smooth instead of rough and rock-like.
Was it worth $20.00? Not even close. It took me roughly 6 hours to win the game and with all the problems described above, I'm not sure I'd really even pay $5.00 for the game. Maybe $1.99 if I had a free afternoon on a random Satruday. The only reason this did not get a 1/10 is because there weren't any game breaking bugs nor anytime the game crashed to desktop. So at least they got that right.

Full disclosure: old friends of mine from art school worked on this game at ION Dallas back in 2001.  Courtesy of them a few of my jokes made it into this game.
Anachronox was a labor of love for its team, the kind you rarely see today, and it shows in hundreds of small touches.  Unfairly dinged on release for using the aging Quake 2 engine (which didn't keep it from having excellent artwork and level design) and the team's proximity to the high-profile flop Daikatana, it's a vast and beautiful thing, with a tone that manages to encompass both warm, strange humor (Tom Hall is a loveable goofball) and universe-spanning epic seriousness.  We'll probably never know how its cancelled sequel, Anachronox Prime, would have wrapped up the story.
Also one of your party members is a planet. So there's that.

If you love saving the universe with a collection of reluctant oddballs, the balls don't come odder.  A sci-fi noir that feels like Deus Ex written by Douglas Adams. and indeed Anachronox was developed at Ion Storm Austin.  As you can see from the pictures it's not just Sly's hair that's late 90's and it is built on a modded Quake 2 engine which was pretty old even in 2001.
Technical Issues - Bizzarely 5 minutes into the game getting trained to fight I experienced a glitch which causes me to drop through the world while going through a repeat of the second cutscene from a minute earlier.  I had to find the noclip cheat and fiddle my way back in (it wasn't even that easy with noclip) and drop down to the training arena thing.  It was odd, I was using a machine with a XP OS, but it was the only single technical issue I had (apart from some of faces which were downright ugly).
Setting - Despite the aforementioned ugly, the setting was pretty varied and pretty fun.  Another late 90's-early 00's thing was the reward for (and desire to) talking to everyone and snuffling around every alley and corner.  It was a golden age for persistent people-poking and cupboard raiding.  This includes weapons, cash and TACO's (Totally Arbitrary Collectible Objects).  I laughed, I totally got the tongue-in-cheek meta irony....I went on hunting them regardless.
Combat is semi-turn based, where the cooldown between actions makes it turn based but if you hang about eating a sandwich the enemy will keep taking turns.  This style of combat suffered from getting a bit tedious early on before having a party, then slid (over many hours) to too easy before a sudden notch up of difficulty requiring collected objects at the end.  The little cutscenes for dramatic weapon actions were nice, but I could have done with being able to press space and skip them after 200 times or something.
The story world is immersive and as you can only have three party members at a time, there are things that happen and dialogue that only happens (and even a special short level for one character which depends one a character taken along somewhere earlier) depending on your choices.  None of them are epic or world breaking, but if you like a character and keep them around you get to see/hear more of them.  Different characters also had powers accessed through minigames, which broke up fights/wandering and it (of course) opened up new areas in places you had been before.  But the story did make me laugh in quite a few places and was engaging.
Overall if you like your RPG singleplayer, not taking themselves too seriously but still with a world to get stuck into, I recommend this game.  Despite my comments on combat for every minute spent being slightly mildly irked there was an hour of exploring and laughing.  So go for it.  Especially given it's only a fiver.

You're in space and you're ruling an empire to conquer the universe. To reach the top you can select one of the 13 very unique races, each race has its own traits, advantages, weakness and history. Additionally you can even create your own custom race, where you can select any boni or mali that you desire. After youve made a choice, you can competete with up to 7 other empires to conquer the stars. You'll be able to plan every of your colonies, decide which scientific field will be the most useful for you, customize and improve your starships, recruite special leaders for your ships or your colonies, negotiate peace, technological trades or multiple other contracts with other empires, command the tactical battles of your fleets or even destroy entire planets. The AI in MoO2 is pretty decent, even compared to new games - its above average. The AI plays to win, different Empires act differently, the AI is aggressive, the AI expands, the AI researches away from you, the AI wins games. Now part of it is, like for nearly any 4x game, on higher difficulty the AI gets extra boni. As already said this is nothing special for 4X games, and I cant name any big name, where this would be different. I knew this game was some sort of side-scroller, and figured that was all there was to it. I anticipated the game being unfun and a complete bore. Boy, was I wrong. That "Metroidvania" tag is seriously legitimate for this game. It's like playing Super Metroid in a modern setting, with a story made up entirely of cheese. The game's intro action lasts about one to two minutes, and it kinda blows, because it has nothing to do with the game's hero, and honestly could have been left out of the game entirely. Everything after that is a path of growth a la games like Super Metroid where you start with practically nothing and end up a high-powered wrecking ball with all the utility skills you need to traverse the entire compound.
I cannot stress enough how Super Metroid this game is. Look at your map, and the rooms are laid out in grid fashion, just like Super Metroid. Shine your flashlight on a door or barrier, and it glows green, orange, blue, etc., each of which has a certain weapon/utility item weakness to bypass...y'know like the doors of different colors on Super Metroid. I'm not even that big a fan of Super Metroid, because the items on the map never get unmarked so you know you've cleared a room of items (some rooms have more than one). I'm pretty anal that way, so that always bugged me in Super Metroid. Here, however, the room has a question mark if there's an item in it, and once you have every item, the question mark becomes a dot.
Within less than half an hour of starting, I'd fallen in love with this game. I would dare say I only have 3 gripes:
1. Obtaining some items using the speed dash is ridiculously difficult and confusing because the game doesn't really train you on all the upside-down-running rules/physics. I had to resort to walkthroughs for several of these.
2. Save rooms can contain items, and they don't get marked on the map as question marks or dots, which means you could be completely lost on where to find an item and have to resort to walkthroughs.
3. Since this is a Metroidvania, going back to old areas is a must if you want to collect all the items, and this game kind of dumps the final battle in your lap without a lot of warning. Once in the battle, you cannot leave or you're killed instantly. If you go back to a save, all the direct routes to where you need to go are closed off. I spent about an hour just trying to get to one area where two items were marked on my map that I had the tools to obtain them now, and never succeeded. I finally gave up despite being almost done collecting the items because it was such a horrible, horrible pain to find the right path to the east side of the map once the final battle blocks you from going there via the surface.
I'm a bit of a perfectionist when it comes to Metroidvania stuff, so although it gets under my skin that the BS with the final battle held me back from getting 100%, I still really dig this game. It was a surprise hit and I totally enjoyed my time with it. The cheesy story, Metroidvania elements, and nice graphics made it a very fun experience. I would put this up there with Dust: An Elysian Tale as far as being really good Super Metroid-esque games. I definitely recommend this to fans of that genre and would certainly love a sequel to this game someday.

I’ll be honest from the outset – Shadow Complex isn’t as good as I remember it being when I first played it way back on the Xbox 360. Maybe it’s just aged a little and maybe I have a faint tint of nostalgia clouding my view, but I think the true reality is that the game does have a few irritations that need addressing. First and foremost; the whole ‘Remastered’ thing is really not that big of a deal. Apart from one or two pretty looking vistas and a few nice looking lighting effects, this isn’t a game that’s super amazing to look at. It’s not bad looking, just average, but the game’s infrequent cutscenes only achieve accentuating the flaws in its visuals. Here, animation feels rough and uneven, and characters hardly show any emotion on their mannequin faces even under the most extreme circumstances. As an added bonus, the cutscenes only exist in the first place to prop up a story that barely exists and is laughable to the extreme; ordinary guy with military training takes down an army for reasons barely enhanced beyond saving his girlfriend. How... exciting.
Some other minor issues seep into the gameplay as well. Camera angles and lighting often obscure the path you need to take, to such a degree that it becomes remarkably easy to miss the desires route and end up highly confused as a result. While the controls are alright and navigation gets fun (more on that later), there is also still a few too many moments where things get rather awkward and fiddly. The main example comes from trying to jump into vents or small gaps, where you have to position yourself in precisely the right place to actually make the jump work... Some other manoeuvres required to unlock every item also veer dangerously close to moving from intricate to exasperating. There’s also moments where the 2.5D feature of the game (which lets you target enemies in the background in addition to those either side of you) completely screws you over, aiming you at the guy in a distant corner over the one directly in front of you who is slowly making cheese of your brain. Combine all these little problems together, and my blood pressure suddenly spiked at more intervals than I care to admit.
Yet, for all these issues and the slight disappointment I had at my memories not living up to my expectations, it doesn’t change the fact that this is a really good game at its heart. It almost precisely mirrors the of the Metroid and Castlevania games – there’s a giant map, which you slowly explore to find new weapons and powers, which in turn make you into more of a perfect killing machine while letting you explore more of the map in the process. Still, while it’s not a unique formula, it’s executed nigh on perfectly here. For one, the map is great fun to explore, staying well away from becoming a dull slog through endless grey corridors. You have underwater sections, you have sections in a mine, others that take in pristine white facilities, and yet more that take in the grand expanse of the great outdoors... Even when it comes to retracing your steps in the endgame to grab stuff you’ve missed, this variety makes it so it never feels like a chore. It’s a nicely created world that successfully makes you want to keep moving.
The sense of progression is spot on as well. Each new upgrade is exciting to obtain and downright cool to use, and its fun to chart your progression from a lowly pistol user who struggles in every fight, to a power armoured juggernaut who enters every room just blindly spraying missiles everywhere. Yet it’s not just in combat that you see improvements – navigation around the map gets its own bonuses. For instance, obtaining the jetpack suddenly lets you zip up ladders at speed, which is such a tiny little thing, but one that never stops being boring. When you add in stuff which lets you run on water and hookshot around like some sort of mechanical Spiderman... Well, things just keep getting more interesting.
In the end, I have to say that the good outweighs the bad when it comes to Shadow Complex, simply because the problems here are so downright insignificant when compared to how enjoyable the game is to play. Sure, there’s a notable amount of moments that may annoy when they present themselves, but a couple of minutes of exploration and downright chaos soon provides the perfect cure to that. When it comes to whether you should buy this game or not, the answer should certainly be in the positive - It’s simply not a decision that’s (shadow) complex.

You know how Goat Simulator started as a joke and then became one of the best games ever?
Well, this is kinda like that; except that instead of trying to simulate a goat the Devs tried to simulate the grass really well.
To be fair, it is really damn good grass... from a distance. The pure visual experience of this "game" is worth checking out when it's on sale. Up close, it's just another basic system of models with "photographic quality' textures that don't scale well, so you can see all the ugly stretching and pixellation when you take a really close look at the grass at your feet.
But the idea here is to stare out over a vast field of grass, so I can forgive the fact that it's not up to the microscope inspection test.
It's really not a GOTY candidate, in fact it's nothing special at all. It's one element of the background from just about every other game, which has been taken to the extreme. In a funny, roundabout way, that makes it interesting; although I wouldn't say it's particularly compelling.
Would I buy it for $5? Never. For 99c on sale? Maybe. But when you throw in the fact that you can make a profit off of selling the emotes (assuming you craft the badge and don't just try to sell the cards individually), and can easily play the game for an hour and then refund it, what have you got to lose?

Personally, I really enjoy Grass Simulator.  Honestly, I don't know what most of the reviewers were expecting- it's a GRASS SIMULATION GAME.  Even so, it actually goes above and beyond just being a grass simulator. Of course there is the grass simulation mode, which is genuinely relaxing with beautiful music and soft, relaxing sound effects. It's perfect for relaxing after a long, stressful day.
If you need more excitement, there are several other modes which have everything from dancing disco cows to the ability to shoot things to a snowy exploration level.
As a fan of simulation games, I genuinely recommend this game. The devs keep adding new things and it definitely gives you a genuine grass simulation experience.

Though when you get passed that learning curve, It becomes really rewarding learning how to do a spin that would decapitate an enemy. Or sweep someone off their feet with a two handed axe/hammer/pole-arm. Or attempting to push someone over with a sheild and well timed sprint.
The only real downside like Ive already mentioned is the learning curve. Its a serious dying simulator at first til you get your feet under you, and learn how to orientate yourself. But its also what adds a unique layer of depth to this game that I personally havent seen in any other. It gives you complete control over your swings and how hard you are hitting and how fast you are swinging.
It's got a large labyrinthine dungeon for the story mode. There isnt much of a story there though. Just some books and notes that you may or may not stumble across. You can get lost easily, since there's no map, only familiar rooms and halways to go by.
Then you have the arena, which i'd recommend hitting first. Practice up in the novice arena, then move on to the expert one. Fighting increasingly better equiped and skilled enemies. Then move on to the persistent arena, where if your character dies in the arena, he aint coming back from the arena, and you gotta start over. But you earn gold to outfit your character and exp to learn new abilities and also hire new fighters to level up in different ways. Like a character that specializes in dual weilding. Or one thats got a preferrence to sheilds/ sword and board.
Definitely think it is well worth the money, Ive gotten more replay value out of it than most other spendy triple A games.

A lot of what is said in reviews is spot on and even more is complete and total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t...
: Flawless. People saying they loved XCOM EU/EW and hate this game because "it isn't balanced" is hilarious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Massive Chalice does a better job at getting me to bring one of each unique class into each battle than any other tactical game I have played. : Great. This one has not been done well in any other tactical game save for some Fire Emblem games (which have even LESS tactical combat) and it has been done well here. Don't listen to the naysayers.  Massive Chalice is strange, quirky, interesting, and one of a kind.
It's get compared to X-Com, and that is not in itself wrong, but it feels completely different.  LIke X-Com, you have both the Strategic Layer, and the Tactical Turn Based combat system.  The difference is the scale is much more massive.  You are playing an imortal ruler and the game takes place over 300 years, with each fight taking place often decades after the last ones.  This means while your heroes level up and gain skills like an RPG, you aren't really leveling them up.  You are leveling up their bloodline.
That's the unique thing here.  You can build keeps and then retire two of your heroes from battle to establish a bloodline.  They won't fight any more and can't normally level up any further, but they will pass on their experience and levels to their children as well as various personalities and traits.  You can also pull heroes from the field to be trainers, further boosting their xp and augmenting their traits and to increase your reseach.
As your heroes only get to fight one or two battles before they grow old and die, it's all about getting them up a few levels, retiring them to pass that knowledge on to the next generation, and engineering a class of heroes with the best traits and abilities.
There's a few more thing, but that's the gist of it.  Go in treating it like a typical combat game with RPG elements and you will get frustrated.  Treat it like the completely unique thing that it is, and you will enjoy it.

If you were looking for an fun and immersive alternative for a turned based strategy game - Seek no more. You just found it.
A brilliant and storyline filled with witty jokes and sassy sense of humour which sets you against the "Cadence", an demon/plague like species which soles purpose is to decimate your people and corrupt your lands.
Seeking a way to defeat the Cadence, you, the master ruler of the lands, seek out  the power of the Massive Chalice, hoping to find a way of cleansing the Cadence. The Chalice is played by to charming voices, an pervy and sassy man and an wise and witty woman, whose purpose is to play the role of advisors trough the game.
The game starts with you waking up in front of the Chalice. The voices are telling you that you manage to achieve what you wanted: An way to purge the Cadence. The punch line? This purging will take 300 years to gather the energy and research necessary to be completed and mastered.
But fear no more! Thanks to the powers of the Chalice you achieved immortality and the power of the "Eye of Thundera" (you basically have an extended vision of the role Kingdom, anywhere you want)! All you had to do was sacrifice your body, becoming entangled to the Chalice. (Y).
Throughout the 300 year timeline, you must build upon your territory different alternative building's and research new and better gear; You must forge an strong bloodline of ferocious fighters to defend against the Cadence to ensure the Chalice is not damaged. For that, you will control the marriage of your warriors, being them infants or nor, transforming this game in an interesting but twisted and  kinda sick,  "Game of Thrones" thing.
Like Pokemon, you will have  3 starters classes: x2 ranged and one melee. Your fighters are sub-classes which are desginated by lineage, thus being necessary the wisdom of Game of Thores again.
What's unique about the level system is you are not investing your time into a certain character but in a lineage/family. You marry your lineage off to another and make babies. These babies have good or bad traits which are then passed down from generation to generation. This traits may be good for combat or bad, like good eyesight, giving you better visibilty of the terrain or alcoholism, meaning your warrior will move less tiles and atack less because will be with hangover. Your lineage determines your fighter class as well. For instance, if you marry off one Caberjack to a Hunter you will be making a Shadowjack.
You will be controlling the family clans  that you send out to defend from atacks in a turned paced duel. Each class will have an amount of tiles that can walk or atack and so does the enemy. With more battles, more experience your warrior get. Experience which that can be later used in a very intriguing skill tree.
With the passing of time and accumulated experiences, your warriors may create legacy gears which, with the eventual death of such warrior, will be passed through his linage, generation after generation, getting stronger and stronger.
Time itself is sped up until an event occurs (research ending, babies being born, old members of the lineage dying, cadence presence,...). With the advent of time, the atacks of Cadence will become more often and in greater number. They start atacking one land in the early game and then, late in the game, three or more, making you have to choose wich terrain you will be sacrificing, since you can only defend one at a time.
For the amount of time you must spent calculating the odds of your strategies to work, for the huge amount of laughs this game will give you and for the connection you will be forging with the families you create (or not, You can be an insensitive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that will be sending young ones to death just to buy time for the true meaning of the game...(No worries, I ain't judging ya)) all I have to say is: Buy this game, it sure is worth playing it.
But be warned, the game may become repetitive, but, since it's cheap, who cares?

Massive Chalice, much like literally every Doublefine game produced since they decided they didn't need publishers or editors, is a bit confused. On one hand, it embraces the purity of XCOM2012-style (or perhaps I should say "traditional board game style") actions and has the trademark Doublefine carefully crafted aesthetic running through every level of the audiovisual presentation. On the other hand, it muddles everything with occasionally pointless RNG and has perhaps three too many systems going on simultaneously in the geoscape.
Did I mention it's an XCOM(2012) CLONE? It's an XCLONE.
There's some interesting bits resulting from the nessesarily disposable nature of your soldiers as you carefully curate their family trees to produce increasingly powerful and skilled individuals in the classes you want. It's a great twist on otherwise normal "level up your units" game design. Sadly this is muddled by the irritiating intrusion of RNG-based inheritance and a bunch of other random crap that turns what should be a selling point into a HR hellscape. Thankfully, the game doesn't randomly choose from the two traits you're presented with when a unit levels up.
Did I mention it's an XCLONE? It's an XCLONE.
The geoscape-level strategic game is neat because it forces you make a bunch of decisions all at once. You can search for new heroic bloodlines, build castles, or research new developments in fighting the corruption that threatens the world. Somewhat irritatingly, the game forces you to choose between building and researching because the titular Massive Chalice can only do one thing at a time. Because reasons.
Every so many years while you
charge the titular Massive Chalice to win the game, there's multiple incursions from

the Cadence and you have to pick which pre-defined region you want to defend (based on rewards and the strategic situation) because you can only respond to one
noise incursion at a time. Because plot reasons. The zones you don't respond to have their
corruption meter increment by one tick and if the corruption meter maxes out they
are lost to the corruption.
Did I mention it's an XCLONE? It's an XCLONE.
Tactical combat is pretty fluid, even though there's a complete dearth of voicework for your units (one of the perils of letting Kickstarter backers do custom war cries for their backer house). Each unit gets two "actions" on your turn, and the turn structure is "my turn your turn". One class snipes with crossbows. One class uses grenades. One class hits things with a caber. There's a bunch of hybrid classes but they're just "Parent class, but with a twist from the other parent". Movement is done on a square grid, and units die pretty quickly on both sides.
Okay so you may have noticed a bit of, shall we say, a theme so far. That theme being "XCOM2012, but with some wierd addons that muddle the everliving crap of XCOM2012's super tight design". Literally the only three big "design elements" that Doublefine didn't T.S. Eliot off of XCOM2012 are the house system, the endgame, and the fact that there are enemies that drain XP from your units when they hit them.
Let's pause for a moment, and let that last one sink in. I'll allow that it's a pretty tiny bit of XP that gets shaved off, but level drain has never, ever, been a good design element. Not even in D&D. It's thematically a cool thing that the enemy does, but it's really emblematic of my issues with Massive Chalice as a whole: The game is so focused on style, mood, and its bloodline stuff that it sorta misses out on why XCOM2012 did things the way it did and tends to awkwardly stumble around depending on it's clever asethetic winks and nods to distract you from the humdrum gameplay. And the fact that the game absolutely nails its aesthetics so perfectly makes its 'original design, do not steal' gameplay all the more annoying.
But no-one buys or plays Doublefine games for the gameplay, really.
Feels a little bit like a re-skinned Xcom, seems pretty good to me.

I mainly played this, just to see how Just Cause 2 got it's roots. I can see that the roots for Just Cause 2 were well fertilized, because Just Cause OG is sh**!
Well, okay, to be fair Just Cause 1 is a lot better than a lot of other games. It feels sort of like playing Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, with slightly less clunkier controls and slightly better graphics. However, the game has some severe problems with both narrative and gameplay that cause it to just truly suffer.
My biggest qualms with the gameplay is how easily cheated it can be. The loading screens advertize all the cool weapons and vehicles you could unlock by freeing more cities, but I got pretty much all the best gear by the end only by playing the regular story missions. And the two staples of the game- the parachute and grappling hook- both absolutely suck in this game. For one, the grappling hook is very selective. It will latch onto any vehicle or person you aim it at, but not trees, rocks, or land- which renders it basically pointless. Plus, parachuting to cars or helicopters is rubbish, since you have to reel yourself close enough to the vehicle for it to work. And Scorpio obviously has some sort of strange disease in his arms, causing them to only aim his grappling hook forward. Once a helicopter flies behind you while you reel it in, you're done. And trying to get onto cars is a massive pain, since you gradually sink to the ground (even if the car is driving at top speed).
The gameplay also takes its biggest dip during the end mission. The game builds up all this variety and open mission play-style, and the end mission completely negates that. You fly in on a helicopter but can't fly it to the island. Cars attract helicopter missiles. And missiles blasting your body cause you to bounce back and forth like a pinball, constantly taking damage. And damage can only be healed by the random health-pack spawning out of dead enemies, which is very uncommon.
The cutscenes are also really weird to watch. The animation studio chose some very strange character models (and some even worse voice actors), and the scenes that explain situations come off as weird, in the sense that characters say sentences in completely off tones, or come off as weird since the characters themselve look very inhuman. In fact, Just Cause has a very toy-ish feel. The cars look like Hot Wheels cars, the characters look and animate like action figures. Even the samey world of San Esperito has a kid's-jungle-themed-toy-box appeal. The game just doesn't have a very fun or realistic draw to it.
I'm not saying everyone would hate this game. Between the wide variety of story missions, vast content, and world to explore- plenty of gamers will enjoy the original Just Cause. It just didn't impress me. I'm very picky with my sandbox games, and if you other 5% of Steam users that agree with my opinions are reading this, then you can be assured that Just Cause is not the game for you.

Just Cause? Just pass. You're honestly better skipping this title and moving onto Just Cause 2, you won't miss anything. Just Cause 1 has a slew of problems, not limited to: poor controls especially when using the grapple/parachute mechanics, vehicle handling is clearly designed with controllers in mind, most notably when using the auto-aiming mounted turrets, a ridiculous cliché story including drug cartels, Nazi scientists and a whole lot of rockets, and finally it crashes alot.
In my 8 hour playtime alone, I crashed six times, three of which where on the same mission, I've Got the Power [#13]. The only real positives I can think about are the graphics are moderately good, ignoring noticable copy-paste jobs on buildings and in jungle, the soundtrack is perfect for the game, and some of the missions including, Some Enchanting Evening [#15],  Dismissed Without Honors [#17] and the last two thirds of Taking Out the Garbage [#19b-c]. If you're going to play this regardless, then I recommend running through the story and leaving a majority of the optional content. The game is only 19 missions long with the last mission split into 3 parts.
In summary, I'd still recommend skipping this and playing the second game in the series as it has improved the core idea/gameplay of JC1 into a more complete and enjoyable game.

I had a friend constantly telling me to buy this game for over a year. Almost everytime I said something about games such as XCOM, Dungeon Keeper, Evil Genius or similar games, he reminded me that I should totally buy this game because I will like it.
A few days ago he went right ahead and bought it for me, even after I told him countless times not to do it. And in the end, I did not like the game that much. As usual, I will speak about the bad things of the game first:
First and foremost, this game tries REALLY HARD to be the Gangster XCOM, but in the end fails hard. During combat, you have multiple units (a max of 4 units with one guy as Support, and in some cases allied units controlled by the game), which aparently evolve as you play. However, I can't really see any evolution. During the almost 4 hours I've played, SOME of my characters leveled up ONCE, and I don't see any "Experience left to LVLUP" anywhere at all. The game didn't tell me at any moment how or when do I level up. Then, we have the weapons of the characters. It's kind of a joke, but pistols felt way more powerful THAN MOTHERF#CKING SHOTGUNS. AT POINT BLANK RANGE. Range on itself seems to be a joke and I don't see anyway of changing the weapons your characters have, while the biggest problem with the game is cover. The maps are filled with objects, but they don't really offer a big advantage, and blow up after getting hit once or twice anyway. In the end, it feels like a poor attempt of ripping off XCOM which backfired.
Outside of combat, we have a Strategy game, really similar of the Tropico games (it's made by the same guys, and it seems to run on the same engine as Tropico 4, as I've seen some models being reused). However, there's not that much to it. There's two kinds of money, you can buy buildings that will get you more dirty or clean money, you can get more firearms... But in the end, I just wish I was playing Tropico 4, as it feels shallow and unfinished. The enemy never seems to do anything that interesting. At times you'll get the police investigating your♥♥♥♥♥ but you can just bribe them off, tell them someone else did it, kill the witness and stuff like that. Maps are also too small on my opinion, at least compared to the huge islands you could have in Tropico games.
Something that also pisses me off, and that this company seems to enjoy doing, is DRM. WHAT IS THE BIG IDEA!? THE GAME IS ON STEAM, WHY DOES IT NEED THIS!? You're forced to make an account on their damn page, and log on everytime you want to play. For me, it just feels amateur-ish. Like they want to do it because the big companies, like EA or Ubisoft do it. Well, that sucks, good job.
I also see that the game has some weird AI. For example, you can steal cars which serve as a ride for your characters, so they move faster. However, your characters will at times take the car and run arround a few blocks when THEY ONLY HAVE TO CROSS THE STREET, TO A HOUSE THAT'S RIGHT INFRONT OF THEIR BASE. It's redundant as hell, makes your characters, at times, TAKE LONGER TO GET SOMEWHERE ON A CAR, THAN ON FOOT. And the cars break down constantly, so I don't even bother most of the time. You can also buy a car, but seems stupid when the whole city is filled with cars that you can steal.
Aim also seems to be a joke. Funny enough, it feels like they based that on XCOM. There, people have felt betrayed at the game because you can miss point blank shoots and crap, which is insanely unlucky, but it can happen. Here on this game, I constantly missed 75% shots, which felt lame as hell because my enemies almost never missed. Now top that with the damn cover mechanics that felt unfinished, and you have an atomic bomb of dissapointment and fustration.
The game also lacks a way to speed things up. You'll be at times waiting for crap to happen, while your resources keep rising and your henchmen go somewhere. If there was the option in Tropico, WHY NOT HERE!?
Lastly, character customization. There's nearly noone. At the start you can choose stats, but it's never explained what those stats do, when will they do anything, NOTHING AT ALL. While being able to select your stats with questions is cool, it would also be great if you could also choose a weapon or some sort of equipment at the start.
So, does the game have good stuff? Yeah. The soundtrack is good. The voices are decent (most characters sound bored as hell, and some even throw unfunny jokes, but outside of that they're good), there seems to be a lot of maps (even though they're small, short and the game sells more in DLC's), you get the picture. However, it's a flawed game that feels unfinished, that might appeal to a small amount of people while being boring to much others.
On my opinion, don't buy it. If you like the economic part of the game, buy Tropico 4. If you like the combat areas of it, buy XCOM; Enemy Unknown. And if you do wish to buy this game, wait for a sale, and probably wait to be dissapointed. It's pretty much a Monopoly game based on the 1920's, that's missing half the board.
Well, at least I got dissapointed for free, this time.

For those old enough to remember, there was once a pretty decent game called Gangsters 2: Vendetta - a game where you could hire gangsters, buy them weapons, cars, muscle (IE - bodyguards), direct them to whatever point on the map you needed them to be, attack rival gangs and their businesses, take over their territory, set up legit businesses, set up illegal businesses, protect your businesses from rivals, all whilst staying hidden from the law.
Now imagine if someone had taken all that, thrown it out of the window, and replaced it with a gangster themed boardgame of Monopoly. Because thats all this is, every mission - buy a fake business, create a speakeasy to sell booze, make money, win level. The cops or rival gangs never barge in on your operations, and if you DO somehow get the cops attention (perhaps by murdering a few people in a boredom induced rage), slip em a few hundred dollars and they'll forget all about the corpses they've just discovered.
Its a sad state of affairs when I can genuinely say that a 16 year old game beats this into the ground.
Pretty but shallow. Go for the older and superior Gangsters: Organized Crime instead.
