3 hours in I'd have given my whole hearted recommendation on this game.  4 hours in and I'm totally done, feeling like I wasted my time.  I want so badly to like this game for so many reasons.  It's incredibly unique and creative.  The story is very well told, the atmosphere is immersive, the jumping puzzles are fair and enjoyable (mostly), and even now I'm extremely interested to see what happens.
Unfortunately though, I'll be finishing this game vicariously through a walkthrough on YouTube.  The entire experience was completely ruined by the Inferno level, which in contrast to everything else thus far is poorly design, poorly lit, and beyond frustrating.  It is in this level that I realized this game has no real gamma setting in the options, and also where I discovered the gamebreaking problem of having to start completely over if you exit the game.  4 hours in and I quit to go look up a walkthrough.  I come back, and there is no saved game to load.  Marvelous.
If the save game issue were fixed and the Inferno level were completely reworked into something even vaguely tolerable, I'd recommend this game to anyone.  As it stands, I am feeling disatisfied to say the least.  It hurts because I was having such a great time with this game up until this catastrophe.  I want to see what happens but there is no way I'm starting all over, much less enduring that lava level again.  Uninstalling and off to YouTube to get some closure...

If you see Lifeless Planet on sale, grab it, otherwise I'm not sure I can recommend it at the full $20 price.
The first 30-60 minutes of the game will absolutely grab you, blow your mind, and leave you excited for more and more.
Unfortunately, as high of a standard the beginning of the game sets, the rest of the game floats betwen okay and good but never returns to the level the beginning led you to believe.
More than anything, Lifeless Planet is a running sim.  It looks like an open world and there is a lot of space in which to run, but by and large there is only one path to progress the story and lots of dead ends along the way.  Lots of running, lots of jumping, and it does get to be tedious after a while.  Every time I ran into a situation where I couldn't progress the story but it seemed like if I just timed this jump just right I'd make the landing and things would go forward, but instead I'd just keep dying over and over, in truth it turned out that there was actually a puzzle hidden somewhere off-the-beaten path that was overlooked so I had to go explore every nook and cranny to find where the puzzle was.  There's a number of 'puzzles' in the game though once you do one or two to understand how they work they are pretty simple to solve.  As immersive and excellent as the atmosphere of Lifeless Planet is though, these shortcomings are pretty easy to overlook.
Atmosphere - atmosphere is what Lifeless Planet does best and at a level not many games out there can keep up with.  The graphics are imaginative and alien and beautiful.  I would love to play this again on a high-end gaming PC just for that experience.  Mine's just middle-of-the-ground PC but the game really begs to be revisited whenever I can upgrade - it's just too beautiful and alien to not.  Music is spot on and never intrudes.  What little voice acting is in the game is done well, too.
Story.........
I don't know if the gamemakers were too overambitious or just lacked a professional writer on the team to tie it all in together better.  There's a few different plotlines and unfortunately they are all undeveloped.  The most story by far goes into what happened with the Russians and that is learned entirely by finding and reading documents or listening to audio recordings.  Far too much of the present-day story that you actually play in is progressed solely by you do this or you go here simply because it is the only thing to do or the only place to go.  Your are given a little bit of backstory for your character at the beginning of the game, which honestly is enough to get things in motion and get the game going, but any sort of character development is pretty much ignored until the very end of the game where those original few sentences of backstory are integral to so the whole thing ends up just coming across as shallow and anticlimatic.
There's also a few transitions between scenes or chapters where the screen will fade-to-black, sometimes unexpectedly, and the new scene starts in a new location and even if there is a cut-scene it lacks any explanation for the transition.  It was twice, maybe three times, I had to pause and look up some YouTuber Let's Play videos because I thought I had missed something.
Conclusion
I enjoyed the game.  Spaceman on a dead planet and all you got is your spacesuit.  "Ummmmmmmmmm......."  Yeah, it's bloody brilliant.
Setting and atmosphere are awesome and at a level all games should aspire to.
It's just the story falls way flat in a game that should be story-driven.
I think you're better off waiting for a sale to buy.  Maybe I'm a cheapskate, but that $10-15 range seems like a fair price for an incredibly atmospheric game, but there's enough story issues I'd feel let down if I paid $20.

I'm having a ball with Shadow Complex Remastered. It's my opinion that they just don't make games like this very often anymore, and this has been a refreshing gaming experience for me. I love RPGs, ARPGs, Metroidvanias, and Platformers. This game as elements of all of these genres.
As a casual gamer, I do my best to avoid permadeath games and those that are unrealistically difficult just for the sake of being difficult. This game caters to both casual and hardcore gamers, because there are mechanisms for turning off the "blue line" showing the route to your next objective and Master Challenges for those looking for a greater degree of difficulty. The blue guide line can be turned off and on at anytime, so if you get stuck or can't figure out where to go, this guide is there for you. Gamers are rewarded for exploration off the beaten path with upgrades and items, but if you stray too far, it's easy to find your way back to where you were.
Another plus for me is full controller support, and this game has very responsive controls. Jumping, shooting, takedowns, it all works just as it should. The graphics are really good, and while it's technically a side-scroller, there's an open world feel to it, because the character can go in any direction, even under water. New areas open up as new weapon upgrades are discovered, and gamers will find value in revisiting new areas to obtain hidden items they couldn't access before.
I can't say enough about this game. I paid full price for my copy, and it's been worth every penny.

This was my first 2D side-scrolling sandbox game with crafting, and I've yet to find one that's as addictive. Perhaps the setting is what grabbed me over similiar games, like Terreria, but for whatever reason, I've sunk as many hours into this game as I have some RPGs.
You start out with a damaged ship and some quests to find the things you need to fix it on the planet below. From there, your journey will take you across the galaxy to find ancient artifacts that open a gate to a showdown with the ultimate evil that destroyed Earth: The Ruin.
That said, most of my time has been spent building complicated and CPU-destroying colonies on challenging planets. Not only will you find yourself collecting all the items you can loot or duplicate for decoration, you'll start trying to "collect" the various types of tenant you can have in the places you'll construct.
Chucklefish has been pretty good about adding updates, having put in mechanics to build space stations (which are still kind of rough compared to what you can build elsewhere) and Mechs (giving the game some space combat aspects), but the real star of the Starbound add-ons is a mod called "Frackin' Universe." Once you've exhausted Starbound's vanilla game, FU will add more items, quests, and complexity than you could ask for.
So if a 2D sci-fi sandbox is something that sounds great with more worlds than you could want to explore, Starbound is well worth your time and money.
Oh, one more thing: The game has penguins. Some wear viking helmets. Just wanted to add that.

The actual combat though, is unfortunately not that great.  It's the one thing I just can't get over. I'm just gonna get straight to the point: do NOT be tricked by the way this game appears to be ath the first glance. The actual battles are pretty brutal even on normal difficulty. Out of your whole roster, you're only able to deploy four characters on a map, not to mention that some additional challenges for moneys and treasures add other deployment limitations requirements. Reinforcements maps are the worst. Nonetheless, combat is the game's best point; the fact that enemies scale with level is a briliat decision that doesn't encourage you to spend hours on grind and always makes sure you're kept on your toes. Every map is able to offer a decent challenge, which, in my opinion, is quite important to a tactical RPG. Here and there there are also tidbits of text-based adventures which is also pretty nice and helps add depth and variety to the game on top of everything. I should also mention that the fishing mini-game is also very nice and doesn't require the most effort and time, yet it's very gratifying.
The visuals are really nice and colourful, with obvious nods to classical JRPGs with character screens and the like. However, the 3D models are absolute cringe. They're very low effort and low quality, yet unfortunately you get to see them a lot – especially during the battles. Combat pacing is still too slow even if you speed it up to the max. I was also unable to find enemy movement indicators so you have to click on each enemy every time to see their movement grid. Considering it's a tactical RPG, it's freaking annoying. Also, some kind of skill check system for the enemies would've also been great. It's not a big issue since you can replay a map at any point and that none of your teammates really "die", but it's those little quality of life things that significantly improve the game's experience.
There's a good variety of characters, each with their own personality, yet again, very befitting of some JRPG. I'm absolutely sure that the devs have played at least one Fire Emblem game because some of the characters appear to be literally copy-pasted from there... Ahem, nonetheless, they all have their distinct role in combat and I don't really have an axe to grind with any of them. The main character is a bit annoying but that's expected. Overall plot premise seems pretty weak if you poke at it but it's not that important since the main point of the game are exploration, castle grounds rebuilding and bonding with your teammates/vassals/citizens.
The only real downside(s) are that the voiceover and animations/3D models quality are pretty cringe, and the combat maps background could've used more effort and detail, but seeing as it's a low budget Kickstarter game, it's already impressive for what it is, so all of it can be overlooked for the sake of a quality gameplay experience.

In Creeper World games, you set up energy collection grid and use collected energy to beat back titular creeper, the blue, oozing fluid whose behaviour (according to extras from CW1) is described by modified heat transfer equations. Every building and weapon costs energy to build, and most cost energy to maintain, forcing you to constantly expand to new areas to build new collectors/reactors to beat creeper back by few tiles more until you can escape (CW1) or kill it for good (CW2/CW3)
That's it. But the way Creeper interacts with shape of the map means that there's a lot of strategy involved: where do you set up a defence? Can you cover the valley with collectors AND fortify it before creeper floods it? Do you go for tight grid of expensive but efficient and easily defensible reactors or for wide and redundant but hard to defend net of collectors? What combination of weapons will you use? How many blasters? Mortars? Sprayers? Maybe use Bombers, Strafers and Cargo planes to open another front on top of the hill instead of fighting uphill? How do you handle valley and mountain ranges?
Not to mention player-made maps of all sorts, including puzzles, "play as creepers" and tricky maps with lots of unexpected scripting.
Bonus highlight of the game is CRPL = Creeper Reverse Polish Language, a built-in scripting language giving map creators total control, even roguelike maps can be made.

All in all, one of my favourites!

I am generally anti-DoubleFine nowadays due to their predatory business practices(releasing unfinished games for full price, never going back to fix them, etc), but I was gifted this game recently.  Being a turn based strategy fan(X-Com acolyte, Fire Emblem slave, etc) I was actually pretty excited about Massive Chalice.  The reviews are good, it has all the flavor of a DoubleFine game which to me is one of their best selling points, and it seemed like a unique and interesting take on the genre - I was a fool. A FOOL!  DoubleFine's honeyed potion suckered me in again, and I wish it hadn't.
The idea is neat - generations of heroes who you can choose to rule, run guilds or fight - and worth elaborating on.  The idea that your heroes have flaws and perks, and you can choose over time how your heroes evolve via bloodlines?  Brilliant. Building and researching and making new items and using unique buildings is, in theory, a great way to spend some time. However, this game is - like most other DoubleFine titles recently - incredibly shallow and gimmicky.  Their titles seem to rely solely on one or two gameplay mechanics and play more like tech demos instead of full fledged games; battles come at random intervals(really?  Are we still doing random battles in the 2010s?) as your kingdom progresses - and when it shows up, instead of something you get jazzed about playing through, the combat is slow, sloggy and boring.  You have very few options(hit a thing, shoot a thing, throw a bomb, or lesser-damage variations of those themes that include knockback), and even your hybrid class characters are lame mishmashes of their predecessors - would you like a shooty guy that also throws potions?  Or a potion guy that also hits things?  Or how about a thing-hitty guy that also sometimes shoots?  And every time I got a new thing researched and got excited for the gameplay to evolve... it just didn't.  Then it was wait some more, more boring combat, wait some more, more boring combat, repeat ad nauseum.
There are no incentives for furthering the bloodlines or making hybrid heroes since they all feel the same anyway: minor variations on the basic melee/range/support classes of stereotypes past.  Even researching new tech in this game - which should be a slam dunk for ANY game of this type - falls flat, as you can only research one thing at a time AND the thing researched generally doesn't add any gameplay value.  Slightly stronger weapons/armor/heals, items with negligible and limited use during gameplay.
If you want a game that is an occasional 45 minute time waster when there's nothing else to do, go for Massive Chalice.  If you want a well thought out and executed turn based strategy game, look elsewhere; Massive Chalice is the shovelware title with the pretty, primary colors that grandma buys fromthe bargain bin for Christmas.  It should come packaged with a generic hidden objects game and a collect-a-thon mascot platformer, to round out the experience.

is a new platformer that utilizes the wind as its main driving force throughout all levels. There are five different worlds with around three distinct sections per world. These sections are called acts which are one way of labeling levels in certain platformers. Also, there are five special levels, one, consisting of a level taken from the Binding of Isaac. The main character in Talewind represents a pilot of some particular kind. We live in a village at the bottom of a mountain; our main goal is to climb the mountain and restore the normal wind speed toward our village and people. This task is rather hard because the wind has decreased exponentially and has continued to decline as all of the levels progress. Talewind takes patience, proficient motor skills that are precise, and accurate pinpoint timing since it places a limit in the whole game to one combat move.

gives a very different perspective towards the meaning of high difficulty in platformers. Unlike traditional two-dimensional platformers,
enemies are simplified; all enemies have a specific pattern, but they are easy first-hand to spot. Okay, since that is the case, then what makes Talewind stand out from other modern-day platformers regarding its gameplay and mechanics involved? There are a few examples that come to my mind when I think of the wind mechanics used in
. The wind is used as a propeller machine to get us to higher ledges, platforms, and areas. There are three main different pathways in which the wind flows. The first pathway, characterized through straight travel, left-to-right movement of the main character and up and down as the wind curves along a horizontal based axis similar to
,
and
.
The second pathway the wind flows is rather in a zigzag pattern. It flows diagonally, increasing the velocity and time it takes to reach the other side. This certain pathway is found most in the third world called the Fieg Snowpeaks. In other words, the first snow level in the game we have that has snowmen buried in the ground, a sasquatch looking creature that hops forward standing in our way and icy glaciers that can make us lose our balance.  If we travel too far and glide, instead of letting go when the wind propels us, each time we will overshoot it and hit the spikes underneath. However, if we let the wind naturally guide us, we will never hit the spikes on each level. The third pathway and my favorite, giving the game its initial excitement, are the loops. The loops function like
that delivers the most precision and incredible speed in the entire game. Sometimes, as in the case in World 3, there is a quadruple loop.
Our character moves throughout a simple layout of controls. How simple? Well, let’s just say that the controls are so simplified that even an animal without a human brain could understand the controls. The controls are stripped down to the very basic of all platformer controls: jump, float, air bast ( whirlwind of air that harnesses crystal energy), and, finally, glide. The controls are very protrusive, or archaic that forms a knockback when approaching enemies. The controls using a gamepad, either an Xbox One or an Xbox 360 controller for the personal computer. They are some of the worst controls I have seen all-year considering all the other platformer games this year that have released for the personal computer.
I wish I could get past the horrible controls and tell you that it has not taken away from my first experience of enjoying this game. However, if I were to inform you that everything was fine, I would be indirectly lying to you. The controls mechanics are not well-designed, although the controls are responsive, doing what the controls are meant to do in the game within the constraints of the actuation force it takes for the floating and jumping to be precise. I have played a handful of platform games now on the personal computer with a Xbox 360 controller, my favorite all-time video game console based controller. However,
does not have that smooth of an experience as I was hoping for when it comes to how the controls feel when I press the corresponding buttons in-game. It feels very contrived as if the developer failed to realize that most gamers do not want to have to approach most enemies within two inches of them for the air bast combat skill to work. There is no variety when it comes to hammering down enemies.
Consequently, because of this one minor flaw, it makes the rest of the game’s strengths stand out immensely in comparison. The air bast mechanism should not be a primary move and the only move you can pull off in Talewind to kill enemies. The rules are impeccable. I cannot change the rules nor the fact that how much I would have liked to jump on the heads of enemies, it is impossible for me to do so. If I decide to go this route, each time I get killed which has no bearing according to my accuracy and my judiciousness. These use of poor mechanics forces both me and all of you who are reading this and wondering if you should buy this game, whether it is worth it or not. The developers coerce me without thinking about us, the gamer playing their game. WindLimit tells me that I have to use air bast to defeat enemies, yet I have no secondary long-range combat options. I have to place myself in immediate danger in the path of enemies with an eighty-percent chance I might get killed doing so because I can only fire,at most, two to three inches in length.

EDIT: Shortly after I wrote my review, the devs released an update that took away the Lives system, making half of my criticism obsolete. Im now forced to change my recommendation to a positive one, and you can skip the second half of my review.
Platforming has been a quintessential genre in videogames ever since we figured out that making something jump over a pit successfully was immensely fun, and there hasn’t been a better time to indulge in that feeling than the indie videogame age we live in. Maybe it’s because the idea of jumping is easily translatable to videogames, or that today’s developers grew up on 8-bit and 16-bit old platformers, but there is a huge saturation of these games in the indie scene. What was once a fairly dead genre has now been resurrected to its fullest with a huge variety of games that experiment with the conventional tropes and mechanics of jumping while also grabbing at your nostalgia for those simpler times. Today, we look at the next in line in this revival, Talewind.
First thing that strikes you right away about Talewind when you boot it up is its presentation. Be it the main character’s simple and cute design and animation, or the green hills whose grass sway with the wind while a soothing and fun soundtrack plays, the game sets the tone right away for a good ol’ time to be had, and wastes no time giving you control after a very brief and unobtrusive tutorial. Levels, NPCs and enemies all feel like drawings come to life like Braid, and the soundtrack, while fairly generic and sometimes repetitive, is pleasant to the ears and fitting.
Talewind separates itself from the majority of its peers by including a gliding mechanic, which lets you have a much tighter and longer air control. Besides this mechanic, it’s the regular platformer where you have a jump and an attack button. You will spend most of your time jumping and gliding over pits and enemies at a brisk pace, with the occasional wind current to launch you into the air and speed you up to the finish goal. Levels are incredibly open-ended and offer a lot of optional routes for you to take, rewarding you for your skills, which is always a plus for a platformer to have in my book. Talewind also uses the archaic lives system, where you have to start the level all over if you lose all of your lives. Nothing wrong with that system, but it might frustrate some players, especially in the latter levels.
Not much can be said about the gameplay department, if you have played any platformer in your lifetime, you know what to expect from this. As for narrative thrust, Talewind tells you that the wind is getting weaker and it’s up to you to figure out why. That’s it. This in no way is a criticism of the game, as I feel that if you don’t have a meaningful or interesting story to tell in a platformer whose main appeal is it’s gameplay, then you shouldn’t force one in it at all, as that would make the game weaker and obtrusive in my opinion. There is however some recurring stone monuments you can find spread along the levels that will give you bits and pieces of the lore of this world, which you can piece together to form a bigger picture of the story. Personally, I found these incredibly uninteresting and cliché, and soon stopped searching and reading them and focused on the gameplay instead, but it's there if that sort of thing interests you.
If I stopped the review right here, I would probably recommend the game and call it a harmless platformer that you should buy and have a good amount of entertainment taken out from it. But I’m going to continue, and I’ll tell you now why you shouldn’t buy this game.
I forgot to mention that this is a one-hit kill platformer. You get hit, you die and start over from the last checkpoint you passed by. Now, there is nothing wrong with that, but when you make a game where you get killed with just one hit, you better have the level design perfectly synced with that idea. And the balance between those two factors can either make or break a game.
Levels are divided by 3 acts, the last one being the boss of the area. Those first two acts are long levels that could take over 5 minutes easily if you don’t already know what you are doing. Getting to a boss and losing your last life to it, means starting the whole level all over again, which adds up to 10 minutes of wasted time, and considering that the levels get longer and harder as you progress, frustration and boredom is bound to set in.
This alone is no reason to not recommend the game, there is nothing wrong with a videogame being challenging and demanding of a player, so I’ll get to the main reason why this game didn’t do it for me.
“Game Feel”. Discussing such a subjective term is very difficult, since it’s own definition is subjective itself. Game feel is when the screen shakes and flashes when you kill someone with a bat in Hotline Miami, it’s when your body move slightly off the chair when you make a hard jump in Super Mario Bros. ,  it’s when the games slows down for a second before the final impact of a combo in God of War.
Pretty much, game feel is what makes gameplay fun. It’s something intangible that causes a positive response from a player. And Talewind severely lacks that response. Once the game starts to get challenging, it soon becomes a slog. Jumping doesn’t feel fun, your character moves extremely slow, and the wind currents, the only moments of the game where you feel some sort of adrenaline, are simply too few and far between and not creative enough.
The gliding mechanic is just not used to it’s fullest, and only serves as a way of maintaining some air control. You only need to compare it to Super Mario World’s gliding cape to see how much potential for gameplay depth is wasted.
It also has a very unforgiving hitbox that constantly makes each death a moment of “it didn’t even hit me!”.  Getting hit in this game doesn’t feel right, it’s sterile and dull, and half the time you are left wondering if it was even fair or not. It doesn’t help that the last levels are filled with killing spikes a-la Megaman and enemies who give you no time of reaction unless you already know they are there.
Add all of this to the one-hit kill mechanic and long levels, and you have an incredibly monotonous experience, and the combination of all these elements are what break the game for me.
There is a reason why Super Mario Bros. worked and something like Bubsy didn’t. One perfectly understood that a one-hit kill system required short levels and precise, fun and player expressive controls, while the other was content with filling the small screen with a variety of enemies and confusing sprawling levels that killed you with every sprint you took. The same reason that made Sonic be able to stay alive if he kept at least one ring.
It feels incredibly unfair to rag on the “little guy”, but when you have such games as Super Meat Boy, Fez and Shovel Knight coming out of small dev teams, you can’t just give a free pass to other games of similar origins, especially when the price tag is this steep.  Overall, I think your money should be spent elsewhere, especially with so many games out there.

I have not finished the game yet. I played through the first 3 acts so far (9 levels). But here are my thoughts from what I have played:
Pros:
Talewind is a lot of fun to play, epecially with a controller. The gameplay is very smooth.
The graphics are very beautiful. The world really feels alive and fluid.
The levels are very well designed, with many alternate paths to take.
Great music as well.
Very challenging - It can take many tries to complete a level and many more to master it.
Lot of replay value - You have goals such as: beat the level in a certain amount of time, collect a certain amout of feathers and find a hidden crystal. If you collect all of them for a certain act, it looks like it will unlock a secret level.
Cons:
The music, while nice, can get a little repetative.
It seemed to be lacking in story early on. There is a strong setting, There are a few people in town that talk to you and some rocks that you can find in the levels that tell you history about the world. but not much I found beyond that. (Perhaps there is more later in the game)
Limited sound effects. It seems like the character should be making noise when he jumps, lands or walks, but he's completely silent. (Correction: The jumpng and walking sound effects are just really quite compared to other sound effects.)
Very Challenging - The challenge can be frustrating at times. Since it's one hit kill, it can feel very unforgiving. If you lose all your lives, you have to replay the whole act (3 levels) which gets longer as you get further in the game (Edit: Latest patch removed lives, so this is no longer a concern). It's nice that you can skip to an act, but I couldn't find a way to skip to a specific level within the act.
If you like beautiful and challenging platformers with fluid controls, this game is for you.
If you want engaging story or get frustrated easily, this game might not be for you.

Retro shooter with minor visual facelift
PRO:
+ Original gameplay, focus on (subtle) visual improvements (but don't expect crisp textures or high-poly models)
+ Eight huge levels which are motivating to explore (to find secrets, parts of a super weapon, keys...)
+ Deactivation of nausea-inducing head/turn/underwater bobbing is possible via menu
+ Great retro jungle atmosphere with fitting (even though a bit repetitive) soundtrack
CON:
- Some annoying jump sequences (failure often has lethal consequences)
- No option to manually switch between ammo types (e.g. Tek arrows vs normal arrows)
- No quicksave or manual save feature (relies on checkpoints and fixed points where you can save)
- Bosses are rather easy to beat (circle-strafing is enough to avoid getting hit), but take tons of damage
- Repetitive levels due to restricted amount of textures/enemies
- Minimalistic story and protagonist remains almost completely silent (besides "I am Turok!" one-liner)
Verdict:
Nice retro shooter which has been updated in a subtle way to add some eye candy and remove a few annoyances of the original. Unfortunately, core weaknesses of the title from 1997 are still there: Visually, the game hasn't aged well at all, the jumping parts are not enjoyable, a quicksave feature is missing and the lack of a real story leaves you a bit clueless sometimes. If you can ignore all this, you still get a rock-solid, fast-paced shooter with huge levels, lots of weapons and tons of enemies to kill.

As you can see from my hours played, this is a game that I actually enjoy. The cardplay is innovative; cards you've played in earlier rounds  get stronger  and 'level up' in later rounds. This adds a great deal of strategic depth as ones must decide whether to trade off one card's immediate utility against another's future 'leveled up' usefulness. I've seen a great many deck types have success, and the available drat-style games are different enough from the constructed variety that there's a great deal of fun to be had here. Why then the thumb's down?
---- One design decision alone: When a game starts, each player is given 20 minutes to complete his game. Usually, at the start oif a game, eaxh player moves relatively quickly. However, when one player appears to gain an advantage, VERY often the other will begin to use the time on the clock as a strategic resource. By this I mean, you'll play 10 turns in fairly rapid succession, each using only a minute or two of time. Then, one player pulls ahead and then will wait 10-15-17 minutes for the other player to move. He may be hoping you'll have lost interest, or just to catch you unawares, attempting to win via boredom what he cannot through skill. This effect is compounded by the fact that one can have a large number of games open at one time.  In constructed deck play, you are rewarded daily through three victories, and sealed deck takes 4 games to complete. Ineither style, prepare to devote majo amounts of time waiting, staring at an unmoving screen, before you can finish up.
Apart from this, the game itself is well-designed and fun to play., It is possible to be competitive without spending real money, though it can take a little patience. The trade-off here is cash vs. time to build reaonable decks, but the mechanic is fair. No real complaints on that score.

I wouldn't recommend this game. The concept of something weird happening on another planet got me interested. I was hoping for the great immersion, tricky story, something different. Sure, the concept is great but the way they delivered this idea - not so. Maybe i get hyped too easily.
What I've got?
Long walks on uninteresting terrain. The landscape doesn't even have any level of detail in most places. It's just as if the level designer put one, big plane, and applied one heightmap on it. I never thought I would see such smooth cliffs. Simple rocks scattered around, smaller and bigger, and more spiky edges could greatly improove the looks.
Story - The lack of exciting things turned me off. I didn't finish the game. Of course I wasn't hoping for AAA quality cutscenes, but the story turned... bland. I remember the trailer, the mystery, the "WTF". It turned out to be the audiobook with text logs and unskippable russian journal.
Level design - sometimes sucks at explaining "what to do next". I remember getting stuck once. For about 20 minutes I was trying to figure out what was I missing. Check through the keyboard instructions, to see if I missed some hist to "press X key" - nope, nothing. I ended up looking up youtube "let's plays" to see if anyone was stuck in the same place as me. Took another 10 minutes before finally realising that I should turn around, go WAAAAAY back the level to pick up some item, hidden somewhere on the second floor of uninteresting looking building...
Performance - I don't think they did any major performance optimisation. The game generally runs smoothly but there was this one, maybe two places where I encountered lower FPS. The whole level loads up and is being rendered as is, without any render distance limit. I suffered 15 FPS just by looking in the fog. The game was rendering/calculating everything that was behind that fog (couple of buildings and props) even if I couldn't see them. I don't recall seeing any LOD being used either (which could greatly help), although I don't remember closely inspecting the screen.

First and foremost, I played through the game with autoaim off and a gamepad. Aiming in the 3D plane felt like luck entirely. Secondly, the pickup placements. They seem by and large useless. I spent most of the game going from objecting to objective, only able to pickup the usual grenade and foam expansion. After obtaining a certain item, I was suddenly able to collect all the previously skipped health and armour pickups. Furthermore, with enough pickups, I essentially became invincible late game (while playing on the second hardest difficulty). I found the overall difficulty curve very unrewarding at the beginning, losing 75% hp if I were unlucky with enemies hitting every shot. A particular example is obtaining the final weapon at the 95% completion mark.
In terms of story, it is worse than none. A seemingly innocent hiking date turns into
. I believe playing this game completely without cutscenes and only objective markers would make for a better experience.
There are way better options for Metroidvania games on Steam, such as Guacamelee, Axiom Verge, Valdis Story or Ori and the Blind Forest, in favour of this title. If you're a fan of the genre and played everything available on PC and on the respective console emulators, this title might be worth considering. Otherwise, it is a very poorly designed video game with the face of a Metroidvania.

Combat mechanics are a lot of fun. The story is tolerable at best and quite skippable, but basically you'll want to be playing for the tactical combat. The strategic layer is mostly just stressful (especially due to limited time and not having all of the objectives at the beginning of the chapter) rather than really enjoyable.
That said, the tactical combat is really quite good. The characters are very diverse with abilities that typically let each of them fill different roles. The passive equips can make a pretty huge difference in how you use the characters. The enemies are pretty distinct and mobility is an enormous part of the tactics. The AI is fairly predictable, which is both good and bad - it makes it possible to come up with good plans but it also makes certain combats somewhat repetitive.
Despite some of the complaints, I found that RNG plays almost no part if you plan carefully. In particular, the main hero has an ability that can debuff an enemy so that any further attacks will not miss; this ability combined with careful positioning can lead to never having to worry about key misses. Later on, you can equip passive abilities that increase chance to hit to the point where misses aren't an issue even without the debuff, opening up tactical options to some degree.
Mainly the tactical combat is extremely dependent on positioning. Your characters are generally relatively fragile with no real way to heal consistently; you simply can't trade blows. Instead, you have to use positioning and turn delays to get off alpha strikes before enemies can hit you while avoiding enemies you can't kill. Skills that can create obstacles or summons are thus extremely strong and you will likely want to build some strategies around those. Likewise having an appropriately diverse portfolio of initiatives (instead of just everyone being as fast as possible) is often a key part of success.
Other good thing is that XP is party-wide, so you don't really have to worry about characters falling behind (except, to a minor degree, gear). I do wish you could select from your entire roster instead of limiting yourself to 5 or 6 per expedition, but it works okay.

I've only played the first two acts (out of five), but here's what I thought of it so far:
* Everything that touches you kills you instantly, which adds to the challenge.
* On the other hand, enemies also die with one shot (except for bosses).
* There are checkpoints every now and then. They look pretty awesome and are quite useful.
* It seems the level designs is inspired by Sonic levels, i.e. you have multiple paths, which is good. There are timerun challenges and collection challenges.
* You start with 15 lives. When you run out of lives, you start in the town again. You can visit the second house and jump into any acts that you've visited.
* I played with a PS3 controller. The controls have a good amount of weight to them, but I wish the shooting had a bit less of a delay between shots.
* I wish there were upgrades or power ups to spice things up.
* Animations are cute and detailed. The world in general has been crafted with love.
* Music is okay. Sound could use a bit more work, I think, but it does the job.
* Bosses are HARD. Especially the second one, because it summons worms all over the place. And worms jump at you in random directions.

* Framerate is super smooth and I have everything set to ultra.
* One thing I'd change: I pressed L2 accidentally, which resets your progress in the current act! A confirmation popup of some sort would be helpful.
Give it a try, if you like a challenging old-school platformer. (:

Lots of new features in there and a complete new way into combat. When the game is finished it might be a good one but for now, there are too many turnoffs.
On the bright side, nice lighting, decent sound and great ambience.
On the neutral side (I haven’t made up my mind on this), the physics… well physics are kind of cool, the idea of damage calculated based on strength, speed, momentum. That’s what made me buy the game. On the other side, when messing with physics, you need to keep in mind the level of control you actually have with a mouse & keyboard. In real life, I can twist around obstacle, adjust my balance, quickly side step, jump or push things around. In this game, you’ll randomly fall because you were running over a pile of junk or suddenly stopped by a box corner you just barely touched or worst, your torch will get stuck in an “invisible something” which won’t allow you free movement while in the middle of combat!
On the bad side:
1) That new combat system really needs some polishing. It's nice to be physic based. Good job guys. But the level of randomness in what you actually do in combat renders it highly frustrating. Yeah, yeah I can hear you "you need to practice in the arena..." Well, know this, I did and I was getting ok so I decided to jump in the game. After all, I bought an adventure not an arena…
2) the AI is again... too random. You go around passing by "passive zombies" and suddenly one of them gets a craving for your brains... So you've been walking around for about an hour without a single fight and all of the sudden, here you are with 2-3 zombies on your back. Well, only one was really aggressive, but guess what?! you don't exactly "target" what you're attacking so, you end up smashing one of the passive and he doesn't really appreciate the hostility...
3) The real killer is that “no save game” feature. To go down this path, you need a perfectly balanced game. Not a huge random death generator like the actual game. There’s no fun in replaying the game 4 times because of a random encounter, random hit or a random AI decision has killed you.
So in one sentence: “This preview is on the right path but it needs major polishing!”

I really wish I could recommend this game, and there are certainly good elements present in this game. The story is interesting, though hardly revolutionary, and the setting and atmosphere are absolutely fantastic. Granted, I'm a big fan of mafia-type stories or stories involving secret organizations in general. And the gameplay can be fun for a while as you try to expand your criminal business. But there's one big, overwhelming flaw to this game: it's damned near impossible to lose. You don't face competition from rival mobs, and the few obstacles you face are a joke. It got to the point where my biggest worry was whether I would have enough time to build all the buildings I wanted before I inevitably won. I don't need the game to be the next Dark Souls, but a little challenge can make victory feel very rewarding. As it stands, victory just feels cheap.
Overall, while this game can be fun for a while, it eventually gets tiring to start up a new level and the only worry on your mind is whether you'll win too quickly. If you really love the prohibition-era setting and stories involving old-school organized crime, then you might find it worth it to pick up this game if it's on sale for 5 dollars. Otherwise, I'd give it a pass, though it breaks my heart to say it.

A Note before this begins: This is my very first Steam Review. Coupled with the fact I'm rather poor at giving feedback, I apologize in advance for this review's probably not being up to par with most peoples'. I'll be returning to this review to alter and add onto it, as I am oft wont to do; and just as well, as a read of what is below will demonstrate that in a single session, I cannot compose anything even remotely approaching the standards of an acceptably comprehensive body.
Disclaimer: This review is based wholly upon my own experience and opinion of the game. I do not claim to speak for anyone else, nor presume to, nor do I believe my opinion to be factual, nor any closer to objective truth than anyone else's. I entrust the reader to understand this applies to the whole of the review, including sentences wherein clauses that disclaim this are absent.
___
Like more than a few 90's kids, I definitely met the Battle Card Genre growing up. The Pokemon Trading Card Game; Yu-Gi-Oh; Digimon; and many more battle card games caught the interest of so many others in my age group (and beyond, even!). All of these were very popular, I took a look at all of them- and I never took to any of them. The Battle Card game genre was simply not for me, and still largely hasn't been.
Even so, there's been something interesting about the genre and many of its products in my opinion, even from a distance. So I've spent time of late looking for one that I might be able to enjoy. Countless ones, I've read of, seen numerous demonstrations for, and found myself uninterested in, just like old times.
Then, the two nights preceding the one wherein I write this review, I gave it another try. I found two very interesting prospective games. One, is Infinity Wars. It looks amazing, and I'd love to try it, but it commands space my potato cannot provide.
The other is SolForge.
Well, I installed it last night, started playing today, and if my impressions must be expressed in a single sentence, let it be this: I, someone who has never played a battle card game before, like, perhaps even am finding love for, this game.
I must start with the gameplay itself. As most reading this probably know, the game's playing area consists of ten spaces in a five-by-two arrangement. One strip of five is used by each of the two players; each space can be occupied by a card. In my opinion, this provides enough room for strategy to truly matter, while at the same time not intimidating a player as the presentation of a vast field can sometimes do. This having been said, a somewhat claustrophobic feeling often sets in when placing a card, adding a feeling of tension that can throw a player off-focus- which, in my opinion, is very satisfying to focus through the fog of.
Cards come in two variants: Creature and Spell. Creature cards have two statistics, Attack Power and Health, and most of them have a special ability (and/or multiple ones, in the case of some cards) There are four main factions, each with its own pool of cards. Once again, simplicity that provides room for complexity.
There are many other rules of the game that I'd love to individually praise, but I realize this is dragging on. I'll probably return to add onto the list and give my critique of each element of the gameplay that I can in kind on one of the aforementioned review edits I'm bound to do. Until then, let us move on.
The instilling of a feeling of tension mentioned in the paragraph about the playing field is just as well, as the cards in this game represent troops fighting and dying within the game's fictional universe. That brings me to what I'd like to talk about next: The appeal thereof.
In my opinion, the creators of this game have done a splendid job of making the lore and universe of this game very interesting. Each of the four main factions has its own unique characters, locations, and (most notably in my mind) culture and elements there-comprising, including their own unique ideals, established government, and general mindset toward life, the world, and even to each other. If you are interested, I'd advise to go to the developers' official website for the game and read their lore section. The descriptions there are highly descriptive, and will give you an idea of the world one is stepping into. There are no direct third-person descriptions of such nature in the game itself, ironically, nor any link to the official website- something I have mixed feelings about.
Even though direct explanations are not provided in the game itself, the game's universe does shine through- and how! In the campaign modes, the "Info" bubbles often relay colorful descriptions of the setting in which your avatar (you?) find(s) her/him/yourself, and/or interactions with the culture of the given faction that one will be facing off against.
Additionally, and in my opinion most noticeably, the images on the cards themselves associated with each faction give insight into the creatures, constructs, and, in particular, the people and, again, culture of that faction. In my eyes and mind, the characters themselves, their attire, their stances and activities, anything they might be holding, the setting each one is portrayed in, even the variations between the images for the different variations in each card, each and all seem to portray living beings with stories to tell, things to show, and a culture/environment/etc. to go back to after the dust of battle has settled. I find myself imagining what they do in peace-time, and in different situations, what a day in each one's life is like. Numerous specific examples swarm my mind, which I've been tripping over myself on my keyboard trying to type as examples, before finally deciding to leave it at this and hope it is moderately acceptable in the way of portraying my opinion of the developers' success. As I look at this paragraph, I am aghast at the degree to which I have utterly failed to express my true wonderment, and opinion of the importance that each card's image plays in picturing the fictional universe. Perhaps I'll come back and go into further detail.
On this note, the artistry of the images themselves is, in my opinion, utterly breathtaking. Even outside of what it does in communicating each character's place in the fictional universe and as an extension thereof, there is much, in my opinion, to be admired. The lighting, shading, and coloration of each item and creature make each one feasible to visualize existing and moving in real, three-dimensional space, even with the obvious fantastical flair of the objects and creatures themselves.
There are other elements of this game that are meritorious of praise. I also fully intend to go back and add onto, edit, and otherwise adjust each and every paragraph to be more descriptive, and adhere more loyally to the purpose of describing the experience that I have with this game. Additionally, there are numerous elements of the game I've not yet experienced, such any of the campaign missions beyond the first four, or the Multiplayer mode.
From one who never liked battle card games before, and is still wary of them for the most part, this game receives a hearty recommendation. If you're interested in battle card games, and/or otherwise turn-based strategy, and you have five-hundred Megabytes to spare on your hard drive, I would recommend giving this game a try. Though there are card packs for sale (none of which I've yet patronized), the game itself is free of monetary cost. Worst case scenario, uninstall if you don't like, no less the wealthy for having tried it.

The game has some very innovative and intriguing mechanics that differentiate it from the TCG genre. Principally the lack of any 'resource' generation and the 'leveling' of cards, allowing for more powerful versions to be played in later rounds. However, it suffers from three major flaws:
1) If you are interested in deck building and/or competitive constructed play, don't bother unless you intend to throw down a significant amount of money, or are patient enough to wait (playing every single day) for several years (and even then, you likely won't have close to a full play-set of all the key cards you'll need to play at the top level).
2) RNG is a massive determinant in games. While this helps keeps mediocre players 'competitive,' it's very frustrating to have game after game decided by a series of bad draws.
3) Power creep. New cards are frequently just reprints of old ones with superior abilities, completely invalidating the older sets. Rather than augmenting existing decks or adding new and interesting folds to the metagame, they simply obsolete everything that has come before.
Draft format helps with this somewhat, but without spending real money, you're only looking to play a handful of times per week.
While these troubles aren't necessarily peculiar to this game compared to many other competitors in the TCG genre, it is enough to keep me from being able to recommend it.

I confess to not having played Turok in its heyday, not having any particular interest in anything involving dinosaurs, though really, I'm honestly not sure why I never played it. I decided to pick it up in the recent summer sale based on numerous recommendations from a friend, who frequently uses it as a point of reference when discussing other games.
For those unfamiliar, Turok began as a comic book in the '60s, concerning Native American warriors accidentially finding their way into a realm known as the "Lost Land", a land forgotten by time, populated with extremely irate dinosaurs. This was kept intact with the 90s reboot by Acclaim Comics, which added aliens and advanced technology into the mix, and told a story of a family line of these warriors, the Fireseeds, and their taking up the mantle of "Turok", Son of Stone, to face the Lost Land's many dangers. This first videogame adaptation concerns a man later identified as Tal'Set, who would reappear in a prequel, Turok: Evolution.
From what I can tell, Turok 1 was considered by some reviewers to be derivitive, praised for its graphics but largely regarded simply as a "doom clone." In particular, the PC version was seen by some reviewers as inferior to Quake. Considering it's largely more of a console game, having released on Nintendo 64 first, this doesn't seem to me like a fair comparison. Others later lauded it as a "system-selling franchise" that established that PC was not the "exclusive realm" of good FPSes. In retrospect, such an assessment may have been premature.
Regardless, Turok 1, and in particular, this Night Dive rerelease, shines through mostly in its controls. I can't speak for the original PC release, but this one handles so well its scarcely feels like im playing a console game, permitting me to straferun and jump with the best of them. It also runs very well, subject to none of the frame loss and distance fog issues of its original N64 incarnation. It does have anumber of odd console-game features, such as its extensive platforming sections, limited lives and fixed save points. My few deaths were found in the bottomless pits, and I can't say I miss that particular aspect of the era. Nor am I particularly enamoured of the game's cryptic item placement. As a child playing things like the Doom and Quake demos, which comprised early, comparitively easy-to-navigate levels, Turok would have driven me up a goddamn wall. It reminded me oddly of Dark Forces II: Jedi Knight, which actually had much more awkward platforming. I don't think less of the game now given easy access to guides, but the game does stand out as an example of a very different era in level design. There's also absolutely no story text or narrative cutscenes anywhere in the game, which even Doom and Quake managed a bare minimum of.
Thankfully Turok also delivers a wide array of nasty weapons and enemies, eclectic and colorful environment design, thematically appropriate music, and some fairly well-executed boss fights. It also has a well-executed hub system with seamless level transisitions, permitting the player to freely explore available areas at will. Compared to the dark and dreary castles and temples of Quake 1, and the grim and gritty military complexes and canyons of Quake 2, Turok's visuals stand out. The hub-based level design is also executed far more smoothly here then in Quake 2, in which one becomes hopelessly lost quite easily.
Turok occupies an important place in the history of singleplayer FPS and this release is certainly worth a purchase.

I'm somewhere around 700-800 hours of playtime, since iOS progress isn't calculated. I've played the game DAILY since January 2014 on iOS, when the deck customization was implemented to the game.
SolForge is one of the two actually proper digital card games around for the people looking for depth in mechanics. The other would be Battle Decks, not Hearthstone, but let's not go there now...
-30 card deck
-Draw 5 cards on each turn
-Start with rank 1 (tech level in game)
-Played card gets a leveled up version to your discard pile
-Each rank consists 4 turns for each player
-Discard pile and the rest of the draw deck gets shuffled when new rank (tech level) begins
-Based on actual effects and combinations, instead of flat out power/health of the cards
-Most of the cards are capped to rank 3, but these are few that have rank 4 as well (not necessarely better)
The table consists 5 lanes. Creatures attack the players, which both have 100 health at the start. The goal is obviously to get that to zero. If there's a creature at the opposing lane, the damage is exchanged. The damage is permanent and not healed on turns.
The reward mechanic is VERY fair for a F2P game. There are no premium only -cards.
1) You get a booster (or better) reward as daily login and silver worth around ~333% of a booster.
2) From a first daily win, you get a draft ticket worth 4 boosters.
3) From a third win, you get a similar reward as daily login - booster (or better) and silver worth ~33% of a booster.
4) Each win also gives you 250 silver, which is 5% of a booster price.
5) With 3 draft tickets, you get to enter a draft where you KEEP the 30 cards you draft. On top of that, you play 4 matches and get better rewards depending on how you succeed. Minimum reward is 4 boosters on top of the 30 drafted cards, which eg. include all the legendary cards in the game.
The only real downside is that the legendaries from the past few sets have been power creeped. Legendaries used to be very situational, but the fact that there are now quite a few lengedaries that work.
I suggest you play the game on iPad. That works wonderfully.

TL;DR review here: All major flaws in the original have been fixed, so if you're a fan of sidescrollers or MetroidVania games, buy this masterpiece of video game development. It's a display of what video games SHOULD be on release day; properly tested and 99% bug free. No rating is high enough, and a full price of $16 is perfectly fair for this gem.
Longer review:
This remaster of Shadow Complex finally fixed a major bug in the original game; getting one of the major, hidden items in the game caused the final cutscene to screw up with Jason's head and hair being covered by an untextured ball. The fix was to just fully show his face in this version, which actually works out better for that final scene, so that bug got squashed.
The main menu music, while always great, is even better in this version, as it's now a great electronic remix of the original violin music. This is really small, I know, but I still found it to be a nice touch and addition to an already astounding game.
Onto the game itself. It's a 2.5D MetroidVania game. A huge map with lots of hidden passages and items, plus full 3D environments where enemies can come from the background but are still able to be targeted and killed. A few points in the game also change the view entirely to give you a full 3D perspective on the player character, Jason's, point of view. Like any good MetroidVania, there are areas and passages locked by doors that require certain weapons or items, as well as upgrades to your main weapon, which has unlimited ammo as per the genre, but as a modern-era shooter, your guns do require reloading. Traps exist throughout the environment to use against enemies, the bosses are unique and one interesting thing is a couple are actually optional unless you're going for that 100% item collection. The enemies themselves have voices and radios, meaning that in some situations, stealth will help you by keeping enemies from being alerted and thus causing more enemies to rush to your location. Other enemies can be skipped entirely, or heard while crawling through a vent above them or sneaking under the bridge they're standing on.
The biggest con with Shadow Complex is its length. It could be a lot bigger, but remember, this was an Xbox Live Arcade title back when XBLA was just starting to really get off the ground and each game gave players a lot for very little. This game is only about 1gb in size, and is packed with a decent (if short) story, a large semi-open world, a plethora of items to collect and secrets to discover, and a variety of enemies in a very near-future setting. Basically, this has everything a good MetroidVania game should have, with no real bugs or glitches to speak of.
I want to be more critical with this review, but the game has aged very well despite maybe lip-syncing that a little bit rough, but this game is an example of good development, with the only game-breaking 'bug' to speak of (if it's even still in this remaster) being that there's a couple points where you can pick up an upgrade to an item before you have the item it upgrades, and doing so prevents you from getting one other item to allow you the full 100% rating on that single playthrough.
I don't really like to do ratings, but for those of you that might need one, this is a rare, unsarcastic, completely serious 10/10. If you like MetroidVania games, get this damn masterpiece.

Had high hopes for this game based on the claim of "metroidvania" and the great reviews over the years. Was excited that this game finally came out on PC as I thought it would never come. However, after playing this game I was throughly let down. This game is nowhere near the caliber of and is actually vastly inferior to games made 30 years ago such as: Metroid (NES), Super Metroid, Super Mario Bros., Contra (NES), Castlevania:SotN. Control mechanics are atrocious: very floaty, imprecise, and clunky. The game isn't necessarily difficult to play because of it, but just isn't honed enough to make this a fun fine-tuned run 'n gun platformer in the style of the games mentioned above. You can tell right away when you start walking and jumping around - just absolute slop.
The game is also billed as a platformer. Platformers require tight, responsive, and precise controls; this game just doesn't have it.
Games of this type which I actually recommend: Oniken, Odallus, Bionic Commando:Rearmed, Exile's End (cheap budget but way better than this junk), Axiom Verge, Super Cyborg (Contra-like), Strider, Vulgar the Viking, maybe Shovel Knight etc.
Game is also bloated with crappy cut-scene story... yes, you CAN skip them, but why should I even have to bother with getting my game interrupted?
I would maybe buy this game for $2.50, but $15 is exceedingly too much. I am in the process of requesting a refund.

Starbound is great in all the ways Terraria isnt. On myold account I had played Terraria for close to 500 hours so I have some experience with 2d sandbox games. Firstly, Starbound is 64bit so you arent limited to only 4gb of ram (that is shared by all other 32bit programs) like Terraria. This means you can have much more mods, much bigger worlds and less memory limitation issues. Secondly it has more content to offer. The weapons and mobs are randomy generated to an extent (even more so if you install mods). There are an almost infinite amount of planets to explore and each planet is the size of a terraria medium sized world. So you will never run out of supplies or building area. Now enough of my comparisons to Terraria. This game has some AMAZING moments. Like when I built a solar system sized empire because three of the planets orbiting the star had mega villages on them. I would recommend NOT to google any tips or gameplay of the game before you play as it will ruin the surprise of it. I have been playing blind and learning as I go and it makes the game 100% better. Another recommendation is to install Frackin Universe mod as well as the Mega Weapons pack for more variability and content (although not needed as it is awesome on its own).

HI,
This game is still in need of some 'rudimentary' code to enable advanced players to play this game without unnecessary difficulties. In this specific case I have spent a great deal of time trying to understand what was going on with my game at the very beginning.
After start up the game starts with the astronaut running in an uncontrollable fashion. which eventually turned out to be caused by the fact that the pedals of the rudder kit were in their rest state which the game interpreted as instructions to walk. Pressing either pedal (i.e. using the toe brakes) causes the astronaut to turn and move in that direction. After some experimentation it seems that if both pedals were pressed such that they were at the midpoint of their rotation all movement ceased.
In  practise the game appears to make use of multiple joystick devices plugged into a platform but fails to take the trouble to identify the class of device. In my case I have the Saitek X52 pro Joystick and the Saitek Rudder pedals connected.
The config screen identifies the throttle quadrant as joystick 1, the joystick itself as joystick 2, but there is no obvious way to disable the use of the rudder pedal (bar disconnecting it [not an acceptable option]). In this case I have attempted to modify the null zones for the rudder pedal but without any impact on the game.
It is requested that the development team look into this problem as soon as possible and hopefully provide a fix.

'Just Cause' is the story of Che Guevara, an Argentine Marxist revolutionary, physician, author, guerrilla leader, diplomat, and military theorist. A major figure of the Cuban Revolution, his stylized visage has become a ubiquitous countercultural symbol of rebellion and global insignia in popular culture.
Playing Che as a young medical student, you travel throughout South America and become radicalized by the poverty, hunger, and disease that you witness. Most of this part of the game consists of quicktime events punctuated by scenes of you jogging down corridors and along dusty streets, but the tight controls more than make up for any boredom you might feel.
Your burgeoning desire to help overturn what you see as the capitalist exploitation of Latin America by the United States prompts your involvement in Guatemala's social reforms under President Jacobo Árbenz, and at this point in the game you join one of three factions which you will stay as for the rest of the game. In my playthrough I joined the 'Reapers' which was more of a fetch-quest based plot but I really like these because I'm a masochist.
The president's eventual CIA-assisted overthrow at the behest of the United Fruit Company solidifies your political ideology and you can start earning perks that upgrade Che based on three trees - Ideology, Philosophy and Taxation Schemes. Ideology allows you to increase Che's intelligence making things like lockpicking and sneaking easier. Philosophy makes people dislike Che more but you're able to find things like hidden doors and alternative roads thanks to 'thinking outside of the box'. Taxation Schemes are probably the most useful tree and are fairly self-explanatory.
Later, in Mexico City, you meet Raúl and Fidel Castro, join their 26th of July Movement, and sail to Cuba aboard the yacht, Granma, with the intention of overthrowing U.S.-backed Cuban dictator Fulgencio Batista. The yacht becomes a hub for you and your men and from here you can use an extensive crafting system to make new weapons. Whilst the other NPCs are in your party you can outfit them with weapons and skills just as you can for Che. The AI is a little patchy in places but for the most part works fine.
You soon rise to prominence among the insurgents, get promoted to second-in-command, and play a pivotal role in the victorious two-year guerrilla campaign that is set on deposing the Batista regime. At this point the game moves to a top-down perspective ala Sim City, and most of the gameplay from now on is based around maps of military strategies and other boring stuff.
I guess it's alright.

Pros:
- Graphic (Characters are drawn in manga/comic-like style and mix up really good with paint-like 2D backgrounds. Looks really good),
- Story [or better "Stories"] (main story isn't something special, similar to zero-to-hero stories, but huge "+" for characters mini-stories. They are similiar to Persona serie Social-Links. Everyone have their own problems and "missions" to complete and fulfilling them give us skills upgrades or perks),
- Characters (they are well written and it's fun to know them better. Bunch of weirdos trying to stick together),
- References to other games, movies, books etc. (there a lot of them and usually it's fun to find reference to Diablo or Disgaea),
- Difficulty (game can be difficult no matter if you just started on it's your last fight. Usually one or two small mistakes can ruin your fight. Add save option available only in city or certain places in dungeons and you have to think really hard until you get a 100% Winrate method.)
- Activites (fishing, city-building, text adventures, crafting, dungeons - quite a lot of it for an tRPG).
- Tacticity (game is clearly inspired by Disgaea series both in humor and battles. Nothing out of ordinary: skills, equipment, two actions per turn (move+skill/item/etc.), cooldowns, attack ranges, character placement - everything is important, especially if there are 2 or 3 more battles before savepoint and you just can't lose anyone).
Cons:
- Time limit (one of mechanism that I hate in games. In Regalia it's not very strict and you usually have enough time to do what you want [except at the beggining], but I just don't like if clock pushing me to do things),
- Level-scalling (another mechanism I don't like. I'm not grinding, exping or crafting to merely bandit or rat become as stong as I am. It helps keeping game difficult till the end, but it's irritating that's you sometimes have to struggle with every fight because enemies scalling themself to your levels and gear),
- Loadings (f***ton of them. There are loadings between every scrren so if you are doing things in city it's taking a loooot of time because of them),
- Few flaws in Polish translation (usually text appear in English in some places).
Overall i would highly recommend this game for fans of Disgaea, or for these who are scared of FF:tactics or Disgaea "size". It's smaller, but you can clearly feel "spirit" of both games in this one. Not too long, but really enjoyable to play.

The game is paced so well that you have plenty of time to complete the objectives and yet still feel the pressure of days marching to the deadline. The voice acting is on par with many profecional games, of course it wouldnt be if the dailogue wasnt so amazing. More than a few times i caught myself giggling and I was at least smiling through every descussion. The characters all try very hard to stand out, not only from eachother but conventional archetypes. It amazed me how the devs could take such a commonly used character like elves and completely turning it on the head. The devs deffinately succeeded in making unique and memorable characters who made an impact both in gameplay and dialogue. The music was another very surprising high point. All the tracks really fit the setting and its beautifully orchestrated. I'm so glad I was able to help this game come out. You should really consider playing if you want a humorous turn based rpg with fun characters and exceptional ambiance.

Regalia is a ride of goofs, followed by more goofs and a very goofy story. I recommend just buying the game to support the team alone. Yet lets get to my honest review of the game.
Pros:
Regalia boast a very rich art style, with some great music choices and some very interesting systems. I enjoyed the choice based story book quest, The sorta timed kingdom quest completion, the relationship side quest and town building aspects. Overall solidly done.
Cons:
Can't have the good with the bad now can we. The tactical combat system didn't feel very tactical and by the end i found it was the least favorite part of the game, and i consider myself a bit of a tactical rpg fanboy. The lack of a stronger defense and normal attack system, makes the game feel very simplistic. While the shield system passing turns to gain or having to have a shield-er in the party slows down the game play given the additional turn limits most matches set.
The other downside, at least for me and many may disagree but i would have loved to see a deeper weapon and armor system setup and a deeper skill tree rather than the allotment system for each character.
Overall:

Having given this game a good couple of hours (spread over a few months, which makes it seem rather sparse), I feel confident in recommending it to others if only for the novel appeal.
In short, drop cards like they're hot!
The "Leveling" system for the cards puts a different spin on play-style, as well as the zero cost for playing them. The only cost you pay is the regret of having to discard the cards you didn't use but ended up needing. But that's all circumstantial and a bit easier to mitigate once you've a better grasp on the cards and mechanisms.
That said, some cards might put you off at first. "Big whoop," you might say, unless it's within the first 'round' or two of hands and you realize, "Holy balls, the level-ups are incredible!" So yeah, drop those cards. Even if your ranks are full and the spells you have aren't necessary, it still pays to play *something* if only for the sake of getting a stronger version of it later, and you're on hand 3 of 4 in the round. And again, no 'mana' cost.
It has a "snowball effect" appeal to it, I guess. Which can be refreshing. While I appreciate the cautious, long-haul strategy of Magic and similar card games a bit better, sometimes I like something with a faster pace and exponential growth - though I seldom see my level 3 cards.
This is all online play notwithstanding. I base an assumption of "Legendary Stomping" on other reviews, and have had enough experience with Hearthstone to be frustrated by feeling incapable of beating anyone. Fact of the matter is, I'm a heavy gamer, but spread my attention across many games. I simply don't invest enough time in these F2P games to build a strong collection and be competetive. And that'd be a lame excuse to pay real life money, so I won't. If I get tired of playing against CPU and draft tournaments feel too noncommital after awhile, I'll just stop playing again.
But again, fun game/concept and worth at least a small chunk of your time to try.

Even though, IMO ranked MP for games like these is a core feature, not something one should plan to implement at a later date. Right up there with "make an online gameplay system" regarding priority.
My gripe with this game is its economy system. I simply have to compare it with Scrolls because there are many similarities. I'm personally not that much into competitive play and in this regard this game really doesn't offer much, past some OK campaign missions and a sub par AI with 0 rewards. Collecting cards and building decks would be interesting to me, had it not been for some problems.
So, in scrolls you had (at the time I still played the game a few months back)
- 360 cards in 4 factions
- possibility to make some 1k gold daily, with a few daily trials and maybe one AI match. 1 hour tops, doable in 30 minutes.
- with 1k gold you could purchase a pack of ten random cards, of which one was guaranteed to be a rare card and another two were uncommons. There was also a chance of about 10-20% to receive an 11th, higher tier card.
- standard decks typically require one faction so upon choosing your color you practically had a pool of 90 cards from which you could choose.
- most expensive cards on the market went for about 1800 gold, which in effect would be an equivalent of 5 LOST online matches, something like 2 hours of your time.
- as long as you managed to put up a decent fight, online losses were rewarded nicely. AI matches were also rewarded, less handsomely, but the same principle applies - more fighting means more gold.
- there were precon decks which went for 5k and 8k gold so all in all, if you wanted to build a specific deck you could do so without grinding to death. Say, two hours daily for a month should net you 60 to 80k with which you can build almost any deck you want. If you were good in competitive play you could net even more easily.
In SolForge you have:
- around 570 cards, not really sure how to check the grand total nor how many are there per faction since the interface is lacking in some regards.
- easy daily rewards which require three victories against anyone, netting about 2.5k silver, two packs containing 6 random cards and a ticket which you need for online events. This requires about a half an hour of your time, if you played against easy AI probably doable in 15 minutes.
- these packs guarantee only one rare card and offer a decent chance of getting some heroic and legendary cards. The problem is you are getting 6 from a pool of ~570. Compared to 10 out of 360 from Scrolls, which also gave one highest tier card guaranteed, this is quite bad.
- to make things worse, forging prices are rather high. Common cards go for 150, rares go for 1400, heroic 32500 and legendary 142500 silver. If you decide to build a specific deck with say 15 heroic and 15 legendary cards you will need 2625000 silver which is an equivalent of about 1000 days of daily rewards.
- online victories net 250 gold, max 10 daily I think so that could split above 1000 to 500 days of grinding, but with a lets say more significant time investment.
- there are preconstructed decks for purchase and a sharing system so that, as long as you can find someone with whom you might share, you can cut deck costs to about $5 a piece.
- there is also the option to earn some cards in the drafting portion of the game, which seems interesting and I'd like to get to know the cards a bit better before getting into that. You can play one casual draft match every three days for free, as things stand now.
All in all, it is my opinion that, as a card collection game, SolForge sucks due to a bad business model. IMO. Even more so for new players.
I'll update this after getting some drafting experience, maybe that can change my opinion dramatically.
