Having played Shadow Complex four times on my Xbox I was very excited to finally see the Remastered version on Steam. Shadow Complex is a 2.5D side-scroller developed by ChAIR Entertainment that originally released on Xbox in 2009. Jump forward seven years and the game has been remastered and released for PC on Steam. In Shadow Complex you play as Jason Flemming, after your girlfriend Claire is kidnapped by a strange organisation you venture into their base to find and rescue Claire. Unfortunately for you this organisation is anything but friendly and they have some serious firepower, you’ll need to learn how to use it if you want to survive here.
Shadow Complex doesn’t have cutting edge graphics but it looked good when it came out and it looks even better with the updated graphics now. The visual effects are also pretty good and all of the in-game models look good too.
The game features a large map with indoor and outdoor portions, it takes roughly 8-10 hours to beat the game. You’ll see pretty much all of the map just by playing through the story but there are some secret areas where you’ll find upgrades. These upgrades range from how many grenades you can carry to how much armour you have and they’re incredibly useful, especially on the higher difficulties.
As you progress through the game it does get a fair bit more difficult, again even more so on higher difficulties. There are a few advanced enemy types but generally you’ll just find more enemies, sometimes in awkward positions making it even harder to fight them. Every so often you’ll also run into a boss. The boss fights are enjoyable and tough to begin with but once you figure out the main strategy to beat a boss they become less challenging. Generally these strategies involve the different equipment items you’ll find over the course of the game: grenades, missiles and a strange foam which prevents enemies/objects from moving. While the main purpose of these items is to break through part of the environment (for example using a grenade to get through a locked door) they can also be used to great effect in combat.
The other item used to get through things in the environment is your gun! Whatever gun you have (the first one you find is a basic pistol but you’ll find others as you progress through the game) can be used to break through some objects, such as metal coverings for vents, allowing you to reach a new area. The gun is also what you’ll mainly use during combat, though you also have a melee attack. The gun is obviously good at range while the melee attack is always your best bet when you’re close enough to the enemy as it’s an insta-kill. The melee attack triggers a mini-cutscene, of which there are a few variations, in which you pretty much beat the crap out of whatever enemy it is you’re attacking. Of course, there are some enemies who can’t be killed with the melee attack but the enemies you’ll see most regularly can.
There are some other pieces of equipment in the game too. You get a flashlight early on in the game which is obviously used to illuminate dark areas in the game but, when shone on objects, it also highlights objects which can be destroyed by your other equipment, for example orange highlighting means it can be destroyed with gunfire. Without giving too much away, you’ll also find some high-tech armour along the way, each piece of the armour adds a new mechanic to the game. You’ll find the armour parts as you progress through the story.
Speaking of the story, it’s actually quite good. The story of Jason trying to rescue Claire is reasonably interesting but it’s the game’s backstory that’s really enjoyable. There are a few points in the game where you’ll be able to listen in to the conversations that take place between some of your enemies in the game. These conversations give you an idea of what the organisation in the game is like and what their goals are. Missing or ignoring them won’t make the game’s story hard to understand but you will really miss out of some cool stuff. The story is based around ideas in Orson Scott Card’s books. While I haven’t read any of his work it seems that he has strong, often controversial right wing views. It’s worth mentioning that Shadow Complex isn’t politically driven so don’t worry if you don’t agree with his views.
Returning to upgrades, as well as the collectible upgrades you find you’re also ‘upgraded’ through collecting EXP and levelling up (an automatic process). The Hardcore and Insane difficulties offer more EXP for killing enemies/completing objectives, meaning you’ll level up considerably faster, but these difficulties are also a lot harder to beat. When you level up, three things happen. Firstly, you’re maximum health will increase. Secondly, you’ll return to full health (this has saved me from death a fair few times). Lastly, one of your stats (such as accuracy) will be increased (some levels also have special bonuses, for example the full map is revealed when you reach level 20). The level cap is level 50 which will take an incredibly long time to get to (after 6 hours I’m level 12, playing on hardcore difficulty) but you keep your level when you start a new game (though you lose your weapons, items etc.)
As much as I love Shadow Complex, it’s not without its issues. The biggest problem I have with the game is the save system, there are checkpoint rooms every so often where you can save your progress and from where you’ll restart if you die or quit and then return to the game later. I always prefer it when games allow you to save at any point and it can be quite inconvenient in Shadow Complex, especially on the higher difficulties, since when you die you’ll have to walk back through a fair bit of the map (dying won’t respawn enemies but when you quit and come back the enemies you killed will be there again). My second issue with the game is with the aiming controls. Being a 2.5D game, not all of the enemies are exactly to the left or right of you, sometimes they’re off at an angle or horizontal to you. The problem is (at least when playing with a controller) that the aiming system is designed for a 2D game, in other words it’s made for you to fire in straight lines in front, behind, above, below or anything in between. Because of this, when aiming at an enemy who’s not in the same plane as you, you have to be aiming at just the right angle so that the gun aims into the scenery/level rather than straight ahead. I realise that’s probably not the best description of the problem but basically it makes some enemies incredibly difficult to hit which results in you spending more time than necessary trying to hit them, often translating into you losing a fair bit of health. Other than that the controls in the game are solid which is important since there’s a fair bit of platforming in the game.
Easily one of my favourite games, Shadow Complex is a great 2.5D side-scroller with enjoyable, challenging gameplay. If you’re a fan of the genre then this is definitely a game you ought to have in your library.

Let me express how good I think »Lifeless Planet« is:
Since summer of 2014 (for 5 months now) I've been binge-watching playthroughs of this game. Now that I'm playing it myself for the first time, I've assumed that no aspect of the game would surprise me anymore (I wanted to play it despite that assumption). But my assumption was wrong: in the first three levels I've stumbled upon goodies none of the players I've watched discovered: tricky ramps and hills, seemingly inascendable, that could be climbed on with a bit of patience; minerals others missed; scripted events (mostly noises and music); a few bugs and quirks here and there -- equally fun, at least for me.
So I'm enjoying every aspect of the game, even after having seen spoilers for months. That's how good the game is in my view.
But the main reason, maybe the only reason, why I love playing this game (which is by now almost completely spoiled for me all to the end) -- it's the incredible atmosphere that keeps pulling me in. The vast landscapes, the part-familiar, part-alien geology, the awesome soundtrack and the unfolding story are part of this atmosphere that just resonates with me.  I recommend playing »Lifeless Planet« and taking time exploring it. And I hope it will resonate with you too.

This game can easily be splitted into 2 parts: a TBS, which is basically an X-COM, and... Well, I would call it a king-pimp simulator with a hint of that X-COM again. The first one is really plain and simple: 5 heroes, some monsters, abilities, 2 Action Points... Nothing fancy here, though fun at times. And the second one is what this game is all about.
To fight off a nasty thing dreaming about consumping your "kingdom" the Chalice from the title must be charged. And it needs just some measly 3 centuries. Good thing you are immortal. Bad thing your heroes are not. And without you they, apparently, can't have sex for some reason. So one of your duties is to marry heroes, hoping they are compatible with each other and capable of producing not only healthy, but also promising offsprings with crazy stats and utility traits and personalities until these heroes die.
Yes, heroes here have not only stats, but also traits and personalities. And if you are bad at pimping, then rather soon the crisis will emerge: all your heroes are drunkards with heart diseases that can hardly hit an enemy right in front of them and you can't even 'produce' more because there are only 2 bloodlines which will lead to incent... Basically, you are screwed.
The game is not bad. This 'marriages and bloodlines managing' is a fresh idea with some potential. But the rest of the game is simply boring. You sit there, waiting for decades until the Corruption strikes (always 2 regions, but you can protect only 1), at the same time hoping the research you started will be finished until then, then wasting an awful lot of time searching for 1 monster hidden somewhere in the corner of the map. And by the next invasion your core heroes will be already long dead, leaving you with rookies who somehow inherit the worst traits of their parents.
Maybe it is just me, but I also noticed that all melee classes are useless compared to ranged classes. With 5 hunters you can hide in shadows and take out 1 enemy at a time without exposing your heroes and risking their lives.
All in all, the concept is interesting, the game is boring and dull. Take it with a discount and decide yourself.

The characters are fun, the character sprites are pretty, the humor is for the most part pleasant. I had fun playing it, was excited to start up the game after work, and was invested enough to redo a chapter three times when I backed myself into a corner by wasting too much time in the previous one. I like it enough that, even though I got the game for free, I'm going to buy another copy and give it to someone who I think will enjoy it - I think it's only fair to pay for a game that gave me nearly 30 hours of solid entertainment.
The plot is good. It’s pretty simple, but effective, with a plot twist and a message I enjoyed and felt fit the theme very well. And simple doesn't equal bad - the story knows what it's doing, and is going towards that goal without meandering or dropped plot points. I found the resolution satisfying and fitting, and even touching.
There’s a lot of characters to befriend - not only your companions, but also the citiziens of your town; each of them gets several relationship cutscenes and a personal quest to solve. None of them are very complex - what you see is what you get - but I still got quite attached to them. I like that you get glimpses of what they might think of each other, too. Sometimes you can find two of your townies talking to each other, and your companions also have dialogues with each other in dungeon camps. The game is very character-driven, and I got pretty attached to them by the end of the game. The humor can be a bit juvenile sometimes - mostly in the cutesy direction.  Even if the characters having days off or going out of town when I needed them was kidn of a hindrance, I still feel it made the town feel a bit more lived-in.
Kay, the protagonist, is very likeable too; I sort of suspected it would be the classic story of a lazy dude that needs to be dragged to do any work and always complains, but he turned out to be a genuinely sweet, well-meaning, hard-working kid, and I’d say he was my favorite character. Bonding with other characters felt believeable; he *is* the sort of guy who’d try to understand everyone better.
Shout-out to the translators/editors - it's a text-heavy game, and I have found maybe two typos/awkward word choices total, so they've done a bang-up job! The dialogue, especially after the rushed beginning of the game, is good, and each character's speaking style matches their personality well.
The battle system was surprisingly fun, too - all the characters have varied skills and weaknesses, and allowed for coming up with different strategies. The time limit could be a bit of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ but not to the point of being annoying rather than a valid challenge. The map challenges were fun - sometimes all you have to do is reach a certain point, sometimes you have to survive several turns, sometimes you have to win quikcly, sometimes you gotta beat up a rock. However: the Line of Sight system was very frustrating. I could never predict when I'd have a clear shot.
There’s some flaws, of course. For one: character design (then: art is my job, and I always zero in on the visual side of game. Most people probably won't mind that part as much as I do). All of the important characters are derivative of something popular, be it an archetype or a specific character. Gwen is Karin Kanzuki, natch; Elaine is every peppy younger sister in 90s anime, Theo is what you get when you type "kid vampire" into google images, so on, so on. At best, it means they aren’t memorable; at worst, copying something results in carrying over the problems of the original, and so we get Haksun, who looks like a 1930s antisemitic caricature, presumably because the team decided they wanted to have a greedy merchant just like in Aladdin or whatever. In all, the characters often look like they don’t belong in he same world; there isn’t much visual unity between them. The sprites themselves are very nicely done; there’s also several more interesting designs hidden on minor characters. But I’d say this was my main gripe with the game.
Also: the color choices for most characters were terrible. Pink hair? Green tunic? Tan boots? MIRI.....
The worldbuilding was also kinda slapdash. You’ve got samurai dwarves, vampires, hivemind elves, undefeatable bureaucracy of a vague higher authority, vampires, knights, pistols, deployable turrets, archers, random spaniards, a german blacksmith… there’s no cohesion to it, and for me, the tongue-in-cheek tone of the game didn’t really offset it.
There were some bugs; for the most part, nothing big - Signy sometimes ending up clipping into an enemy after her attack, I ghost-deployed Kay during Aliss’ quest and couldn’t do anything, so on. Nothing game-breaking or even overly annoying. The one that did♥♥♥♥♥♥me off was that I could SWEAR the game doesn’t always save my perk distribution/character inventory, and I had to redo it several times. >:|
Also: the dang fishing minigame. In theory, a good way to fill in a lull between bonding days/quests; in practice, a ticket to carpal tunnel syndrome.
All this might sound a bit unenthusiastic, but I very much enjoyed the game! It’s charming, nicely balanced, and just… fun. I slammed 25 hours into it within a week, and I’m kinda sad that I finished it.

Creeper World 3 is an interesting variation on tower offense... You build towers to limit the spread of "the creep", something that spread like goo over all areas of the map like the Flood in Halo, except smaller. Weapons can limit them, but the only way to stop them on a world is to destroy the creeper emitter on the world by building a nullifier near it. However, nothing can survive in the creep... thus, you need to build a network of nodes to power the turrets, push back the creep, and eventually reach the emitter and shut it down.
As you advance from world to world, system to system, creeps get... creepier. They get spore throwing towers (shoots a blob of creep anywhere on the map), but you get beam towers to defend against such. The defense "digitalis", which was supposed to destroy creep at the molecular level, had been subverted and now creates "pathways" to spread, but cannons and such can roll back such until you can destroy the digitalis emitter. Runner nodes generate small runners that can suicide, but you have "sniper" turrets against such. Then "glider" nodes with weapons defend against intruders near its paths.
To counter those, you get better turrets. Mortar (ignores terrain), sniper turrets (mentioned before) that goes after runners and such but limited to line of sight, beam turrets against incoming spores (some are launched up to 4 at a time), sprayer to spray "anti-creep" (AC), bombers to drop larger qty of AC, strafer to slow a valley of creep, Guppy transport to move AC, energy, or ore around maps that has disconnected islands, Big Bertha cannon (takes out a big chunk of creep), better control nodes (longer range) and much more.
Your command module along with collectors and reactors generates the power to power all the turrets. The trick is find control terrain to limit the creep to a section of the map, then roll it back section by section, by controlling key terrain much like all RTS games, without running out of power.
You are some sort of warrior awakened after millenia of sleep, only to find desolation all over the galaxy, ruins everywhere, signs of combat and creep everywhere as well, shields and warp inhibitors did not save the worlds, but your strategy and deployment of units may. As you advance from world to world, star system to star system, your encounters gets worse and worse, enemies gets more and more complicated, but you get more and more toys to play with.
While graphics are low-fi and 2D only it does not distract and in fact, keep the frame rate high and creep is sufficiently creepy enough. There are also visibility options to turn stuff on/off to help visualize the battle, with zoom. However, there is no edge scroll... You have to use WASD to scroll if you are zoomed in.
It is different enough from regular tower defense to give you a good challenge, but it does get a bit boring after a while, or frustrating, as energy management is crucial, and there is no manual. Read beginner's guide on Steam before getting started.
Verdict: Try. It is a very unusual RTS.

It's an educational game, yey!
helps one practice basic arithmetics by addition and subtraction, you know, the old pals plus and minus.
As a game it is pretty much just a excessively graphic arithmetics game. However, it is aimed at
, so the visuals might appeal to them. The difficulty is pretty good for practicing the simplest operations in math.
For an adult though? Well, you can use it to practice sums like you were back to grade school, or if you're into that sort of thing, you can speed-calculate to grab those precious achievements.
There's easy (numbers 0-20), medium (0-100) and hard (0-100 with max. two operations) math problems. To fare best one has to choose the computation that amounts to largest result and then provide result correctly. Difficulty affects the number of the potential computations as well.
Everything works just fine with keyboard: arrow keys pick the computation and then you enter the number that you think is the answer. The game provides feedback immediately. There's a bonus for picking the computation with the highest result, though the rest of them are not penalized either.
For kids it's a brilliant way to render math practice into a game. Game also rewards completed sessions with exciting (?) bee facts.
Adult gamer will likely be bored after a quarter hour, having likely beaten or laid down the game by that point. One grindy achievement makes sure that perfectionists will stay for at least an hour or two.
I wouldn't recommend it as a paid game with its currently repetitive, simplistic content. However, being free makes it quite accessible and potentially useful for parents with little children. Therefore, here's thumbs up for its continued discoverability.

It looks good but the gameplay is quite boring. Just outlast to level 3 units where you will actually duke things out.
PROS
1. Nice Visuals
The artwork for the cards are great.
2. Easy to Learn
Just play 2 cards every round if possible. Preferably choose units over spells as the stat point growth for units far exceed spells. E.g. Stone Giant 6/9 to 20/20 vs a 6 damage to 12 damage.
3. Interesting Abilities
Armour (Negates X damage on the first hit), Aggressive (Attack on Summon)
4. Campaign is okay
It's still another AI battle but it's campaign is better than some other online TCGs that I've played E.g. MMDOC (Google it)
CONS
1. Peculiar mechanic
The idea of a default mechanic where you gain a higher level card by playing a lower level card first is quite strange. E.g. Play a Level 1 card to gain a Level 2 card of the same card.
2. Repetitive cards
Card Levels go into 1, 2, 3. The next level is merely a buffed up version of the first card. E.g. Cull the Weak: Destroy any creature with 4/8/12 attack and below.
3. Pay-To-Win
You get normal booster packs with Silver (in-game currency) and rare booster packs with Gold (cash currency). People who spend cash on this game will get better cards than those who don't.
4. No Trading System
Can't see anyway to trade your cards so your cards are valueless.
5. Low Multiplayer Count
Hardly anyone playing.
6. Tournaments
Minimum number of event tickets to enter is 2. You need to pay cash to get these tickets. With such a low player count, I wonder why they even charge.
7. Bugs
Lot of bugs
8. No unique narrative
Standard undead horde, wild animals, technology city and primordial tribe cards. This is the same story as Infinity Wars. There is nothing unique.

Ah, a classic 3D FPS. This of course comes with a familiar set of good and less good aspects:
Pros
- Good old run n' gun combat. Like other shooters of the time (and stuff like Doom 2016), it's worth staying on the move to avoid getting shot and/or torn apart. Add on top of this the fact the game will periodically spawn in more enemies, and there's almost always some kind of action to keep you on your toes.
- Large arsenal of weapons with plenty of variety, from the mundane but effective (shotgun, assault rifle, a knife that, unlike Doomguy's fist, is actually fairly useful in a pinch), to the unusual and flashy (energy weapons and explosives of various sizes and effects).
- Element of exploration in the levels. While the level layouts are mostly linear, you are rewarded for going off the beaten path and checking all the nooks and crannies. Usually this bags much-needed health and ammo, but there's also the possibility of finding a new weapon early or a nifty powerup. And you WILL have to do some searching if you want to collect all the pieces of the Chronoscepter, this game's ultimate weapon.
- Plenty of intersting enemies to use said weapons on. Of course you'll have dinosaurs and humans to shoot, stab and blow up with explosive arrows, but the Lost Land is a weird place filled with all kinds of crazy stuff. Expect every level to throw something new at you that you haven't faced down yet.
Cons
- To get to new levels you need to find keys in previous ones to unlock them. Fortunately keys are usually not that hard to find if you're already hunting around everywhere for goodies, but nonetheless if you miss any it means taking another trip through the level to find what you missed. Level 5 in particular is a kind of a maze, and I wouldn't blame anyone who misses at least one key during it.
- Remember when FPS games thought they should have platforming as a key element, without fantastic controls to back them up? Yeah, this game looooves its precision platforming over perilous pits of alliteration. Obviously this remaster's mouse and keyboard controls help a lot compared to the old N64 incarnation's janky setup, but you can still expect the game to punish you with lost health and/or lives when you screw up even a single jump. And it's still not hard to screw them up, even with modern controls.
- Speaking of lives, you have limited lives and save points. Just one of those things I suppose the genre hadn't grown out of yet at the time. Not the friendliest thing to have to deal with when you consider how quickly enemies can tear you to pieces on higher difficulties, plus the aforementioned platforming. If it's any consolation, the game is designed around this, with it not being TOO difficult to get more lives if you remember to explore for resources and grab the bonus stage portals when they show up. Also, slain enemies stay dead between lives and bosses retain whatever hurt you put on them before they killed you, meaning you won't lose quite as much progress as you may normally expect.
So overall, we got an old shooter with old design quirks, given a fresh coat of paint and controls that won't make you tear your hair out. The original N64 version would be a bit hard to recommend today, but having a mouse and keyboard to use makes a huge difference (or a modern controller; I played this all the way through with an Xbox One controller and, thanks to the sizeable amount control customization options, had a ballin time that way too). Given that huge change, this is now totally worth playing, whether you're an old player going back for that sweet nostalgia or a new player wanting to check out a fun bit of gaming history. Either way, I can guarantee this one still delivers.

TL;DR - Easier than Banjo Kazooie remake. But not really able to recommend to newer players.
Do I enjoy the game? HELL YEAH!! It's fun, it's frustrating, it's old-school quirky and fast paced. Do I recommend it? Hell No! The reason I don't recommend it, is the only people whom it would need recommending to probably won't see the same game we all enjoy.
Turok is 100% a product of it's generation. That doesn't mean it's a bad game. It means this game will only really be enjoyed by those who grew up at that time. The first problem this game has is it's level design and engine. It reeks of N64! Which the game was built for, I know. However, the limits of that console keeps this game feeling cramped. Keep in mind this was the same time games like Blood, MDK, Quake II, Hexen II, Tomb Raider II, & Star Wars Jedi Knight II were coming out on PC.  Those games had a much more open feel. Their level designs still hold up today. Turok does good for the tech it was built for, but it does lack in comparison to these titles.
Weapons are another concerning factor. There is variety, but they don't have range. Enemies can shoot you further than you can. It's strange to be taking damage from someone and when you shoot at them the bullets don't reach. The shotgun is underpowered imho. Why does it take 2 hits to take down a raptor? You have limited ammo and a long animation sequence between shots. Unless you have explosive shells, this gun is hardly worth it in most situations. The bow and arrow is another one. Other than hitting large enemies, this weapon leaves a lot to be desired. And why can't you switch ammo? You have to use your best ammo no matter what. Then there's the knife. It doesn't 1 shot even some of the most basic enemies. You take a big risk using it, but the reward is not there. That's just my take on things.
The limited lives and spaced out save points are another throw back to an older generation. I doubt most new gamers will appreciate mini-bosses standing at every save point. Exploration is punished by enemies respawning. You have to play the levels a few times to get all the niche's figured out. The secret warps are limited. Although spread out nicely throughout the levels, they repeat and bring you to the exact same secret you entered at the last checkpoint.
It also must be commented on that a crazy faced, fully stereotypical, Native American may put an itch under the skin of SJW's. But this game came out in a time when that wasn't considered taboo or even that bad. Carmageddon had just been released rewarding players who murdered innocent people. Shadow Warrior was making fun of Asian stereotypes. GTA 1 had just been released. Duke Nukem was objectifying women. It was a different time for sure.
These are just a few quirks that Turok has. Do I think they are barriers to enjoying the game? Depends on the type of gameplay you were raised on. If Halo was your first game, and you were raised on infinite, op, pistols, and the ability to hide in a corner until you regained sheilds, then this game will feel very unfair. If you were raised on Doom, and sometimes running for the exit switch was your only option, then this game is a nice balance between FPS speed-running and exploration/platforming.
But hey! At least it's not as hard as Banjo Kazooie!!

I got it while it was on sale during Black Friday week.
My first impression:
It's a very relaxing game. you can just build to your heart's content, without worrying too much about micro-managing every little thing. you also don't need to worry too much about your citizens hating you and telling you how much you suck... because they don't stay unhappy for very long anyway. It would actually take a lot for them to become so unhappy that they leave the town in droves.
The simple cartoon-like and block-like appearance of the world is aesthetically pleasing to the eye. It adds even more to the relaxation factor of the game, ya know?
So if you wanted a stress-free experience and just wanted to completely relax while doing something? Then this game is for you.
HOWEVER!! It does have a few negative points, because no game is completely perfect.
Number one: The game feels like it's a closed-beta game. There's actually not much in the way of buildings, and you can't really upgrade anything. You can't upgrade the wooden huts into stone buildings so that they can't catch on fire, for one thing.
And there's only two farm plots-- a grain plot and a tree farm plot. There's no animal farm or any other resources there.
Number two: There's no challenges or anything like that. The Dragon and the Vikings come around once in a while, but they're not really challenging at all... they just seem like elements that come around to liven up things now and then.
That's not really a negative for me as seeing I just want a stress-free game where I can build to my heart's content.... but at the same time I can see how that would be a major negative thing for other gamers who want a more exciting experience.
That said... I'll be playing it now and then when I just want to completely chill the ♥♥♥♥ out.

The graphics are not going to set any new standards in 2016 (they rocked in 2009, though), but the developers were thoughtful enough to do a proper HD upgrade to the game and you also have some advanced graphics controls that can dial things in. At high resolutions, the game looks great and plays smooth. I'm on strong hardware for 2013, but I get the impression you really don't need a monster rig to run this thing at all. I mean, it was a 360 game, no amount of HD textures is going to change that :)
One thing I loved:
The shooting gameplay is nice and tight, with a hint of a twin-stick twitch shooter feel if you disable the auto-aiming.
One thing that bugged me:
Save points seem a little infrequent. For a game that lived on HDDs from its inception, sure does rely on the old "Save Room" mechanic heavily. It's somewhat frustrating to die after getting a pickup, for example, but before saving your progress. But this isn't a game defining frustration, just a minor annoyance and a common problem for the genre until more recent games mostly opted for autosaving on important things like item pickups and boss fights, in addition to save points.
Great game though, so far, really immersive and the gameplay is right up there with Axiom Verge for enjoyable, Metroid-inspired side scrolling shooter gameplay (though less inventive, at least so far - no out-there weapons).

I really want to like this time game - the concept really caught my attention and the movie was enticing.  But this game has so many mechanics that suck the fun out of it and it really prevents me from recommending it.
Allow me to elaborate.
TLDR;  great idea, poor execution.
To start, the game is set up such that has the enemies will attack every 10-20 or so years.  This is otherwise fine except that time affects your heroes - they will age and they will die.
This mechanic poses the greatest challenge to the game.   Essentially, the game ceased to be a turn based tactics game and instead gets overwhelmed in favor of, "let's pray to the RNG gods and hope we have the elements we need to continue playing the game".
The primary challenge of the game is maintaining a set of troops that will be ready to fight the enemy threat when they appear.  You can't rely on the same ssquad you had before because your heroes eventually age (lose stats) and die.  Throughout the game, you'll assuredly be going through new set of troops every 1 or 2 of these enemy waves.
To maintain a standing vanguard, you need to build keeps to preserve the blood line for the next generation of heroes.  But instead of being a mechanic that helps you, that adds a layer of problems - your heroes can have bad traits that make them undesirable to sire the next generation.  Not having enough of the right gender, the heroes could be infertile, random events cause their heirs to become unusable and other random events cause you to lose the heroes that you've painstakingly prepared.  Heroes are also needed to become sages, do little side quests that have the possibility of taking away from your pool of available heroes when enemies attack.
Additionally, maintaining 1 keep isn't enough as the developers have thoughtfully disallowed inbreeding.  This means a minimum of 2 keeps are needed.  Which means another 2 heroes that you have will have to be be removed from your standing reserves - and yet another set of problems that comes with it.
Aside from these balance issues, AI is fairly weak, and missions don't require much thought.  Overall, it really feels like a pale reproduction of X-Com.  At this time, X-Com 2 is due to come out soon, and I would recommend you save your money and buy that instead.

If you are a fan of the hex turned based strategy games - this will not let you down.
A brilliant but basic story-line which pits you against the Cadence, an alien like species which comes to infect your lands, set over a 300 year time-line.
Throughout the time-line you build upon your territory and research better gear for your group of fighters to defend against the Cadence and ensure the Chalice is not damaged. The leveling system from your class of 3 fighters (x2 ranged and one melee) is a two tiered 10 level system. Your fighters are sub-classes which are desginated by lineage.
What's unique about the level system is you are not investing your time into a certain character but in a lineage/family. You marry your lineage off to another and make babies. These babies have good or bad traits which are then passed down from generation to generation. Your lineage determines your fighter class as well. You marry off one Caberjack to a Hunter and therefore you make a Shadowjack for the next 40-50 years.
Time itself is sped up until an event occurs (research ending, lineage monarch dying, cadence presence etc etc). As time progresses so does the level of Cadence and how Advanced they get... the latter years gets harder.
All in all takes about 20 hours to finish the game, but a definately replayability for another go at it, because you will make a lot of mistakes.
Worth getting.... because I actually finished this game.

Shadow Complex Remastered is a remake of the critically acclaimed Shadow Complex, which was released on the Xbox Live Arcade back in August 2009. The remake was released on Steam in May 2016, with a console version of the game being released in March 2016. The Microsoft Windows store offered the game for free back in December 2015 for a brief amount of time. Having no exposure to the console version of the game, I went into this game only with the knowledge that it was one of the better games to come out of the Xbox Live Arcade.
Game play is done in a 2.5D platforming style which includes a handful of 3D elements.  Your movement is restricted to two-dimensional systems though.  You find yourself in the middle of a huge spy plot, as you explore an underground base which is holding an entire army ready for overthrowing the American government. Throughout this underground complex, you are faced with plenty of different puzzles to solve. The puzzles aren’t massively complicated; they normally involve some sort of jumping mechanic. Other puzzles will require the use of other pieces of equipment which you will discover throughout the course of the story.  These pieces of equipment vary from different weapons such as rocket launchers, grenades, foam guns (question mark?), grappling hooks, all the way to supersonic speed for running through walls and boosted jumps for scaling walls.
The gun play in Shadow Complex is a little tricky to get a hang of. The game uses twin stick controls for aiming meaning you don’t always get a huge amount of accuracy.  The 2.5D environment also causes a lot of confusion and hassle when trying to aim at enemies but you have to be in a certain position in order to shoot at enemies in the rear of the scene.  You will come across plenty of enemies whilst exploring, these can be dispatched in a number of ways, using range combat, or an easy to use melee combat system which changes style depending on where you are attacking for example, if you are jumping from above, you’ll land on top of the enemy to knock them out, whereas attacking from behind will result in you being a little more stealthy.
Boss fights throughout the story mode differ a fair amount between them. None of them are your usual style fight where you just volley a ton of ammo in their general direction. A lot will take into consideration the environment you are fighting in, such as needing to throw grenades underneath a tank to hit its weak spot. I found the boss fights to be a nice challenge which you wouldn’t otherwise get from the regular enemies you’ll come across.  As you unlock new abilities and pieces of equipment, you’ll often find yourself in a position to be able to backtrack to previously visited locations.
Even though this is a remastered game, which runs on the Unreal 4 Engine, I was a little disappointed with the graphical fidelity of this title. The environments look really poor, and at times you are able to see the textures quite close up and they are really pixelated which take the edge of the remastered effect. The character models look average, nothing special sadly. Animation in character’s faces can be a little off-putting at times if you focus on them whilst they are speaking, as well as a few awkward movements in cut scenes to boot.
Plot wise, the game is fairly interesting but somewhat cheesy at times. The opening prologue of the game bares no relevance to the actual story itself so I was a bit confused as to why it was included. The main protagonist is Jason Flemming, who happens to be on a weekend away with his new girlfriend, Claire. Your new girlfriend gets kidnapped and you are tasked with finding her and bringing her to safety. As the plot unravels everything turns out not to be the way it seemed. Although a lot of it is largely predictable, I still found myself interested in finding out what happens at the end. The dialog between Jason and Claire can be quite cringy at times and often felt like it was written by a twelve year old.  Thankfully you don’t need to follow the story too much in order to get the most out of Shadow Complex.
The voice acting across the game is nothing special, and you may even be better off turning it off as it did make me wince with awkwardness at times. The rest of the game’s sound effects are as you’d expect from an action game like this. There are moments where you really should be hearing a sound effect, such as background noise when you are on a factory floor, but you don’t hear anything. This can really knock you out of the immersion of any game, and sadly it happened all too frequently throughout this one.
Shadow Complex comes with a variety of different difficulty settings, most will be sufficiently challenged on the normal mode and however you can change the settings on the fly, and so I would advise start as high as you can to see how well you handle the combat. The easy mode is no challenge at all and you may find yourself getting bored of the combat system if you aren’t being challenged.
I wouldn’t consider Shadow Complex Remastered to have any replay ability unfortunately. There are a number of achievements which people may be after which will force a number of different play throughs, but the regular gamers amongst us will find themselves being satisfied with the single play through of the story. I did like the in game leader boards comparing your progression with people on your friends list who also have the game though; it adds a little competitive nature to an otherwise single player experience.
Other than the control issues being a bit of a pain in the 2.5D environments, the only other technical issue I had was that even when playing in full screen mode, your mouse does not get locked into the game window, meaning anyone who plays with more than one screen will find themselves minimizing their game more times than you would even believe to imagine. The only way I was actually able to play the game without this happening constantly was to move away from my preferred control method of keyboard and mouse to use an Xbox controller. Granted this got around this annoying technical problem that brought along its own problems with the lower accuracy when shooting due to using the joysticks rather than the more precise mouse movement.
Shadow Complex Remastered shouldn’t really be classed as a remastered edition in my opinion. This is the first time the game has come to the PC platform, and it doesn’t really show off the platform to its full potential.  The game play itself is enjoyable with a lot of interesting and unique abilities at your fingertips, but there is so much room for a potentially amazing game here that I was left feeling disappointed at the end.  The $14,99 price tag is probably nudging the boundaries of being over the average for this game so you may want to wait till the drops in price a little bit before picking it up.

There's honestly not much positive I can say about this game, it's a disappointment in plenty of ways. It's not horrible in any way, either, but a lack of positive elements isn't much better than incredibly negative elements.
For one, the game's physics are kind of iffy and the platforming is harder than it should be. Building up momentum is inconsistent and plenty of times I found myself slipping off the side of a rock or whatever. It also asks for more precision than it provides, at times, with narrow paths to walk across or somewhat strict jumps to make.
There's also just no sense of direction half the time. The puzzles are more "find where you need to be" than "figure out the solution" and at times where you need to be is practically a non-sequitur. The inferno area is awful about this, looking incredibly samey to the point where finding where you're supposed to go next is harder than anything else about the area. There's also a point where you have to traverse a large, open area to find one narrow passage with a switch you need to trigger. It's just... tedious, very tedious.
The plot's alright but nothing special. I don't want to spoil it but the plot at points could be compared to a rather-well known sci-fi movie with blue humanoid aliens... more near the end than anything though. Transitions between areas are also incredibly rough, just happening literally out of nowhere more often than not. It lacks a sense of cohesion to it, which is a bit of a problem in a game as linear as this.
And I was sort of expecting a bit more than a purely linear path, too. A bit of ability to explore around would've been nice. Sure there are a few secrets to find but they're not that far out of the way.
And the game's just a glitchy mess overall. At one point I had to go back to a previous area because the NPC I needed to follow me glitched out and wasn't where they were supposed to be. Apparently not having this NPC causes a glitch in the ending, too, so it's kiiiind of important. The only way I could fix the problem created was to reload and lose a fair bit of progress. It doesn't help that the "save and quit" option literally does not work. I've only ever been able to exit by closing the game window. Some of the achievements are bugged, too; Lifeless Astronaut seems to be utterly borked, and Planetary Historian seems to require more documents than exist in-game. Plus, I'm pretty sure I did not complete the game fast enough for Rocketeer but it gave it to me anyways.
There's just so much wrong... the game is a chore to play and the glitchiness doesn't help. Not particularly good performance either, I've played games more graphically advanced than this that ran better. I wish I could like this game, but I just can't, it's not close to being good.

It's always both surprising and depressing when a video game uses only a single game mechanic for the entirety of it, and that mechanic is implemented as poorly as possible.
I cannot even fathom what others here who claim that this game has no bugs played but it certainly wasn't Lifeless Planet. You see, this game is one of those which wants you to experience the views and vistas while having minimal interaction with anything else. No shooting, no big puzzles. Running and jumping.
The story starts out very intruiging and leads to a sub-standard and cliche'd ending. Running and jumping at first seems enjoyable and even quite fun and exciting until you jump from one rock to another for the 1000th time and wish the game would throw something different at you already, or just end. The jumping mechanic itself is done as poorly as possible. Yes it works, but barely. I kept getting stuck on rocks and canyons and the almost non-existent air control after a jump mostly lead to an untimely death.
The best thing about Lifeless Planet is the music and the artistic concept of some of the environments. Because even though technically this game is nothing to look up to, it definitely has great atmosphere and you almost always feel alone and helpless on an alien planet. The orchestrated music, as I previously mentioned, is brilliant. I would recommend listening to the soundtrack because along with the atmosphere, it's the only thing holding this game up.
Definitely not worth full price and definitely not for those who are looking for a long or special experience. The abundance of graphical glitches and audio bugs (music and sfx would suddenly disappear in many of the levels) hold this title back from becoming a true triumph.
Treat the game as a 5-hour experiment from a promising bunch of indie developers and you'll probably find something to like. If you approach it with hopes of experiencing anything above standard (except for the music) it will lead to sour disappointment.

Lifeless Planet is a walking simulator. Now normally I use that term as a kind of endearing, tongue-in-cheek term for narrative-driven exploration games like Dear Esther, Gone Home, etc. which I enjoy greatly. However Lifeless Planet is much closer to a literal
simulator. You spend the vast majority of the game trundling along... well, a lifeless planet. The game is drab and brown and and boring looking. There are light platforming sections as well, which are serviceable but nothing really special. The jumping physics feel a bit off but don't get too frustrating.
The excessive walking sections might be tolerable if paired with an interesting story (like "Eidolon") or beautiful visuals (like "Mind: Path to Thalamus"), but they're not. The story is mildly intriguing, but never really goes anywhere outside typical sci-fi fare, and journal logs and story tidbits are too few and far between. You spend most of the game chasing after a mysterious woman, even though you don't really know why other than "there's nowhere else to go". It just feels kind of aimless.
It's a 5ish hour game, but it still feels like it drags on too long. It just wasn't my cup of tea.

One of my favourite games as a kid was Raft Away River on the Apple IIe - a game where you were shipwrecked on an island and had to manage food, shelter, warmth and the like before making your escape. The notion of a modern take on this was quite appealing, and Dead in Bermuda made a solid first impression. Unfortunately, the cracks appeared very quickly.
It is a hard game, and not in an enjoyable way. There are a number of interlinking mechanics which conspire to lock you into a tailspin of failure from the early stages. A number of early upgrades are essential. Each requires a substantial number of resources. However, you must also spend those resources to maintain your existing structures, otherwise they become starkly less effective.
This can leave a situation where you cannot build the upgrade allowing you to collect the resources you need because you're spending your dwindling resources constantly trying to maintain your shelter, since without that maintainance your people will be perpetually tired and thus ineffective in every task (if not dead).
There is an easy mode (which the devs strangely dub "normal" mode, as opposed to the default "hard") buried away, but it may as well be casual mode because it makes the game a tedious clicker with no real challenge.
If there was a good story it might be worth it, but it doesn't even have that. It's linear and one-note, just a bunch of random attempts at humour and weird misspellings - it's like they decided to just spell some words phonetically without even bothering to look them up. It all culminates in a boss battle which is a choose your own adventure with RNG, a tedious and frustrating experience.
That all leads to an ending which is so lame that I'm grateful that I wasn't invested in the game, because it'd be a big slap in the face if I was.
This all sounds rather harsh, and I didn't realise how annoyed with the game I was until I wrote it out, but unfortunately this is the impression which it left.
Dead in Bermuda is very challenging but from the great challenge comes great satisfaction (or frustration).

2. Got to about day 10 and realized that the plane was running out of resources and I would need to find a new way to produce food

6. Sat everyone down at the campfire on day 16 hoping they would go happily, all but the little girl starved to death.
7. She died of exhaustion on day 17.
This all amounted to 1.8 hours of gameplay (including the slower gameplay during the tutorial) and I was having fun for about half of that time, the period where things were somewhat working out for my group.

In conclusion, I would definitely not waist 15 dollars on this game, 5 dollar price tag and I would recommend it.

In it you manage 8 characters each with their own backstories who survive a plane crash on an island. To survive you must gather resources such as wood rocks food and herbs, while using them to heal and feed your survivors and build up your base. There also is a very interesting map system where you send people out to explore then you can explore and scavenge the place. Once there you will have to pass rng tests of stealth to do anything. You have the trade off of either using as strong character to not take as much damage or a stealthy character who can try to not take damage via rng or take more damage if they fail the stealth check.
TL;DR if you enjoy survival games pick this one up its mostly unique and fun to play for more hours than the price suggests.

Everything is where it needs to be, and no piece of detail is left out.

You hit enter. And that's when quite possibly the greatest moment hits you. Your body already so full of ecstasy, that you're not quite sure you can comprehend what's currently unfolding in front of you. Your eyes cast a gaze on the screen, and as they follow from left to right, you see it...
“Rise my Bee’s, morning honey is the sweetest honey!”
I can’t describe it. The feeling is nothing short of overwhelming. To see such shakespearean writing takes such dedication and craftsmanship, you almost feel like you’ve known the characters for your entire life. You start to picture moments of your childhood, reimagined. The front porch, as Becky the Queen Bee cradles you in her arms, her gentle antenna caressing your face as she gazes into the blooming fields beyond. Worker Bee #37 mowing the lawn as the scent of freshly cut grass wafts through the air. You feel at peace. You feel at home.

The campaign is ungodly long for how shallow the actual gameplay is. You play an overly simplified city builder for half an hour, interrupted every once in a while by "tactical" combat which requires no real thought or planning. After you win, you repeat this again a dozen times until the campaign ends.
For the city builder portion, a quarter of the buildings are so situational that you will never actually build them in the campaign. Another quarter is so clearly inferior to your other choices that you have to wonder why you would build them except for the missions that restrict you from constructing the better buildings.
The only progression you have in the game is the perks you get when your gangsters level and the weapons they can buy during the missions. Unfortunately the game handles this too poorly to actually make you feel like you're making any progress. Many of the perks offer only small numerical bonuses, while the good perks don't even really matter since you can almost always just shoot your way through a mission as long as you don't make any obviously bad tactical decisions. The weapons carry over through the campaign, but if you want them you'll end up just waiting in a mission long after you've won, just to make money to buy them. Later you can sell all the extra crap weapons you've bought to try and speed up the missions so I guess that's something.
The story which is the best part of the game, is fairly charming but wouldn't stand out if the rest of the game wasn't so poor. And this is a massive problem as the tiny chunks of plot each mission doles out, is almost unbearable for the repetitive gameplay that you put up with in the campaign.

This could really be a great game if not for some pretty major issues. I'm not talking technical issues either (allthough it has those), I'm talking major design flaws in the game itself. I've been playing Solforge for some time now, over 200 hours so far, and while this game has the usual balance issues, and other minor technicalities associated with an early release game, the real killer (and why i no longer play) is the rediculous tedium of having to wait...and wait....and wait...and wait some more just to take each of your turns. For some ungodly reason your given 20 min per game each for a total of 40 min, but no time limit on each individual move, so you find yourself quite often que'ing for a game, about 20-40 sec, loading the game screen, about 5-10 sec, THEN STARING AT YOUR MONITOR FOR LITERALLY 15 MINUTES WHILE YOU WAIT FOR YOUR OPONENT TO MAKE THEIR FIRST MOVE!!! But here's the real pinch, the game also allows you to create what seems to be an unlimited amount of games running at the same time. So not only do you get people who enjoy letting the timer run from 20 min down to 3 min before they make their first move, or people who "give up" by simply moving to another game and letting what remains of their 20 min timer run to 0, but you also have to contend with the fact that in 95% of all Solforge games, your opponent will without a doubt have at least 3-4, maybe even 7-8 other games running at the same time, which means while your making moves in 10-20 seconds, your opponent is take 4-5 minutes per move because they're jumping from game to game, and not actually even in your game looking at the same screen you are. This to me is a MAJOR design flaw, and a source of a lot of complaint and debate on the Solforge forums. When you actually get lucky, and happen across another player who seems to only have the one game open like you, and moves are happening in usually less than 30 seconds or so, then the game is actually quite fluid and enjoyable, to the extent I'd even spend real money on it to bolster my collection and "finish off" a few of my decks. But as it stands you spend far to much time doing nothing but staring and waiting. Not cool. In fact its just plain boring and quite frustrating. The Dev's say the official release is on the horizon, and i pray they dont leave the game the way it is, because the "influx of people" they're hope'ing for wont stay for long i can assure you. Which would be a real shame, this could be such a great little game, but for now, ill be off playing something else.

When reviewing "old" games, I tend to be tolerant in regards to technical aspects such as graphical fidelity, animation quality and overall presentation.
, released in 2006, is not a bad looker. Cranked up to the max, its video settings allow for some pretty stunning vistas in the huge tropical island of San Esperito.
However, that's pretty much where the praise ends.
The story has no depth at all. You're a US agent and your mission is to overthrow a Latin American dictator. Along the way, you'll be assigned some the most forgettable seek-and-destroy missions the gaming world has ever seen, usually consisting of:
1. Being briefed by terribly voice-acted, stereotypized characters;
2. Getting to terms with the nearest vehicle's shoddy handling in order to reach your objective as quickly as possible;
3. Storming a government base, guns blazing (forget about stealth), walking through fire from a hundred mindless, respawning enemies (good luck getting cover from helicopter miniguns, though), planting a few C4 charges and leaving.
That's it. Very simplistic gameplay coupled with terrible artifical intelligence. That's
in a nutshell.
I wouldn't recommend it by 2006's standards, and I most certainly won't recommend it now.

For starters, the game just looks horrible. The whole thing looks like it was drawn by a 10 year old over the duration of a half an hour, TOPS. The font is blocky and annoying to read, all the characters are just outfit swaps, and everything just looks unappealing and bland.

I first rented this game back in March 1997 when it was originally released, then purchased it outright later that summer (along with an N64 Controller Pak, because god forbid you try to beat this in one sitting).  I went on to love and complete all 3 of the mainline Turok games released on the system (even Turok 3, which was lowkey garbage), and this rererelase does an exceptional job of wiping away the thick fog and wonky controls of the 64-bit original and playing the way Iguana likely intended it to.
Draw distances are vastly, vastly superior, you can turn on a reticle to fascilitate actual, proper aiming (and turn on a "precision aiming" mode to trim down the bloated, console-friendly hitboxes of enemies), and most importantly, you get fast, responsive keyboard and mouse controls that make the game play like a modern release.
Of course, this is still 1997 design, and gameplay never evolves beyond simplistic shooting, keycard collecting, braindead enemies, and a shocking amount of 1st person platforming (which is actually manageable now on Kb+M).  But it all works, really well, and it's fun.  If you're a younger player who's never experienced Turok, but enjoy modern shooters like Shadow Warrior and Doom 2016, there's real fun to be had here beyond just nostalgia.
It also has to be said that the game looks absolutely decrepid, low-poly chunkiness liberally smeared with Vaseline textures, but it's so aged that it almost crosses over from being a relic to being downright A E S T H E T I C.  It's very much of its era, which is bad, but in a good way.

I figured out how to load mods without using the editor:
Step 1: Go to - (Your Drive):\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\SteamLibrary\steamapps\workshop\content\405820 - You will see folders with different numbers, inside these folders are your mods.
Step 2: Take out all the ".kpf" files in each of these folders and copy them to the main directory for Turok - (Your Drive):\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\SteamLibrary\steamapps\common\Turok - Dinosaur Hunter
Step 3: Set go to the game properties in steam, and click "Set Launch Options". Once here you'll need to enter the command "+KexPakFile::LoadZipFile:" (Without the quotes) And then enter the name of the mod after.
- [EXAMPLE] -  "+KexPakFile::LoadZipFile: turokrevampedstartmenu.kpf"
Step 4: Do this for every mod you have installed.
ENJOY!

Exanima is unique and yet will probably feel familiar for those of you who were playing hack'n'slash and cRPG during the late 90's early 2000's, the grim visuals and macabre atmosphere brings me way back and touch my feels in places I thought long dead.
I even felt unease and stress when walking these long pitchblack corridors, my torch in one hand, a barrel lid in the other, going deeper and deeper into darkness, from which anything could emerge and pounce at my face... and then♥♥♥♥♥♥goes wrong : panic-running back to the nearest fix source of light to draw my weapon and face it (or them), stumbling and falling on the way, I could die at any moment. And I did, and I will again. Because Exanima is hard !
It's hard and I love it ! The game is very challenging, it doesn't guide you, it doesn't help you nor pats you on the shoulder, it just kills your worthless peasant's butt ; it's up to you to take a stand and prove you're a fearless survivor and a talented fighter.
And that's another point I love about the game and the unique fighting mechanics : you're a nobody, you're not a hero who can finish his/her foes single-handedly, you need to be tactical, careful, cool headed and smart ; you have to keep your composure or else you WILL make costly mistakes and probably die. Surviving and progressing really feels rewarding ; even more considering checkpoints are scarce, but fair.
Controls are very different from anything I've played so far, it takes a bit to get used to, and hours to master (I'm far from having mastered them after 23h ingame, but getting there!). Under pressure it works magic : if you can't keep your calm your character will feel clumsy because of your lack of precision as a player.
Right now the game feels more like a (really good) Hack'n'slash, considering it's under development and the more RPG-y aspect of the game will bloom later. But it sure is going in the right direction.
Oh, and the Arena mod is a botomless pit of entertainment !

BUY. NOW. The most worthy of your patience game ever.
-This would be the opposite of No Man Sky, looks deceptively simple but has infinite deep and subtlety. The graphics seems simple but the attraction is that even at low dpi you see no pixels at all, with nicely grained textures.
-By far the most important feature is the constant ragdoll physics, this is no fixed animation system! when you hit you are not merely substracting hp, you are affecting enemy impulse, to the point of twarting an incoming attack. I cannot emphazise the importance of this design choice enough, it is groundbreaking and every hit, miss and block is unique, you will remember epic blows given and received forever, it really grows on you.
-This imposes particular problems, like having some "puppet" feeling. The input was the second most obvious hurdle. Both issues had the most intensive work and i can attest a solid leap, having played since before steam greenlight.
-If you are ready to try, please take time to start arena "story" mode, even if its more difficult than straight practice. Just because of the pugilism mode added not so long ago, it is both massively fun and very forgiving and helps you familiarize with input and timing with lower frustration factor.
Im not very fond of learning new ways of playing since im and old gamer, but this game will reward you like no other if you take it easy, forget big shiny critical numbers to make you feel like you hit something good, you will grin and laugh like a madman when you connect good whacks here and those impacts will affect enemies while they are still alive, no ragdoll when dead ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. This is a true gem.

Hard, Strange and yet brilliant!
Exanima, despite being one of the many early access games on steam, has no comparable games that i know of. From imagery or a written review alone it would appear another dark fantasy dungeon game, it's only upon closer inspection or a video review that you see the unique and complex combat system which is at it's very core what exanima is about. Exanima is at the moment a little less content rich than many would like but the game is in effect a fund raiser and proof of concept for another larger game that the devs are working on and so while it will likely continue to be worked and inmproved it will never be a huge game.
All considered the game is definitely worth a look just for the fact that it is so different from the many other combat games out there. When chivilary medievil warfare was released many praised it for it's complex and innovative combat system, and yet it pales in comparison the sheer ingenuity of Exanima's system.

After hours of playing. I can confidently say that I am satisfied with my purchase of this game. Imagine if a game with clunky as hell combat (like Mount & blade) had a baby with a unforgiving difficult game (like dark souls) and this is the game you get.
So what's the story? Honestly, I'm not sure. As a proctor, I'm investigating the dissapearance of somebody in this dungeon, and that's all you're told when you start. Much like Dark Souls, experiencing the story is up to you, as most of it is found in journals, and parchments. Often times, it's easy to miss important notes. I will say though that this mystery adds substantially to the interest of the game. You will see rooms in the game that are pretty interesitng. "What's with this planning room?" "Is this some sort of council room". You will find yourself trying to put the pieces together with the story, and I found that kind of fun.
More importantly, the gameplay is what is fun about this game. I will say though that it can be very frustrating in the beginning, and learning to fight takes patience in this game. Once you learn to fight though, the game can be really fun. I reccomend trying out the Arena for practice. It iwll make you better at the campaign, and half the experience is in the Arena. The combat uses ragdoll physics. Your character can get hung up on stuff like chairs, walls, doors, weapon racks, and will also trip over these things if you run into them at full speed.
Exanima is a dark game, and at some times can be creepy. this mixes really well with the tense combat, as you know anything can be a threat. Anything can kill you, and anything can jump into the fight to team up and can kill you. Often times you won't even see enemies coming because when I say this game is "dark" I mean it literally. Without a torch you are doomed.
Now on to some negative stuff. You can spend 10+ hours on this game, and have your character end up in a situation of being totally doomed. For example, if you first/main character dies in Arena, you have to start all over again. Or how about in campagin, there are no potions. You can take what is called "Lethal damage" This damage covers your yellow health bar in red. This damage is never recovered. There are 3 salves that will heal this damage all the way spread out accross the 5 floors that are playable right now. What if you lose your torch? You can't see anything (and this will happen at level 5 btw) you can either walk blind in the dark, let yourself die, and come back to life in your torch (which is a big set back) or you can find this "Special item" hidden in a secret door in level 3 that let's you see in the dark.
There's also quite a few mazes, and timed switch doors. Personally, I did not find these parts fun. a lot of the time, the game doesn't acknowledge me clicking the levers, and I have to stop my forward motion to pull them, creating a frusterating experience.
You can interact with items in this game a feature that I loved in games in Skyrim, and it's a weclome addition to this game). Often times, you can use this item interactions in puzzles. For example, take a plank of wood, lay it over a trap door. Press a button to open a gate on the other side as the trap door falls open, the walk accross the plank. I think this was a really cool part of the game. Item palcement tended to be slightly difficult, and sometimes items would refuse to cooperate with me, and not allow me to play them in certain areas.
I should also point out that the updates for this game are slow as molassis. There's been 11 updates in the past year. And the most recent one as of this review was just a week ago. Before that, there had not been an update since May. Thankfully, they do add a lot in these updates, but they are coming rather slowly.
In the end, due to this games addictive gameplay, creepy dungeons, fun combat (once you're good at it), in addition to it's item interactions, I have to reccomend this game. Updates for this game don't come often, but I will say that's because this small studio is working on a second game that seems very similar to Exanima. however, the updates are *big* when they do happen, and I can't wait for the next one, and I can't wait for their next game.

The ending ruins the game
As for the game itself, I'll try to go over my thoughts playing it, both the pros and cons.
The music was a nice listen, but not exactly memorable - and it didn't get to the point of being irritating and sets the mood, so it's a net positive even if there's nothing to write home about. The graphics and art direction are probably the high point of the entire game. Every character looks unique, and you can tell at a glance their general personality and attitude, and they have differing expressions during conversation scenes, something most games don't bother with. The Gods are suitably strange and enigmatic, even if their symbolism was about as subtle as Lord of the Flies - same goes with the various objects you can find, from a WWI-era plane to a bishop on a toliet - the only things I would hold against is the random monsters looked more like they belong in a JRPG.
The gameplay is simple to pick up, and it's got some depth. Every character has something they'll be better at, characters they get along better with than others, and with randomized traits, there's some flucations in what works and what doesn't, and the fun thing is their traits reveal their background - Why is Julia so good at combat related stuff? It makes sense once you get the relevant fireside chat. There are a couple ways to lose people, so it's important to watch your negative stats.
Now the big part of the game aside from exploring and minor crafting is relationship building, which is a great concept but is somewhat flawed execution. Least when I played, if the RNG is not kind about the placement of plot locations, you can very easily run out of conversation midway through the game - or sooner if someone dies - which is very likely to happen, as one or two characters will outright attempt to murder another member of your group if their relationship is too low - and this can happen randomly. There is another flaw as the conversations don't always account for overall mood, so even if someone's 5 hearts with everyone, he can provoke everyone to the point of causing depression, and while there's some interesting plotlines, most seem to have gone nowhere in my play, and the clearly intended canon romance is rather rushed.
There is a hitch at the end game - a required bossfight that is entirely trial and error, while it's repeatable, it's a brick wall - when the player is close to the goal with nothing else to do, you have to keep the momentum up, to keep them interested and excited, but the way the boss works, it's in-games of frustration as your main combat character fights, you ditch to make sure they don't die, wait for them to heal, before going back - killing the momentum.
The game only has one ending, the only reason to play through the game is to earn all the achievements.
And I already said my piece about the ending.

I left this game with extremely mixed feelings. I enjoyed the art style, the diversity of characters, and the overall tone. Unfotunately, the story and mechanics rip apart what would have otherwise been a true gem of a game. The resource management is tough -- it's supposed to be -- and you do feel pressure to manage your survivors' needs vs. the demand for new materials, food, and water. It's just hard to find the will to continue when the game goes out of its way to hate you.
1. The story is a bite-for-bite rip off of Lost, from beginning to end. They've changed a few things, added a dash of mythology to spice up the soup, but you realize exactly how things are going to play out within the first twenty minutes of game time. It takes a lot of the meaning away, once you realize you're clicking through a story you already know.
2. Characters have relationship levels with one another, but it dosen't seem to matter. Each day ends with a vignette between two of your survivors. Most of these events are negative, which is a fine way to add tension into the game. Except one character decided to♥♥♥♥♥♥on another character's food despite being max relationship, doubling the amount she needed to be fed that day. Another started an argument with the entire group, again at max relationship, and tripled the amount of depression that needed fixing the next day.
Either relationships matter, in which case the code should care too, or they don't, in which case why are they in the game?
3. Holy Jesus the boss fight. There's only one boss in this game, and you will hate to fight it. The entire fight is a choose-your-own-adventure style, "decide what move to use now" click-a-thon. Except there is no choice, because your charater will only be high enough in one of three major stat areas, so you'll pick that one every time.
Failing at any part of the seven or eight even sequence starts you over, with the success rates falling each successive round. "Beating" the boss is essentially no more complicated (or easy) than rolling a dice six times, and getting six ones in a row. Uninteresting, repetitive, and wholly subject to the in-game RNG with no input from the player.
Buy it if you're willing to overlook those flaws, but wait until it's on sale.

Review:
We all know that despite many titles wearing the label of survival game, there are very few survival games that deserve that name. Even less of them are considered "finished" and out of Beta or Early Access.
This game is neither simulation, nor survival, nor RPG, nor strategy, nor heavily focused on crafting.
So if you are looking for the title that will scratch that survival itch we all have, this game simply isn't it.
Graphics: 7/10
Colourful, 2D graphics, nicely done locations, some ridiculous character graphic etc.
Overall it is nice and welcoming.
Sound: 4/10
Annoying ambient and music, no Voice Acting.
Music is basically few 15 sec loops repeating over and over and over again.
Gameplay: 5/10
This game is resource management game, not survival.
You have to manage certain resources and keep states of characters down to a minimum.
It becomes tedious AF very soon, due to very broken and imbalanced mechanics.
Seriously.
Unless you abuse game mechanics, RNG is going to whip you silly and fukk you stupid death spiralling out of control.
If you do abuse game mechanics, the game turns into a breeze and you drown in resources.
Here is how it works:
The result of an action, for example, fishing, depends on the following:
- states of the characters (all affect results negatively)
- a condition of the item used (cut off is extreme)
- skill related to the action
- character stat related to the action
- and finally, if two characters are performing the action, on how much they like or dislike each other
Therefore game forces you to pair characters in a very predefined way to achieve the desired result. And as they work together chances are they will like each other more and more and more, they will level up their skills and stats and deliver an outstanding performance.
However, if you would like to have some freedom, and pair toons with lower stats or who do not like each other yet, you will get so little resources, you will be running from one bottleneck to another just to keep yourself afloat.
What is possibly most incredible is that game actually becomes easier with fewer characters. Because two at the fruit collecting job can collect enough fruits to both feed 4 to 5 people and build up water surplus, while the other two gather resources or explore. This will give you even ability to call days off for toons to rest.
Or, more importantly, have them talk to each other. Characters in this game will die from dreadful "Not-being-talk-to-enough" syndrome.
Well, so far so good. But then, the worst part of this game.
Storyline.
The storyline in this game is bad, I actually think this game was made as a joke.
It is so poor, tied to exploration, and so ridiculous with all those blue people and mystical crap, it will just make you shake your head in disbelief.
Oh, and there is only one ending. A bad one, actually.

Lifeless Planet is a walking simulator. Now normally I use that term as a kind of endearing, tongue-in-cheek term for narrative-driven exploration games like Dear Esther, Gone Home, etc. which I enjoy greatly. However Lifeless Planet is much closer to a literal
simulator. You spend the vast majority of the game trundling along... well, a lifeless planet. The game is drab and brown and and boring looking. There are light platforming sections as well, which are serviceable but nothing really special. The jumping physics feel a bit off but don't get too frustrating.
The excessive walking sections might be tolerable if paired with an interesting story (like "Eidolon") or beautiful visuals (like "Mind: Path to Thalamus"), but they're not. The story is mildly intriguing, but never really goes anywhere outside typical sci-fi fare, and journal logs and story tidbits are too few and far between. You spend most of the game chasing after a mysterious woman, even though you don't really know why other than "there's nowhere else to go". It just feels kind of aimless.
It's a 5ish hour game, but it still feels like it drags on too long. It just wasn't my cup of tea.
