More than a review, this simply aims to be a collection of thoughts on my experience with the game.
I was honestly very excited when I first heard of this title. Sadly, it didn't really live up to expectations.
Not that it's a BAD game, it's just not consistent and often breaks the immersion and atmosphere. Which is a shame: this game would otherwise really do a great job in creating a haunting experience.
One example:  roughly a few minutes into the game, after the impact, you find your oxygen levels are dropping dramatically due to a leak. After running to an oxygen tank, you will be able to fill up (and magically fix the leak) and be left with an autonomy of approx 8 hours.
Shortly after that you will find your way to the Russian town where, among other things, you'll find another oxygen tank. Remember where it is, because you are likely going to use it more than once, as oxygen will run out within minutes and you'll have to track your steps back to it quite often until you unlock the next zone - which is where the game just resets its own rules: for most of the time your oxygen will last you days, with the exception of a few areas. You can argue that, as the game has cutscenes, you will have filled up in the period of time we weren't in control of him for - but there are plenty of areas you'll be roaming for a relatively long time without a worry.
This may sound like a really minor thing to complain about, but it's one of many the immersion suffers from.
Another aspect that feels often unnatural is that of puzzles: more often than not, the puzzles will feel completely irrelevant - you can safely pick up the green stones with your hands, but you NEED the robotic arm to place them in a slot roughly at the same height as your head, triggering a mini game. When you feel you might actually have found a use for the arm it won't be available for use, as it's only triggered when close to an object it is designed to interact with.
The puzzles overall are never overly challenging, with the game mainly focusing on jumping, and simply feel out of place - situations that require you to interact with objects to actually clear a path are scarce, and when you do come up with a clever idea, the game just won't cooperate with you.
It's not a bad design choice in itself, it just feels like the dev threw any potential the game had out the window.
As for the story, it is obviously the aspect that should keep you playing the game until the end - but again, it starts with an intriguing premise and loses it's strength in the later chapters.
What the game does achieve though, is in creating its atmosphere through haunting sound effects and a well placed soundtrack, which alone manages to keep the player on edge.
Overall, I'd still recommend this if you can overlook it's flaws - the story is not without surprises, and the atmosphere it creates tries hard to make up for most of what the game lacks in mechanics.

I really enjoyed this game. It's an engaging story - actually several stories, intertwined - that sucked me in right away. The atmosphere of uncertain danger and mystery is very well done. The story unfolds slowly as you wander through the world, and in between the moments of discovery what it all means is left to your imagination. A lot of time is spent wondering just what the heck is going on, which is a really nice change of pace from always knowing your mission.
I was a little hesitant to buy this game at first because my enjoyment of both puzzle-heavy games and platformers is very hit-and-miss, but the story intrigued me enough that I was willing to give it a shot. I'm glad I did. The puzzles are straightforward - nothing that requires the internet to solve. Any time I got stuck, a little wandering around led me to whatever I was missing.
The first jump puzzle was almost a dealbreaker until I figured out how to use the jet pack properly, but once I got the hang of it it was easy. There was also one level where I got hopelessly lost for awhile, but otherwise the game played out very smoothly. Overall this game makes the platforming pretty painless, and there are some jump sequences that are acually bouncy fun.
That said, if you're looking for a puzzle-platformer you'll probably be disappointed with this. The platforming consists solely of jumping (and one high-wire sequence you'd have to be drunk to fall off of) and the puzzles are very easy. This is really more of an interactive story, and the game elements seem to be there mostly to make it more, well, game-y. On the flipside, those game elements are unobtrusive enough to make this a good interactive story, so if you like story games, this won't disappoint.
As far as the story goes, I enjoyed it, though I did think it could have been fleshed out a bit more.
I didn't encounter any bugs or other technical issues, aside from the mouse cursor appearing in the game if I alt-tabbed while playing fullscreen.
The game is short - though I took almost 6 hours for my first play through, you could easily finish it in 4 - so the price seems a bit steep. But looking at the achievements I can see that I even missed some pieces of the story, so it's also worth another play through.

Pros:
This is an easy strategy game.
Great for casual players... Kind of...
The turn based combat is simple...
Cons:
AI is abysmal.
Balance is nonexistent.
Economic side is dumbed down to facebook level.
Equipment is impossible to get what you want.
Let’s just say the cons are the game seems like the alpha of the game was released where they were just trying to figure out what they were trying to do... Then never came back and finished the game and released the first almost playable concept...
Let’s start with character development. There is an attempt at it. It is not based on combat, kills, damage, jobs/missions, or anything that should cause your character to increase. The only thing that triggers level advancement or character progress is certain pre-scripted missions that grant you a level. This dumbs down progression and makes it anti-climactic and tedious. No matter if I play a level completely through conquer all the properties and finish every detail, or do the bare minimum it does not change the character development. This is obnoxious.
Equipment is like an afterthought in this game. You have 1 slot for 1 weapon. That is it. 1 slot. You can equip a single weapon. No body armor, med kits, or any of a countless other standard fare in these games. No switching between primary and secondary weapons. You get ONE weapon. And most of what you are offered is baseball bats and knives to fight people with tommy guns and flame throwers. For every three melee weapons I was offered a ranged weapon. And most levels (streets) allow you to buy 0-3 weapons. There are no equipment drops during combat. You find yourself quickly using pistols and revolvers and melee weapons against much more powerful items. Seriously, the balance on weapons is non-existent, but helps balance the poor AI.
The AI is horrific. Some missions you swear they are scripted and others if they can't see you or your target, they don't get to move. I have had combat where I have two enemies with a divider wall between them in a U shaped room. As I moved I spotted both but I am obscured from the one and he is not in my direct line of sight. They are less than 10 move from each other. I shoot the exploding barrel next to my target as it was both his cover and a way to do more damage. The fire crosses the divider immediately and will soon start the hidden character on fire. He doesn’t spot me yet. What? I shot the barrel in front of him and he is on fire and does not get to act??? I shoot and miss, still oblivious. I shoot and hit with my final shot and miraculously he spots me. End turn. He runs further INTO the fire and shoots at me from there with a flame thrower… Ok, ironic and a bit funny… I am now on fire, he is on fire the fire he is standing in is spreading. The guy on the other side of the divider doesn’t come out. My turn, I move back to cover and shoot at him until I am out of actions. His turn he stays where he is and tries to flame me again. Still waiting, the other guy does not get an action. I take him out finally. One of my other character gets in position and the other guy was just standing in the flames like nothing was wrong. Awesome AI!!!!
Your economic side is deciding which prefab buildings to rent or attack and rent or buy out… And set up enterprises to make money. You can’t build more. You can’t upgrade sites. You get a category per site with set selections and then you can “improve” the selected business. Or you can buy residential and a small house, apartment, or factory all cost $1000 and make you $80. No balance, logic, reason, or anything. You have limited choices and it plays like a phone app or facebook game.
Heat is how much the police have noticed your criminal activity. And it doesn’t matter if you are running legitimate businesses only or criminal ones you are going to gain heat just for existing. I have tried even going as far as not owning anything, not running a single mission, and just sitting there. And yes, even if you do NOTHING and own NOTHING the heat level increases. It appears to have a minimum increase over time with modifiers depending on mission.
I so wanted to like this game. But alas Jagged Alliance I was better and Jagged Alliance II blew the doors off of this game. Kalypso, please finish this game… or at least advance it to BETA from the playable concept you released…

A combination of business management and tactical turn-based combat, Omerta - City of Gangsters will scratch your Mafia itch like you wouldn't believe.  The atmosphere is absolutely incredible and you feel like you've hopped into a time machine and traveled back to the 20's.  The single-player story was far deeper and more enjoyable than I had first expected it to be.  You create your character by answering about half a dozen questions regarding their past and begin play at about the time they step off of the boat in the United States.  From then on, you begin to form connections, set up (or extort) little businesses (some legitimate, others as fronts for the illegal activity taking place within), rob banks, chase off other gangs, etc.  All of this takes place while an overarching storyline with several twists and turns plays out along the way.
The business management side of the game is entertaining, and simple enough to learn quickly without a significant time investment.  On each map there are dozens of lots that can be built on (if there isn't already a building there), purchased, taken over, or firebombed by your gang.  On these lots are everything from pizza shops to speakeasies to casinos to gun shops to smuggling rings, each with their own purpose and choice of upgrades.
The combat aspect of the game is can most easily be compared to XCOM.  It's a turn-based tactical combat system that utilizes a variety of unit stats, skills, and equipment to engage in battles where a limitless number of approaches are possible.  Though you can only ever have six members of your gang working directly with you at any given time, every single member of your gang levels up at the same time - a massive convenience for those Dons who prefer to swap gang members in and out on the fly.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys tactical turn-based strategy, light business sims, and that Mafia-era Roaring Twenties setting.

If I had to sum up this game in one word, it would be "Enjoyable."  The artwork is great, the voice acting is as good as I have ever witnessed, the story is clever and unique with all of its' characters being quite original, and most importantly the gameplay itself is well-tuned and fun.
Fans of SRPGs will appreciate the battles.  Every character you recruit is entirely different from the next.  The path to upgrading characters involves a sort-of skill tree, where you have a number of passive abilities to choose from (Health +100, damage +3% etc) with a few unique individual skills that upgrade their battle abilities.  Leveling up has a sense of importance to it, and as you graduate skills and stats, you feel a real sense of accomplishment after seeing how effective your characters now are in combat.  There are a thousand ways to win a battle with the varying make up of your party at anyone one time.  My only knock here is that you have free reign to choose your entire squad for 99% of the fights, which at least for me fell into a pattern of the same team almost half of the game.  I would have liked to have seen more variety, with story related battles forcing the usage of certain characters and combinations.  The enemies are well varied, and several stages have interesting circumstances (survive X turns, one battle with a mother bug and the field is surrounded by eggs that turn into bugs in X turns.)
Fans of story driven RPGs should also be in for a good time.  The story itself is perhaps a bit short, I suspect I will be completed with the game around the 30 hours mark.  But the best part of the story isn't the main plot itself, it's the development of the individual characters through a series of Personal Bond quests.  They are all at times hilarious, sad, and even philosophical, but consistently well written and thought out.  These quests are also rewarding, as they unlock abilities for use in the skill tree I referenced earlier, and also allow you to upgrade stores in your castle.
My only knock on the game is that it appears incomplete, which you can read about more in the Discussions.  I don't know if the intention is a paid DLC or an update in the future, but I don't intend to replay the entire game again once released, so now I feel like I am potentially missing out on something.
I'm hooked on this game, I dare not look at how long I have spent playing it.

This game is the best tactical RPG I've played on Steam thus far, and compares remarkably well to classic JRPGs considering the resources the developers had to work with.
The game's best quality is its well thought out combat system which is challenging and diverse. The game has around a dozen characters each of whom are powerful in their own right, with unique abilities that give them a really varied feel in combat and allows for a wide variety of strategies. The characters also have a lot of personality out of combat. Each has a quest chain and many, many chances to interact through conversations.
The writing is excellent, and although I don't say it lightly, sometimes even laugh out loud funny. It frequently uses subtle geek culture references, from Warhammer 40k, to Recettear, to Dr Who, to Despicable Me to Fallout. It feels to me to be a labour of love for the writers.
The graphical quality is excellent and you can judge this for yourself from the store page. Music and voice acting are also very good, and after seeing the credits I was surprised to see the game had more voice actors than developers.
In summary, I was very pleasantly surprised by this game. Despite some flaws, I feel it's well worth a purchase for those of us who would like to see more quality TRPGs made. I finished the game in just over 30 hours, with many dungeons still available to complete once the main story is over.

Regalia: Of Men and Monarchs is a fantastic tactical RPG with some gorgeous artwork and writing. Truthfully, the writing is actually what pulled me into the game to begin with! It also features an extremely interesting and useful feature for a game in its genre: the option to skip battles entirely! When I first saw this, I was immediately intrigued. How does that work? Well, pretty well, because Regalia is all about it's story.
==========
A short intro cutscene to the world of Regalia greets you as you start up the game. You are introduced to Kay, the sole heir of the Loren family and estate of Ascalia. Joining him are his entourage of a protective knight and two sisters. Upon going to visit the estate that is his inheritance, Kay discovers that the castle and village are rather run-down and in rather bad shape. They decide to just cut their losses and leave, but upon leaving they are approached by a member of the Furtive Union. It seems that their family had accrued a large amount of debt from the estate, and are pretty much forced to take the land and estate and restore it to its former glory to make up that debt.
Even though it's a tactical RPG, Regalia is very story driven. There are cutscenes and dialogue aplenty, with battles peppering the experience here and there. Thankfully, both sides of the coin are very well done. Cutscenes are usually fully voiced, and you can definitely tell that the voice actors were quite experienced. They became their character, and brought them to life on screen through their voice acting.
On the battle side of things, Regalia is surprisingly deep. At the start of each battle (assuming you didn't skip it!), you are allowed to choose who to send into battle. Once placed on the starting grid, you can view your character's stats and abilities, as well as how far they can move, at any time. Turns play out in a certain order depending on your characters and actions taken. Each entity in battle gets their turn one after another until the battle ends. As far as actual combat, it's more of the same from the rest of the genre. Fans of tactical RPGs will know exactly what to do.
In addition, you also get to manage, repair, and upgrade your castle town as you go. Resources can be gathered in and out of battle, and spent on your estate to improve it. Doing so can help you establish trade routes with nearby towns, which in turn improves your reputation and level with them. After certain levels, you can recruit special characters from said towns and their factions, which in turn helps you in battle. Everything you do can benefit you in some way or another.
==========
The artwork of this game just drips with love and detail. Everything is lovingly crafted and painted in such a way as to make the world feel very alive and vibrant. One of my favorite parts of Regalia is definitely the artwork. Every character is well animated, which compliments the excellent voice acting. I can't find anything bad to say about this aspect of the game!
==========
Aesthetically speaking, the music and sound effects of this game are somewhat basic, but they lend themselves well to the world of Ascalia. Battle themes blend in well with the mood and tension of your fights, and the cutscene music reflects what's going on in the story very well. Not much else to say here, except that the audio of Regalia does it's job quite well.
==========
I had no problems with this games' performance. I played exclusively with mouse and keyboard. My controller didn't seem to work at all, but that's fine, as mouse and keyboard work better for this type of game. Great framerate, no lag or stuttering, and no random crashes. Near perfection on my 5 year old mid-ranged custom rig.
==========
If tactical RPGs are a thing for you, you need to add Regalia: Of Men and Monarchs to your library. Just do it, you won't regret it one bit. The enchanting storytelling, amazing artwork, terrific characters, and well-paced battles will keep you playing far longer than you might expect.
==========

SHORT VERSION:
Solforge is way deeper than Hearthstone, way easier to play without spending any money, and more fun/rewarding imo.
Strongly recommend.
-----------------------------------------------
LONG VERSION:
I'm going to compare Solforge to other card games I have played.
So first of all, I would like to start out saying that I was seriously into playing Magic the Gathering until Ravnica (the first one, not return) rotated out of standard and all the money I had invested in dual lands was worthless. I ended up just playing proxy decks with my friends, but no longer showed up to tournaments/etc. Magic the Gathering is just way too expensive to play, as the cards rotate out of standard too quickly. Extended/Modern is even more expensive to play if you don't already have the cards from when they were in the Standard rotation.
So then Hearthstone came out, and I started playing it. Had no cards so I was playing zoolock/hunter (when uth was broken). Nax came out and I didn't wana spend 20 dollars on it, so my decks stopped being competitive and I quit for about three months. GVG came out, bought packs with gold i had saved up. Still wasn't competitive. Decided to buy Nax for 20 bucks. Turns out Sludge Belcher/Loatheb win games. Also mad scientist pretty much needed in every hunter/most mage decks. Then Blackrock Mountain came out. I haven't bought that one because i don't think it brings anything to the table besides Thaurissan/Flamewaker/Quickshot. I have a pretty good set of legendaries and have fun playing the game, but that is only cos I sank a lot of time into it since it came out of beta. Everytime I try to get a friend to play it, they get turned away by the inability to acquire cards for free. The quests require you to win games, which is really hard with the starter cards, and you will only get a pack every 2-3 days assuming you do the quests. The arena, at 150 gold, is prohibitively expensive for new players, and since theyre inexperienced they usually go 0-3. You don't get to keep the cards either.
Now to solforge. I started playing this game a couple of days ago and I have to say it's great. A lot of the card abilities seem to be Magic abilities with a name change, but that's fine. What is great is the ability to be able to play it for free. Completely for free. You get a pack just for logging on every day. You get another pack after three wins every, which can be against the computer. Free packs for no reason.
But card packs aren't what make this game, it's the drafts. To get into a draft you need 3 event tickets. You get an event ticket for your first online win of the day, every day. That means you have to beat a guy, but you will probably get wrecked if you're a new player with no cards who hasn't mastered the game yet. What I recommend is you make a second account, and every day you make the accounts play each other and get an event ticket on each. That way you can draft 2 out of every 3 days (one day on one account, the next on the other).
The drafts are like in Magic. You open a pack, pick a card, then the computer passes you their pack, which is now missing a card. Maybe I'm biased because of my Magic experience, but I much prefer this to Hearthstone's "pick one out of 3 cards" method. Anyway, you get to keep all the cards that you draft, so it's really easy to build your collection.
The first few drafts I played were stomps. I went 0-4 multiple times, but it is nowhere nearly as frustrating as the first few arena fails in Hearthstone because you keep the cards. You also get 3 card packs for going 0-4. The game is extremely friendly towards new players.
Assuming draft is not for you and you want to play constructed, you can just go to
and sign up for the unheroic ladder. This means that you play against other people using only commons or rares, no heroic or legendary cards. Commons or rares are very cheap to craft. I was able to craft an unheroic netdeck on my third day of playing just from the login rewards. Of course, I still got destroyed because I wasn't used to the game mechanics yet, but at least I knew that it was my fault and not the fault of my poor cards. Losing mirror matchups in unheroic ladder made me realize ways in which I could improve my play, which ended up boosting my draft win rate.
Solforge is truly a free to play game. Way more accessible than Magic/Hearthstone
-Paper card games like Magic are definitely pay to win and prohibitively expensive.
-Hearthstone isn't really free to play due to the single player adventures, which require you to shell out cash. You can be competitive if you grind Hearthstone without spending money, but you would have to be some sort of arena wizard or grind quests for months.
CONS OF SOLFORGE
-the client is ugly. super ugly. Hearthstone is extremely beautiful in comparison.
-Some mechanics are ripoffs from Magic
-The unheroic ladder has long queue times unless its nighttime in the US
-There are like five people total who play this game (draft queue times are almost instantaneous though)
Still, greatly recommended over Hearthstone. Really don't understand why this game is so shunned.

In the standard tradition of Steam Summer Sales reinvigorating Bargain Bin Breakdowns I bring you, Just Cause.  I picked up the first two in the series, and their included DLC content for an amount low enough not care what the games were. Having been part of a franchise that I recognized I knew they couldn’t be total crap, right?
Purchased and installed they sat there, icons on the desktop, being ignored while double clicks would happen elsewhere.  Two icons over LEGO Worlds gets a double click, on the other side of the screen Quake 4 is the proud recipient of a click followed by and press of ‘Enter’ on the keyboard.  Team Fortress 2, Fallout 3, Resident Evil 4, Race to the White House, Minecraft, Chips Challenge, even the Recycling Bin were all getting more click-action.  Until I finally decided to hover the cursor atop its icon and give it the grace of the double-click.  Why, after all this time did I finally take this step?  Just cause.
As of writing I’ve logged five hours playing Just Cause and while that’s not enough time to provide a fair and honest review, I’m gonna do one anyway.  Just cause.
Things start off with a free fall from the back of a plane where I need to meet up with a contact on a beach.  The first time I did this I opened my parachute earlier than I meant to, then closed it and reopened it again, and again and again, and again. I guess Rico(the main character) has a hundred reserve chutes or maybe he can fold them up and repack them quickly?  After a while I just decided to belly flop into the ocean, die, and start this crazy mess over.  Only I didn’t die.  Falling from really high up, gaining speed by holding my body tight and pointing down and I just splash like it was a five foot high dive.
I stared at the screen for a moment or two, awe struck, slightly annoyed. Seconds went by and I noticed the lack of a breathing reminder. So I waited, and waited, and waited some more.  Never did I see anything informing me of a need to exit the water to breath nor did I suffer to the fate of suffocation.  I’m going to hope the developers went with this route because of some aspect of the game I haven’t experienced yet, and not just cause.
Once I restarted and made it to the beach proper I helped my contact guy fight off some other people and then we left in his truck. During the truck ride I got to see the auto-aiming performed by the mounted gun in the back of the truck. I’m starting to notice a trend of ‘easy mode’, is this because I’m playing on an easy difficulty?  Maybe, I don’t know, but I’m not complaining about it.  I’ve reached the point where I’d rather have a enjoyable casual gaming experience than getting worked up because its too much of a challenge.
We make it to the base or hideout, or whatever it is, where I get a cut scene leading me into the first real mission.  What that actually is I haven’t a clue since I’m focused on how this guy talking to me is completely trying to be Sam Axe from Burn Notice. But whatever, lets get this pony show on the road.  I leave that place check around my surrounding and find a motorcycle, so I hop on and start driving towards the point marked on my map, just cause.
At some point I passed a police car and they yelled “Stop!” and hit the lights/sirens combo.  I thought ‘Wow, that’s awesome it detected me speeding, this is going to a fun challenge to play!‘ So I stopped, and the police car pulled up and they got out.  I got off my motorcycle, not knowing what to expect, then they shot me. I guess I should have expected this.  Although I don’t know what it was that triggered them to attack me, but the police yelling at you constantly is an annoying part of the game, just cause.
I think it was somewhere around here that I realized I was playing a mob-less tropical-island-based Grand Theft Auto. Don’t immediately take that as a bad thing, the GTA franchise is one of the best ones out there.  And sure, there are other games out there that put you in an open world like that, Mafia is another that comes to mind.  But I mark GTA with that distinction since it was at least the first one I played.
The main story didn’t grab me as I had hoped, I went and broke some guy out of prison and instead of him wondering why I would do that having never met me, he had me join him.  Which was good, since the reason why I was to break him out was so I trick him into letting me join his group. I feel like the leader of a rebel group would question the guy  he’s never met before that breaks him out of prison. I guess he decided to just cause.
I did a couple main story line missions before I discovered the side missions.  Missions where you help liberate small villages from different armies or something.  Those were fun, repetitive, but fun. You would basically work your way up a road taking out roadblocks along the way until you reached either a flag that needed capturing or a leader that needed killing.  I would fly my helicopter to a mission marked on the map, liberate the town, and then steal the helicopter parked on the roof of the building.  Then fly off to the next one. I did this for a couple hours, and I had more fun than I had playing the main storyline. I’m not trashing the story or anything, it just didn’t grab me like liberation missions did.
From what I’ve seen Just Cause is the child of Far Cry and Grand Theft Auto’s wild night in Vegas. They’ve taken pieces from both and created this whole new thing. Its not terrible, its not amazing, it just is, just cause.

Massive Chalice is a good example of a game that went through the Early Access phase and was eventually followed through to successful completion.  I've seen several games that went through Early Access and were later abandoned by the developer, so it's nice to see an example that turned out to be a polished and fun game.
You'll see a lot of people commenting about how the play style is similar to Xcom, and they're right.  I do like Xcom, but I actually like Massive Chalice better than Xcom because of the way heros can be married together to form families and offspring, and eventually new heroes.  The traits and stats of the parents influence the traits, stats, and initial experience level of the next generation of heroes.  With some clever planning over which hero I marry to another, I can have a batch of fresh new recruits leveled up and waiting to replace the aging (or dead) ones.  Contrast that with Xcom, where you lose one of your soldiers and they're just gone.
I feel like Massive Chalice's building placement mechanic improved on the 'base building' mechanic seen in Xcom.  I don't have to worry about excavating some area, and providing power or anything silly like that.  Instead they added bonuses based on what building you place and where.  They simplified the building concept while also improving on it.  I also like the random events that come up and require a decision to be made.  The decisions made for those events have lasting effects on how the game progresses, and add flavor to the story.
I hope the developers consider making a Massive Chalice 2.

I picked Massive Chalice up on sale and while I enjoyed the game, I'm very glad I didn't pay full price for it either.
The game starts off fairly quickly giving you a taste of everything. It quickly abandons you as you start to progress through the 300 year war. The combat while not extremely challenging or varied is enjoyable throughout your first play through. The random events come semi frequently and offer a lot of possibilities. During my second play through I used the wiki to look at the outcomes just to see the potential of each situation and was pleased by the range and pros and cons of each decision. I found the art style very hit and miss but I can't fault the game nor praise it either. The music was appropriate and enjoyable to listen to while playing but the two "voices" of the chalice I found incredibly annoying and within 30 minutes of playing dropped their volume to nothing and used subtitles instead.
I had a few issues with Massive Chalice besides the annoyance mentioned above. I was really hoping for more from the eugenics side of this game. It's not often that a concept like this comes up, especially within gaming. I found the pairing / breeding system of the game at best disappointing both in the long and short term game. The 300 year war isn't long enough to selectively breed a really decent army and for the "hero's", the best of the population. Undesirable traits seam fairly common. I really thought there would be a lot more depth and variety in the actual game play. Instead of fighting the same 5 or so enemy types on different maps in different combinations and numbers constantly throughout the game. Finally without spoiling anything I found the end of the war to be anticlimactic.
I mostly enjoyed my first play through of the game even after restarting about 175 years into the war due to some poor prior planning. My second play through was dull before I had even clicked start, I got to 200 years and stopped because I realised I had not been enjoying it at all. I think Massive Chalice had some great ideas and seamed great from the outside and while enjoyable the first time around, it really didn't deliver what I had expected from the game.
If you enjoyed the eugenics side of games like Crusader Kings 2 this game might give you a bit more (but not greatly) of what you are after but besides that, it's a dull game with great ideas and great random events but that's it. Buy it on sale, it's worth $5 at the most. 6.5/10

Exanima is a smaller prologue to a bigger game, called Sui Generis. It's basically an ARPG with a extremely deep combat and many innovative features. The combat, in primis, is incredible, probably the most revolutionary aspect of this genre in almost 10 years. Is physic based so there may be silly movements, but other than that it works great: it's fun, it's really challengind and - for this reason - really satisfying.
Every hit does damage based on the speed, the distance and the movement of the wielder, the combat system is so deep that you can even "hug" the enemy to reduce the impact of a hit you couldn't avoid.
If that's not enough, the game is really stunning and immersive. You can move almost every object around, open every door and pick up every single useless item (and a motherf***ing compass!). There is no minimap, no "visible objective" and no helping tools to assist you. You have to get your♥♥♥♥♥out of there by yourself, trying to search for the right keys and - in the meantime - a good equipment to survive.
And if you love to characterize your character, well, it's still in Early Access but you can already give a look at the armor system, divided by many different pieces and many different armor layers (cloth, jazzeraint, armor, etc..).
It's true that they're working slow, but they're doing an awesome job. As soon as the core will be polished the story content will be easy to develop.
There is still no tutorial, if you need anything feel free to ask or check the Steam hub.

Oh were to start, This is possibly one of the best 2D style Metroid/Castlevania games I have played in a long time. The premise is simble, America in the future, has a home grown group of terrorists trying to force a civil war, Jason Flemming (the main character you play as) Meets a girl at a bar and decide to go exploring a cave as a date. The cave turns out to hold the main base of the terrorists and she gets captured and you have to save the girl and save the day. There is some fun dialogue and the writing is entertaining but not memorable.  What is memorable is the gameplay. If you ever liked the Metroid series or Castlevania series, you know exactly how this game works. Find a interesting bit of gear, this gear lets you explore the area until you either fight a boss or find new gear. Once you get the new gear, you can carry on forward or go back to get to areas you could not get to before and find more goodies hidden around the map that way.  Repeat. The combat is fun and entertaining with ever improving quality of guns (5 total) and uprades for your character, Either Missles, grenades, Foam gun, Hook shot device, or even double and triple jumping and hyperspeed running where you can even go zipping by enemies while on the roof!
The only real negative I have for this game is I originally bought and played this on my Xbox360 and it played completely fine, smooth frame rates and seemless transitions between sections of the map. Here on PC, I can get frozen screens, stuttering and for some reason the game likes to default to the lowest quality graphics settings whenever I exit and log back into the game, forcing me to change them back whenever I start playing again. All in all, the stuttering and temporary freezes happen enough to be noticed but not enough to really interfere negatively with the game experience itself. I Do have to wonder if the devs ported this without being fully optimized properly. I have other games with much higher system demands than this that I can run without these problems, and other games using the same engine as this don't have these problems either.
To sum up, If you have missed the old school Metroid style of exploring for fun and profit, You will most likely love this game and is well worth the price.

Somewhere in rural Catalonia in 1937 an unusual painting is taken by force by a man with fascist connections. Much more recently, in Paris, the same painting is stolen from an art gallery by a pizza courier and with the gallery owner shot in the process. Witnessing the second crime is amongst a few other people George Stobbard, an American in Paris representing an insurance company, and Nico Collard, a local journalist. These two have a history together investigating mysteries (the four previous games in the series), and they naturally begin to investigate what is really going on. A story is uncovered involving high level art dealings and higher level gnostic gospels, and possibly also the future of the world as we know it.
Broken Sword 5 – the Serpent’s Curse is a classic style point-and-click adventure game but with a modern polish. It feels comfortable and relaxing to go back to that kind of game, especially when the overall story is well-written such as in this game. The plot is a bit too linear to offer any alternative routes to solve prolems, which is not unusual, but there are also restrictions in the order that new information is uncovered. Some items can only be interacted with after some other action has occured, for no obvious other reasons than that the story says so, and that is annoying. The game also suffers from other issues that is inherent in this type of games: Some of the problems are solved in a far-fetched manner and other problems are truly elementary. Luckily, there is a good stepwise hint system built into the game to help when the inspiration of the player is running low, which helped me a couple of times when I had missed to pick up some piece of information or inventory. The dialogue also feels quite sluggish at times.
Now that I have written a lot about negative aspects of the Broken Sword 5 – the Serpent’s Curse experience, I must say that almost everything else in the game is good. I really enjoyed the story, the bantering, the characters, the cheesy music, the atmosphere, most of the scenery, and the religious history. However, the final punchline is truly horrible…

This game is not at the level of the first two "Broken Sword" games but is still a good adventure game to play and truly comes close to the ambiance of the initial games of the franchise. The scenario lacks a bit of action though but is still pleasant to play. Well better than BS 3 and 4.

I found this game to be a fantastic entry in to the Broken Sword series. After the last two games terrible turn in to 3D, going back to the series point-and-click roots is a breath of fresh air. I've played all of the games in the series, and this one fits perfectly with I & II.
Overall, I found the game throughly enjoyable. It is fairly short (10-15 hours) but that is fairly standard in this genre, though YMMV depending on how good you are at these types of games and if you're familiar with the tropes in some puzzles. The built in hint system works well, though I only needed to reach for it once or twice when I was doing puzzles out of order.
Visually, the game look great. It isn't animated like the first two games, but the cell-shaded graphics give the same feeling and I'm sure make the developer's jobs easier. It was jarring at first since I expected hand-drawn characters, but by the end of the game I was totally happy with the art style. Even though it is different, it still captures the spirit of the original games.
Most of the puzzle are perfectly logical, which is rare for this type of game. I only encountered a few puzzles, that after using the hint system, felt kinda cheated due to the puzzle not being well defined. I only found one section of the game unenjoyable
, it was also the only part of the game where I needed to use hints.
Overall, this is a fantastic game and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys point-and-click games of old. It is a perfect example of how to do this genre correctly. I hope to see more games like this from Revolution Software.

I'm still making my mind up about this game as I write this review. On one hand, this is a very interesting survival game with so-so graphics. On the other hand the difficulty is rigged for you to lose. I think I would easily say this game is worth the purchase if it weren't for that last point. Let me explain...
So the game increases in difficulty as you play it. The principal mechanic is that you get less loot for the same action as time goes on. Down the line, mistakes in how you task your people can lead to them being too tired or depressed to do the actions required to keep the group alive. However, there are more than a few mechanics that break the standard of "fair" in a game, and no I'm not talking about "le rogue skillz" that you see in that tired genre. I'm talking about a mechanic where as a character gets fatigued they can't sleep to remove the fatigue, and sleep is the only option to remove said fatigue (other than a random chance location/item).
The real mechanic is this:
Character A does a task that increases fatigue. To reduce fatigue, Character A must sleep. Fatigue reduction from sleep is based on Character A's constitution stat. The constitution stat is reduced by Character A's fatigue.....
As you have probably noticed, we have a closed loop that will almost always lead to Character A dying ultimately the game ending. And as stated above, there is no way around the mechanic. Put in simpler terms, your character is too tired to sleep.. which doesn't make sense. Also of note is that all characters (presumably) sleep at night, yet they only acquire negative statuses and do not remove fatigue.
There are other examples of faulty mechanics but this one is the most obvious. And the more I think about it, the more I think that I can't recommend this game. It's a shame really, because despite the game having some interesting elements, and although simple in some regards (graphically, camp activities, etc), it offers up some enjoyable moments and really makes you think about how you are going to help this group to survive.
I could easily see this game being rated higher than what I'm going to rate it; if only it were better balanced. But the issues like fatigue/sleep are fundamental design flaws. You can make a game tough and still make it fair. And at the end of the day this game just isn't fair.
And I guess I've made up my mind and I'm not going to recommend this game. If the issues were fixed and the game balanced I could easily flip my review to something I'd recommend. However, the current issues are game breaking. 5.5/10.

With this game being one of the so-called "walking simulators" with very simple and straightforward puzzles which include placing object A in slot B, pushing buttons in specific order and jumping puzzles, it is the story, themes and setting that is making this game shine.
Without giving too much of the plot away, I will describe first half an hour of the game, which will make it easier to talk about the themes that the story explores later on. You're playing one of the Astronauts sent to a distant planet that is thought to be filled with various kinds of life. With the journey taking more than a dozen years to reach it's destination, even though the spaceship is travelling twice the speed of light, the crew is put into a cryosleep. On reaching the planet something goes terribly wrong and a landing pod with all of the crew still asleep is crashed into the planet's surface. Some time after the crash landing, the protagonist regains consciousness only to find out that all of the crew is gone, landing pod is damaged beyond repair, his space suit is leaking oxygen and the planet itself turns out to be the wasteland with no signs of life. However after spotting and following the footprints in the sand you discover a derelict Soviet Union outpost, and this is where the protagonist starts to question if their mission was a hoax.
With the game starting out as a more straightforward sci-fi thriller, especially after encountering a strange woman who can walk the surface of the planet without the need for a special suit with the supply of oxygen, even with the influences of the early science fiction films of the first half of the last century (particularly
and
) it is very interesting to watch how the game expands it's story into a more intelligent and thoughtful themes. If you're familiar with the works of the great
, particularly the ones that explore attempts at communicating with an alien intelligence (see: "Solaris", "The Invincible" and "Fiasco") you will know what I mean. Having said that, I also have to say that as other great pieces of art
is using those influences to tell it's own story. With the main themes of game being the ones of ecology and how species interact with the biosphere;
and the concept of otherness; and of course the story of the main protagonist, which ties it all together through his own personal loss in the past that he overcomes by finding out the story of that mysterious woman and the chain of events that led the planet to a state in which you found it.

Big congratulations to the gaming designers and programmers...superlative achievement!

This is a very interesting, well-written concept. Unfortunately, it falls a little short on the design and execution of the product - so much so that you can almost feel what David Board had intended with it, but didn't manage to pull off entirely.
I'm still recommending this game though, as you can really feel the level of scientific literacy in the writing, and the story gives room for some interesting afterthought. The best part about the game, is perhaps discussing the story with other people, afterwards. It also has its moments where the ambience strikes the right chords, making for some memorable events here and there. But they are a bit far in between, which is a shame.
Perhaps if he had been a little more experienced in game design, this could have been a really great game. You can feel that there's a lot of influences from places like Stargate, Alien, Space Odyssey and perhaps even a bit of Shadow of the Colossus? But it all wraps together in an, unfortunately, slightly monotonous jumping "road-trip" where not that much happens throughout it.
I'm not sure if I can say that it's entirely worth the 20 euro it costs now, but you should consider it, if you ever see it on sale.

An amazingly atmospheric game that is let down slightly by its final stages.
Lifeless Planet really does achieve everything it set out to do. It provides the player with an incredibly moody game world, interesting platforming, and a touch of puzzle solving. The real meat of the game is its environments, and they are on full display here. If you love breathtaking scenery, doted by strange and lonely structures, then this is the game for you.
However, the strongest part of the game is definitely its early stages. Once you reach the midpoint, and you start to uncover the mysteries of the planet, the game loses a lot of the mystique.
The use of documents to provide exposition is nothing new, but this is perhaps one of the worst implementations of it. There’s no way for the player to discover or interpret any of the plot, because everything is clearly spelt out in the documents. You might be wondering what happened in a specific location, only to pick up a note and have it told to you. For a game that reveals in the idea of exploring an empty planet, I find this extremely strange.
There are also some transitions towards the end that don’t make a lot of sense. You might be walking in a cavern one moment, then a transition will shoot you outside and you’ll be notified, via the document system, what happened. This was incredibly jarring, and threw me out of the fictive dream.
Without spoiling anything, the story is rather silly, and there is literally no foreshadowing of the two final plot-twists. I’d almost say that both break the game’s own atmosphere, but I recognise that might be my own subjective view. That being said, however, there’s no excuse for informing me via text what the outcome of an event was; especially if my character apparently bore witness to it. Just show it to me and I should be able to infer its meaning.
The final revelation is also just plain stupid, and literally introduced in the last ten minutes of the game. While it does provide a sudden burst of energy to push you through the ending, it was so convenient that I almost forgot the amazing sense of place leading up to it. And this is coming from someone who really likes happy endings.
Oh, and there was also a subplot about a dead wife that literally goes nowhere.
In conclusion, Lifeless Planet is an atmospherically impressive game that is let down by its poor story. It manages to capture the feeling of being the lone human on an alien planet, but shoots itself in the foot with terrible explosion and a ham-fisted ending.
It is worth a buy if you’re interesting in the concept or atmosphere, but I wouldn’t recommend it at full price. And now I have to figure out whether to give it a thumb’s up or down. Bloody binary review system.

Overall, I thought this was a pretty good game.  You play an astronaut exploring a planet, but it's pretty linear -- for the most part, you're following a relatively fixed path and having to solve a few puzzles along the way to progress.  The story is kind of interesting, but there didn't seem to be a whole lot of it; there's enough to keep things moving, but it's told in small pieces with longer stretches of silence (well, environmental sounds) in between.  It took me around 9-10 hours to get through the game, looking up some info/hints when I got stuck in a few places, and generally not too difficult.  But around the middle of the game, one sequence of ~7 jumps in a row had me stuck for a long time (easily 30+ minutes of play time).  I knew what to do, but had a lot of trouble actually doing it and that really annoyed me.  That could just be me and my game-playing skills, but that part really disrupted my enjoyment of the game.  I eventually got past it and finished the game, but it just wasn't quite the same after that point.  I was a little disappointed to find out that I had missed some things along the way (I still hadn't earned some achievements), and you only get a single save point that's automatically determined by the game as you go, so I'd have to start all over again from the beginning again if I wanted to look for what I missed.  Yes, there's some replay value here, but having seen the story and everything once already, I'm not sure I'd enjoy it as much when I'd really just be looking to find some missing pieces / get some achievements.  Also note that once you finish the game, it's impossible to "resume game" from the main menu; it just crashes.  I was hoping to go back and see the ending bit again, but I'd have to play the whole game again now to do so.  :(  So as I said at the start, I think this game is good overall, and would recommend it if it sounds interesting to you or you generally like games of this type.

The game uses the same engine as Quake 3, which explains the dated graphics.
At first, you may simply try to run and gun down the enemies. Don't try that, you'll just die before you know it.
The second thing you might try is simply putting a lot of machine gun turrets around. Useful, but they'll get destroyed without anyone nearby to repair them.
Building AT Turrets costs a lot of power and makes them really big targets for tanks, walkers and rocket launcher enemies, so leaving these unguarded is a terrible waste.
After a while, you may notice that you can find stuff lying around inside the may buildings in the maps. This loot actually gives you extra power, which makes exploration worthwhile. It also respawns in semi random places, so there's always a trophy or other shiny thing around.
Lastly, enemy officers don't charge straight like the rest of the footsoldiers, they always try and hide somewhere, which makes exploration doubly neccessary.
Now, the game could use some extra balancing. The default reload speed is sluggish. For the rocket launcher, even at max upgrade, it still takes 3 seconds to reload, leaving you very vulnerable. Most guns fire from a point slightly up from where your weapon is, you can actually see the yellow streaks coming out of nowhere, as if your guy was actually hovering a bit up and to the left than where you are. On medium is where the game seems most balanced (at least playing solo). Bump the difficulty to hard and you'll get your♥♥♥♥♥handed in 5 minutes.
One thing this game really could use is advanced settings, like number of enemies spawning per wave, their types, speed, accurracy, health, how much power you get per turn, how much morale each team has, etc. There is nothing like this you can set up for a match, and it's a real bummer, because these settings alone could vastly increase the fun factor of the game.
Still, it's worth playing. Really wish the devs would at least read that last paragraph of mine!

Before you buy, consider..
- Limited resolution support
Game displays optional resolutions as low as 640x480 to 1600x1200, but only 1280x1024 is the max, selectable resolution for the game. And editing config files won't do crap for you.
To get your game to run in your monitor's native resolution, you're gonna need one of two versions of this program called res changer..
Version 1 or 2. Try 2 because it's newer. If it doesn't work, 1 might. 2 didn't work for me, so I had to use 1. Only drawback to having to use 1 is that it has no support for windowed mode like 2. And that alt-tabbing with 1 crashes your game. But, hey, it works. And I almost refunded my game. Looked awful downscaled. Game may be old, but still should have had more resolution support.
- Very few graphics settings.
You're gonna need to force AA, AF, etc on from your video driver control panel. Everything in menu only affects quality of textures, shadows, and post-processing FX.
Overall, the game is a good game. I have less than an hour on it over Steam, but I speak from experience from having played it on console years ago.

A fun platformer, Super Smash Bros-esque fighting game, where you control one of a few dozen cuddly pixelkids in adorable Halloween costumes and make them instagib eachother. One of the unique features of this style of fighting game is the "one hit decides all" factor (for most characters), making for fast paced matches, where precision and timing is everything. there are only two ways to actually damage your opponent, through the use of a basic standard attack, and a special move. Each character has a fairly diverse playstyle, some requiring optimal distance and planning in order to devestate their opponents, others, well, not so much. (LOOKING AT YOU, CLAWS.)
My favorite character by far, although perhaps a bit of a spoiler as they are an unlockable character, is Bee. Bee is a perfect example of how disparate yet complex the character selection can be, as Bee does not directly damage anyone with their skills, but instead relies on short-lived summons and a non-damaging slowing trap of honey to slowly whittle down the enemy. So fun!
However, the game doesn't seem to be as lucid as I'd like it to be in the multiplayer department, but that is to be expected of an indie game that hasn't gotten the reception or attention I believe it deserves. I don't know if the devs are still around, but kudos to them for making a very creative, easy to jump into and hectic brawling game!

I bought this game last year, and sank only about 2 hours into it in total. That will likely be all of the time I give it, which is a crying shame, as it seemed like it would keep my interest.
The game itself seems very interesting at first. It's basically Dark Souls meets Diablo, which, to many, would be a fantastic thing. However, for this one player, and many others, it just made things far too difficult, especially for a casual player, to sit down and play. Allow me to tell you why.
The visuals, the idea, and the concept are perfectly fine to me. It's the combat mechanics, however, that I can't stand, nor understand. Really, I struggle to understand why any developer would want to create a game that focuses on combat, but has overly-complicated combat mechanics that require you to sink a lot of time into the game to even become adequate.
The way combat works is based upon physics, character build, and positioning, for the most part. You have to take into consideration your movement speed, your facing, your weapon, even your height and weight, which often completely changes the way your character wields cerain weapons, the way they move, etc. You also have to keep an eye on where your mouse is, where you are in the room, where your enemy is in the room, where any items you may trip over are (yes, you can TRIP over items on the ground), where doors are, where fire is, where traps are...It becomes a mess very quickly, and while you can run away to regen your stamina, healing is done through rarely-found items. This makes it a bigger pain for newer players to even get into the game.
Look, the game looks interesting. If you seriously want to try it out, go ahead. But if you really don't want to put in Hearthstone-levels of hours to 'git gud' (as many of the elitist players seem to spout left and right), my advice is to stay away. I myself may never pick up this game again, unless some drastic changes made it more accessible and playable for others.

The first two Broken Sword games are classics in the point and click genre. Broken Sword 5 returns to the roots of the beloved series.
Playtime: 15 hours
I've played the first two installations in this series, but skipped out on the 3rd and 4th games (mixed fan reactions about horribly clunky controls and 3D movement). This title feels quite like the beloved games that I played, with gripping mystery, some sort of ancient magic or ritual that could destroy the world, and solid point and click puzzles.
The previous BS games had puzzles that were quite difficult or roundabout, as was the norm in point and click games back in the day. The focus on this genre overall seems to have shifted from providing players with extreme challenges, to having manageable challenges and letting players enjoy the story.
Broken Sword 5 provides a good mix of both: in Act I, most of the puzzles were intuitive and logical. While they still required imagination and had me puzzled several times (e.g. how to set up a cockroach trap with collected items), I think frequent point and click players could figure them out without getting overly frustrated.
Act II had more challenging puzzles, including deciphering messages. Apart from the deciphering/translation puzzles, the general puzzles were more difficult to me as well than those in Act I. This act took me much more time, and I actually had to look at a guide for a couple of hints. For people that love a challenge, these will scratch the itch of the older titles (to what extent may depend on the individual).
The story is quintessential Broken Sword, where the main characters George and Nico run into some murder or world-destroying event. To the general public, I'd describe it like a Dan Brown novel in game form (though BS1 was published before Dan's first novel Digital Fortress)!
This title follows a similar structure to previous BS games: George and Nico gather clues, which leads them to some person that might be related to the murder(s), which leads them to some mastermind, which leads them to something even bigger and deeper than they imagined... If you like mystery with a touch of mythical, these games will be a pleasure to play.
However, as people have pointed out, there's not much going on with regards to character development. It depends on what the individual player values more, a mind blowing story or fun puzzles. I'll say that the story mostly serves to connect the puzzles, and motivate the player to find out what happens next.
Broken Sword really excels in the art direction and atmosphere of the game. Each scene was breathtaking, and really brought the locations to life, set in multiple countries. I really enjoyed the puzzles, and didn't have an issue with the difficulty.
I have some gripes with this game however. The biggest frustration was that the character Nico, whose witty and sarcastic personality was a big reason the previous games were loved, doesn't play much of a role in this game. I remember using her special reporter perks to navigate so many dangerous situations and unearth ancient mysteries.
In this game, we use her special perks once or twice (in really safe situations, not life or death), and maybe use her reporter ID card as a prop to get things stuck in holes. While I used to be able to explore vast areas and fill up my inventory with Nico, in this game there's only a couple items she uses. While I liked George and Nico equally, having one of the main characters basically drop out of the story was jarring to me.
One technical issue I ran into was an achievement not unlocking. I emailed the developers and got a save file promptly, allowing me to unlock the achievement. Some people have encountered other save file issues, but the forum has many threads on how to resolve them. I personally didn't encounter other issues apart from the achievement.
I enjoyed Broken Sword 5 for its art, environments, mystery elements, and its puzzles. Additionally for players that loved the previous games, this game will bring back a lot of nostalgia. However, for players who are expecting a mind blowing story, or well written character development, and do not care about point and click puzzles, this game might not be for you.

As probably every reviewer will agree this game mixes strategic decisions like recruiting, research and so on with (somewhat) tactical tb-combat. Both parts feel a lot like the X-Com remake, which is why a lot of people compare it to this title. While it may be unfair to judge Massive Chalice in comparison to a multi million dollar project, the simillarities are so striking that it can't be avoided. Heck, the combat part looks more or less identical. The problem is that Massive Chalice looses battle against X-Com in all it's core elements.
There is considerably less to research, the combat is simplified to the extreme and the AI (haven't tried the highest difficulty yet) is basic at best. True, X-Com's AI isn't exactly the strongest part of the game, but in Massive Chalice enemies seem to wander around in groups in a predesignated area until they see you/you attack them. Then they start charging at you, sometimes alone, sometimes drawing their group with them.
Without a system of cover and very few support skills combat starts to get repetitive after the first few hours. At that point you have met every kind of enemy, later enemies are only beefed up versions with more HP and damage.  That is really sad as the existing enemies have some interesting features like letting your heroes age, teleporting them around or stealing their experience. Still, after a quarter of the game you have seen all of it.
The strategic part is pretty linear. Mixing your houses for classes and special traits is fun and I'm sure I've only seen the surface of it so far, but otherwise there isn't much to be done. Then and there are little events which is a nice idea, but all in all it is just waiting for the next attack. X-Com has the upper hand again for adding simply a lot more to do between fights. Also researching and reequipping your heroes did not enthrall me like it usually does in similar titles.
That your heroes age and die on the other hand is a clever and interesting design feature. Kudos for this idea!
From the technical point of view the game is solid. Graphics are the way they are, but for me that's all right. The actors of the chalice did a good job, too, while the rest of the sound setting isn't spectacular.
The german translation is somewhat funny, for example the "Klugmachergilde", but than again I guess "sagewright guild" isn't exactly a common english term, too, so you can't realy blame the translators.
As far as I can tell the game comes without any bugs, which sadly is something worth mentioning nowadays.
I bought Massive Chalice at 4,99 at the current winter sale. At this price I can recommend it despite my various critics. It is simply depressing to imagine what wonderful game Massive Chalice could have been.  Sadly, the developer stoped working on the title. As there seems to be no mod support (or no interest by skilled modders), chances for new content and a polished gaming experience are pretty low.

I was prepared for the same disappointment with Massive Chalice as I was with Spacebase DF-9. Long story short, people paid money and the Double Fine gave up on making the game, leaving everyone with a game that essentially never left alpha. But funnily enough, that wasn’t the case. Massive Chalice is essentially XCOM cross the map from the Game of Thrones introduction.
The enemies are varied and you can use their corpses ro craft new weapons, items and armor. Someone dies and there’s no getting back up again. Every mission is very simple: Kill all the Cadence monsters. With no variance, the game can be a little repetitive at times. But I don’t enjoy this game for the combat.
Almost unheard of, but one of the best parts about this game is the micro-managing between battles. And here’s where the Game of Thrones comes into it. You have several families/clans under your control which you place into keeps around your kingdom. Each clan has a dominant class and by intermingling different clans, you can produce hybrid classes and place emphasis on certain traits. You are an immortal dictator with complete oversight of your kingdom, the oversight and totalitarian control needed to save the realm.

The schtick of the game is that you manage a fantasy realm for 300 years in a prolonged seige from an otherworldly badguy.  You have a few bloodlines of heroes, and the top-level gameplay sees you assigning them to a few different roles.  They can be part of your vanguard (strike team used in tactical levels), you put them in
keeps to produce more heroes (cause the game goes for something like ten generations), they can take on the white to become a sage (speeding your research times), and your most awesome heroes can become standards in the training crucibles (boosting all heroes kingdom-wide).
Meanwhile, the badguy threat the "Cadence" attacks your lands (in which you build keeps, crucibles, and sagewright guilds).  You send in your vanguard and play a blessedly short tactical exercise to take them down.  There are always more attacks than you can address, though, and the Cadence's corruption seeps into your lands, eventually destroying them.  So you're constantly triaging your threats, knowing that you won't be able to keep everything, but holding out for retaining enough to make it to the endgame.
The endgame, by the way, is when the titular Massive Chalice fills up and can destroy all the Cadence forever.  That takes 300 years.  But you're immortal thanks to the power of the Chalice, so you can manage things until the endgame… assuming you can hold everything together until then.
Dividing your resources (ie heroes) between vanguard, breeders, sages, and standards is surprisingly difficult, challenging, and consequential, and continues to be so throughout the game.  Your heroes have various traits, both genetic and acquired via training, and they pass these down to their kids and their trainees (and sometimes their comrades-in-arms).  There is a whole lot of fun fiddling and arranging what traits you want your
keeps to produce.  Or who you're willing to put into the sages instead.  Or who's going to fight for you, or who's going to train the kingdom's heroes.   This is, from a game design standpoint, a real victory.  It is some seriously elegant, downright exquisite, design.  So the strategic level of the game gets an A+.
The character classes are amusingly different from your standard fantasy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  You have caberjacks, whose weapons are giant, iron-shod logs.  You have alchemists, who sling explosive potions.  Lastly you have hunters, who can stealth and shoot things with their crossbows.  You can shunt these into the tank/dps/aoe structures you're used to, but you don't
to.
You also get hybrid classes (when a mommy caberjack and a daddy hunter love each other very very much…) which make for interesting combinations.  Trickshots shoot arrows tipped with explosive potions.  Shadowjacks can stealth and then leap out of the shadows with their massive cabers.  And so on.  As you can see, as you start figuring out hybrid classes, things get weirder, not more predictable, and it's lots of fun to explore those new options.
And there are relic weapons that get passed down from generation to generation, leveling up as they get used, and becoming incredible items of power.  Nothing says dynasty of super-powered warriors like a crossbow that's been passed down within the noble house for 200 years.  Towards the end of my playthrough, which youngster got bequeathed a relic more-or-less determined who was going to be in the vanguard.  There's a lot of thematic power in that decision, where you're figuring if this 13-year-old lordling shows enough promise to be given the mighty Monarch crossbow.  I really got into it!
While there are a lot of Game of Thrones elements in there, it's also notable what things are _not_ carried over from the most popular fantasy property of the day.  Namely, you have all these noble houses in your kingdom, but they do not conspire or scheme or complain to you.  They don't have petty rivalries, they do not undermine the realm with their ambitions.  This would be a natural development to pursue, but ultimately it would detract from gameplay.  Your job isn't to convince the realm to fight against the
Cadence, it's to manage that fight.  Good on the designers for
falling down that rabbit hole.
Also the game is pleasantly gender-neutral in regards to you, the sovereign, even though it sticks pretty strongly to the gender binary for your
regents.  I'll take my victories where I can get them on this front!
The game suffers from the common trope of the Big Final Battle being unlike any other battle you've fought before, so all of the expectations and strategies that you've honed over the course of the game are just slightly off-base.  (Mild spoilers; skip to next paragraph to avoid…) Instead of using your team of five heroes sweeping an area for the 15-20 badguys hiding on a map, you set your team of five heroes to defending a single target against wave after wave of badguys who teleport in every few turns.  Worse, there is zero indication if you have four waves to go, or one, or fifteen.  Given that part of the game is resource management, withholding this information does not do the endgame scenario any favors.
More mundanely, except for that last one, the battles all have the same objective: kill all the badguys.  Every once in a while, the game mixes things up and has the badguys attacking a keep and you have to defend the regent of the keep… by

Luckily a quick internet search will answer these questions, but still: not something I should have to do to understand the game.  More puzzling, this is a known problem and could be addressed in a very simple patch, but it hasn't been.

Starbound is very fun. Compared to Terraria, there's some things it does better and some it does worse. It's different enough to warrant playing.
Pros: There's some definite QoL improvements like longer item placement range, easier liquid manipulation and being able to set teleport points easily and cheaply. And moving betwen planets with different biomes is itself a pretty fun thing, more fun than just running through the desert to get from your base to the jungle or whatever. Also, searching for caves to explore is a lot less tedious than Terraria (no mandatory hellevators here). The instanced mission dungeons also just work better than any of the bosses in terraria or its two dungeons. Pets and party members can be obtained more reliably and are fun to have. Also, it's way easier to mod this.
Cons: Much less exciting item progression, with less variety in weapons and armor in the base game. Less enemy variety. More linear progression. Annoying "examine racial items" sidequests needed to advance the main quest. There's no equivalent to the guide to tell you what a crafting ingredient is used for.
Do yourself a favor and if you do buy this, immediately add some of the mods, in particular Frackin' Universe (adds more of everything, fixes the linear progression problem and lack of weapon/armor variety, makes enemies and biomes more exciting). That and some QoL ones.

I played this game through once; took approx 14 hours. Overall, somewhat enjoyable, but there were enough annoying aspects that I don't think I'll be playing it again.
First off the good stuff: The art direction and implementation is great. It really helps set the tone of a desperate situation, which becomes increasingly otherworldly. The gameplay is a pretty decent sweet spot between sufficiently complex as to avoid being boring, while still being easily understandable. With the possible exception of how relationships between characters vary.
The characters are interesting, at least at first. However they're so... static. The nature of the interactions between characters don't seem to change at all, regardless of how much they "like" each other, etc. This largely determined by whether or not you assign two people to the same job together; but how this actually affects the relationship, up or down and how much, comes across as random. Perhaps that's intended. There's also nightly random cut scenes that play out, which can affect the relationships between the characters and other stats.
But there's nothing that I'd really say is akin to player driven choices affecting the relationships between the characters. I suppose this is by design, but it seems a bit strange to me. Regardless, if those stats between particular characters reach certain levels, you might trigger a cut scene. But I don't really see much in the way of change between the character interactions beyond that. Jacob stays an abrasive paranoid♥♥♥♥♥regardless of how much he's actually supposed to like people; he always accuses Bob and Illyana of not pulling their weight, regardless of whether or not they've been the only ones getting any food or not.
I played through on the easy setting, which was too easy TBH. I attempted the normal setting, and it seemed too hard.
The UI is a tad annoying. Dragging characters around to deploy them in the various spots is irksome at best. The stuff you use, from the fire to the bow and arrow to water degrade over time, and need to be topped up using various resources. This is, well, annoying busy work. An option to automate some of these tasks would have been ideal. Such as something to allow you to make it so that you always kept the fire fed above 30% (assuming you didn't run out of wood) or auto-topped up the water supplies from fruit (assuming you don't run out of fruit) would have made playing the game far less annoying.
A "fast mode" for the actions would have also been ideal. Near the end, I was trying to get the "survive 100 days" achievement, and had gotten to the point where I was a bit over 20 days away, but had enough wood, food, water, etc that I didn't actually need to do any more work to continue surviving. So I set everyone around the campfire and just had them talk for a couple weeks straight. But by god, getting through those weeks was annoying. Even just clicking on the next button, you'd still have to sit and watch as the results of everyone's chatting filtered in one by one; clicking the mouse button helped speed it up somewhat, but not nearly enough. And then there was the manual feeding. A rules base system of allocating food would have worked wonders there too.
