It is much more likely to perish in this game due to conflicts between characters pushing people into a position where they no longer can survive effectively.
The inhabitants of the island are mysterious enough to want to continue to engage with, threatening enough to pose risks in making decisions, and just enough of a pain to want to screw them over in interactions.
Getting achievements in the game requires planning, as some do not follow natural progression, and many are conflicting and will require multiple playthrough to obtain. This game easily will provide 6 to 12 hours of gameplay to pass the learning curve and obtain an ending. A good value on sale, and a fair value at full price.
I would recommend this at full price for fans of adventure PaC style survival, and wish list for the next sale for anyone else who just enjoys playing this genre.

Shadow Complex was originally a 2009 Xbox 360 title, but has since been ported over to PC.
Before talking about the game itself, I'll just mention that the PC port is great. You have all of the graphical options you'd need, and it runs at a constant 60fps for me.
The game is a metroidvania game, in the sense that you have a vast map that you can go back through at any time. As you progress through the game, you will unlock new upgrades and weaponry that allow you to access areas you couldn't get to before.
It's incredibly fun to slowly grow stronger and stronger. Eventually you'll be going through previous areas much faster than before, because you're now more experienced at the game, your upgrades make you a badass, and the enemies will crumble under your might.
The game will still pose a threat to you in later areas. Different enemy types will force you to react differently. There are multiple ways of disposing of your enemies to keep the game fresh. Not only do you have different weapons you can use, but the environment can be used to your advantage. Many rooms allow you to flank enemies from underneath or above, and you may shoot drones off of walls, which will then explode. If enemies are caught in the radius, they will go flying. If the game is too easy/hard, you can change the difficulty, which will also reward you with less or more XP depending on how difficult it is.
The combat is actually incredibly satisfying. Headshotting, exploding and meleeing enemies has them ragdoll away, while it rewards you with XP. The PC version allows for keyboard+mouse or gamepad. Both systems work totally fine, and you can actually switch between them on the fly. Throughout the game, I've been using an Xbox 360 controller to play, but during the 2-3 turret sections in the game, I just switch to the mouse because the game allows for totally free aiming during those points, so the mouse is far superior. Throughout the rest of the game, I found both control schemes to be equally as good.
The story is the game's weak point. It's really quite stereotypical and forgettable. You try to save "the girl", and that's more or less the only real plot point. It doesn't bother me, as I just play the game for the gameplay, and it's quite evident that the devs didn't put too much care into the story.
Overall, I really love the game. I've played through it 3 times now on different platforms, as the gameplay always grips me. Even though I've gone through it that many times, I barely remember the story. (That's how non-existent it is). If you enjoy the genre, you should definitely pick this game up, I had an absolute blast with it.

What I really like is you can complete the game with 100% items (which is quite satisfying, as most games won't let you do that until
the game ends) or with the least amount of items you possibly can. Whether you're wanting to do a speedrun or absolutely complete the game, it's all fun.
The only negatives I really have about this game is that the graphics aren't completely "remastered." They look just a bit worse than I remember them looking back when I first play this. That doesn't take away from the fun at all.
Pros: Great for speedrunning, great for taking your time to complete 100%, super fun combat, smooth gameplay, replay value (leveling up, trying different approaches), overall a unique game.
Cons: Graphics are old looking.

Buy it :)

So basically, it's an RTS with a twist - the enemy is (mainly) some toxic slime and you need to get rid of whatever is spewing it out. There's a fluid mechanism that makes it possible for the slime to build up and spread out, which is kind of neat (e.g. if you're on top of a hill, the slime will take longer to reach you and it flows into cracks and valleys first).
So, the one player campaign begins nicely enough, you get introduced to units and game mechanics. The story is also interesting (and is mainly what kept me playing). However, it seems that on every mission there is always something new; a new unit or building you need to take into consideration that does one special thing which you need to take out some specific enemies. They're not exciting or add much to your strategy, except "to kill unit X you need unit Y". Which doesn't give you much choice of an attack strategy at all, except to build whatever is required to make it through the level.
And this is where the game fails the most - every level is a
. You quickly set up your defense perimeter, but once you manage that, it's slowly building up an attack force and inch by inch moving away enough slime to get to an "emitter", destroy that, and do the same for any other stuff you need to destroy. You know you'll make it, it just takes time and there aren't many surprises.
So, on top of not being very challenging or exciting except the first five minutes of every level, it takes between 45 minutes to over an hour to finish one. When you're finally done trudging through, you breathe out in relief - not satisfaction. Then you get annoyed because it has taken so damn long, and 90% of it was just waiting for things to happen.
So, to sum it up:
Yays:
* Interesting campaign story
* Fluid dynamics are nice
Nays:
* Levels are a grind
* Too specialized units make things more annoying than exciting
* Tactics are more or less the same every level
* Takes too long to finish a level
* Only exciting first couple of minutes on every level, after that it's just routine

Solforge is a card game with a new formula, and it's leveling up cards while playing a game.
Each turn you draw 5 cards and you get to play 2 of them.
When you play a card, you discard a higher level copy into your discard pile.
Cards you don’t play get discarded themselves with their current level.
PRO:
+ Lots of different & beautiful cards
+ Updates also add new cards, besides fixes and so on.
+ New idea of leveling cards is refreshing for a card game
+ SAVING WHEN IN A CAMPAIGN MISSION: press return to menu, you can find your unfinished game in the play menu. Other (card) games can learn from this feature.
+ Campaign is challenging, first some proving ground tutorials, then mastery games,…
(winning a mastery gives you a legendary card of your opponent !)
+ There are tournaments: constructed (your deck against another), draft (pick cards and make a deck), expert draft. (higher position in tournament, higher rewards) (Losing in a tournament still gives you card packs.)
+ Some cards can be forged cheap (most of them are not)
+ You earn cards& card packs by playing the campaign (also rare, heroic and legendary) (Yes, I got a lot of heroics and 2 legendary by opening packs the game gave me.)
+ Daily rewards (win 1 game a day, win 3 games a day) will get you a card pack and other rewards (win online game, win 10/100/1000 online games) give you even more. 10 online games completed => legendary chest !
+ First items from the store are at a discounted price, so you can buy these by playing a little
( got enough silver& gold &2 decks via a humble bundle)
+ You can buy additional deck slots in the store.
+ Price for card packs in the store is ok (but I never did)
 
CON:
- Booting up issues
- Collection loading issues
- Collection: the button to switch from list view to card view is hiding itself very good, took me a while to notice it.
- The font used for the text is somewhat blurry, but you can adjust that. (But the text itself is nicely done.)
- Very short campaign.
- Mastery missions in campaign => excuse for the game to cheat on you, this wouldn’t work in real life ! Example: only 1 card may be played when you begin the match, they play 2,…
- Decks, event tickets, legendary chests, daily cards, special packs, are expensive ! Even the ‘discounted chests’ are expensive.
- Constructed tournament is pay to win, they all have superpower decks, including new cards you didn’t buy or legendary cards which are just too expensive.
- Access to tournaments is expensive from 3-7 event tickets, to large amount of silver you can’t obtain by just playing the game, quantities of gold that require real money !
- Alternative legendary cards not forgable, you can buy them in a daily rotation card scheme (card of the day), but this rotation scheme also includes normal legendary cards.
- You can only break down a card if you have 4 copies of it.
- Breaking/forging cards can be accessed by clicking on a card in your collection. Maybe say it somewhere in a tutorial ? Make an extra menu option for breaking/forging cards ?
- Breaking/forging cards doesn’t really pay off. => expensive !
There are better (Magic) and a lot more more renewing (Card City Nights) card games out there, try them instead.
If you already played all other card games, you can try this game.
Try the campaign and the drafting tournament.
Avoid the constructed tournament, so you won't experience the pay to win story.

SolForge is a F2P (don't stop reading, trust me) trading card game. It sets itself apart by being made by ex Magic and by having a unique take on things. As an example. You have some lanes and each card can take up one lane.  Once that card is in the lane, you cannot move it (unless it has movement) until it is destroyed.
It is unique in that sense. The game revolves around a hand of 30 cards, cards come out each turn and stay for the duration of the turn. You have no mana costs so you can throw down any card in your current hand in any free lane (or no lane depending if it is a spell card (up to 2 cards per turn)). But each card does have a level. As you level up, so do your cards. And each level makes them stronger.
As said it is F2P, so you'll be expecting the costs of the game. Well there really isn't any. You can play and enjoy the game "as is". Each day you login, you get free silver and a free booster pack of cards. You can spend silver to get boosters or misc items. And if you really start to feel the vibe, you can lay down some actual money on gold. Which is not needed to enjoy the game. I have been playing for a few hours and I have to say, I log in each day, and claim 3 victories against the computer for my goodies and enjoy every minute of it.
Enjoy the game for what it is, a F2P game that wont rip your purse from you.

If you enjoy turn based RPG-Strategy hybrids (so more Fire Emblem-inspired than XCOM) you'll enjoy this. Maybe a more limited roster of characters than you'd expect from the genre but the characters play very distinctly; each with a very different set of resource/positioning/combat role considerations. This game is clearly indie, but the production quality on everything is top class. Clearly some very talented people behind this game.
Scattered thoughts:
*Difficulty curve was a siggly line - Get the weakest point out of the way first. There was absolutely a learning curve, first few instances of combat seemed very difficult and then I figured out how to manage the 70~80% hit chance you are stuck with for a while. Then some later party members are comically overpowered, and then some late game enemy types are living nightmares. Overall it was appropriate but there are some enounters that are serious outliers, so be ready for the occational whiplash.
* Overarching time management system - there's an overarching system of days to complete a set of X objectives from a master list in each chapter with each town building/overworld movement costing a few days. If you don't plan out how you will tackle them you will run into the day limit. They are easy to reach though unless you were looking to mindlessly wander through the game. I enjoyed it as a solid balance between letting players sandbox thier way through the content and providing the structure needed to challenge the player's planning ability.
* The shield/health system I felt was very well executed, you can't stonewall a choke point forever with a healer, tank, and a ranged class. Using terrain to maximize the number of 2v1 situations in your favor or forcing enemies through environmental traps you lay down is vital.
* The plot is servicable as a method to help direct your focus, but not much else. However, the inter-character dialogue is perhaps best described as a similar flavour to Borderlands 2: the 4th wall is frequently MIA, its on the groan-inducing side at times, but I'd be lying if I said I didn't laugh and enjoy it. There is a suprisingly large amount of fully voiced dialogue. Every line has a professional production quality.
* There is some hard core waifu bait. There are husbandos as well, but the waifu bait is more intense than I expected from something from outside Japan. So I guess there are Fire Emblem comparisons to be drawn here as well.

TL;DR: Overall, this game gets a 6/10. I recommend it for anyone really itching for a tactical RPG without a heavy emphasis on story who can overlook some significant design flaws.
Pros:
- The art style is well done.
- The voice acting, overall, is very solid. The characters feel like characters and are written well. This is especially important because you're going to spend a LOT of time interacting with your character, as it's the only way to avance the plot and to open new skills, items, weapons, and mini games.
- The battling, the game's bread and butter, is CHALLENGING. But after an initially steep difficulty curve and once you start getting used to how the skills and characters interact with one another, it becomes pretty rewarding to take down enemies in battle. The reason this game gets a 6/10 instead of something lower is simply that the battling is rewarding and feels challenging without being overwhelmingly hard (once you get used to it). The lack of healing but instead relying on "shields" to absorb damage was a refreshing spin on the genre, and it never felt like there was a super heavy emphasis on shields despite some other reviews (for instance, I focused more on dodging and high initiative for defensive purposes and never really went heavy into shields...in fact, I wasn't using Kay by the end of the third chapter).
- The choose-your-own-adventure style dungeon interactions were pretty fun and were also rewarding without feeling too cheap. There were some that should have been improved or scrapped, and a few had some silly references/jokes (Lassie, the Empire Strikes Back, etc.) but overall they were pretty enjoyable.
- First, the whole game is formed around the idea of 2-month sprints in which you have to achieve a series of "kingdom quests". I actually liked this, and never felt rushed. In fact, I had lots of extra quests done at each deadline. However, the things you spend your days doing that weren't exploring dungeons and fighting will be covered in the "cons" section.
- There is a good amount of variety in how you choose to build the characters, and even though you start with every skill you'll ever get for each character when they first join the party, you can upgrade each of the skills (through the silly personal relationship system) so I liked that.
Cons:
- The personal relationship system is one of the most annoying systems in a game I've ever suffered through. Some people seem to be okay with it but I just think it was a huge overcomplication that really brought the game down a few pegs. You are required to have interactions with the characters in your town in order to unlock the ability to craft weapons, craft items, use the store (at all), upgrade the rewards from battles, make money, unlock the battle-character-specific upgrades for the characters you fight with, etc. You need to "spend a day" with a character to improve your relationship and "level" it up. However, certain characters are only available on certain days of the week and the number of times that I had to put off going out and getting more quests done so I could wait a couple of days (wasting time, usually) for a character to become available to me was infuriating. Who thought this was a good idea? It's awful.
- The statuses that get applied during battle are largely ignored, which I think may be buggy. There were many, many times when my "vanished" character was still targeted directly even though the point of that status is that enemies do not target him.
- The percentage chances for abilities to land (chance to hit, for example) are way wrong. I experimented with this for a while when I was missing >30% of my attacks on abilities with an ~85% hit chance. I kept track of this over hundreds of attacks. I don't understand how they could be so off.
- There are other bugs, like the town screen showing you that you can interact with a particular character (by placing a heart in their avatar icon) but then not allowing you to actually interact with them.
- The line of site is implemented horribly. Why does the front square of a 2x2 square enemy block line of sight from the back square? Why is a perfect diagonal sometimes within line of sight and sometimes not? The LOS implementation was maddening.
- I didn't use a single item until the final fight. Not sure if this is just my play style or other people found them as useless as I did.
- It's too long. Way too long, and there's really no story to speak of. Each character has a tiny little arc you can view through the personal relationship system, but the main story arc is about 40 minutes long and the game took me 30+ hours to finish. It's WAY TOO LONG.
If you're looking for a successor to Final Fantasy Tactics or Vandal Hearts or other classic era tactics games, this ain't it. The complete lack of a meaningful and engaging story kills that. But if you're in it for the character building and battling, you could do much worse. 6/10, slight recommendation.

If you really like Broken Sword 5, you might want to buy it, but only on a discount - 50% at least.
The game starts well enough. A murderer in the gallery you are at, some religious voodoo as a theme, some puzzles ready to be solved.
Unfortunately, it gets worse along the road.
I enjoyed playing the game, but I'm not sure I can recommend it if you're not Broken Sword fan.
First, the ending was just bad. It isn't "Life is Strange"-level bad, but it's pretty bad. It also really exposes its second weakness:
The characters are shallow, uninspired, boring. Some of the potentially interesting characters are never developed. Even when you meet them, it's usually just a short meeting and you don't hear of this character(for the long time). Their motives are unclear, some characters undergo a change of character that's surprising at least, if not outright dumb. There are no memorable characters in this game.
Because of that, the plot suffers. It looks like most characters behave certain way just for the sake of behaving this way(or, which is probably the real reason, becacuse the writers didn't have any better idea).
The game has many unsatisfying side plot's endings, including the main plot and many promising characters/plots aren't developed. This makes the game look rushed or incomplete.
Oh, and the UI sucks. It is the first Point and Click game that I had to order character something multiple times, because UI sent him to my cursor instead of interacting with the item.
And the animations are long and impossible to skip. I wonder if that's another way of making the game look longer than it really is.

Game Corp DX is best described as an excellent entry level management game. It's cheap, charming, easy to learn and compelling, but clearly targeted at a casual audience. Veterans of similar games such as Factorio or Prison Archtitect will find no challenge here. As a near total newcomer to this genre of video games, I find the afore mentionned games difficult to get into, yet I was able to understand and "master" Game Corp DX's main mode with relative ease. After I reached the "end game", I was left craving for more options, more layers of complexity and especially more challenge.
As of writing this review, I must have produced and published over a hundred video games, and all of them end up turning a profit and helping me grow my virtual developement studio. I've long ago left my AI competitors in the dust, as my studio dominates the Top 10 chart with games 4-10 times superior to the competition. I never had any need to grab loans, fire a difficult employee or work really hard to optimize the efficiency of the studio as a whole.
This is not to say Game Corp DX is a bad game and in fact its possible the hard mode could grant me the challenge I crave, but that wouldn't be enough to compel me to play more of it. 15 hours was enough to experience what is on offer here. I had fun the whole way througth and I hearthily recommend the game to anyone willing to experience a "light management" game. Maybe I'll come back just to produce Half life 3. ;P
All in all, its a great low pressure game and I give it 8 out of 10.

This game is a steal at any price $5 or less.
It's a funny, quirky little tycoon game that let's you very quickly and easily create your own game studio and start cranking out games for profits.
The fun (for me) comes mostly from being creative with studio and game names, creating horrible franchises and manipulating the game industry to buy whatever you shovel out the door based on meeting market demands.
On the plus side this is a very easy and simple game to pick up and learn. You'll quickly master the setup of making games and then the rest is tweaking your developers skills and learning how to read the industry trends.
On the down side: it is really simple. There's probably 5 hours of real content here before you totally master the game. You can probably go another 5 hours if you really want to churn out every achievement for the game (some are just random ~ which legendary developers show up to be hired to hit those achievements) and some are just a matter of time (you'll have long since mastered the game before you get to a billion dollars a couple of hours later)
I had fun with my 10 hours in game getting 100% achievments. And it's the type of flash game I'll probably replay once a year or so for a couple of hours.
As a fun little game it's easily recommended at it's low price point.
I can only wish they created a deeper more intricate version that would be worth a higher price tag.

I have had played Starbound before it hit version 1.0 and I didn't like it as much. There weren't much to do other than to progress through the Techs and getting to the endgame gear.
Now that I have achieved every achievement, I am more than happy enough to write a review of my findings.
Since version 1.0, there has been a storyline to follow. It seems rather under developed but it is serviceable enough to keep driving me forward to see the ending (This could be an exception if the player has skipped the prologue as it is an option when creating your character).
You can play the game and not give a toss about the main storyline. Once you've got your ship repaired, you are free to do whatever the hell you want to. I have played with multiple friends and they all have their own unique experiences.
- I personally have overprepared on everything I did. I fought the third boss of the main story having achieved endgame gear. Once I've beated the final boss, I went on a journey to collect everything and achieve every achievement.
- One friend setted out to explore the universe as a pirate pilaging every settlement he comes across.
- Another immediately begin to colonize a planet when he found out how to use the Colony Deeds.
- One other friend begun life as a full time farmer and earning money then forgetting about the main quest entirely (Took him about 20+ hours to finally get the first artifact).
- Yet another friend immediately went exploring to pilage every settlement but he does it in utmost caution as he doesn't want to anger any of the occupances, he just wants their nice looking furniture (Nothing in his home nor his ship is crafted by him). I did tell him 3D Printing becomes a thing later on in the game, he just didn't listen.
I don't know how to describe the soundtrack. It just feels right. Sets you in the right mood as you run across a thick jungle trying to find for a friendly settlement just so you could empty your backpack and continue to spelunk for that sweet sweet Durasteel. I guess the Starbound OST is rather melancholic.
Ultimately, if you want a game that is basically a Universe-Sized Sandbox filled with options and things to do, get Starbound.  At the current price, it is a literal steal with the amount of content already present. Some would call this the "Poor Man's Sky" but I am ready to debate that this is so much better than No Man's Sky.
NOTE: The game is still being updated noted by the recent Spacefarer update and the coming Bounty Hunter update. More things to come.

Exanima is a hidden gem of a game. The best way to explain how excellent this game is is to provide a timeline.
First, I fought in the practice arena to learn and hone my skills. Clearly, the gameplay is the highlight. To my surprise, there was simply no cheap way to beat enemies. The AI adapts to your actions and will learn to backstep if you constantly step in for swings and then step out (as many guides suggest). Of course, still play defensively, but understand that there is no way to cheese enemies in this game. As I practiced more, I realized the significance of the motion of the mouse. Wide, fast swings resulted in heavy blows that would deal great damage but also leave me open should I miss. Landing my first headshot felt more rewarding than any other action in any other video game I've ever played. This just applies to the two handed heavy weapons. Different weapons offer different play styles, and the combat never gets old or repetitive. It's meaty, raw, and gives complete control to you, the player, over these marionettes.
After the practice arena, I tried the real arena. It's an interesting game mode, with a real sense of progression, albeit slow. Without the option to save, there are real stakes in the game, and I would highly advise not using the main character in life-threatening situations, because if he dies, your "guild" dissolves and the game ends. I enjoyed this feature as a game mode, but the lack of a way to save also hurts this game mode, more than it hurts the campaign. Speaking of which...
~~~~~~~~~~~~~
CAMPAIGN
I have never been more surprised by a game's campaign. To begin, the campaign is structured in 5 levels currently with about 14 total expected upon release. The first 3 are considered "tutorial" levels, but do not be mistaken; you recieve NO help and they are NOT easy. They are essentially a pretest, making sure the player can handle the challenge. At the end of level 3, the player encounters the first and only checkpoint. There is no indication that it is a checkpoint, and this story event is spoiled in the steam videos, so I might as well just tell you that it's the blue portal. In these three levels, there are eerie stories unravelled similar to the way Dark Souls tells it's story through items, settings, and text rather than dialogue and cutscenes. This trend continues throughout the rest of the game, but leaves many holes for the player to fill in, like Dark Souls. It's an overall immersive and atmospheric experience that absolutely captivated me. Exanima challenges many AAA games in terms of immersion and atmosphere.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
GRAPHICS
The game is further boosted by it's perfect graphics that are dark, drab, and fit the game perfectly. The lighting, however, is the real highlight. Light is scarce and often dim. It is dynamic and the torch even loses intensity if you swing it around.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
MUSIC
The music, although I expected it to be generic and mediocre, surprised me too. It is fitting for the atmosphere. Foreboding but somewhat goofy horns give way to more threatening strings, until at one point, the game is silent.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
SOUND DESIGN
Sound design is excellent, too. Meaty slugs, crisp slices, crunching blows, clatter of debris and surrounding objects, clanking of weapon against armor, there appears to be a different sound for everything. Again, the game goes beyond expectation, and conquers AAA games like Dark Souls, which seemed to use the same sounds repitched and lacked variety, or skyrim, which lacked weight.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
In the end, Exanima is an impressive techincal achievement that has revolutionized combat, and will forever ruin hack and slash games for me; I can't imagine touching skyrim again at this point. But what's most impressive is that this is an Early Access title with a long, immersive, thoughtful campaign, an additional endless game mode (arena), a practice arena, and NO CRASHES OR GLITCHES despite it's revolutionary combat system. I am simply amazed and would honestly reccomend this game to anyone. This game has even captivated my older brother who typically laughs at these "nerdy" games. I return to my computer and often see him sitting in my chair playing Exanima. The game clearly has had a similar effect on him as it has on me.
If you're just looking for a number score, it's a 10 for me. It's a diamond in the rough of awful early access titles, whether they are abandoned or buggy, glitchy messes that crash, or just garbage games. In a sea of Pixelcraft Survival Open World Simulators beta 0.1.2.4.2, Exanima is a beacon of hope. It is an already complete package with promises of plenty more coming.

If you can get passed the simplicity, small amount of land, lack of building variants, poor management options for peasants, lack of customization, and no sandbox mode (or ability to change difficulty in game at any time) then you might like this game.
On the surface this is your average city builder. You have your homes, defenses, production, and transportation. If you're looking for a more in depthy game where you can micro manage everything, this isn't for you. Or if you want to play around with it and make giant kingdoms without the burden of lacking resources. But if you enjoy a time waster and managing a kingdom where much of the management is taken care of for you, then this is your type of game.
PROS
-Music is good
-Graphics aren't bad
-Optimization options
-Simple enough for most anyone
-Randomly generated maps
-Easy enough to start for new players
-Peasants have names
CONS
-Lack of building variants
-Lack of management options for peasants and buildings
-Peasants die to often of pleagues (In my experience)
-Lack of customization options
-No sandbox mode
-Very little land to work with
-Gets repetitive and boring after awhile
Overall, if you want to buy it and are okay with a simple game to waste a few hours on then go for it. But if you want a game like Banished or Ancient Cities, you best be moving on from this game. I overall like it and believe it has a lot of potential to get BIG! However it's been out for a year now and there hasn't been many dramatic changes other than enemy spawns being increased. I hope that the game gets updated with a few major updates to make it more involving.

Basically I didn't like it - the game is very short, finished it under 4 hours and more than half of it was simply running - and the half of other half was reading log entries. You might think that I should've been enjoying the scennery - but there isn't much to enjoy, everything is pretty monotonic - starting from orange and brown hills, through grey and black hills and even some blue glossy hills that probably were meant as glaciers, finally finishing with green hills.
Graphics of this game were pretty outdated, which would be hard to notice, since most of what you see are rocks and hills, but... well, suffice to say that I've seen better character models in games made ten years ago. And you'd think that gamedevs would put some more work into character models, since there are about THREE of those in the entire game.
Dying - dying was pretty annoying. I understand the fact that dropping from 100 feet to the ground is lethal, but seeing me fall and turn into bloodied ragdoll about 30 feet above ground is laughable. Similarly, I understand that stepping into lava is lethal, but ragdolling with the cheerful sound of flatline after one step into a burning rock? Am I to understand that burning your toe causes immediate heart failiure?
Well, you might say that this is a story-driven game and what I should look for is good story - and the fact is that story in this game is pretty interesting. But the way it is delivered is, in my opinion, horrible. Voice in this game is used only as single sentences spoken by main character (in plain, monotonic voice) or single words by the Russian girl (which are, obviously, in Russian). Pictures are so confusing that without reading full logs you're not sure what exactly is happening.
So to sum up, what we have here is neglegible quantity of voice acting, couple of nice pictures and several pages of text. Good enough for a sci-fi novel, not good enough for a game, not nearly enough for this price.

It's hard to pin down the genre of Lifeless Planet. It's part walking simulator, part platformer, part puzzle game, with an overarching strong story focus. You're an astronaut sent on a mission to explore a lush planet but end up on a deserted wasteland. Questions like "What happened to the planet?" soon meld into questions like "Did something happen to me?" when all kinds of weirdness starts popping up.
Elaborating further would steer the review into spoiler territory, so I won't go there. But unfortunately I have to report that while I make the game sound very mysterious (and it certainly is that, up to a point), the final answers provided do not end up being nearly as satisfying as I would've initially hoped they'd be. There is some neat psychological ambiguity lightly sprinked around, but most of the story is rather standard sci-fi fare.
While you wait for the game to reveal its next story nugget, you'll traverse through some pretty arid environments and do a lot of jumping. And I do really mean a LOT of jumping. Most of the actual gameplay in Endless Planet consists of jumping and platforming, and it ends up being more of a nuisance than interesting or rewarding in any way. I feel like majority of the bouncing around could be replaced with just bog-standard walking sections, and the game would work a lot better. A few simple puzzles also felt a bit hastily thrown together.
Lifeless Planet is heavily banking on the player finding its story worthwhile, but at least for me, it just didn't hit home at all. The most interesting facets of the story are hardly explored at all, and the least interesting ones are shoved into the limelight and paraded around. I just can't root for this one.

Although this game was very entertaining and very fun to play for ten minutes, all in all, based upon the content, it's a waste of money. It doesn't cost much, no, but you do have better games for the same price to spend your money on.
Classic Mode:
Has no objective at all. You walk around in a reasonably small world filled with a single cabin, grass, fences, trees and cows with buggy heads. Shooting the cows makes them explode but once you've seen that once and you've giggled - do you want to see it again?
Grass Mode:
Why would you even put this into a game? You don't spend money on a game to watch grass grow. You can't move or equip anything. All you do is sit in your chair and watch grass grow. Paint-Drying simulator will be the next release.
Dubstep Mode:
I laughed for about six miliseconds. Stingy cow animations with some tacky lighting effects and some terrible dubstep music. Putting two-and-two together, yes, it's just spinning cows dancing to music. Done.
Ranged Mode:
Um, this is meant to be a "Grass Simulator", not a FPS. Completely irrelevant to the game, and once again has no clear objective. The mace is pointless; you can't kill cows with it and you can't actually get out of the cabin that you spawn in on this mode.
Snowfall Mode:
This mode is the only one which actually has detail. Probably my favourite mode because the map is actually extremely well modeled, but much like the Classic Mode, has no objective whatsoever. Just walking around in a snowy place with, oh! Guess what! Cows!
At first I thought it was a direct model from KHOLAT.
Bad Party Mode:
This mode does one thing, and one thing only. Generate lag. Guess what! Cows again! Superspeed cows with lights hanging off their backs and dying. For people to laugh at that they really must have a bad sense of humour. Sorry, but why would you put things like that in a game, especially since people actually paid money for this?
Online Mode:
Gah, what do I say about this? Like I said before, if you call a game "Grass Simulator", you must be mad to turn it into an FPS. People seem to be invincible, the aiming sucks, the bobbing of the weapons, although it's realistic, makes it extremely difficult to see what you're doing.
All In All, this game is just a waste of money. This game would be perfect if it was a Free to Play game and is very good at pointlessly consuming 20 minutes of your life. You're better off just watching videos of this game and saving your money.

This is more of a clicker-game than an actual management or economy.
The game is solid, bug-free and has some appealing concepts.
However it feels like it just came out of alpha. Every aspect of it is trivial, without any sort of challenge or feeling of accomplishment.
Competitors in campaign mode won't get too much ahead of you even if you stop making games for years.
There are only 12 items in the game, all of which can be bought, used and then sold back for 100% of the buy-price; that absolutely should not be the case in a game tagged as "economy" and "management".
There's a special machine which can remove negative traits and add positive traits for your workers: everyone can reach the perfect worker state in a relatively short time.
On the quality side of things only the UI is lackluster: Esc doesn't close windows, new windows open on top of eachother instead of closing the previous, no worker list, only small things, really.
It's a 4€ game from 2015, and as I said there are no serious problems with it.
But it's a very empty sandbox with only hints of economy and management, or mabye just an intricate clicker-game.
You can get much better value out of Game Dev Tycoon, but to be honest I've had more fun even with AdVenture Capitalist..
Pointless, waste of money.

There exist numerous bad reviews for this game, but I thought I'd try it for myself. I am not one of those people who blast a game after playing it for 35 minutes, but trust me on this one, in 35 minutes I checked out
this
had to offer.
There is no story, no intro, no video, no cutscene, no dialog at all. Just the obnoxious music at the start screen. You start Classic mode, to find yourself in a random field with cows (wooden, low geometry idle models) grazing grass made up of 2-D models that will remind you of Midtown Madness (the 1999 game by MS). If you name a game Grass Simulator, for the love of Cthulhu, at least render the freaking grass nicely! And to think that
maxed out my decent laptop system at second-best graphics quality (fell below 30fps). What is it using the memory for? Definitely not rendering anything in the game!
Okay, so you're in the field. Now what? You have a crosshair in the center of the screen - that's all. Since this is obviously not your first game, you click around buttons, and realise that number keys bring up different weapons. You can shoot cows with a Glock, an old-timey Revolver, a Tommy-Gun, and apparently what looks like a swinging mace. After 3-4 bullets the cows explode. That's it. The worst part, is that the budgeoning mace ironically does no damage. The "world", i.e., the random field, has invisible borders you can't cross (but your bullets can) and there is no map, no HUD, nothing at all that can tell you where you are and what, if anything, are you supposed to do. Oh, and there are no Ammo indicators, it just runs out when it wishes.
Next is the "Grass" mode, where you can be a strand of grass on the ground, and can see the Sun set and rise every few seconds, seeing up close the pathetic 2-D grass models around you grow in height as days go by. I don't know if this bit was some satire on the overdose of crappy, mindless simulator games flooding social media, but this is truly pointless. Also, satire works best if there is something of use to complement it. Someone tell that to the Devs.
Then there's a Dubstep mode, where some groovy music plays and you have cows spazzing in circles about their fixed axes. You can just watch the light-and-sound show, walk around and watch cows flashing in bright colours rotating to trippy music that repeats every 2.5 mins. The Bad Disco mode is a worse version of the same, with series of glowing disco lights replaced by the cow models. Frankly, seeing this does give you a laugh for the first 20 seconds, but after the joke is over you kinda wonder why the hell this game exists
The Snow Forest is actually a decent-looking stage which again clearly shows that the trees are much better-designed than the grass. Again, you have guns and you shoot cows to explode them.
My absolute crappy experience was the Range: There are targets for you to shoot. That's it. No count, no score, no ammo indicator.
Throughout the game's various levels, you:
-Can't switch to guns if you die. Gotta reboot the game (oh yes!);
-May randomly just die, while walking or standing (I even died randomly in the Range); of course, no guns IF you manage to respawn;
-Exploding cows, if too close to you, push you back and their explosions are lethal (no health bar whatsoever);
-Might face a simple crash;
-Might face the game's level loading but you freezing, with the Menu still functional.
I had chanced upon this game in Greenlight, and voted yes because the idea seemed new, hilarious and really satirical. But the game has absolutely nothing in it. I expected something like Goat simulator, maybe. What I got was an 800 MB download that basically consisted of 2 MP3 files, 2 terrain models, 1 animal model, 4 weapon models, 2 tree models and maybe 5-6 grass PNGs. I later came to know that if the game got through Greenlight, the Devs would gift a key to those in the group following the game. They did not ask anyone to promote the game in any way, and the group was closed, so I don't know how ethical this whole deal was, but I am pretty sure that shady releases like these are a major reason why the Greenlight system got shut down. If I am feeling so bad over spending less than an hour, and a little bandwidth, I cannot imagine the plight of those who shelled out 10 Euros for this piece of absolute defecation.

Pretentious plot? Check.

Puzzles that are senseless? Check.
The further into game, the more there are.
Stiff, unskippable animation of movement? Check.
Imagine situation, where you have to walk from left side of the location to right, and main character walks his way slowly, taking up to a 2 minutes of game. Repeat few times a location, since some of the puzzles will work on the second try, after adding up unrelated item to a puzzle.
Unskippable dialogue? Check.
While the dialogue boxes are skippable, any movement during dialogue is not. This makes waiting even worse.

Where to begin. This game has a lot going for it. The physics engine is unlike anything I’ve ever experienced. Every object, enemy, and weapon has a distinctive presence and weightiness to it. Deep and interesting combat, challenging dungeon crawling, a fun arena mode (Which I’ve wasted over 150+ hours on) and so much more.
PROS:
+ Unique combat system based on physics.
+ Weapons and armor that behave like real weapons and armor. Armor layers in a natural way to create unique combinations of clothing and armor. Armor and clothes are procedurally generated creating unique stats and colors on the same armor / clothing piece.
+ A huge variety of weapons ranging from Swords, Axes, Maces, to improvisational weapons like steel rods, brooms, and farming tools.
+ Challenging and rewarding gameplay. Main campaign can take between 30 minutes (if you’re good) to 20 hours.
+ Unique character creator where height, weight, and physique impacts combat in unique ways.
+ A interesting story to unravel, in the spirit of Dark Souls.
+ Runs well on my toaster of a PC
CONS:
- Updates are fairly spaced out, however are released mostly bug-free.
- Can be crushingly difficult and has a deep learning curve (not a problem for me, but I can see this turning off certain people)
- Many of the features from the 2011 Kickstarter are still being worked on.

Cutesy ridiculousness done right.
I don't usually like 'humourous' games, nor the characters that typically comprise them, but Regalia manages to get (most of) the humour right. Pop culture references abound, both brick-to-the-teeth obvious ones and those as obscure as Vinicius Quesada, and more often than not - which is a massive step up from most such outings - they actually manage to be entertaining.
Bear in mind, this isn't really the sort of game you play for either the character development or the plot - both are ludicrous, and you shouldn't expect either to leave you thinking for more than 2 seconds after you close the game.
Thankfully, Regalia has some reasonably meaty turn-based tactical combat to enjoy. A cast of 12 characters - each with 5 unique active skills and a passive skill, and a maximum party size of 6 with 4 typically being deployable - offers quite a variety in approaches one can take to fights. Characters can be tweaked with perks and 3 pieces of equipment to suit your style even further. There are some pretty groovy combos between characters to pull off, and most characters have clear synergies with others. Many fights will see you up against unique or relatively rare opponents, and each has up to two optional tasks to complete for a minor benefit (but mostly for the challenge of it).
The game operates on a time-limit per chapter, a feature which immediately turned several of my friend off playing it, but the time-limits are incredibly generous and unlikely to impact anyone but the most negligent, wasteful players. They serve more to progress the story than anything else.
The music and art have both had a great deal of passion lavished upon them, though the art does perhaps give one the impression of some of the more well-developed flash games, which could turn you off if you only looked at screenshots. Suffice to say, this is not a cheap, quickly-turned over title. The developers have done an amazing job in the style with which they've worked.

TL;DR: There is nothing badly done or incompotent about this game, but almost every facet is done better in another game.
This is a turn based tactics game. It has some sembelence of relationship management. It threatens to have kindgom building without getting quite there in the first 4 hours.
The combat is okay. Battles feel challenging enough while staying fair, but there is no real basic attack to be found. This means that at times, you might need to use a character to get a kill, but because of how their most basic ability works, you will be forced to hit one of your own units as well. Everything has some kind of added (sometimes bonus) which in theory is cool, but is far more limiting than you would think. Want a better tactics game? Play Fire Emblem or Children of Zodiarcs when it comes out.
Then there is relationship management. You can spend a day talking to someone to increase your relationship with them for some benefit. The characters, while relatively interesting (at least in the first 4 hours) dont have very much to them. You have the stingy shopkeeper, the burly feminine man, the ridiculously obsessed/danger ignoring journalist. The time you spend with them just feels like a chore and a waste of time, and the dialogue choices (3, picking the best one gives better increase in relationship) don't feel like they give you a fair chance. For example, once I had the choice between 3 forms of the word "no." I guessed the right one, maybe you got an increase in relationship for all of them, i dont know. Either way, you want good, time based, relationship mechanics? Play Persona or Stardew Valley.
The game starts with our main character moving to an abandoned kingdom he has been told is his, and he has to build it up. As far as I can tell, you really have no choice as to how this happens. Sure, you can upgrade buildings, but its pretty clear that you just upgrade whatever is going to give the best rewards. Also, you dont choose the order people come to your kingdom. Want a blacksmith? Cant build a forge until the blacksmith guy comes in the story. Want some kind of enchantor? Probably not in the game, but you wouldnt be able to build an enchantors lab until the enchantor came in the story. It doesnt feel like you're building a kingdom, and I guess that wasnt what the devs were going for when they made it, but it feels lacking because of that. I can't think of many examples of this off the top of my head, but I'm guessing things like Little King's Story or even Terraria do this better.
I think this game should have focused more heavily on one thing. There is nothing terrible here; nothing specifically that makes me think its a bad game. Altogether though, I would not recommend this.

Edit: After completing the game I'm happy to say I still stand by this review. There's still a big list of things that need fixing.
This is one of those reviews where I wish there was a neutral review! As there is so much to love about this game.

But here is the TL;DR: Regalia is a game that just oozes with surprisingly high production values, art, voice acting and music (Fully orchestrated!) but stumbles with a long, long list of core gameplay bugs and head scratching choices.

When it comes to presentation Regalia does have that unity engine game "feel" with chunky buttons and menus. However the artwork for the game is bright, colourful and clear. It's an absolute joy to look at all the characters portraits and expressions during cutscenes. Voice acting ranges from "Hey that's pretty good!" to "Ehhhhhhhh" but it’s all very welcomed. The music is a highlight with some nice tunes.

The game has social links and a calendar much like the persona franchise. Each couple of in-game months required you to complete a number of tasks (mostly simple ones that benefit you generally for doing them) and a general quest. Coming from Persona 5 only a few weeks ago I had no issues with this system at all. I enjoyed doing the little social links with various characters as it makes them feel a whole lot more alive and not just "shopkeeper" or "weapon crafter". I had a close call at the end of chapter 5 to completing the quests but managed alright.

Going onto the main map has you going from location to location doing dungeons with various nodes that will be a battle, campsite or a choose your own adventure like story. Campsites are where you can save and revive dead party members and on release you could only save once at a campsite, but this has now (THANKFULLY) been changed so you can repeatedly save but only revive your party members once. The choose your own adventure stories are usually fun and you can get some fun little quests, items, stories or just end up going into a battle.

Battles are the the real let down of the game though and the main reason for why I give this a negative. Most characters have some fun powers and passives even if it might seem strange at first they have all their skills available from the game go.  The enemy designs are good with their own passives, skills and such that are all fitting to what you’d expect. However most enemies are masses of HP and sometimes possess skills and abilities that punish you in overly for merely attacking. A good example of this is an enemy that gains extra turns when you miss it or another that will regain all of its HP back and more in the form of shield points which might as well be normal HP when fighting most of your characters.

If you've seen the other reviews or discussions you will see that accuracy in the game is a big point of contention and I agree. There are ways to make sure your attacks always hit with a number of unmissable abilities but when you are swarmed with enemies that benefit each other with large health pools and abilities that make them stronger the more you hit them. There's a frustratingly high amount of enemies that gain benefits when score a hit. I have sunk all of the characters weapons and perks into boosting accuracy which seems to only very slightly offset the issue, but this accuracy doesn’t appear to account for the enemies dodge stat. The accuracy issue also seems to come from, if I'm not mistaken, that the chance to hit is essentially rolled twice: Once for the players accuracy and then once for the enemies chance to dodge. What makes missing so frustrating is that a lot of battles can feel like a slog with your whole team surrounding one moderately powerful enemy and each character taking anything from 10-15% of its health each turn. I actually kept getting flashbacks to this CLASSIC movie scene as my party repeatedly poked an enemy:

One reviewer pointed out that (while I haven’t confirmed but seems to be true) enemies scale with your characters level that only makes their attacks hit about as hard if not harder as the game goes along and their pools of HP a slog to get through when it feels like just under half of your attacks are missing.

Line of sight can be extremely annoying as well when your party members block the line drawn to enemies. It makes using “large” characters that take up four tiles more of a hinderance. There are perks that remedy this for some issues but it’s not great.

Each battle will have challenges as well to complete. I recently replayed Chroma Squad and remembered the fun challenges at the start of each mission that you could do for bonuses at the end. However these challenges range from “possible” to “are you actually joking”. The worst ones are challenges that want you to not use your character's main skills, not enter battle with a full party, not lose a point of health on any character and never miss an attack. A lot of these challenges are simply based on dumb luck if you want to succeed. The rewards just simply aren’t worth it.

I do enjoy the perks part of leveling up though. Having a bunch of small perks you can unlock and then stack up on your party members that change their skills to ignore line of sight, do more damage, shorter cooldowns, etc.

...Also I don’t like fishing. I’m not a big fan of any game that has you hammering a button for an extended period of time over and over. Should of just copied Torchlights fishing mechanic, wouldn’t even of been mad.

The bugs are what really brings the game down currently. Many of the skills, perks, status conditions and other various parts of the game are bugged and don’t function correctly making it even more frustrating. I could go on about these but this review is already so long I’m sure most of you have switched off. I’ve seen the devs been so kind to take people's saves and edit them so they can continue with their progress in the game. Which is super nice of them but still won’t feel like a true solution.

To end this review I want to say I kickstarted the game and don't regret it for a moment! Regalia has the potential to be an absolutely excellent tile based RPG but it currently isn't in that state. I'm also a strong believer a game should be reviewed in the state it launched in (or within the first few days) and not after X amount of patches. I'm sure I'll be changing this review to a recommended in the future once issues are solved. Devs are quick to answer any bugs people have come across though. I will likely finish the game in time and maybe even do a second playthrough when they add all the features they didn’t have time for in the initial launch and patches that help the game. I’m excited for when this game is fully ironed out!

TL;DR at the bottom.
Lifeless Planet is an incredible game filled with atmospheric joy and a story that only gives you just enough to figure out what is going on. You play as an American astronaut that is sent to explore a planet that your readings suggest is brimming with life. Upon arrival you find that this planet is nothing like you expected. It houses strange secrets of past explorers and a nation trying to find the perfect life away from Earth only to find that meddling with things they don't understand almost never ends happily. An interesting mix of casual exploration and platforming, it keeps things relatively fresh most of the time. You should feel the want to get to the end to see how everything pans out and what the mysteries of this Lifeless Planet are, but at the same time your feeling of eerie isolation and the ambient sounds of the world make you want to take your time looking at the planet and chilling out as well. I became lost in the isolationist atmosphere and didn't want it to end.
If you peer at the store page for this game and look at the user tags you would think that this is a game in the same genre as Dear Esther and the other "walking simulator" sorts of games. In some instances this is accurate, but in Lifeless Planet you have more than just your feet to work with. You are in a space suit with a jetpack! So while this game is semi-casual most of the time, there are a fair amount of platforming situations in which you must use the jetpack to make some pretty intense jumps now and then. I wouldn't say that this is extremely difficult to do, but you don't just walk from point to point here like a "walking simulator" would suggest. Not only that, but there are puzzles that you will come into contact with that force you to ponder the environment a bit as well as some technology to help you solve these puzzles. So it definitely delves into much more gameplay than just walking from story point to story point.
Besides the tags being somewhat misleading, that META Score is completely off base in my opinion. Lifeless Planet is a fantastic game with a fantastic atmosphere, a cornucopia of map changes that will give you an explosion of color in some areas that is intensified by the more “Lifeless” areas you will find. The game has about 20 different areas with about 15 of them feeling like something completely different from the rest. Each area can be blown through in 10-15 minutes if you want to unless there are puzzles to get through, but anyone that enjoys looking at scenery and taking their time to explore game worlds should find more joy. (While discussing the want for even more little discoveries outside collectibles like random gravestones and such to add to the flavor of the world on the forums the developer said that they will be adding in more of this in a future patch.) It is not open world, but the areas feel wide and spacious enough that you will be able to wander a bit. Not to mention that there are some collectible items such as minerals and documents found in the game to give you a reason to check some of the back corners. Documents, which add a great deal of the story aspects to the game tend to be on the main path, however so you shouldn't miss any of these.
The soundtrack is used sparingly, but feels like when the music comes into play it is escalating the situation and your feeling of isolation and the importance of where you are. It creeps into the feeling of the game and gives you the impression that it is pushing you towards an important moment when it begins to quietly chime in as you move forward. Most of the time, however the isolation you feel is intensified by the ambient sounds of a barren world. Winds and other strange sounds like rocks falling while looking into a great chasm add to the effects of your play.
The story is mysterious, creepy, and interesting. While the main protagonist is your view into Lifeless Planet, you can hear the echos of others throughout your exploration in documents. Some documents contain a sound file in which you can read along as a Russian speaker transcribes it in their own language. It is a Russian speaking voice from someone native to the language as well so it feels authentic. Based solely on the game's title graphic, it is obvious that there is a Russian aspect to the game, but a Russian aspect from the Soviet Union of old. While you are an astronaut from the United States, and there is a Soviet Union background within the game, it does not delve into politics of any sort, nor does it make any statements about either of these nations, or any conflict they had other than maybe a passing note here, or there if necessary to understand the story within the game. The story is one of DISCOVERY, and what it would be like for someone to travel many light years away from Earth and to explore a new world. Their excitement with seeing new forms of life, as well as their struggles with dealing with the unknown.
The best part of the story to me, however is your own discovery of something else being there, and your interactions with it throughout the game. Very little communication is had as you feel it out and it brings an aspect of humanity to the game that is wonderfully done I feel. Without talking, or actively communicating you do feel a sense of closeness to something while making your way to the end. It is too spoilerish to discuss it really, but it is something I feel should be mentioned because the impression you will get mostly looking at this game is that you are fighting the planet and the story is just one of looking at the past more than anything else. This is a major part, but there is the sci-aspect that all good sci-fi stories have in which humanity and human experience comes into play.
Graphically the game is solid and gives you a great many screenshot opportunities. TL;DR/BOTTOM LINE: Lifeless Planet is a great game that will appeal more to a casual gamer from a gameplay standpoint, but to a wider audience of gamers who like sci-fi mysteries, exploring new worlds, and feeling the isolation of a lost planet. The developer, David Board and his team should be proud of their work and congratulate themselves on an epic and unique game. I loved it all the way through and plan to play it again. There is an Achievement to beat the game in under 4 hours, so it could be completed in under that time, however it would be a complete waste to blow through it that quickly. It took me close to 10 hours to finish the game taking my sweet time. There is an Achievement for playing 10+ hours in one game as well too, and I got that without actually having to just idle the game so it is possible to spend over 10 hours in it easily.

Let me start by saying that this game definitely does a few things right. The atmosphere is great and the overbearing loneliness of the situation is made very appearent, especially because of the soundtrack. Now, that being said, this game does fall flat in a few aspects. The journey is long, and I'm not saying that that's a bad thing, but it suffers from something that I think a lot of games are sometimes a culprit of; waiting.

Example: There's a rocky platform that I need to get up onto in order to progress the narrative. Although, instead of just being able to scamper on up to it, I have to use a lift. Unfortunately the power is out so I need to follow the cables to the source to get it back on. I do that and then the path I took there crumbles and now I have to take a longer way to get back to the lift. Once I've made it, I then have to turn it on and time my jumps carefully to get from ground to platform, and finally, onto the path to move forward. The platforming in this game is very basic to say the least, but to put off the story to go make the player perform a tedious and time consuming jumping puzzle just to get back onto the right track is pointless. Why? Why couldn't I have just flipped a switch next to the lift to get it going, or maybe a master power switch just a few yards away? It constantly makes you stop and worry about doing the next thing to make a door open or a path become available.
There are other areas where the only way to go is onward, but you have to make it across multiple platforms. This isn't so bad, but the jumping mechanics aren't very fun to begin with. The astronaut has barely any weight to him and his movement is slippery making for a few frustrating retries at certain points. The jetpack only adds to the grief, sometimes causing you to overshoot a jump, die, and be taken back to the beginning of the platforming encounter to try again.
Overall I enjoyed the first 1 or 2 hours, but then all of the problems I mentioned above started impeding my progress and began to drag it out way too long. Once I reached the end, instead of feeling accomplished for what I had done, I just felt relieved that it was finally over. It all felt like a chore. You can call this game a platformer but the fact that it can't do that right makes it a mediocre experience. The story is the high point most definitely. If only the controls were tighter and the level design wasn't so focused on having platforming obstacles just for the sake of platforming.

Back in January, I was a relatively new Hearthstone player who was also relatively new to card games in general. I was watching Brian Kibler's stream when he mentioned he was a developer for another free to play collectible card game: Solforge. He spoke a bit about it and I was intrigued enough to check it out.
Now, in April and having played Solforge for a few months, I think I can speak enough about the game to warrant a review. Solforge has four factions and hundreds of cards. Games are played with creatures and spells, the former being placed in any of the five lanes and the latter having various effects. Creatures in lanes will "battle" opposing creatures in the same lane. If they are unopposed, they attack the player, removing a given amount of base HP. The first player to drop to zero, naturally, loses the game. As cards are played, they are discarded and "leveled", and when a rank is gained, the discard pile is shuffled and becomes the draw pile.
If you enjoy CCGs, you will *probably* enjoy Solforge. It has a generally great community, many of whom are always willing to share cards with new players to help them get on their feet, which is really important because, as with any CCG, new players begin with an inherent disadvantage as all the veterans have more cards. This is something that all CCGs struggle with, and not even Hearthstone has a solution for it. Another thing to note is that the developer, StoneBlade Entertainment (SBE), seems to really enjoy ridiculously strong cards. They update often (new cards, nerfs/buffs, etc), but in the few months that I've played they've nerfed some strong cards while leaving other glaringly, fun-suckingly strong cards like Wegu untouched. The card Herald of Destruction recently received a massive buff that makes it as un-fun to play against as Wegu. Luckily (?), there's no ranking system, so games can be conceded without a second thought when you discover your opponent is running one of those decks. (Caveat: beware that complaining about cards will occasionally be met with "get better" replies or other variants of the same thing from veterans who have played the game since Kickstarter and will defend all of SBE's decisions to the death)
Solforge has some incredible art, like the
and the
, and some pretty bad art, like the
and the
, though apparently many of the latter cards are from the Kickstarter, where backers were somewhat poorly photoshopped onto cards.
I would be remiss if I didn't mention the incredible Kaelari and his unofficial
, where you can chat with other players, participate in tournaments of various kinds (the best are the unheroic and unlegendary ones, where the really strong cards that new players won't have are "banned") for different prizes, set up trades, and actually participate in a ladder ranking system. Most of the stuff that Kaelari's site does should ideally have been done by the developers themselves as opposed to an unpaid third-party, but SBE is seemingly more focused on pumping out cards than they are with smoothing out what they already have. There is a downside to this ladder, however, and it's that most of its users are veterans, so if you queue up for a ladder or tournament game, it's very likely the person will be better than you. Other than release day for new sets of cards, the number of people who concurrently use the Ladder sits around 50. That means that if everyone's queued (which is never the case), you've got a solid chance of playing the same person more than once. Not enough of Solforge's several hundred daily users either know about the Ladder, or care enough to use it, which is a damn shame, and it'd probably be a different case if it wasn't third-party. Indie developers only have so much money, though.
As I said, I think StoneBlade needs change the focus from more new cards (which everyone loves), to doing things like meshing most of the Ladder's features into the game, overhauling the UI, and actually advertising the damn game. That being said, I'd still be hesitant to label this an Early Access game if it weren't for the big blue label on the store page (otherwise it'd just look like an indie game). Despite all its flaws, I do enjoy Solforge a whole lot and I implore you to give it a shot if you're even remotely interested. It's easier to get into than Hearthstone, as packs and cards in general are easier to acquire. SBE recently revamped the Draft (Arena) queue, where now you can pay 2 event tickets (acquired from your first win of the day) to draft 30 cards that you KEEP after the tournament, which is a fantastic value for new players.

This review is mostly about the local-multiplayer aspect.
Fighties is a very fast-paced local-multiplayer game which feels like a combination of the platforming and unique character abilities from something like smash bros and the quick one hit kills from a variety of other local mp games.
On paper the game is very much like smash bros. A diverse roster with unique moves, dashing, double jumps, stock mode is better than other modes and a goofy collectible mini-game. However a few things make it feel very different.
1. Animations are super simple. One or two frames really.
2. Two moves per character and almost all of them are one hit kills.
3. Floaty. No character feels as if they have much weight at all.
All of this leads to a game that plays very fast and very slow. Every character has their two moves which all have different levels of cooldown. I must commend the creators for making each and every character feel unique. However some of them are maybe 'too unique'. If there were a tier list for this game half of the roster would be piled up at the bottom. Still me and my friends have come up with very creative ways to use even the worst characters.
However most people I try to play with give up after a game or two. The insta-death is very discouraging in this game compared to other games with one hit kills. The reason most have given me is that they feel like they had no options for dealing with the death. They think that due to their character choice they stood no chance against whatever the others were playing.
The characters all look cute even if they are a tad generic. The stages all look fine but I think they would benefit from some animation, even some simple stuff like leaves or rain. I really detest the music, I get that his is supposed to be cutesy game and all but the music is just flat out bad. It doesn't match the pace of the game at all and to be honest barely sounds like music.
In conclusion this game is not for everyone. I would give some videos a look and maybe give it a try if you can before buying as this game really rides on its first impression.

Summary: This is a beautiful game resource management/worker placement game that has high aesthetic appeal and really engaging characters that do draw you into a island world. The game hits the mark on many levels of design but the core elements of the gameplay are riddled with an overwhelming number of dice rolls and convoluted algorithms that ruin an otherwise simple game.
Dead in Bermuda hits alot of things that makes this a very visually appealing game. The parallax style that it uses in almost of it elements gives it a very unique style and overall visual approach that you don't find anymore. Compared to many other games of this genre finding a game with a moderen design is really rare.
Another high point is the dialogue between the characters. While the main story may be dry, the 8 characters each have very distinct personalities that play very well off of each other. You don't really care where this characters are going you just want to see them interact. It's more like a drama with no plot but still a more engaging than some other games.
I was draw to this game for two reason. One; I love worker placement games, mostly board games, because it's hard to find this genre in video games. Two; I'm really in love with its visual design, because I'm a graphic design student. After playing the game I was met with a large amount of disappointment. One of the appeals of this genre is that RNG or dice rolls is kept to a minimum. Bead In Bermuda has so many dice rolls even a DnD player would roll their eyes.
Each character  5 states that you must monitor and keep as low as possible as if one fills that character dies, and also 16 stats that detemine their effectiviness in a certain action or the ability to resist state changes or to recover from state changes. The 16 stats are pretty munch sismply to old school western style rpg design, but what's different is that each skill will raise in level as you use it. This makes no sense in this style of game as you will be so stressed for resources you will need people to what their best at not what thier worst at to skill farm, beacuse of that having skills raise in level seems pointless.
But then again performing any actions seems pointless when having a higher skill level barely raises your min. value. Yes, the first to raise is your max value, not your min. value. Exampe, the fishing action will show 0-8 as a possible outcome. Meaning it is still possible to get 0 fisth despite the fact your fishing skill is 100. Meaning for most actions raising skills ls like instead of rolling a 1d4 you get to roll 1d8 instead. Now if  you're unlucky like me then you rolled in the lower bracket pretty much everytime. It just doesn't make sense. Similarly, the relationship between the states and the stats doesn't make sense. Fatigue lowers your condition, but you need condition to lower your fatigue. There are many instances where this happens and honestly it should happen in this genre of game where you get into an uphill battle but it happens way too soon and just turns into a lockdown for any character that has too low condition. Namely this happens because as with gaining fatigue to lose the fatigue you have to roll for it. Not to mention you gain fatigue even when you sleep at night, also  determined by another dice roll. The pentalies for having high states just becomes so high that if a character gets  3 or more states to even 40% at the same time they are basicly just marked for death as they will have no way to recover from that unless you use an item, which don't appear alot.
I wanted to love this game but having dice determine literally everthing makes it feel like I'm not really doing anything and that I'm losing not because of my bad choices. As for turning it to easy mode it because so easy it was basicly a just a waste of time. This game in its current state, as I have read it has changed, is basicly more like a punishment game for people that love survival games and staring RNG in the face.

The guns feel and sound weak, though they are vastly improved from the single player guns. The controls can be painfully awkward and are not rebindable. To quit multiplayer I have to Alt+Tab and close it as I cannot find an option to return to the menu or quit the game.  Finally, the Grass Simulating mode has the worst graphics of any mode, featuring 2D 'sprites' rather than 3D models of grass (this is most noticeable with the green silhouette of corn.)
Despite the updates the game has received, essentially no significant improvements to individual modes have been made as far as I can tell. New modes get added, and nothing gets fixed. Despite a HUD and all guns being fully animated in multiplayer, the single player modes still have unfinished animations for guns and no hud at all.
Perhaps someday, if the dev is willing to fix and expand existing modes instead of randomly adding new ones, the game may end up ok. However, until that day comes I advise you stay clear of Grass Simulator.\\
V0.2.1 Update:
Just performance fixes and maybe(?) some bugfixes. No new content. Multiplayer still ugly and empty (fun fact: it's impossible to use up all your ammo in a match.)  At least if you now find yourself playing Grass Simulator it will run better.

MAIN MENU BUG FINALLY FIXED. You can properly change game modes now. Unless you start multiplayer, then you have to restart the game. :/

While it was nice to see an update that actually addressed problems and attempted to add 'new' content, I still cannot recommend this game to anyone.

Anyway, I'm just going to address the main complaint I see here in the reviews: the combat.
