What is this game?
It's a an rpg with turn-based combat on a grid field. There are elements of base management, dungeon crawling and 'choose your own adventure', but the combat is the 'meat' of the equation, so to speak. You are tasked with completing 'x' tasks in 'y' of in-game days in order to not fail, although there is a fair bit of flexibility in terms of what objectives you can accomplish in what order.
Combat gameplay manages to balance being both simple and complex at the same time, in my opinion. On one hand, there is no difference a unit's facing makes and the playing field is a flat table with some line of sight and movement blockers placed on it, on the other hand there is enough variety in field layouts, enemy types and player character abilities and their interaction between each other to keep it all engaging and challenging throughout the game.
Party member customization does the same approach: there are no individual levels (everybody levels up as a group) and all characters have a predetermined set of abilities and stats, but there is enough room to customize your build with perks, equipment and character combinations to keep an enjoyable level of variety among the effective loadouts you can bring into combat.
My biggest complaint here is the draconian party size limit - it's four in most scenarios, sometimes less. And there is no option to tag a party member out in exchange for somebody out of the reserve or some kind of reinforcement mechanic either. Reserve characters can't provide off-field support as well. I maintain that this kind of game would only benefit from being able to field bigger parties, or, better yet, the whole party at the same time.
I also disagree with limiting times at which you can save your game - it is very easy to get locked into a half an hour or longer of tough combat to go through without any opportunity to quit the game without losing progress in between. Seems like a bit of a hassle and artificial difficulty that is completely unnecessary.
UI seems a bit bare at a first glance, but is surprisingly functional in terms of what information is available at a glance or one click away. Some things could've been done better, but it is a solid job as is regardless.
Music and sound effects don't irritate me, but they also don't stand out in my memory. Some songs sound pleasant to my ear, some leave me indifferent; overall my biggest complaint for the soundtrack is the lack of tracks - the basic combat theme is used for almost all fights, for example.
VA work varies from okay to excellent. I think that in some cases the voice director dropped the ball; a couple of actors seem to struggle with staying in their assigned roles too much to allow for much range on their part, but otherwise I feel that it adds to rather than detracts from the experience, as all properly done voiceovers should.
The story doesn't stand out to me as particularly engaging. It is one of those cases where the burden of success hinges more on characters and delivery in general than in the underlying plot, setting, themes and all that jazz. I feel the writing of said characters is good enough to do it in this game though.
The narrative is generally humorous through and through, starting from loading screen messages and all the way down to tooltip popups. It is not an easy task to make a game consistently fun throughout its entirety, much less funny. I believe Regalia manages to accomplish just that though. You may or may not find the particular brand of tongue-in-cheek humour jell well with you, but the project lead and the writing team should be commended for a job well done on this front, in my opinion.
Overall impression: worse than I hoped but better than I feared. I found this a surprinsgly enjoyable experience even if lacking in several areas (base management in particular feels vestigial). I would recommend it if the gameplay footage looks like something that might interest you.

All the pieces are there for this to be a very enjoyable game. The story is interesting and has enough references and humor to satisfy anyone looking for a laugh. Unfortunately; the execution of the combat system and the difficulty ruins the entire experience. There are only two difficulty levels: way too easy and way too hard. Especially considering there is no way to level up or really get stronger outside of story battles.  At least unless you want to spend hours upon hours fishing to make money. And that is a significant problem. I don't want to play on the easy setting as I enjoy some challenge; but I am unwilling to spend a full day fishing in order to make enough money to upgrade my equipment to the point where the fights are possibly winnable.
Basically the combat system and difficulty of fights combined with a lack of options to advance in other paths ruined this game and that is a shame because it is otherwise a game I would recommend to anyone looking for a tactical rpg. I can't even recommend this to people who enjoy stupidly hard combat games because it's not a fair difficuty level. The enemies have better stats, better abilities and better passive traits than your party and there is no method of healing in combat, The shielding system has a significant problem in that it is effectively unavailable at the early stages of the game due to a lack of characters which can generate them, particularly in regards to shielding other characters in any meaningful amounts, Out of the first seven characters there is only one which can reliably generate shields on anoter character and that is only 20% of the target characters maximmm and is limited to line of sight, which deserves it's own section on how much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that is. Contrast this with enemies who gain 10% of their maximum shields when hit with any damage, can instantly generate 50% of their maximum shields while removing all negative status effects (though I believe it does come at the cost of two minor status effects that are applied for two turns incluuding the turn it was  applied during) or generate 100% of maximum shields and deal 70% of maximum health to any enemy who is too close to them when they end their turn.  All three of those enemies are in the regular dungeons and hit as hard if not harder than my units while having similar hit points and a numerical advantage in every single fight. Hell; they even have larger movement ranges than my units so kiting isn't even an option. Which I would like an explanation on why a dwarf gets 50%+ physical resistance and a spear which can hit two squares yet can move as far or farther than any of my units. They suffer from initiative but that isn't as important as it doesn't allow me more turns, I just get to move before them which is less important when compared to the other factors.
Regarding line of sight issues. There are way too many objects which block it and the rules that govern it are ridiculous. Basically if you are not in a straight line in one of the four cardinal directions with nothing between you and the target you will not be able to attack that target. Even typical rules regarding LoS are not applicable here. If someone is standing in front of a doorway there is no way to attack anyone except that unit. No angles allowing attack to another unit, which is a serious problem when many of the enemies have abilities which don't require LoS but almost every singe abiity available to the player requires it. You can use your limited perk slots to help with that in a very small number of cases; but out of the first seven characters the number of non LoS abilites that are available even with perk slots can be counted on one hand. Your own allies both block LoS and block friendly movement so if one of your characters gets stunned in a bad place you literally cannot help them in any way shape or form until they either wake up or die.
Which brings us to death in the game. You can take a maximum of 6 units out with you and deploy 4 of them in  a battle. If they die in a battle they are unavailable for any other battles until you rest at one of the very limited number of rest spots or finish the dungeon. I don't mind this at all as at the point I got to as there were always enough rest areas to handle the situation. The individual fights on the other hand were the problem.
The fishing system is fine for small stretches but as it is button mashing it gets very tedious after a fairly short time. It being the only method of generating resources outside of combat makes it an obstacle to overcome rather than a diversion or something to supplement the combat, If I ever play the game again I will be looking at probably two hours of fighing in order to generate the resources to craft/purchase the equipment necessary to be successful at any of the combat locations.

I'm going to be honest, I pirated this game before buying it.
Then I accidentally played this game for two days without realizing I hadn't bought it yet. I won't be giving arbitrary number values or positives/negatives, I'll just talk about my opinions of the game.
Gameplay
------------------
I didn't know what I was expecting at first, but the combat in Regalia plays just like other tactile RPGs; you move, you perform a skill, maybe you move again. What took me a little getting used to is the lack of a standard attack. In Regalia, there is no regular stab or slash, instead characters will have a Signature Move with no cooldown that serves as their standard attack (Not all characters have an attack here). Authority Points are great. Whether it was for activating special skills or chaining attacks, it was a mechanic that I very much enjoyed, despite my stinginess with them. The combat stats are nice and simple as well, no crazy pages of minutia to pore through.
Enemies and Allies will all scale to whatever level your party is, so there's no need to individually manage your characters. Any character will be viable to use at any point in the game without grinding.
The Text Adventure portions were also fun to go through. There's nothing quite like dancing to please a crowd of drunks in text form.
The time limit situation isn't a problem at all. It requires you to complete a certain number "kingdom quests" within a certain number of in-game days, which I often completed in excess just by playing normally.
Personal Bonds
------------------
I'm a sucker for this type of stuff. And it happens to be very easy in this game so that's a plus. Leveling up your bond with a character will unlock perks, be it a skill improvement, crafting better items, or higher bond increases. Maybe I'm just a pleb but I found the characters to be likable and interesting (Max bond with everyone except the Merchant and Alchemist as of writing).
Character Customization
------------------
This is also pretty simple as well. Characters will have a number of perk slots equal to the level of the party. A nice sense of balance arises due to more powerful perks taking up more slots. So unfortunately, I can't turn Signy into an ultimate death machine, but I guess a regular death machine will suffice.
Characters will have 1 slot for a weapon and 2 slots for trinkets. Doesn't get much simpler than that, does it?
Miscellaneous
------------------
The writing is cheesy, but I love it.
The music is great, especially the boss battle music. I knew I was in a boss fight before I even read anything just by hearing the music.
The art for the characters is amazing. I can't say so much for the in-game character models, but the character portraits were very pleasing to look at.

Reading other reviews: Most complaints revolve around being supposedly pay-to-win. It's a TCG. I've seen a few cards that use a "gain between 1 to 20 health" and similar, but frankly it doesn't detract that much from the game as you're just as likely to roll crap as you are fantastic.
Start out facing the weakest AI level, build up your collection a little bit at a time. When you have collected 3 Event Tickets, start doing the Casual Draft - you keep the cards you draft, which will often include half a dozen Heroics, and are guaranteed at least 3 booster packs after you've played 4 matches with that deck. It's the fastest way to boost your collection. Don't bother buying booster packs with your earned silver, you can collect enough of those by playing, save it up for a Legendary chest.
One thing I wish would be implemented is an inbuilt chat and trade function: maybe it's already there but I haven't seen it. Cross-platform is cool too, but the game runs like♥♥♥♥♥on my tablet anyway so whatever.

The atmosphere and immersion are actually quite good and dialogue and relationships are decent (although it gets repetitve on the second playthrough). Gameplay is fun, and it took me some hours of trial and error until I found a strategy where I could juggle all the different needs without loosing any of the characters.
This is a good game. I would recommend it to players who like these gaming genres.
Conclusion: 7 out of 10.

I like this game, but somehow I feel like I spent 15 bucks for several tedious replays and frustration. Steam does not offer a grey zone, but thats where this game would fit.
Since it came out, it seems to have been re-balanced. And the "normal" mode is way to harsh and somewhat "unrealistic" or lets say "implausible". I know, its a game and such, but since its set in a half-realistic enviroment, some things really annoy me. But lets get the great things first:
The visuals are nice. The sound is charming and - thats somewhat paradox - calming. The characters are well written and differ from each other. Every single one is special. It makes a real nice first impression.
But there are so many things that will effect your gameplay in a negative way, that the game itself will become a burden. The setting is on "normal" by default. There is also an easy mode, but normal should be for normal people. But it is harsh, very harsh:
Everything will wear your team down. There are nearly no positive effects during activities. The hobby fisher gets depressed while fishing, even when has the maximum success. Everything you build is extremely expensive. While 2 good people manage to get 4 units of wood, crafting a single fire place will cost you 10. Hunting equipment, which is basically a bow is above 20. The loner will be depressed when doing activities alone. The people do not seem to sleep at night, since they are never well rested in the morning. Getting fatigue down is annoyingly harsh. Exploring the map is not fun. You will know where to find what and once you used it, its gone. In the midst of the jungle is a huge tree, you can chop it down. You cannot chop down other trees. The sunny island seems to be cold as the alpines at night, since if you sleep without a burning fire, youre a goner. Putting two people that like each other on a task will still cause depression. And if the RNG fails you, they will lose their relation to each other.
If you want to survive, you have to go exactly one way. Every one of your guys is a specialist and shall be used for his specialty. Learning new stuff is rather useless. Everything will rapidly fall apart and maintaining it gets very costly. And once you hit the downward spiral, there is no way out. Food will decay rapidly. Bob will steal plenty of your food reserve and still be hungry. He even mentions that he has a secret food stack but can still die of starvation on the first try. When an encounter with an animal appears, you can hunt it and will get a good amount of food if you succeed. But you cannot send out anyone to go hunting without having the costly equipment. So before and after this encounter, no hunting. That makes no sense. You will find a place with plenty of fish, but after fishing they seem to be extinguished. Even 10 days later, you wont find any fish there. It will just be an empty square you left behind. Found a sand castle, use it once to get depression down, but never again. There is basically sand on the entire island. Its made of sand.
Many values and abilities of the game are not explained good enough, so that you have to go by trial and error. Everything in this game is against you, which is not bad by default, but it limits your management down to an one-way level. And that is the point why I felt like 15 bucks was way too much for such a tiny, limited game. Even if it looks beautiful and has its charme, it does not feel like being worth its price.
And yes, I know there is an easy mode. But I want a challenge, that can be handled. A fair challenge. A team of specialist should be able to maintain to survive for some time without dying of depression, hating each other, starving or freezing to death. There should be a balance. Bad event - depression rises. Good event, like hunting success and plenty of food - depression sinks. Sleeping at night, fatigue gone.
Some last words: I wish the devs the best they can get for their future. I am sure, many good games will follow. I see that they tried to create something of beauty and value. But as a customer, I really did not feel like getting a fair game for a fair price.

Dead in Bermuda is a management sim with RPG elements in which you try to help a group of strangers survive in the aftermath of a plane crash on a remote island. Their survival hinges on your ability to properly utilize their skills, monitor their mental and physical well-being, and stave off any homicidal interactions.
I tend to enjoy management games and RPGs, and I was pleased to find that their marriage worked pretty well in this case. I found the management aspect to be pretty challenging at first—my first couple attempts ended with everyone dying of either hunger or sickness—but since figuring out how to survive is the point of the game, I think it was appropriately difficult and the challenge added to my overall enjoyment. I also thought that the characters were generally well done: everyone has a pretty distinct personality, and everyone’s character is revealed and developed fairly naturally using conversation around the campfire at the end of each day.
I do have a couple nitpicks with the game, however. I understand that this game was translated from another language, but despite an English proofreader being listed in the credits, there are still enough errors to merit another pass at proofreading. Pretty minor stuff, admittedly—awkward phrasing, incorrect capitalization, etc.—but still not something that should be present in a complete retail product. Another issue is the limited dialogue pool. I mentioned earlier that I thought the campfire conversation was well done, but there just isn’t enough of it. I’ve played through the game twice now, and the significant overlap in dialogue events that I saw does nothing to encourage me to play through the game a third time. Finally, the mid to late game is pretty boring. (And I’m saying this post-patch 1.1, after they apparently tried to address this.) Once your survival situation has stabilized, you end up just passing the days until you’ve explored enough of the island to end the game. I actually think that this is a symptom of having made the island too large: I bet if the devs made exploration easier (so island areas were revealed more quickly) but reduced the number of helpful areas, the game would retain its difficulty in the beginning without dragging at the end.
Despite my criticisms, I enjoyed figuring out how to help these people survive (sometimes despite themselves). I can see this game appealing to other casual management sim fans who don’t mind failing a few times while figuring out what to do.

Since I was a young child, I was crippled with an allergy to grass.
I used to spend my weekends sitting mournfully on my windowsill as my friends played out in the fields.
My mother even installed a plastic lawn around our house so I could play without fear of dying, but the experience was too false as the lawn could not simulate the true freedom of a field.
Eventually I sunk into depression and decided to commit suicide by playing in the field that my friends had invited me to all those years ago. I did not get far before my body had completely shut down from exposure. Luckily I was found and managed to reach a hospital before the exposure managed to kill me.
Upon recovery I was under 24-hour surveillance to ensure I did not go near the field again - a fact that plunged me into depression even further.
It was upon the 2nd of April, 2015 that I planned to take my life again where, by luck, I noticed the release of "Grass Simulator" on Steam. Fearful it would not match my preconceptions of grass, I bought and installed the game.
Grass Simulator provided me a rich and beautiful simulation of how playing in the fields was to my friends and, I daresay, saved my life. So I thank the creator of this game. You have saved my life, but think of how many others you have saved, who have not spoken up.
Thank you.

Lifeless Planet is an odd little beastie, ill-suited to the industrial production line of today's gaming world. Of course, this is what makes it all the more endearing. The premise is instantly appealing and the ability to just wander this strange, seemingly lifeless world and its mysteries is fun. It's always linear, but the open spaces (compared to your little astronaut chappie) are vast, and rarely do you feel funnelled. Maxed out, it's also rather pretty, with a neat DOF effect and the only decent film grain I've ever seen in a game. The most exciting weapon you find is an extendable arm - woo-hoo, I hear you cry - but LP is a game that reminds you of the simple joys of the gaming days of yore, such that every opportunity to use said arm, brought a little cheer to my heart. Oh mechanical arm (thought I), how I long to reward you for your reachy-button-pressing and green-rock-thing-lifting by taking you back to earth in place of my missing wife. It also has a functional jetpack, which is 5/10 straight out of the box.
Overall, while some may find this a little empty, dwell on the title and you may realise your error. It looks nice, has great sound design, solid controls, great variety of areas and a story which reveals itself over 3-4 hours as you explore firsthand and discover the relics on the planet, rather than being battered by hours of cut scenes and terrible dialogue. It's something of a cross between Dear Esther, LucasArts' The Dig and classic 2D platformer Another World. LP may not be very challenging, but it has charm and immersion, and you really feel for the lonely little astronaut chappie. Is he the first to visit this world? Is the planet really lifeless and, if not, do you get a refund? Is his story real or just lovesick hallucination? And if you have a jetpack, who cares? 7/10

Incredible.  This game is excellent.  Immersive, emotional, and surprising.  The gameplay is simple and engaging.  The story is compelling, but also sparse and not intrusive.  There is plenty of empty space, as there should be in a game where you are a lone astronaut on a desolate planet.
I found the puzzles to be the perfect amount of challenging.  I got stuck a few times, but never reached an infuriating level of frustration.  I felt a true sense of reward upon figuring something out.
Lifeless Planet is a very linear game.  I actually found this to be quite refreshing.  Compared to today's sandbox, procedural, open-ended games, this one stands tall in its assertiveness.  Even though there is usually only one way to go in this game, I never felt limited.
The atmosphere is breathtaking.  So immersive.  Tense and frightening at times.
If you're interested in an innovative and interesting science fiction aesthetic & story in an engaging, non-violent game, you must buy Lifeless Planet.  We need more games like this.

Oh man Turok was the first M rated game I ever played as a kid. I had no idea what the game was about, what my objective was, or why everything wanted to eat me. Playing this remaster was a major nostalgia trip for me, and it was interesting to see how much of the game I had not yet explored as a kid. As far as the game itself goes it is a very high octane shooter with a pretty large selection of weapons. Your mission to mission goals are exclusively centered on gathering keys to unlock the next level, and perhaps a piece of the game's penultimate weapon. When compared to its sequel, Turok Dinosaur Hunter really isn't all that special; it is definitely a relic of its time. Having said that, for those of you who may have played bits and pieces way back when, I would recommend traveling back in time with this game. It was extremely satisfying to see this journey come to an end 16 years after I first played it. If nothing else, that was worth it for me. For newcomers however, I would suggest you skip directly to the sequel and then contemplate picking this game up. The storylines are only connected through the brief description of Turok 2's store page, so you won't be missing anything. You will also have an objectively better experience, with better hit detection, fleshed out music, mission based objectives, more powerful weapons, and the ability to save where you please

Do you want to fight evil monsters and world-threatening horrors with a Vampire Hairdresser, a Pirate King Elf, an Arabian Pyromaniac, and a Half-Naked Amazon Lady?
Do you want a rich, deep RPG full of story, charm, and world-building that is incredibly colourful, lighthearted, and funny, while still managing to be serious?
Would you like your gameplay to be full of humour, bordering on the ridiculous with deadly, adorable kittens that shoot lasers and sprout wings, to the meta, with the main currency Dilac being "DLC" for short, and the hilarious exploits of a manly blacksmith with a pink apron and an adorable pug in a tutu?
Then take a look at Regalia: Of Men and Monarchs.
There's so many things I can talk about with this game, but I'm not a comprehensive reviewer, so I'll just go with the part that resonated with me the most:
The Characters.
I love that this game has the Personal Bond system, where you, as Kay, the monarch of the kingdom, hang out with, bond, and get close to your subjects in purely platonic relationships. No romance to be found here, just befriending folks, earning their trust and learning their deep, dark secrets, and ultimately helping them achieve their goals in life, while also getting perks and abilities to help you in the combat.
Among my favourites of this system are:
Baz and Lillka, the co-owners of the Placeholder Inn. What might at first seem like a giant who only speaks in grunts and his hyperactive preteen daughter actually turns out to be

Valen, the Pirate King Elf (and I should mention, Elves are Blue-Skinned Vikings here and I love them) talks about himself in the third person, is boisterous, loud, and proud, but underneath it all he
along with being universally loved by his crew, and being a nice guy, all in all.
(The figurehead you help build for his ship is also just majestic. I wish I had taken a picture of it.)
Then there is my first favourite, Signy, a wild woman who goes around headbutting moose, suplexing wolves, and petting kittens in her search for her totem animal, will rip and tear her enemies with vicious claw attacks, and speaks almost exclusively in really obscure nature koans with a sexy, growly voice, along with being hot as hell.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Regalia: Of Men and Monarchs is a new console-style RPG from indie developers, Pixelated Milk.
In Regalia, you play Kay, the only heir to House Loren and the long-ago-defeated city of Ascalia that is your legacy. On your father's deathbed he tells you of your heritage, and you venture forth with your two sisters and your bodyguard to restore Ascalia. (No, I'm not sure why your sisters aren't considered heirs either. I suppose it's a heavily patriarchal society.)
Finding Ascalia in ruins and inhabited only by an ancestral ghost, you quickly run into a powerful debt collector, who tells you that the city also has an astoundingly large debt owing. He makes a deal, though, and allows you time to rebuild the city and the kingdom to greatness ... as long as you meet the regular payments.
Graphics - A mix of hand-painted 2D backgrounds overlaid with 3D models for obstacles and characters. The backgrounds are nice, though completely static, and the 3D models look good when still. The mix of the two is not that great, however, with the characters often looking like actors on a green-screen background from a low-budget TV show.
Where the graphics really shine, though, is in the 3D animations, which are really rather nice. Some characters appear to have different walking styles, from a swagger to a bit of a wiggle, or even a beast-like gait. Attack and ability animations, too, are well done, though there's not enough variation in them. I'd like to see some more fancy special effects, particularly for the magical abilities. And most of the animations, lovely though they look, are a bit too slow for the action.
There are no in-game graphics settings, but there's a basic low/medium/high detail setting and resolution available through the launcher.
Sound - Sound effects are good and there's a full musical score, which often fades into the background. Both are appropriate for this grand fantasy style of game.
Cut scenes are fully voiced, but the voice-acting quality is extremely variable. Griffith, the bodyguard, is not bad, and the same goes for some of the other characters. But the narrator at the start, and Kay and one sister, in particular, are gratingly bad.
Gameplay - Regalia plays like a traditional JRPG, but with a more 'European feel' and some extra gameplay elements thrown in.
The game starts with a lengthy tutorial that introduces you to the setting and characters, as well as the interface and basic concepts. There are two modes of play: real-time, used for accessing the various kingdom management features; and turn-based, used in combat. So far I seem to have spent slightly more time in combat than in kingdom management, but the proportions are more equal than I had initially expected.
Your kingdom begins with a castle, an inn, a town square, and a pier. Initially you can't do anything at any of the locations except talk to the characters that happen to be in the area -- which you can predict based on the personal calendar feature -- but you'll soon meet a merchant from whom you can purchase goods, and unlock the ability to develop and improve the locations, as you meet the characters that will populate them.
In your castle you can access the diplomacy menu, for developing relationships with the four factions, as well as the world map and your family tree. Unlike traditional console RPGs, the world map itself is unexplorable; you don't wander about, running into random encounters. Instead, you select the world map and see the available 'dungeons' in the surrounding area. You can then elect to travel to one that you've unlocked and explore it with your chosen party. Exploring a dungeon involves progressing through a connected graph of up to three different node types: combat (duh), adventure (plot development, with choices), and camp nodes (develop character relationships and save game).
Once the tutorial is complete and the game begins properly, you're given bimonthly periods to meet the various demands of the money lender, or it's game over. These demands typically take the form of completing a certain number of kingdom quests, such as building or upgrading some buildings, completing dungeons, or developing your friendships. The order you fulfil these objectives is up to you, as long as you've completed enough of them by the end of the period. The demands can also include story quests, which help to move the plot along.
Saving is only allowed in certain areas, which seems to me like an artificial way of increasing the game difficulty; I found it frustrating. The debt collector's time limit, too, I found a bit annoying, as I like to explore, but at least that has a valid plot-based explanation for it. I can't imagine going back to replay the game with a different focus, though; I would have preferred to be able to do it all in one play through.
Like the rest of the game, character progression is a blend of styles. You earn experience points from completing quests and battles. When your party levels up you gain perk slots for each character, to which you can assign abilities. Kay's abilities are unlocked through play, but his companions' gain abilities by developing Kay's relationships with them, which sometimes requires other actions as well.
The writing quality is excellent for a modern indie game, though I have seen a few errors. It's unfortunate that the script itself is not that great, containing too many modern contrivances, and coming close to breaking the Fourth Wall. This is no doubt supposed to be funny, but mostly comes across as a bit weak.
Though I'm far from finishing the game, I believe it runs for one year of game time, based on the Achievements. There's a lot to do, which is fantastic, but once you get started it all starts to feel like a chore. Though the combat engine itself seems good, it quickly becomes grindy. I'm also not convinced that the basic characteristics are applied as simply as the tooltips imply.
Pros:
+ There's a lot to do!
+ Character animation is excellent
+ Good range of characters
+ Few grammar errors
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- Some voice acting is atrocious
- Inappropriate script in some places
- Fairly 'grindy' once you get into it
- Loading screens get a bit tiring
Regalia: Of Men and Monarchs is a good console-style RPG with some novel features and likeable characters. But it's let down a little by the script and the voice acting, and it feels like more of a chore to play than it really should.

Omerta - City of Gangsters is a strategic simulation that puts you in the shoes of a small-time mafia don running a very small outfit during the height of Prohibition. The game is reminiscent of Gangsters 2 and Gangland, utilizing similar economic and battle mechanics, but lacking some of the depth and scope of the older games.
The gameplay is divided amongst "levels," neighborhoods of a city in which a specific mission must be accomplished to continue to the next. Most of the missions are relatively straightforward and do not require a great deal of strategy to accomplish. The battle mechanics are also somewhat clunky and unrealistic, and is by far the most challenging aspect of the game due to the limitations. When the mission is completed, the level ends abruptly without an option to continue building your empire in that neighborhood.
Sandbox mode offers more of a challenge, allowing you to set the police coverage to high and offering rival gangs that can quickly move in on your territory, take over your businesses, and attack your "hideout." The neighborhoods are rather small, however, and really restrict the scope this game could have.
Despite the problems, however, this is the best organized crime strategy game that has hit the market since Gangland was released in 2004. It has been enjoyable for hours and I recommend purchasing it on sale.

Was it worthy of the hype? If only we could rate episodic games per episode, instead of the whole thing. Broken Sword V definitely requires that. It was a great return to form with the first episode. Everything a player of the series could ask for - a punchy start, immediately eye-catching and beautiful surroundings, good voice-acting et cetera. By all means, Episode 1 was all I could expect from the Broken Sword. Episode 2, on the other hand...
By and large, Broken Sword series work on a rather simple formula. The story is built upon an ancient artifact, lost in ancient times. It is sought after an antagonist, George and Nico are inadvertently drawn into the conspiracy et voila! This formula has worked for so long and was remarkable in the first two games, the Shadow of the Templars and the Smoking Mirror. Even the forced 3D layout of the third game, the Sleeping Dragon, was actually not bad at all.
The main issue about the Serpent's Curse is that its episodic structure was a bit tacked-on. Most episodic games feature choice and consequence - your choices carry across the narrative and the episodic structure allows a cliffhanger, leaving you in suspense regarding how your choices changed the story. But Broken Sword has, and has always had, a linear structure. There's only one way to skin a cat here, so what's the purpose of the two-episode release? One could argue that the studio would be able to gauge reactions with the first episode and act accordingly, but this is not a new title - it's probably one of the oldest adventure game series out there with a dedicated following.
I would have interpreted all these as a nod and a continuity to the series itself but when you go through them after a very long time (the time between E1 and E2 was quite, quite long), it feels a bit bland.
However, the game is now a whole piece with no interjections or cliffhangers so current experience will be quite different. Fan-teasing features as well as returning characters (and that damned goat) from earlier games also help giving a feeling of continuation overall. It's one of those classic, old school point-and-click games that is lucky and fortunate to garner so much attention. It's by no means "bad" enough not to be bought, but it's not a game-changing, mind-blowing blockbuster either.

The game is playable and reasonably entertaining from a basic playability standpoint; but deck building is an exercise in needless frustration and there are massive issues with competitive online play that doom SolForge to meet an early grave. I won't waste time describing the same issues others already have:
Instead, I'm going to focus on a single point that has grown to end any chance of the game being playable for any incoming player. At this stage, there's no realistic way to compete with players that have been around for months because their decks are loaded with the rarist cards in the game (legendary and heroic). Catching up at this stage would require an investment of several hundred, or even thousands of dollars.
I've played dozens of people, to the point that I see certain names often enough that I know their decks and what to expect; and every card in their deck is wildly more powerful than almost every card I've been able to get in more than a month of play. At this point, I'm pretty sure the only people still active in the game are long-term players. The few new players come in briefly, see how much of a mess it is, and promptly leave.
It's a complete waste of time to invest in this game, even if the balance issues are worked out, the cheating/trolling is curtailed, and more players join. Save yourself the hassle and find something else to do with your time.

The good:
There is pretty deep strategy to this game that isn't immediately obvious from the first couple of plays. It has some neat mechanics that I haven't seen in any other CCG.  I have 700+ hours on record, so it cant be that bad, or can it?
The bad:
ITS SLOWWWW: About that 700 hours.  A  lot of that time was spent playing other games or working while waiting on a slow opponent to take their turn.  Games take too long and players are slow. The only game mode is a 20 minute timer on both sides. Many players rage AFK when losing making you wait for 15 minutes to collect your win.  Many other players play so slowly they take their whole 20 minutes. This is really frustrating to me, as I rarely use more than 5 minutes of my time.
NOT FTP FRIENDLY: Decks are 30 cards, and most top tier decks use 9 legendaries or more. That makes it very difficult for FTP players to be competitive. Spend money or you will be locked out of competitive constructed games.
POWER CREEP: Power creep seems to be a real issue.  Every set has a couple of godawful broken cards that are then nerfed later on (after the paying player base got a chance to abuse them, of course).
NO MARKET: There is no public market for cards, instead there is a trade system. Its okay, but a market would be much preferable. As it is now cards have little value.
COPY_PASTA: Copy-pasta meta.  I have played CCGs quite a bit, never have I seen a meta so dominated by builds that are blatant copies of winning decks. It makes things really dull.
SWINGY:  Recently the game has become much more swingy due to uber powerful cards and combos. By this I mean you may be 10 turns into a game, have your opponent locked down at every turn, ahead on life, ahead on board position, then suddenly you lose. Its pretty frustrating.
I dont enjoy the game anymore.  I liked it the first hundred hours or so,  now I just play it due to inertia.

Reviwing Creeper World 3: Arc Eternal.
Note: This is just my own opinion on the game, and I am but a regular gamer and not a professional games designer or critic of any sort. It is up to the reader to decide whether the statements found in this review is favorable or otherwise.
Introduction:
Creeper World 3: Arc Eternal is a RTS strategy game whose role of the player is to stop a corrupted fluid-like army from invading the galaxy. You command an army of automated buildings that shoot lots of stuff in order to prevent the fluid from spreading and destroying your base. These buildings are your bread and butter to fend off and destroy the fluid emmiters and win the game.
Pros:
1. The gameplay and its mechanics are really in-depth, and in each situation comes with a new strategy towards the game. Fend off even terrain with fast-firing cannons and low-land areas with strong long-ranged mortars, moving your base across space with, as well as weakening the enemy with ships and AC bombs. The campaign is designed for the players to explore each of these mechanics, as well as taking advantage of them in order to gain an advantage over the enemy.
2. There are tens of thousands of maps to play, both from the original official maps and custom-made maps from the workshop. Each map brings a different situation for the player to deal with. Besides that, creating a custom map is relatively simple and does not require any advanced form of coding or game designing knowledge.
3. The player is given a great amount of flexibility with various amounts of structures for them to build and control the game with, each being unique in their own way while complementing others.
4. The game kept me playing for longer than I've expected. Despite it being repetitive after some time, it was still pretty fun to play. An affordable game for a reasonable price.
5. When playing on a larger scale, the animations look kinda cool. It's always fun to watch your beloved "minions" go fight it out and do stuff.
Cons:
1. The soundtrack is too limited, repetitive and lacks randomization. I can memorize all of the battle songs after a few hours of play time.
2. The graphics are a little basic and simple, but this is not a big deal as the gameplay is much more significant in this situation.
3. The game acts sort of like a math question without much penalty Once you reach a stage where your buildings are self-sufficient in defending against the enemy, you can just sit back and don't do anything. From this point onwards, it will just be clearing out what's left of the enemy army, slowly but surely. Not much of a challenge up to that point.
4. To be honest, I was not very intrigued by the story, and I found myself skipping the storyline after playing the first few missions of the campaign. The method of presentation was tedious and boring.
Possible Improvements:
1. Ambience in the game would be nice. The songs do not have to be in a consecutive loop without end all of the time. Just play another song in a-minute-or-two intervals, something like Minecraft or Starcraft. That way, the player would appreciate the songs even more, and it brings a more exciting atmosphere into the game.
2. The presentation of story would easily be more attractive by using methods such as vocalized dialogs, pop-out characters, cutscenes (if budgetable) and subtitles.
3. The GUI and graphics could be improved.
Conclusion:
Creeper World 3: Art Eternal is a must-buy game for those who love tower defense and puzzle games. With an affordable price, the game is a pretty good choice in comparison to the more expsensive AAA games in the market. If not, the mechanics is something that makes the game worth exploring and trying out.
I would give this a 7.5/10.

The first time I heard the name was with Just Cause 2. "The game seems to be good" I told myself. In a discount, I bought both games (Just Cause and Just Cause 2). To be fair, I must say that I expected to play only Just Cause 2, not the 1. Since I like to play games in order, I tried to play the first.
At first, the graphics didn't looked like something really impressive. They aren't. In none moment I was impressed by the graphics. The first mission appeared to be "simple" and not very interesting. The game, literally, throws you into action and you should shoot to the bad guys. Nothing really impressive. I wasn't expecting a big game during my first 10 minutes.
I was wrong.
The game implements some interesting game mechanics. The gameplay is good, and the story... well... the story is interesting (cliche after cliche, but that isn't bad). The main "storyline" is fun to play.
I first played throughout the main missions. There aren't many missions, so, you can pass the main missions in some hours, but, I think, not in a single try. Some missions are really easy. "Go and destroy this". If you get an helicopter with missiles, some missions are completed in a couple of minutes, or less. Other missions (in special, the final 4 or 5 missions) will require you to try various times, since is almos a deal that you will die. A lot. So, the main missions are ok, they are fun and, by the nature in the game, you keep wondering "In which other ways can I complete this mission?". The main missions, I think, have good replay value.
The game has various extra components, like liberation missions. These missions are intended to remove the power of the government over some small places. At first, these missions are ok, but, as long as you keep liberating more and more zones, they start to feel a little bit repetitive. I stopped liberating zones since I get bored (since they are repetitive) and I get stressed because of a spawning problem in the game. When liberating a zone, reinforcements keep coming, and some are spawned riding a car. The problem is that sometimes they are spawned right behind you (if you are in the middle of the streets) and advancing, so, they can kill you without warning if you are in the middle of the streets, and dying means failing the liberation. If you don't mind that problem, and doesn't get bored so easily, then these missions are ok.
Other side missions are about recovering "hidden" elements (they are perfectly marked in your map). This is interesting, but, also, after a while, I got bored of flying from here to there in an helicopter to fetch these things. If you enjoy a lot flying over the islands, these things are for you.
The side missions in the liberated zones are ok, but within some minutes, they will start to repeat themselves, so, you can't expect a lot from these ("Go kill these people", "Go destroy this", "Go and retrieve this", etc, you got the idea).
So, these are my results of playing with the game:
Good:
- Really cheese story.
- Funny ending (so exagerated that made me laugh).
- A big open world.
- Lots of things to do.
Bad:
- Liberation missions are a little bit of repetitive.
- Side missions in liberated zones are repetitive.
- You can die very easily due to apparent bugs (like cars spawing behind you).
So, I can recommend this game? Yes. The game is better than what I really expected. I can't compare it to Just Cause 2 since I have not played it yet, but is a game that can be re-played various times and you can finish the game doing various things.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of the Strategy/Survival Simulator Dead in Bermuda. Dead in Bermuda was brought to us by Developer CCCP and Publisher Plug In Digital and was released on August 27, 2015.
(NOTE: This was a review from a game in my own Steam library, it was NOT provided by the Developer and/or Publisher)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
Nice, easy to learn management simulator focusing on survival. Solid game.
4/5 and worth the dough. Try the Demo for sure.
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
Dead in Bermuda is a management sim, at it's heart. Tasks, time, resources, making sure the right people are doing the right things, etc. It is a full-on management simulator, with the goal being survival. 8 survivors have survived a plane crashed and are stuck together on an island. You must manage them daily, and nightly, in order to survive. Your survivors will level up as they complete tasks, allowing you to raise their stats in areas and making them better at certain things. Some people are better at some things, others are better at other things. You have to kind of fiddle around with it to maximize your efficiency. Otherwise, for example, you could be Scavenging for days and yielding little-to-no rewards. There is a learning and crafting system woven into the game, and their is also a pretty entertaining story among the survivors and the island itself that you are exploring. This game plays out MUCH better than your typical management simulator. The story is good, the interactions are great, the ar is of good quality. All in all we've got ourselves a solid, fun, challenging game here. Don't let this one pass you by, I almost did. 4/5 and worth the dough all the way. Try the Demo, available right there on the Steam page, for free. You'd be crazy NOT to!

Started playing this on a Friday night and basically didn't stop until Saturday night. This game has a "just one more turn" factor like Civilization. You play a group of 8 people who have crashed on a desert island. While doing the normal resource management stuff - finding food, crafting things, gathering materials - you explore the island and run into mysterious beings who mention a prophecy that can get you off the island. The goal is to find out more and fulfill this prophecy before you all starve to death, get sick, or kill each other. The encounters while you explore the island are quite amusing.
The game is really attractive with a nice, clean interface. It's not overly complex once you get the hang of it, and it does save your progress each day, so you can go back and try again if everyone dies. A big part of the game is levelling up your characters - there are 16 different skills that all impact some element of the game in some way.
There's not a ton of incentive to replay, as it seems that very little of the game is randomized aside from where exactly everything is located and a few character interactions. I had a lot of fun with it though. Recommended for those looking for a good survival/resource management game that doesn't take itself too seriously.

I was torn whether to thumbs up or thumbs down this game.  If you judge it according to other indie horror games, this is most definitely a thumbs up.  If you play a lot of those, this game is for you.  If you judge it according to AAA or simply bigger studio non-indie horror games, this is mostly a thumbs down.
Ultimately, to be fair, you have to look at its content for what it is and what it was trying to do and whether or not it succeeded.   The answer is:  sorta.  Not really.
The production value is pretty decent.  The sound fits right in and the whole game is creepy as hell.  The atmosphere is done right - in the beginning.
About a third of the way through the game you meet the second kind of "specimen", and..... that's it.  That's all there is.  There's a one-time encounter with a third that isn't hard to deal with, and you can SEE a fourth later on, but there are no real interactions with it, and it shows up only once.  The problem with this is that once you realize this is all you're getting, the tension is pretty much gone.  The primary two types of specimens in the game are rather badly animated, but again - would you rather compare this to other indie horror games, or ones from bigger studios?
The writing starts off okay and descends to a kind of "eh" throughout.  There are film slides and written paper logs for you to read to fill out the rest of the incident in your mind, but very little of it actually matters.  You won't care about any of the characters, and many events feel tacked-on.  There's a HUGE lack of payoff for the end.
I fell through the floor twice in the game, and I'm sure it would have been more often if I hadn't avoided certain spots, both related to ventilation shafts.  Invisible walls abound.  Collision detection is rather poor, not only from monsters but movement in general, and it definitely killed me on parkour parts more than once.  Sometimes you can see through wall edges to other rooms.  This lack of polish really breaks the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the immersion every time it rears its indie head.
The game often appears to be non-linear, but it isn't.  Many, many rooms and hallways exist simply as dead ends with nothing in them.  There are really no items, just fuses to open doors, and metallic fragments that I apparently never got enough of to find out what they do.  There were so many pointless areas and doors that were unopenable that it felt as though the devs intended to add a whole lot more, and just never got around to it.
And then there's the length - five hours?  Really?
If the game goes on sale for around five bucks, it's worth a play, no matter who you are or what scale of horror games you prefer.   But ten dollars?  No, absolutely not unless you are a hardcore fan of indie horror.  If the game had been longer, had more depth, more mechanics, more specimens, more craftsmanship, I would have been all over this thing, but it's just too short and mediocre in its overall impact.

Quadrant is an episodic first person horror game made by a very small team. Unlike many other horror games on the market, it doesn't rely on jumpscares and cash from screaming YouTube kids, instead it focuses on the adventure itself, story and atmosphere. It was supposed to be a 5-episode deal, but then the whole story was cut to just three episodes (the price has been lowered as well).
When I started to play it, the game reminded me a lot of the first F.E.A.R. game, by the Episode 2 it already was like Half-Life 1. Speaking of which, if you played They Hunger mod for Half-Life 1, this game and that mod has lots of things in common.
The graphics are like in the first Half-Life (low-poly models, primitive animations, old looking effects), but with the modern shaders and higher resolution textures (physics based shaders of Unity 5). The latter make the game look great and blood stains, for example, look REAL.
Also, coherent style in everything all the way through the game. I never felt like some texture was out of place or had a lower resolution than the others (maybe there were such ones, but I didn't spot them and they weren't obvious), the same goes for models and sounds.
It may be all low-poly and old-looking, but the game is pleasant to look at, which is much more important and certainly better than games with super-fancy shaders and effects thrown in without any thought.
The game has weapons and combat system, but the weapons were completely useless for me and I couldn't kill a single enemy with them, always running away. You have a delay for attack animation and enemies kill you with just 1-2 hits. It doesn't matter if you run forward and back while attacking, their attacks will still reach you. Combat system is useless for big enemies and only OK for killing those alien things on the walls which shoot with some goo or something. So run, run and run.
You can also break the walls with a pipe, but as you could guess, these are very specific walls which you need to destroy to proceed further in the game. Still, it looks cool.
I enjoyed playing Episode 1 and Episode 2, but forced myself to go through Episode 3. The last episode was pretty weak (aside from environments, they were great, as usual), just walking in the pure darkness with barely anything happening. Which would be OK, but these new action “trial and error” sequences made it worse. You need to learn every turn just to make it in time and total darkness and many enemies running after you don't help at all.
Also, those “jump down the cornices in the vent” parts get really old by the end of the game, they were used too much, in my opinion.
But the game definitely has some surprises under its sleeve.
When I met the first spider, I was somewhat hoping it'll glitch in its way so it'd be easier to deal with while I was running around, but then it just started to throw tables around, going right at me. When I first met the creature which senses your movement, it was pretty terrifying to walk around it. And there are many other memorable moments like these ones.
The pace is about right and the game is never boring to play (even the last episode).
Quadrant has controller support and it works great. However, there are action parts in the game which I highly doubt you'd be able to complete with the controller. Right stick sensitivity is set to low, which is good (in my opinion), but in the fast action parts the sensitivity makes it impossible to turn as quickly as you need. Just be prepared to switch between controller and mouse+keyboard.
There were some bugs (like falling through the map, objects without physics colliders, a bug with animation of the doctor) and many slowdowns (especially in the Episode 2), but overall it's a well-polished product.
It's a very low-budget game (the developer said it was “zero budget”), but it's a low-budget game done right and there was a lot of care put into it. It's an interesting, quality old school horror, which you don't want to drop until you complete it.
It's three episodes now and Episode 3 is not as good as the 1 and 2, but for 10$ it's completely worth it (just the very first episode alone is worth 7$, in my opinion).

Massive Chalice is very, very close to being an excellent game. Meaning it isn't, but it's nonetheless a fun twist on an old shtick. The pitch - turn-based combat married to kingdom management in service of fighting a generations-long war against monstrous invaders - is dynamite, and it marries the tactical and strategic layers together better than any other game I've seen. If there's a "but", it's the game's small budget, which shines through pretty noticeably at the nation level. It's not
so much as it's
, so for all of Massive Chalice's strengths, it's a much better fit for Fire Emblem or XCOM fans than those of Civilization or Crusader Kings.
The 300 year timeline immediately sets Massive Chalice apart from your average turn-based strategy, and the best bits are those that reflect it most strongly. Character permadeath isn't new, but zooming out to such a long timeframe makes it an inevitability rather than a fail-state. That gradual, unstoppable changing of the guard ends up being the game's biggest strength, since it ensures that your tactical team's composition is constantly changing. Marriages you make in the kingdom produce different unit types, and you'll also be juggling units' genetic and personality traits, plus the kingdom's greater needs and the particular enemy types being battled. It's dynamic in a way that no other tactical game is. Also praiseworthy are the enemy types. While there aren't many, each functions fundamentally differently, and most are threatening not just for the damage they deal to your heroes, but to the threat they represent to your long-term plans.
The strategy layer itself is where things fray, unfortunately. The hold-out-until-battles structure is lifted almost wholecloth from XCOM - despite it being unquestionably XCOM's weakest element - and while the addition of dynasty management, legendary weapons, and random events add some spice, the overall experience is frustratingly static. Also not helping matters is the lack of attachment to your heroes, houses, and kingdoms. Watching 300 years drain from the hourglass was always going to distance you from the individual people you're ruling over, but it doesn't feel like you're missing those day-to-day details so much as it feels like they simply don't exist.
And ultimately, that's Massive Chalice in a nutshell. The core systems are all there and range from fine to perfect, but it doesn't have the bits of polish that would make it an instant classic. It's very much worth a playthrough, but will not be the kind of game you'll sink thousands of hours into.

Slow and shallow.  I believe those two adjectives best describe this game. Which is really sad, since it has a lot of charming elements, but even with all that charm, it can't overcome its pacing and lack of content.
Massive Chalice is made up of two parts. The combat is turn base squad game, where you move your squad of 5 (usually) through a map in order to kill everything. The other part is a meta game where you build structure, research, arrange marriages, and deal with random text adventure events.  Sadly, both these parts end up feeling slow and shallow.
Combat feels dull due to the fact that every mission's objective is nothing more than to kill all the enemies on the map.  This is fun the first few times, but it quickly loses it charm, and ends up feeling like a loose collection of skirmish maps stringed together.
The meta game on the other hand feels unbearably slow.  The premise of the game is that you have to hold out for 300 years in order to charge up a super weapon to win. And at first I found this interesting, but that quickly changed, and in the end, I felt like I was on a super long defend the npc while he opens a door really, really slowly mission.
In the end, this game made me sad. Mainly due to the fact that I want to like this game, but ended up hating it instead. I like double fine (the company that made this game), a lot of their older games are great. However, I don't think the same about most of their newer ones, and that makes me kind of sad.
*Note, i didn't finish this game, got about 75 years in before i couldn't take it anymore. So there always the chance that the latter half of the game is amazing, but even if it is, I don't want to have to play through the start of the game to get to it*

Game Review:
I have not completed the game and will update this review upon completion (May take a while). The game is a FPS game originally released in 1997 for the Nintende 64. You play as a Turok, who has to go through 8 levels and collect 3-4 keyes per level and a piece of the Chronospetre. The Chronospetre is needed to defeat an evil alien called the Campaigner. I have only played level 1-3. I have collected everything for level 1 and level 2 but I still need to get a key in level 3. The keys are hidden fairly well in this levels and in two levels I didn't find all the keys. If you don't find all the keyes, you have to replay the level to find the keys. The Chronoseptre parts are usually found in secret areas. The guns I got so far are fun to use, although not super creative. There is a bow (with explosive tipped arrows and regular arrows), a pistol, a assault rifle, a shotgun and automatic shotgun (both with explosive shots) and finally a plasma rifle. The enemies are varied and interesting. I have encountered mercs, raptors, natives with melee weapons and blow darts, grenade throwing mercs, monkey like things (Aliens or dinosaurs, not sure what) and bugs. The game is really fun so far and I haven't encountered any problems I had with it. (Some people may be bothered by the replaying of levels to find keys)
Remaster Technical Review:
This remaster is really good. I never played the N64 version of the game, but I did look at gameplay videos to get a sense of the graphical improvements in the remaster. The fog has been reduced, giving the game a much bigger draw distance. There have been various effects added and the game is playable in any resolution up to 4K. The texture resolution didn't look much better, but to me its part of the games charm (being a real old school shooter). The game runs buttery smooth at 60 frames on my average pc. This is a remaster done right.

I had low expectations based on previous reviews. But I disagree with them: this game is great.
The concept is very interesting. The key is not to get too attached to your heroes. They are tools, you are an immortal planner. You can't get bogged down when they die.
And while the heroes aren't the most unique characters, there are fun stories the game generates. I still remember when two heroes I threw into a mission alone together (I was stupid) somehow managed to kill almost all of the enemies. I had a breather when I realized how close they were to surviving. But there were still enemies left, and they were basically dead. So these two heroes - the last of their bloodline - walked to their inevitable doom.
Definitely not all happiness and roses, but the concept is unusual, the enemy types are mechanically interesting and fun, and the game isn't too long (~8 hours for game 1).

This game is a real mind bender. It wants to be so much: A sim/tycoon game, a turn-based strategy game and to some extent a story-driven RPG. I just can't say that this game is not enjoyable at all, because it is, although it is over-complicated, the atmosphere and setting, the graphics, the voice acting, everything is done with great attention to details in order to immerse you into the infamous era of prohibition. The controls are rather easy to pick up (especially if you use a controller) and the first levels get you going pretty fast. The turn-based combat is probably the biggest caveat of this game. It wants to be so much like X-Com, but just ends up being a huge pain in the rear with no real tactical options as some cover is just purely ignored and you can shoot through walls. If you want deep city-building, this isn't the game for you.  What we have here mirrors the amount of depth you'd get in one of those cookie-cutter browser mmos, where you place and upgrade buildings.  Less so, each slot in your city is for a specific building and can never hold any other.

I found there to be far too many electronics based puzzles and not enough actual logical ones that required investigating or thinking, which is a shame. The main highlight is the actual game itself, the look of it is so gorgeous and rich that you will want to visit Paris in a heartbeat. Nico is not as hard-faced as she was in the Sleeping Dragon, however isn't the ultra-feminine 'tard that she was in Templars either. The good thing about this one as well is that there are countless favourite characters returning like Lady Piermont and Hector Laine so it offers more treats for dedicated fans of the series. The good thing about Broken Sword however is that you can literally jump in anywhere in the series and begin enjoying the game.
I haven't run into any bugs or anything as of yet. Well-rounded game overall and good addition to the series! 7/10.

I've been pleasantly surprised by this game. While there is a power advantage to having rarer cards, there is enough of a synergy requirement, and a large enough playerbase, to prevent it from being too annoying thus far.
The card-leveling mechanic is really engaging and refreshing. It adds progression to a CCG that isn't found elsewhere, along with another strategic layer. The small deck size (30) helps mitigate the odds of not drawing the card you want. This creats a slight negative in that deck variety is a little limited, but after 100 wins (which I reference because that's the achievement that just came up) I'm still excited to load up a match.
The tounaments are a lot of fun, and seem to be pretty accessible (~2 per week as a free player, maybe more). I got in through the Humble Bundle, which gave me 2 starter decks, and I've been pretty competitive (though I wouldn't recommend buying the packs, as the cards have been powercreeped out), winning at least half my games, though I have a lot of CCG experience. The 4 factions have distinct styles, and seem very well balanced.
The interface leaves a LOT to be desired, but it gets the job done. Hopefully it gets a serious makeover in the near future.

Exanima
Gameplay Time : 100+hours
After putting in some well spent time in this game I have had enough time to write a review.  Exanima is not a game you can fit into one single category.  Its adventure, action, strategy and a little on the creepy side.  At first I was frustrated because I struggled to learn how the game mechanics worked.  After spending much needed time in the Arena fighting became a lot of fun.  This game is not a button smasher and does require some skill in order to survive.  Below are my thoughts, I kept well in mind that this is not a finished product.  Exanima has a mountain of potential and in my opinion the developers are on the right track.
Pros
Visually great and suspensful
Custom characterization
Combat -tricky to figure out but very rewarding
Weapon selection ranges from all different types
Variation of enemy NPCs
Cons
Poorly lit areas - even in the aren "Never Lose Your Torch"
Single player only, hopefully in the future this will change
Save Points, after level 3 there are no more
No map as you explore, fortunalty players created maps to use on google..Thanks :-)
That is all I can really say as this game is in development.  I have enjoyed playing andI hope more content comes out soon.
Thanks,
Update 9-14-17
It is time to update the review after a year. There has been little to no change. The developers have even admitted they have done a poor job to communicate to the player base. There are some die hard fans of this game that continue to play. I do not recommend this game for purchase in its current state. Especially with the lack of updates and silent communication from the developersl. Maybe an update will come out at the end of the year or maybe not.  Who knows.

This game is one of these titles that are good, but just not good enough..
Simplifying my experience and trying to be short:
-A very nice setting, the nature design and the size of the map are nice for a 2006 game of the genre. Note huge, but not small either.
-Pretty nice graphics texture and color wise, the sea and the jungle were very beautiful and offered a great tone during the gameplay.
-Great variety of weapons and neat explosion effects.
-Though simple but satisfying enough weather effects.
-Faction based minigames and side missions that offer some replayability (though it depends how easily bored you can get consider the whole)
-The sound quality is a buggy mess. You can keep hearing shouts "freeze citizen!" and "alto alto! this nis the police!" even if you are like alone in the freakin woods, hell you even hear them when you are driving a plane 10 miles above ground. You also get to hear vehicle sounds that are unnaturally far away from you.
-Too many helicopters flying around. I mean seriously, TOO MANY.
-Grappling hook only works on moving vehicles. For some reason anything esle is pure glass surface (thankfully this was fixed in Just Cause 2)
-Cheesy characters with stupid lines, hard to feel any urge to connect with them. Even the main hero is so out of interest.
-Physics that are not good at all.. You can't have rock hard car suspensions and airplanes that fly like pieces of woodsticks when games like GTA San Andreas have already been out there setting the example.
-A main story that's not interesting at all.
recommended?
Not really sure.
If you are a fan of the genre and you like trying old games, juicing out ideas and gain opinion on some things, its not a bad title to play.
In any other case I can't recommend this game. I doupt it's even worth buying even if its cheap as hell right now. There's so many other titles out there that can offer you a far better experience and you get nothing to lose story-wise about the franchise since Just Cause 2 stands alone on that matter.

Summary:
Assume the role of the flamboyant Rico Rodriguez – an undercover CIA operative specializing in regime change - as he tries to overthrow the corrupt government of San Esperito. This rogue South American island is suspected of stockpiling WMDs and it’s your job to negate the threat to world peace. It could be to your advantage that this tropical paradise is about to implode as various factions vie for power – it just needs a gentle nudge in the right direction. Just Cause offers the freedom to tackle your assignment however you want: play the island’s factions off against one another; incite a rebellion among the masses; or build alliances with rebel forces and drug cartels. The game world consists of 1,225 sq. miles of mountains, jungles, beaches, cities and villages which can be explored by land, sea and air. And you will have at your disposal a varied and exciting array of vehicles, planes and watercraft.
7/10.

Dead in Bermuda is, all things considered, a noble effort and a successful survival simulator. It displays an almost insane degree of granularity and focus on fine details, which micromanaging players will probably enjoy. Its failings lie within its own ambitions: to be more emotional and personal rather methodical and mechanical and even in that I would not say it completely fails rather than falls a bit short.
PROS
- Beautifully drawn graphics
- Very complex stat system
- Some replay value due to random events
CONS
- Characters lack expressivity
- Music and graphics fail to match the tone
- Eventually becomes repetitive
Full Review here:

Dead In Bermuda is filled with clever and novel ideas. It manages to pull off the survive-on-a-mysterious-island thing impressively and in a most atmospheric way. Very addictive, very well presented, very interesting and filled with lovely little moments too.

is an 2D indie survival strategy game with an excellent look and entertaining gameplay.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.
Eight survivors have landed on a desert island and have to use their best skills to survive. You have to take care of they fatigue, depression, injuries and other stats. You have to last as long as possible with as many characters you can save until maybe, one day, the rescue ship comes by and picks your people out.
Yes, yes, and yes. I'm not a big fan of survival games, but this one definitely hits the right spot. The atmosphere is great, the gameplay simple yet challenging and, last but not least, the way all of the characters behave. You have to take care of each one of them and it takes a great deal of skill and persistence to help them survive.
If you're a fan of survival games, this should be an insta-buy for you. If you're not, you should still consider this.

Dead In Bermuda is a survival management game with some rudimentary RPG elements. The premise of this game is very simple - a plane has crashed, with only eight survivors and your goal is to survive and escape the mysterious island.
Each survivors characteristics are predetermined. In other cases, lack of customization can be viewed as a flaw, but these characters are designed excellently. There is your typical big brawny Russian guy Yuri, the middle aged couple whose strengths are cooking and fishing and of course the guy who goes completely nuts and so on.
Gameplay is very straightforward. Every day is split up into three turns: sunrise, sunset and nighttime. In first two you manage resources like wood, water, food etc. by scavenging, gathering and exploring. You can also research and craft new constructions, which will help you to gather resources more efficiently. Besides various resources, you also manage survivors health like sickness and injuries, hunger, depression and more. If one of the statuses hits 100, the survivor is dead. In nighttime your survivors will have conversations, which will change their opinion about each other, increase or decrease their depression accordingly.
The simplicity of the gameplay can be mistaken for its low difficulty or others even say that this game is casual, but I strongly disagree. It’s not casual but rather laid back, because it’s turn based and doesn’t have any action in its classical sense. Also in my first playthrough I found it quite difficult, but on the second one, yes, it was very easy. (On replayability I will touch upon later)
Story. By exploring you meet other people (?) who are also stranded on the island. By having conversations and doing tasks for them you unravel the mystery and by completing the last “mission” the truth is reviled and you escape the island (or do you?).
The story is captivating but very predictable and quite shallow and reminds me of the TV show Lost. After meeting the first two NPCs I already understood what they are and what the island is all about and the endings plot twist wasn’t “twisty” at all. But I am more of a gameplay person rather than story one (at least in these kind of games), so it really didn’t take away from my enjoyment of the game.
Aesthetic. In my opinion, the game looks sooooo pretty, because I very much like this cartoony, hand drawn look, but that’s very subjective matter. The one thing I can criticize is the music. The background music is very monotonous, you get sick of it in five minutes, and because there is no voice acting, I just listened to my music, which I do very rarely while playing a video game. I think this game could be improved a lot if the dialog would be voice acted, because it is actually very well written, it’s witty, provoking, sad and even depressing at times.
Replayability.  This is the games biggest flaw, for me. If I like a geme, and I certainly liked this one, I want to replay it multiple times. BUT the game has very low or even no replay value. Because it is linear, there is one or very few optimal ways to complete it and there is only one ending. Usually games will have different endings depending on how many and which people will survive but this game has only one. After playing it for 14h and completing it twice, I have no desire to go back. If they add new content I will definitely play it again, but it seem not very likely because game feel very polished and complete.
My final verdict is that I recommend Dead In Bermuda if you like management games with superb management mechanics and don’t mind spending 15EUR on a game you will play for max 15h.

The game is turn based, with a morning and afternoon phase. You can assign your survivors to various activities around the camp, depending on which improvements you've already researched.
There is a character level system, which greatly influences your progress. Also, your characters are susceptible to death by various means (hunger, depression. injury, murder).
The game can be very punishing in the early stages, especially when you follow an inefficient strategy. On the other hand, it becomes a little too easy, once all the research is completed.
Nevertheless, it is quite balanced - and loads of fun to play. As stats, dialogues and events are sort of randomized, the replay value is not too bad, I'm on my second playthrough and still excited.
