I've been waiting for the full game to come out before doing a full playthrough and writing a review. I would have rated Chapter 1 negatively itself, in it's early stages. However, playing the full game all the way through really is the only way to experience it properly.
CONS:
I'll begin with the cons, which are as follows. The collision seems really buggy, I'm almost afraid to walk certain places for fear of falling through the floor or getting stuck, which only happened 2 or 3 times, but really it shouldn't have happened at all. The story and game design is all over the place, in the sense there's gameplay inconsistencies, where some areas you'll have puzzles that are difficult to understand, and other places you'll have platforming for no reason. Some of the creatures are creepy, some are just silly. Graphics and textures are alright for an indie game. From what I understand, this game was created by just a few people, so some of these issues are excusable.
In general, I felt hardly any dread or horror from the creatures themselves. A few exploits of the AI are that some of them you're able to just run right past and it kind of negates any horror or suspense that comes from avoiding the creatures. Combat is pretty useless, I'm not sure why it's even an option, aside from using pipes to break through to other areas.
There are a few really long cutscenes and monologue exposition. To be completely honest I tabbed out and checked my email while one of them played in the background for something like 3 or 4 minutes.
These, along with a list of other smaller things (too many flickering lights, repetative environment/empty environments etc.) are my main gripe with this game. But to be fair this is an indie game and I did expect some of these issues. The price though, maybe a little high at $13.
PROS:
Although it does have it's fair share of cons, some parts of this game are actually really well done in my opinion. The sound design for the most part is incredible, and is responsible for most of the game's horror. The sound is what made this game hard to play at night, it's actually quite scary when you don't know what to expect. The story does have some things that are a little out of place, but as you learn more and go deeper it really does come together quite well in the end and touches on some very interesting concepts. The music is incredible, I know music is subjective but I personally loved the soundtrack and I'll be buying it when it's available. Some environments actually have some really cool storytelling going on and it's worth playing through a second time to see it all. I can tell a ton of work went into creating this. It's not the next Outlast by any means, but it is an indie horror worth playing at least once.
You can tell the devs got better as they made this, you can see the environments and game design become better as you progress. Which, personally, is a good thing to me, since it ended the game at a high point for me.
Short Version:
Yeah, this game has bugs, and glitches, and some odd design and story choices at some points. Some monsters aren't that scary, it's got a lot of exposition sometimes. There's a lot of scavenging for fuses and notes, and some odd puzzles that are either too easy, or a little difficult. It's what you'd expect from an indie horror game.
But, atmosphere is incredible, and the game itself is more story-oriented than puzzle-platformer. The horror comes from the implications of the events that take place in the facility, rather than relying on cheap jumpscares (although there are a couple). Quadrant is borderline Lovecraftian, and the story really opens up at the end and provides answers to things previously unanswered earlier in the game, which I was hoping for.
Like any indie horror, it has flaws. But, when it does something well, it does it very, very well. It's a solid effort by the few devs that worked on this and completed it.

Massive Chalice puts you in command of a kingdom to watch over for 300 years.  It features turn-based combat as the core component.  It also has a kingdom building and unit management aspect to it.  The most interesting concept is the breeding system I'll go into more detail so you can see if this is worth picking up.
The core game play is centered around combat, unfortunately it is a poor execution when compared to X-Com, Fire Emblem, Heroes of Might and Magic or any other turn based game I can think of.  Very rapidly I found myself feeling bored of the bland combat system which is littered with issues.  Your ranged units also happen to be your best scouts, which means you will be moving them around ahead of your melee units often enough.  I assume you can breed some of these scoutlike qualitys later on into the melee units (didn't play enough to find out), but as a baseline it feels horrible.
There is
in the game and it's somewhat difficult to be sure weither or not your units are within line of sight with the enemy.  It leads to a gameplay style that is sluggish, wherein you are moving very slowly and eventually setting up for a turn where you can destroy all the enemies within a specific area or suffer the consequences of a nearly non-existant cover system.
The meta of the game revolves around triage, as periodically two zones within your kingdom will be attacked at which point you must choose which to defend.  If you neglect to defend an area to much, then it goes bye bye.  This is a cool concept and one of the better aspects of the game in my opinion.  A lot could have been done to make this screen more interesting, as a fair amount of your time will be spent looking at it, but in general I give it a pass.
You will have the option to develop your kingdom by building structures and finding new units, or you can research new technology and combat upgrades.  You can only choose to upgrade one thing at a time, which will take years of gametime (300 year span remember).
A big focus of the game is on breeding new units.  All of your units will have perks or problems which can effect them in a number of ways.  You can assign units to breed or to help the kingdom in other ways, but once you do they will be stuck there until death.  There are 3 basic unit types: A melee tanky unit,  A roguelike unit that can throw flasks (bombs) and a ranged hunter unit.  Crossbreeding the units will make offspring that have mixxed characteristics of both classes. It becomes a question of who should you choose to breed together.
The big issue I have with the the units is that they simply grow old and die to rapidly for you to really care about them at all.  You will only ever use a unit in battle 3-4 times.  So you tend not to give a damn about their traits and stats all that much, it's just to much to keep track of when you know they are going to be dead soon anyway.
Sadly the core game play just isn't there, if it was I would be interested in the game, but when the thing that should be the most compelling in your game is the most tedius there is a problem.  I almost wish they would have focused soley on everything you do outside of combat, then the game might be interesting... fun even.  As it stands though I can't recommend Massive Chalice, and with so many cool ideas I just wish it was executed better.

It is a single-player monopoly.
The main problem with the game isn't the poor combat or the fact that there's no point in strategically building your buildings for one purpose or another.
The core problem is that you can't lose.
There is no competition trying to compete for the same areas that you are. Imagine a strategy game in the style of Starcraft where you find a set of minerals but there's no point in rushing to build there because no one else will take it. As a matter of fact, there is no point in building bunkers or base defences either, because the only time you will get attacked it will be scripted.
Additionally the multiplayer is a joke. It only allows you to do a small number of pre-created missions. There were gangster games made over ten years ago that have higher quality than this!
The only good thing I can say about this game is that it has a good atmosphere. Worth 20 Euros? No, absolutely not.

A very fun Tactical RPG with some Resource managment, companion friendship, rebuilding a lost kingdom.

Another thing i liked in the combat was Authority point, it gives you character an extra turn of sorts, they cannot move any additional movement, but they can attack or use items. Some characters like Griffith can charge towards an enemy, this does not count towards the amount of movement he has done, and since you can move after doing an attack and not only before attacking it will make it possible to move much in a single turn and as some quests have a lot of enemies but all you need to do is to kill a single target, usually leaders or bosses of sorts this can be done to quickly position Griffith in a battle with the boss or leader, using his taunt ability to keep them occupied.
Personally i prefer to use:
Kay, his character abilities are low offensive but powerful for support.
Griffith is a decent tank, moderate dps with the option to equip a talent to make his main attack impossible to miss or get dodged. making him a very stable member of your team.
Alissa is a ranged fire mage, with a fire wall attack and a powerful summoning that can really turn the tide, her main attack is somewhat like a chainlightning in other games jumping to more opponents, in short a powerhouse in dps and her best weapons even build up Shield, which is a form of HP in this game. Making her able to survive a lot of trouble
The last spot is usually filled with Theo, great aoe and status effect attacks with amazing dps potential as he has an attack that deals more dmg depending on the various debuffs the target has, this include debuffs from other characters and items, easily dealing 2-3k damage at max level.
The only times i replace Theo is against enemies with high ice dmg resistance, and i only replace Alissa during fights with high fire resistance. I replace them with other high dps or debuff characters.

TL;DR
I can only "recommend" this game to any die-hard fans who played similar games because this one has major design flaws. I absolutely adored games like FF Tactics/ War of the Lions, Onimusha Tactics, Tactics Ogre etc which is why I had high hopes for Regalia
The flaws
a) Personal Bond system
b) timetable
c) optional mission goals
d) save mechanics
The Personal Bond can best be explained like a "friendship bar" that goes from 0% to 100%. Once you reach 100% you take the bond with that character to the next level ( 5 in total), unlocking perks (which can be used by anyone like +3% damage) and skill mutators unique to that character like -1 second cooldown on x skill or general benefits like +5% more gold.
Personal Bond is increased when you spent an ingame day with a character. Either it's a generic cutscene you can skip or it's a dialogue which you can't skip. In these dialogues you will be presented with 2 questions, each having 3 answers. Based on what you pick, the Personal Bond will increase by a certain % amount.
The characters either
- fully agree ( 3 arrows pointing upward)
- agree ( 1 arrow pointing upward)
- disagree ( 0 arrows pointing upward)
I'm not sure about the specific % values, but I think every arrow represents 20% on that Personal Bond bar. That means if you don't pick the optimal answer everytime it takes a ridiculous amount of ingame days to unlock all the stuff.
This leads to -> saving before the dialogue -> hoping you get the right answers -> if you fail, reload. And that for every character! It's insane how much time you have to spent leveling up that Personal Bond. But you can't really skip them, the benefits are either too good or simply necessary to make a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ skill decent.
b)
This game some sort of an ingame timer, after you complete the initial part of it. Each chapter you have ~50+ days to finish a certain amount of quests. The problem is that many things cost ingame time.

- Talking to a character to increase Personal Bond: 1 day
- Upgrading a building: 1 day
- Constructing a new building: 1 day
- Moving on the world map: 1 day for each station
- Fishing: 1 day
- Clearing dungeons: 6 to 9 days
c)
Optional mission goals grant you extra EXP as well as an increased chance of finding treasure. The problem here is that these goals are atrocious most of the time like fighting with 3 instead of 4 people or never missing a single hit the entire battle! Or never using a signature ( as in basic) skill. They are not challenging, they are badly designed. The difficulty they add is artificial, nothing else.
d)
You can only save in the main city or while you rest at a bonfire in a dungeon. However, you only visit that bonfire once and the whole dungeon has between 3 and 5/6 battles.
If you find yourself overpowered because you didn't level up the Personal Bond enough, you still lose all the days you invested already should you leave the dungeon.

Loveable characters, check.
Enjoyable character by character stories, check (I liked Theo the most)
Great artwork, check (Sometimes the backgrounds reminded me of Deponia style artwork, which I loved!)
GREAT voice acting, check (I didn't feel dissappointed in anyone's voices)
Excellent RPG quests, check (I thought it was intuitive to give you around 55 days to finish a few main quests, then see the story, I often found myself having 20+ days where I could just go around and spend time with the inhabitants, and I never felt like there were long streches of me doing nothing)
Enjoyable battles, check (Only once did I feel like the battle was total bs. At the beginning a battle against those tree guys where I had I think 3 characters, once they put up the petal shield and I couldn't walk without taking damage was hell. Really balanced otherwise.)
Good character dialogue when not fully voice acted, check.
I could sing its praises all day, or I could say something like "oh I wish there was more of this or that" but really, cmon, it's a 25 dollar game. It's a fantastic piece of work and really shows how much blood sweat and tears pixelated milk and the guys put into it.

Pros:
Nice big colourful battlefield where you don't have to strain your eyes reading tiny text
No mana dependence
Easy earning of ingame currency with daily logins and 3 wins
You can buy any card with your earned currency (though getting a legendary can take up to 15 days of play)
Interesting and complex card interactions
Cons:
Newbie decks are often matched up with legendary filled decks - this is probably one of the biggest reasons why new players will get discouraged and not stay with Solforge - a newbie would rather wait to be matched up with another newbie than be matched up fast with a super deck
You can only play 2 cards per turn usually, which feels too limiting and drives players inevitably towards the cards which help break that rule - 3 would provide better balance and create even more interesting interactions. Seriously only being able to play 2 cards per turn is a major drag lol. It almost makes me want the mana/resources system back so that I can get to play more than 2 cards
Screen layout and decor still feels a bit stiff and amateurish
Most of the strong decks all pack in Nekrium ('black') legendary cards - that is so obvious an imbalance that needs to be addressed and I'm very surprised they haven't yet - are they Satanic programmers or something hehe
Conclusion:
If you're a newbie, play it daily for just three wins (can be against computer) until you strengthen your card collection and you won't get frustrated. Remember you can forge any card you want with the silver you earn ingame.
The game has great potential, perhaps as much as Magic The Gathering when it first started out, and with new cards introduced regularly and speedily to compete with other card games, especially non-Nekrium legendaries, the game will be more colorful, balanced, varied and interesting. Those are imho the only ways it can genuinely catch up with MTG.

When I first picked this up a few months back for an hour or so I shrugged my shoulders and tossed it aside (foolishly) having just spent a day or two on the vastly inferior bloodrealms I felt the similiarity of the lane style one card face off style fooled me into thinking they were the same game. I was wrong and the beauty and the simplicity of this game is that the choices you make early can completely change your end game strategy.
As a CCG I will personally score this game highly because it breaks away from the Magic the Gathering formula that many recent ccgs are clutching to (Hearthstone, Hex). Though I love the game in the case of Hex, Shards of Fate, the best way I can put it is that they made some very basic and simple modifactions to MTG mechanics and cards and tweaked it to take advantage of digitial playing field. To be honest its nearly a blatant copy and some will hate on that but Hex took a great concept and made it better. Given that MTG has failed miserably and shamefully to be able to do the same with their own product I will just quitely applaud that the product is there to enjoy. I will however stand up and applaud louder when someone strikes out into some different territory and manages to make a few decisions (usually only two or three per turn) evolve into a complex web of moves and counter moves. There's alot here to love and I am ashamed I missed out on it the first go round.
There are some weak points I will touch on but I would like to point out that there seems to be alot of hate in this review sections for this game that are centered around the "pay-to-win" aspect of this game. EVERY colletible card game has some element of this (Scrolls comes close but you can still get an advantage by tossing in some extra coin) and If your passing this one by because of all the hate you see in the forums or on the internet you are making a mistake. I paid absolutely nothing into this one for the few weeks and acquired a MASSIVE collection of cards to play with. There is plenty of fun to be had here without paying a dime.
The worst thing far and away about this game is the User interface which I have found to be awkward and counterintutitive. There are achievments that can not be found anywhere in game which is a bit odd to me. The collection screen where you make decks is frustrating to say the least. This is a real shame because all the accessibility bonus the core mechanics offer to draw new people to the genres is lost pretty quickly when you can not figure out what is what after the brief tutorial.
Overall Solforge offers something great from a mechanics standpoint and the f2p factor gives it a big boost for me (don't believe the hate).
Recommended if your a fan of TCG's and want something a bit outside the box.

Unless you're a diehard Broken Sword fan, I can't honestly recommend this game. The plot is uninspired, the characters are paper thin, and the puzzles are inconsistent.
Somewhat a retread of the first game's story, George and Nico find themselves once again embroiled in a cold-blooded murder which drags them into a world full of ancient religious sects. Instead of the shadowy Templars of the original game, this time George confronts the Cathar heretics of the Middle Ages, but perhaps because it feels so similar to the first, it's just not very exciting. It's compounded by the fact that the game was originally released as two episodes, so the pace of the story is uneven. Furthermore, every character except George and Nico was irritantingly two-dimensional, to the point where I was skipping dialogue because their lines and personalities were so boring.
What makes or breaks a good adventure game though are its puzzles, and it's here where Broken Sword 5 feels undercooked. Some of the puzzles are brilliantly designed, and it's normally the ones that are integral to the main story (there's one involving an ancient object you have to translate from an ancient script, and despite spending an hour on it, it felt genuinely thrilling to solve). Others, however, were so obtuse and lacking logic that you know it was simply done to pad the game out (anything involving goats, for example).
I did end up finishing it because I'm a Broken Sword fan, but I do not have the urge to play it again like the original game, which is a classic.
Not recommended unless you've played the rest of the series and simply want more.

Lifeless Planet certainly sold me on a unique premise.  An American Astronaut lands on a planet 30 light years from earth, only to discover that not only did the Soviet beat them there, but that they've all mysteriously disappeared...
And so begins what is probably the best 'Walking Simulator' I've played in the last three years, and all the usual suspects of the genre are here; diary entries, simple puzzles, no enemies, and most importantly, an atmosphere so thick and intoxicating that it just makes the games many flaws all that more tragic.  The majority of the games 'walking' involves linear pathways with simplistic jumping challenges and the occasional 'put the battery in the battery slot' puzzle, while gravity and vegetation serve as the games biggest threats.  It's certainly more involved than the other mascots of the genre, like Gone Home and Dear Ester.
The graphics in particular deserve attention.  Specifically, they're terrible.  Even while playing on the highest graphical settings it felt like I was playing a game from the middle of the PS2 era.  Hope you like your worlds full of terrain morphing, because that's what you're getting, texture stretching on cliffs and all.  This plain geology is broken up with some simple rock models here and there, but it's no where near enough to fix how bland some environments feel.  The man-made structures are a mixed bag.  The simple utilitarian houses are well modelled and fit the theme well, while the larger structures are blocky and kind of silly looking.  The character models are also horrendous, and have such a cheap, low quality appearance.
The games plot is also a bit of a mixed bag.  Earlier parts of the game sprinkle bits of character back-story on you, before deciding the to leave that arc alone until the end game.  In fact, so many plot points occur in the opening segments of the game that a lot of the middle section simply feels like filler.  On the other hand, this 'quiet' gives the game, and the player, a chance to take in the scenery, and with a full play through lasting three and a half hours, it's not that big a deal.
Even with the visual and story pacing issues, I found Lifeless Planet to be a generally pleasurable experience.  It's aura of mystery and discovery kept me interested enough to see it to the end.  That said, it's a bit steep at $20, so you're better off waiting for a sale or bundle deal.

It's going to be hard to articulate what I really want to say about this but here goes.
I found this game via the discovery queue and saw from the images that it looked simillar to Diablo, Grim Dawn, Titan Quest type games, I was wrong. It is in as much as it's top down and you kill an enemy, proceed to loot it and get better equiptment/items needed to proceed. The thing that puts this FAR apart from those games is how much

The combat is a fairly steep curb, sure it takes getting used to, sure it can seem counter-intuative. It isn't though, I promise. Within a couple of hours of practice (Which is provided in-game) you will have enough skill to get further and feel like you're getting somewhere. The beauty is, complicated combat mechanics means that there is so much you can practice and attempt to increase damage output. Spin your character with the momentum of your weapon? More Damage. Aim your weapon to collide with the enemies head? More damage. Get to close and collide early? Less damage. This basically translates to you getting even more engrossed as you try to up your game.
I mentioned combat first as that is a staple for this title, it seems to be the most fleshed out aspect of this game and it is done incredibly well, I strongly advise you watch videos about it to see if it interests you, then perhaps trial the game to see how you get on.

Dead in Bermuda is a game about a crashed plane on an island in the Bermuda triangle. The 8 survivors from the crash must find a way to rally themselves, survive, and eventually escape the island. Sounds simple enough, doesn't it? Well, it is not!
As I usually do in my reviews, let's take a look at the good and the bad about this game.
The GOOD:
1. The artwork is very thematic, the models are great and the locations that you will visit are unique.
2. The characters in the game (the 8 survivors) aren't just names in a spreadsheet - every single one of them has a story, a personality, a pattern of behaviour and/or an agenda that they will follow throughout the whole adventure.
3. The interactions between the survivors are very interesting to follow and read. It is a story of friendship, intrigues, stupid remarks, psychotic outbreaks and a lot of heart, all in one neat package. The interactions also vary, based on what kind of state the adventure and the person is, which is a very welcome design decision.
4. Every character has a skillset that is randomly determined at the start of the game, without deviating too far from their personality.
5. The is an RPG progression in the game, which is comparable to that of The Elder Scrolls franchise - the more you do a certain activity, the better you get at it. However, you also get a number of skill points to distribute based on the Intelligence of the survivors, which can lead to various "builds".
6. The survivors also gain various character traits based on what is happening during their adventure. They can be either positive or negative and you have no control over them.
7. It is very easy to relate to one or more of the survivors, which forms a deep connection between them and the player. You will love and hate some of them, or all of them.
8. A good challenge - the game is very challenging, especially until you manage to get a good survival system up and running. Once you do, there are still factors that can ruin your adventure, which I find extremely important. This lets the game transcend the simple point and click adventure.
9. A nice base to look at, which changes depending on the time of day.
10. A fool-proof system - you get a warning about pretty much anything that could result in a game over, which is a very welcome addition to the game.
11. You need to make a number of very, very hard choices, from who gets which meal to who gets to live or die.
12. Good value for the money - it will take you at least 10 hours to get used to the game and win,  and even more of you want to have a second go at it and unlock all the achievements.
Now let's take a look at the BAD, or the things I found lacking or I didn't enjoy in the game.
1. The game has a very steep learning curve which may irritate you on a number of occasions.
2. The story is... passable. It's not the best out there but it's not the worst. I could tell you more, but I don't want to let any spoilers out.
3. Luck plays a huge factor in this game. While better skills result in better percentages to succeed, the almighty RNGesus might still make you look like a fool - for example by failing a 99% chance to succeed roll.
4. You have no control over the traits your survivors gain, meaning you can sometimes end up with a guy who gets easily sick, hungry, and tired at the same time, which is not a pretty sight to endure.
5. The English in the game is sometimes a bit wonky, misrepresenting a fact or two in the game.
6. If you are a sensitive person, you will not like the fact that you might sometimes have to send someone to their death or see them perish because you were forced to choose one survivor over the other.
7. The base, while looking pretty, seems quite outstretched, making you move the screen left and right a lot. While the devs made a few recent changes to remedy the situation, it is still a slight annoyance.
8. It seems that there is a problem with some achievements - while I am not an achievement hunter, it might irritate some players. The devs are hard at work to fix them, though.
9. The replayability - only the map layout, the starting skills, the traits that you will gain during your adventure and the character interactions based on the state the adventure currently is will change the way the game plays. Everything else stays the same.
The conclusion:
I am going to give this game a careful recommendation. The beautiful artwork, the interesting character interactions, the exploration factor and the rpg-like elements are a strong selling point to this game. I have felt a very strong connection to every single sirvivor and felt compelled to do my best to keep him/her alive throughout the adventure. Learning more about them, their past, and their agenda is extremely satisfying and keeps you either entertained, or on edge throughout the game. The game is only hindered by its mediocre main story, the replayability factor and the steep learning curve. While it can easily reel any type of gamer in, it can also irritate you the hell off and force you to shelve the game. It is up to you to decide if the positives outweigh the negatives.
I, personally, had a very good bit of fun with it.

Explanation:

The mid-point of the game hits a plateau and then the last few hours of the game crash and burn in a boring downhill slog. By the time I had uncovered half of the island everyone's statuses were well under control. By the time the game was over I had over a hundred dried meals, plenty of fresh ones, and probably like four or five of those fire crystal things because I never ended up needing them again.
That's not to say the game is easy. I restarted twice while I was learning the ropes and that actually made me happy. I thought this was going to be more along the lines of "This War of Mine." The translations and dialogue are really very poorly done. This game probably should've been released as a beta first because it definitely feels unpolished and unfinished. The ending was highly disappointing especially because I was really intrigued by the mystery surrounding this island.
I could probably go on, but I'll refrain from listing all of my complaints here. Suffice to say that if the game gets cleaned up and rebalanced then I'll probably change my recommendation. For now, however, you're probably better off spending your money elsewhere.

Just finished the game. It was a long ride, but totally worth it.
A lot of people compare this game to XCOM. There are some shared principles, but you should not see it as an alternative to XCOM, because Massive Chalice is different im many aspects.
What really makes this game shine is Double Fine's humour. The enemies, the items, the stories, the heroes have some nice touches that are weird in a good way. There is just nothing more awesome than the warm and fuzzy feeling that you get when a Wrinkler hits one of your wünderpants-wearing heroes.
The management of your kingdom does not require you to do a lot of planning (at least not in normal mode). What could really be improved is the management of heroes, because you will have a hard time remembering them all. It makes sense to use a paper notebook to keep track of your plans of your heroes. One very central problem of the game is that it's much harder to get attached to your heroes than in XCOM, because your heroes can simply die of old age. The relic system tries to compensate for that, but it could be more epic. I still got attached to some of my heroes during my playthrough, but it was much later in the game. But once the attachment is there, it's just awesome to kick♥♥♥♥♥on the battlefield with your favorite heroes.
The battles start rather easy, but get a lot tougher in the course of the game. The artificial intelligence is not that clever, but if you don't pay attention, it will still eleminate your heroes with unpleasant efficiency. There were many situations where I really thought that I was screwed but with some thinking and planning I could usually find a way out of the situation. And that was just awesome.
But even if you fail during battles and lose some or all of your heroes, the game still gives you plenty of chances to recover. It's certainly not too easy (imho) and you can still play on hard mode with iron mode if you like a challenge.
In a nutshell, you should get this game if you like
- getting out of sticky situations
- weird humour
- Combining traits, items and seeing how things synergize.
- Round-based battles with lots of positioning and special abilities
You should not get this game if
- You are impatient (A battle takes around 30-60 minutes)
- You want a really complex game
- You want a deep story

Like XCOM, this is a game about fog-of-war-focused tactical combat with a greater strategy layer above it, best played in Ironman Mode. XCOM is better, but this game is still worth experiencing.
Rather than being about cover management, the tactical combat part is about trying to kill enemies before they ever get a chance to attack you, where the enemies are dumb as bricks. So, sometimes entertaining, and sometimes rather unimpressive, and on the whole a bit less great.
The strategy layer is a closer match though; it's got the same level of researchyness, with the additional hero breeding mechanic. I think the tactical combat's balance kind of wears down on the strategy layer though: there are many elements that make it easier to focus on upgrading and breeding only one class, but the tactical rewards for diversifying do not really make overcoming those elements worthwhile.
Oh, and the voices in this game are rather unimpressive. Every once in a long while during a battle, one or both of the chalice-people will say something useless from their rather small set of things they can say. My favorites being "Good riddance!" when an ally dies (if an enemy was killed in the crossfire), and "Ha! Following my advice paid off!" (or something like that) when nobody has said anything. There are individual Red Alert 2 units that have more lines than this game. Almost.

I wasn't expecting to enjoy MASSIVE CHALICE as much as I have done thus far. I suppose it is similar in a lot of ways to the recent X-COM games in that the game requires you to succeed at both managing a base and also managing the strategic battles, and like X-COM if you fail at either element too badly you stand a good chance of losing the game.
The "Base" component of MASSIVE CHALICE places you as the immortal leader of a small kingdom that spans several hundred years over the course of the game. You're expected to manage the continual repopulation of your roster of heroes as they die to old age through a Game Of Thrones-ey family system where you build keeps and assign lords and ladies to have lots of heroic children. These children may inherit some of the personality quirks or physical traits of their parents as well as experience points or even family heirloom weapons. This ensures that over the course of the game you can maintain a sense of growth in your hero roster as the game progresses through the family ties.
You can also spend time researching new weapons, armours and items for use in the field and the game occasionally throws up points of contention amongst the populace for you to make decisions on which will have either positive or negative effects, similar to what you may have seen in The Banner Saga.
The battles themselves present you with a variety of legitimate threats that I'd rather not spoil for you that escalate as time progresses. Enemies are interesting in that the threats they pose are often not necessarily tied in to their raw power in terms of health pools and damage they can deal. Encountering them in unexpected combinations can make for some interesting tactical puzzles and this is doubly true with the nature of your ever changing roster of heroes. You may not have a full set of tools available for you to tackle these problems with depending on how the baby-making situation goes.
I've got a fair amount of experience with games in this genre and for me this game was refreshingly different and thoroughly enjoyable.

What is "Game Corp DX"?
Game Corp DX is a game studio management simulator. It is a rather casual game, seeing that you will - at least on the normal difficulty - steadily progress until you are able to create the largest and best games - such as Half-Life 3.
The gameplay, controlled entirely by the mouse, consists of buying furniture such as training stations, worktables, etc, and hiring game developers. After you hired them, you assign them to a project, and when that project is finished, you publish it with an advertising campaign based on its size and quality (although I always chose only according to size).
In the campaign, which can also be seen as a tutorial, you have 28 tasks to fulfill. Your small studio soon grows and you can relocate to new towns where you can buy bigger studio space for more growth, and so on.
In the end you make large games which you can polish at post-production. For some achievements you must match real game titles, including Game Corp DX. Other achievements can be gotten just by playing through the campaign or after it - when you beat all tasks, you continue in an endless mode, enabling you to get whatever achievements you still need.
The entire duration of the campaign was around four and a half hours for me, but although the game is just a repetition of the same actions again and again I enjoyed most of the game. Only when the studio gets too big, it feels more like work.
All in all, Game Corp DX is a game that can be recommended for its small price, as it can be played through in one afternoon and evening, but in that time you will have quite some fun. That is, if you like this kind of games. If you don't like management games, this won't be for you.
A word to the sound: The soundtrack is okay, but there is nothing special. The sound effects are mostly typing and your actions. The graphics aren't too good - see the screenshots in the store - but they work for this game. The controls are mostly intuitive, only that you can have multiple windows and actions open, all of which overlap then, can be annoying.
Recommended: Yes

Quadrant didn't look that appealing to me at first. I could hardly hear what the characters were saying and there had been no actual jumpscares. You cannot interact with friends in any way, as soon as you go upstairs and use the outlet you never see them again.
The game is extremely atmospheric. Based in the
, in the distance you see silhouettes of many strange shaped statues, figures and occasionally flickering lights. I love that in Horrors.
Throughout the game you find fuses, audio clips, newspaper clippings, email snippets and video tapes, each one revealing more and more of the story.
Emails and letters go on about rocks arriving in the quadrant and begin showing signs of life.
one states. Progressing into the game more and more is revealed about these strange rocks, showing photographs of extraterrestrial giant spider-like creatures. Are they really rocks? Where are the spider creatures now?
It seemed like I was going through the same coridoors almost all the time. I'd find the amount of fuses required, I'd open a vent, and I'd go into an indentical coridoor. They're increasing the level design in Chapter 2, so I wish them luck on that!
The character animations are, if I may say so, awful. Our character always has his arms by his sides, when sprinting, running, or hitting a giant spider with a fire extinguisher. What was the point in the fire extinguisher, by the way? I hit the spider several times, I seen blood but it never died...
Quadrant really made me jump. It made me sit on the edge of my seat and it sent shivers down my spine. Not many horrors have done that to me.
I await Chapter 2! With increased level design, some minor bug fixes and some sound-effect splicing this could be one of my favourite horrors.
Based on Chapter 1, I give this game a 7.5/10.
Not all about the jumpscares, Quadrant delivers a fine share of every aspect that horror games should require. With edge-of-your-seat intensity, this game will seriously send shivers down your spine.

Just recently bought and tried out chapter 1 to its fullest. Not much else since its only the first episode and I have heard others are on the way so this review will only be judged on the first episode.
This review will change as more episode are released overtime.
Pros:
Solid Horror atmosphere
Some good tension here and there
Solid attempt from Indie-developers
Sound Design is spot on.
Cons:
Character Animation is terribly done (Do stuff while staring at your shadow, you'll see what i mean)
Level Design repeats itself a lot (Felt like i was walking through the same corridors and offices for 75% of the game)
Questionable objective markers (*Walks Outside, must get to roof for whatever reason?*)
Some Bugs (Was stuck in crouch mode and was unable to stand for a while at the keycard part)
STORY & ATMOSPHERE:
Starting this game up, I was somewhat intrigued with the beginning aspects of the game but it really shows its limitations which will be discussed in a different section. Starting with the story, it follows a guy named John who, unexpectedly, has to work a night duty at a research center which has pushed the panic button. 2 guys and a girl (from the voices) have arrived at the research facility to investigate what's going on and its your job to get to the bottom of things. For the most part, its more just a rinse and repeat of traditional horror games. Something goes wrong ---> main character goes to investigate ---> Stuff happens ----> Main character must escape facility or find out what's really going on. Their are some other stuff horror games throw in but that's the gist of it. The game sets the atmosphere up well for the most part but towards the end, it kinda loses it after the 2nd level transition. It definitely has its scare moments but they get repetitive and dull while having some tension throughout the game but not much else. The characters, however, are completely forgettable because their is very little given about any of them. After the first 5 minutes, you basically just follow this hidden path with little context outside it. I mean, if the lady was alive, why is she unable to communicate to you through normal means? She didn't state her communication device broke or anything. She also walks around the facility just fine despite stating her leg broke and wants the player character to find them.  Towards the end of chapter 1, the horror elements become lost and confused and rely too much on cheap jumpscares. For the most part however, it's an ok starting story that sets the game up in a nice but bland way. Hopefully, we'll see some improvements come episode 2.
The Rest:
The rest of the game however, does not hold up very well at all. Graphics are meh, animations are very awkward, the layout of the levels repeat several times, some bugs here and there, and very questionable objective markers. When it comes down to it, story and atmosphere need a substance to hold it up throughout the game. Too bad its being carried in a poorly designed vehicle. First up, the animations are terribly done. Running without hands moving, holding a flashlight without it showing in the character's shadow, running up and down the ladder, and even jumping felt awkward (i think holding the jump button allows you to jump higher?). While these may be some minor things to pick on, they, nonetheless, make up the game. I also ran into some bugs such as being unable to pick up a fuse even though i had no idea why I was picking up random fuses without them serving a real purpose. The monsters didn't do much despite being spotted by them as sometimes they would follow me slowly, and sometimes they would ignore me. Not sure what was going on there, might have been a bug or something.
The level design, for the most part, was disappointing. I couldn't tell if i was really walking through a research facility, or if I was just walking through some random office building I found in the middle of the woods abandoned. Nothing in the building makes it seem like an actual research building, just some offices around with a cafeteria and some elevators. Nothing really stood out to me as being "woah... That's cool! I wonder what kind of research was going on." The only reason I remembered it was a research building was the fact I was in a hazmat suit and the beginning of the game which stated it. You mainly just go through the motions, walking through a ton of vents and following the linear path set before you. Their is very little optional exploration besides the rooms you are forced to go through.
The game does have some puzzles but they, for the most part, are too easy/too few. I think I only ran into like 2 puzzles (Elevator and solving an encrypted message). Hope to see more in episode 2 to break up this walking forward monotony. Some of the object markers, felt like they appeared too early or just didn't do anything after they were completed. I guess for the most part, your overall objective is to escape but I couldn't even tell as the game didn't bother to tell me after the first time it did, and swapped objectives. One of the objectives stated I needed to get to the roof for some reason, and then proceed to walk back inside for no apparent reason. I mean, couldn't we have technically escaped the facility at that point by just climbing a tree and jumping over the fence? Not really sure what was going on there but well, went back inside for some reason.
Short Review:
For the most part, you walk down this hidden path, some jumpscares happen, you run into the monster a couple times, and that's it. In its current state, I can't entirely recommend this game as its short, and has way too many technical issues that plague the game. I hope the developers bring more to the field than what has been shown so far since most of it has already been done in plenty of other games more effectively. I also hope they fix a lot of the technical problems holding this game back such as the character animation and interactions. If this is all this game has to offer and the following episodes just bring more story, it's gonna be hard to recommend suffering through all of its problems just for some story and a couple jumpscares.

It is hard to say, as I am torn on this one. I would give it a 6 out of 10. If it is on sale, Pick it up, it is fun. But sadly, it gets old fast. There is barely too much for replayability - in fact, after the first few levels, you start noticing there is barely too much for advancement.
First of all, I loved Mob Rules from back in the early/mid 90s. I'm also a fan of stories about the prohibition era. I don't think society would cope with prohibition now, and much less in the 20s when this took place. That is why stories are so fascinating to me. But every game about the mob during prohibition is the same, more or less, and they run dry after long.
I'll sum it up with a list of pros and cons:
Pros:
- Good story line. It isn't strong, and in fact, far from original. But it is still a good story line. It is a little unique, but nothing special. Start small, build a reputation, and become big. It even spans the full prohibition era, for the most part.
- Pretty decent city management sim. Again, nothing special here, but it is fun for a bit. There are quite a few options.
- Plenty of maps. Each one increases in options and difficulty - but again, nothing too spectacular.
- A lot of weapons and skills. Henchmen have plenty of skills to choose from, and each one can bring unique things to the table. You also have plenty of henchment to chose from based on play styles, so if you want a team of masterminds, or maybe thugs - there is room for this.
Cons:
- Every level, you start fresh. You bring a little bit from previous missions, and you get more increasing difficulties.
- Every map starts becoming the same thing - over and over again. Start small, build up without becoming too noticed by the cops. Bribe them, and keep a low profile. They become terribly easy and uncreative after long, especially when you start learning what to do.
- The learning curve isn't great enough to keep a steady interest. It is easy to learn, and easy to master. Again, once you find a good solid stratagy, every map is the same. There may be one curve ball here and there - but nothing to special.
- The game only becomes more "difficult" because people rat you out (to be expected) and because the prohibition is coming to an end, cutting into your profits (again, to be expected). No real sense of accomplishment, more a sense of "Well, I survived and made a profit early on..."
- The story can be exceptionally predictable. No real surprises, and very few curveballs to keep you on your toes. Easy to go on autopilot.
- After finding a winning stratagy, the game turns into "Send henchmen somewhere, afk for a few minutes, come back and check on profits and missions completed."
- Rival AI is.... lacking. Seriously, there is no challenge from them. They litterally let you walk all over them and don't try to stop you. You can raid their places too easily, but nothing from them to retaliate. It's like they don't care at all they are losing to you.
- Severe lack of a hard mode at all... At least, I didn't notice any difference on the difficulty settings.
Again - It is a good game, don't get me wrong. but not really a $30-40 game.... Maybe a cool $8 game on holiday/summer sale, when you want to see what the prohibition is like.

Long and short:
The Short:
Simple without being patronizing, with a good ramp, room to correct mistakes, charming style, and great little score.
Well worth the money at full price.
The long:
It has an almost Black and White feel to it with a heavier emphasis on the Sim City aspects, but not too much. Very chill and relaxed vibe but things can get hairy when ogres start showing up. There is a kind of natural ramp that gets you extending your borders in search of the resources and balancing plates for gold, stone, and wood, with some extras that build on those economies giving better buildings more of an investment weight. It’s not going to have you micromanaging exact numbers of workers for each resource and instead opts for a more general management approach that sits comfortably in that warm fuzzy area between macro and micro management.
The fact that there is still more promised and seem to be pretty regular feed updates on the Dev’s social media is also a big plus.
At 10 bucks, you can’t beat it. Hell I spent $10 on coffee this week and got far less enjoyment out of it.

- The Castle system is really well designed with the modular walls and tower parts you can add. Hopefullt this will be expanded on in the future to make this even more indepth.
- Infinite rocks and iron nodes. This seems like a small thing but having a finite amount of stone or iron sucks and this game avoids that nicely. Also doesn't require ugly quarries like Banished that leave a stain on the land even after removal.
- Almost bug free (from what I've seen). I experienced no bugs in my 12 or so hours before writing this, which is great for an early access indie title.
- The dangers and enemies are great. In a lot of these type of games the main things that end your game are passive (Starvation, Plague, etc) but the active enemies like Raiders and Dragons are a great way to spice up the game and the castle system is a great way to build up defenses like Archers, Ballistas etc to fend off these threats. Puts a nice spin on an otherwise quite passive and relaxed genre.
- Active developers that interact with users. Sadly this isn't a given in today's marketplace, but LionShield do a great job bringing out new content and listening to feedback to improve the game.
Cons:
- The worker system feels a bit underdeveloped. From what I've seen there's no way to manage which workers go where without closing down certain buildings. A way to re-assign workers from a menu WITHOUT the need to close buildings and pray that the workers do what you want them to do.
Like, I feel you should be able to assign some workers as dedicated Woodcutters (Not foresters) to cut trees you assigned to be cut. And to be able to move a quarry worker to a farm without needing to close the quarry.
- Small thing, but there needs to be a way to mass select stuff. You should be able to click and drag to select a big area of trees to cut etc.
- Not massively rich in features at the moment. Of course it's an early access title and I'm sure with future updates there will be more added but right now there is a small shortage of stuff to build and farm. A variety of crops and the addition of livestock as an alternative food source would be great, for example.
Overall, this game has a solid foundation to build upon on it's journey through Early Access. As a base game I'd say it's definitely worth getting if you're a fan of the genre due to it's cheap price. It's only gonna get better as more content and features get added so in my opinion it would be a good investment. Even as a base game right now it's worth the price, but as more gets added it'll only get better.

I really wanted to like this game. I was really excited because at it's core it has a lot of things I like
PROS
+ Strategy RPG: I am a huge fan of FF Tactics and Tactics Ogre
+ City/Base/Army: The City building mechanics is one I was waiting for a long time. Far too few games allows players to build themselves a base.
+ Party Level / No grinding: Basically all party members share the same level which is good because all party members all relevant and available for any content.
+Visuals: The game looks really nice. I like the art style and the painty backgrounds.
+ Character relationships: Just befriending your people. Building your relationships give you unique bonuses based on the people you are befriending. (like in Persona Series)
So I said I really wanted to like this game, but there are too many things that annoy me.
CONS:
- 20 Mins of dialogue before the game really starts...
- Story: Lazy hero learns that he is the sole heir of a prestigious family and is forced to restore the castle againsts his will.
- Protagonist has no agency: He is given quests to restore the castle by his grand-father who's ashes he drank. All his choices are who to spend time with. I long very much a game when the protagonist decides by himself what he wants to do and why, instead of being given arbitrary choices.
- Characters: Cliché characters are cliché. I just didn't find any of them likable.
- Humor: Sorry, the humor of this game doesn't reach me.
- Voice Acting: typical anime-like voice acting that usually is the reason why I watch anime in jap with subs.
-Music: If you like elevator music, buy the OST! (The battle music is good though.)
-Time limit: So you have a limited number of game days to complete a number of quests. each interraction that you do take 1 day. if you reach the limit and you failed the complete the number of quests, it's game over. I don't like it. It's just a personal preference. Also what this means is that you'll almost always want to really get the optimal outcome in each encounter otherwise you would be gimping yourself (catching up to a bad interaction will cost time, and time you don't have).
- No Grinding: and by grinding I mean, taking time to get stronger in order to complete difficult content. There are a limited number of battles in the game, and limited time to complete them. So basically, the devs have set a very specific progression of battles that you should do. And each of these battles are hard (even harder if you try the bonus objectives). So if you find some content too difficult, then tough luck... git gud or play story mode.
- The enemies scale based on your level: So basically, the only reason to level is for perks. The rest of the stats mean nothing because wherever you go, the enemies will scale.
- Character skills: right from the get go, all characters have all the skills they will use in the game. They don't seem to learn anything new. With some progression,  you will be able to modify/upgrade some of these skills. Also, skills have cooldowns, I don't like this. Again, personal preference.
- Protagonist is THE main healer: so basically there is no "healing" in the game. Your characters get shield points that allows them to prevent future damage. At the begining of the game, your main tank has 1 ability to generate shield points which is a melee aoe with 2 turns cooldown, which is bad considering it does not generate that much shield points anyway. The only other character that generates shield is you main character, who is a leader type (does not fit his personality at all IMO). He has a ranged no-cooldown spammable give ally shield ability. and there is no reason to do any other ability (except his ultimate, which gives lots of shields, and a banner that is very situational). Personally, I find it boring.
- Almost all enemies are have ranged attacks: So basically positioning your tank becomes almost useless when enemies can circle you and do ranged attacks
- Characters get unconscious after battles: If a character falls in battle (no possibility of revive during battle mind you), the character is out for the rest of the dungeon (you can revive them once in consumable camp). That means that if you fail to protect your party members early in the dungeon, it will only get harder and harder (the game is already hard as it is). That would normally not be a problem but since you can't grind, it's going to be that much harder. Again the git gud or play story mode.
- Rewards vs Failures: The rewards are ordinary, some XP and trinkets, nothing fancy. Loot is boring. Even doing the super hard battle objectives give you just a little bit of XP and a +15% chance of getting loot. But when you fail, you not only did you waste real time, but you also wasted game time, and game time is important because it's limited and it's counting down to your doom.
Save Locations: You can save anytime when you are at home. But when you leave, you can only save at camp. You'll have maybe 3-5 battles per dungeon (earlier dungeons) but only 1 save point. And it's consumable, meaning that if you save to soon, you'll have to go through many battles without saving. This is what the game would call risk management, while I just call it annoying.
- Save Scumming: because of all the mechanics in the game, you will save scum a lot. If you don't know what that means,  it's when you save at a specific point and get throught content, and if you fail (or don't get the outcome that you want, you reload and retry until satisfied.) Dungeon are the worst offenders.
Conclusion:
I'm happy I got a refund after 3 hours.

Regalia: Of Men and Monarchs is such a weird game. If you go in expecting a light RPG with some funny moments you're certainly in for a treat.
Combining everything from diplomacy and castle building, to exploring different areas, developing personal relationships for perks and bonuses, and even fishing, I was quite amazed by how well they actually fit together and give life to this little gem. Granted, most game mechanics are very simple at their core, but as a whole it really does shine.
The story, characters and their interactions are hillarious, the actors doing an amazing job, the graphics are colorful, but what really makes it impressive is the combat. Including line of sight, buffs, debuffs, friendly fire, quite a lot of characters with a nice assortment of skills and perks, troops placement, and different types of main objectives for battles, the combat in Regalia proves to be quite difficult and well thought out.
The main issues with Regalia is that it is a race against time, and its slow pace, meaning it's not a game that everyone will enjoy, but those that are just fine with spending a lot more time reading and listening to the conversations than fighting will have a blast with it. Not to mention it includes Text Adventures. That's right, TEXT ADVENTURES! Like in the last millenium, but so satisfying.
Even at this price point, Regalia is very easy to recommend to those searching for a turn-based RPG that's a bit different. Offering around or more than 30 hours of gameplay, depending if you're trying to 100% it, certainly tips the scales in its favor. Plus, it has a teen vampire that "vants to suck your blood". That, or become a hair stylist...

I'm just gonna say it, this game is amazing.
I love tactical rpgs anyway, so this game is right up my alley, and I've been following the dev team since PAX, so I may be a bit biased in that regard. That said, there are several reasons why this game is worth buying at its price point.
The gameplay: gameplay is tight, feels fairly balanced from what I've seen of it, which, arguably, isn't much yet. Quest and overworld system is really refreshing and unique, and I really enjoy the battle/dungeon style the game offers, as well as the exploration and character interaction in the town and while camping.
The characters: the characters are lovable, quirky, unique, and feel very real. The character interaction and dialogue is really really well done, and I found myself getting through the gameplay to get to more narrative, which is telling in this kind of game's experience. (Note: the gameplay isn't bad at all, I just really enjoy the narrative + character building.)
Enjoyability: I really enjoy the game, as can be seen from the favorable review. It just feels like a really tight tactical rpg with interesting mechanics that I haven't seen in a lot of the genre.
Cons: These things said, the game isn't perfect. There are a few bugs I've encountered, which is to be expected on days 1 and 2 of release. This said, none of the games have really impacted my experience outside of minor annoyances here and there. There are also a few QoL changes that could be made that would make a difference. Not being able to leave from the town menu (having to enter the castle and click the globe to leave) is a bit annoying and largely unnecessary in my opinion. Movement in battle is also a bit off at times, which isn't a huge deal due to the ability to cancel movement (provided you haven't done or taken damage) but can at times be frustrating.
Overall: Excellent game and worth 25 dollars for sure. Gameplay is intriguing and solid, overworld is unique, and the characters and story are top notch and are worth the lion's share of the dosh you'll be paying for this game. Honestly, even if you removed the gameplay, I'd still enjoy the game for just the dialogue and characters.

I was one of the kickstarter backers, and thank god this one turned out great. There is a lack of strat-rpgs these days and this not only provides the expected combat experience from strat-rpgs, but it also pushes the genre a bit further by mixing in features from games like Persona and Suikoden where you have your own castle and need to upgrade it and find new party members out there etc.
Overall in a world devoid of this genre I cannot recommend it enough, the dialogue and characters are fun and the combat is not as simple as other strat-rpgs where you just bumble through attacking most of the time and occasionally healing. There is no heal mechanism here, but there is a damage mitigation system and every character has their own unique movesets which lend themselves to different approaches of combat.
One other thing to note is that this was a kickstarter that delivered as promised, I have backed a number of other strat-rpg kickstarters and they are either cancelled, silent, or no where near completion, so this was a welcome release and I hope to see more from these guys!
== Update ==
I am seeing a ton of bad reviews which mainly complain about the bond and date system, which I can appreciate may not be for everyone but is a game mechanic used in highly regarded games like Persona, so it may be slightly simpler but the concept itself is fine.
One other thing to think about is that the date deadline is also a game design mechanic to give you some goal of what to achieve, I appreciate some people may want to do a skyrim and just go off exploring everywhere which would be fun too, but I assume you end up exploring most of the world throughout the main story anyway, so I dont see any of these negative points as negatives, I dont know how it can offend anyone really, its more like The Banner Saga than FFT but that is fine too.
Ultimately if you liked The Banner Saga and you like Persona or other JRPG games you will probably like this.

Don't bother.
Just Cause is an open-world action game with a lot of self-humor and 90s style cheesiness. "Cool guys don't look back at explosions" atmosphere. That's fine and fun, not every game needs to be dead serious, and this one doesn't shy away from its craziness. The writing is cliche, the music is light-hearted and the action is over the top. Well, in theory at least.
You have boats, planes, helicopters, tanks, motorcycles, even an attack jet by the end. Rico, the agent you play, is always equipped with a parachute, for those instances where you feel like jumping off a cliff for kicks and giggles, and early on in the game you receive the franchise's signature grappling hook. You remember in Ace Ventura 2 when he spies on the jeep while gliding in the air? That. Only here you can do it to boats and aircrafts as well, jumping from one to the other and hijacking them. It sounds good, but the execution is clunky, which is a shame, because it could really change navigation in open-world games. Gun fights aren't anything remarkable, either, and you might rightfully wonder, "Well, what's left?" Not much. Not enough.
The world is huge, but boring. It's all one sort of landscape without any variation - islands with lush forests, and that's about it, with the occasional city here and there. I had no incentive at all to explore, let alone to do the side quests. Everything outside the main storyline (and I use the word 'story' here very lightly) is absolute filler content. Grab 5 pieces of this gun, bring us this stolen car. Really, you have better things to do with your time.
You have small Liberation missions, which are some hectic fun at first.  See, the map is separated into regions\islands, and at the beginning of the game they're all under the control of the regime you're trying to overthrow. These Liberation side-missions are where you join the rebels in attacking a settlement, an army base, a city, and conquering it. It's not complicated - it's just you with a bunch of endlessly respawning allies rushing to raise hell among the lines of endlessly respawning enemies, until you either capture the flag, or kill the boss. I enjoyed it, at first, for the chaos. But all these liberation missions accomplish is just opening up more filler side quests for you to undertake. I can't be bothered, so after liberating a few towns, I stuck to the main missions and finished the game in less than 10 hours. And that's despite the frustrating checkpoints.
Seriously, what is the purpose of limiting my saves in a huge, open world game? I don't get it.
By all accounts, Just Cause 2 is a much better game. The action is improved, the grappling hook is improved, the vehicles are improved, the map is improved. Heck, you have support for wide screens. If you want some mindless, mayhem-wreaking fun, skip this game and go straight to its sequel. You're not missing out on anything, and you certainly don't need to play the first to understand the second. These aren't story focused games.
This island must have a high procreation rate to make it possible for me to mow down thousands upon thousands of enemies.
Just Cause will win over many viewers who are fans of open world simulation games and for the fans, it's another colorful burst of manic fun.

Having just uninstalled the game after 70 hours of playtime the reason can be summed up to a single word "greed". Now as a gamer one has to think what is the value I am getting for my money. When I compare the value I have gotten for my money from current master of digital CCG's Hearthstone one has to conclude that Solforge is a ripoff in comparison.
There are a few reasons for this lack of value:
A) The rewards for tournaments are weak for example one has to win all matches to get enough game's F2P currency of silver to play another.
B)The rewards for playing the game are at most an insult i.e. you will get 100 silver per win and less than 10k for dailies and you need 60k(casual) or 140k(competative) to enter a draft so you do the math.
C)So as the prices of everything are beyond reach of F2P currency one has to spend a lot of money in order to actually play the game and then feel bad as you will probably lose at the tournament and get nothing for you money.
Now obviously as I spent over 70 hours on the game I actually liked the game mechanics, but come to realize that I like roller coaster rides as well but doing them daily is just not economically viable. So back to Hearthstone wherein I am happy to spend some money as I don't feel rippedoff at the end of it all.

The latest (not the last, I heard they're working on a new BS) chapter of this saga comes back with a classic yet renewed style!
After the questionable 3d and keyboard input experiments with the 3rd and 4th chapters, this 5th chapter presents itself in a classic aspect, the way we used to know Broken Sword as in its most appreciated chapters (1st and 2nd). 2d characters (actually 3d, but then exported in 2d) on 2d beatifully drawn ambiences.
As usual the story starts very quickly: George and Nico meet up by chance for work reasons at an art gallery in Paris and they both witness the homicide of the gallery owner and the theft of a particular painting, which is the core of this story as the entire adventure revolves around it. Obviously this time the purpose will be to find the killer, who's behind him and what is the story behind that particular painting.
The spirit of the game is back at its origin, we'll see new characters but also old acquaintances (a special mention for the Goat), the game can be played with just the mouse again and the interface is very intuitive.
We'll be visiting many locations and almost all of them are well realized, with details, or great sceneries or good old humour (special mention for Pugs), which is always present in George's speech.
Dialogues are always important, they reveal informations and even though they're not always essential they give shape to characters (special mention for the "gardener" with Nico).
Riddles sometimes can be hard to understand or solve (special mention for the "sancuary" and the dark cave) but there's nothing that can be impossible if you try to understand all the elements around you and try with logic and George's logic, according to the situation.
The story is very pleasant to follow, a thrilling starting point, hideous characters, old acquaintances, many plot twists and revelations, everything with a touch of classic humour in the right points.
To make it short this chapter is another one of my favourites among the frist two chapters. Good job Revolution, I can't wait for the next chapter!

I originally purchased this game a long time ago, with the intention of saving it as backup for a rainy day.
When I buy games I will normally get a main title that I am really interested in for $60.00, as well as a couple other cheaper games that I am not really interested in, just so I can try them out.
Based on the trailers, I thought Starbound would be a cheap 2D Minecraft clone that I could probably get 2 or 3 hours enjoyment from before getting bored of it.
Two weeks ago I finally got round to installing Starbound, and was pleasantly surprised by how good it was. I am now thoroughly hooked, with a good 200 hours of play on record, and I still feel like I have only seen about half of what the game has to offer.
I was expecting the game to be a cheap 2D Minecraft clone, but instead I was presented with a highly addictive and original game that is a lot of fun to play, specially with a friend.
The game has all the elements that makes a 2D platformer fun, as well as an easy to understand crafting and building system, and much more.
You can explore space in your ship, complete the main story line, take part in side quests, build a base, ride around on a mech with powerful weapons and mining tools, craft 100s of different items, as well as build colonies and farm livestock and produce to trade or consume.
You can upgrade your ship, you can upgrade your character, you can upgrade your mech, and you can upgrade all the crafting stations in order to unlock more things to build.
The game is like a mix between Mario Brothers, Mega Man, No Man's Sky, Minecraft, The Sims, Farmville, and a few others games. Taking all the elements that made those games fun, while cutting out the bad stuff.
The only negative thing I can say about the game, is I would have liked it if there was some voice acting so I did not have to read so much,  other than that it is more or less perfect.
I would rate this one 9.8 out of 10.
At the current price of $15 bucks they are practically giving the game away, with each hour of entertainment the game provides costing you less than 10 cents, assuming you play it as much as I have.
This is a must have game that people are going to be talking about for a long time to come. I can already see me and my friends comparing other games to this game and getting nostalgic about it years into the future, just like we do now days with games like Mario 1, Doom 1, Diablo 1, and all the other great games from the past.
This is probably one of the top 10 games on Steam right now. 100% Get it.

At the time this review, I have just completed the game for the first time, clocking in at 5.9 hours of playtime. I'm assuming that those reading this are familiar with the original PC/N64 releases, so bear with me not going into too many details on gameplay and story.
Wow, what a remaster. It kept everything I knew of the original game and put a bunch of changes on top, that, in my opinion, improved the game quite a bit, but not to a degree that it felt different from what I remember.
The annoying view bobbing that plagued the original game can be turned off now and the draw distance (fog) can be increased (but not entirely removed). Sounds are decent (and easily moddable!) and are based on the N64 version.
The higher resolution and improved lighting makes it a good looking game, although the textures are merely upscaled, not necessarily HD by today's standards, same with character and item models. Basically it looks like a more polished version of the original game.
As far as my 6 hour playtime is concerned, you have to know that I used to know this game inside-out as a kid, around 15 years ago. I barely ever got lost this time, and even then, just paying attention to the environment helps. Increased draw distance helps a ton in this regard as well. While the level design can be confusing (especially for first time players), it can eventually grow on you, barring initial annoyance. Never before were keys this important to find.
So the game can be short, but with stuff like finding the Chronoscepter pieces and (truly well) hidden secret areas, there's reason for further playthroughs.
I recommend this to anyone who liked the original and everyone else who wants to play a classic shooter that was a bit different from the masses at the time, both in style and in gameplay, as this game can almost be seen as an FPS/Platformer hybrid.
