Goddamn, this has aged well. Not quite as well as Quake, maybe, but I expected Quake to age well. I had no expectations whatsoever for Turok, but lo and behold, it's a really fun game. Not perfect by any means, but definitely really solid and enjoyable.
This was one of the first FPS to be on consoles, to prove that the genre could exist on more than just PC. A lot of the design decisions reflect this: there's a fairly generous auto-aim feature to make up for the lack of mouse, and the weapon select feature is clearly designed for scrolling, not selecting with specific keys. There's also no "Use" button, probably to make up for the relative lack of buttons on a controller compared to a keyboard. More generally, however, there's a more arcadey feel to the mechanics. Your character can jump really high, swim for a very long time, and not take any fall damage whatsoever. This complements the near-omnipresent platforming (another arcadey touch), which is surprisingly good for an FPS. Additionally, there are pickups scattered around that, if you collect 100, give you an extra life. These arcadey features seem more geared toward the consoles of the 90s than PC, and give Turok: Dinosaur Hunter a very different feel to most FPS of the time.
There doesn't seem to be any plot whatsoever, only circumstance. You are Turok, a baffling Native American stereotype living in some weird world that seems to combine elements of prehistory, such as dinosaurs and extensive jungle, with elements of the future, such as laser guns and high-tech bases. For whatever reason, you've decided to kill every living thing in sight and assemble the eight pieces of the Chronoscepter. I don't know anything more about the plot than this, but it gives me an excuse to shoot cyborg Deinonychus with an explosive shotgun, so I'll give it a pass.
The gameplay is ♥♥♥♥ing great. Besides all the platforming, the main focus is shooting, which feels wonderful. It's fast and frantic and almost effortless at times, the difficulty curve is well-managed, and there's lots of variety to add interest to proceedings. There's an excellent selection of 14 or so diverse weapons from all sorts of time periods, although it's pretty poorly balanced (I couldn't find any use for the Alien Weapon or the Shockwave Weapon). A couple have different ammunition types, but you can't toggle them, so all you can do is wear out the better type before moving on to the normal one. That's dumb, but it's not enough of an issue to really be worth complaining about. Ammo caps are also kinda low, but the Backpack powerup remedies this to some extent. There's also an AK-47 that fires 9mm pistol rounds, which I thought was interesting.
The enemies are about as diverse as the weapons, in both design and gameplay execution. There are some fun enemy death animations, and you can shoot random harmless animals for health pickups. The game is also very bloody, but not gory; defeated enemies practically gush blood particles, but other than that appear untouched. Unfortunately, enemies spawn infinitely even though ammo does not, but this can be worked around to some extent by simply ignoring and running past them.
The levels are pretty well-designed. The game forgoes the usual structure of 15-30 normal-sized levels in favor of 8 massive ones, each with tons of secrets and alternate pathways. These levels can be replayed as often as you want in order to get enough keys to unlock later levels. The level design is often quite maze-y and easy to get lost in, but it has the same odd property as Quake where the levels are intuitively designed enough that you can often have only a vague idea of where you are, but as long as you keep moving forward you can usually get to where you want to go. This works well enough that I barely ever needed a walkthrough. I can only imagine the backbreaking amount of effort it took to design the levels to work this way, but I certainly appreciate it.
There are no quicksaves. Instead, there's a system of checkpoints and lives that can be gained by collecting enough points, as mentioned above. Occasionally, there'll be a statue where you can save as often as you want, but they're generally limited to 2-3 per level. This doesn't work as well as quicksaves, of course, but it's basically fine; checkpoints are spaced well enough to avoid serious frustration.
The camera jerks around constantly in response to various actions, such as climbing, swimming, and turning sharply. I got used to it fairly quickly, but if you have trouble with FPS-induced nausea, be warned.
Overall, Turok's a very solid game that has certainly stood the test of time. The gameplay is enjoyable, there's a lot of variety, it works to set itself apart from other FPS, and what issues there are are generally minimized as much as possible. I recommend it.
EDIT: $20 is a bit steep for a game this old, though. You should probably wait for a sale unless you're dead-set on getting this.

So it doesn't make sense to craft the bow and arrow, but there's no way to know this beforehand.

This is a great remaster of an alltime classic shooter.
In Turok you play as Tal'set who is a time travelling Native American warrior who goes to a world called The Lost Land to stop someone called The Campaigner from ruling the universe.
The game is split up into 8 very large and open levels in which you collect keys to open later levels, collecting hidden pieces of a weapon called the Chronocepter, jumping across difficult jumping puzzles and killing enemies ranging from poachers to dinosaurs and cyborgs with weapons ranging from Shotguns and Rifles to Rocket Launchers and Plasma Guns.
Visually the game was one of the best looking 3D shooters at the time (1997) and the remaster has done its best job trying to make it look acceptable to a modern audience while still catering to the old fanbase.
Audio ranges from a funky Electronic and Tribal soundtrack to meaty weapons and enemies who die in exagerrated and humorous ways which pay homage to its comic book roots.
There are still a few issues that might the game hard to recommend to new people, for one the jumping sections can be rather difficult and tedious to get through and some of the levels can suddenly cut off which will force you to revisit and backtrack through if you missed some of the earlier keys.
Overall though Turok is still a highly entertaining oldschool shooter and the remaster does a fantastic job keeping it up to date and along with workshop support there is plenty to sink your teeth into.

The top rated reviews had me a little wary on this title, but since they were all Early Access complaints, and the game previewed positively, I decided to give it a shot. It's a blast! It's a fantasy cousin to XCom, with neat visuals, warm character voices, and all of the fun feels you'd expect from a production of DoubleFine. Games last from 10-20 hours, and it starts very easy, and quickly becomes highly challenging.

Story:
After an air crash on an island 8 survivors try to survive and find a way to get off the island. All characters greatly differ from each other. You have a guy who thinks to know how to survive on the island not being very likeable for the most of the people, as well as a bookworm who survived the plane crash with her father and stepmother, having a strong relationship with her father and apparently not having much normal fun in her life so far, another on is an agent who believes a spy is among the survivors and so forth.
The game has a unique way to convey the story. At night, before distributing the rations, a dialogue (which may influence the needs and relationships of the characters) triggers, depending on what happened the day, who worked with whom, what was discovered on the island and so on, what kind of means that you won’t have the exact same dialogues on each of your playthroughs. You get to know the characters and their relationships better. I really liked that part and it feels like the characters truly are different personalities.
Gameplay:
You have to manage the castaways on their daily life on the island. They need to collect resources, craft as well as research new buildings. But that’s not all. Considering the needs of every single survivor is much more important which are as follows: depression, injury, hunger, fatigue and sickness. Neither of these must become 100% as the character die hence. Though the game isn’t over when a character dies, it becomes just harder as there is one person less to help around the camp.
The characters have relationships with each other which influence the efficiency of the activities the survivor do together. So if two gather resources together and don’t like each other (relationships increase/decrease when working together) they’ll find less resources in contrast to two who like each other, having the same needed skills as the first two. Talking about skills, there are 16 skills which are diverse on each character. Some cook better, scavenge better, are better at exploring the island and et cetera. Due to that you have to think about who should do what. Should somebody with a high skill do the job, resulting in a high outcome or can you afford to place somebody less skilled there (becoming better after a while of course) so that the other one can rest for awhile or perhaps another crucial activity? All characters increase their skills by perform the corresponding job. And after a few skill increases the characters levels up and receive skill points which can be used to improve the individual skills.
Graphic/aesthetic:
Everything is beautiful drawn and the game has its’ own style, a bit cartoonish but still realistic enough to convey the characters and the environments.
If you are now interested in the game, you should give the demo a try. It’s only a few days long but I think that’s sufficient to get to know if the game is for you and the savegame can be used in the main game too. The price is very low compared to the quality by the way and the developers still listen to customers suggestions (at least when this review was written ;)).

Great example of a "Just one more mission I swear" sort of strategy game.
It's a little odd seeing so many down-thumbs in the user reviews talking mostly about what the game didn't manage to be. I approached it simply as a scaled-down XCOM with a bit of a fun blood-lines system that you would have expected from Rogue Legacy. It seems that a number of the negative reviews are mostly people who expected the moon with their early access game and felt suckered when a neat strategy game didn't transcend to another realm.
Not all games need to blow your mind. But it's something when a game is able to grab me for fifteen hours in just three days.
Comparing it to XCOM is shorthand. It's a slimmed down and more pure experience with far fewer annoying bits like resource management and research (though there is some, it's opportunistic), and it's replaced with a system of bloodlines, marriages, babies, and combining classes.
I want to mention that for the first 200 years of the game it's fairly easy once you get a grasp of the mechanics - the first mission I lost two members in the first turn due to carelessness, but after that rarely made similar mistakes. On normal it's quite a bit easier than XCOM, but by the last three battles in the last 50 years or so I was really sweating a number of battles, having to restart a large number of them.
Unlike XCOM I wasn't afraid to let people die in battles. In XCOM I was a bit of a pansy, saving and reloading multiple times in a level, but in the estimated 20-25 battles I faced in the 300 year campaign I at most restarted a level due to some boned headed mistake I couldn't stand to live with. The march of time and the raising of heroes from birth means that you get a steady stream of heroes.
Oh, and about the bloodlines concept, this game isn't one you should fret over who's best married to who; with tons of time speculating on stats and perks. I never spent more than 20 seconds deciding on who to marry who or who to take into battle over another.
I believe things could have been improved to make your familes and vaguards more visible on the kingdom screen to help communicate the flow of heroes being born, aged, and buried. Instead I was left viewing most of my families and soldiers as anonymous people until later in the game when two families started to stand out. One was just a family that bred like rabbits and gave me what felt like dozens of caberjacks.
The other family was one that I ended up cheering on as father to daughter, mother to son, etc etc as time went on producing my star unit in every battle from around year 50 to 301. I even went so far as to write down their history and anticipate their nicknames. When the thrower weapon "Dream Crusher" became a relic that passed between six different generations it became a tool of nearly guarenteed one-hit-kills. When the holder of the relic died it was always a serious moment when I decided who of the holder's children would be able to carry on the legacy and become my next great vanguard.
It all started with the team of Mael "Rusty" Fu and his daughter Eleandra "Wildcard" Fu blowing things up together. Then came Aaron "Clam" Fu, who I felt was a poor substitute for his late mother. He ended up having a quiet career until late in a mission he accidentally killed his daughter and heir apparent Jacqueline Fu. With his elder sister dead "Dream Crusher" passed to Bloodroot "Heavyfoot" Fu where he became my most vicious warrior. His son Kane "Red Hands" Fu continued the bloody mantel, but he wasn't able to make it to the final battle in year 301. His daughter Rebecca Fu took up "Dream Crusher" to the final bout where she met her fate. I don't want to spoil it but the ending had me truly excited.
I would happily recommend this game and would give it a solid 8.5/10. I'm not eager to return to it after finishing the campaign in 15 hours, but I was addicted and felt accomplished to finish it.

One of the most interesting games I've played in awhile.  Firstly, this is an FPS.  Secondly, it is also a simple strategy game.  Thirdly, it is around 800 mb of space.
Basically, you and your "rebels" fight off thousands of enemy imperial soldiers.  You must defend your rebel stronghold, while the enemy must kill it off.  The main game is in FPS mode.  Every player though, depending on how well they do, gains power.  With power you can buy traps, guns, bombs, support crates, turrets (both troop and vehicle), among other things.  The strategy mode isn't another main mode.  Rather every person has it with the press of a button.  You can still control your character's movement in this mode.  So if you want to plant a trap while running away from gunfire, you can do so.
The maps are set up so that attacks can come from any area, but you also have a good defense and each round is about 30 to 40 minutes of play.  You also have the option to repair anything, every character has molotovs, and every character has a knife, pistol, and rifle.  Buying weapons with "power" is what customizes your character.  Once you buy something in terms of weapons or bombs, you have it forever.  When you die, you respawn with those armaments.  Spawned turrets have unlimited ammo, and health that you can repair as well.
It is really fun to play this game.  It isn't graphically advanced, but it doesn't need to be.  A very simple strategy/fps game with a tower defense like mechanic, that doesn't involve any towers.

I got this game when there was a good sale, and I've loved it ever since. Orcs Must Die! 2 is a first person shooter slash tower defense game, and it seamlessly brings these two genres together. I didn't get the first game (although I am planning to) but I was able to understand the general plot, and it still leaves questions unanswered that I can learn later (when I play the first game). Orcs Must Die provides you with a slew of unique traps, weapons, and AI guardians, which are all beautifully implemented and effective and powerful in-game. This game successfully differentiates itself with others in the tower defense genre by allowing you to actually participate as a warmage in the game, and also by its unique trap mechanics. However, I do have two complaints. One is that the gameplay does get a little monotonous after a while, but this is a very minor complaint. My other complaint is that I've found a bug. When I tried to place a void wall on a wall, the game wouldn't let me. The outline of the void wall didn't even show up when I pointed my cursor toward a wall. Don't know what's up with that. Despite this, Robot Entertainment made an excellent game that I would definitely recommend.
Edit: Turns out the void walls take up a 2 x 2 space, so that nulls my point about the "bug," as I was pointing only at 1 x 1 spaces.

This is 3rd in the Creeper series and it shows;
headline feature from previous entries now casually sit in your tool box, and years of polish and good UI choices run through the experience.
This is the Creeper series at it's very best,
The core game is a pseudo tower-defense game, where the enemy "creeper" is modeled on thermodynamic movement (enemy propagates through the level like heat through a medium), and your personal infrastructure in modeled on packet switching.
The benefit of this is a game that's a very unique variant on the genre, and visually is wholly singular.
Packets zip about your network as they beat back the horrors of living entropy!
Worth highlighting is the story; minimalist in a very impressive way. A few text back-and-forths at the start of a level are all you get, but they deliver fully on the feeling and weight of being trapped at the end of a dead universe; alone in the empty infinity but for your sole friend.
It would be nice if production values were a little higher. Sprites could be better; and the music though good, does get repetitive with it's few songs. Though the core experience is never deeply hurt by these weak points.
The game's single biggest flaw is in it's dynamics. If you survive the first few minutes of a fight it becomes a rather rote process of slowly expanding your territory, until 30-60 min later you've zapped the last enemy.
There are frequent small decisions to make, but very few large ones.
Despite the narrative weight of the-end-of-all-things and the cool high-energy packet switching & blasting of your little empire, the game ultimately feels like a casual experience.
Mellowly click away, pruning your little bonsai death machine until you've won.
A fine experience, but RTS and 4x fans will be yearning for more difficulty and substance.
Though some will wish it had more challenge, "Arc Eternal" is still an excellent little game!

The actual review:
Story: This game takes place 5 billion years after CR2, that's all the story for now because i don't want to spoil things.
Gameplay: Every level except for the 2 systems leading to Prospector and Tormented zone, and the system which has Farbor in it introduces new mechanics. Such as Vapen which gives you your final command node, or Arca which gives you Thor. The gameplay is mainly build weapons to fight off various enemies and advance.The enemies are runners, spores, and the creeper. In addition to this you also have digitalists which can transport creeper over terrain instead of the creeper having to flow over. Many levels will introduce a new mechanic whether it's a permament enmy, a new tech, or a custom enemy, such as Ormos which has no emmiters, but creeper stuck in space and will come down once you land. Also on Ormos you get Terps whichcan terrraform the land. The terrian is in 10 levels. 1 being the lowest and 10 the highest, the previously mentioned digitalists can ignore this boundary and can jump terrain even if the emmiter strengh is at 3 (yes in the main campgain there are emmiters that emits 3 creeper every five seconds). You paint the terrian with whatever level you want it to be and the terps will slowly work on it. This can be sped up by a powerzone. The terps reqiure energy and the area they are terraforming cannot be covered with creeper. The powerzone enhanch all of your units abilities such as being able to make terps work faster and have a longer range or turning the motor into a fast firing, long range beast. The creeper is like CR1 so nothing to say there. However, the runners must be connected to digitalis to spawn and to survive. The runners will come out of runner nests and will stun your units, the best unit to kill them are snipers. The spores are like the ones in CR1 and CR2 they must be killed by beams and will drop a payload of creeper if not destroyed. The AE fields prevent your air units (guppys, bombers, and strafers) from flying over them. Your air units are guppys, bombers, and strafers. Guppys will transport  packets to your units such as AC, energy, or ore. Bombers use AC to spray down AC on an area and are the most powerful air unit. Strafers use energy and are essentually fighters. AC is short for anti-creeper and is gained from ore which comes from ore mines which can only be played on special spots or else you would win every mission too easily. There are 2 AC units, sprayers and bombers. Sprayers will spray AC that automatically fights creeper. It works like the AC from CR2 and it will protect your units if creeper hits them meaning that reactors will be safe if ac is on them. The main units are collecters, relays, reactors, blasters, motars, and nufflifiers. Collecters, will give you some energy and will expand you energy network, place these as far away from each other as possible since the energy production doesn't stack (they collect energy from an area like the ones from CR1). Reactors can be and should be placed in tight packs since they always give .4 energy, that can upgraded in the forge or using power nodes. Blasters have to have a line of sight and fire fast. Motars don't have to have a line of sight. Nuffelers can destory emmiters. The forge can upgrade things such as packet  speed, energy effifency, or weapon range (and yes move speed does apply to guppy's).  This review is getting very long and i covered most of the things i wanted to covers so now onto bugs.

Oh and this game has maybe 30 story levels, 30-100 alpha levels (levels that were made in the alpha) a random generator, close to a thousand user-made maps some of which allow you to play as the creeper, and 2 areas with thousands of levels which add a new mechanic in addition to the regular stuff and an extra credits mission which turns it into a third person shooter so maybe 10 or infinity hours of content for you to play until you get bored

Fairly typical free to play CCG, this game doesn't really do anything special to separate it from the pack. The UI isn't as nice as it could be, and frankly it feels worse than Hearthstone overall. And, like all F2P CCGs on the computer, it is vastly inferior to Magic: The Gathering.
Why can't any of these games be as good as Magic? Who knows.
This game's central mechanic is the idea of levelling cards during a match - by playing a card, you get a better version of the card shuffled into your deck in the future. This means that over the course of the game, your cards (and your opponent's cards) get progressively stronger. This leads to, in principle, an interesting tension of now vs later, but the reality is that the best cards are simply good now and even better later, and while there are some trade-offs, and there is some strategy involved, in the end it isn't really all that amazing.
It was a valiant effort, but frankly, you're better off playing a real game.

So apparently this game was made early last year?  Graphics aren't everything for sure, but this game looks like it could've been made a few years ago as one of those completely free flash games.  While playing Solforge I've been trying to look past it, but unfortunately this game has too many parts that seem to have been totally overlooked.
My biggest complaints:
No tutorial that goes beyond "drag and drop to play your cards, press these obvious buttons to end your turn, here's a quick explanation for the leveling and rank system, here's how spells and effects sorta-work, good luck!".  The game doesn't really explain the various factions in any form or the way that thier ally abilities work, now does it go on to explain any sort of basic strategy in this game at all.  There's so much missing for a game that's already a year old.
The card balance is pretty bad.  There are several cards that are simply better than other ones.  There are several clones of Zombie Soldier that have the same stats as well as an added effect, for instance.
There's no undo button, which is pretty vital for a card game.  You can't undo any actions whatsoever.  This is especially annoying when you start to realize the full potential of the battle and turn phases being seperated.
The interface as a whole isn't as streamlined as it could be.  It works better than most games that have recently come out, with thier 20 buttons and 50 menus at least, but it's much nicer to click on a button that says "settings" over fishing around for a cog symbol....
There's only 4 factions, and no lore.  I don't understand why factions even exist except to have those little ally effects, but almost all of the ally effects pool into Tempys so they don't matter very much.
There are too many similar cards, except for spell cards.  The spell cards tie into my aforementioned gripes about the card balance in this game, where one faction has many powerful spell cards while another faction has some OK ones to get by on.  I could understand it if 1 of the factions had particularly strong spells and particularly weak creatures, but this isn't the case.  Because half of the monsters in this game could be clones with very minor stat differences.
In summary, I'm glad that I got these starter packs in a huge Humble Bundle, because I would have regret my starter pack puchase if I had not.  I'm going back to Infinity Wars, I'll take its' more punishing economy over this game's less fun, less explodey, less varietal gameplay.

Every now and then, one of my less open-minded Steam friends asks me a question to the effect of:  "Why do you keep buying and playing all those crappy indie games?"  It's always nice to have a simple one or two word answer to such foolish enquiries, and I can now safely add the words "Lifeless Planet" to my list of possible responses.

Think Dear Esther on a mysterious alien world, with a third-person perspective and a great deal more "gameplay" and danger added to the bargain; mostly of the 3D "platforming" type, if a tag MUST be placed on it.  Like Esther, it has gorgeous graphics, a genuinely interesting storyline and mood aplenty...with a fair few more "action"-y elements added for those who might require such things. This still isn't a title likely to appease the aggro-gamer crowd who require something to be relentlessly "hard" in order to enjoy it, but for those of us who don't mind oodles of atmosphere and adventure along with our little bursts of action...it's a right little gem.
Let me put it another way: while the game is still REASONABLY fast-paced - providing you follow it in as linear a path as possible - you're not liable to fully appreciate it unless you fancy yourself playing a kind of intergalactic "tourist" on a bizarre alien planet (hence the Dear Esther reference earlier...a game which really is, when all is said and done, a slightly spooky and visually stunning sight-seeing tour across an interesting landscape).

Which isn't to say that Lifeless Planet is a mere "walking simulator" as the cynics like to term such games, but, well...about half of it is, unless you speed-run the ♥♥♥♥ing thing.  And let's face it, if you're one of those speed-running types, do us ALL a favour and look at the ♥♥♥♥ing screenshots on the Store page. Does this REALLY look like your kind of game? Of course it doesn't.
Now ♥♥♥♥ off and play Serious Sam 7 for the twenty-second time, you boring plebs, and stop criticising games which are clearly labours of love, created for the primary purpose of taking those of us endowed with sufficient imagination on an enjoyable and - upon occasion, at least - genuinely AWE-INSPIRING journey.

So, one of the Kickstarter projects I backed over a year ago finally came due. Regalia: Of Men And Monarchs just came out on Steam and I am pretty impressed with it so far.
It is a tactical RPG (combat wise) with a lot of emphasis on resource management between battles: managing time, money, the growth of your city, your relationship with your party members, exploring different regions, etc.
It has a lot of humor, enjoyable characters, and an interesting world, even if the story itself is pretty straight forward so far. The combat system is pretty good as well, introducing some unique concepts (you can increase/recover 'shields' during battle, but not health, for example). The dungeon system they use is really interesting.
The only real frustration I've had so far is that the combat system has very strict Line of Sight rules, making it difficult to plan your actions at times (especially given some of the battle layouts), but I assume it will just be a learning curve.
It's $25 on Steam right now and it seems to be a pretty polished project. I'm only a few hours in, so I don't know for sure how long it is or whether the ending pays off, but so far it looks like there may also be several paths through the game with rival factions and such as well.

9 hours played so far.

Some of the writing is funny, while it could be better in other parts. The game uses party level instead of individual level, which I find refreshing. Regalia has been a great ride and I'm excited to see what game comes next in a couple years.

Regalia: Of Men and Monarchs is a solid turn based strategy game. I recommend it for SRPG and/or Turn-Based Strategy games fans.
+ Good writing - funny dialogues and witty conversation
+ Fun combat - exciting combat, mechanics are neither too simplistic or too complicated
+ Diverse battle skills - every character has different skills, instead of sharing boring generic skills like in other games
+ No grinding - experience is gained party wide, so you can use use that party member that you never use without drawbacks
+ Relationship building - think like Persona games, you get perks by building relationship with your party member and townsfolk npcs
+ Time limit - makes you think carefully of what to do instead of doing everything in one playthrough, but endless mode option is there for completionist
+ Choices matter - makes for great replayability
+ Fast loading time - after dealing with horrendous loading time of other turn based game such as Expeditions Vikings, Shadowrun, Wasteland 2, etc, it feels good to finally play something that loads fast.
- Challenge in battles. Not a fan of "bonus objective" system; I'd like to take my time and enjoy battles, not min-max to win in less than X turns.
- Can't pan camera with WASD, this is rather unintuitive in my opinion. I accidentally used whirlwind on the second battle while trying to move the camera
- Can't compare equipment. For some reason you can't see currently equipped item when trying to switch equipment.
- Can't save the game anytime I want, only in town and dungeon camp (save point).

Starbound is a 2D side-scrolling sandbox game, kinda similar to Terraria. But it's SO MUCH MORE than Terraria. After logging almost 200 hours into the game, i'm still not bored of it, and see myself coming back to it almost every day.
I give ratings on a scale of 0-10, 10 being the best I've ever seen and 0 being a rating that would be better than something I'd give to No Man's Sky.
Graphics: 9/10
The pixel art done in this game is fantastic. You can tell exactly what something is the moment you look at it, and everything fits together into a wonderfully cohesive design.
Soundtrack: 10/10
Most AAA titles have what? 50 minutes of soundtrack? Maybe an hour? Starbound? An indie game made by a super small team? 6 HOURS of beautiful, unique soundtrack that I never get tired of listening to. So good.
Story: 7/10
If there's one thing I don't like too much about this game, it would be the story. Don't get me wrong, it's good. But you can tell it's not the main focus of the game. It's pacing is a little shakey, and it's a bit generic. The characters on the other hand, are FANTASTIC. I just wish we could've had more interaction with them. The story goes as such, You are one of the sole survivors of a terrible attack on Earth by a creature known as "The Ruin". You flee with only you Matter Manipulator, and your ship. Your ship's FTL Drive fails in orbit of an unknown planet, and you must survive, and find a way to get your ship back in working order. But once you do that, it's your job to help find the artifacts that form the key to "The Ruin" and destroy it once and for all.
Gameplay: 9/10
In Starbound, you find resources, craft items, build buildings, and explore a MASSIVE universe, Kinda like No Man's Sky. But ACTUALLY GOOD. Every planet is unique and an absolute joy to explore. And great multiplayer funtionallity makes it even better.
Verdict: 8.75/10
Starbound is a ton of fun, and with friends, you'll lose yourself in the massive universe waiting to be explored. The story insgood, the soundtrack is fantastic, and gameplay doesn't get old fast. and it's only 15$! Take that No Man's Sky!

I've backed this game on Kickstarter because it looked fun and I liked Psychonauts and Brütal Legends.
To make it short: It was not worth backing. If you can get it in a sale though, you might hit that buy button.
That said, this game doesn't feel finished. The basics are there, and some of them are really fun and promising, but on a whole this feels more like a preview than a finished, polished game.
The Kingdom: There's hardly any UIs to manage your kingdom, giving you infos about family trees, birthrates etc. You know, some dashboards giving you an overview of how well, or unwell, your kingdom is functioning. The nation building is very limited (3 different types of buildings), no politics, no managing your citizens (like happyness etc.) and absolutely no visible changes to your kingdom. There could have been different regions with different climates etc. like a harsh north breeding strong heroes or a desert or a swap-region that would benefit alchemists but maybe bring more sickly children forth... nothing of that sort.
Combat: Take any turn-based strategy game, deduct most of their depth and you end up with Massive Chalice's combat system. The fights quickly become redundant, the different maps offering almost no distinctions. No environment that would impact your strategy (f.e. foggy weather that yould lower sight and hit-chance for hunter-types). hardly any interaction with the terrain, no cover, flanking, almost no buffs/debuffs. no summons etc. etc.
tldr: If they had put DOUBLE the effort into this project, this could have become a FINE game. But probably 3/4 of the budget already went into another PRODUCTION :-(

Massive Chalice is a blatant fantasy clone of the new XCOM, minus the tactical depth offered in the aforementioned title (deep or shallow as it was, depending on your opinion). The game is lacking in several key areas, as explained below.
1) No explanation of range for hunter weapons - you are left to guess whether your crossbow is in effective range. This should be stated upfront, in number of tiles.
2) There is no point to utilizing any other class in combat besides hunter - enemies such as Wrinklers (melee enemy, they age your hero on any successful hit by 5 years), Ruptures (explode when killed) and Lapses (explode when killed, possibly stunning anything in range) make close combat units a gamble, at best.
3) Mixing the three basic classes (caberjack, alchemist, hunter) does nothing of particular interest  (except for shuffling class skills and adding a few questionably useful new skills).
4) AoE attacks don't function unless targeted at specific enemies (except for alchemist grenades). In other words, you can't utilize the majority of AoE attacks as indirect fire / artillery. They MUST be targeted at an enemy.
5) Most 'heroes' that are recruited are typically stacked with negative attributes that make them useless in combat and useless for generating further hero bloodlines.
6) You can use only 5 heroes in any given tactical combat, but the Cadence have typically 3-4 times more units. Regardless of what skills are used against them (for example, Taunt) they still maximize their effectiveness in terms of hitting multiple units. A Taunted unit should not be able to move to where it wishes and hit multiple units - if it is Taunted it should only be concerned with directly attacking the unit that Taunted it.
About the only thing that was done correctly in this game was the music.
If you're looking for a turn-based strategy game I would recommend avoiding this, unless you're willing to deal with ridiculous odds, horrible random events that can destroy your heroes, and weapons that lack any sort of explanation regarding range and capability.

I can't recommend this game. The control scheme is beyond terrible: having the WASD controls vary based on where the cursor is was a terrible design decision, especially when the cursor also controls where attacks come from. I went into this game knowing the controls were difficult after watching Let's Plays, but this is an exercise in frustration. It's like those old console games where the camera flips and suddenly your controls are inverted. If it was just movement, it'd be at least doable but the cursor also controls attacks and blocking which makes it a chore to even attempt. I was hoping the controls were improved in the last year but it appears not to be the case.
Here's how it works: WASD moves the character up, left, right and down in relation to the cursor. Unlike most games with similar controls where pressing W moves you toward the cursor, this just moves you up in whatever direction that happens to be at the time. It's infuriating trying to map your movement and control your weapon while trying to block and move while derply sidestepping around the place in who knows what direction at the same time, all the while trying to control the camera. There's also no real tutorial to slowly introduce you to this odd mechanic.
The characters walk around like they're perpetually drunk, getting caught on small obstacles and generally looking very derpy. The very first monster I ever encountered ran away and the chase was a tedium of switching out of "combat mode", running and then trying to adjust the camera while also making Senor Derpenstein not trip over every little obstacle only to get clobbered by the monster when I finally caught up because I wasn't in "combat mode" so my character didn't block.  Devs, you have a great concept here but it seems the idea of making it a good game was lost in the nuance. Without a solid control scheme it doesn't matter how fun the concept or potential of a game is.
I want to state my point once more: I cannot play this game at all due to its control scheme. Literally. It's a shame because I can see this game being great fun if it had better controls.

(TL;DR – pros and cons at bottom)
In an age where RPGs are perk-laden and low-skill, open-world yet surprisingly dilute of content, and full of loot but mostly devoid of true value, Exanima drags the player into the darkness to offer them something fresh and innovative.
Learn unique and highly rewarding fighting mechanics, explore and fight your way through a dungeon, and unravel the mystery and the physics-based puzzles.
At present, Exanima has three modes of gameplay: dungeon crawl, practice arena, and career arena.
The main part of the game is the dungeon itself and you have two options regarding how you wish to approach it. You can either choose to be a hero who’s descending into its depths of his own volition, or you can choose to be a nobody who’s been abducted and thrown into the labyrinth. Ultimately, both options play the same, but they affect your motives for pushing forwards into the dark, and (most importantly) they change what equipment you start with. A knight who’s stepped forward to brave the unknown starts with good-quality plate armour and a weapon; conversely, a kidnapped peasant starts with nothing but the shirt on his back. This decision greatly affects the early-stage difficulty of the game, and newcomers may find it more beneficial to try their first run at the dungeon as a well-armoured knight.
The career arena mode is fun and a complete game in its own right. You start off armed only with a meat cleaver, but as you win fights and earn money, you buy better weapons and armour, and slowly ascend the ranks. In addition to fighting by yourself, you can hire AI controlled combatants who can enter the arena when your character needs to rest and recover from injuries. These companions also fight alongside you in team battles.
In addition to the standard armed duels, the career arena offers pugilistic brawls, a fray (in which you’re thrust into the pit with several others fighters at the same time), and an elimination tournament that offers a large pot of winnings if you successfully fight your way through all of its adversaries.
As well as being a fun way to spend many hours, this part of the game offers great training in the combat system for when you try to fight your way through the main game dungeon.
When in comes to looting corpses and treasure chests most RPGs seem to place an emphasis on finding that great new weapon that will take your undead slaying to the next level. Exanima turns the convention on its head by getting you excited about your newly found armour upgrade instead. New and better weapons are nice; but improved and extra armour is what you’ll be most grateful for finding. The game does this by providing the mechanic of wearing multiple pieces of armour simultaneously by layering them over the same body part. (For example, you can protect your chest by wearing a padded coat over your shirt, by putting on chain mail on top of that, and finally donning a steel breast plate.) Aside from historical accuracy, and the absence of this mechanic from the majority of other RPGs out there, this is a very welcome addition to Exanima due to the fragility of your character. Just a few careless moves in battle could bring your dungeon crawl to an alarmingly abrupt end, to a degree that shows just how unforgiving Exanima loves to be. You truly will want every piece of protection the game has to offer.
This will have you scouring the dungeon for every last shred of padded leather and chain mail you can find to protect your fragile hero from the hoard of undead that roam the forgotten corridors.
However, all this protection comes at a price: each piece of armour has its own encumbrance based on its size and the density of the material. A full set of steel plate armour with underlying chain mail will offer great personal defence, but will slow your hero down considerably when running and fighting. Worse still, if you lose your balance and fall over it will take your character considerably longer to stand up again. During this time they’re utterly defenceless against incoming attacks, which can be far more damaging than having worn only very basic armour would ever have been. The key in Exanima is to find a good balance between protection and manoeuvrability.
The combat system in Exanima centres on precise placement of the mouse cursor and then careful movement of the mouse. Pressing the attack button triggers a standard right to left swing of your weapon. Moving the mouse from right to left during this process adds momentum. Stepping to the left at the same time, as well, adds even more speed to the blow, causing that much more damage to your enemy. However, this has to be done very carefully, as too much mouse swinging or too great a step can orientate your character off target, spin them around, and even knock them off balance leaving them completely exposed as they pick themselves up off the floor.
If you wish to swing from left to right, you begin your attack with the mouse cursor to the left hand side of your character on screen instead.
In addition to the lateral swings, you have an overhead swing and a stabbing thrust available to you.  Both of which can have their force increased by crouching at the fastest part of the downward movement, and lunging forwards - respectively.
Learning to combine precise mouse movements with gentle keyboard tapping is the key to successful and deadly attacks, while keeping your hero in a good defensive position.
Blocking works by placing the mouse cursor between yourself and the enemy and then moving it in the direction of an incoming attack at the right time. This isn’t always perfect so learning to move out of the way of with graceful movements from the keyboard will greatly improve your chances of survival.
This physics-based combat system is even more innovative and satisfying than those of Mount and Blade, and Chivalry. But as you can imagine, there is a lot of skill involved in picking up and mastering such a fighting system.
It is for this reason that the developers have very wisely included a practice arena in the game. This allows you to hone your fighting skills without taking the risk of losing your hero’s progress in the main dungeon run. Trust me: you will be very grateful for its inclusion in the game, as death in the main game means having to restart your entire adventure.
With both a novice and expert arena, and with 8 successively more difficult opponents in each, you’re sure to improve your odds of survival in the main part of the game -  with enough practice.
+ Unique physics-based combat system that’s very rewarding and satisfying.
+ Plenty of loot to find in a low-fantasy, medieval RPG that emphasises layering of protection.
+ Expansive dungeon to explore with plenty of enemies to fight off.
+ Has a wonderfully dark and ominous atmosphere.
+ Interesting storyline to pursue - at your choice - in a world that’s rich in its own lore.
+ Excellent sound effects that add a surprising amount of depth to the atmosphere.
+ Excellent detailed graphics with a very polished presentation. The dynamic lighting is truly beautiful.
+ With all the polish and content already present you’d easily be forgiven for thinking that Exanima isn’t an early access title.
- Steep learning curve for the combat system – you will need to spend several hours mastering it in the arena.
- It’s possible to get stuck on some parts of the environment. This usually isn’t much of a problem unless you’re engaged in combat at the time at which time it can be utterly devastating.

This game is garbage. First off, if you thought you'd get to do things like move around outside, look at castles, be in the sunlight, look at green plants, or teleport - things you might have seen in trailers by this company - you thought wrong. This game throws you into a dungeon and that's it. You stay in a dungeon for the entire game. It doesn't tell you anything unless you go to the options menu and read about how the game works. Even that didn't tell me how to block - I had to learn that from a loading screen tip! An essential skill of the game has to be learned in a loading screen tip.
There are two modes: adventure and arena. Adventure is the one that throws you into the dungeon. Arena is even worse. It's supposed to be a gladiator thing where you fight, earn money to buy better weapons and armor, and fight some more to earn mroe money. However: to start a fight you have to click a poster on a wall, and to see that poster you have to rotate your camera. You have to do this every time you want to fight, you have to rotate your camera. The developers were clearly too incompetent to put it in a visible area or adjust the starting camera angle so you can see it. You may also be looking for where you buy items. Well, you have to click the empty stool in the place that looks like an item shop. The developers were clearly too stupid to put a person there to be a shopkeeper, so instead you have to take a guess and click on an empty stool to get to the purchase menu.
The arena fight mechanic itself is trash. You start with virtually no money. The items available for purchase are random, and often cost far more than you have. On top of that, you won't be able to equip anything except a shirt or pair of pants, even if you do buy it, because gear is also limited based on rank. Your fighters are all at the lowest rank, and it takes a great deal of fighting experience to go up even one rank. This means most of your fights will be with crappy weapons in no armor - not what I expected from a game that bills itself as medieval fighting. (Speaking of money, you have gold, silver, and copper. Do you want to know what the conversion rate is between them? Too bad! The game doesn't freaking tell you. I think it's 12 coppers to 1 silver. Why would anyone make such a system?)
On top of that, the fights all have terrible payouts! The only fights you can do at your rank, against enemies also at your rank (so you don't get blown out instantly by guys with way more Skills than you), pay terrible returns. You have to bet some amount, and if you win you get some amount back. The only type that pays well is Elimination, but I've never won one. It seems to involve at least 5 fights in a row without stops, and any "lethal" damage you take to your health bar carries over from fight to fight. My enemies didn't seem to be getting any weaker even though I was.
Oh and your entire Arena mode system has permadeath. If you take too much "lethal" damage, you die forever. So if you die, that's it, you lose everything. Why anyone thinks this is fun is beyond me.

A Real Time Strategy game that emphasizes buildings over units.
The third entry, I assume, in a series. I haven't played the other games, but was able to get into the story and gameplay with no issues. You are allowed to save at any time during a mission and in my experience the early story missions take roughly a half hour and the later more complex ones can take an hour to two, so if you can only spare a little bit of time per day, this game is very accomodating.
I normally enjoy RTS games for the interesting units and buildings over strategy, so I tend to spend more time building and upgrading than being any good at completing objectives. In this game, though, base building is the core. You are given the entire map to see, so you always know what is coming at you and what you need to prepare for. There are never sudden unexpected onslaughts of troops rush through your defenses. If you prefer to take your time in an RTS, this is a game that encourages it, with the exception of certain timed missions in the later story sections.
The main gameplay is set around starting a base and protecting yourself from the map-enveloping creeper and fighting it back enough that you can destroy the sources producing it. As you progress in the storyline you will be introduced slowly to new tech to help you and new threats from the creeper, such as missiles launched at you from towers. The game does a good job at teaching you how to use your new resources to deal with new problems and then challenging that new knowledge by mixing threats together.
A complaint: Many, though not all, of the buildings can move themselves where you choose, which I don't believe the tutorial missions mentioned, or at least did not reinforce as well as the other gameplay mechanics. Since buildings consume energy and creeper that has reached them will damage them, it is very useful to know you can pick up and move rather than potentially kill your energy reserve with more weapons or helplessly watch a building get destroyed.
Potential negatives:
Once you've established your base and are ready to push the creeper back, the game tends to be fairly similar each mission, especially after you've gotten all the buildings available through the story missions.
There is one mission per planet and typically 1-4 planets per system. When it starts getting to an hour or two per mission. It can add up to a lengthy game with less variety than you might like.

I'll be frank. The original Just Cause was extremely advanced for the time, allowing for vertical gameplay, an absolutely MASSIVE world map, capture-the-territory regime change mechanics, car stunts and a politicized CIA story archetype which is pretty distinctive in its conceptualization by Avalanche Studios. I originally played this game for the Xbox 360 at a friend's house and was completely blown away by the freedom the game afforded, its solid controls and its then-gorgeous graphical detail.
The PC port does it a disservice by being so janky. I personally believe it's almost impossible to advance in the game because the vehicular and combat controls were originally designed for the 360 version and were then effectively rebound to a mouse and keyboard as the only change... this makes the entire game feel stiff and hard-to-adapt-to when you're actually playing it.
Combine this with numerous graphical, AI, UI and other kinds of issues (Regular crashes to desktop? Really?) and you have, without hyperbole, what is one of the worst PC ports I have ever seen. I would gladly recommend you play this game, just not this version of it. It's overpriced at $6.99 unless you really don't care about it being playable and only want to collect it.
If you loved Just Cause 2 and want to harken back to the genesis of the franchise, go do yourself a favor and pick up the Xbox 360 version. Maybe that's mostly nostalgia talking (I have yet to have bought the 360 copy for myself after all this time), but you have a far greater chance of beating what is an ultimately good game hampered by an awful port.
Oh yeah, and you can't do 16:9 in this game either. Yep. At least the PS2 version (also flawed, but much easier to play) had an excuse, being a last-gen port.

is the last part of Broken Sword series, coming out in 2014. Yup, our lovely duo is back in our lives again, nearly 20 years after the release of the legendary first game. We have witnessed George and Nico evolve throughout years - and devolve in some games, to be honest - yet after the commercial and presentational failure that we'd know as
, I wasn't expecting much from a new game. I had come to accept that even though it had a marvelous beginning, Broken Sword series were dying in our age. Now I am thrilled to announce that I was tremendously wrong after playing this adventure gem. George and Nico are back, and they are at their best!
Some years after the 4th game, George and Nico run across each other by another odd chance in an art exhibition. They are back in Paris again: the city that holds many memories for both; of cafés, of music, of love and of death. Where it all began years ago. This time, George is working for the insurance agency which the gallery owner made an arrangement with, and Nico is simply there to catch a scoop of the gallery opening. Just before they can catch up or get on a nostalgia train through longing looks they exchanged, they witness an art theft and an accompanying murder! Gallery owner is shot and
- a religious Gnostic painting by the mysterious artist El Serp - is stolen. As fate pushes Nico and George into each other to run through a final mystery, we take on yet another mystical yet hilarious adventure with them.
Okay, from this point, it might very well become a love letter and a summary of the whole franchise and narrative, so feel free to skip this part if bored. Narrative pace, presented lore, character interactions and humor are incredibly well here! I was really worried - and a bit depressed after playing the 4th game, since it was obvious that with each new game hailing from the series, the quality of all these aspects dropped down a bit more. Legendary with the first, well-done with the second, quite nice with the third and... Downright horrible with the fourth. Now this game, brings back George and Nico, and what made both their personalities and the stories revolved around them special. We'll meet new characters, catch up with old ones and work on a full blown conspiracy with medieval background yet again. This time, the lore focuses on a less known - and mostly apocryphal side of Christian history: Gnosticism. It is a different approach with authentic scriptural storyline, compared to the millionth Catholic witch hunt we've seen in video game history so far. It is refreshing.
Environment design is again 2D classic point and click, with 3D depth enhancement. Keyboard interference is completely gone once again. Artworks are marvelous, and site transitions are wondrously smooth. You keep playing the game without a notch of display quality dropping down. Character designs are marvelous cartoon exaggerations again, with some comic art shading, which is a tip of hat to older games yet a refreshing redesign when it comes to animations. I have to add that the soundtrack was also the best in the series since the first one. Kudos!
This is a text-book classical P&C adventure if I've ever seen any. We have inventory collection, NPC & environment interactions, and of course puzzles to solve. Now that we are not dealing with 3D environments anymore, all box-pushing puzzles we've suffered through in previous games -3rd and 4th, to be specific - are gone. Yay! A breath of fresh air for stretegy-enthusiasts!  An IMMENSE amount of customization in HOW the game unfolds.  There is no "right way" to play Massive Chalice, but all the ways you'll try will feel balanced to perfection.
I absolutely LOVE this game.
Massive Chalice is unlike any other strategy/tactics game I've ever played.  Originally, I was intrigued by the description promising different forms of strategy combined with a standard tile-based tactics system.  However, I had no idea how complex theses elements would be, and the result is a truly unique, pleasantly deep game.
The game is split between battles and planning stages, but the "planning" isn't as simple as outfitting heroes with gear, or leveling up attributes.  You can do all these things, but additionally, you actually have to populate your army by mating your heroes in hopes they are fertile enough to produce babies.  The offspring inherit traits of the parents, and can form unique classes based on how you mix the parents' classes.  Also, be sure to keep an eye on the age of your heroes, because unlike any other strat game I've ever played, your heroes actually die of old age.  You'll want to continue their bloodlines, and take advantage of relics (super-weapons) that can be passed down through bloodlines.
Then on top of this there are random events, choice of what battles to fight, options to retire heroes for use in research and general army-level boosts, structured all around a "passing timeline" which beautifully incorporated into a consistent style.
In addition to the typical grid based battle system like so many turn-based strat games, I found an astounding number of "new ideas" for weapons, attacks, skills, environments, etc.  Example:  One environment/map-type has tall weeds you can hide in to increase your evasion.  This is nothing new to strategy games--tall grass/mountains/swamp tile, etc always make it harder to hit you... but in Massive Chalice, these weeds only show up in ONE environment-type--it's the ONLY time you find a tile that increases your evasion.  I took advantage of these weeds twice, in 25 hours of play.  Each bio-style has its own little exploit.  Some I like more than others.  But it completely keeps the turn based battles from getting repetitive.
Another example:  There's a weapon that has a chance to knock an enemy "into the future"; you don't understand at first what this means, but then, (years :P) later, during your NEXT battle, those enemies show up and hopefully you're more prepared this time.
And this is just one weapon you can research to develop--that is, if you want to research weapons at all.  I got to the end of the game only ever researching 2 things from the "items" category (health potion, and health buff) and never got to try the other 15+ items...
And I know next time I play through, I can focus my research into a different category and completely change the way the game is played.  And the nice thing is, I WANT to play again.  Especially now that I'm becoming more of an expert in the game's mechanics.
Lastly, art is SUPERB, music never dull or repetitive, story/depth feels personalized and is never disappointing, reply value is definitely there.  There isn't really any "fluff" in this game.  Everything has been refined to perfection.
The ONLY criticism I'd have for this game:  Sometimes it'd have been nice to play through battles at 2x speed.  If you had the option to speed up an enemy reveal, or enemy turn phase, this would be cool.  But really, that's it.  It'd be cool.
If you've been bored with new developments in tile-based strat games (but still love them) you will be over-whelminging engaged by this game.

In Japan, there is a category of games called “Mazoge”, the contraction of MASOchistic GAmes - a genre in which the design and the rules are aimed at putting the player in the worst position. It is oftentimes a derogatory term.
Just like Brütal Legend was an RTS under its ARPG guise, Massive Chalice advertises itself as an epic fantasy take on XCOM, while it really is such a “Mazoge”.
The odds are so much against the player it can be intimidating at first, but it also eventually builds up a world view that while only outlined, is very grim - I personally digged that aspect of the game.
This would yield very little rewards if the game didn't offer what I consider to be the best melding of strategic and tactical gameplay I have ever experienced. The family building, the research, the combat, the events - all tie up to create an absolutely chaotic and unfair experience, but a wonderfully creative one too. Never had I felt so tense in a strategy game, fearing that the difficulty might catch up to the progress of my families, or that a cataclysmic event might destroy one of the bloodlines I careful crafted. Unfair in a sense, yes, but those are the rules of the game and they create a really cohesive experience. Again, “Mazoge”.
The randomness of it all also means, sometimes, all goes so well, the game turns mundane - until the next crisis, “hopefully”, if I may say so.
I really, really like this game. But in all fairness, it asks a lot from the player : to play for 15 hours a couple of 'normal' games to grasp the rules ; to accept the randomness of what might happen to all your work thanks to odds turned against you ; to cope with the same limited recordings of the androgynous chalice...
Here is hoping that when watching at that Chalice, you might consider it half-full as well!

I like Double Fine, no, love is more accurate, but this is a serious misstep.
Gameplay: This is a pared down version of the latest XCom games that ramps up the frustrating parts right over the garden wall. That may seem facetious, but it even observes the same adherence to the passage of time, the meticulous planning of building and research, and the bitter mocking when a hero dies. They haven't included injuries sustained during combat, deciding instead to build those directly into a heroes core statistics by the usage of "traits" and "flaws". Your heroes do feel a bit more powerful as you can mow down twice as many enemies in one battle as you ever could in XCom and the monsters do provide a nice palette of obstacles to overcome. Of course, your heroes only live about sixty or so years which goes by surprisingly quick, so it is difficult to form much attachment. I suppose one is supposed to develop a fondness for a clan of heroes that you breed over generations, but it seems rather pointless when you're maintaining the houses much in the same way one takes care of an ant farm. Normally, I would not directly fault a game for copying another game's mechanics, but DoubleFine is a studio I look to when I want good design, gameplay, and solid writing. Which leads me to my next point:
Story: The writing is weak. There's a diad of narrators that fall so predictably into bad cliches and poor acting that I simply had to turn the sound off; no hint or narrative point could be worth that. Despite the game allowing you to choose a "Silly" and a "Serious" mode as far as randomly generated names go, I lost all love and respect for the heroes I was grooming when their nicknames arose as "Fishfingers". The game flits between wanting to be a comedy and wanting to be a grim war and mortality simulator so nervously that I can't commit myself to any emotion other than anger when I play it.
Sound: Aside from what I've already mentioned there is nothing special here, the sound is just passable and you will get tired of the soundtrack before your first playthrough is up.
I was very much looking forward to this game and was elated to see it pop up on sale, I will have to give DoubleFine a second look before I plunge into anything of theirs again.

So, when this game turned up here on Steam, I assume that most of people thought the same as me: This is like playing Terraria in space, with the ability of visiting and colonizing different places along the way.
I think that it would be fair to have that first impression. I mean, ever since the Early Access phase, there's been so many changes. Some were for good, others, not as much (at least for me). For instance, I really disliked what they did with the ship's fuel system. Either way, now it's a finished product, so it's useless to cry over the spilled milk.
Well, even though you have total freedom to roam around the universe (as long as you have the necessary resources and equipment for it), there's still a main plot to keep you focused on what you're supposed to do. The graphics are simple but ok, the sound effects and music are nice too. The gameplay makes a good combination of the keyboard + mouse combo, even though there're people who would rather play it using a gamepad.
Ok, so unlike Terraria, it's kinda senseless to build bases around the cosmos. That's because the fun factor of this game is to explore all around, so I assume that most of people would rather build their "operations base" inside of their ship. There're many crafting possibilities available, and NPC interactions, which can fetch you a quest every now and then.
Overall, while you have goals to meet, this game is really interesting and addicting. After you're done with them, not as much. I'd still recommend it to whoever is considering to invest their time and money into it.

By all means this game should not be fun but for some reason, I like it. Let's first see why it shouldn't be fun and then I try to explain why I enjoyed it anyway.
I first played Turok on the original Nintendo 64, many years ago. At the time, the game had a lot of problems, some of them still apply, even to the remastered PC version. The game was still praised back then because at the time, there wasn't much else on the N64 and it was kind of a new experience on console. Among the issues are the incredibly short viewing distance (improved in the remaster) and difficult controls (also not an issue on PC).
The problems that still apply, even to the remaster, are some ridiculous jumping sections, unnecessary tedious back tracking if you miss some required keys and constantly respawning enemies. Some secrets are a bit too obscure for my liking, like jumping into a random wall from some random ledge to find an illusory wall.
But that is a minor thing. The later levels, especially the last level, get really big and boring and you start to realize that it's better to just run through without fighting much. This is possible because Turok is fast, like, really fast. I think that is one of the reasons I like this game anyway.
The gameplay is really frantic, fluid and fast. There aren't any cutscenes interrupting you constantly which actually makes the game better I think. You are always moving, running and gunning. You have cool weapons which make you feel powerful. Also the world in the game has a pretty unique style to it, with that dinosaur and jungle theme. I always liked that threatening and dangerous feeling atmosphere in Turok.
The game isn't overly long, it took me around 7 hours to complete everything but I think this is OK. After that amount of time you have seen all the tricks the game can throw at you. This also makes it less of a problem that you cannot save the game anywhere but some sparsely placed save stations.
Repetitive gameplay with increasing difficulty. Get this only on sales or in a bundle.

The easiest way I'd describe this game is "strategy lite." There's an X-Com-like fight system, which can be a little unfair at times: every combat encounter brings the sometimes unwelcome surprise of a more powerful and more numerous enemy. It feels to me like Kalypso tried to nail the appeal of an X-Com combat system but fell woefully short. The larger world is straight-forward and reminded me of the gangster-business end of Godfather 2 (PS2), but is largely just a means to the story end - there's no real challenge to it. The story is good, and presented in a style which many Kalypso fans will recognize.
I would recommend this game to anybody looking for a break from the more challenging strategy games that we all enjoy dumping so many hundreds of hours into. I would not recommend it to anybody who is looking for a well-wrought combat system or challenging strategic game.

Omerta is not a terrible game, and I'm almost inclined to give it a thumbs up. Heck, I spent 30+ hours playing it, so you might think that's an implicit recommendation right there. But it's not.
There's enough going on in Omerta to keep you occupied in a pleasant, cow-clicker kind of way. But the strategic/RTS layer lacks enough depth to be really satisfying - every mission plays out in pretty much the same way, tilting from "how long do I have to wait until my next building? I hope I don't run out of money" over to "I'm printing money and the police are in my pocket" in about 10-15 minutes each time.
The tactical combat is pretty fun, but unlike XCOM EU, you don't feel like you're really making many interesting choices in the team construction. I've carefully balanced my squads between AoE shotgun-types and single-target pistol/rifleman. I've also just thrown a bunch of characters in with the best-rated weapons that happen to be in my inventory. Either way you'll find a way to win without too much sweat. So leveling up gang members and choosing their skills/perks becomes a forgettable side note, not the kind oi high-stakes, nailbiter moment it should.
I picked up Omerta as part of a Humble Bundle so I'm plenty happy with the purchase. If I'd dropped north of $10 on this, though, I'd feel cheated. Omerta has some nice production values, but the gameplay is a lot more like a Facebook/casual game than a real AAA title.

Just completed the game. Took about 10 hours from start to finish, though I restarted at one point so my whole playtime was longer.
Short version: I liked it. It’s got a nice visual style. It falls somewhere in between a casual game and one of those that takes forever to learn and takes over your lfe. It's definitely more complex, difficult and well-made than a casual game. I was impressed by the way everything was presented in a very accessible way, despite the mechanics actually being fairly involved. I wouldn't replay it (mostly because there doesn't seem to be much else to uncover), but thought it was great while it lasted. It's actually harder in the first half than after (basically once you’ve unlocked all the research it gets a lot easier, probably a little too easy). Even still, the developers still have a few tricks up their sleeves to keep things interesting at that point.
In Dead in Bermuda, you control eight characters who are stranded on a Bermuda island after a plane crash. You assign each person two tasks each day, collect and use resources, and manage their various maladies. The goal is to survive, explore the island and find a way off it. The characters each have vastly different stat attributes and various relationships with one another (there’s a husband and wife, father and daughter pair, etc.).
For the most part, this is a management-style game. To a smaller extent, there are small quests, dialog, but much of this is pretty linear, so you have limited control over it. There's also some plot twists that may come up also that complicate things a bit, once you're further into the game.
Your main points of concern are: their stats/skills, their maladies (fatigue, hunger, depression, sickness, injury), their resources, and relationships. Their stats, skills, maladies, relationships with each other are all interrelated and correlated in various ways and impact their effectiveness at tasks. Managing these elements is at the heart of the game, and striking a good, complex balance is what the game does really well.
To survive, you need to manage their maladies – if any reach 100%, that character dies. Ideally, you want to leave the island with everyone! As you research, you will gain access to new tasks which give you access to new resources or easier ways to produce certain resources. Meanwhile, you're also exploring the island, which consists of 100 plots, which nets you resources and sends you off on various quests. The quests are pretty simple and don't significantly affect gameplay, but I thought they were fun, and you meet some colorful characters.
One big plus for me was how the main points of concern shifts as the game progresses. For example, at first, finding food is your main problem to contend with. However, very quickly, you notice your sicknesses are building up and things you were ignoring before might kill you. (Which is why I had to restart, haha) But as soon as you sort that out, then other concerns take over, etc. Kept me on my toes.
To win the game, you need to explore the island, and I won’t give away the rest, but let’s just say yes there's a way off the island. In terms of strategy, it doesn’t have a huge effect, but it brings some variety into the mix.
I would say that this game is much harder and more interesting in the beginning half than the ending half. The hardest part is staying alive the first 15-20 days. Since you have limited access to resources, you have to be very strategic. I loved the first half of this game. Thought it was delightful and interesting and a very healthy level of difficulty. It’s well-paced and well-designed.
The second half or so, for me somewhere around 50 days in I think, gets a little tedious once you have researched everything and have consistent access to all resources. The quests provide some entertainment to get you through it. (The plot twists are also thrown in there, which may impact your strategy as well, but they involve a little more guesswork than I'd prefer. Not my favorite aspect of the game.)
There’s not much variation from game to game, apart from some randomness in the locations of occurrences when exploring the island and personality modifiers for the characters. As far as I can tell, there’s no new content that I’m missing out on by not replaying it, so I think the replay value is pretty low. I wish there were at least alternate endings depending on how quickly you finish the game or something, but whatever.
Overall, I really enjoyed the game, even if it was a little of a grind towards the end. For me, it hit a sweet spot of being both strategically complex and also accessible. Even though I would not replay it, I thought it was well worth my time and money. Definitely one of the better games I've played in a while.

First of all I would like to say that I'm in a grey zone if I like this game or not.
The Drafts/Tournaments are super fun while the regular vs-mode is "meh", and if you plan to play a lot of drafts this game will probably require money.
I would also like to point out some of the reviews I've seen here. Some reviews claim this game is pay to win. It is not. If you think about it any TCG is "pay to win" at the start. You should never start playing a TCG with the belief that you're going to be on par with players that have played several weeks more than you, it doesn't work that way. This is the nature of any TCG. You can't believe that you will be able to beat any player with more experience and invested time than you in any TCG with your starter pack. Be it an IRL TCG or a computer TCG.
Let's compare SolForge to some other TCG's like Hearthstone and Scrolls. In all these three games you can pay real money for booster packs. Does that make them pay to win? Well, maybe. But let's compare them to some IRL TCG's... NO WAY! You pay MONEY for CARDS that may or may not be better than mine!?!?!++ PAY TO WIN!!! PAY TO WIN!!!
You see how silly this becomes? Yes, a core element in a TCG is that it IS pay to win. But in all the TCG's I mentioned above there is the option to "grind" for in-game gold that you can buy cards for, and doing casual drafts in SolForge will surely get you started!
Another complain I've seen is that some reviews claim RNG is a major part of SolForge. I'm baffled.
In SolForge you play with a deck with 30 cards. You are allowed to have 3 copies of a single card. This means that you could make a deck of just 10 separate cards (such constistency!). In SolForge you discard your hand (5 cards) and draw a new hand every turn (in which you may play 2 of them). This means that you in theory can go through one copy of each of your cards in just two turns, and there are a lot of cards with good synergy!
Compare this to Hearthstone. You can have 2 copies of a single card and a maximum of 30 cards. This means 15 different cards in your deck, minimum! You can also only draw one card every turn (with some exceptions). This means that you would need atleast 15 turns to go through each separate card in your deck.
It does not take a math genius to tell the difference between 2 and 15...
Except from this the whole "So much RNG"-point is strange since RNG is a core element in any TCG. Some TCGs have more and others less.
TLDR; Do not listen to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t reviews, try the game because you may or may not like it.
