Iron Grip: Warlord is a game built on cool concepts that could have used refinements, and a bit more variety. I assume you saw that it's an FPS/Tower Defense game. There's not a whole ton of these, so it's good to see another option. Iron Grip: Warlord is neither among the best FPSes nor the best TDs. In a number of ways it falls short. Sound design is nothing special. The sound and music isn't bad, but it's not memorable at all. However, the game has a cool aesthetic. The visuals aren't very unique or inspired, but at least seeing some airships and soldiers in suits of conquistador or gladiator armor and stuff like that strays from the norm and sets itself apart a bit.
When it comes down to gameplay, I also have mixed feelings. It's tough and punishing, sometimes fun and sometimes bland. But at least it engages you. If you don't carefully plan, and then react on the fly (you get a bit of time before the first wave and then it's continuous), you will fail. The game allows you to rapidly switch between your FPS view (where you'll do all your combat) and your overhead build view (where you'll build one of a few buildings or traps), and it's kind of engrossing that the game doesn't give you any shortcuts around the map, or allow you to take breaks. The game plays at a rapid pace if you're on a small map. Enemies are good shots, and numerous. You need to choose your emplacements carefully, and your personal upgrades perhaps even more carefully. There's nothing worse than picking up a sniper rifle and shotgun and not being able to take down tanks, or any troops within long or close range. The build view is okay I suppose, it just takes a second to get used to. You'll understand if you try the game. My major complaint with building though is a slightly obvious one. There's not enough options. That really is dissapointing when you realize that there's essentially two towers-one for people, and one for vehicles- and two traps-one for people, and one for vehicles- and two assist buildings- a supply building, and a rebuild for your base. So it's very limited. You'll also find yourself counting on any member of your team to keep themselves upgraded and reinforced, because if a path even slightly starts to fall, you're screwed. Medium difficulty, is perhaps a little bit more than one might expect. You have to juggle a lot of problems at once. When it comes down to it, there's not a ton of enemy variety, but the ones that are in the game feel interesting enough(well except the cannonfodder), filling roles between being tanks, asassins, supports, and generally tough commanders.
So, in summary, the game is not going to blow you away by any measure. That said, for the price it's pretty fair. $8 for a decent co-op game isn't a bad deal, even if you only play a little bit. Just make sure you play co-op, as bots can't compare and very few people play online. 6/10

I'm very impressed with Massive Chalice so far.  The deceptively tricky resource management of heroes reminds me of a European board game.  Massive Chalice is the X-Com / Crusader Kings II mashup that I didn't know I wanted.

A breeding simulator bolted on to an excellent strategic turn-based tactical game in the style of XCom.
There's a threat to your kingdom, one which will try to consume and destroy everything - very slowly.
You have a stable of heroes... however, at best, even the most vigorous of them will only live into their 80s or 90s, and most will die in their 50s or 60s. Given that you must survive for 300 years, you're going to have to get new generations of heroes to continue fighting.
So you pick two young heroes with the best traits (hearty, strong, bright, etc.) to wed, and over the next several decades, they will produce children, who will grow to become the next generation of heroes to fight the good fight.
I felt that both the breeding and combat portions were equally compelling - you start with three types of heroes (hunters, alchemists, and caberjacks), and depending on whom you breed with whom, there are a total of 9 classes which you end up with, which combine traits of their parents to get unique skills (such as the trickshot - a hunter/alchemist, who is able to fire an exploding arrow.) Combat-wise, you've got to deal with the fact that you've got only five heroes (unless you're protecting a keep, when the two rulers will also come to the defense) to deal with potentially dozens of cadence.
The game also features typical Double Fine humor, which makes the game that much better.
Overall: I was a KickStarter backer at $20, and I felt that I got my money's worth out of it. From what I understand, it's been on sale recently for as low as $8, at which price I would say this is a total steal, and should be purchased by anyone with any kind of interest in the genre.

Massive Chalice is a turn-based strategy game that has the player rule over a land that is under attack. The defense force consists of heroes, which battle in short, turn-based skirmishes against invading forces. Heroes live for 70 years on average, but the player has to defend the land for 300 years. Therefore the player has to marry off heroes so that they produce children, which get some of their genes and personality traits from their parents. This way, the player attempts to breed heroes of good stock, so that future generations are better able to defend the land against the invaders who get stronger all the time. Sometimes a hero may leave behind his weapon upon death, which then becomes a family relic, that gains better properties over time when it is used in combat.
While the game has some original ideas and can be fun to play, it also has some very noticable flaws. What irks me the most is the lack of control that the player has over important parts of the game. Even on "Normal" mode, the game is really hard. Being hard is not a negative by itself, but Massive Chalice is hard because of randomness that is beyond the player's range of influence.
The most prevalent example of the game's randomness are the events that occur regularly. An event is a story moment in which the player has to make one or more choices, picking from several textual options presented. Some of these choices lead to slightly beneficial results, some of them lead to very bad results. But what result you get is completely random! There is no way to influence the outcome. You pick and hope for the best. A hero gets a positive trait, or a negative one, or your best hero might die, or you might lose a relic, or you might lose part of your land to corruption (and once you go down that road, you are on the losing track).
You also have relatively little influence over what genes the heroes get. Yes, they are likely to get some genes from their parents, but these might be good or bad, and they might get new genes that their gene pool did not contain before. Since parents only get a few children, it is not uncommon for a family of good stock, which you carefully bred, weeding out all the bad offspring by sending them into battle or to the Sagewright, to get wasted in one generation because the offspring gets inferior random genes or there is no more good partner available. There is almost nothing that the player can do to protect a family against that. Basically, the only thing that may help is calling forth new heroes, which takes about 5 years of research, and produces 5 new heroes with random attributes. Usually all of them are crap -- Infertile, Sickly, Clumsy, Nervous wrecks. Again, complete randomness.
Finally, there is the issue of the combat. The enemies are relatively weak for the first half of the game, but after the halfway point they ramp up in difficulty in big strides. And then the combat rolls are really starting to get on your nerves, as a hero that gets attacked might evade the attack, or might lose one or two hitpoints, or lose all of his hitpoints in one go. There seems to be very little in between.
The game has been compared to XCOM, and it definitely has a lot of similarities. But XCOM offers the player many more ways to mitigate the random effects of the game, both in strategic decisions and tactical approach.
Making the player suffer badly from the whims of random events is a serious design flaw for any strategy game. I therefore cannot recommend Massive Chalice. I have had some fun with it, but I am always interested in seeing what Double Fine comes up with, and got the game at a big discount. It may be worth a couple of dollars or euros to you, but do not get it at full price.

It's a great concept for a game. The idea is a tactical turn based strategy game that is drawn out over generations. So you don't simply manage a squad of heroes, but rather a dynasty and genealogy that you have to develop overy many years in order to breed great leaders and fighters for you to combat this ever-present demonic army threat.
As such, many of the threats you will face are not simply the battles but rather the slow passage of time, and the random events that can either benefit you or lose your heroes.
I find it very difficult and deeply frustrating but at the same time, I enjoy how involved it is. It brings other elements of strategy into the mix that regular games don't.
There's a bunch of small nitpicky things that bother me about it, but it's a good experience overall. If you're a strategy fan, it's definitely worth checking out.

Considering how old this game is it's amazing that it's more captivating than many modern FPS' I've played.
There is not really a story or much of an introduction, the game throws you right in to kill dinosaurs, natives and aliens. Sadly more of the latter two than the first one, but the dinosaurs are usually the tougher opponents.
If you care to explore and use the map feature you will most likely find all the secrets pretty easily and get rewarded with a weapon that can basically two shot the final boss (if you hit him well, I needed all three shots it had).
The bosses, outside of the first one, are a bit too easy, because you can easily run away and shoot them without taking any damage if you do it well. The regular enemies are fine overall, but I would have liked more variety at times (there is a decent amount, but not within the stages) especially in terms of dinosaurs. There are raptors and dimetrodons with and without guns and triceratop riders. other than that the dinosaur-like opponents could just be considered aliens as well. There's also dragonflys and beetles, which are merely there to annoy you.
The biggest issue in terms of enemies for me was the respawn rate. Dinosaurs always respawn after a while, and later on even the cyber seargents, which take lots of ammo and deal good damage respawn quite a bit (even though not infinitely I believe). I'd rather have more initially than run back and get randomly attacked in an area I believed I cleared out.
There are also quite a few platforming sections, but outside of a few exceptions they are pretty easy and give you a safety net early on. The hardes ones are ironically inside of secret portals where you can't die anyway.
Last but not least you sort of have to manage your ammo occasionally. It's not a big deal most of the time, and basic enemies early on can actually be one shot with a knive, but later on you might get phases where you get low on ammo for a few minutes. I repeat it's managable and adds to the difficulty in a nice way, but you can't just randomly shoot at everything without aiming and hope for a quick ammo refill. I would also recommend, unless you got really far into a level to simply reload a save instead of respawning. You keep your ammo but loose your backpack, armor and health above 100. So load your save and simply be more careful, because especially the backpack is very important.
Overall Turok is still an excellent game, and even though I would be hesitant to buy it full price I couldn't resist during a sale and I wasn't disappointet.

One of the most fun and unique RTS/Tower defense games I've ever played. Basically, you're fighting a liquid. This liquid flows from higher elevation to lower elevation (like liquid does). There are emitters that pour this liquid out of them at specific intervals. You have several ways of corraling and destroying this liquid. Destroying thin liquid with laser turrets, deep liquid with mortars, or distant liquid with strafers. Corraling liquid with terraformers to lower or highten the terrain or shields that shove the liquid around. Or, even combinations of the two with anti-liquid that doesn't damage your towers and can destroy the bad liquid.
There are several play-modes too.
The campaign starts you off with very little unlocked and very easy missions. As it progresses, you unlock more turrets, learning what each does with the missions getting harder and harder. Eventually, you have nearly everything and the missions have reached alarming difficulty, requiring epic strategy to beat, making each mission defeated a great accomplishment and very satisfying.
Colonial Space has a huge array of player created maps given ratings for each one with varying difficulties and extreme customization for each level.
Alpha Sector is filled with misisons created by alpha testers of the game.
Tormented Space and Prospector Zone have maps randomly generated by the engine.
This game is all about strategy, and nothing to do with luck. Love it.

If you've played Creeper World before, know that this is an
sequel. If you liked it before, you'll love this.
If not, then you're also in for a treat! CW is very, very good. People compare it to tower defence, but I usually describe it as a computer network fighting a liquid. The lines you see in the screenshots are the links between your units - if a unit becomes disconnected, it won't get resupplied and will eventually become defenceless. So, keeping supply lines going is incredibly important. The other thing is that your primary enemy is a corrosive purple liquid - it has no AI whatsoever, it just flows following the terrain. (Or sometimes it moves in other ways - the more scripted maps can have it behave in stranger ways.) The third thing is that terrain is everything. Perhaps the best defence in this game is just a really high wall... until the creeper overflows it!
This is a game about attacking, not defending however. Pushing forwards, often uphill, can be very tricky because most of your units can't attack upwards, and the creeper naturally flows down on top of you. Then you have to handle beach landings, and spore towers that will dump creeper right in your base, and runners that stun your units, and then all of these at the same time, uphill, with a time limit, along with all kinds of one-off scripted challenges too!
Later in the campaign you'll unlock units that can modify the terrain (slowly) and let you build a series of stepping stones above the creeper, or build walls to protect your home, or produce helpful "anti-creeper", or send supply ships to bridge between islands, or try to push the creeper away with force fields, or all sorts of other cool things. The fact that it's so freeform lets you find a style that's comfortable. I'm a big fan of terrain fiddling myself.
Seriously, this game has so many original ideas, and it's executed really well. Perhaps not the prettiest of games, but it's very clever, and it'll make
feel clever when you finally conquer a map that's taken you hours. I can't recommend it highly enough.

The game can be very difficult to get used to but
.
First off, the character controls like a tank. W/S to move forward and back and A/D to turn left and right. Remember those early games such as Doom where this was the default, and Q and E were 'secondary' movement keys to strafe? Nowadays keys for turning have taken a backseat to strafing, but this game goes back to the bad old days.
Secondly, the camera does not follow the character, so if the character is facing towards the camera then W will move him down instead of up.
If you turn on combat mode, A/D change from turn to strafe and your character will always face the cursor (which is strangely off by default), which makes a huge difference. Press TAB to turn on combat mode. In combat mode you will be unable to interact with objects in the world but you can hold CTRL to regain this ability (however, your character is frozen in position when holding CTRL so you can't hold doors and move back to open them, you actually need to pull them with the cursor while your character stands still - not a big issue but it's odd that you can do this with the tank controls but not the combat controls - hopefully the devs will fix this in an upcoming patch).
This however does not fix the camera and you will still feel like you are playing an RC game (controlling a Radio Controlled vehicle where controls will be reversed when your vehicle is facing the camera), which will still be awkward for most people.
So for fix #2 you can hold SPACE to keep the camera centered behind the character. It is annoying that you need to hold it and there is no toggle option but hopefully this will be fixed in an upcoming patch as well as the game is still in early access and the devs are still figuring out what works well and what doesn't. The cursor will be a fixed distance away from your character but it doesn't really serve a purpose anyway as your character will always attack forwards.
Combining these two fixes you can get the intuitive controls that we are all used to:
WASD to strafe + mouselook to turn the camera.
This makes the game 100x more playable and much easier to pick up and start learning (as it eliminates needing to learn the camera facing and old fashioned tank controls before playing), and players can dive straight in and start learning the combat which is really satisfying.
To swing your weapon hold the left mouse button. If you let go it will cancel the swing. You can also swing the camera around while holding the mouse button to perform stronger swings but I've found this unnecessary. What is necessary is to move your character forward while swinging. You will need to judge the timing and distances to achieve the best results but this is obviously made much easier with enemies always being in front of your character (instead of to the side or below in the standard view); it means you only need to learn one distance instead of several.
Ideally, you will begin to hold the left mouse button then as the swing is moving forward you want to hold W to make your character hop forward. This will give more power to the swing and hopefully you've judged the distance correctly and the swing will impact the enemy's head with the outermost edge of your weapon for maximum force. 2H axes are perfect for practicing this as when you connect with the wooden shaft you will have no effect, but when you connect with the axe head you'll get a very satisfying collision.
One this that is annoying however is in combat mode the character will only move in hops and cannot run. If you need to run away then turn in the appropriate direction and press TAB to toggle off combat. Keep holding space but be aware that with combat turned off your character won't necessarily move in the same direction as the camera - you are back to tank mode where the forward movement of the tank and the turret (or camera) can point in two different directions - ideally you should point them in the same direction but as you improve you can look around as you run.
The graphics and sound are simple but great; they are detailed up close and look good from a distance. There are lots of browns and greys which gives the appropriate sense of foreboding and hopelessness, and you will need the sound and enemy shadows to detect their presence around corners.
The game cleverly blacks out rooms as you move away from them so you can usually only see the contents of your current room and you'll need to get close to another room to begin to see inside even if the door is open. This is a nice touch and really helps with the claustrophobic atmosphere (you're in an underground dungeon so this is perfect).
You can inspect almost every object in the world and most ordinary objects can be used as weapons. Different items have different stats for impact, reach, slashing, crushing etc but unfortunately there is not an automatic equip compare function so you need to manually inspect what you're wearing and then manually inspect the item you're considering, you will also have to drag the inspection window a short distance so that it does not disappear when you open the new one. This does allow you to have both open at the same time for comparison purposes but it takes a bit of fiddling around each time you want to compare a new item. The inventory is just drag and drop which is nice and there's no limit on the amount of items you can carry but you will have a lot of stuff piled on top of other stuff.
The options menu has different sliders and the size of the sliders easily convey the amount of levels per setting.
eg. if the slider is 1/3 the size of the bar this means there are 3 different levels for that setting.
This was my first experience with the interface and it was a very positive one. The menus open and close quickly and there is no mouse lag or window lag.
Overall, the atmosphere is great and the input is smooth and responsive. There are a few gripes with the interface and character control and while these have workarounds, they are not perfect and can still cause small issues (moving around the game world in hops instead of a simple walk may get annoying). The game is still in Early Access so there is still time for these issues to be fixed. At this stage I would recommend trying the game to see if these issues are a deal breaker for you right now, and hopefully the developer will fix them before release.
At this stage I cannot recommend this game 100% but once these issues are corrected the game will easily get my recommendation.

One of the most addicting and promising games I played so far given the fact its still in Early Access stage:
* Innovative, physics-based combat mechanisms which require a decent amount of practice before getting somewhere. Once you accomplish to master them even at a basic level, combat turns out to be a rewarding experience other games simply cannot provide. One of the key factors is the mouse movement being used to create momentum and direction for each hit.
* Instead of distributing points on character creation for strength or stamina, the game lets you "form" your players body literally whereas height or body mass are part of the equation when it comes to character movement, resistance to hits, speed etc.
* Great atmosphere achieved through beautiful lighting, detailed graphics and a dark, ambient soundtrack.
* Once you are dead, you have to restart the current level which also adds to the menacing experience and leads to a cautious gameplay. If you exit the game, your current position and overall game state is saved though.
* Pretty cool inventory and equipment system enabling the player to wear numerous layers of clothes and armor, each of them adding different kinds of protection to the respective body parts in a fluid, non-static way (no slots for body parts).
* Great attention to detail, let it be the physical interaction with your environment, highly dynamic fights, sound effects indicating the clothes and armor you are wearing or decent AI reacting to players behavior and remembering his actions.
* 5 campaign levels so far and ~10 more are coming.
* Addicting arena mode where you can fight alone or with hired AI players in various modes (1 vs 1, 2 vs 2, 3 vs 3, Elimination, Fray, Pugilism). Requires some grinding to buy the good stuff, but helps a lot to get better in combat which on the other hand helps to survive in campaign mode.
10/10

It's...eeehhh...
I'll do a pro/con with more explanation in the paragraphs below.
I bought this because it had a "tactical, physics-based" fighting experience, or so it offered.
Skip to end for TL;DR
PRO:
-Great Atmosphere
-Incredible lighting
-Runs pretty smooth so far
-Fairly good customization (I didn't see any face-customization, though.)
NEUTRAL:
-Doesn't hold player's hand, makes them find out things on their own
-Unique, physics-based combat
-slow paced
-Exploration relies totally on memory of the dungeon
CONS:
-Physics-based combat feels incredibly goofy, like marionettes trying to make love
-Disorienting controls for both movement and camera.
-Unclear combat instructions may make some players think that the learning curve is too hard, though it's actually pretty easy to pick up
I think the idea's good. Execution doesn't really work right now though. However, I believe they can refine it into a better working model soon enough.
Here's my problem with the combat as is:
The "physics" part of the combat basically turns your character's arms into half-ragdoll half-animation that does more/less damage based on your mouse interaction. You can (almost) tell if your swings are timed right when your Player Character makes an attack grunt. You also have side-step dodges that can close distance between you and your target, or duck out of the way of an incoming blow. You can use these dodges to slam into your enemy, causing them to not land their hits as well, or outright miss by putting them off balance. Sounds cool, right?
Unfortunately, the combat doesn't really look (or feel) good. It's not to say I didn't get the hang of it--I've killed plenty of enemies without being hit once. But when the animations make the game look like two marionette dolls having a goofy slug-fest, it kinda ruins the feeling of the "dark-atmosphere, low-fantasy, tactical experience." Furthermore, swinging your weapon also feels goofy--this is partially caused by the combat-mode causing your player to look in the direction of where your mouse is pointing.
"But wait," you may ask. "Isn't mouse-look kind of a normal thing in vidya?" Well, not in this game. While not in combat-mode, your WASD keys run on tank controls. It's really disorienting and hard to get the hang of, and to have it switched-up all the time only makes the experience more frustrating. (I think this could be remedied by having a toggleable difficulty "training-wheels" setting that allowed the player to press middle mouse button to lock on to an enemy, and then show traceable in-game guides that allowed the player to practice their swings in combat, as practicing in mid-air/against the dummies doesn't really help in real applied combat.)
Another big problem I have with this game is exploration/looting. There's no shortage of armor/weapon related loot throughout the game. However, picking up a new set of armor doesn't really mean that much when I can't tell how much of a difference in damage It's making. There appear to be "stats" for all clothing/armor that shows you the amount of protection, and how much of a particular part of your body is protected. I suppose this only makes a difference in later parts of the game when enemies have better weapons, but I didn't notice much of a difference in damage after I layered my leather armor with friggin' chainmail. (I find it necessary to mention here that I also upgraded my arm/leg protection at around the same time, so it wasn't simply that the one section of my body that was most likely to be hit just wasn't armored as well) Save for the aesthetic pleasure, looting doesn't feel that rewarding.
Exploration. This is kinda neutral for me. I'm the kinda guy who draws maps on paper so that he can more easily navigate games (one of my friends who 100% the OG LoZ taught me how to map games like this). Yet, I can imagine a lot of players who would be totally turned off/ frustrated by not having at least the classic "dungeon-map that becomes more clear as you explore the gameworld" in the corner of their screen. I noticed the game had a compass, but it felt totally useless.
Finally, the lack of health items.

A surprsingly addictive game with some fun "RTS-like" features added in, Iron Grip: Warlord was one of my very first purchases on Steam and remains a favorite to this day. Unfortunately, what little community the game did have seems to have dried up and multiplayer is almost nonexistent. The single player campaign (featuring bots) is still enjoyable, but be prepared to carry your team to victory EVERY. SINGLE. TIME.

Iron Grip: Warlord is an interesting game. It's a combination of RTS and FPS gameplay (somewhat like the Sanctum series), with a gritty, almost steam-punk like feeling to it. There's plenty of weapon variety, and the game doesn't really artificially limit you in terms of what weapons you can use or have at any moment. The enemies come in vast waves, and sometimes include large, hard to destroy vehicles. The maps are all pretty well thought out and sometimes quite challenging.
The RTS aspect is somewhat akin to tower defense - you build fixed structures, and they employ either an attack (like a machine gun or anti-tank unit) or else are triggerable (mines, exploding barrels) or otherwise help your troops (by healing them or refilling their ammo). The main limitation is that you can only put them on flat ground, and there's a point-cost for each item you place.
The FPS aspect is more or less horde-defense. You deal with enemies in any of a variety of ways (ranging from mowing them down with machineguns to setting off explosive barrels to using a flamethrower or what have you). The FPS gameplay's not inspired, but it's definitely challenging at times, and can be very situation-oriented.
All told i recommend it because it's a good synergy between two different types of gameplay, and seems to have a lot of replayability to it. My only wish is that it had more maps.

Extremely nice to see game developers actually letting people play the first 5 days of their game.  It lets you see exactly how it plays.  The game becomes more complicated and difficult past those first 5 days too.  The game is clearly pitched at the survival aspect, but the social management side is well developed and interesting as well.  I feel like I am watching the first few episodes of Lost as I play the game, solving small problems, dealing with clashing personalities and figuring out what everyone is good at.  Then of course you will eventually lose someone, probably, and you have to learn how to survive without their expertise.
Don't forget to use your items, I have absolutely been saved by them.  Make sure you keep up with all the actions, maybe you will research a book which shows you how to solve your current shortcoming, or maybe you will find a location in the jungle that happens to have the very resource you need.  You can get your group in a holding pattern and stabilise, but eventually you will have a lack which forces you to move on or perish.
Lastly, I feel like the game is replayable.  You can work with your people a different way, or perhaps try to explore a different stretch of terrain earlier, or approach an unexpected encoutner differently.  It certainly is not infinitely repeatable, but I will certainly get a second playthrough and perhaps even a third out of this game.
I have only encountered a single bug so far.  After a character in my camp died, they no longer showed up at the evening conversation, but the others would still refer to them as if they were still alive.  A small bug, but a little immersion breaking.
Either way, I still very much recommend this game if you liked Lost or would like a slower, more relaxed survival and social puzzle.  Everything is turn based, so you can think about what you want to do.

Pretty interesting strategy and interactive indie game here.
See my "First Play on Launch Day" Episode 1 video here:
The game starts off with a very predictable start as a plane engine goes up in flames and sends it smashing into a forest in Bermuda below.  Everyone onboard evidently dies except for the eight random people that we have left at the beginning of the game.
These eight people are our game.  We need to look over them and try and keep them alive.  The game lets us know that if any of our survivors have any single state reach 100, they will DIE!  {gulp}  These five states are Hunger, Sickness, Depression, Fatigue, and Injury.
To make things more complicated, each person has their own thoughts and traits about them that will determine how well they succeed at different tasks you might give them, and even how they get along with all of the other survivors.  Only two of each persons five traits is revealed at the beginning of the game, which should offer plenty of surprise element as you play the game!
Sounds complex?  Fear not!  The game is well explained in a nice tutorial at the beginning of the game, and this is what I work through in my above linked video.  It looks like the game will offer a good challenge and you better have your leadership thinking cap on when you jump into this game!
I like the exploration part of the game the best so far I believe and that's where you send three of your survivors out to explore the island you've crashed on.  You'll come across different items scattered about and you must have one of your survivors take a "risk" to discover what is inside of it each time.  This is a skill check of their skills and if this check fails, a dangerous animal will pop out and attack your survivor!  It feels fresh each time and definitely keeps the game interesting!
So far, I like this game.. and will offer up a more thorough review after I complete more of the game.  For now, all I have is the gameplay video(s) I have linked above.  (When I play more of the game, I will link the new video above until I complete my first full game)
I hope this review helps in some way along with the video(s) I have provided.

Dead in Bermuda is like what if Lost and Gods will be Watching had a baby together. After a mysterious plane crash you are left with 8 survivors and must do everything in your power to stay alive. Balancing hunger, depression, injury, sickness, and more. On top of that you have social aspects such as love or people getting on each others nerves. There are things to help you through your journey of the island. Each survivor comes with a set of skills and specialties, that can be applied to multiple tasks such as crafting, hunting, gathering, exploring, researching and more. Survivors may be good at certain skills and terrible in other skills, each character is different and many elements to this are also randomized per playthrough. If you love management there is plenty to enjoy in those aspects, on the other hand if you love a mystery and story that progresses at your own pace then exploring the island is amazing fun. This is where Dead in Bermuda truly shines and where it truly immersed me in the world.  Where most games go for a super realistic tone, Dead in Bermuda doesn't mind straying into the supernatural. Aside from there are many things to enjoy here, leveling/skill system, great replay value, love interests, randomized environment, and plenty of Gilligan's Island shenanigans. The graphics are simple but have their own unique tone and flavor, there are times that I felt it reminded me of a bit of a visual novel.  One minor complaint is that moving 8 characters about by dragging them across the screen became tedious however, this is a minor complaint. In all I really enjoyed Dead in Bermuda and encourage you to explore the island...or else.

Dead in Bermuda is a Survival/Management game, where you the player get to control 8 survivors who are stranded on a island because their plane crashed. I know what your thinking, another survival game. But i can tell you that this game is far different from all those other out there, and that’s a good thing.
Dead in Bermuda does a lot of things different, for instance you get to keep not one person alive, but eight. And that is where the management aspect of the game comes to live. Each character has their own stats on what they are good at, and what they are not so good at. Sending out a character with the scavenging skill out to explorer, will not give you the best results obviously. So you need to be careful on where you send your survivors to. There is also a bit of a RPG style to it, as you can also level up your characters during your play session, and increase their skills.
There are a couple of things you can do during a single day. each day allows you to take 2 actions for each character. During the morning you can send people out to scavenge food, wood etc. And then again during the mid-day. So each part of the day takes a turn. Setting your priorities is very important in such a game. During the evening you get to divide the food for the entire party. And i really love how they did this, because with a lot of these survival games, a character takes a absurd amount of food needed to survive. in this game they are very happy with a normal single meal. You have different choices on what to give each person. a small meal which brings the hunger bar down to 10% to 20% or a bigger meal that does 20% to 40%. There are also smaller bite size snacks that will help with the lower percentage hunger. But in my opinion this is a very cool and realistic method. Obviously if you do not feed them, their hunger bar will rise higher and they will then need more food to survive.
Your goal in this game is of course to survive as long as possible and while doing so you get to research items and craft them for your base or for your exploration missions. Having people explorer the island you are on will reveal new locations where you can find items and other things to interact with.  Besides the normal stat bars, your characters also have other bars that need your attention, cause it’s survival game, so not all happy times. For instances you got to keep track of their fatigue when they are doing tasks. Their depression bar, which goes up when they see dead bodies or other party members talking bad stuff about them. But having a rest and let them talk to other people in the group will lower those bars again. I could go very in dept in to the stats and bars, but i am sure you get the point to it. keep the bad stats down, and increase the good stats. Another thing i just mentioned i really like about this game, is the interaction the susrvivors have with each other. You really get to learn who they are, and what is on their minds. A story is being told as you play a long. And that is something you do not often see in such games.
Another thing about this game that stands out is the graphics style. A 2D hand painted look, which looks beautiful in my opinion. Also the music in this game is very soothing to listen to, from relaxing moments, to the more intense ones. It really captures you in that moment.
But don’t get me wrong, while it looks beautiful and seems easy enough by my comments about it, it is a pretty difficult game as well. My first couple of play through i reached around day 13 and 15 before everyone died. Well who knew you would need water to survive. So a lot of trial and error here. But it is very worth it to play it again and again, because every day something new can and will happen. From what i could tell so far it has a lot of replay value.
For me personally this has been one of the most surprising games to come out this year, and i can full heartedly recommend this game to anyone, especially if you are into survival or management games.

Massive Chalice is X-COM plus King of Dragon Pass.  It's a neat game concept that doesn't make it all the way to being a good game.  I like the slightly zany art style.  The narrators get stale long before you finish one playthrough.
The events add nothing.  Do you want to pick door A, B, or C?  It's OK that you have no way of evaluating the options, because it turns out all of them will kill your hero.
Do you like Punnet Squares and genetic engineering? Too bad.  All the heroes are limited to 3 traits.  Also, the heroes play the same way whether they have +5 hp or -5 hp, so it's not really worthwhile to put effort into crafting a super-race.
Sagewrights, your researchers, are tedious at best.  You put your oldest people there, because age correlates with research speed.  Then they die, because they are old.  Then you stop gameplay, zoom into your research house, and take ~20 seconds to pick your next oldest person.  This isn't a feature, it's a chore.
Relics are a neat idea, but they stick with a hero until death.
This would work better as a turn based game at the strategy level, because there is no situation in which you adjust your play style to adapt to changing situations.  You just wait an indeterminate period and then choose options.  Heroes are assigned for life, so there is literally nothing you can do except wait until your heroes die in order to choose their replacements.

My only two complaints about Massive Chalice:
-The Children
This may seem like a minor issue, but if you’re going to use a style as minimalistic as Massive Chalice’s, you need to make sure the game looks good where it counts- in this case, with the characters. The designs of the children in this game look more like something out of Rule of Rose, and don’t compliment the art style.
-The Difficulty
On paper, the way this game handles difficulty doesn’t look bad- introduce beefed-up versions of enemies already presented after the halfway mark of the game. The problem is that this concept doesn’t compliment the experience- ideally, new enemies based around the strength/weakness aspects of those attuned to the chalice are what would show up instead, creating a kind of puzzle element to compliment one of the main selling points of the game- having to deal with good and bad genetic traits. The main difficulty for the player would be trying to deal with these new specialized enemies on top of the broader ones already introduced. The game would be taking what players have been trained on and forcing them to face the consequences of choices that they made all the way back to the start of the game. As it stands, the enemies are just there to make life harder for the player and are far more frustrating than challenging.
It’s these problems that hold this game back from being worth the price it’s asking for.

Certainly the best Broken Sword game so far, and one I can easily recommend--although with some reservations.
Despite loving adventure games, I can say I've never really been a big fan of the Broken Sword Series, the first one was alright, but due to the similar subject matter felt a lot like the third Gabriel Knight game, but with worse puzzles and less charasmatic leads.  The second Broken Sword game makes my list of worst adventure games, and the third was fun enough, but its pleasure came in the unusual platforming and stealth areas at which other games have done much better.  So it was that I never really jumped at buying this one.
That turns out to be a mistake.  First of all The Serpent's Curse is gorgeous.  I didn't mind a bunch of simple puzzles that did little other than waste my time in the first act, just because I loved seeing every environment.  So much attention to detail in the art too I loved the inside of Bijoux's apartment for instance, which caught her personality even better than her dialogue did.
In the second act the puzzles improve quite a bit.  It does in that act include one puzzle they should have axed involving a cockroach that is on the level of the cat hair mustache in GB3 or the inflatable duck to get the railway key in Longest Journey.  However, that excepted, Act 2 has a very nice assortment of puzzles including some particularly memorable ones in which you must decode a map and decipher a hieroglyphic language.
The plot is fairly interesting throughout, if a bit safe.  It goes exactly the way you'd expect and never really explores new territory, but that is okay if it's a story you don't mind hearing again.  And it is one which allows the artists to dazzle you.  Also on the negative side is a number of tiresome comic relief characters and an uninspiring will-they-won't-they dynamic between the leads.  Especially considering they have before.
I must agree with reviewers that you control George too much and Nico not enough.  There really should have been more balance here and in one place where you DO control Nico, it makes little sense.  There is a scene in which George and Nico must pose as insurance investigators.  George is an insurance investigator in his daily life, yet Nico--who is a reporter--takes the lead? Later, or possibly right before that scene, George interrogates a man who has come to see Nico because of a report she wrote on a robbery--wouldn't it make more sense for Nico--the reporter--to have conducted that interview?  It is bizarre.  And then, of course, there are numerous scenes throughout where it wouldn't matter which character you control except that it is almost always George.  Ah well.  I suppose it is a little thing really.
Buy this for the art and the puzzles in the second act.  There is also a story and some characters, those shouldn't annoy you enough to keep you from enjoying it.

Absolutely brilliant. I'd forgotten just how good this game was/is. One of two first-person shooters - the other being Exhumed/Powerslave - that took the genre and redefined it for a console audience in a way that didn't make it feel like we were being given a cut-down, second-rate experience, but instead something that was polished and thoroughly entertaining, while still designed specifically around the way that console games are played. Games for playing on the television, sat on the sofa, controller in hand.
Turok consolises the FPS experience fantastically well. Secret bonus levels! Collect 100 things for an extra life! JUMPING! Most developers *still* can't get first-person platforming right. Iguana perfected it the first time of asking.
The sense of movement and momentum in this game is spot-on, from the character's walking and running speeds - it's here that we're introduced to analogue speed control in an FPS and what a diffrence it makes - to that tilting thing that the screen does when you strafe.
Little tricks that you discover the more you play. Want aiming assistance? Turn the mini-map on. Not sure precisely when to jump when running to the end of a platform? Keep going until the view dips a little.
Everything else about the game is nuts, in the way that the FPS used to be before developers started introducing missions, "reality" and po-faced storylines. Who the hell are these people you're fighting? Why are some of them dressed in army fatigues and armed with automatic rifles and shotguns while others are in skull costumes blowing darts at you? Where the hell did the dinosaurs come from? Where the hell did the bloody *aliens* come from?
Also, dat weaponry. Every single gun is satisfying to use, not just the later, nuclear-powered madness. There's a sense of impact and power to your attacks that marries to the movement brilliantly.
Yeah, there are aspects that weren't great originally and remain kind of rubbish now. That first boss is a real pain in the backside and, I'd imagine, a potential sticking point for many. There are too many identical-looking caves linking areas together. But those things are forgotten about once you're past them. Everything else is good enough to make you forget them.
When this version initially came out, the 'overwhelmingly positive' reviews baffled me. Surely it was just a nostalgia thing, people's memories clouded by the fact that there wasn't really anything else available on the N64 at the time, once you'd polished off Mario and Pilotwings? But no. In its own way, Turok is as enjoyable as anything else that ever hit Nintendo's machine. Playing it again now is an absolute joy.

This is an excellent version of the N64 classic which feels 'exact' to the original, though with the advantage of keyboard and mouse. Truth is it's not exact - the fog is much further away, and the textures are better (though I didn't really notice this until looking back at the N64 version).
Whilst I struggled through the levels on the N64 game, I was now able to whip through them, slowed down primarily by the maziness of some of the levels which Turok 1 and 2 are known for. The AI definitely feels somewhat nerfed to cater for the expected N64 controls and pace, though I did lose a few lives here and there regardless.
The final level feels a bit too big for the sake of being big, but at least it didn't involve monotonously getting lost for hours. Some of the plasma weapons felt useless too compared to the other options, though these are critisisms of Turok 1 itself, and not this release.
The map editor is a fantastic bonus, though custom-made maps are few and far between. Shame, because there's some good potential with the objects provided by this game (as opposed to other options, such as Duke3D).
Overall I am very pleased with this. It was nice to run through the game and to spend an hour or two afterwards with the big cheat enabled, playing with slow motion enemies and way over-powerful weapons.

You can see from the big blue thumbs up that I'm recommending this game; so it must be good, right? Well, actually, no, it's not. I'm recommending it because of nostalgia, nothing more. If you never played the N64 original then you might as well consider this review a thumbs down. Despite the many refinements Night Daive have made to the original game it's still not good, and never will be.
So what's wrong with Turok?, you might ask. Well, other than the obvious aspect of the visuals, which can be excused due to the game being 20 years old, there's a list of problems that exist not only in this port, but in the original game too. The port is actually very good, and credit to Night Dive for a job well done.
The main issues with Turok, mostly left over from the original version, are as follows:
-Poor level design. There are many areas in the vast, sprawling levels where it's very easy to get lost or turned around. The map helps to alleviate some of the issues but is not really dequate. In many places vital areas are hidden like secrets, making progress difficult and replaying the levels a neccessary chore.
-Terrible hit boxes, both for enemies and your own weapons. The hit boxes tend towards the large side which isn't so bad for enemies, although it does look stupid, but will lead to cases of shooting the ground at your feet when you know you were aiming clear over the edge of a ledge.
-Poor audio/visual feedback. It's often unclear whether or not you are hitting an anemy, and even when you do the response from enemy is very unsatisfying. Enemies have no stagger animation, or indeed any response to being hit.
-Nonsensical arsenal layout where redundant weapons are not replaced or removed, but exist in the player's inventory alongside the superior version of the weapon.
-Lack of challenge. This is more of an issue with the port than the original game, as having access to mouse and keyboard controls in a game made for a controller with a single analogue stick makes everything a lot easier.
Those are the main problems I found with Turok. There are others but those are mostly nitpicks so I won't go in to them here. But even so, if you played Turok when it originally released then go ahead and give this version a try. The port is better than the original, certainly, adding many quality-of-life features that we have come to expect from modern games, but doesn't detract from the nostalgia feeling. I had a lot of fun with Turok, despite the game itself being pretty awful, as it always has been.

Coming from a long time MTG Player and Hearthstone player I really enjoy this game. I got turned on to it because I found out a long time MTG pro named Brian Kibler was one of the driving forces of this game.
This game seems to be one of the best games to limit the amount of randomness that can happen in games that have a resource system. You get to play 2 cards a turn (as long as they have targets when applicable), discard your hand at end of turn and draw 5 again. Whenever you play a card a leveled up version goes into your discard pile which gets reshuffled into your deck every 4 turns. So there's a neat strategy in which cards you play and when. Most cards have 3 different levels (with some having 4 and some that are just 1 but that get buffed based on what turn it is). All combat takes place in lanes (5 of them) which creates some interesting strategy.
You can buy packs and gold in the game but you don't have to. You only need to win 3 games a day to get all the special bonuses (which include packs/cards and silver) and you also get tickets for tournaments. My favorite game mode is there version of draft. You start off with 6 cards that are figured out based on a logarithm of which cards get picked higher. No waiting on other players to choose their cards as yours are all generated just for you. It's a nice approximation of a traditional magic drafting but without having to get 8 players gathered and without waiting for others to choose their cards,

Tactical hero breeding roguelike!  Thats something you don't see every day.  Obviously you get a combination of xcom like tactical difficulty thrown in with a relatively unique flat polygon heavy 'retro 3d' look which I'm actually quite fond of, mixed up with some rpg elements and a relatively fixed timeline to work against.
Yes, this is not going to be the easiest game in the world, and yes you can totally screw yourself  by making a relatively poor choice of family matriarch/patriarch pairings early on and ending up with an entire battle force of dim witted, puny, sickly heroes before you even realize what you've done... but the whole point is to take those lessons and try again to do better the next time.
Replayability is relatively good since you will likley absolutely have to restart the clock a number of times before you really master enough systems to nail everything perfectly.
I also appreciate the game offering you a choice of either 100% serious in-character/genre hero conventions or some lighter hearted, sillier hero names etc.
This is not going to be a game for everyone, but if you do like xcom, and more broadly tactical turn based games in general, this is by far one of the most innovative games to come down that genre in years.

Read the other reviews for in depth content of this game, I might not get too in depth about mechanics and such, I'm just gonna blabber for a bit.
I personally enjoyed this game and have played through it multiple times. It starts out as interesting considering it's initial concept involving heroes and trying to create and maintain bloodlines with good genes that can carry on to future generations, while hoping the bad ones don't... While it's true that heroes are bound to die, whether from time or battle, and thus you can't get "too attached" to them, you still can have favorites and favorite bloodlines. I've noticed a bunch of reviews whining about not being able to keep the same hero forever, but that's what happens over 300 years. People die. I always liked the system and felt it was pretty neat that my favorite heroes can live on in their kin with their genes and house name.
Make your favorites advance in level through battle, do what it takes to keep them alive for multiple battles, then make them a regent before they're too old to make heroic babies that have potential to be your new favorite! It's not hard to understand. Hell, if they kill enough cadence and get enough xp, their weapon becomes a relic that can be passed down to others in their bloodline. Cool.
I'd recommend playing this game on easy the first time around to get the swing of things, then try it on hard (if you feel confident about things), then try it on hard with IRON mode enabled (which just means you only get one save that's overwritten after each action you take)... I also played it on Brutal difficulty with IRON mode and I guess you could do that too, I just hope you don't start out that way.
The different difficulties are there so that once you pick up on the game and figure things out, you can apply the strategies you've learned from a previous playthrough and make sure you don't repeat your mistakes, while having a greater challenge to keep things fun...
The game is replayable, at least in my opinion. The combat system isn't the most exciting, and that's what makes it tough to want to play again, so I wouldn't recommend sitting down and marathoning it as if you had to beat it as soon as possible. Just take it easy.
Think about your choices carefully and decide what would be the best course of action and things like that, and if you mess up, then load a save and learn from it (unless you're playing IRON mode, in which case try your best to not ♥♥♥♥ things up anymore). At first, I played for hours, but for my following playthroughs I played for maybe 30 minutes to an hour or two a day and got plenty of enjoyment out of it. I now currently have 100+ hours and I haven't played it in a while but I noticed it was on sale for only $7.99 right now and thought I'd write a quick review. It kinda makes me wanna play it again actually, and I think I might.
Long story short, it's a pretty good game, though not without its faults, I'll admit. I do recommend it though, especially since it's on sale for less than half price... Give it a shot.

Fun game overall and a good, casual city-building game. Worth the $11, but don't expect tens of hours of gameplay.
It's light on content which means that this is a easy and quick game to pick up, and this is facilitated by excellent interface design. There's no tutorial at this point, but it's hardly needed, because the interface is intuitive and the tooltips are very helpful. Information on buildings, production, and needs are efficiently displayed making city management an exercise in judgement instead of a guessing game.
Resource management is also straightforward. Mines and foresters provide limitless supply, but some attention needs to be paid to the labour supply. Every resource and service building needs to be staffed, but you also need resources and services to attract and keep inhabitants. At the same time, the game is designed in a way reduces micromanaging - you won't be assigning jobs to individual inhabitants.
Combat is also very simple: there are occasional raids by vikings and dragons that will kill/kidnap your villagers and destroy your buildings. To counter this, you need to build walls and staff archer towers/ballistas and maybe even maintain some armies, of which you are limited to 3, which each operate as single controllable units.
There are some quirks to the game.  One is an absurd castle wall height limit, which I have not reached even after making towers whose tops have an altitude several times that of the clouds. I've also noticed a bug in which a selected army can't be directed to attack ogres; instead, you just order the army to the same tile that the ogre is in and it will attack it while they're near it but won't follow it as it moves.
Overall: well designed, easy to play, light city building game. Good for city-building fans and casual gamers. Will likely provide you at least several hours of entertainment.

The game is extremely easy to pick up. As of now, there aren't many things you can build but it is diverse enough to have a slight learning curve. After only 15 to 20 minutes, I understood almost everything that needed to be done. My first playthrough, I built a basic city on a peaceful difficulty to learn the mechanics of the game. After I finished, I continued to both difficulty levels. I'm still playing my current game and am really enjoying it. I had minor issues whilst playing but none of them really affected gameplay; the biggest issue is the game crashing to the desktop which is not too bad. All in all, nothing terrible.
The gameplay itself is interesting enough to keep your attention for the first 4-5 hours. After that, it does feel a bit boring due to lack of game content. After 4-5 hours, I personally had done almost everything there was to do in the game other than achievement completion. People who really love these types of game would really enjoy this area of the game. Pressing forward at this point and completing your kingdom is a fantastic feeling. Expanding to the borders of the map whilst still maintaining my kingdom was and is the only reason to keep playing after hour 5.
If you have $10 USD to spend on a city building and strategy game and have already explored other games like Cities Skylines, Sim City, and Age of Empires, this game will fit right in with your strategy library. While it feels far from finished, the developers are working hard to add content to make this game feel like a polished strategic experience.

Starbound is a solid entry to the survival genre that reimagines the familiar open-world-sandbox-survival format as a space opera, spanning (so the math says) 12 quadrillion planets. Without spoiling much: you play as a member of one of six races, and begin the game limited to the exploration of a single planet, but hunting for resources and fixing your ship will allow you to begin travelling between planets and stars, progressing an overarching plot that's linked to how you first ended up in the middle of galactic nowhere.
Of course, the beauty of open-world sandbox games is that you could let that grandiose mission fade into the background, and simply travel the universe for its own sake.
Starbound certainly goes to lengths to craft a multifaceted experience for the player; like any good sandbox title, it presents an amazing range of activities to choose from: you could start a mega-farm, build a space station, make like Indiana Jones and loot ancient tombs full of guards and traps, play landlord to a village of tenants...the list goes on. You could quite possibly never run out of things to do, granting this game incredible longevity.
Here is where it must be said: Starbound is not a game meant to be sped through. While it has its intense moments, players seeking constant high-stakes tension are probably not going to find it here. Even progressing in the plot requires some intervening periods of farming, base-building and exploration. It is best enjoyed by those who take pleasure in tinkering with the environment and its inhabitants, and in meandering gameplay where the journey, not the destination, is the reward.
The galactic sci-fi setting definitely helps make that journey all the more riveting. Whether intentionally or not, the vastness of the universe—and the manner in which the player traverses it—invites a certain kind of existential contemplation. You will visit settlements on countless planets throughout your sojourn, but most of them, you won't ever return to. All at once the universe seems both teeming with possibility and soberingly unfamiliar, and oftentimes you find yourself all alone in its remote reaches, wondering what makes any given planet—our planet, even—special.
This sense of unfathomable vastness that is so central to Starbound hinges, heavily, on its procedural generation.
An admirable amount of love and effort has gone into designing and programming the base templates: massive varieties of biomes, weather, furniture, clothing and architectural structures abound, quirky and visually-arresting, and often featuring unique descriptions.
The AI is also surprisingly complex: the NPCs interact organically with the environment and each other, rather than standing in one spot with the sole purpose of repeating a single line to the player. There's a lot of material for the algorithms to work with, and combined, they serve to make the universe feel endlessly expansive and detailed.
That said, when you've played for more than fifty hours, the templates underpinning the procedural generation become obvious. Architecture sometimes repeats, monsters often share features, and yeah, it could use a few more quest generation templates than the ten-odd it currently has.
Whether or not this works for you depends on whether you're able to suspend disbelief whenever you see a monster that kinda looks like another one you saw five planets back, or when you notice that a structure you're traversing is almost identical to one you've visited before.
To me, this has never mattered: after 200 hours of gameplay, I have yet to encounter two experiences that felt truly similar. If ever a building is the same as another one, it is populated by different people, or set in a different biome, and will probably play host to different events—and that can make all the difference.
Mechanically, Starbound is quite polished: aside from the occasionally clunky matter manipulator (the tool you use to manipulate the environment) that can cause misfires with object- and block-breaking, it plays well, and combat does have an intermediate skill ceiling—more than typical of the genre. Multiplayer is intuitive and adds value, especially to story progression and fixed missions.
The game also undoubtedly has problems that can pull some players out of it—most significantly the pacing of the early game, and the sometimes-repetitive procedural generation. That said, it also has fantastic modding support, and an active community continually putting out mods that enhance the game to suit all preferences—so if some aspect of the base game irks you, chances are, you'll find something that improves it in the mod gallery.
For what it's worth, this is possibly my favourite game that I've ever played, and I continue to find it thoroughly absorbing, even 200 hours in.

When you are admitted to a hospital, they place on your wrist a white wristband with your name on it. But there are other different colored wristbands which symbolize other things. The red wristbands are placed on dead people.
There was one surgeon who worked on night shift in a school hospital. He had just finished an operation and was on his way down to the basement. He entered the elevator and there was just one other person there. He casually chatted with the woman while the elevator descended. When the elevator door opened, another woman was about to enter when the doctor slammed the close button and punched the button to the highest floor. Surprised, the woman reprimanded the doctor for being rude and asked why he did not let the other woman in.
The doctor said, "That was the woman I just operated on. She died while I was doing the operation. Didn’t you see the red wristband she was wearing?"
The woman smiled, raised her arm, and said, "Something like this?"

The Broken Sword series had a middling time of it after the breakout first title, now considered a classic piece of gaming from the 90s. Between then Charles Cecil has dabbled in tone and format; The Sleeping Dragon was a foray into console platforming, while Angel of Darkness experimented with a decidedly mature narrative. But The Serpent's Curse is thankfully a more cohesive affair, one that stays closer to the series's earliest roots. Once again you assume the role of resilient lawyer George Stobbart and his opportunistic on/off journalist girlfriend Nico Collard. This time, while back in Paris, they witness a murder during a robbery at an art gallery. Cue convoluted religious infractions on the plot, casual globe trotting and some mystic revelations and the fifth game in the Broken Sword canon just about hits standard mileau. And though not nearly as well written as the first two games, with neither the profundity and humour to be seen across the many characters, The Serpent's Curse is still a charming adventure that fans will be proud of.

I still have a copy of Turok: Dinosaur Hunter for the Nintendo 64, but each time I go back to play it I simply can't control it. The outdated controls ruin it for me, making Turok lost to me... until now.   
I think it is important this remastered version exists; projects like this are great for the preservation of video games. Custom controls, improved resolution, and reduced fog in the game make me feel like I am playing Turok the way the original developers intended.
  
Turok consists of eight fairly large and open environments packed with clever level design, platforming, and gunplay that is heavily inspired by early Id Software First Person Shooters.
 
The weapon variety in Turok keeps the shooting mechanics fun and fresh.  With the exception of a cheap sniping enemy and some inconsistent boss fights I really enjoyed the classic shooting style of Turok, it is fast paced and keeps you on the move.
 
The speed of Turok and the clever level design make the exploration in Turok fun. The in-game map is basic but I found it essential to helping me navigate Turoks worlds. There is a lot of swimming, climbing, and platforming involved in the exploration, the latter of which can be challenging depending on your experience and skill level with platforming in a first person view.
  
I enjoyed Turok a lot and think it is a great classic First Person Shooter. The shooting mechanics are good but it is the level design and exploration that I enjoyed the most. If you are new to Turok and are expecting a straightforward shooter just keep in mind there is a lot of exploration and platforming involved. Turok is just as much about navigation and fast paced exploration as it is shooting.
(I played on Windows 10, no crashes, overall the game ran very well.)

Ahhh, the N64... While the controller looked like it was designed by aliens for people with more than two hands, the games it had and the way it utilized that controller cemented it into the hearts of gamers in all corners of Earth.
And when it came to the top FPS titles, there was GoldenEye... And then there was Turok.
Turok: Dinosaur Hunter was the first FPS I ever played, and it is one I have fond memories of. And while I loved the second in the series the most, I will never forget this game.
Story:
Oddly enough, the story was not told in-game, but was hinted at in manuals and other forms of media.
You play as Tal'Set Fireseed, a Native American from the Saquin Tribe as he is transported to Galyanna, The Lost Land, a land where time has literally NO meaning and is inhabited by all sorts of aliens, peoples, interdimensional beings and DINOSAURS.
However, this new world and ours are now under a terrible threat.
The Campaigner, a meglomaniacal cybernetic tyrant, has devealoped a superweapon that threatens not only The Lost Land, but also our world as well, as he masses an army of cyborgs and cybernetically-enhanced dinosaurs in a terrible plan of universal domination.
It is up to Tal'Set to become Turok, the Son Of Stone, and end the diobolical machinations of The Campaigner once and for all.
Gameplay:
I'll admit, the N64 verson was a lot harder to play, but this one is definitely better to control, though the difficulty is still there.
The game really does handle smoothly, and it does manage to feel fluid, without any hiccups at all.
The enemy AI is very notable, as they are vicious and can think cunningly and gang up on you, so be wary what you do.
Graphics:
Sadly, the graphics look very dated, but that is not imprtant to me. You can be a delicious cake even if the frosting looks as old as your granny running in terror in the rain. Even so, the graphics add to the charm, and to be honest, they aren't the worst.
Weapons:
There is an INSANE amount of weapons you can hold and carry, from the usual pistol, shotguns, assault rifle and bow, to a minigun, rocket and grenade launchers, a cannon that unleashes a NUCLEAR BLAST, and a fair bit more. Whatever you decide to tackle your enemies with, this game will give you those options.
Sound:
The sound has upgraded quite a bit since the N64 version, and while it does have moments where it could have been better, it is a far cry better than it once was, and the N64 version was pretty good for it's time.
Rating (1 being the best, 10 being the worst) 3.2 (Gold Rating, Four Stars out of Five)

Good old school FPS fun (1997 is old school right?).
Turok does not stray an inch from the tried and tested Doom formula: There's just about no in-game story, you run around, you shoot things (in this case "things" tend to be dinosaurs, aliens and robots), find secrets, and try to make your way from point A to point B in a series of increasingly complex levels.
Fortunately, while it may not be the most innovative game of its generation, Turok does all those things pretty damn well. The levels are largely fun to explore, you have a fairly wide arsenal at your disposal and most (but not all) secrets aren't excessively obtuse to find.
I would definitely consider this game to be a must-have for any fan of the genre who's already played the classics (Doom, Quake, Unreal) and who seeks something fresh to scratch that itch.
It's also worth noting that Turok was originally meant to be played with a controller on an N64, so you may want to up that difficulty a notch if you're going to be using mouse+keyboard.
Finally, if longevity is a worry, all I can say is that it took me somewhere around 10-11 hours to complete it blind and find the "main" secrets linked to an endgame unlockable. This was done in 'Hard' mode, which is not the hardest setting, so your experience may vary.
For those who like meaningless numbers I rate this game 7 Triceratops out of 10.

Lifeless Planet is a 3rd person adventure game about an American astronaut who crash-lands on a mysterious planet and discovers the ruins of a Soviet settlement.
The biggest thing you need to know about this game is there is so much walking.  Your feet may hurt by the time you're done playing.  This game is 70% walking, 15% story, and 15% puzzle.
That being said, the story is pretty good.  The pacing seems off because plot developments are bookended by miles of walking.  Honestly, the story may have worked better as a novel, but perhaps that's due to the literary influence on this game.

Unfortunatly, nearly every aspect of this game, from the visuals, to the story, to the sound editing, leaves something to be desired.  However, I still enjoyed making my way through the vast environments and discovering what this game was all about.  While the idea of a planet exploration game seems like it could be rather easy to pull off,

I made two maps, a normal map and one with scrips.
The programming language used in scrips is based on "reverse polish notation" concept:
- you put the values into the stack and the operand afterward on top of them
- the operand will combine the top elements (these are consumed)
- the result is being placed back to the top of the stack
The concept is very different from normal programming languages.
They say on the wiki that you do not have to be a programmer to learn this language.
I say this is true for any programming language.
And after you learn it, you are a programmer. Not an experienced or profesional one, but a programmer nevertheless.
Regarding the maps: I made them for myself, as hard as possible. Some people do not like hard maps.
I will continue occasionally to make maps inbetween other games.
I avoid playing custom maps to avoid being influenced by their ideas.

I've only just started playing, and while my TCG exposure has only been a few matches of Magic, and 10 hours of Hearthstone, I have to say that this is a super fun one. The card art is great for the most part. Each creature card has 3 levels, and the card art changes as the card gets stronger mid game. A really unique mechanic and it's fun to have the game evolve to a stronger and stronger level as time goes on.
There's no mana in the game, so you can play any two cards in your hand during you turn, with the hand being entirely rerolled each turning, giving weight to the decision of which cards to play. This is because each time you play a card, you level it up, so the next time you draw the card, it'll be one level higher, often unlocking new abilities.
The game's not flawless though, there's not nearly the same amount of polish as a game like Hearthstone, and there's no visible ranking, although the game has a hidden ELO system, and there's a new UI incoming.
There's a great card selection, easily over 400 cards, if my math is right. A bunch of different types of spells and creatures, although there is some overlap between them. The best part about the game is that it basically throws currency at you, so you're able to buy a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of basic cards. You get about 2000 to log in each day, and the most common of the cards can be bought for 150. I respect that, and I'm alright with there being rarer cards worth up to 34k. The game's free to play, they need to make money somehow.
Overall, I heartily recommend the game.

Pros
- Very strategic at times (wide decision trees for those who like to mull it over)
- Very intuitive at times (narrowing those decision trees, on the surface, can seem quick and easy)
- Brewing (executing that master plan with your quirky combos is excellent)
- Drafting (picking and pairing happens asynchronously, no advantage for whales)
- Free currency (daily rewards in order to collect currency and cards are not tedious or overbearing)
Cons
- Interface for all devices is slow (you will think sometimes that you are disconnected from the world, but you're not)
- Interface for all devices is bugged (which means learning how to play the game well involves a period of trial and error regarding some game input/output, e.g., time clocks, cancelling card effects)
- Some card rules and interactions are not made clear (and after researching this a bit, it appears to be more of an issue of lazy programming than it is an issue of making the game newbie-friendly)
- Features which have been promised for a while (single-player campaign) have been put on the backburner in favor of some which weren't ever really needed
This game is always changing, but this list of pros and cons has remained the same since I started playing the first Steam-released version.

ORIGINALLY NOT EARLY ACCESS, SolForge is a decent free to play card game with some of the easiest mechanics of any card game I've ever played. Choose cards from four factions (nature, fire, death, and robots), make a 30 card deck, and fight the computer or an online opponent. You get two actions per turn (except for the first turn, when the player can only play one card), and as you play you gain levels in order to play higher-level cards. Any cards you don't play don't gain levels, and any cards you don't use get discarded.
Several cards synergize for higher levels of strategy, but overall this is a simple game anyone can play. If you don't mind being limited to only two actions per turn, that is.
