Despite overwhelmingly negative reviews, I decided to give Massive Chalic a chance and have really enjoyed myself. I'm close to winning the game for the first time and will do another round. I still fondly remember Ume Graymarch, my first and best warrior and regret accidentally killing off her line 100 years later with a misthrown bomb by a drunk near-sighted Alchemist. My only really issue is with the two 'god' voiceover characters with their annoying voices and chatter.  If you grab the game on sale, it is worthy of your time and don't let everyone comparing it to other games cloud your decision.

While MASSIVE CHALICE proudly wears all its influences (Crusaders Kings 2, XCOM remake, Game of Thrones) on its sleeve, ultimately it does not feel like a castrated version of something grand - it is a fine game for its price and set scale.
The central gimmick of managing bloodlines is very entertaining, especially when you realise that marrying random people is not the way to go (by year 100 when you need diverse classes).
Tactical battles exchange XCOM cover management for knockbacks and stuns, forcing you to constantly be in motion, slamming heads into solid objects.
The length of the game is a bit frustrating - playthrough on normal took me 16 hours, while my first XCOM playthrough was only a bit longer - 20 hours. With a game much more abstract, leaner on story and systems, it drags, but by the year 200 (of 300) the "caring about troops" aspect kicks in and you just cant leave the clans that you have been fostering for centuries.

Mind-numbing drudgery.
Massive Chalice borrows from the popularity of Game of Thrones by putting in bloodline houses. Only people of special bloodlines can fight the cadence. These bloodlines come in the form of houses, each with their own name, banner, motto and castle name. Houses are completely cosmetic and at the start of the game you are able to choose five to be your vanguard at the start. It’s a nice little aesthetical feature that tries to make you care about your characters. The problem is it doesn’t work, because you progress through the game in years, passing ten years is nothing meaning that your characters die often of old age. In fact characters die so much that unlike a game like X-Com where you really care when someone dies because you have spent a lot of time investing in their abilities and appearance. In Massive chalice, the games time progression and lack of character customization means that you become numb to characters. It was to the point that I did not care to learn their names and rather solely based their usefulness on their age, level and traits.
Permadeath by its nature is only an impacting mechanic if you care about the death. Massive Chalice’s core design almost forces you not to care about your units. Because time passes so quickly it means that characters never really level up to a significant point so they never become irreplaceable. In fact the game design makes units become as meaningful as pawns on a chess board. They are very useful but highly expendable and you don’t put much stock in them as you do the other pieces.
Ruling your nation is very simplistic and keeps the focuses on making sure you have enough babies being born to provide soldiers in the coming years. It’s a case of building castles to house bloodlines and produce children, building the occasional building that helps with research or training and of course researching new technology. Researching tech allows you to unlock new weapons, items and armor, it’s also where you can recruit a batch of heroes if you’re running low on troops and it’s the tab where you build the few buildings available. There isn’t much in terms of choice when it comes to new weapons and armor, there’s a couple of interesting items that you can research once a certain number of enemies have been defeated. These items tend to share a trait that relate to the monsters it requires such as the boneshell armor that covers your soldier in a protective shell after one hit like the Bulwark monster.
The UI in the overworld parts of the game looks and responds like a touch screen port. The UI is overly large, bulky and provides no feedback upon clicking it. It’s almost as if the overworld UI design was made with the thought of a mobile release in mind, and to be honest this wouldn’t be very surprising. It does however leave a negative impact on the game, it stands out as not being the correct UI for a PC game, the size of the menus is a perfect size for a touch screen, not for a 2080p monitor with a mouse a keyboard.
Massive Chalices combat is modeled from similar games like X-Com. The game does not really do anything unique or particularly innovative with combat but it’s a solid tried and tested system that works well. There is a variety of factors in battle you must think about which usually comes from the combination of monster mechanics and the variety of armor and weapon effects. Sadly there is not a large amount of variety in enemies. Each enemy has a unique mechanic tied to it such as wrinklers who will add age onto a character if they successfully hit or lapses who if they hit you drain you of XP which can lower your level mid battle which will cause you to lose abilities. The problem with the enemies rears its head later on in the game when you’re just facing the same enemies over and over and the game just throws ever increasing numbers of them at you to try and make battles difficult.
The game is just a characterless husk, it works sufficiently well in terms of stability but gives no immersive experience. Double fine tries to put in charm with the voice acting of the magical chalice but it fails to charm and instead only serves to annoy and make you cringe. Massive Chalice is light on its content which was surprising when you span three hundred years and it simply does not stand up to games like X-Com. It has promising ideas that were not explored properly which are also spoilt by conservative combat design and a garish aesthetic.  It is certainly not something I would play again and people looking for a X-Com like experience from this should instead just go play X-Com. It’s a sad, deflated disappointment from Double Fine, who have once again turned a promising idea into mind-numbing drudgery.
I could sink my teeth into it. And it will hold you over until XCOM 2 comes out this fall. 7/10

I'll confess that I never did get the whole 'Massive Chalice' thing.
When I explain this game to people, I breeze pass the name, cop to the presence of a big stupid cup and go on to tell them that it's a fun turn-based tactical combat game, matched with am even better eugenics simulator.
The mixing and matching of various heroes provides a wide-variety of blended character classes derived from the basic Alchemist, Caberjack and Hunter (the Rock, Scissors, Paper of this game) archetypes. But deeper than changing the skills, the joining of bloodlines supplies a variety of Traits that modify heroes in ways ranging from how many babies they're likely to have (and of which gender) to increasing their basic attributes, which is a direct increase in combat damage, to how likely they are to drop dead from a heart attack.
Many times I found myself weighing who should marry whom, since characters made heads of households can no longer join in battle. Similarly, building the Sagewright's Guild allows you to permanently retire characters for a reduction to research time for new technologies and nation-wide buffs. Finally, a Crucible structure allows you to retire a single exemplary hero to train the next generation (providing bonus experience points) and shape their attitudes (by imparting Personality on others, a learned version of the Trait system that you breed for in order to create the best heroes). Selecting proper breeding stock and maintaining enough quality heroes to repel an enemy attack can be a challening balancing act.
As far as the tactical combat goes, it does not fair so well in comparison with its most obvious inspiration: X-Com. The lack of variation in maps becomes crushingly tedious over even a single playthrough. The small number of enemy units is disappointing, though they are interestingly rendered, looking like enemies unique to this surreal fantasy universe. But the Caberjack and other melee combinations are punished by the enemies' proclivity for stunning, knockbacking, hurting and aging (yes, age attacks are to be feared since you're spending 300 in-game years breeding heroes. You wouldn't want your prize stud going gray before he's had a chance to pass on his swell Traits).
Also the lack of any kind of overwatch command and no modifiers because of elevation or posture choices further limit the tactical options. Frequently I found myself wishing for more imaginative gear to research. I wanted items that affected the battlefield or changed the way you fight in more tangible ways than providing simple buffs, healing or immunities (the Skipping Stone being an exception).
Since you're cast as an immortal sovereign, shepherding your kingdom in a three hundred year holding action until the Massive Chalice charges up like a Death Star in a pint glass, various conundrums and questions come up along the way. These opportunities to pass judgments often create lasting consequences that take a few years to show themselves. While being simply text and two or three Choose-Your-Own-Adventure style choices, they add a welcome break from the immediacy of tactical combat and the more considered, long term choices in your breeding program. Unfortunately, there don't seem to be nearly enough of these events, with many of them repeating on a second play-through.
All in all, I enjoyed the cubist fantasy art and the unique enemies. Though I wanted more from the combat, I still enjoyed it, even if some of the maps sprawl too much for my taste. The eugenics simulator was entertaining, and I enjoyed (at least on the first playthrough) the occasional problems that my subjects would require my judgment on. I wanted a little more from every system in the game, but if you're a fan of turn-based tactical simulators and are willing to explore a fresh take on how one recruits the units for one's army, I recommend trying Massive Chalice... just ignore the premise of the big stupid cup and enjoy the rest.

I don't normally do reviews, so I will keep this brief.
This game is the start of something great. In massive chalice I see the seeds of the game which any warhammer/game of thrones/lord of the rings fan could love and harbor as a true classic. I will cover these seeds below.
- You are the immortal blood emperor of what remains of mankind, thats awesome!
- You command aging, powerful heroes to save the world agains TEH DERKNESS!
- You have immense magical powers, and total Dictator level control of your kingdom, as well as two hilarious advisors.
- You get to create noble houses and powerful blood lines who become more epic as time goes on, asigning them to the roles that will determine their lives.
- There are events which occur while "sleep" that prompt your waking which are not enemy attacks, such as hero fueds and such.
All that said, there are some other things that keep this game in ther "seed" stage, as opposed to the actual dream game we all want. I will list these below.
- The game tries to be silly and serious at the same time, sprinkling bits of a serious plot amidst two bickering magical halves a big♥♥♥♥♥cup (Guess which), heroes who range from silly to insane (not the good kind), and in general a lot stuff which broke me out of my epic role and screwed with my immersion.
- NO HOUSE POLITICS. Heroes and the noble blood lines and houses are completely loyal...maybe to loyal. Outside of events which are personal to individual heroes, and which may not occur at all, they never fight amongst themselves and never seem to be "alive". Though some of my heroes had some epicness tied to them. it required a lot of imagination on my part.
- No armies at all. Just the heroes and stuff. The humans, outside the usurper queen when she appears, are pretty bent on obeying you and doing nothing else, so you never need to use them, since monsters are not fought with armies in this game. Hard to feel like an Emperor without armies or politics.
- Not enough effect from events, not enough customization. I love my first playthrough, but sadly, the second playthrough was nearly identical to the first. I can't customize my heroes appearances very much, nor can I alter the appearance of...almost anything at all aside from placing buildings. And that is far from satisfying my builders craving.
- Lack of enemy units and type of attacks. To keep it short, there are not enough of them. The ones we have are great and unique and do require a stratigic approach (Wrinklers and lapses anyone?) to properly enegage, but the fact stands that there are not very many of them.

Bought this game on a whim a few weeks ago and decided to try it out just now. I've been hooked for the last 4 hours. Exanima is one of the most fun, well made, and challenging games I've played in years. Difficult to learn, harder to master, every combat encounter could mean life or death with oine wrong move. The story mode is labrythine and requires a lot of searching and exploring, and it feels highly rewarding when you make progress.

The long and short of it: Neat idea, clunky execution, combat isn't all it's cracked up to be, music/controls/UI are terrible, game will probably never leave early access as Sui Generis (the larger kickstarted project the Exanima serves as a prequel to) is stuck in development
So, the whole idea behind this game is that it has some physics-based combat. And boy howdy does it! In fact, this game has physics-based everything, which means you can get tripped up in some tables and your warhammer or torch will frequently get caught in the door because you the 3D equivalent of the puppet-animated sprites from the Sega Genesis era. Sometimes it's cool, sometimes it ain't, but it always feels like a complete mess. Despite everything the developers claim (you get a -really- smug little text wall the first time you load the game in which the devs tell you how deep and complex their combat system is), there's really not much to the fighting at all.
There's little variety in opponents: most of them (or all, if that doesn't change by the endgame) are human/oids wielding one of the weapons you can pick up yourself.
Combat boils down to this: swing right, swing left, swing down, thrust. Of the four, swinging right is the quickest and easiest option, while swinging left can be spotty since it's dependent on your position, facing, and where your mouse cursor is. Swinging down is perhaps the most limp and feeble animation I've seen this side of a Bethesda game, and thrusts feel ineffectual even when you're hitting with them over and over. You automatically block as best you can when you're doing nothing. You can do some neat things like put your hips into your swing to get more power out of it, but it's entirely likely you'll miss or hit too closely to your hands (basically think about hitting a target with a baseball bat with the bat impacting at a point only an inch or two from your hands -- you miss out on a lot of the momentum that way), so it's only helpful if you're in a great spot or you're really lucky.
The camera's awful and stuck at too steep an angle to really get a good look at the action. It also causes some pixel-hunting scenarios, as most items in this game are normal-sized and don't really indicate if they're useful in any meaningful way, so you'll have moments in which you're looking for an iron-grey key amongst a background full of dull grey stone which very well may end up shot into some corner of the room the camera can't see at all because keys are still physics objects.
On that note, the controls and the user interface are both a nightmare! You have to select the exact pixels of an object to pick it up, and sometimes you can have your mouse cursor clearly directly over the line of pixels that is a sword you dropped or a hand-sized item you can barely see but Exanima doesn't like your attitude or something and forces you to adjust until it decides to work. Just getting around is also needlessly complex with three types of movement: normal movement, which is straight-up early Resident Evil tank controls; combat movement, which is when you are in fight mode and you do this really bizarre drunken shuffle that centers your facing and movement around the position of your mouse cursor; and Diablo-style movement, in which you just walk or run toward wherever your cursor is while you're holding down right click. The way the different movement styles interact adds to the frequency of dumb situations, like getting limbs stuck inside doors or finding yourself tangled up in some clutter on the ground when you're trying to murder a dude.
At some point in the game I thought my hard drive was dying, but then I realized that it was just the game's music. After listening to it loop 20-30 times, I had to turn it off; I have no idea if there's any other music in the game besides that and hte title screen stuff. The crunch of a beefy hit with a sledgehammer or equivalent sounds good, at least.
Another problem is this: who knows if this game will still be in development this time next year. Exanima originated from a kickstarter project called Sui Generis, which is a much larger and more ambitious fantasy endeavor. Exanima uses assets and the combat system from that game as a testbed, and also to act as sort of a prologue to the events in Sui Generis. The issue is that Sui Generis has missed its mark by two years now, and Exanima is still very much an Early Access game. I would not recommend it unless you're -really- hungry for some dungeon crawling and you've got fifteen dollars that are burning a hole in your pocket.
It's a damn shame, because I would really like to see an interesting fantasy/dungeon crawler with some kickass combat, but this is simply not that game yet.

Creeper World 3 Arc Eternal is a fluid time strategy game,
that is a game where you can pause and even speed up the time, just like in city builder games.
Creeper World 3 focuses heavily on base building. All buldings need to be connected to a resource network and many of the buildings can be moved in a way similar to the Terran buildings in StarCraft.
The main enemy is the creeper, which is a fluid flowing out of emitters.
This fluid will flow downhill which is usually towards you.
You cannot build in creeper and it destroys your buildings if it touches them.
The maps have 10 height levels and you can build terraformers to change the terrain gradually. This gives you tons of tactical options. The simplest example would be to build yourself a high wall as protection against the creeper.
Beware that creeper levels accumulate and if you do not destroy some, it will flow over your precious walls.
You have various guns and mortars in your arsenal to destroy the creeper and you can even deploy your own anti-creeper, but this is just pushing back against the endless flow.
To stop new creeper from forming, you need to push towards the emitter and build a special building, the nullifier, and protect it until it powers up enough to destroy the emitter.
There are other interesting foes and obstacles, which I will not spoil here.
The bread and butter of the enemy is the creeper emitter.
Most of the tension for me was usually in the early game, where I needed to stave off the creeper while building my resource economy and it's often about eeking out tiny little advantages until I could stably match the creeper. After that, the aggressive phase starts.
There are dozens of interesting story missions with diverse leveldesigns where you need different strategies to win.
After beating the story missions, which took me about 30 hours!, you have a sheer endless supply of challenge maps, as well as tons of user generated maps.
Though I find that the challenge maps aren't as diverse as the story maps, so once you find your dominant strategy, they tend to play out similarly.
Creeper World 3 is also an excellent podcast game, since all relevant information is presented visually.
The game gets a clear purchase recommendation from me.
You can play the demo version beforehand, you can find that on the developer's website.
Creeper World 3 has a crazy high rating of 97% on Steam, which I think is because the Trailer shows you exactly what you can expect from the game.

Back by nostalgic demand, this fifth installment of the franchise is something of a return to form, albeit one that is as guilty of replicating the faults of previous games as it at revisiting the strengths.
Abandoning the 3D worlds and returning to a 2D style, reminiscent of the first two installements, helps the game recapture the appealing artwork style that enhanced the atmosphere of those first two adventures. Not to mention the return of Barrington Pheloung on soundtrack duties. Meanwhile voice work is largely of a good quality, spear-headed by Rolf Saxon's now iconic performance as George Stobbart.
However, it's the story that really starts to let things down, with the plot taking some silly turns that push the player out of the narrative, keeping you at arm's length from really engaging with the events unfolding on screen. There are also a handful of puzzles that are frustrating in a way that stops you feeling like you're really experiencing the thoughtful adventure, meaning that you spend ages pursuing an idea that seems right, receive no confirmation that you're making any progress, and then feel lost, only to realise that you were right to begin with... and not in some sort of rewarding "I'm a genius!" fashion, sadly.
It also feels terribly anti-climatic, though that's been a problem of every single Broken Sword game, but, for fans of this series, this is a much appreciated step back in the right direction, and undoubtedly the third best game in the series, though that's both high praise and something of a back-handed compliment.

A Review after a year in Solforge(from someone who's not a prior TCG player)
Summary right at the bottom.
After having played SOlforge for over a year now(having started during early access in August last year), I would to say a few things(good and bad) and hopefully new players can decide if the game is for them and whether they would want to spend more money and contribute to the development.
For those who are not familiar with this genre of games, Digital card games(DCGs) or Trading Card games(TCGs) probably first gained prominence through Magic:The Gathering some 20 years ago. Most have a system where there are multiple colours/factions/races and there are some differing mechanics to how you can construct a deck.
Ok, onto the game itself. The first thing will strke you about this game is the ease of learning it. I remember learning the mechanics in maybe 15minutes after playing the tutorials and a game or two - something not even remotely possible for more complex games like M:TG. This is actually good for players new to the genre, so as not to build fustration before getting into the game. Play on a bit more and you will also learn that learning is not mastering, and to beat other human players(and the hard AI as well), you will likely need to build a decent deck -- which brings me to the concept of deck building and building the collection of cards(because you obviously can't build a deck without cards).
Deck building in Solforge is super simple, with less things to ponder about like lands and the other myriad of card types in other card games. In Solforge, there are only two card types -creatures and spells- and no consideration of off turn acitivity like counterspells and such. Your deck can comprise of up to 2 factions(there are 4), and must have a minimum of 30 cards. That's pretty much it, but as I said if you are new to the genre, you will probably need some time to build a good deck. Along the way, you will realise losing is part of the process of deck-building-- what works in theory may often not pan out in actual games.
I will imagine new players having a little trouble getting some decks up in the first month or two while they build up their card collection. I started with 20 blue packs(some early puchase deal of sorts) as well as having the early access benefit of having access to all cards to experiment(just to play, not own them). However, the one BIG plus about the game is the speed of earning rewards. In solforge, there are 3 daily rewards(login, 1win and 3 win reward) and 1 for winning an online game. You may get boosters or individual cards, and will always earn silver, which may be used to buy any card which you already own. This system is especially useful if you dont wan't to blow like $10?(not sure how much exactly) on a single legendary which you may need more copies of to play around with.I recommend new players to play the easy/normal AI for a week or 2 to earn some rewards and build a deck before playing the hard AI or humans.Overall, having recently tested a couple of other games, I will say the rewards system in SF is pretty generous.
The gameplay mechanic revolves around the "ranking up" system of cards where often cards that are weaker early on are more powerful at rank 2 or 3. There may be a few exceptions to this balance, but these are almost always legendary cards. Actual turns consist of 2 actions - either a spell, or a creature played down to one of the 5 lanes. Creatures in a lane fight against the opposing creature in the same lane every turn, so no tapping or assigning blockers needed. Despite the relative simplicity of the game I feel like it remains relevant and fun.I came from being in the chess club back in school and my only gripe is the RNG factor of drawing the big rank 3 cards during the first turn of rank 3, but coming to a card game you have to accept some random luck factor will be unavoidable. Overall, for players like me who may not want to spend hours everyday figuring out the next meta-defining deck, combining generous rewards and simple gameplay makes Solforge a good 30minutes-a-day to destress type of game. For more experienced card gamers looking for a complex challenge, I'm not the right person to give you an opinion - however, having dabbled with M:TG like 15+ years ago I'll say that M:TG definitely feels more intense to me.
Lastly, I would make some suggestions which would make the game enjoyable. First, would be to slightly lower the prices of the cards. I'm not sure about the rest, but the only time I've spent money on this game is during sales. I have spent $100, which for a year isn't that much but not that little either, but overall I think the prices on decks/packs as well as tournament tickets to be a little too high. Regarding the gameplay and game types, the developers are currently working on a campaign, but if they are reading this, I would really like to see downloadable AI decks. This is a really fun card game.  If you like card games, you will probably like it a lot.  If you don't, you might still like it because it has a very unique and intuitive ruleset.  I love the card transformation mechanic, I like that decks are consistent (discards are shuffled back into the deck).  I like the five lanes and the way creature battles work--it simulates a battle on multiple fronts--though I think I would like it if you could choose on your turn for your creature not to attack (you could make it a defender, but that's a permanent solution to a temporary problem).  Because of all of these mechanics, this is also a good example of a card game that wouldn't work at all in physical form--it would be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to do all of that by hand.
The deck builder is rather well done, though I wish I could rescale the card size so I could view more of them at once (you can do it in text only, but I like to see the card).  The number of cards of that type you own is also right over the flavor text, which is annoying.  Deck building mechanics are similarly simple, yet interesting; there are four schools/kingdoms/worlds/colors/whatever and you can have no more than two in your deck.  You must have 30 cards in your deck.  Easy.  I normally don't like deck building--I'm a draft/arena kind of guy, from my M:tG days to the present with Hearthstone, but this game makes it simple enough to be fun.
The AI is also really good. I like to play against the computer primarily because I mostly just build decks and test them.  Hard computer is formidible enough to be interesting. If I've built a solid deck, I can beat them almost every time, even if they're using the same deck.  It is tuned to be a rather good gauge, I think.
TL;DR: It's free, it's easy to learn, there are a lot of interesting mechanics and interplay between them, and it's fun as hell.

Okay, just to get it out of the way, yes, this game is flawed. What game isn't, right? It's a platformer at it's roots, and the controls just aren't dialed-in enough for that. There's a lot of landscape to explore, and nothing much to discover in it. The areas that are dark are so incredibly dark and muddled that it's close to impossible to navigate unless you simply use logic to guess where you should be blindly jumping off into (once you get to a certain firey stage, you'll know what I'm talking about). The visuals and animation mostly seem like a game from over a decade ago (minus the shadows). It has flaws.
However, I absolutely loved it. The visuals though dated, lent to the overall feel of the piece being an homage--intentionally or not--to the kind of psychological sci-fi fiction from the 70s-80s I dearly love (the original Solaris, anybody?). It starts off feeling like somethings slightly amiss, then things get very grand very gradually. And it's the kind of subtle story you "feel" more than you actually understand in detail. All of this I love. The gameplay is also not the worst around. It's mechanically very straight forward, and once you get the knack for jumping and boosting, you'll be blazing through like a natural. The puzzle solving is spare, but enough to keep this from being simply an interactive visual novel.
Granted, my tastes aren't everybody's, but I greatly enjoyed it. It resonated with me in it's simplicity, yet implied depth.

World War II GI is the sequel to NAM, a broken Duke Nukem 3D ripoff that I don't think anyone was asking for a sequel to. Like NAM, it's on the Build Engine, and if releasing a game on that was audacious in 1998, it was nuts in 1999. Also like NAM, it's really bad.
Most of World War II GI is exactly like NAM, but in World War 2. You have to configure the controls beforehand to not be completely stupid, it reuses a lot of Duke Nukem 3D assets and mechanics, there are 2-3 kinds of enemy, the game is a constant storm of explosions and white noise, there's a woeful attempt at a plot, there are two short episodes, and you die constantly because of things you could not possibly have seen coming (unless you use Godmode, like I did). Therefore, the rest of this review will just be the handful of things that are different from NAM.
Sometimes a few buttons, like Fire, Jump, and Weapon Select, just don't work.
The enemy and weapon sprites are digitized instead of drawn now, which makes them look even worse somehow.
At least the land mines and airstrikes are gone now, or at least far less common. It'll mostly be soldiers you didn't see killing you without warning, not unpredictable explosions.
There's some sort of Morale stat that I couldn't figure out, although drinking and smoking seem to raise it.
There's an escort mission at one point, which is unforgivable given the game's faults.
I also couldn't find a list of levels or walkthrough anywhere on the Internet, which I think makes this the most obscure game I've ever played.
So yes, World War II GI is just a reskin of NAM. I'd say it's almost worse, somehow, with the unresponsive controls and uglier assets and escort quest. I'm not sure why it's on Steam, but please don't justify it being here by buying it.

Legit one of the worst games I've ever played. The over the top lethality would be awesome given the setting and themes, but World War II GI is only hard by way of stuffing every nook and cranny with soldiers to the point that every level is less "FPS" and more "Simon Says". You just have to memorize where everyone is each time you die and constantly be quicksaving. The game is a sequel to NAM and I'm not saying these kinds of situations never ever happened in WW2, but you can tell the developers just reskinned everything from their previous project. It doesn't transfer well at all, despite kind of working in it's favor with the Vietnam flavoring.
One of the worst parts of the game is that the artificial nature of the  props and enviroments is badly evident  Everything is just so fake looking. It's like the community theater version of World War II, and it's crazy, because as said, the engine could do way better with more talented developers(just look at Blood, Shadow Warrior, or even Duke 3D, which this is essentially a mod of). It's not like it was experimenta new technology either, considering this was released in 1999 and outdated even then. There's just no excuse for how cheap and lazy the whole thing is.
The one thing GI really has going for it is that getting a kill is incredibly satisfying, with good gun feedback and death animations. However, even this is spoiled by the extremely off hit detection(which is never a problem for the enemies, of course). World War II GI is just irredeemable garbage, but I guess that's quality in it's own way. I sure had a lot more fun noting everything wrong with it and writing this review than playing the game.

This game is good.
But most people make a mistake - they compare it to X-COM and expect an X-COM-like game. That's totally wrong. This game focuses on pre-planning, planning in advance and preparation much more than X-COM game and while strategic mode in X-COM serves to support tactical one - by unlocking more guns, armors and stuff for destruction of aliens in tactical mode - in Massive Chalice tactical mode would be a test of your strategical decisions and ability to allocate your main resources - time and people.
The main idea of the game is not turn-based battles - the main idea is managing of your heroes - which is both simple and complicated. Simple - because there are three positions to which you can assign your heroes. You can have them reigning (supposedly) in a castle, where they would produce more heroes (assuming that you've found a fitting partner for it), you can have them doing research in sage's guild, which would speed up many other things or you can have them training other heroes at crucible, which grants a steady supply of exp for all your heroess and allows them to also pick some good or bad traits from the teacher. All assigments are life-long and you can't undo them. All heroes, who are not assigned can participate in fighting off Cadence (though you can take only five of them into battle - you can choose those five out of all your unassigned heroes).
And then comes the complicated part - the higher level of the hero - the more effective he would be at those assigments - he would be able to train his children, so they'd start with several levels already, he would be able to give all heroes more experience at crucible and... no, he won't be more effective sage, as wisdom comes with age and certain in-born traits. And, of course, high level hero would be able to fight off Cadence better. The other thing you should take into account are traits - they are divided into inborn ones and 'gained' ones. Inborn ones are simple - characters can be strong or weak, have inborn heart problems or be very bright and so on. Those traits can be inherited from parents and can't be changed, so you should look - who are marrying with whom. 'Gained' traits are a bit more complicated - as character can pick them after parents, after the crucible instructor and even after his teammates during the mission, so one drunkard can quickly turn the whole group into drunkards - those traits add a layer of complexity as well.
And only after all that complex strategy layer comes tactical one, where your heroes are sent to fend off Cadence in an X-COM-like fashion - tactical mechanics are close to what you get in X-COM - every hero has two actions, attack ends his turn, so you can either move twice or move and attack or attack without moving. Instead of cover mechanics - there is positioning and visibility, since enemies that you can see may not see your characters, even without using all sorts of hiding abilities. Many abilities affect areas or lines or pierce through multiple enemies, so you'd need to do some positioning, before engaging them (and keep an eye on enemies trying to do the same) and eventually you'd get cool stuff, like bombs that create walls and so on.
So, in general, I'd give this game 4.5/5 - but I warn you that this game may be not fitting for people, who love only tactical games or only strategical games, as it would require combination of both to win - without good strategical management of your heroes you'd get an army of low-level weak clumsy dimwitted characters, who'd miss an elephant at a point-blank range. Without tactical abilities - your army of super-soldiers won't be able to win battles, which would lead to an obvious defeat.
Also, I've encountered some people, who don't like the graphical style, the style of weapons (a log as a main melee weapon and giant crossbow turned sideways as ranged one - that's too hillarious for them) or find the fact that there are only three main classes a bit lacking for their taste (though there are hybrid classes, which add some to gameplay - for example, caberjack (fighter with that log as a melee weapon) married to hunter would produce shadowjacks - still fighters with a log, but they sacrifice some of their combat abilities for ability to turn themselves invisible, like hunters do). So, if you are among those people - approach this game with some caution.

Just Cause is a 3rd person shooter with a forgivably cheese ball story and a lot of cool ideas. You play as Rico Rodriguez, a suave secret agent type on a mission to overthrow the dictator of the Caribbean island San Esperito. There's a giant open world, a set of factions warring against the currently established government, a grappling hook that can shoot you towards cars/boats/planes/etc, and a parachute you can pull anytime your high enough off the ground. Unfortunately, it is in the execution of these ideas that the game starts to fall apart.
To start, the world of San Esperito is truly massive and pretty impressive for such an old game (2006). This seems great until you realize that it consists mostly of long stretches of dense forests and tall mountains that make traversing it a huge pain. The various planes, jets, helicopters, and boats all do a well enough job at getting you from point A to point B, heck even jumping off a high mountain and gliding with your parachute is a pretty quick way to get around, but running on the other hand is completely off the table and the ground vehicles are arguably just as bad of an option with crazy amounts of oversteer making driving less of a convenience and more of a challenge.
San Esperito is also populated with a few cities, some villages, and a couple of army bases. These all start off as government/cartel controlled but can be taken over. This is accomplished by first completing the story mission in the given area which will shift the surrounding areas from "Government stable" to "Politically unstable", unlocking the liberation missions for the respective group you will be aiding in the takeover, either the Rebels or the Riojas (an anti-government drug cartel). During these mission you run in with your allies and try to raise hell by shooting as many enemies as you can and generally blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up. Again, this is a pretty cool idea, except in practice it can quickly turn into a♥♥♥♥♥♥show. Accidentally shot one of your allies while he was running around wildly in front of the enemies you were trying to take down? It is now his sole purpose in life to kill you dead. Did an ally bump you with his slow moving car when riding in to join the fight? The wonky vehicle collision will almost ensure that even at full health, you wont be getting back up. All of this gets even more chaotic in later portions of the game when both the police/army and your allies start bringing tanks and attack choppers into the fights and a stray missile sends you straight back to your safe house. Your reward for soldering through these missions is an area full a friendly faction members and some faction points which you accumulate in order to rise through the ranks of that particular faction, unlocking bases, weapons, and vehicles along the way.
Aside from these issues, the combat can actually be pretty fun and creative. The shooting is pretty basic (Headshots aren't a thing? come on!) with dropped health packs in favor of regenerating health, but cool tricks like throwing a grenade and then shooting it in mid air or raining bullets from above as you parachute across the battlefield help to spice things up. You can also highjack anything with an engine by aiming your trusty grappling gun at it and then reeling yourself in close enough to jump in the drivers seat, or just hitching a ride. This can add a whole new layer of mobility and strategy to large scale battles that you don't really see in most games. Its a shame that you can only use the grappling gun directly on vehicles as this could have led to some very inventive stuff.
Just Cause also makes sure to include the obligatory racing missions and collectables we see in most open world games. The races are pretty basic; you are the only participant racing to get to the next checkpoint on the map before a timer runs out. As tacked on as these are, I actually found them somewhat fun even though 8 of the 9 races involve the previously mentioned terrible driving mechanics. The collectables are out in the open for the most part and kind of a bore to collect. They don't really add anything to the game but you do get some faction points for collecting a full set. Speaking of which, before and after a liberation becomes available, the factions contact will be waiting nearby the settlements they are assigned to and will allow you to partake in side missions for some faction points. These boil down to fetch quests and "go kill/blow up X/Y", which are far from the most exciting things to do but will once in a while lead to an interesting offshoot, like "go kill X" but this time he's on a lightly guarded tanker on the ocean.
The core game is pretty short taking less than 5hrs to get through if you choose to ignore the fluff, like taking over settlements etc, in favor of rushing through the story missions. I also ran into problems with the games sound where I would be miles above the ground in a plane and hear a police officer shouting as though he was standing right next to me; not to mention not once being able to tell where a helicopter was in the sky based on the blaring propeller noises coming from seemingly nowhere. There were a few glitches as well where I would spawn inside buildings, fail to respawn completely, or have my helicopter zoom off into a wall or the ocean on its own after landing and getting out, but these were infrequent enough not to be much of a problem.
Overall, Just Cause has not aged very well. It can be a fun game when everything works as intended but it's short story with repetitive side content and a general lack of polish in some key areas all wrapped up in an 8 year old game keep me from being able to recommend this. 4/10.

I'm not sure I've ever felt so engaged in a fight system before in my life.
There are a few things you have to understand in order to have a fun time with this game.
First off, you have to understand the controls. Go into the practice arena mode, have a few fighs. Or, hell, go into the real Arena mode, grab a weapon, got the hub area, and just swing around a weapon at the training dummies. You have to learn the controls. You just HAVE to. If you think "ah, it'll be fine", go into the Dungeon, and get killed by the first enemy, I'm going to be very upset with you if you write a negative review with 30 minutes of game time citing "bad controls" as your reasoning. Shame.
Second of all, you have to understand that you will STILL DIE. Whaaaat? Yeah, I know.  Blew my mind. When I beat the novice arena I thought I was hot stuff until I took on two enemies at once and was bed-panned to death. Yes, bed-panned.
Third of all, and perhaps most importantly for enjoying this game, is that the characters in this world, the dungeon, and the inhabitants of it, existed before your character. You have to understand that you, the player, are not the focus of this world. That the Dungeon existed before, will exist alongside you, and will exist after you've left. This game is not player-centric. You are merely dropped into this world as a player, just as your character was mercilessly dropped into the horrible Dungeon. The mysterious rotten inhabitants were there BEFORE you. They aren't there to just to kill you, they aren't there just so you can get EXP. They are there because of reasons in the story you can only understand if you look.
Fourth, not all of the enemies are hostile straight off. Infact, the AI of the game is pretty stellar. They are programmed with expertise to act realistically stupid. They can become accustomed to your presence, they can become threatened based on your actions, they will attack if they feel they have the chance. It's really good.
Okay, so now let's get onto what this game has to offer.
-An excellent learning curve.
It was a blast to learn this game.
-A deep and well unfolded lore.
Finding letters, piecing together environments and character locations, (I think that all of the "enemies" are really their own characters) and all that jazz is really fun. This place feels as alive as a dungeon full of dead people should be.
Hm. That doesn't sound right.
You'll get what I mean if you play it.
-The most engaging combat system. (At least, from my experience)
The intense physics of the fights, how unpredictable yet predictable they are... it's amazing. The fights feel so personal. I've said insults to the inhabitants of the dungeon while playing this game. And not through rage, just because I got so into it. I cannot stess enough how stellar the combat is. It's intense. It can be stressful, if you let it get to you, so just remind yourself that it IS a game every once in a while. But that'll be hard because...
-It's incredibly immersive.
The physics, lighting, lore, non player-centricity (centricity? eh, whatever) of this world sucked me in and kept me trapped there like...like... like a vacuum made out of jello.
Let's go with that.
-An arena!
Not only does this game have a little practice arena for 1v1 fights (just for practice and fun), it also has an Arena mode. Permanent characters, buying equipment, hiring mercenaries, and a plethora of game modes. One of my favorites is Fray, which is a six-gladiator free for all.
-Updates
This game is actively being developed. Don't expect weekly updates, they are infrequent. However, when they do come, they always add something substantial to the game to keep you playing until the next one. Even if you run out of story content, you can always just play the arena mode (which is also being updated!!!).
-Different every time
People often complain that because the dungeon is "static", that every playthrough is the same. I argue differently. I've never had a fight take the same course. I've made friends with some of the inhabitants some times, only to have them turn on me other times. One of my favorite moments is when I had a fight in what looked like some sort of restaraunt tavern area. Cups, bowls, board games, and wooden stools flying every where as me and this "zombie" attempted to battle each other in this hectic environment. It was great.
-Beyond the portal
The first three levels take place in a dungeon. The time I become good enough to beat all three levels took upon me suddenly. My playthroughs never got me past the first area of the first level. Then, suddenly, in one life, I took myself all the way through. There's also checkpoints throughout the first three levels, so you can still continue playing until you get to the portal. The momentum you can pick up is astounding for the first three levels.
The portal changes everything. Suddenly you realize that everything before this has been a tutorial for what lies beyond that glowing blue entrance. And it is. I won't spoil anything, but things get pretty crazy. By the third level, you may think this game is getting too easy. I did. The portal...let's just say the fourth level changed my mind.
Negatives?
I have to talk about negatives, I guess.
First negative...
Well...
I mean it can be hard.
Difficult.
Challenging.
But never unfair.
Well, see, now it's not a negative anymore.
Honestly, for what this game sets out to accomplish, it does so perfectly. This game has a niche audience, if you don't happen to fit into that audience, don't feel bad. Another thing, the people who play Dark Souls and the people who play Exanima are not one and the same. I'm not a big fan of Dark Souls, but I love this game. Some people like both games, some people like one or the other, some people like neither. That's just how it is with all games.
But, for people like me, I enjoyed the game the minute I started playing.

Wow. Where do I start?... This game is amazing. First thing you might want to do is start the main story. I personally do not like it so I can't give you much info on that. There are classes, sorting kind of "Difficulty modes" Persay, like knight, which has full plate upon start.
Let's start mainly with development. Bare Mettle is a responsive, hard working team that I respect to all ends. They release updates (mostly on time, but then again bug fixes) And release patches bug free.

Combat? Oh boy.  Some people might want to say it's "Clunky" "Stupid" or that the camera is annoying and hard to control. But it takes time. I'm no master but I am decent and the controls are perfect for the style this game is played. There is a training arena, with 2 difficulties. Novice, and expert. Novice has less tactful AI and worse gear. You can pick up gear as you move along the opponents, same as in expert. Expert is pretty much the same except smarter AI and better gear, forcing you to change style to compensate for the gear. Then there is the other arena, which is much better if you've got time, the practice arena being more of a get in and go type. The actual arena has ranks, shop, different kinds of gameplay such a duels, (Selft explanatory) Elimination, where you go enemy by enemy but the thing is if you take damage it won't regerate for the fight. There is a hiring system where you can hire AI to fight battles where you heal, and a recruit system if you prefer playing still. Hiring AI is needed for 2 modes, Doubles and skirmish. Doubles is slef explanatory, while skirmish is 3v3.
Now to the physics, which is a main part of the combat. There are 4 attack modes. Let's cover the basic, normal swinging. You hold down your LMB and your character swings, 2 times depending on the weapon. It is a top down game and you can get more info from the trailer. 2nd attack is a stronger swing, This time you move your cursor and therefore your body with the swing, giving momentum and damage, But leaving you exposed. 3rd attack is overhead strike, double click and hold the second click for an overhead strike, Dealing tons of damage. You usually want to do this when opponents with 2 handed weapons swing and leave themselves exposed, Perfect for the strike. And the 4th final kind is stabbing. I don't see much use in this if you're not using a stabbing based weapon, But it is good if you're getting trapped as you can keep the enemy at a distance and try to get to a better position. Other things in phsyics include dragging items (story mode now) into your inventory or out the way. You can make barricades from things found around a room. There is weapons all around. An axe on a shelf? You can take it. There is lots of opportunities with the physics. Also fun ragdolls, Tripping, A certain enemy can send you flying with a single hit. Very fun.
Now to the music, Not much I can say but it most definitely is immersive, and matching the tone and general feel of Exanima with of course dedicated tracks for the arena and such things.
Well I think this wraps it up, But 2 more things. This definetly might not be your game if you're not into a slow paced sometimes even grindy skill based physics combat. But if you're willing to put yourself through that this game easily gets itself a 10/10. Beware the dagger. OP.

I'm finding it very hard to give this a recommendation, yet also feel rather bad for giving it the thumbs down.
It starts off as a great return to the old classics that were 1 and 2. The atmosphere is great, it's visually pleasing to look at and the voice acting is really well done. The puzzles are, at the start at least, well done and requires quite a bit of 'out of the box' thinking.
Old characters return, which is always nice, but some are just there to be there and be even more ridiculous than before.
And here comes the part... Later in the game, it doesn't just require the player to think outside the box, it actually gets down to, should I say, ridiculous puzzle solving. Trying not to spoil too much, I managed just fine on my own with the game, until there was a puzzle that just made absolutely no sense (to me) in any way. I thought that was fine, but then came another one and... Dare I say, even another one. Sure, not all puzzles are meant to be easy, but I found these to be a bit too over complicated, as if the developer thought they were clever.
Another gripe I have is that the voice acting of minor characters is off. A french person with an american accent or a rather obnoxious actor trying to imitate spanish. A pet peeve because it started off so well, then this happened.
When acting with a certain object, it sometimes doesn't even change to be interactive until the playe has looked at or interacted with something else. At the start, it's very minor, but later, it became a bugbear.
Then the typo's, there are so many in this game that it became bothersome.
Then there's the pacing. There's no quick walk or sprinting at all, nor double click to skip to next scene. Everything is very slowly paced and even the dialogue sometimes waits for several seconds to actually start. It drags the game out so long for no good reason.
And it's a shame, because the first half of the game is really damn good. After that, it starts to become a drag. I wanted to get on with the game, but it wouldn't let me. Throw in some obnoxious puzzles, have backwards logic, like not being able to interact with something when it made sense and that's pretty much Broken Sword 5.
I would commend it for being rather true to what it started out to be in the past though, but I simply can't recommend it like this. There are many point and click adventures out there that make more sense while having puzzles that work outside the box (Book of Unwritten Tales) that actually work.
If you're a fan of the series, it's a rather good addition to the series, but I'd suggest waiting until it's in the bargain bin.

I really don't know where to start, It's simply superb. The atmosphere, the scenario, the story, everything. Revolution took it back to the old days of broken sword making this game in High Quality but with pratically same mechanics from BS1 & 2, which are my favorites. Enigms, dialogues, everything is in place.

Overall I enjoyed this and am grateful to see that another BS game has finally been made, but I must admit that it wasn't really until I got through the first 1/3 of the game that I started to enjoy it. While there is a lot to like about this game -- the art, music, story and puzzles (in the latter part of the game at least) were well done -- by the time that it got interesting the game was almost finished. The main problem with this release is with its first half, as it spent far too much time self-consciously trying to reassert itself as an old-school point and click adventure game, which made it feel a little tired, like an old band trying to make a comeback after many years out of the scene.
In saying that, I still really enjoyed it but am not sure if I would have persevered past the first quarter of the game if I wasn't such a big fan of the series.

Updated 6/10/16 for the new client:
Hoo boy. The long awaited new client is... certainly something.
Pros:
-Much cleaner looking. I haven't tried it on mobile yet, but it fits my laptop screen flawlessly, rather than being locked into a square shape.
-Menus are easier to navigate, once you get used to the sub-header-like-buttons.
-I've experienced far less lag. Again, yet to try on mobile.
-Greatly enjoy the changes made to forging costs and returns.
-Battle flow is MUCH easier to follow, and there's a small card-log-bar-thing on the side of the battle.
-Filtering cards in collection no longer takes a small eternity.
Neutral/YMMV:
-Not a fan of the 'everything looks better in 3D' school of thought. I miss the 2D rewards chests.
-The main theme no longer plays in battle. It's replaced by something much quieter.
-Not a fan of the new card borders. Attack and health are easier to read, but compared to the old ones, they look lackluster.
Cons:
-There is a lot of feature loss:
--Untimed battles had to be reimplimented at popular demand, and is currently friend-only.
--There doesn't seem to be a way to sort cards in your collect; only filter.
--Spacebar will no longer initiate battle or end of turn.
--The 'Random Deck' button in single player games has disappeared.
-When selecting decks for play, there is no scroll bar to indicate the deck buttons can be dragged upwards.
-Many of the visual effects are very slow, and many of them are unnecessary. You must wait for them to finish before continuing on.
-Single player battles no longer appear to contribute to daily rewards.
-'Newest Set Only' packs are still gold only.
-There no longer seems to be a booster pack reward for logging in.
In my opinion, the pros of the new client do not outweigh the cons at this time. After such a long wait, it's frustrating to have the client take away so many of the features that were crucial to my enjoyment of the game. I primarily played SolForge on my breaks and lunches at work, earning my dailys vs the computer because of slow and unreliable connections.
On top of that, many battles now take several minutes longer because of superficial visual effects that cannot be turned off, only toned down. Turns used to be able to be played in a couple of taps and around ten seconds each.
I admit the client looks, and feels, more polished, but it is ultimately disappointing. I had hoped the new client would bring in improved functionality, not... unnecessary new glowing, 3D effects. The team has promised that they will be reimplimenting a number of features in time, but who knows when those days will arrive.

Broken Sword 1 and 2 were truly brilliant, clever, inspiring and enjoyable games, and I am one of the many who feel the move to 3D for Broken Sword 3 and 4 was a tragic, but understandable mistake.
Broken Sword 5 has finally recaptured the magic and charm that the first two games brought us. It's engaging, full of life, mystery and oozes such appealing gameplay. I am so glad they have finally brought us a Broken Sword worthy of the name. I would, and do, recommend this game and it's predecessors. If I could, I'd throw any amount of money they needed to make Broken Sword 6, the games are that good.

Summary:
Constructed: Pay to win.
Draft: Fun.
Let me tell you a story why you don't want to play constructed with a slim wallet.
At the beginning, my starter deck was fine, I tried to make the best out of it with more or less success. Then I was lucky enough to open a Tarsus Deathweaver from a booster pack, forged 2 more, and built a whole new synergy-based deck around it. Only commons and rares, a couple of heroics and no legendaries. It worked literally awesome, I won 80% of my matches even against players with better cards overall.
After a while, I felt, I'm being paired agains players who had spent a bunch of money to buy the same starter deck 3 times (since this is the most reliable way to get legendaries). Now, I can only win 20% of my matches because in the other 80%, my opponents present more legendaries in their first 4 turns then I have in my whole collection.
You might feel tempting to buy legendary chests. Once you spend money on the game to play better constructed deck, you are part of the big grinding. The daily rewards are far not enough to get good cards.
On the other hand, drafts are suprisingly good. The system works differently than anything else I've ever seen. You draft alone, which means no other players are involved in your draft procedure, thus you can draft in your own pace. Once you drafted the 30 cards, it becomes your deck and you are now ready to play your matches. However, you don't need to play them on the spot! Play them whenever you have time. If you're too tired in the evening, you can draft the cards and play the games on the next day or whenever you want. This means you  don't need to spend 1-2 hours to draft and play at the same time.
The game itself is fun, but the power creep between rares and commons is ridiculous. I've never seen a game with such a "pay to win" level.

I've followed the creeper series since it began and each game has been rewarding and worth each hour spent playing it. If you are looking for a strategy game to burn hours on with a degree of challenge and occasional thinking outside the box, this is your game. Also, there is player content and countless other implemented game types which keep you playing the game even after you've beaten the core element.

It's a RTS that's all about area control and down-to-the-second resource management. The puzzle of a map's solution can be digested simply, piece by piece, but by the end of each match you'll have built an eye-bogglign mesh of energy and weapons. The craziest innovation is: the enemy is a fluid, occupying a volume of space and flowing down hills, not a set of discrete units coming at you one-by-one.
Building upon CW1 and CW2 combines best of both of them. Highly recommended.

A simple yet amazingly versatile concept: Build against goo.
In Creeper World 3 you take command of an automated base that gathers energy and ore and uses it to supply a diversity of weapons and utility tools, such as terraforming, to survive an seemingly endless onslaught of an oozy, purple substance called "Creeper".
Much like the Creeper that some of you know form Starcraft, this slow flood will damage your buildings.
In order to obtain, hold or destory a range of objectives, you will have to protect your base by clever build defences, until it provides enough energy to conquer and scrub-free new land. New land means new buildingspace and more energy and the circle repeats till victory.
The strong side of this strategy puzzle game is, that the way you expand is totally up to you.
Artillery and dropping additional bases is my recommended tactic.
It is not an easy game.
Players of Starcraft or similar micro/macro skill based RTS games will probably enjoy the level of APM that is needed to hunt the online highscores in this game.
Apart from being a challenging and fun strategy and puzzle game, Creeper World also has an own storyline.
A space captain and an ancient AI take on a seemingly hopeless battle against an alien race that teleports emitters of Creeper onto every planet which ever existed. As they try to understand the relentless hatred of their alien adversaries, the duo of lone survivors discovers a conspiracy that seems to be encoded into the very fabric of the universe itself.
It tends to stretch dialogues to create tention, which works but is a bit exhausting. Also the characters are aggressively unaware of the mysteries that surround them. But perhaps that's just me.

Lifeless Planet is a beautifully atomspheric adventure game, throwing you in the space suit of an astronaut who, after a long journey through space, reaches a mysterious planet in search of life & potentially a new home for humanity. On arrival, you discover you are alone, isolated on a planet seemingly devoid of life, yet strangely there is a Soviet town abandoned long ago. How can this be & what has happened here? As the story unfolds, & you explore more of this intriguing alien world, you soon realise there is a much more going on than meets the eye. The planet is not as lifeless as it seems...
The sense of exploration, uniqueness in the alien world along with the snippets of story that you unlock through your progression was most enjoyable & kept me wanting to progress to reveal more.
Sound effects & musical score were also strong, & graphically there is also a cool film grain effect & blurring of the edges of the screen that add greatly to the experience. Would have been epic in first-person view to really enhance the claustrophobic feel of being stuck in the space suit on an alien world.
For those who love their Sci-fi movies, you will also come across many scenes throughout that feel somewhat familar (in a good way), yet meld together well. Futuristic yet retro, reminding you of old classic 50-60s B-Grade Sci-Fi, cold war era themes & some modern storytelling elements.
When looking past these positives there are some parts of the game that I found lacking from making this a really excellent game. The controls for one, although basic & suitable for the layback style of gameplay are awkward. It is easy to mis-jump, your jetpack is limited in function (essentially only providing a double-jump type mechanic to traverse larger areas) & the puzzle elements feel somewhat clunky & difficult to complete. Even though the puzzles themselves are rather simple. It also didn't help things when you respawn (this will happen a lot!) facing the wrong direction all the time is very disorienting.
Dark, creepy sections that occur in several stages are way too dark, with only a tickbox option to lighten the scene in menus. You have a flashlight, but does little which is most frustrating at times. It really needs a gamma or brightness slider.
There are also the 'emersion breaking' elements, such as there always being an oxygen tank just when you need it, or dynamite just near where you need to blow your way through a blocked path or a nice round rock (unlike anything else in the surrounding enviroment) just at the right spot to jump to a higher platform. It seemed to lack some creativity in level design in this regards when elements like this are introduced essentially just for the sake of it.
Most cut-scenes are limited being less than 30secs with most of the story elements experienced through translated logs found. This felt like a bit of a missed opportunity to really expand on the adventure; still good overall (& I am being picky to a degree) but could have been exceptional if the story continued as strongly as it began!
Some later sections of the game feel padded out, with no real content or interesting things to see, just more running & jumping. Other parts are really awe-inspiring so it quite a mix. Some of the final levels just seem to go on & on without any purpose other than to lengthen the game. The experience would have more impact if the overall length was reduced by maybe 30% or so in my view. While shortening some areas, some larger cut-scenes & more back story to your character (only touched on for most of the game) would have been great!
Although not quite as good as my expectations coming into Lifeless Planet, I still thoroughly enjoyed the story, the implications of the story (not to give anything away) & the final reveal. It was an interesting conclusion. Overall a fun & occasionally disturbing experience!

World War II GI is a first-person shooter set during the events of World War II, developed by TNT Team and published by GT Interactive Software and released in 1999 as the direct sequel to NAM.
World War II GI was later re-released on Steam at the end of 2015, with Retroism and Night Dive Studios as the publishers.
The Steam version of World War GI  also has the Platoon Leader Expansion which contains three single player levels. One WWII Pacific and two Vietnam War scenarios with many new effects and features not seen in the original game.
In World War II GI you play as G.I. (Government Issue) Corporal Gerardi of the 101st Airborne Division, sent in to wipe forces of the Wehrmacht and Schutzstaffel (SS) soldiers. The game sets the player in the middle of  World War II scenarios like the D-Day beach landings during the Invasion of Normandy, assaults on equipment and supply depots throughout 30 levels divided into four episodes.
During the game you to deal with different types of enemy infantry, mine-fields, air strikes, tanks and many more that will block your path towards the end of every level.
Different from NAM is that when you pick up medic packs, you have to stand still in order use you bandage to receive health, the environment and weapons and their functionalities.
For me the game was very exciting but quite hard. I had a hard time dealing with the first mission on D-Day to get through because there is little to no cover. I noticed that several weapons functioned strange and it looked like it made use of a burst mode. Sometimes I clicked but the gun didn't fire as if a trigger did not respond . I also had find it hard to deal with tanks when not having rocket launchers but only C4 charges which makes the game quite challenging.
Saving multiple times while playing World War II GI is a good thing to do but don't do this when you are being shot or wandering through large open areas otherwise your saved progress can be a total disaster by limitless dying when the save game is being loaded.
I really enjoyed this game because of the complex level designs and variation of locations and scenarios like assault or defense. If you have played the Doom series, Duke Nukem 3D, Blood (One Unit Whole), Shadow Warrior, Redneck Rampage you will probably like this game because of the Build game engine.
I highly recommend this game to people who like challenging retro pixelated first-person shooters with great gameplay and level design, certainly when the game is on sale!

I know that giving a game a recommendation for having a lot of potential is generally frowned upon, what with so few games actually delivering on their promises these days. So let me start off by saying that this game is a charming, addicting little game, and well worth the price of $11 CAD.
The graphics are pretty basic but the simple colour-enriched style coupled with the calm soundtrack give this game a really cute charm. It's downright relaxing at points. It's a very fun game for people who like tycoon-style games, a pointless city-sprawl that requires a bit of forthinking and a lot of trial-and-error. It gets more intense as you try to defend this thing you've built from dragons and vikings, and this helps lend some validation to what you're doing, knowing you're not just this derping on this tiny island, and honestly it breathes life into these little cube men in the same way dwarf fortress has a lot of life to it. The gameplay can get samey at times but the satisfaction from the game comes from seeing your city go from one building to an island-spanning metropolis.
I'm giving this game a reccomendation, though, because I also see huge potential in the game. First off, I don't know why this game doesn't have workshop support. That seems like a no-brainer which I'm hoping will be rectified soon. But this game has the potential minecraft had back in the day. The territory and army mechanics, while rather basic, could be retooled to serve as the base of a kingdom building RTS. Add in bigger maps with multiple kingdoms and it could make for really interesting vs. and campaign modes. What if it wasn't just islands, but a whole continent to explore and spread to? Cities of tens of thousands of people across a state-sized territory. They could add magic, dungeons to explore, new heroes to train. Here is where the simple graphics are a strength, because there's no limit to where it can go.
I really hope the devs are listening to the community, and quick with those updates, because this little addicting game could go a lot of places. I can't wait to see what future updates (and workshop support, SERIOUSLY) bring.

A fantastic strategy game that subverts the standards of the genre in some very pleasant ways. Many have complained that the nature of the game (the entire game takes place over 300 years, during which your heroes that fight for you WILL die of old age, as the average lifespan in this game is about 60-70) is such that you can never get attached to the heroes.
But indeed what is so awesome is that instead of getting attached to the heroes, you get attached to their families. THIS family makes some badass alchemists, and THIS family I can rely on to make great tanks. After 150 years of marriage choices, perhaps a family who made awesome heroes dies out due to some poor choices. Maybe a family of miscreants with crappy traits becomes amazing heroes after some good choices 100 years ago.
Meanwhile as family members have success in combat, they might christen their weapon a relic that is powerful and levels up, and can be handed down from family member to family member. Essentially what this game does is abstract away the individual heroes, leaving you more concerned with bigger choices that ensure that when heroes are needed, you will have them in quantity.

Let me preface this review by saying I am not a Double Fine fanboy (I've played a few of their games, but would never buy one merely because it is DF). I also did not back it early. I have no bias to say this is good if it isn't. I bought it on sale. I've also beaten it on Normal Ironman mode, so I've seen the whole thing.
This game is not going into a Top 10 for me or anything, but it is quite good. I'll try to address the concerns you may have from the other reviews.
"The game is not XCOM." This is a strangely specific complaint. Are we to judge whether a game is good solely on whether or not it is XCOM? The games have different foci. Any of the myriad complaints along the lines of "you can name your characters in XCOM but you can't here ... this game sucks" are nonsense.
The goal in XCOM is to keep people alive. One of the main mechanics in this game is to get time to progress so that people die and new, better ones take their place! I'd be overly annoyed if they wanted me to name the 200 people I went through. Not naming is a good design choice. Anyone that says otherwise has misunderstood what the game is about. This goes for the other "this is not XCOM" complaints as well.
"The tactics are limited and shallow." This complaint is a thinly veiled "This is not XCOM." The depth doesn't come from pure tactics like XCOM. The depth comes from the large scale strategy of bloodlines, buildings, researching technology, setting standards, and so on in a limited resources environment. Time is a resource. You only get so much. I'd like to see someone with this complaint beat it on Brutal Ironman difficulty. Yeah. If it's so shallow this should be cake for them. That's what I thought.
Look. The general idea of some of the complaints stand. It gets mildly repetitive. I plan to take a short break before starting some attempts at Hard/Ironman for this reason. But it has some strategic and tactical depth to it. It is fun. It has some unique, new ideas. It is certainly worth the price. I'd be surprised if I got less than 50 hours when I decide to call it quits. Not game of the year, but certainly not bad.

So if you're looking for a version of XCOM as I was from other reviews, you may be a bit disappointed.  I like the idea of the game spanning numerous generations, but in practice, it just meant that my heroes never lived long enough to fight more than a couple battles.

Probably the worst game I have ever had the misfortune to play. Do not bother with it, skip straight to Just Cause 2, forget this was ever made.
The side missions that let you gain control of regions are hugely repetitive. There seems to be no advantage to gaining control of regions, or doing tasks for the two factions you are supporting, other than getting better vehicles and access to safehouses. The driving mechanics feel floaty and leave you sliding all over the road.
During these side missions, there is no checkpoint system, if you die, you will be transported to the nearest safehouse, leaving you often taking several minutes just to return to the area you were in, where you will promptly be randomly exploded again.
Despite the somewhat random nature of death from vehicles or explosions, you can take ridiculous amounts of bullet hits before appearing injured, at which point your health will regenerate, but only to around 20%. Although your health doesn't regenerate, apart from some NPC drops there is no health-pack system, meaning the only way to return to full health is to go back to a safehouse and use a medical box there.
The almost invulnerable period and the total lack of anything even remotely approaching a cover system means often the best technique when liberating settlements is just to run in and destroy the necessary items before capturing the flag, almost completely ignoring the enemy NPCs to complete it as quickly as possible. It doesn't feel like any progress is made when you're fighting the NPCs as not only can they take a huge amount of bullets too, but they seem to endlessly spawn, and will quite happily do so behind you, leaving you running around in the open shooting randomly (at which point you'll likely be run over and die).
I'm not sure if they're glitches, but the police will constantly be shouting at you even if you have no "heat", and there is permanently a helicopter hovering somewhere near you. Which sometimes decides to shoot at those nearby. This probably wouldn't be a concern if I knew why it was there, if only I didn't have to constantly listen to a helicopter, which means if I'd like to peacefully explore the game's huge and impressive environment, I have to do it chaperoned by a damn noisy hovering annoyance. It's annoying when it turns out to be a police helicopter, which will start raining down missiles when you scratch someones car.
There's a bizarre targeting system too, which sometimes auto-aims, and sometimes doesn't. Several times I blew myself up when the game decided I was aiming missiles at the guy who had just appeared three feet to my left, rather than the fuel tank which was my objective 50m away.

I bought this game to tide myself over until I could muster enough money to buy a machine that could run Just Cause 2 at any decent frame rate, and I definitely can't say I regret my purchase.
