Even some recent  titles struggle to compare- it is visually stunning; the  screenshots on the store page don't do it justice, on higher graphical settings it feels like you're on holiday, the most danderous holiday you'll have. Although saying that, there is very little variation from mountainous forest to tropical beach,and the cities are not quite GTA V's los santos. The downside being, of course, that many such toys are locked away untill you've completed dismayingly similar missions numerous times. Which may have been more interesting for much longer had the hostile NPCs been given any form of a competent AI, and the friendly AI seems to be all too intrigued about what's coming out the end of your gun, though I shouldnt complain about AI from that era.
Also I can't tell if any of the guns do more or less damage. A stats screen wouldnt have gone amiss, if the different gun shapes aren't purely for aesthetics. As a result the side missions are an absolute chore and still necessary to get anything large and flammable. From the little Just Cause 2 I've been able to play, the grapple hook and parachute system is much more fluid, but don't get me wrong, the system in the original works fine.
The animations in the game such as Rico's running looks pretty dodgy and can be pretty amusing at first, but is distracting from there on out. The story isn't brilliant, but who's playing games of this genre in place of a bedtime read? The greatest annoyance I have with this game are the NPC voices; the developers seemed content to hire just two voice actors for the entire civilan population, though, it's nothing a low flying plane can't fix.
All in all, Just Cause is definitely worth your time, whether you dont yet have the computing power to run Just Cause 2, just enjoy the genre because this is a great game in it's own right, or have already completed the Just Cause 2 and want to experience it's roots, and for under £5 is a bargain. If you can get it on sale, all the better. however if it's between Just Cause and it's sequal, Just Cause 2 would be a better use of your cash.

Extraordinary game, active development, low price for a great deal of content, and you're funding an incredible project (Sui Generis).
The Good Things:
++ Incredible, realistic physics.
++ Extremely innovative combat system. Very satisfying, skillful, and fun. And this is coming from someone with several hundred hours in Mount and Blade.
++ Beautiful graphics/visuals. Dynamic lighting is spot-on.
++ Lots of content. I have 20+ hours and I've never gotten passed level 2 (5 levels total as of this review, planned for 14).
++ Interesting story.
++ Great character customization.
++ Great, beautifully simple equipment system.
++ Active development.
The Bad Things:
-- Navigation. Seriously, this game NEEDS a map. These levels are huge and maze-like. I get you're trying to create a difficult, confusing experience. But it just feels frustrating, and doesn't make sense from a narrative nor mechanical perspective. You have a journal; there's no reason you can't draw a map.
-- Replayability somewhat lacking. The only randomly generated elements of this game are the items in chests. Everything else is static. This detracts from replayability.
-- Unsophisticated puzzles. This game describes itself as something of a puzzle-solver, when really the puzzles are no more than exploiting game mechanics or doing speed-runs.
-- AI is dull. All of the enemies have just about the same fighting style (wildly swing and walk towards you).  This can, at times, make one of the most creative combat systems I've ever seen very dull. EDIT: After playing for a while longer, I've encountered new enemies with new and vastly different fighting styles.
IN CONCLUSION:
This game has more potential than I've ever seen from an early access title. The developers are dedicated and communicative. I look forward to Exanima's future, and look forward to the release of Sui Generis. Great job Bare Mettle Entertainment.

I DON'T like Solforge. Even though the game has everything a good cardgame should have: Cards, strategy, a specific playtime period and the oppertunity to get better cards via playing, tournaments and other forms matches!
What I don't like about Solforge is the following: The amount of luck u need in order to win a match is staggering.....so much so that all the tweaking and gathering of cards is pure and simple a con to pull  some more money out of the players. Pure and simple.
Luck plays too big a part:
The 'luck' factor is way to high. With that I mean the chances of one player drawing lower level cards (consistently) and the other player drawing higher level cards is devastating in any match. No amount of strategy or color of cards can make up for that. I dont base this on 1, 2 or 3 matches but many matches and draft tournaments.
There is simply no telling what u get but u can be damn sure the opponent gets better cards. U try to improve the odds with cards like 'meta transfer' or 'technosmith' and other discard and level up mechanics but the result is still the same... the chance u get lousy cards late in the game are simply too damn high... getting your first lvl 3 card(s) in round 3.3 or later is going to devastating for any match especially if the other guy is playing them from the start of 3.1
Server connection:
There is also the server connection. For any online cardgame to work u need a stable connection. At the moment however that  stable connection is not there. To many times during a tournament the error message is shown that the client is unable to communicate with the server, frequently resulting in a big amount of lost time that u dont get back...and could mean the difference between winning a match or losing.
9 second refund:
There is also the point where u get about 9 seconds back after each turn to make up for slow connection between u and the server but it also means u can play whole rounds without losing any time at all...why have a maximum playtime if u are goimg to build in a way to cheat the given time? Something to look at for sure!
All in all this game could become a favorite of mine but for the moment with the above mentioned problems being what they are... this game is irritating as hell...
I will keep playing though in the hopes of it getting better but for now the tournament is off limits due to the extreme luck or bad luck u generally have as a player!

First impression:  'This is close enough to Terraria that I'm not sure if I made a mistake buying it.'
4 hours impression: 'This is WAAAYYYY better than Terraria!'
Starbound is a crafting and exploration game.  The premise is that your spaceship only has a functioning teleporter, so you can beam back and forth to the ship, but the ship isn't capable of leaving orbit without you finding all the materials and technologies needed for repairs.
That one premise goes a long way in changing the gameplay mechanics for the better.  For example you can plant flags and teleport to them, without any need for being able to walk/climb back to your base.  There's also no penalty for recalling to the ship - so if you are worried you might die, you can "beam me up Scotty!" in the heat of a battle and then teleport back to a flag or to your base to regroup.
There are also pets that can fight for you, upgradable building stations, and eventually once the ship is repaired, other planets to explore that may have different mineral compositions or atmospheres.
Is it worth full price?  Hard to say.  I can say that 2 hours is barely enough time to figure out some of the offerings the game provides over Terraria, but if you enjoy the crafting and exploring it should be enough time to get the general idea.
If you've never played Terraria, buy this first.
----
Update after playing "normal" mode:  the game is more challenging as you can't beam up to the ship if you are underground.  This requires more planning and can be more intense.
I get the feeling there are basically 3 main play screens which are:
- Current planet's surface.
- Space flying/fighting in the mech
- The main storyline city
On the planet's surface the area in 2D of any given planet is roughly 1/5 of the Terraria planet - so it's not very hard to run the whole surface, yet there's still a large amount under the surface.  Yet the universe is full of these planets and moons, and they have different biomes and atmospheres and weather conditions.  They are also rated by difficulty.
Space flight in the mech is roughly identical in gameplay to the old "Asteroids" videogame.
The main storyline city is where you access the old lady who tells the storyline, and where the major store access is (although minor shops can be found on some of the planets).
Other mini-games:
There are boss challenge areas and random doors that have one-time challenges (i.e. if you die the door disappears and you can't try it again).
There's also a minimap you use to fly your "mothership" around in which adds oh-so-tiny hints at orbital dynamics.
Outpost deeds allow setting up housing for tenants.  See
Criticisms:
Yes the UI is deplorable.  The X key switches between 2 banks of numeric hotkeys, and each hotkey can be assigned left and right mouse actions associated with selecting which weapon/tool or what food/medkit a mouse button will shoot/use/eat.  I found it really unfriendly because all actions are mouseclicks.  Storage usage is equally bad.  Some function keys are remappable - and there are some mods to help - but I do find the UI frustrating.
Non-memorable:
The music I immediately shut off.  [This is in stark comparison to Terraria, which has some of the best music of any videogame.]
At the core Starbound is a platformer with crafting thrown in.  I still have to say this is hands-down my first choice over Terraria, as it spreads the gameplay over many planets.  Yes both are great games and right now Starbound is a noticeably more casual, but for the average non-hardcore player this is the better choice.

In the opening moments of Broken Sword 5, I was cast back to playing the original Broken Sword game back in the 90's. A peaceful afternoon in France is quickly transformed into a murder mystery... The story beats are classic Broken Sword fare; a crime is committed, there may have been a deeper motive behind this crime than is first apparent, and digging deeper begins to tug at the threads of a historical conspiracy.
At first glance the 3D models used for the characters draw more attention to themselves than their hand-drawn and animated sprite counterparts of old, but this passes quickly. The background art is bright and vibrant and characterful, reminiscent of the previous old games (1 and 2, in particular). Voice actor Rolf Saxon returns for George Stobbart (and let's face it, it wouldn't be George without the same voice!), although Nico's voice actor has sadly been replaced. I must admit, however, that the change for Nico is not particularly jarring, with the new voice fitting in alongside George's well and you'll quickly forget that her voice was ever any different.
I found the puzzles mostly satisfying, only getting stuck a few times over both episodes, and fortunately the game has a built in hints system that works really well. It's a tiered system, first offering a vague hint, then building as you ask for more info until it just gives you the complete solution. I feel this is the best possible system a point-and-click game can have in place, allowing you to still feel like you've solved the puzzle on the first few hints, and ultimately saves you alt-tabbing out of the game for a guide in the worst case scenario. I felt comfortable negotiating most of the puzzles myself, but a few tricky and obscure puzzles had me stuck until a few hints pointed me back onto the right path.
A must-play for Broken Sword fans, and a great point'n'click game for those new to the series too. A few in-jokes may be missed, but you'll still enjoy the ride.

This is my first Broken Sword, and it lives up to the hype. I'll definitely now buy and play all the others.
The story, visuals, characters and voice acting are all strong, but what sets this apart from other point-and-clicks is the execution of the puzzles. With the exception of a few late on, this game's puzzles avoid the common pitfalls of not communicating themselves well enough to the player; they are a challenge, not a nuisance. The hint system also comes with various tiers, therefore catering to players of all skill sets.
Worth the full price for anyone interested in a good 8-10 hour point-and-click with an engaging plot.
